title: The Relationship of Space Adaptation Syndrome to Middle Cerebral Artery Blood Velocity Measured in Flight by Doppler
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Space Adaptation Syndrome (SAS) has an incidence of approximately 73 percent in first-time flyers, typically occurs during the first three days of space flight, and can include many symptoms ranging from malaise to repeated bouts of vomiting. The pathophysiology of SAS has not been determined, but one etiology may be related to the head ward fluid shifts that occur during this adaptation period. These fluid shifts may cause changes in cerebral blood flow as well as intracranial pressure (ICP). Symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, lethargy, and malaise may be manifested by those with increased ICP as well as by astronauts with SAS. To study these phenomena as they relate to SAS during space flight, a noninvasive method of measurement was sought. Transcranial Doppler (TCD) uses Doppler technology to noninvasively measure intracranial blood flow velocity through a window in the temporal bone of the skull, where the bone is thin enough to permit insonation. From this window, the middle cerebral artery (MCA) is typically the only artery found at depth between 25 and 50 millimeters, making it relatively easy to locate. Since it carries approximately 80 percent of the blood flow to the hemisphere and does not exhibit acute changes in diameter, the MCA is often chosen as the optimal vessel to study for indications of cerebral blood flow.
approach: Crewmembers on three Space Shuttle missions volunteered to be subjects for TCD MCA measurements preflight and in-flight. Each subject was studied a minimum of four times preflight and two times inflight. Preflight data were collected in both the supine and sitting postures. Three of the subjects were trained as operators and assigned subjects on whom they collected all data. At the beginning of each data collection session, the operator measured the subject's pulse rate (at the radial artery) and blood pressure (by ascultative sphygmomanometry at the brachial artery). The operator then obtained the MCA flow velocity in a reproducible sample volume using a plastic template. These templates were developed to locate the optimal temporal window and sample depth previously determined for each subject by an experienced operator. Space motion sickness symptoms were reported for each day in flight on a symptom response sheet. This sheet included the following symptoms: headache, malaise, sluggishness, impaired concentration, disorientation, decreased appetite, stomach awareness, nausea, vomiting, and a space to indicate other symptoms. Each subject's symptoms were evaluated by the investigators and each subject was assigned a general score from 0 (no symptoms) to 3 (severely ill) for each flight day. Doppler data were analyzed postflight using a system developed by Micco and Dietrich at the University of Colorado. The tape recording of each session was divided into 30-second segments. After the 30-second segments of data were analyzed, the segment with the greatest number of cardiac cycles having the highest velocities was analyzed in greater detail. Systolic and diastolic blood pressure data were also compared, and systolic resistance (systolic blood pressure/maximum velocity), mean resistance (mean blood pressure/mean velocity), and diastolic resistance (diastolic blood pressure/minimum velocity) were calculated for comparison. Preflight and in-flight data were also divided into post-sleep (morning) and pre-sleep (afternoon and evening) groups to study diurnal variations. The terms post-sleep and pre-sleep are used because morning and night do not apply in the same context while in Earth orbit. Thus, one preflight post-sleep data set and one preflight pre-sleep data set were established for each subject. In-flight data were also diurnally grouped by flight day (FD). The only in-flight pre-sleep data collection occurred on FD 1; all other in-flight data collection occurred in the post-sleep period.
results: Preflight Trends When general comparisons were made between all preflight data, there were no significant differences between TCD or any related parameter. When viewed with respect to diurnal (post-sleep vs. pre-sleep) variation, there were significant increases in mean velocity, maximum velocity, pulsatility index, and blood flow acceleration. Diastolic blood pressure decreased significantly from 68.9 to 65.25 mmHg, as did systolic resistance from 1.87 to 1.51 mmHg/cm/s, mean resistance from 2.21 to 1.79 mmHg/cm/s, and diastolic resistance from 2.58 to 3.22 mmHg/cm/s. Preflight to Inflight Changes Preflight and in-flight general data were grouped according to SAS scores: subjects with a score of 0 or 1 (well) and subjects with a score of 2 or 3 (sick). Using the SAS groups from FD 1 (five sick, three well), there were no significant SAS main effects and no significant day main effects between the preflight general average and FD 1. However, there was a significant SAS-by-day interaction between the preflight average and FD 1 for mean velocity and mean resistance. For the preflight averages only, the two SAS groups did not have different mean velocities or different mean resistances, but on FD 1 only the SAS groups did have significantly different mean velocities and mean resistances approaching significance. These changes in significance of the SAS main effect across days explain the SAS-by-day interaction. In-flight Trends There was a significant general in-flight decrease from 5.56 to 4.16 mls/s in blood flow acceleration between FD 2 and FD 5. No in-flight diurnal effects could be determined from FD 3 or FD 5 data. SAS in-flight effects were not calculated due to the fact that different subjects were sick on different days, so there was no uniform way to group subjects for multivariate analysis.

title: Behavioral Issues Associated with Long Duration Space Missions:  Review of Astronaut Journals
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: (2003 - 2010) : The Journals experiment was a focused study of human factors, behavior, and performance issues during expeditions to the International Space Station (ISS). The investigator has studied conditions analogous to space craft in previous projects, including a two-year study (conducted for NASA with the cooperation of the European Space Agency and the French Polar Institute) in which content analyses were performed of diaries maintained by the station leaders and physicians at the Antarctic and South Indian Ocean remote duty stations. That study provided the first rank-ordering of the behavioral issues in terms of importance associated with isolation and confinement, based on quantitative data. This experiment used the same content evaluation techniques on journals kept by ISS crew personnel during ISS expeditions. The experiment tested the hypothesis that the analogous conditions could provide an acceptable model for space craft (i.e., to validate or refute the
approach: Approximately seven days before launch (L-7), the participating crewmembers complete a very brief questionnaire. While on orbit, crewmembers made journal entries at least three times per week in a personal journal. The journal was either electronic (e.g. using a laptop) or paper. In addition to the journal entries, participating crewmembers also complete a brief questionnaire at the mid-point of their respective expeditions. Approximately 4-6 days after landing (R+4 to R+6), the crewmembers complete a questionnaire identical to the mid-point questionnaire.
results: of the previous study). Specifically, the study was designed to 1)evaluate how isolation and confinement on long duration space missions can affect crew health and morale, which are important factors that can influence mission success, 2) convert behavioral and human factors data contained in journal entries into quantitative data on the importance of the various behavioral issues involved in long-duration isolation and confinement, and 3) systematically analyze the content of astronaut journals in order to enhance the design of procedures and equipment to support human performance during exploration of the moon and Mars. (2011 - forward) : The original study period of the Journals experiment (2003-2010) tested the hypothesis that the analog conditions provided an acceptable model for space operations. Substantial support for the hypothesis was found, but ISS crew size has increased since then. The Journals experiment is being continued to collect data from members of larger crews to determine if there are differences in behavioral issues that could be attributed to crew size. The objective of the study extension is to obtain behavioral and human factors data relevant to the design of equipment and procedures to support adjustment and sustained human performance during extended duration isolation and confinement. For the continuation of the experiment with 10 additional subjects, the specific objectives of the proposed study are to 1) collect data concerning the relevant behavioral factors from 10 additional astronauts while serving as members of 6-person crews onboard the ISS; 2) compare the experiences reported by members of larger crews to those of the two and three-person crews who participated in the original journals study; 3) assess the effects of other changes that have been implemented since the journals study concluded (e.g., cupola, sleep chambers, procedures); 4) further test the third quarter phenomenon; and 5) provide a safe and constructive outlet for the frustration and irritation that usually accompany isolated and confined living. The ultimate objective of the study is to provide data-driven recommendations to inform decisions concerning the priorities that should be placed on the various behavioral issues to prepare for and manage future space expeditions. Study results can be applied to improve selection, training, support, scheduling, and the design of equipment and procedures. APPROACH: Approximately seven days before launch (L-7), the participating crewmembers complete a very brief questionnaire. While on orbit, crewmembers made journal entries at least three times per week in a personal journal. The journal was either electronic (e.g. using a laptop) or paper. In addition to the journal entries, participating crewmembers also complete a brief questionnaire at the mid-point of their respective expeditions. Approximately 4-6 days after landing (R+4 to R+6), the crewmembers complete a questionnaire identical to the mid-point questionnaire. RESULTS: (2003 - 2010) : Personal journals that were provided by ten subjects during ISS expeditions were analyzed to obtain information concerning a wide range of behavioral and human factors issues. Astronauts wrote most about their work, followed by outside communications (with mission control, family and friends), adjustment to the conditions, interactions with crew mates, recreation/leisure, equipment (installation, maintenance), events (launches, docking, hurricanes, etc.), organization/management, sleep, and food. The results were presented in a final report that was published in July 2010 by NASA as NASA/TM-2010-216130. The study found evidence of a decline in morale during the third quarters of the missions and identified key factors that contribute to sustained adjustment and optimal performance during long-duration space expeditions. Astronauts reported that they benefited personally from writing in their journals because it helped maintain perspective on their work and relations with others. Responses to questions asked before, during, and after the expeditions show that living and working onboard the ISS is not as difficult as the astronauts anticipated before starting their six-month tours of duty. Recommendations included application of study results and continuation of the experiment to obtain additional data as crew size increases and operations evolve. Astronauts have reported that participating in the Journals Experiment has helped them adapt to the isolation, confinement, and other special conditions of the ISS. (2011 - forward) : At the conclusion of the experiment, results will be posted when data becomes available.

title: Pre- and Postflight Measurement of Cardiorespiratory Responses to Submaximal Exercise
experiment_type: Shuttle Extended Duration Orbiter Medical Project (EDOMP)
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: It is known that regular aerobic exercise can maintain aerobic capacity during bed rest. Therefore, aerobic exercise might also be able counteract the deconditioning effects of microgravity on aerobic exercise capacity. The objectives of this study were to document the degree of aerobic deconditioning after space flight and to investigate the use of aerobic exercise during flight to reduce the severity of postflight deconditioning.
approach: The study included 39 astronauts (35 men and 4 women) from missions lasting 8 to 16 days. The astronauts performed exercise tests on an upright cycle ergometer at increasing rates of work until they reached 85% of their age-predicted maximum heart rates. A monitor recorded the heart rate every 15 seconds during the tests. Aerobic capacity was defined as the peak oxygen consumption during the tests, which was measured with a Q-Plex system. The Q-Plex system is a computer driven device for cardiac, respiratory, and rehabilitation stress test (similar to an EKG stress monitor). The composition of exhaled air was analyzed either with a mass spectrometer preflight or with zirconium oxide and infrared sensors postflight. Oxygen consumption during the last minute of exercise was used as the index of cardiovascular performance.
results: from tests performed 10 days before launch were compared to results from landing day. The astronauts exercised on a cycle ergometer during flight. No specific exercise protocol was required. Heart rates were recorded every 15 seconds during exercise. The frequency and duration of in-flight exercise sessions was noted, and the intensity of the exercise was quantified as the percentage of age-predicted maximum heart rate achieved during a session. RESULTS: Lower work rates were achieved on landing day because the target heart rates were reached sooner, ending the tests. The rate of oxygen consumption that corresponded to a given heart rate was lower after the flight than before. At 85% of predicted maximum heart rate, the decrement in oxygen consumption was nine percent for astronauts who exercised during flight for more than 20 minutes at least three times a week at more than 70% of their predicted maximum heart rate. The decrement was greater for astronauts who exercised less often or at lower intensities. It was 15% for astronauts who exercised more than three times a week but achieved lower heart rates, and 23% for astronauts who exercised less frequently. The decrease in oxygen consumption did not correlate with flight duration. Because the exercise tests were performed upright, both exercise deconditioning and orthostatic deconditioning would have contributed to the higher heart rates during exercise. In this way the tests were similar to an emergency egress from the Shuttle. The results showed that in-flight exercise can help to maintain postflight aerobic capacity and that the intensity of exercise is important. On the basis of this and other studies (see DSOs 476, 608, and 618), it was recommended that space crews exercise for more than 20 minutes at least three times a week at work rates that elicit 70% of maximum heart rates, but that the maximum heart rates should be determined in preflight maximum exercise tests rather than estimated by age.

title: Renal Stone Risk During Space Flight:  Assessment and Countermeasure Validation
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: The purpose of this study was to assess the renal stone-forming potential of humans as a function of mission duration and to determine how long after space flight the increased risk exists. In addition to the analyses of mineral components, this study was designed to determine levels of the naturally occurring urinary protein inhibitors of calcium crystallization. This investigation provides a direct understanding of and overcoming human limitations in space that may affect crew health and potentially mission success. If a crewmember were to develop a kidney stone, only supportive action is possible at this time. Medical support would involve pain relief through on-board medication with the hope that the crewmember would pass the stone over time. The afflicted crewmember may not be able to perform his/her duties or, more significant, cause the mission to be aborted and return to Earth. Previous data have demonstrated that human exposure to the microgravity environment of space increases the risk of renal stone development during and immediately after space flight. In-flight assessment has shown a greater risk of calcium oxalate, calcium phosphate and sodium urate stones. Postflight changes to the urinary chemical composition increase the risk of uric acid and calcium oxalate stone formation. Astronauts in the U.S. program have experienced multiple postflight stone events (2 crewmembers had 2 postflight stones). The length of time for appearance of symptomatic stone formation ranged from 9-120 months. Six of these postflight stones have occurred since 1994 and have taken place concurrently with the beginning of the extended shuttle missions of greater than 12 days in space. Discussions with Russian medical science investigators have noted multiple stone events among cosmonauts, with one in-flight renal stone episode nearly causing the crewmember to abort the mission. These epidemiologic data may suggest that that risk of stone formation may extend beyond the testing period implemented during this investigation in some crewmembers.
approach: Potassium citrate (K-cit), a proven Earth-based therapy to minimize calcium-containing renal stone development, was tested during space flight as a countermeasure to reduce the risk of renal stone formation. Preflight baseline data collection sessions were performed at approximately L-180, L-60 and L-45 days. Two 10 mEq potassium citrate tablets (total dose 20 mEq) or placebo were ingested daily with the evening meal beginning three days before launch, all days during flight, and following landing through R+14. Urine was collected before, during, and after flight. Food, fluid, exercise, and medications were monitored before and during the urine collection period in order to assess environmental influences other than microgravity. During ISS operations, 24 hour urine collections and 48 hour dietary monitoring were performed early ( Subjects were active astronauts and cosmonauts who were certified for space flight. There were no gender specific requirements, therefore both male and female crewmembers participated in this study. This investigation was designed as a double blind study with neither the investigators nor the subjects knowing whether the subjects were ingesting potassium citrate or placebo.
results: This investigation was successfully completed by 19 crewmembers. The majority of renal stones are composed of calcium containing salts. The risk of calcium oxalate stone formation as determined by the urinary supersaturation of calcium oxalate was observed to be lower in the potassium citrate treated group. The decreased risk was evident during the in-flight and immediate postflight assessment sessions. The risk of calcium phosphate (brushite) risk followed the same trend observed with the risk of calcium oxalate stone formation. This study also evaluated the effect of fluid intake and urinary output on the supersaturation of the urine and the potential risk of stone formation. Regarding the correlation between 24-hr urinary volume and the risk of calcium oxalate stone development, data indicate an inverse relationship between urine volume and risk of calcium oxalate stone formation. Approval for elimination of the double blind requirement was received from NASA in December, 2005. As a result, the participating crewmembers ingested only potassium citrate as a countermeasure to the risk of renal stone formation. Data from all the ISS missions were combined for a detailed analysis involving statistical analysis and evaluation of the pharmacologic countermeasure to reduce the risk of stone formation. Potassium citrate-treated crew members had decreased urinary calcium excretion and maintained the calcium oxalate supersaturation risk at preflight levels compared to that in controls. Increased urinary pH in the treatment group decreased the risk of uric acid stones. Results from this investigation suggest that supplementation with potassium citrate may decrease the risk of renal stone formation during and immediately after spaceflight.

title: Inflight Aerobic Exercise
experiment_type: Shuttle Extended Duration Orbiter Medical Project (EDOMP)
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: It is known that regular aerobic exercise can maintain aerobic capacity during bed rest. Therefore, aerobic exercise might also be able to counteract the deconditioning effects of microgravity on aerobic exercise capacity. The objectives of this study were to measure aerobic exercise capacity before and after space flight and to investigate the use of aerobic exercise during flight to reduce the severity of postflight aerobic deconditioning.
approach: The 24 astronauts in this study completed one or two exercise tests before space flights of six to 11 days and another test two or three days after landing. The exercise tests were performed on a treadmill according to either a longer or a shorter protocol (sometimes the protocol was shortened due to scheduling conflicts). The astronauts were instructed to exercise to the point of fatigue. Heart rate, heart rhythm, and blood pressure were monitored during the tests. Aerobic capacity was defined as the peak oxygen consumption during the tests, which was measured with a Q-Plex system. The Q-Plex system is a computer driven device for cardiac, respiratory, and rehabilitation stress test (similar to an EKG stress monitor). The composition of exhaled air was analyzed preflight with a mass spectrometer or with zirconium oxide and infrared sensors postflight. Most of the crewmembers exercised during the flight using a rower, a cycle ergometer, or a treadmill that had a harness and tether to simulate gravity. While a monitor displayed and recorded their heart rate, they followed continuous or interval exercise protocols with target heart rates intended to correspond to 65 to 85% of preflight maximum oxygen consumption. Several subjects had difficulty achieving these heart rates on the treadmill. The total exercise performed during flight was quantified by multiplying the percentage of the maximal heart rate by the number of minutes per exercise session and by the number of sessions per week.
results: The data from this study were combined with data from DSO 608, and the combined results were as follows: The amount of exercise the astronauts actually performed during flight varied widely. Astronauts who did not exercise and those who exercised with the cycle ergometer lost approximately 12 to 13% of their preflight aerobic capacity. For astronauts who exercised with the treadmill or rower during flight, decreases in aerobic capacity were smaller and not statistically significant. However, the timing of the postflight exercise test confounds the interpretation of these results, because aerobic capacity partially recovers within three days of landing (see DSO 618), and the subjects who were tested on landing day versus two or three days later were not evenly spread among the various exercise modalities. Also, astronauts who used the cycle ergometer tended to be on longer missions, but this may not be a confounding factor because the preflight to postflight decrease in aerobic capacity did not correlate with the duration of the flight. These results indicated that the capacity to perform aerobic exercise is reduced after space flight (see also DSOs 608, 618, and 624), but that aerobic exercise during flight attenuates this effect. The results did not indicate the optimal exercise device or protocol for maintaining aerobic capacity.

title: The Evaluation of Concentric and Eccentric Skeletal Muscle Contractions Following Space Flight
experiment_type: Shuttle Extended Duration Orbiter Medical Project (EDOMP)
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Loss of muscle strength and endurance after long exposure to microgravity can interfere with the safe completion of critical tasks during space flight, emergency or routine landing, or during egress. Decreases in leg strength have been documented after Skylab missions as well as after Russian space flights. The objectives of this study were to assess pre flight-to-postflight changes in muscle strength and endurance and to evaluate the effect of in flight exercise on these changes. Changes in muscle performance after missions of shorter or longer duration were compared.
approach: Muscle performance was tested before and after space flight in 19 astronauts (3 women, 16 men), 10 from 5-day missions and 9 from missions lasting 9 to 11 days. LIDO isokinetic dynamometers were used to measure muscle performance in the back and abdomen and at the knee, ankle, shoulder, and elbow. These dynamometers provide variable resistance so that movements will continue at the same speed (i.e., they are isokinetic) regardless of the force applied. Both concentric and eccentric strength were measured. Concentric strength is the strength of a muscle as it contracts to move a body part, while eccentric strength is the strength of the muscle as it is gradually lengthened while resisting the motion of a body part. Endurance was tested during 25 repetitions of concentric knee flexion and extension. The eccentric torque maximum was 400 foot pounds. Subjects abstained from food for 2 hours before testing, from caffeine 4 hours before, and from exercise 12 hours before. The dynamometers were calibrated externally and internally (electronically) before each test session. Joint configurations and ranges of motion were recorded for each subject and reproduced for each test session. Testing of the limbs was unilateral with the dominant limb, unless contraindicated. Verbal instructions were consistent and given before each joint test. No verbal encouragement was given during the tests. Mean
results: from tests conducted approximately 1, 2, and 3 weeks before launch were compared to results from landing day and from 7 days after landing. Only 17 subjects were tested on landing day. Losses greater than about 9% were considered to be operationally relevant. Four of the astronauts also performed in flight exercise as part of DSO 476, using a treadmill with a tether system to simulate gravity. They followed continuous or interval exercise protocols with target heart rates intended to correspond to 60% to 85% of preflight maximum oxygen consumption. The percentages of change in their strength and endurance test results were compared with those of 5 astronauts who did not exercise during the flight. RESULTS: From before the flight to landing day, large decreases in the strength of the back and abdomen occurred. Strength had decreased by 23% in the concentric tests of the back, 14% in the eccentric tests of the back, and 10% in the concentric tests of the abdomen. The loss in back strength was greater after flights of 9 to 11 days (concentric, 28%; eccentric, 17%) than after flights of 5 days (concentric, 18%; eccentric, 11%). Eccentric abdominal and concentric back strength had recovered significantly 7 days after landing. A significant (12%) decrease in concentric strength of the quadriceps muscle of the thigh was also seen on landing day. No significant loss of strength was seen in the hamstring muscles or in the tests at the ankle, shoulder or elbow, except for a few minor losses that were not considered operationally relevant. The four astronauts who exercised during flight actually gained eccentric strength of the gastrocnemius muscle of the calf. Although the exercising astronauts lost concentric strength in the quadriceps, the percent change was significantly less than for the four nonexercising astronauts. For the other results of the knee and ankle tests, decreases in strength were generally smaller in those who exercised; although, the differences between exercisers and nonexercisers were not statistically significant. Treadmill exercise did not prevent losses of strength in the back or abdomen. Decrements exhibited by muscles of the five astronauts who did not exercise during flight indicated that muscles are less able to maintain endurance and resist fatigue after space flight. The astronauts who exercised had no loss of endurance. There was no change in endurance after 5-day flights, but the endurance of the quadriceps decreased after flights of 9 to 11 days. Endurance recovered within 7 days of landing. These results showed that space flight results in losses of skeletal muscle strength and endurance, and that the losses are greater after flights of longer duration. Strength was lost primarily in the antigravity muscles of the legs and torso. Exercise may prevent losses of muscle strength and endurance.

title: Stability of Pharmacotherapeutic Compounds
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Analysis of certain medications returned from the Space Shuttle and the International Space Station (ISS) have indicated that some pharmaceuticals are significantly degraded in space, and this may compromise treatments and the health of crews on future exploration missions. Data gathered from past Space Shuttle missions suggest that some of the medications packed in the Shuttle's medical pack degrade even after relatively brief periods (less than 20 days) of space flight. The observed degradation included both physical and chemical characteristics of medicine formulations. Physical and chemical instability of medications could render treatments ineffective for assurance of optimal crew health during long duration space exploration missions. An evaluation of subjective data on medications used by crewmembers during space flight indicated that 8% of all treatments administered in the Space Shuttle program were reported ineffective. Pharmaceutical instability may modify effectiveness and safety, and is one possible cause of the ineffectiveness of treatments. The objective of this project was to identify the pharmaceuticals that degrade in space by collecting data on the magnitude and time course of degradation of select pharmaceuticals. This investigation studied the effects of radiation in space on complex organic molecules, such as vitamins and other compounds in food and medicine. This could help researchers develop more stable and reliable pharmaceutical and nutritional countermeasures suitable for future long-duration missions to the moon and Mars.
approach: The pharmaceutical kits contained 35 types of pharmaceutical drugs, including tablets, ointments, suppositories, and injectable solutions. In addition to the food and drug items, the kits were equipped with two temperature loggers and a dosimeter to measure radiation.
results: There was no crew interaction with the contents of the kits, which were configured to prevent them from being inadvertently opened. One of the kits was immediately returned on STS-122 after 13 days, while the other three remained aboard ISS for 353, 596, and 880 days of spaceflight. Each kit was returned on subsequent Shuttle flights. The flight kits were analyzed in parallel with the eight ground control kits, identical to those flown. Results from this investigation designed to examine changes in chemical content and physical attributes of dosage forms stored aboard space missions suggest that there may be differences with respect to potency and rate of degradation of formulations stored in space compared to those on the ground. Some APIs and formulations may be more sensitive than others, and specific chemical and formulation characteristics may influence the stability of medications in space. Cumulative low dose radiation and dispensers used for solid dosages in space appear to influence stability of pharmaceuticals in space.

title: Promoting Sensorimotor Response Generalizability
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: The goal of this study is to develop an inflight treadmill training protocol that enhances adaptive generalization of locomotor function to facilitate rapid and robust recovery of functional mobility after long-duration space flight. Specifically, the investigator hopes to determine whether subjects exposed to a special inflight treadmill protocol will have greater proficiency in reassembling an appropriate, full-body postflight locomotor response. Will they recover locomotor function sooner than subjects not exposed to the inflight treadmill protocol? Data from this experiment are planned to be used to develop a countermeasure system.
approach: Locomotor function were assessed before and after space flight using two tests of gait function. Test 1: The Integrated Treadmill Locomotion Test characterizes alterations in the integrated function of multiple sensorimotor subsystems. This test required subjects to walk on a motorized treadmill while researchers assessed changes in dynamic postural stability, head-trunk coordination, visual acuity and lower limb coordination strategies. Subjects walked at 6.4 km/h on a motorized treadmill while performing a visual task consisting of identifying the position of the gap in the letter "C" that is presented centrally on a laptop computer positioned 4 meters in front at eye level. Each trial lasted approximately 30 seconds and was repeated four times. Subjects also walked at 6.4 km/h on the treadmill while performing the same visual task described above, but in this case, with the letter "C" presented centrally on a micro-display positioned 50 centimeters in front at eye level. Each of these trials lasted approximately 30 seconds and were repeated four times. While subjects were walking on the treadmill and performing the visual task, 3-dimensional full-body motion data were acquired using a video-based motion analysis system; gait cycle timing was measured using foot switches placed in the shoes and dynamic visual acuity was assessed by the visual task described above. Test 2: The Functional Mobility Test provides a corresponding assessment of the functional and operational changes in locomotor function by testing a subject's ability to negotiate an obstacle course placed over a medium-density foam floor. Subjects walked at a preferred pace through an obstacle course set up on a base of 10 cm thick medium density foam. The foam provided an unstable surface that increases the challenge of the test. The 6.0 m x 4.0 m course consists of several pylons and obstacles made of foam. Subjects were instructed to walk through the course as fast as possible without touching any of the objects on the course. This task was repeated three times in the clockwise direction and 3 times in the counterclockwise direction. The dependent measures are time to complete the course and the number of obstacles touched or knocked down.
results: Test 1: Integrated Treadmill Locomotion Test Results showed that subjects exhibited postflight changes in head-trunk coordination, toe clearance and gait cycle timing during treadmill locomotion. Dynamic visual acuity was decreased postflight, followed by an improvement in performance during the postflight recovery period. An analysis of the relationship between inflight treadmill usage characteristics and postflight functional mobility performance revealed that subjects who exercised on the iRED with greater body loading had enhanced postflight (R+1) functional mobility performance. Test 2: Functional Mobility Test Results indicate that adaptation to space flight led to a 62% increase in time to traverse the obstacle course on one day after return, and recovery of function took an average of 11 days after return. In conclusion, recovery of functional mobility after long-duration space flight is composed of two distinct but interrelated motor learning processes: 1) rapid on-line strategic change characterized by immediate onset after landing and 2) slower adaptive change requiring days to complete after landing. Postflight (R+1) changes in gaze control produced decreases in dynamic visual acuity (DVA) during walking. For some subjects, the decrement was greater than the mean acuity decrement seen in a population of vestibularly-impaired patients (collected using a similar protocol). The population mean showed a consistent improvement in DVA performance during the two-week postflight recovery period. Post-flight neurological exams conducted by flight surgeons have rated gaze and ocular symptoms from mild to severe in over 50% of returning Shuttle astronauts. These observations are consistent with the decrements in visual acuity during locomotion described in this report. Future work should focus on the addition of a “field” test of dynamic visual acuity that could be incorporated in the postflight examinations. This research should focus on the development of a portable system that will provide passive body motion (i.e. seated subject on a motion base) while subjects perform tests of visual performance. Astronauts should be tested as soon as possible after landing to assess the early effects of gaze dysfunction related to sensorimotor adaptation. This will allow a better determination of the potential impacts of changes in visual acuity on landing performance. This research led to conduct of ground-based studies focusing on developing adaptability training programs that include both gait and manual control training. In addition this research is investigating the retention capabilities of adaptability training, allowing this type of training to be conducted preflight and therefore reduce the requirement for an inflight training component, thus saving inflight crewtime and upmass hardware requirements. It will be useful to examine the relationship between other in-flight exercise modalities (cycle ergometer, upper body resistive exercise) and post-flight functional mobility performance to determine if a relationship exists. The current in-flight exercise data set includes only average data from US crewmembers over the entire duration of the mission. The exercise prescriptions to US crewmembers are graded over the duration of mission with the intensity (especially loading) and duration increased towards the end of the mission. Hence, the above analysis may be overly conservative in its estimates and should be extended with data over separate in-flight periods to confirm the relationships observed in the present study. Results obtained from this research helped motivate the design of the Functional Task Test, a pre/postflight battery of tests used to assess performance of astronauts on functional tasks that are representative of critical mission tasks for lunar and Mars operations. The Functional Task Test will allow better definition of the linkage between physiological change and functional performance including across several physiological systems (sensorimotor, cardiovascular, muscle performance).

title: Canal and Otolith Integration Studies (COIS)

approach: The COIS experiment was composed of three different protocols: Voluntary Head Shakes (VHS), Smooth Pursuit Tracking and Optokinetic Nystagmus (OKN). The VHS and Smooth Pursuit Tracking protocols were always performed at the same time (first VHS, then Smooth Pursuit Tracking), while the OKN protocol was not necessarily performed on the same day. During the VHS and Smooth Pursuit Tracking protocols, the subjects were seated and the lower body and trunk restrained. The subject wore a vest called the Instrumented Vest Assembly (IVA), which contained amplifiers and data recorders (called the Superpocket Assembly) and provided the connections to the peripheral hardware. The peripheral hardware included an electrooculograph (EOG) to monitor eye movements, a triaxial rate sensor to record head movements, the Luminous Target Display (LTD) and the Electronic Light Occlusion Goggles (ELOG). The LTD provided a cruciform array of Light-Emitting Diodes (LEDs) and was used as a visual target. The ELOG goggles occluded vision under normal conditions and were translucent when a 30-volt DC electrical current was applied. The VHS protocol included two test conditions, both featuring voluntary head shakes at two different frequencies, 0.33 and 1.0 Hertz (Hz), in both the horizontal (yaw) and vertical (pitch) planes. Instructions were given to the subjects via a prerecorded audio tape that played a modulated tone. The subject was asked to move the head so that during the lowest tone the head was at the far right and at the highest tone it was at the far left. During the first test condition, the subjects performed the head shakes using the central light of the LTD as their visual target. During the second test condition, the subject's vision was occluded using the ELOG goggles. The subject was asked to move their head according to the auditory cues and use an imaginary target to fixate gaze. Smooth Pursuit Tracking required the subjects to track a moving target in two ways. In the first type of tracking, the head was held stationary, and the target was pursued with eyes only. In the second type of tracking, both the eyes and head were allowed to move. Two frequencies, 0.33 and 1.0 Hz, were used for both the horizontal (yaw) and vertical (pitch) planes. The diodes of the LTD functioned as targets, providing a peak amplitude of 25 degrees. During the Optokinetic Nystagmus (OKN) protocol, the subjects wore the Optokinetic Stimulus (OKS) goggles. The head-mounted OKS goggles provided the stimuli to provoke optokinetic nystagmus by means of a pattern of red and black 4-degree-wide stripes viewed through a Fresnel lens. The stripe pattern could be moved at a constant velocity of a maximum of 40 degrees per second in the horizontal, vertical or 45 degrees oblique direction. The optokinetic stimulus was maintained in one direction for 20 seconds, followed by 10 seconds in darkness, during which optokinetic after-nystagmus was observed. This was followed by 5 seconds with a stationary display to visually suppress any remaining after-nystagmus before providing 20 seconds of OKS in the opposite direction, followed again by 10 seconds of darkness. During the initial darkness period, eye movements (EOG) were recorded with the subject looking straight ahead to quantify any spontaneous and/or positional nystagmus that might be present. In space, the subjects were free-floating during the OKN trials to avoid external orientation cues. For pre- and postflight testing, the gravitational effects on the OKN were inferred by evaluating the horizontal-to-vertical cross-coupling effects with either visual stimulus by tilting the subject's head by 30 degrees with respect to the spatial vertical. Crewmembers participated as test subjects and operators for COIS, obtaining measurements before, during and after flight. Three preflight data collection sessions were used as a baseline with which to compare inflight and postflight data. Space flight data collection occurred four times for each subject -- two times early and two times late during the mission. Postflight data collection occurred on landing day (R+0), and continued on R+1, R+2, R+4 and R+8.

objectives: Exposure to microgravity is known to have profound effects on fluid homeostasis within the human body. The headward shift of fluids which occurs in microgravity
approach: Flight Requirements and Procedures Preflight, In Flight, and Postflight: 1. Participants drank enriched water, which contained naturally-occurring stable and nonradioactive isotopes after taking baseline urine and saliva samples. Void-by-void urine samples and two saliva samples (at 3 hours and at 5-7 hours) were collected post isotope ingestion according to the timeline in the activity schedule. Samples of galley water were collected once every 24 hours in flight to monitor the isotope enrichment that occurs onboard. At L-3 days a dose of enriched water was ingested to increase the background of stable isotope concentrations. No samples were required on that day. On L-15 days through launch and at landing through R+6 days, participants (not the control subject) ate prepared meals which they had chosen from a menu. A control subject was required for EE. Preflight activity included one training session at L-4 months, and saliva and urine collections according to the timeline in the activity schedule. There were no postflight requirements, and the only ingestion of enriched water was at L-3 days. In-flight, the control subject collected one saliva and one urine sample each flight day (FD) plus follow-up samples on test days. 2. Extracellular Fluid Volume (ECF): ECF was determined through measurements of bromide dilution. Bromide is a stable compound that distributes throughout the extracellular space. The technique involved the collection of a 2 milliliter (ml) baseline blood sample, followed by ingestion of a specific amount of bromide. After three hours, a 2 ml blood sample was taken. Subjects were fasting and did not exercise for at least 12 hours prior to ingesting the bromide. 3. Blood/Serum Analyses: Blood/serum was obtained via an indwelling catheter preflight, in-flight, and postflight for biochemical and hormonal analyses. Preflight and postflight, a 20-minute rest period was required after catheter insertion to restore resting catecholamine levels. Whenever possible, testing was coordinated with Medical Operations' activities to minimize crew time. In-flight catheter insertion, blood draws, analyses, and preparation of blood samples for storage was required. 4. Urine Collection: All preflight and postflight urine samples were collected using void-by-void techniques. In-flight urine collection involved drawing syringe samples from a urine collection device (UCD), which contained lithium chloride inside as a marker. Specified syringes were frozen, and others were stowed along with UCD's in the urine sample containment bag. 5. Intake/Exercise Log: Food/fluid/medications/exercise was recorded preflight and postflight according to the activity schedule. In-flight, the participants used bar code readers to record this information. Weighed (pre-proportioned) meals were provided from L-15 days through R+6 days. 6. Peripheral Venous Pressure (PVP): A peripheral indication of central venous pressure was measured preflight and postflight using a strain gauge manometer. Inflight, the PVP measurements were taken using equipment in the Life Science Laboratory Equipment (LSLE) In-Flight Blood Collection System. Preflight and Postflight Only: 1. Plasma Volume (PV): PV was determined using a nonradioactive indicator dye (indocyanine green) injected through a catheter after the 2 ml baseline blood draw. One ml blood samples was drawn each minute for 10 minutes, then at 15 and 20 minutes. PV was performed simultaneously with ECF testing preflight and postflight. 2. Renal Clearance (RC) Tests: Two indices of renal function, glomerular filtration rate (using inulin) and effective renal plasma flow (using para-aminohippuric acid [PAH]), were measured preflight and postflight. After a 2.5 ml baseline blood draw was taken via catheter, the insulin was infused at 0 minutes, and the PAH at 40 minutes. At minutes 90, 108, 126, 144, and 180, 1 ml blood samples were obtained. 3. Measurement of Body Weight (in conjunction with dietary intake monitoring): Participants were weighed daily on calibrated scales preflight and postflight during L-15 days through L-0 and R+0 through R+6 days, in conjunction with the pre-proportioned diet. Crew Training: Training sessions were required for achieving proficiency in phlebotomy (i.e., venipuncture techniques), PVP, tracer handling, sample processing, and urine and saliva collection techniques, as well as blood sample analysis for specific in-flight portions of the investigation. Hardware training sessions covered the bar code reader and LSLE equipment.

title: Orthostatic Function During Entry, Landing and Egress
experiment_type: Shuttle Extended Duration Orbiter Medical Project (EDOMP)
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Several cardiovascular parameters were measured during entry, landing, and egress in order to develop and assess countermeasures designed to improve orthostatic tolerance upon return to Earth.
approach: Heart rate and rhythm, blood pressure, cardiac output and peripheral resistance were monitored during entry and landing of the Shuttle, and during crewmember egress from the Shuttle.
results: Systolic and diastolic blood pressure increased during space flight and were highest when gravity reached its peak during entry and at touchdown. Systolic blood pressure decreased significantly when the astronauts first stood up from their seats after landing. Heart rate increased at the time of peak gravity during entry and at touchdown, and it rose even higher when the astronauts first stood up. The increase in heart rate varied, but was generally substantial.

title: Cabin Air Monitoring
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: This experiment used the Solid Sorbent Air Sampler (SSAS) to continuously sample the Shuttle orbiter atmosphere throughout flight. This SSAS was used to verify that volatile organic contaminant levels in the Shuttle internal atmosphere were within established safety levels. The SSAS was flown on first flights of a new vehicle, first flights of a vehicle after extensive nonmetallic materials refurbishment in the orbiter cabin, and on all Spacelab manned module flights. Examples of refurbishment are interior repainting, extensive addition or replacement of wiring, and equipment, or other similar modifications which would make a significant change in the off-gassing products to the orbiter atmospheres.
approach: The SSAS was placed in a designated sampling location either in the middeck or in the Spacelab. A crewmember activated the switch on the SSAS and recorded mission elapse time (MET). After 24 hours of sampling, the valve was placed in the next sampling position and the MET was recorded. This procedure continued for the duration of the mission. Five minutes was required for a crewmember to destow, place, and activate the SSAS during flight. An additional five minutes was required to deactivate and stow the samples prior to landing.
results: STS-37: A total of 31 contaminants were desorbed from one or more of the five SSAS tubes exposed during the mission. The collective toxicity potential of the chemicals found in the cabin air was estimated by adding each ratio of compound concentration to a 7-day spacecraft maximum allowable concentration (SMAC). Based on the analysis of the atmospheric samples collected on STS-37, the air was deemed toxicologically safe for crewmembers to breathe throughout the mission. STS-40: A total of 108 chemical contaminants were desorbed from one or more of the six SSAS tubes exposed during the mission. Analysis of orbiter and Spacelab atmospheric samples collected throughout the mission showed the air was generally safe to breathe. The only exception was the air quality degradation caused by the Orbiter Refrigerator/Freezer (OR/F) malfunction. Odors and symptoms reported by the crewmembers during the malfunction, as well as postflight failure analysis of the OR/F, indicated that while the SSAS was in the middeck area early in the mission, crewmembers were temporarily exposed to harmful concentrations of thermodegradation products.

title: Energy and Metabolic Requirements for Extended Duration Space Flight (Energy Utilization)
experiment_type: Shuttle Extended Duration Orbiter Medical Project (EDOMP)
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: An astronaut will lose lean body mass if energy balance is not maintained. This is especially true if energy expenditure exceeds energy intake. However, astronauts on Skylab lost lean body mass in spite of the apparent adequate intake of energy and protein. Energy requirements could be affected by microgravity and by the limits on physical activity in the close confines of the spacecraft. Before this study, energy requirements during space flight had only been estimated from metabolic balance studies and food intake records. The objectives of this study were to measure total energy expenditure (TEE) during space flight and to compare the
approach: Two five-day test sessions (one before and 1 during flight) were completed by each of 13 astronauts on six Shuttle flights lasting eight to 14 days. The astronauts consumed doubly labeled water (labeled with the heavy isotopes 2H and 18O) and periodically provided urine and saliva samples. It was necessary to account for baseline differences in the isotopes of hydrogen and oxygen in the Shuttle's drinking water, which is made by fuel cells from liquid oxygen and hydrogen. Total energy expenditure was determined by indirect calorimetry and was corrected for body weight and fat-free mass. Energy intake was calculated from records of food and fluid intake. One-way repeated-measures ANOVA identified differences in energy intake and expenditure between the preflight and postflight periods. The Student-Newman-Keuls test was used for post-hoc comparisons. Paired t-tests were used to detect any differences between preflight and inflight dietary intake.

The astronauts consumed doubly labeled water (labeled with the heavy isotopes 2H and 18O) and periodically provided urine and saliva samples. It was necessary to account for baseline differences in the isotopes of hydrogen and oxygen in the Shuttle's drinking water, which is made by fuel cells from liquid oxygen and hydrogen. Total energy expenditure was determined by indirect calorimetry and was corrected for body weight and fat-free mass. Energy intake was calculated from records of food and fluid intake. One-way repeated-measures ANOVA identified differences in energy intake and expenditure between the preflight and postflight periods. The Student-Newman-Keuls test was used for post-hoc comparisons. Paired t-tests were used to detect any differences between preflight and inflight dietary intake. RESULTS: Energy expenditures were similar before and during flight. However, energy and fluid intake were lower during flight (energy intake was 23% less; fluid intake was 19% less.) Weight changes ranged from a gain of 1.0 kilogram (kg) to a loss of 3.9 kg, with a mean weight loss of 1.5 kg. In flight energy expenditures were similar to estimates published by the World Health Organization (WHO) of energy requirements for healthy adults. The results indicated that energy expenditure was not changed during space flight and that the WHO estimates of energy requirements were appropriate for estimating the dietary needs of space crews. However, most of the 13 astronauts were in negative energy balance because they had reduced their caloric intake. This is undesirable because the loss of lean body mass reduces work capacity and promotes the loss of electrolytes that are important to muscle function and cardiovascular function. The astronauts also consumed inadequate fluid. The importance of maintaining adequate food and fluid intake should be emphasized in future flights.

title: Magnetic Resonance Imaging after Exposure to Microgravity
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: A number of physiological changes have been demonstrated in bone, muscle and blood from exposure of humans and animals to microgravity. It was hypothesized that during space flight, all of the following would increase: atrophy of the muscles, the intervertebral disc space, and percentage of fat in the bone marrow. It was also hypothesized that the changes in bone marrow fat would be accompanied by a decrease in the cellular component. Determining the mechanisms of space-flight-induced physiological changes and the development of effective countermeasures for long duration space missions is an important goal of the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA). Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) scans performed on the leg and lower back muscles of the crewmembers of the Spacelab-J (STS-47) mission showed significant muscle atrophy after only eight days in microgravity. The 17-day Life and Microgravity Spacelab (LMS) mission provided the opportunity to determine whether long duration space flight would
approach: Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) was used to measure changes in the volume of individual muscles (soleus, gastrocnemius, quadriceps, hamstrings, adductors, intrinsic low back, and psoas) and to determine the degree and rate of recovery to their preflight states. During all MRI sessions, measurements were made in the same order, starting with the spine and back, and followed by the limb measurements. For spine imaging, subjects were positioned so that the imaging area was centered within the L3 vertebra. The cross sectional area of the disc space was measured for the T12-L1, L1-2, L2-3, L3-4, and L4-5 discs. For imaging of the back muscles, twenty (20) 0.5 cm slices, centered on the L3 vertebra, were obtained. For limb measurements, the feet were positioned in a holder to minimize movement during image acquisition and to ensure repositioning. For the thigh and calf muscles, thirty-two (32) 1 cm slices were taken. The calf muscle transverse relaxation time (T2) was measured by repeating the calf region scan using the same receiver gain with a longer echo time. The T2 values of each pixel were determined by comparing the image intensity at two different echo times, Te=10 and 50 msec. The determined T2 value represents the averages of the individual pixels taken from each muscle. To measure fat and water percentages in the vertebral bone marrow, volume selective proton spectra were obtained using a surface receive coil. A cubic volume of interest of 15mm x 15mm x 15mm, located at the center of the L3 vertebra, was selected from the scout scan. The spectra were obtained at four echo times (Te = 12,18, 24, 30 msec). Bone marrow cellularity was determined from the fat to water peak areas. At the end of each MRI session, a whole body Dual Energy X-ray Absorptiometry (DEXA) scan was performed as well. The DEXA scan required approximately 15 minutes and gave a radiation exposure of less than 1 mrem. The whole body scan was analyzed for bone mineral density (BMD), soft tissue, lean tissue, and fat. In order to examine fluid redistribution between the upper body and the lower limbs, the soft tissue values of the legs were divided by the whole body soft tissue minus the legs. This ratio was used to compare preflight status with postflight status. MRI and DEXA scans were performed on four crewmembers two times preflight, at 50-51 and 29-31 days before launch. The scans were repeated postflight within 24 hours of Shuttle landing (R+0), and 2, 10, and 30 days after landing (R+2, R+10, R+30).
