title: Sleeping Short
variables: Center for Epidemiologic Studies depression scale (CES-D)
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: For various reasons, astronauts typically "sleep short" in space, seldom getting the 8 hours intended by the time line schedule. For some, this may not present a problem, because they are naturally short sleepers who can get by with 5 1/2 hours of sleep, for example, without any consequent daytime sleepiness. For others, sleeping short inevitably leads to impairments in mood, alertness, and ability to perform at full capacity. This project comprises a detailed investigation of "sleeping short" using ground-based studies of healthy men and women (20y-59y). This study sought to address three critical questions: 1. Which countermeasure or combination of behavioral and physiological countermeasures will optimally mitigate specific performance problems associated with sleep loss and circadian disturbances during a Mars mission? 2. What individual biological and behavioral characteristics will best predict successful adaptation to long-term space flight of sleep and circadian physiology and the neurobehavioral performance functions they regulate? 3. What are the best methods for monitoring the status of sleep and circadian functioning and for assessing the effects of sleep loss and circadian dysrhythmia that are also portable and non-intrusive in the spaceflight environment? It has three aims which coincide broadly with the three years of proposed research. In Year 01, we will develop a questionnaire/diary instrument (the "Sleep Length Index" - SLI) designed to identify those who are naturally short sleepers who can thrive on less than 6 hours of sleep (as opposed to those who restrict their sleep inadvisably and suffer from daytime sleepiness). Year 02 will be concerned with determining the sleep and circadian rhythm, mood and performance differences between short sleepers (as identified by the SLI) and age and gender matched controls. The study will use an enhanced laboratory version of the 72-hour measurement block we have used in previous bedrest and astronaut studies. Year 03 will test the efficacy of Modafinil as a countermeasure when medium sleepers are required to "sleep short." The drug will be tested in a double blind placebo controlled cross-over design, during a week of severe (40%) sleep restriction in the laboratory, involving detailed sleep, circadian, rhythm, mood, and performance measures. The project seeks not only to provide findings of operational benefit to NASA, but also to provide tools and information of general benefit for those of us on the ground who have to restrict the time available for sleep because of occupational and/or care giving commitments. This experiment sought to provide questionnaire and diary instruments designed to assess habitual sleep need, and to assess the circadian regularity of human behaviors. It also had the aim of testing a particular pharmacological countermeasure (Modafinil) to reduced sleep amounts. In particular, the experiment involved a double-blind placebo-controlled trial of Modafinil as a countermeasure to five consecutive nights where sleep was restricted by 60% (i.e. to 40% of habitual durations). The 3 specific aims are: development of questionnaire instruments to assess habitual sleep need and timing, to identify “naturally short sleepers”, assessing the personality and circadian characteristics, also the evaluation of the consequences of unmet sleep need (thus identifying short sleepers who were sleeping short unwisely); continued development and testing of an easily administered diary instrument to assess circadian regularity in human behavior (the 5-item Social Rhythm Metric SRM-5); and a double-blind placebo-controlled trial of Modafinil as a countermeasure to 5 consecutive nights where sleep was restricted by 60% (i.e. to 40% of habitual durations).
approach: Aim 1a: Identifying and characterizing naturally short sleepers While most people require more than 6 hours of sleep to feel well rested, there appears to be a group of people who can function well on between 3 and 6 hours of sleep. The aims of the present study were: 1) to compare 12 naturally short (3.0h-6.0h) sleepers recruited by a media publicity campaign with age and gender matched medium length (7h-8.5h) sleepers on various measures; 2) to determine the prevalence of naturally short sleepers in a volunteer sample of 71 University alumni; and 3) to examine the distribution of the various measures from the alumni study, and the position of the 12 naturally short sleepers identified in #1 on these distributions, determining the extent, if any, to which they were outliers. Measurement instruments included diaries and questionnaires to assess sleep duration and timing, as well as questionnaire assessments of sleep pathology, morningness-eveningness, extroversion, neuroticism, pathological daytime sleepiness, perceived competence, optimism, depressive symptoms, exercise, and work habits. Aim 1b: Development of a questionnaire instrument to assess sleep duration and timing The initial proposal called for a development of a Sleep Length Index (SLI). However, rather than limiting ourselves to sleep length only, we felt it better to develop an instrument yielding measures of both timing and duration of the habitual sleep episodes. This
results: ed in the development of the Sleep Timing Questionnaire (STQ). The objective was to develop a single-administration instrument yielding equivalent measures of sleep to those obtained from a formal (2-week) sleep diary. Test-retest reliability was examined in 40 subjects who were given the STQ on 2 occasions separated by less than one year. Convergent validity was measured both by comparing STQ derived measures with objective measures derived from wrist actigraphy, and by comparing STQ derived measures with other subjective measures derived from a detailed 2-week sleep diary in 2 non-overlapping samples. Correlations of STQ measures with age and morningness-eveningness (chronotype) were also examined. Most subjects were healthy volunteers; some subjects were patients (enrolled in research protocols). Aim 1c: Consequences of sleeping short unwisely In order to provide baseline data for various research studies at the University of Pittsburgh over a 10-year period, 266 healthy subjects meeting certain criteria each completed a 14-night sleep diary. For each night, the diary allowed the subjective measurement of bedtime, wake time, Time In Bed (TIB), sleep efficiency, number of minutes of Wake After Sleep Onset (WASO), alertness upon awakening, and percentage of mornings needing an alarm (or a person functioning as one). Weeknight versus weekend night differences in TIB (TIBdiff), weekday alertness, and reliance on alarms were examined as possible indicators of sleep debt. Additionally, general descriptive data were tabulated. Aim 2: Continuing and testing a brief diary device to evaluate daily lifestyle regularity A brief diary instrument to quantify daily lifestyle regularity (SRM-5) is developed and compared to a much longer version of the instrument (SRM-17). Three studies are described. In Study 1, SRM-17 scores (2 weeks) were collected from a total of 293 healthy control subjects (both genders) aged between 19 and 92 years. Five items--(1) Get out of bed, (2) First contact with another person, (3) Start work, housework or volunteer activities, (4) Have dinner, and (5) Go to bed--were then selected from the 17 items and SRM-5 scores calculated as if these 5 items were the only ones collected. Comparisons were made with SRM-17 scores from the same subject-weeks, looking at correlations between the 2 SRM measures, and the effects of age and gender on lifestyle regularity as measured by the 2 instruments. In Study 2 this process was repeated in a group of 27 subjects who were in remission from unipolar depression after treatment with psychotherapy and who completed SRM-17 for at least 20 successive weeks. SRM-5 and SRM-17 scores were then correlated within an individual using time as the random variable, allowing an indication of how successful SRM-5 was in tracking changes in lifestyle regularity (within an individual) over time. In Study 3 a SRM-5 diary instrument was administered to 101 healthy control subjects (both genders, aged 20 – 59 years) for 2 successive weeks to obtain normative measures and to test for correlations with age and morningness. Aim 3: A controlled trial of Modafinil as a countermeasure to sleep restriction This study was a small-sample (10 subjects) double-blind placebo controlled study of Modafinil as a countermeasure to 5 consecutive nights of partial sleep restriction (to 40% of habitual time in bed). The study was a within-subjects cross-over design in which subjects experienced both drug and placebo conditions in 2 week-long sessions, separated from each other by 2 weeks. Each session involved the subject living in a time isolation apartment with no time cues or knowledge of clock time. The routine was specified by technicians who informed the subject when to get up, go to bed, take meals, etc. All sleeps were polysomnographically recorded, rectal temperature measured continuously, evening salivary samples collected (to detect the timing of the Dim Light Melatonin Onset - DLMO), and a battery of mood, alertness and performance measures (5 times per day) taken on each day of the study. On the final day of the study (before the recovery sleep) a Multiple Sleep Latency Test (MSLT) was given to assess daytime sleepiness under drug and placebo conditions. Bedtime and wake time on the first night (of each week) were at the subject’s habitual times. On nights 2 through 6, bedtimes were made later and wake times earlier (by equal amounts) until time in bed (TIB) was at 40% of baseline levels (a 60% reduction). A placebo pill was taken at breakfast on the first morning (after the full night of sleep) and a pill (either placebo or drug depending on condition) at breakfast on the mornings following nights 2 through 6. The first 2 subjects also took a pill at lunchtime. The dose of Modafinil at each administration was 200mg. In all cases, between 100% and 150% of habitual TIB was made available for sleep on night 7 (the recovery night). With the exception of drug versus placebo, the procedure was identical for the two sessions for a given subject. One subject terminated the study early for family reasons, thus data analysis is proceeding using nine subjects (6f, 3m, age 21-58 years). RESULTS: Aim 1a: Identifying and characterizing naturally short sleepers Few measures showed reliable differences between naturally short sleepers and controls except the obvious ones related to sleep duration. There was, however, some evidence for subclinical hypomanic symptoms in naturally short sleepers. The prevalence of naturally short sleepers in a volunteer alumni sample was about 3% after shift work, daytime sleepiness, psychopathology and sleep disorders had been excluded. Aim 1b: Development of a questionnaire instrument to assess sleep duration and timing Test-retest reliability for the STQ was demonstrated for estimates of bedtime (r=0.705, p Aim 1c:Consequences of sleeping short unwisely On average, bedtimes were at 23:48 and wake times at 07:23, yielding a mean TIB of 7 hours 35 mins.. As expected, bedtimes and wake times were later on weekend nights than on weeknights. Bedtimes were 26 minutes later, wake times 53 minutes later, yielding a mean weekend TIB increase of 27 minutes. Overall, subjects perceived their sleep latency to be 10.5 minutes, reported an average of one wakening during the night (with an average of 6.4 minutes of WASO), had a diary sleep efficiency of 96.3 %, and awoke with an alertness rating of 69.5%. These variables differed little between weeknight and weekend nights. Subjects used an alarm (or a person functioning as an alarm) on 60.9 % nights overall, 68.3 % on weeknights, 42.5 % on weekends. When TIBdiff was used as an estimate of sleep debt (comparing subjects with TIBdiff>75 minutes with those with a TIBdiff Aim 2: Continuing and testing a brief diary device to evaluate daily lifestyle regularity Measures of lifestyle regularity from SRM-5 correlated quite well (about 0.8) with those from SRM-17 both between subjects, and within-subjects over time. As a detector of irregularity as defined by SRM-17, the SRM-5 instrument showed acceptable values of kappa (0.69), sensitivity (74%) and specificity (95%). There were, however, differences in mean level, with SRM-5 scores being about 0.9 units (about one standard deviation) above SRM-17 scores from the same subject-weeks. SRM-5 scores also deviated more from a Gaussian distribution than did SRM-17 ones. In a study with a sample size of 101, the new SRM-5 instrument yielded scores with a mean of 4.11 and a standard deviation of 1.13. Correlations between lifestyle regularity and age, and between lifestyle regularity and morningness appeared similar whether 5-item or 17-item SRM measures were used. When a gender difference in lifestyle regularity appeared, it was detected by both SRM-5 and SRM-17 measures. Aim 3: A controlled trial of Modafinil as a countermeasure to sleep restriction The tenth subject was only completed at the end of September, and data analysis is ongoing, so the final results of this study cannot yet be reported.

title: Crewmember and Crew-Ground Interactions During NASA-Mir
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: During future long duration missions, international crews will be engaged in complicated activities over long periods of time. A number of interpersonal issues likely to impact these missions must be addressed to ensure healthy crewmember interactions and optimal performance. The objectives of this study were to measure and characterize changes over time in a number of important interpersonal factors, such as tension, cohesion, leadership role, and the relationship between space crews and ground support personnel during the NASA/Mir missions. The formal hypotheses addressed a number of aspects related to crew and ground control tension, cohesion, and leadership role. Over the course of long-term space missions, tension in the crew environment and crew cohesiveness were expected to change. Researchers expected an association between the level of tension in the crewmembers and their relationship with people on the ground, and between tension in mission control personnel and their relationship with management. Also, it was hypothesized that the perception of both the leadership role and outside monitoring support would change over time. Although specific stressors that occur during the mission, there is evidence, can influence these issues, that time alone may be a factor. One
approach: , the biphasic model, proposes that significant psychological and interpersonal difficulties may occur after the halfway point of a mission. Hence, a sense of relief that half of the mission is over is outweighed by the realization that another half is yet to come, and this
results: in decrements in mood and interpersonal functioning of the crew. The triphasic model describes three phases of reaction for people working in isolating and confined conditions for long periods. The initial anxiety in the first few weeks are mainly due to the novelty of the situation; depression during the long middle period of the mission are mainly due to monotony and homesickness; and euphoria and adolescent behavior during the last few weeks due to anticipation of returning home. When crews are composed of people from different countries or different ethnic backgrounds, language and cultural differences are important since they may lead to intra-crew tensions and disruptions in cohesion, and this in turn may negatively affect morale and interfere with the performance of mission tasks. Issues related to language and cultural differences have been reported in both simulation and space environments. Language and cultural issues also may adversely affect the interactions of mission control personnel on the ground, although these individuals have not been studied previously. The relationship between the crewmembers and their mission control support personnel is important, since miscommunication or insensitivity between these two groups may lead to misaligned work schedules or inappropriate responses during times of danger. A phenomenon that may negatively influence crew ground communication is displacement, which occurs when tension and distressful dysphoric emotions (e.g., anger, depression) that arise within the crewmembers during the mission cannot be expressed openly and are instead transferred outside to ground personnel, who are perceived as unsupportive and negative. Interactions suggestive of displacement have been reported during space missions and during space simulation studies on Earth. In simulations, crewmember anger directed to outside monitors has been especially observed when overt anger and tension were not seen between the confined subjects, and vice versa. Earlier work explored several of the above psychosocial issues in confined groups and included a questionnaire study of 54 astronauts and cosmonauts who had flown in space and a study of three male Russian subjects who were secluded in the Mir space station simulator in Moscow for 135 days. The study described in this paper involved a series of space missions in which two Russian cosmonauts and one American astronaut worked together on board the Mir space station for periods of four to seven months. The objectives of the study were to determine how tension, cohesion, and leader support affected the space crewmembers and mission control personnel on the ground and to determine how these factors changed over time. Several of the hypotheses predicted decreases in crew behavior during the second half of the missions in accordance with the biphasic model. The value of the triphasic model was also explored and other time effects that might be present while the crewmembers were on orbit. As stated in the hypothesis, displacement of tension and dysphoria would occur from crewmembers to mission control personnel and from mission control personnel to management; differences in response between Russians and Americans and between crewmembers and mission control personnel, were explored. We made no predictions concerning these differences since little empirical evidence existed that would allow us to form hypotheses related to these socio-cultural factors. APPROACH: American astronauts, Russian cosmonauts, and American and Russian mission control personnel who were involved with the Shuttle/Mir space program were asked to participate in our study. The number of subjects who volunteered, gave informed consent, and participated in the study during the on orbit periods included 5 astronauts (in 5 U.S. missions), 8 cosmonauts (in 4 Russian missions), and 42 American and 16 Russian mission control personnel, who included flight surgeons, operations leads, engineers, mission scientists, spacecraft communicators, and psychological support staff. To measure mood state and group interpersonal climate, standardized measures were used which have been shown to be valid and reliable in a number of studies on Earth. To assess emotions, we utilized the Profile of Mood States, or POMS, which consisted of 65 adjectives describing various affective states, such as "tense" and "cheerful", and were rated on a weekly basis by the subjects on 5 point Likert scales: 0 = Not at all 1 = A little 2 = Moderately 3 = Quite a bit 4 = Extremely To assess the interpersonal climate in the crew and mission control groups, subscales from two well-known instruments: the Group Environment Scale, or GES, and the Work Environment Scale, or WES. Both of these instruments measured dimensions of a group's interpersonal environment through subject endorsements of statements as being either "true" or "false" of their particular group during the previous week. An example of a question is: "There is a feeling of unity and cohesion in this group". Subscale scores were determined by summing the scores from related POMS, GES, or WES items. Examples of subscales were Tension-Anxiety (from the POMS), Cohesion (from the GES), and Supervisor Support (from the WES). Changes in subscale scores over time were regarded as alterations in the subjects' perception of mood and group climate. Descriptive analyses of the data suggested that the subjects considered the full range of responses when completing the measures. For example, on 63 of the 65 items from the Profile of Mood States, subjects gave all possible responses from 0-4 with exceptions for: "spiteful" and "forgetful", and on all 126 items from the GES and WES, subjects answered both true and false responses. For most items, however, the distributions were skewed in the direction of adaptive functioning (i.e., low values on negative subscales and high values on positive subscales). The above measures comprised our study questionnaire, which was available in both English and Russian computerized and hard copy formats. The questions took 15-20 minutes to complete. Both crew and ground subjects completed the questionnaire with reference to the preceding seven days Overall, 82% of the expected questionnaires were received from subjects participating during the on-orbit periods (70% from crewmembers and 85% from mission control personnel). This totaled 212 from crew subjects and 1,088 from ground subjects. Data analysis strategies One analyses examined the data for differences between U.S. and Russian subjects and between crewmembers and personnel in mission control personnel. Mean scores were calculated for each subject on each of the POMS, GES, and WES subscales. Subsequently, the number of observations that contributed to it weighted each mean, and a two-way repeated measure analysis of variance (ANOVA) was performed. The model included main effects for country (American, Russian), group (crewmember, mission control personnel), and their interactions. A second set of previous analyses dealt with hypotheses related to the displacement of negative emotions for both crew and ground subjects. Displacement was operationalized as the negative association between measures of tension and dysphoria with WES Supervisor Support over the course of a mission. For the crewmembers, supervisors were defined as members of the outside monitoring staff in mission control, and for the mission control subjects, supervisors were defined as members of the American or Russian space agency management staff. A mixed model analysis was used to test the effects for each measure of tension or dysphoria. During weeks that there was high tension and dysphoria in the "in-group" (i.e., the crew or ground), we hypothesized that there would be a tendency to displace these feelings outwardly to the respective mission control or management "out-group" and to perceive these supervisors as not being supportive. A third set of analyses examined hypotheses related to the biphasic model, which predicted decrements in crewmember emotional state and interactions during the second half of the missions. Before analysis, the distribution of the raw data was examined for normality. Several subscales (dependent variables) had scores that were normally distributed. Others were successfully normalized using a logarithmic transformation. Still others had greatly skewed distributions and needed to be dichotomized. Cutoffs were made as close as possible to include 50% of the scores in the "high" category and 50% in the "low" category. These dichotomous variables were analyzed using Generalized Estimating Equation (GEE) fixed effect models with logit link functions and binomial variance. All other variables were analyzed using a mixed model approach that modeled random intercepts and slopes and assumed a decreasing correlation as the lag interval increased. Both the GEE and the mixed model approaches accounted for the effects of autocorrelation and were not handicapped by missing values in our longitudinal data caused by random events that prevented the subjects from completing the measures during a given week. The bi-phasic analysis used a piecewise linear regression approach. The weekly subscale scores for each subject for each mission were arrayed around the midpoint of the mission (counted as week = 0) because the launches and mission periods of Americans and Russians were staggered in calendar time and were of differing lengths. The missions varied from 16 weeks (an American astronaut) to 28 weeks (two Russian cosmonauts). From the actual weekly subscale scores, overall estimates of the average slope in the first half and in the second half of the missions were calculated, with these slopes intercepting at the midpoint. Another analyses also tested for the effects of time during the on-orbit period but modeled the effects of triphasic rather than biphasic changes. A regression approach with a quadratic function was selected to test for a pattern indicative of the presence of three phases in all crewmembers and in the Americans and Russians taken separately. For example, the literatures have suggested that crew tension levels would be high initially, and then drop during the middle phase of the mission. Tension would then rise again at the end as the termination approaches. Since quadratic functions describe curves with one bend, this analytic procedure was a reasonable way for us to test for U-shaped patterns among the variables in the data. However, since other curvilinear patterns may give a significant quadratic result as well, we had to visually inspect the data to see if a U-shape or some other curve best defined it. Since the regression models with a quadratic function included tests for linear functions in the analysis, a comparison of the quadratic pattern with a linear pattern was explored for the subscales throughout the course of the mission. If both of these tests for a given subscale are significant, then it is appropriate to present only the quadratic results. It is important to realize that the pattern of change in the actual data for a given subscale variable may not in itself be linear. For example, for variables that were dichotomized and subject to a GEE analysis, what was being evaluated was the presence of a linear pattern in the logit transformed values, not in the actual data. The most one could infer from such a case was that there was an overall tendency for a variable to increase or decrease versus showing no change over time (e.g., the tension level rose or fell during the course of the total mission versus staying pretty much the same). Therefore, one needs to visually examine the plot to deduce what kind of pattern is evident. A second set of new analyses was conducted to determine whether crewmember subjects differed from normative samples on Earth. T-tests were used to compare mission means with normative scores from other groups on Earth, both in terms of all subjects pooled and in terms of American and Russian subjects taken separately. A third set of new analyses tested for differences in the subscale variables during the missions compared to pre- and post-mission. Mean scores were calculated for each subject on each of the POMS, GES, and WES subscales for the mission itself and for the pre- and post-mission periods. Subsequently, each mean was weighted by the number of observations that contributed to it, and a one-way repeated measures analysis of variance (ANOVA) was performed that compared crewmember subscale mean scores during the missions with pre- and post-mission means. Again, we looked at all crewmembers pooled and at Americans and Russians taken separately. All of the previously conducted and new regression analyses were performed using a SAS macro based to execute the GEE analysis and the SAS MIXED procedure for the mixed models. The t-tests were conducted using the SAS t-test procedure, and the ANOVAs were conducted using the SAS GLM procedure. To control for a possible inflated Type I error rate associated with multiple significance tests, the false discovery rate procedure was utilized to determine an adjusted significance threshold. This procedure controls the expected proportion of falsely rejected hypotheses (i.e., the false discovery rate). For each effect being evaluated, the actual p-values from each of the total number of N subscales being tested were rank ordered from smallest to largest. Multiplying .05 by the rank number of each subscale result and then dividing by N calculated a cutoff significance threshold. The p-value from each subscale result then was compared against the threshold p-value until a comparison was found that did not exceed the threshold. This p-value became the significance level threshold for that particular effect. The results reported below have been interpreted with reference to the appropriate calculated Benjamini and Hochberg adjusted significance threshold. RESULTS: Interpersonal and cultural results To examine the potential impact of interpersonal and cultural factors, we used an analysis of variance to explore differences between Americans and Russians and between crew and ground subjects. Seven of the total of 21 subscale comparisons gave p-values lower than the adjusted significance threshold for the country main effect: Americans scored higher than Russians on POMS Vigor-Activity and WES Work Pressure, and lower on WES Managerial Control, GES Task Orientation, GES Self Discovery, WES Physical Comfort, and GES Leader Support. For the group main effect, four comparisons were significant, with mission control subjects scoring higher than crewmembers on four POMS measures of dysphoria (Tension-Anxiety, Fatigue-Inertia, Confusion-Bewilderment, and Total Mood Disturbance). There were significant country by group interactions for three GES subscales: Leader Support, Expressiveness, and Independence. American crewmembers scored lower than any other group on all three measures. Taken together, these findings suggested that Americans (especially U.S. crewmembers) experienced more emotional and work related problems than Russians, and that mission control personnel were more dysphoric than crewmembers. Displacement results Strong support was found in favor that displacement would occur for both crewmembers and mission control personnel using a mixed model analysis. Six subscales were picked to evaluate displacement (POMS: Tension-Anxiety, Depression-Dejection, Anger-Hostility, Total Mood Disturbance; GES Anger & Aggression; WES Work Pressure), and the phenomenon was indicated operationally when there was a significant negative association of each of these subscales with a measure of outside support (WES Supervisor Support). All six predicted associations were significant for the crewmembers, and five of the six were significant for the mission control subjects with the exception of WES Work Pressure. These results strongly suggested that crewmembers displaced tension and negative emotions to mission control personnel and that mission control personnel displaced tension and negative emotions to management. Biphasic model results According to the biphasic model, as hypothesized, there would be a significant rise in measures of crew tension, a drop in measures of crew cohesion and leader support, and a drop in measures of mission control leader support during the second half of the missions. The cohesion hypothesis was tested by examining six subscale variables: GES Cohesion, GES Task Orientation, GES Order and Organization, POMS Depression-Dejection, POMS Fatigue-Inertia, and POMS Vigor-Activity. We tested our tension hypothesis in terms of four variables: POMS Tension-Anxiety, POMS Anger-Hostility, GES Anger & Aggression, and WES Work Pressure. Finally, leader support was examined for both the crewmembers and the mission control personnel by exploring two variables: GES Leader Support and WES Supervisor Support. Using a piecewise linear regression approach with the appropriate mixed model or GEE analyses, only one of the, variables was significant when the Benjamini and Hochberg adjusted significance threshold was applied: there was a significant drop in GES Leader Support for crewmembers in the second half. Overall, the results did not indicate the presence of a moderate to strong biphasic time effect. The findings reported below deal with triphasic and linear time effects and with emotional and group climate responses reported by the crewmembers during their time on-orbit (the mission period). Unlike mission control personnel, the crewmembers were confined in space during the missions in an environment quite different from that on Earth. This isolation made them especially vulnerable to group and time pressures. Consequently, the results will have special relevance for the crew subjects. Quadratic (triphasic) model results The triphasic model was evaluated in terms of a regression approach with a quadratic function, since this gives a reasonable test of the U-shaped pattern one would expect to see in the subscales over the course of the missions if this pattern was in operation. However, since quadratic functions also describe non U-shaped curves, it is important to inspect the data visually to see just what kind of curve is depicted. A significant quadratic component in the model indicates that the quadratic function is a better representation of the data than a linear function. For the crewmembers, all of the 21 subscale variables from the POMS, GES, and WES were tested. After applying the Benjamini and Hochberg procedure, the results indicated that none of tests for the quadratic function in these subscales met the adjusted significance threshold (p = .0024). Additional evaluations were made of the quadratic function in the 21 subscales for Russian and American crewmembers taken separately. For the Russians, none of the tests resulted in significant findings. For the American crewmembers, three of the subscales were significant for quadratic functions, with the p-value being less than the Benjamini and Hochberg adjusted significance threshold of p =.0024. These were: GES Order & Organization (beta = .007, p = .000); GES Task Orientation (beta = -.007, p = .000); and GES Self Discovery (beta = -.099, p = .000). Since all three of these variables had a skewed distribution and were dichotomized, they ~ere analyzed using a GEE model. Linear model results For all the crewmembers and for the Russians taken separately, regression analyses for the linear model were made on all 21 subscales. In both cases, none of the subscales resulted in p-values that were less than the Benjamini and Hochberg adjusted significance threshold (p = .0024). For the American crewmembers taken separately, only one subscale variable (other than GES Self Discovery) had a p-value that was less than the Benjamini and Hochberg threshold of p = .0048: GES Cohesion. A GEE analysis had been performed on GES Cohesion since the data were skewed and needed to be dichotomized, and this resulted in findings of beta = -.144 and p = .003. The negative beta meant that the probability of achieving a high score decreased in some manner from the beginning to the end of the mission. Although the shape of the logit curve was better described by a linear than a quadratic function, this did not imply that the actual data necessarily would plot as a straight line. Crewmember results versus scores from normative samples on Earth For nearly every subscale, the crewmember means were in the positive half of the subscale range. That is, where a high score defined a negative outcome (e.g., POMS Tension-Anxiety), the crew mean was below the scale midpoint (18 for this subscale), whereas where a high score defined a positive outcome (e.g., GES Cohesion), the crew mean was above the scale midpoint (4.5 for this subscale). This suggested that the crewmembers generally endorsed positive adaptive responses, especially for the POMS emotion variables. The normative means and standard deviations were determined from several thousand people participating in non-patient work and task groups. The POMS sample consisted of 1,130 adult males who participated in a smoking cessation program; the GES sample consisted of individuals who participated in 101 task-oriented groups in health care, correctional, and educational settings [41]; and the WES sample consisted of 8,146 individuals who participated in 116 general and health care work groups [42]. Using t-tests and the Benjamini and Hochberg procedure, a total of 13 subscales resulted in p-values that were below the adjusted significance threshold of p = .033. For all six significant POMS variables, the crewmembers endorsed significantly less dysphoria than the POMS normative sample. They also scored lower on GES and WES measures of group expressiveness, independence, anger & aggression, and innovation; and higher on measures of cohesion, leader control, and managerial control. The subscale means and standard deviations for Russian and American crewmembers were taken separately, along with their respective comparisons with the normative samples; a given difference did not always reach significance (probably due to the smaller sample sizes). One notable new finding is GES Self Discovery, where the Russian mean is significantly greater than the norm, and the American mean is significantly smaller. Mission versus pre-and post-mission results Crewmember subjects were asked to complete the POMS, GES, and WES questions each week during the time they were on the Mir. They also were asked to complete these measures for four consecutive weeks pre-mission, ending at one month before launch (i.e., baseline data collection period), and for two consecutive weeks after they returned to Earth. However, it was discovered that during the post-mission period the American and Russian subjects were separated from each other, so there was no group environment to evaluate using the GES and WES items. Consequently, only POMS data were collected. To look for differences in subscale scores before, during, and after the missions, mean scores were calculated and compared using a repeated measures ANOVA (pre-mission versus on-orbit versus post-mission for the POMS subscales, and pre-mission versus on-orbit for the GES and WES subscales). After applying the Benjamini and Hochberg procedure, none of these comparisons were significant in terms of all crewmembers, Russians alone, or Americans alone. CONCLUSION There was no support for the triphasic or linear models for all crewmembers or for Russian cosmonauts alone when the Benjamini and Hochberg criteria were applied to contol for Type I errors. Although there were three significant quadratic findings for American astronauts, only one variable, GES Order & Organization, showed a U-shaped pattern consistent with the triphasic model. This finding suggested that Americans in space felt that their interpersonal environment was comparatively more organized at the beginning and end of the on-orbit period than during the middle. This makes some sense because the new astronauts were formally oriented to the Mir shortly after arriving by the departing astronauts and by the continuing cosmonauts, and because the preparation for the return to Earth required the astronauts to undergo a number of specific procedures during the end of their on-orbit period. The other two significant quadratic functions for the Americans, GES Task Orientation and GES Self Discovery, gave a different pattern, with the probability of a high score being greater during the beginning weeks of the missions, then declining as time progressed. This pattem also was evident for the significant linear function finding for GES Cohesion. Taken together, the results from these three subscales suggested that the American crewmembers might have been impacted by the novelty of the situation during the first few weeks of their missions. They perceived the crew environment to be one where orientation to tasks was high, where they could grow individually, and where there was a strong bond among the crewmembers. Over time, there was a significant decrease in these areas. Perhaps the novelty of the situation simply disappeared. Alternatively, the decreases may have reflected an emotional change in the Americans due to homesickness or asthenia, although one would have expected to find some POMS changes as well if this explanation was valid. The above results were found only for American astronauts. The Russian estimated probabilities for high scores were in the .4 to .8 ranges for all four of the subscales shown in the figures, and they did not vary significantly over time. Thus, the cosmonauts were much more likely to endorse higher scores throughout the mission than their American counterparts. This difference may have reflected actual cultural differences or differences based on interpretations of the English and Russian versions of our measures. But it also might have reflected the specific interpersonal characteristics of the Shuttle/Mir missions, where there usually were two Russians and one American on-board, where the leader was always a Russian, where the Mir and its operation was in Russian control, and where the predominate language being spoken was Russian. Thus, an American astronaut was psychosocially isolated during these missions, and the U.S./Russian differences may have been more a reflection of the crew composition and operational situation than of characteristic cultural differences. First, although the estimated curves were significant, an inspection of the figures suggests that the estimates are not idea fits of the actual proportion data. The smooth estimated probability curves contradict the variation that is occurring in the mean weekly responses. Only biphasic, quadratic, and linear functions were tested, and perhaps some other function would give a better fit to the data. Second, for GES Order & Organization, GES Task Orientation, and GES Cohesion, the high/low splits were at 9/8. This means that about half of the total responses were the highest possible value of nine, and about half were eight and below. Therefore, in many cases, the indicated drop in scores was from a high of nine to a low of eight or seven, still in the upper part of the subscale range. In contrast, the high/low split for GES Self Discovery was 5/4, which gave more room at the top and bottom of the subscale range for the subjects to score. Little support was found for the presence of moderate to strong time effects in the crewmembers during the Shuttle/Mir missions. In comparison with other work and task groups on Earth, the crewmembers were significantly less dysphoric and perceived more cohesion and direction from their leaders and managers. They also felt that their group environment allowed them less opportunity to express themselves and to be independent and innovative, and they reported lower levels of group anger and aggression. American and Russian subjects taken separately generally echoed these overall findings. In addition, unlike many work environments on Earth, the Shuttle/Mir missions were busy and highly structured, with many timelines, procedures, and directions from the ground that needed to be followed. One interesting difference between Russian and American crewmembers pertained to GES Self Discovery, with the former scoring significantly higher than the normative sample and the latter Scoring significantly lower. Although the Russian crewmembers perceived their interpersonal environment as conducive to such discussion (compared with the normative group on Earth), the American crewmembers had an opposite perspective. Perhaps language differences and a sense of psychosocial isolation handicapped the latter and prevented them from learning about themselves through such informal group interactions. No significant differences were establish in crew response before, during, or after the missions in terms of all crewmembers or Americans and Russians taken separately. Significant pre/post seclusion differences using the same measures were found in our 135-day Mir simulator study, and we expected to replicate some of the findings. For example, POMS Tension-Anxiety levels were significantly lower, and GES Leader Support, Expressiveness, and Self Discovery levels were significantly higher during the Mir simulation seclusion period than before. However, the psychological meaning of this simulation was much different from the Shuttle/Mir missions in terms of anxiety and perceived danger, and one must be cautious in extrapolating the findings from earth-bound psychosocial simulation research into space. Crewmembers may be more comfortable with their work environment in space than mission control personnel are with their work environment on Earth, and it is possible that for astronauts and cosmonauts, the excitement of being in space offsets any negatives from living and working on earth. Thus, crewmembers perceived their work environment differently form people on Earth, and they demonstrated equanimity in mood and group perceptions, both in space and on the ground.

title: Microcirculatory Adjustments to Simulated Microgravity Exposure in Humans
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Exposure of an individual to microgravity activates a series of compensatory alterations. Reduced tolerance to orthostatic stress is a primary concern when the individual returns to a 1-G environment, whereas reduced thermoregulatory capability could affect performance in space, as well as following the flight. This investigation included a series of experiments that addressed both issues by assessing the effects of simulated microgravity on the control of the cutaneous vasculature at the level of the microcirculation. These studies were performed using non- and minimally invasive techniques to assess skin blood flow simultaneously with administration of vasoactive substances primarily via intradermal microdialysis. Dose-response relationships were constructed with this information. It is recognized that the cutaneous circulation may not be significantly involved in the maintenance of blood pressure during orthostasis in normothermia. To this regard, two important points should be made, a) information regarding the effects of simulated microgravity on the cutaneous microcirculation may be valuable in identifying mechanisms associated with altered control of the microvasculature in regions more important to the regulation of blood pressure, but less easily studied; b) in hyperthermia 50-60 percent of cardiac output is directed towards the skin. In this environment the skin represents the largest fraction of total vascular conductance, and its control is, therefore, critical in the maintenance of blood pressure. The following five hypotheses were tested. In each case microgravity exposure was simulated via 14 days of 6 degree head-down tilt (HDT) bed rest, and a subset of these subjects exercised throughout HDT exposure to see if impaired responses could be improved by aerobic exercise training. Prolonged HDT exposure decreases cutaneous adrenergic vasoconstrictor responsiveness. Prolonged HDT exposure reduces cutaneous vasoconstriction associated with the venoarteriolar response. Prolonged HDT exposure reduces maximal cutaneous vasodilator responsiveness. Prolonged HDT exposure impairs sweat gland function. Impaired thermoregulatory responses due to HDT bed rest will be preserved in subjects exercising through bed rest exposure.
approach: Twenty-two subjects (19 male and three female) were exposed to 14 days of strict 6 degree HDT bed rest. Fourteen of these subjects were randomly assigned to an exercise group (including two females), while eight subjects served as control subjects and thus did not exercise during HDT bed rest. This study was a component of an 18-day HDT bed rest study. However, the reported data were obtained from subjects after 14 days of HDT bed rest. On the final day of HDT bed rest (i.e., day 18) subjects in the exercise group were further subdivided to investigate questions unrelated to the present findings. Thus, for the reported data there are an unequal number of subjects in the control and exercise groups. The subjects' average age was 34 ± 2 years and all were of normal height (180 ± 2 cm), weight, (82 ± 4 kg), and health. A written informed consent from each subject was obtained prior to participating in the institutionally approved study. Bed Rest & Exercise Strict bed rest was maintained in the 6 degree HDT position for 14 days. Subjects remained in this position at all times, except they were allowed to elevate on one elbow for meals and were horizontal for exercise, transport, and bathing. Subjects were housed in a hospital-based general clinical research center and given a controlled diet, while fluids were allowed ad libitum . Pre-bed rest data were obtained within a week of the onset of bed rest. Post-bed rest data were collected on day 14 of bed rest. For the exercise group, exercise was performed at 75 percent of pre-bed rest heart rate maximum for 90 minutes per day using a supine cycle ergometer. Subjects chose to exercise for this duration either in two sessions of 45 minutes or three sessions of 30 minutes per day. Hypothesis #1: Two intradermal microdialysis membranes were placed in dorsal forearm skin. This technique involved placing a small (200 µm outer diameter, 10 mm length) sterile, semipermeable membrane intradermally using a 25-gauge needle. The microdialysis membranes were perfused with Ringer's solution at a rate of 2 µl/min via an infusion pump. The protocol commenced once skin blood flow (SkBF) returned to normal levels after needle insertion trauma (~60-120 minutes). Local temperature was controlled at 34 degrees Celsius via a local heating element that housed a laser-Doppler flow probe centered directly above the microdialysis membranes. Once SkBF stabilized, eight doses of norepinephrine (NE) were delivered (in 10 fold increments) at a flow rate of 2 µl/min for 5 minutes per dose. Data are presented from doses of 1x10 -9 to 1x10 -2 M, which represent both threshold and saturation for the subjects. Microdialysis membranes were placed at similar regions of the forearm between pre- and post-HDT bed rest trials. However, it is recognized that slight variations in probe placement likely occurred between these periods. For each period (i.e., pre- and post-HDBT), responses between the two sites for each dose were averaged. Hypothesis #2: With the subject in the supine position and the arms and legs at heart level, the forearm venoarteriolar response was assessed by inflating a cuff placed around the upper arm to 45 mmHg. The same procedure was performed to assess the venoarteriolar response of the lower leg except the cuff was placed around the thigh. The cuff remained inflated at this pressure for a minimum of two minutes. SkBF, assessed via laser-Doppler flowmetry, was measured at two sites on the dorsal forearm for the forearm assessment. For the lower leg assessment, laser-Doppler measures were obtained from nonglabrous skin over the tibialis anterior 39 ± 1 cm from the bottom of the foot. When SkBF from two sites were measured, the laser-Doppler signals were averaged between those sites. Anatomical measurements were obtained to place the laser-Doppler flow probes in the same region between pre- and post-bed rest trials. However, as indicated above, given the small sampling area of the laser-Doppler flow probes, it is doubtful that the probes were placed at the exact location between trials. Hypothesis #3: Assessment of maximal cutaneous vasodilation was accomplished by exposing the subject's left forearm to 42 degrees Celsius for 45 minutes using a cylindrical water spray device that encircled the subject's forearm. A thermocouple was attached to forearm skin within the cylindrical water spray device to verify skin temperature was held at 42 degrees Celsius. Prior to and following the 45-minute heating protocol, the average of six forearm blood flow measurements was obtained using venous occlusion plethysmography. Arterial blood pressure was obtained under both conditions via R-wave triggered auscultation of the brachial artery, and forearm vascular conductance (FVC) was calculated from the ratio of forearm blood flow and mean arterial blood pressure. The units for FVC are ml/100ml tissue/min/100 mmHg, however for clarity these units will be reported as FVC units. Since local heating of the forearm does not alter muscle blood flow, elevations in total forearm blood flow and FVC were due solely to elevations in forearm skin blood flow and forearm cutaneous vascular conductance, respectively. Hypothesis #4: Two intradermal microdialysis membranes were placed in dorsal forearm skin. Probes were placed a minimum of 3 cm apart and at the same location for both pre- and post-HDT trials. This technique involved placing a small (200 µm outer diameter, 10 mm length) sterile, semi-permeable membrane intradermally using a 25-gauge needle. Both microdialysis membranes were perfused with Ringer's solution at a rate of 2 µl/min via an infusion pump. The protocol commenced once skin blood flow returned to normal levels after needle insertion trauma (~60-120 minutes). Chambers having a small window (10 x 5 mm, i.e., surface area of 0.5 cm 2 ) were positioned over each membrane to measure sweat rate by the ventilated capsule method using compressed nitrogen as the perfusion gas. The gas was delivered at a rate of 150 ml/min. Location of capsule placement was aided through the use of markings on the tubing that indicated the center of the membrane portion of the microdialysis probe. Humidity of the effluent gas was measured via a humidity/temperature probe that was positioned one meter from the capsule on the skin. The humidity/temperature probe connected to a humidity data processor that calculated absolute humidity from the measurement of relative humidity and temperature. Local skin temperature around the microdialysis membranes was maintained at 40 degrees Celsius through the use of a lamp and a thermocouple. Sweat gland function was assessed by perfusing nine doses (1x10 -6 to 2 M) of acetylcholine through the microdialysis membranes. Each dose of acetylcholine was administered for 5 minutes, while sweat rate over the microdialysis membranes was continuously recorded. Sweat rate during the final minute of each 5-minute period was averaged and used for the statistical analysis. Sweat rates from both sites were averaged and are reported as a single value for each dose of acetylcholine. Following the acetylcholine challenge, with the sites continuing to be perfused with the highest dose of acetylcholine, the number of activated sweat glands was assessed in triplicate over the microdialysis membranes using the starch-iodine technique. Hypothesis #5: For this component ten subjects (nine male and one female) participated in the study. Throughout HDT bed rest subjects exercised at 75 percent of pre-bed rest heart rate maximum for 90 minutes per day on a supine cycle ergometer. Heart rate was monitored during these exercise sessions. Immediately prior to beginning HDT bed rest and on the 13 th day of bed rest, thermoregulatory responses were assessed throughout 25 minutes of supine cycle ergometry exercise tested in a room held at 28 degrees Celsius. The same absolute workload was performed during both the pre- and post-HDT testing. Upon entering the laboratory, each subject was instrumented with six thermocouples placed on the skin. The weighted average of the six thermocouples was used for the measurement of mean skin temperature (T sk ). Internal temperature (T core ) was measured by thermister or telemetry pill. A thermister probe measured esophageal temperature and was inserted through the nose to a distance equal to one-quarter of the subject's height. A telemetry pill was used in a subject who refused to insert esophageal temperature probe, and was swallowed two hours before the thermoregulatory response test. Heart rate (HR) was monitored using the ECG. Arterial blood pressure was obtained under both conditions via R-wave triggered auscultation of the brachial artery. Mean arterial pressure (MAP) was calculated as one-third of pulse pressure plus diastolic pressure. Skin blood flow (SkBF) on the chest and forearm was measured by laser-Doppler flowmetry, and sweat rate (SR) on the forearm by the ventilated capsule method using compressed nitrogen as the perfusion gas delivered at a rate of 500 ml/min. Cutaneous vascular conductance (CVC) was indexed from the ratio of SkBF to MAP. CVC was normalized relative to maximum CVC obtained via local heating of the skin to 42 degrees Celsius for 30 minutes. Humidity of the effluent gas was measured via a humidity-temperature probe that was positioned one meter from the capsule on the skin. The absolute humidity was calculated from the measurement of relative humidity and room temperature.
results: These data were obtained to identify the effects of 14 days HDT bed rest on the control of the microcirculation and sweating. Moreover, the effects of aerobic exercise training during bed rest on the hypothesized impaired responses, as well as on thermoregulatory responses during exercise, were assessed. The primary findings were as follows: a) HDT bed rest does not alter cutaneous post-synaptic vasoconstrictor responsiveness; b) vasoconstriction associated with the venoarteriolar response is impaired following HDT bed rest regardless of whether the subject exercises during bed rest; c) maximal cutaneous vasodilator and sweating responses are impaired following HDT bed rest, however these responses are preserved if the subject exercises during bed rest; and d) aerobic exercise during bed rest preserves thermoregulatory responses previously shown to be attenuated after HDT bed rest. Hypothesis #1: The mean goodness of fit (R 2 ) of the dose-response model was high both pre- (exercise: 0.94 ± 0.02 and non-exercise: 0.95 ± 0.03) and post- (exercise: 0.93 ± 0.02 and non-exercise: 0.95 ± 0.03) HDT bed rest. Neither HDT bed rest alone nor exercise during HDT bed rest had an effect on the concentration of norepinephrine (NE) that caused 50% of maximal cutaneous vasoconstriction (i.e., EC 50 , HDT bed rest: P > 0.30; exercise during HDT bed rest: P > 0.15). Similarly, maximal and minimal responses from the dose-response model were not altered by HDT bed rest (maximal: P > 0.30 and minimal: P > 0.40) or exercise during HDT bed rest (maximal: P > 0.50 and minimal: P > 0.15). Finally, no interactions were observed between main factors of the ANOVA for any of the dose-response variables. Hypothesis #2: The magnitude of forearm vasoconstriction associated with the venoarteriolar response was not affected by HDT bed rest regardless of the group (pre- HDT bed rest non-exercise: 53.1 ± 4.2 percent; post- HDT bed rest non-exercise: 52.2 ± 4.5%; pre- HDT bed rest exercise: 56.6 ± 2.1 percent; post- HDT bed rest exercise: 52.7 ± 3.0 percent). Probability values from the ANOVA were P > 0.30 for HDT bed rest, P > 0.70 for exercise during HDT bed rest, and P > 0.50 for the interaction found between pre/post- HDT bed rest and the exercise/non-exercise main factors. In contrast, cutaneous vasoconstriction of the lower leg due to the venoarteriolar response was significantly attenuated following HDT bed rest in both groups (pre- HDT bed rest non-exercise: 51.0 ± 5.0 percent; post- HDT bed rest non-exercise: 43.0 ± 6.6 percent; pre- HDT bed rest exercise: 48.4 ± 7.4 percent; post- HDT bed rest exercise: 36.4 ± 8.5 percent). Probability values from the ANOVA were P 0.50 for exercise during HDT bed rest, and P > 0.60 for the interaction between pre/post- HDT bed rest and the exercise/non-exercise main factors. Hypothesis #3: In the non-exercise group both maximal FVC (21.5 ± 1.3 to 18.7 ± 1.7 FVC units; P=0.01) and the change in FVC with local heating (i.e., ”FVC; 18.1 ± 1.2 to 15.9 ± 1.7; P=0.01) were significantly attenuated following HDT bed rest. In contrast, in the exercise group, these responses were not significantly different between pre- and post-HDT trials when reported either as maximal FVC (21.8 ± 2.0 to 21.4 ± 2.5 FVC units; P=0.39) or as the increase in FVC due to local heating (17.7 ± 1.9 to 18.4 ± 2.4; P=0.32). Hypothesis #4: In both the exercise and non-exercise groups the EC50 of the sweating response was unaffected by HDT bed rest. However, maximal stimulated sweat rate for the non-exercise group was significantly attenuated following HDT bed rest (0.63 ± 0.06 to 0.42 ± 0.03 mg/cm 2 /min; P=0.001), while no significant difference was observed for the exercise group (0.81 ± 0.15 to 0.77 ± 0.10; P=0.31). Regardless of the group, HDT bed rest did not significantly change the number of activated sweat glands during administration of the highest dose of acetylcholine. Hypothesis #5: Exercise during HDT exposure preserved VO2 max, blood volume, and plasma volume relative to pre-HDT bed rest levels. Internal temperature prior to exercise and at the end of exercise was not different between pre- and post-HDT trial. The onset of sweating and maximal sweat rate during exercise were no different between pre- and post- HDT trials. Moreover, cutaneous vascular responses were also preserved by exercise throughout HDT. Taken together, these data indicate that 90 minutes of exercise throughout HDT bed rest preserves thermoregulatory responses.

objectives: The importance of nutrition in the adaptation of man to weightlessness was recognized early in the United States manned space flight program. Investigators were concerned with the possibility that exposure to microgravity would impose high demands on micronutrients and would therefore lead to nutritional deficiencies. Experiments conducted during the Gemini program led space life scientists to believe that some physiological changes associated with space flight were related to nutritional imbalances. Numerous studies documented that imbalances between bone formation and resorption can lead to clinical disorders such as increased calcium in the blood and urine and osteoporosis. approach: Food analysis: All foods were analyzed for nitrogen, fat, carbohydrates, crude fiber, phosphorus, iron, sodium, potassium, and magnesium content. Some composite Apollo menus were analyzed for water- and fat-soluble vitamins. Dietetics: The menus used by the Apollo astronauts were formulated from flight-qualified Apollo foods in combinations that complied with the personal preferences of the crewmen and that met the Recommended Daily Allowance (RDA) requirement. The menus were primarily composed of dehydrated foods that were reconstituted before eating. The foods were consumed in a prearranged sequence, but could be supplemented by additional items. Nutrient intake measurements: Each meal was composed of a predetermined number of food items. Records were kept on any foods omitted or incompletely consumed. Snack items consumed that were not part of the programmed meals were also recorded in the flight logs. All food residue and unopened food packages were returned from the missions. Residue was weighed to provide more precise information on inflight nutrient intake. For the Apollo 17 mission, a five-day metabolic balance study was performed approximately two months before the mission by using the flight menus and collecting urine and fecal wastes. Fecal measurements: Fecal samples were returned from all Apollo flights and analyzed for a variety of constituents either by nuclear activation analysis or by wet chemistry techniques. Metabolic balance: A partial metabolic balance study was performed on the Apollo 16 crew. Urine and fecal samples were returned for analysis and the data was compared to the inflight nutrient intake data. For a more detailed metabolic balance study in conjunction with Apollo 17, accurate measurements of fluid intake and output were performed approximately two months before the mission. A five-day food compatibility / metabolic study was performed in which three Apollo 17 prime and backup crewmembers consumed their flight foods and participated in metabolic collections. The study was designed to obtain baseline data on the excretory levels of electrolytes and nitrogen in response to the Apollo 17 flight menu. One duplicate of each meal was analyzed in addition to the residue from the meal that was consumed in order to measure nutrient intake and output. Every food item consumed inflight was derived from a group of foods that had been analyzed for nutritional content. All deviations from programmed food intake were logged and reported. Inflight water consumption was measured using a beverage dispenser. All urine was collected, measured, sampled and returned for analysis. Inflight urine samples were collected by means of a biomedical urine sampling system (BUSS). Each BUSS was marked with the name of the crewmember and the time of collection. Following each collection period, the urine pool was thoroughly mixed before a sample was taken. The urine samples represented a 24-hour void and were subsequently analyzed for electrolytes, nitrogen, and creatine. Complete stool collections were also performed. Body density was calculated from body volume and weight. Density was used to calculate the percentage of fat. Changes in calculated lean body mass and total body fat were converted into caloric equivalents. Total body water was measured using a potassium-42 dilution technique.

RESULTS: Food analysis: The overall nutritional analysis indicated that the typical Apollo diet was composed of protein, fat, carbohydrates, fiber, and minerals in the following percentages (percent of dry weight): 18.0, 17.0, 61.0, 1.0, and 3.0, respectively. The results of the vitamin analysis indicated that the Apollo diet provided an excess of some vitamins (A, E, C, B12, B6, and riboflavin) and marginal amounts of others (nicotinate, pantothenate, thiamine, and folic acid). Nutrient intake measurements: The daily intake (grams) of protein, fat, carbohydrates, and fiber averaged over all Apollo missions was 76, 61, 269, and 5.4, respectively. The daily intake (milligrams) of calcium, phosphorus, sodium, and potassium averaged over all Apollo missions was 773.0, 1121.0, 3666.0, 2183.0, respectively. The average energy intake (kcal/day) for the Commander (CDR), Command Module Pilot (CMP), and Lunar Module Pilot (LMP) was 2403, 1565, and 2366, respectively. The average daily inflight potassium intake for the CMD was 113.6 milliequivalents (mEq). title: Aerobic Capacity (Flight Analog)
variables: Perception of effort, Borg Rating of Perceived Exertion (RPE)
archive_status: Data preservation is complete.  All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: To assess cardiovascular functional performance, maximum aerobic capacity was measured in each subject before and after bed rest using a graded cycle exercise test. The peak maximal test was performed on an upright cycle ergometer on each bed rest subject to assess cardiovascular health and aerobic fitness.
approach: Maximal aerobic capacity was assessed in each subject before and immediately after bed rest using a graded cycle exercise test. Subjects pedaled a cycle ergometer at increasing work loads of 50-350 Watts while heart rate, blood pressure, and oxygen uptake were monitored. Peak cycle exercise tests were conducted prior to bed rest and following bed rest. The test measured metabolic gas analysis parameters, blood pressure, workloads, and perception of effort (RPE). From these measures peak heart rate (HR) and peak oxygen consumption (VO2) were established. Subject began with a very low workload as a warm-up. The workload was gradually increased in an incremental manner until maximal exertion was reached. The protocol was appropriately configured to the body size and fitness level of the subject such that maximal exercise was reached in approximately 8-15 minutes. The first stage lasted three minutes and was set at a light workload. Each subsequent stage was one minute in duration and the workload was gradually increased until the subject reached peak effort. During the exercise test the subject was asked to wear a nose clip and breathe in and out of a special mouthpiece. The expired air was analyzed for various fitness related parameters. The upright cycle ergometer test was performed at each session to measure HR and VO2. Blood pressure, workloads, and RPE were also measured.
results: Results from the Artificial Gravity (AG) Pilot Study indicate that bed rest decreased peak VO2 in the control group while the AG treatment attenuated this drop. The mean peak VO2 after bed rest was 12% lower than pre-bed rest in the control group but was 6% lower in the treatment group. When these results were expressed relative to body weight, there tended to be a group by bed rest interaction in peak VO2. Tabular results are available for the public. .

title: Cardiovascular Conditioning
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: The cardiovascular system was the first major body system to show physiologic change following space flight. As a
approach: One astronaut from each of the Gemini 5 (8-day) and Gemini 7 (14-day) missions participated as a test subject, described here as subjects A and B respectively. The remaining astronaut aboard each respective flight acted as a control subject (subjects C and D.) In-flight, the two test subjects wore cuff devices designed to maintain venous pressure in the lower extremities. The experiment equipment consisted of a pneumatic cycling system and a pair of pneumatic cuffs. The cycling system alternately inflated and deflated the cuffs that were form-fitted to the proximal thigh region of the test subjects. The bladder portion of each cuff was positioned on the dorsomedial aspect of each thigh. Upon reaching orbit, the cuffs were automatically pressurized to 80 mm Hg for 2 minutes out of every 6 minutes. The system was capable of continuous operation during flight, but could be switched off for sleep periods if required. The experiment imposed no operational requirement other than activation of the device after reaching orbit and deactivation prior to reentry. The experiment lasted for the first 4 days of the Gemini 5 mission and for the first 13.5 days of the Gemini 7 mission. During the Gemini 5 mission, the cuffs were to operate continuously for the full 8-day mission. After 4 days, however, the pneumatic programmer stopped cycling when the oxygen pressure in the storage vessel dropped below operational levels. Before and after flight, all Gemini Program astronauts, including the subjects of this experiment, were given a series of tilt table tests to measure orthostatic intolerance. Parameters measured included heart rate, blood pressure, pulse pressure, and leg volume. Leg volume was determined by the strain-gage technique. Changes in blood volume, plasma volume, and red cell mass were determined using radioactive isotope (125I, 51Cr) techniques. Body mass was also measured. The tilt table test protocol was as follows: each subject lay supine for 5 minutes. The subject was then elevated into a +70 degree, head-up tilt position for 15 minutes. Leg volume was measured for the duration of the 15-minute tilt. After the tilt was completed, the subject was again supine for 5 minutes. Leg volume was measured for an additional 5 minutes after the tilt was completed. Heart rate and blood pressure were monitored continuously throughout the 25-minute test. All subjects completed three preflight tilt-table tests. The astronauts of Gemini 5 completed 6 post flight tilt table tests, while the astronauts of Gemini 7 completed 4 post flight tilt table tests. Post flight tests for the Gemini 5 astronauts were conducted between 2-104 hours after recovery. The Gemini 7 astronauts were measured between 2-56 hours after recovery.
results: , it was extensively investigated by various means during the Gemini missions. The purpose of the Cardiovascular Conditioning (M001) experiment was to determine the effectiveness of the pneumatic cuff technique in preventing orthostatic intolerance to a 1-G stress after space flights lasting up to 14-days. Water immersion studies in support of this experiment indicated that pneumatic leg cuffs alone, when inflated to 70 to 75 mm Hg for 2 out of every 6 minutes, provided protection against cardiovascular deconditioning. Four healthy, male subjects were immersed in water up to neck level for six hours on two separate occasions, two days apart. Before and after each period of water immersion, the heart rate of each subject was measured during a tilt table test. Data analysis indicated that the first water immersion period, during which the subjects' did not wear leg cuffs, resulted in cardiovascular deconditioning. This was evidenced by cardioacceleration in excess of that observed during the tilt-table test prior to water immersion. Also, syncope occurred in two of the four subjects. Tilt table responses following the second period of immersion, during which leg cuffs were utilized, revealed that a definite protective effect was achieved. Cardioacceleration was less pronounced, and no syncope occurred. The physiological mechanisms responsible for the observed efficacy of the cuff technique were not completely understood. It was hypothesized that the cuffs prevented thoracic blood volume overload, thus resulting in the Henry-Gauer response with its resultant diuresis and decreased effective circulating blood volumes. It was also postulated that the cuffs induced an intermittent artificial hydrostatic gradient (by increasing venous pressure distal to the cuffs during inflation) across the walls of the leg veins, mimicking the deterioration of normal venomotor reflexes. It was theorized that this action would decrease the pooling of blood in the lower extremities and increase the effective circulating blood volume upon return to a 1-G environment following weightlessness or its simulation.
