archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: The negative effects of space flight on cardiovascular health has been demonstrated and documented over many years. One of the body’s normal vascular repair mechanisms is the recruitment of adult stem cells from bone marrow to integrate into the vasculature. These recruited cells are involved in blood vessel wall repair and the formation of new blood vessels. This proposal seeks to study the effect of microgravity on adult stem cells. Of specific interest is how well these cells can differentiate into vascular cells under altered environmental conditions such as microgravity, and how well these cells function as healthy vascular cells once differentiated. Differentiation studies using a bioreactor will be conducted to expose the cells to microgravity conditions. Once differentiated, the cells will be exposed to several stimulatory environments that will demonstrate their functional ability. Molecular biology techniques, such as gene expression studies, will elucidate the effect of microgravity on these cells. Studying adult stem cells is a means towards the goal to develop countermeasures for the negative effects of space flight on vascular health. This proposal addresses one of NASA's research interest, specifically, studies of the effect of gravity and the space environment on cellular and molecular processes. In this proposal, the cellular and molecular processes under investigation are stem cell differentiation and the corresponding molecular changes the stem cells undergo.
approach: To achieve our goal, we have established 2 specific aims, briefly, 1) Differentiate circulating stem cells into vascular endothelial (EC) and smooth muscle cells (SMC) under conditions of microgravity and normal gravity; 2) Assess the functional potential of the microgravity exposed differentiated cells. Our approach to achieving these goals involves first isolating blood derived stem cells, then culture under microgravity conditions in a rotating wall vessel bioreactor or static (normal gravity) in tissue culture polystyrene (TCPS) plates. Following dynamic and static culture, the cells are assessed for differentiation. Our assessments include both protein and gene expression changes, using western blot analysis and real-time quantitative polymerase chain reaction (rt-PCR), respectively. We are interested in the loss of stem cell protein and gene expression and upregulation of endothelial and smooth muscle cell protein and gene expression. For our second aim, our goal is to assess the changes in functional capacity of the differentiated cells, particularly the changes in function as a
results: of microgravity. To assess SMC function, we proposed to evaluate the ability of the differentiated cells to respond to contractile stimulation, migration, secrete extracellular matrix proteins, and modulate between synthetic and proliferative phenotypes. Our approach involves culture under stimulatory conditions where appropriate and assessments of SMC functions can be made. For endothelial cell functional analysis, we are interested in assessing the production and secretion of antithrombogenic factors, nitric oxide (NO) and prostacyclin (PGI2) by the differentiated endothelial cells. In addition, our approach involves assessing the hemocompatibility of the cells in terms of clotting and platelet activation when exposed to whole blood from human subjects. RESULTS: 1. Goal: Optimizing bioreactor and experimental set-up and methodology with Human Umbilical Vein Endothelial Cells (HUVECs) The experimental set-up we proposed using a commercially available rotary cell culture system (RCCS) bioreactor (Synthecon) was optimized using HUVEC cells. Our goal was to optimize various bioreactor/experimental parameters such as microcarrier bead handling and protein coating, cell seeding density and culture parameters, bioreactor rotational speed, culture maintenance and sample extraction from bioreactor chambers, as well as overall training within the experimental system. Early project challenges such as low cell adhesion on microcarrier beads and cell detachment under dynamic conditions in the rotating wall vessel (RWV) were eventually overcome by changing our experimental design. Our results show successful cell attachment and faster proliferation of HUVECs under microgravity than under static conditions. 2. Goal: Isolation and culture of human endothelial progenitor cells and differentiation into endothelial cells Once our bioreactor and experimental setup was optimized, we extended our work to the target cell population that is the focus of this work, human endothelial progenitor cells (EPC) derived from circulating blood. The human EPCs are a rare population of stem/progenitor cells that are isolated from the peripheral mononuclear cell (PBMNC) fraction of whole blood. PBMNCs were isolated from human blood obtained from donors as per Institutional Review Board (IRB) guidelines. Circulating progenitor cells contained within the PBMNC fraction of whole blood were differentiated into endothelial-like cells, as confirmed by the formation of colonies (within 2-6 weeks) with EC specific ‘cobble-stone’ morphology, and positive expression of EC specific proteins. 3. Goal: Study the effect of microgravity on the differentiated endothelial cells in culture We assessed the ability of these cells to adapt to simulated microgravity conditions after short term culture and expansion. More specifically, the functionality of the differentiated ECs following exposure to simulated microgravity assessed conditions such as proliferation, release of soluble factors, changes in gene expression, and anti-thrombogenic potential was investigated. The results of the present study demonstrated that the populations of human blood EPC derived ECs when exposed to simulated microgravity proliferate faster, release higher amounts of soluble NO and lower amounts of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6, when compared to their normal gravity cultured controls. This can be possibly attributed to the ability of the cells to sense simulated microgravity as a “stressful” condition and adapt by upregulating gene expression of hsp70. However these secretory as well as proliferative functions had no effect on the anti-thrombogenic functions of these cells. Their anti-coagulative and anti-thrombogenic ability as assessed by both upregulation of tPA as well their ability to delay plasma clotting, were impaired upon exposure to simulated microgravity. This study is the first step towards understanding the ability of these repair cells to regulate clotting mechanisms and cardiovascular health in space. Further studies to assess alternate and synergistic mechanisms involved in regulation of cardiovascular health as well as inflammatory dysfunction under microgravity are required to develop possible cell based countermeasures to prevent cardiovascular deconditioning due to space travel. 4. Goal: Expand to include porcine EPCs to further study the effect of microgravity on differentiation of the blood derived EPCs. Due to the initial challenges we had faced with differentiating as well exposing human blood derived progenitor cells during the pre- differentation stage under simulated microgravity, our goal was to extend our work to an alternative cell source, porcine EPCs. Our lab has previously obtained porcine PBMNCs (under University of Florida IACUC approval) and differentiated these into cells with endothelial cell phenotype (PE-like cells). Circulating progenitor cells contained within the PBMNC fraction of porcine whole blood were exposed to simulated microgravity, using a RWV bioreactor. After exposing the circulating progenitor cells to 6, 12, and 18h of simulated microgravity, the cells were then cultured on fibronectin coated TCP under static conditions and their ability to differentiate into endothelial cells was assessed by the formation of colonies with EC specific ‘cobble-stone’ morphology and confirmed by immunohistocytochemical staining for CD31 as well as eNOS. Our results showed that longer exposure to simulated microgravity delayed the onset of differentiation of EPCs to PE-like cells. Clotting behavior assessment showed that following the clotting rate for 6h-µg exposed cells are the clotting times for the 12h and 18h-µg exposed cells. Normal gravity cultured cells clotted the next while the last to clot was the plasma exposed to the EC control cells. Similarly, the whole blood clotting kinetics showed that the kinetic profile of whole blood when incubated with PE-like cells differentiated after exposure to simulated microgravity, showed faster clot formation than normal gravity controls. However, longer exposure times showed greater inhibition of clotting. Collectively, the data shows that within the 3 time points of µg exposure, the longer exposure times showed greater inhibition of clotting, which may be attributed to the increased ability to release soluble anti-thrombogenic factors, NO and PGE2. While both the migration and proliferation of cells were inhibited by microgravity exposure, prolonged exposure of EPCs to microgravity resulted in decrease in the migration abilities of EPC derived EC and the proliferative capacity of the ECs seemed to recover on longer time of exposure. The initial decrease and subsequent increase in release of soluble factors such as NO and PGE2 reaffirmed the possibility of recovery mechanisms being involved on prolonged exposure to weightlessness. Finally the assessment of whole blood and plasma clotting, indicated that microgravity pre exposure at the progenitor stage caused inhibition, in the ability of PE-like cells to delay blood or plasma clotting while this effect was again nulled with increase in time of exposure of EPCs to microgravity. This data collectively provides some insight into the role of short term exposure to low shear stress environment due to simulated microgravity, on cardiovascular deconditioning during space travel.

title: Skylab Oral Health Studies
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Oral health is important to effective work in space, and is also crucial because the oral region serves as an entry point for pathogenic agents, acts as a reservoir for infectious microorganisms, and plays a role in cross contamination and disease transmission. Oral health studies were performed during all Skylab missions. Three general areas were studied: clinical dentistry, provisions for in-flight care, and research dedicated to the identification of potential oral problems in long-duration missions. The emphasis of clinical dentistry was on the prevention of dental disease and included pre- and postflight restorative procedures, measurements of oral health indices, and in-flight provisions for emergency dental care. Inflight care dealt with the risks of an unanticipated problem, which could impair effective work. This risk was computed at 0.92 % for a 3-man 28-day mission, was based on studies of dental experiences in other isolated environments and on a 3-year study of the astronaut population. The two most likely problems were a painful tooth due to pulpitis or severe, localized gingival inflammation. Dental caries was not considered a problem in missions up to 3-month duration, because of the high level of oral health of all crewmen and the frequent dental evaluations they received. Oral research was conducted on Skylab by monitoring the crew to assess the effects of the space flight on the population dynamics of oral microflora, the secretion of specific salivary components, and clinical changes in oral health. Laboratory intraoral changes can precede clinical manifestations of acute and chronic infectious disease. Clinically detectable alterations of oral tissue can identify changes caused by local and/or systemic disorders of microbial and nonmicrobial origin. Changes in saliva composition and volume may also reflect local and systemic disorders. One objective of the Skylab oral health studies concerned metabolic profiles that were established to discern microorganisms associated with oral disease conditions. In addition, effects of space flight on salivary electrolyte levels were determined. A practical and reproducible method was needed to definitively identify closely related strains of oral microorganisms associated with dental disease. High resolution gas liquid chromatographic (GLC) techniques provided a means of effectively establishing metabolic profiles between physiologically and serologically closely related, potentially pathogenic oral microbes. Emphasis was placed on the definitive characterization of Streptococcus mutans since this microorganism has been directly implicated in the etiology of dental caries and indirectly associated with periodontal disease. A high prevalence of S. mutans in the Skylab crew provided the interest for discerning the different strains of this organism. Salivary electrolytes were also examined in this study. Changes in the concentration of such electrolytes may be due to emotional stress, drugs, drug toxicity, metabolic changes, and systemic disease. If the mineral imbalance revealed by the urinary and fecal elevations in specific electrolytes during the Skylab missions is also evidenced by electrolyte changes in saliva, prolonged spaceflight might have an impact on the buffer systems in saliva and upset a basic homeostatic mechanism in the oral cavity. Thus, this study had two specific aims: 1. Adapt and/or develop analytical chemical procedures to establish metabolic profiles for fingerprinting microorganisms associated with oral disease conditions. 2. Assess the effects of the 28, 59, and 84-day Skylab missions on the salivary electrolytes.
approach: All Skylab crewmembers took utmost oral care during the preflight timeframe. Oral hygiene procedures consisted of brushing the teeth two minutes twice a day and flossing once a day. Regular topical applications of stannous fluoride were provided to all crewmen up to six months before launch; oral exams and evaluation were performed every six months. Because of the risks of inflammation to the dental pulp, no dental restorations were provided during the last 90 days prior to flight. Complete oral Panorex radiographs were made of each crewman prior to his mission. All crewmen were placed on a space food diet about 21 days before flight. The backup crewmen continued on the space diet until launch and prime crewmen until 18 days after recovery. Prime and backup crews of all Skylab missions received two days of training in pertinent dental procedures to be able to treat the most likely dental problems that might arise. Training included lectures, demonstrations, and supervised clinical procedures, which were as complex as tooth removal, and were performed on volunteer patients. Instruments and medications were part of the In-flight Medical Support System-Dental, which also included a manual with line drawings of complete intraoral radiographs of each crewman and integrated, illustrated diagnostic, and treatment procedures. The crew also had air-to-ground communication access with a dentist and/or surgeon. The eighteen prime and backup crewmembers of the three Skylab missions were monitored for quantitative changes in oral microorganisms, saliva partitions considered potentially important to oral health, and alterations in clinical indices of oral health and preexisting dental disease. Over 100 saliva samples were analyzed. All samples were collected before oral hygiene and breakfast. To produce stimulated saliva, crewmembers chewed sterile paraffin and spat into a sterile cup, measuring and recording the time each took to produce a 5-ml volume. This time was used to calculate the saliva flow rate. The samples were grouped into three categories, which were preflight/conventional diet, preflight/space diet and postflight/space diet. High resolution GLC and pyrolysis-GLC procedures were used to obtain distinctive metabolic profiles of closely related genera, species and strains of oral microbes associated with dental caries and periodontal disease, with emphasis on serologically unique strains of S. mutans . Uninoculated culture media and pure cultures of known strains of the same and different serotypes of cariogenic and noncariogenic S. mutans , Streptococcus sanguis , and Lactobacillus fermenti , along with uncharacterized strains of S. mutans isolated from the crew were analyzed. Microbiological Assessments: Oral specimens were collected from the crewmembers weekly or semiweekly from three intraoral sites from 31 days preflight to 18 days postflight for Skylab 2, from 51 days preflight to 20 days postflight for Skylab 3, and from 57 days preflight to 17 days postflight for Skylab 4. All collections took place between 7 and 8 am, before oral hygiene procedures or breakfast. The specimens included dental plaque, crevicular fluid (exudates absorbed from the gingival sulcus area), and stimulated saliva (all sites associated with the development of dental caries, periodontal disease, and alveolar bone loss). Serial 10-fold dilutions of each specimen were plated onto a variety of bacteriologic media for the enumeration of up to 17 microbial categories including mycoplasma and yeast. Duplicate platings were incubated at 37ºC either aerobically or anaerobically. In addition to microbial assessments, stimulated saliva was used to determine total protein, secretory Immunoglobulin A, and lysozyme.
results: All preflight dental conditions were resolved before launch. The radiographs revealed two asymptomatic, previously unrecognized areas of disease conditions about the apex of the teeth of two crewmen, which were successfully resolved. During the last nine months prior to the Skylab missions, six crewmen required treatment for dental problems, which were other than routine replacement of restorations and dental prophylaxes. All dental problems were resolved successfully with no recurrence. No in-flight dental problems requiring the use of the Inflight Medical Support System-Dental occurred during the Skylab 2, 3, and 4 missions. Laboratory and clinical parameters related to dental injury were evaluated in order to monitor mission-related effects on oral health. The most distinctive changes observed concerned microbial and IgA concentrations, and analysis of calculus and gingival inflammation. Increased counts of specific anaerobic and streptococcal components, primarily of the saliva and dental plaque microflora were observed, and were more diet related than flight related. An elevation in secretory IgA occurred with a reduction of salivary lysozyme. Also observed was an incidence of increased increments of dental calculus and gingival inflammation, especially on Skylab 2. There was less increase in the scores of plaque, calculus, and inflammation in the Skylab 3 mission despite this mission being 59 days in length rather than 28 days. The lower scores are believed to be due to better oral health status of the prime crew of the Skylab 3 mission. Thus, the preexisting state of dental health was believed to be responsible for the clinical changes rather than any adverse space-flight effect. These studies show that the better the preflight oral health status, the lesser the flight-related changes on oral health. The high resolution GLC techniques on oral microbes disclosed pronounced metabolic distinctions between two physiologically related genera of the same bacterial family ( Streptococcus and Lactobacillus of the family Lactobacillaceae), and between two closely related oral species of the same genus ( S. mutans and S. sanguis ). Differences between and within serologically unique strains of the same species of S. mutans were detected, but were less striking than between inter-species profiles. Overall, the GLC procedures provided a practical and reproducible means of obtaining metabolic markers for identifying closely related strains of pathogenic oral microbes unattainable by conventional techniques. The major pathogenic microorganisms present in crew specimens the morning of launch of Skylab 2 included Klebsiella pneumoniae from the gargle of one crewmember, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus from the gargle of another crewmember. None of these species created any problems during and after flight, although the S. aureus did spread to the mouth and scalp of the crewmember during the mission. From the gingival fluid, counts of bacteroides, veillonella, fusobacteria and leptotrichia increased significantly in all crewmembers after the initiation of the space diet at 18 days before launch. Similar increases were noted for species similar to S. mutans and Neisseria sp. Counts of S. mutans , which were relatively high in the prime crew at the onset of the study, appeared to increase during the recovery period, but this was not statistically significant. In stimulated saliva, significant increases occurred in mycoplasma, streptococci and bacteroides. Enteric bacilli, which were unusually numerous in saliva at the onset, declined during the investigative period. These enterics included isolations of Pseudomonas aeruginosa , Klebsiella pneumoniae , Enterobacter cloacae , and Achromobacter lwoffi . Changes in microorganisms in the dental plaque were within the expected range. However, bacteroides, veillonella and lactobacilli increased significantly after the initiation of the space diet. The conclusion drawn from Skylab 2 was that extensive microbial sampling of the crew before and after the mission revealed no changes of medical significance. The most distinctive changes noted from Skylab 3 assessments of gingival fluid, dental plaque and saliva include elevations in counts of specific anaerobic components of the gingival fluid microflora, increased counts of streptococci, enteric bacilli, and specific anaerobic components of saliva, and increased numbers of streptococci, lactobacilli, and leptotrichia in dental plaque. Except for the post-flight increases of enteric bacilli, the diet was believed responsible for the oral microbial changes. Preflight regular diet, versus preflight space diet data were compared, along with postflight space diet data. Specifically, increases were noted in Fusobacteria, Bacteroides melaninogenicus , and leptotrichia in gingival fluid. Streptococcus salivarius , enterics, fusobacteria, veillonella, and leptotrichia were elevated in stimulated saliva, and S. mutans , lactobacilli, and leptotrichia were elevated in dental plaque. The microbial changes observed in Skylab 3, with few exceptions, were similar to those noted previously in the ground-based trial and the Skylab 2 mission. As in the prior studies, the changes occurred during the preflight period after the incorporation of the space diet. The changes detected in Skylab 4 were very similar to those observed in the ground-based study and the two previous Skylab missions. Most of the microbial changes were diet-related rather than flight-related. This was shown by statistical comparisons of cumulative counts from the 18 crewmembers before and after the incorporation of space diets during preflight samplings. The most distinctive changes noted in Skylab 4 included increased counts of specific anaerobic and streptococcal components, primarily of the saliva and dental plaque microflora. The most significant finding from Skylab 4 and previous Skylab missions was the decrease of intraoral changes. Most of the chemical composition changes in saliva were minimal. There was an increase in saliva flow rate that was observed with the space diet. Investigators hypothesized that this increase could have been caused by flight-associated anxiety since stress can affect salivary flow rate. The total salivary protein decreased in combined missions, although this finding was downplayed since it was significant in only one mission, the 59-day mission, and that corresponded with the increase in salivary flow rate. The changes in the saliva electrolytes were a decrease in sodium along with an increase in magnesium concentrations. The increase in magnesium was significant, but since its concentration was extremely low, it was probably not clinically meaningful. Investigators suggested that the sodium decrease might have stemmed from higher production of adrenocortical steroids, especially aldosterone, which was elevated in urine over each mission. The increase in IgA was the most prominent compositional change. This finding was explained as a possible response to a subclinical infection that could have spread among the crew during preflight activity. This result is similar to the 56-day land-based, simulated Skylab mission. No clinical problems were detected despite the rise in IgA. Lysozyme, which is 0.5% to 1% of the total protein, decreased in the middle of the preflight stage, and continued to decrease throughout the study. This result was unexpected, and investigators were not able to explain the cause. No changes were noted throughout the missions in saliva calcium, potassium, chloride, phosphate, albumen or IgG concentrations. The salivary electrolyte changes did not parallel the increased urinary electrolyte excretion observed during each mission. Thus, the indication here is that saliva does not play a decisive role in regulating the water and electrolyte balance of the body. The Skylab oral health studies results showed that the better the preflight oral health status, the lesser the flight-related changes on general oral health, such as occurrence of cavities, plaque and gingivitis. Most of the microbial changes were due to switching from conventional diets to space diets, and all Skylab mission data showed only a small effect of microbial intraoral changes. Chemical changes in saliva, such as protein and electrolyte levels were also minimal. Thus, the most significant aspect of the investigations was the relative nonexistence of health hazardous intraoral changes during Skylab missions.

title: Water Microbiological Monitoring
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Maintaining crew health during extended periods in space can be complicated by contamination of the general living environment. High standards for air, water, and radiation shielding quality have been established to ensure the continued health and safety of long duration crews. Water provided for crew consumption has either been launched from the ground or produced in flight by the recycling of humidity condensate. Water delivered from Earth can be tested for microbial contaminants before leaving the ground, but the water produced on orbit must be analyzed to determine its potability. The water must therefore be tested for the presence of microbial contamination, such as bacteria and fungi. In the past, this analysis has been done in Earth-based laboratories after returning to Earth. This investigation allowed water testing in-flight by the crew. The Water Microbiological Monitor (WMM) was one of several technology demonstrations planned for the NASA-Mir missions that were aimed at developing and testing in-flight, the sampling kits needed to support quality assurance for future space platforms. Having the capability to conduct the analysis during the mission gives both the crew and researchers feedback about the quality of the water in a timely manner. The experiment objectives were to quantify bacteria in potable and hygiene water in a space environment, characterize the microbial population of a reclaimed water system, and have a water microbiology analysis system ready for the International Space Station (ISS). Findings from this investigation will help in redesigning water-sampling hardware and microbial procedures for future routine application on the ISS. Successful completion of the proposed investigation was expected to validate technology for in-flight detection, quantitation and limited identification of waterborne bacteria. Lessons learned from this technology demonstration will be applied toward the development of the ISS Crew Health Care System (CheCS), which will ensure the maintenance of high water quality standards.
approach: Water samples were scheduled for collection and processed on flight days 15, 55, 85, 115, and 135 during the NASA 3, 4 and 5 missions. Samples were collected in Teflon bags, and known volumes were processed through a microbial capture device (MCD) contained in the Water Experiment Kit (WEK) using a syringe pump assembly. Each sample was processed through three MCDs, one with 10 ml of water, a second with 50 ml, and the third with 100 ml. A modified R3A nutrient broth growth medium was added to the MCD by syringe to cultivate microorganisms trapped on the filter. Mir sampling locations included the galley hot and cold water ports (reclaimed water) and the SVO-ZV port (ground-supplied water). MCDs were incubated at 25-35 degrees Celsius in an area of the spacecraft chosen by the crewmember to promote bacterial growth. Cultures were examined after 2 and 5 days of incubation for bacterial growth. Growth on the filters was matched to a bacterial colony density chart, and
results: were recorded in the flight data file and on the MCD using a "Sharpie" marker. Video and photographic documentation of the bacterial colonies were also performed. After examination on the second day, MCDs were returned to the incubator. After incubation was complete (at 5 days), samples were stowed at ambient temperature in a return kit and returned to Earth for complete analysis. Aerobic bacteria and fungi were identified using a Vitek Automated Identification System, Biolog Automated Identification System, or by classical means. Species not identified by these means were sent to a microbial reference laboratory for identification. RESULTS: This investigation verified the ability of the WMM to provide the means to detect and quantify bacteria in potable and hygiene water supplies during spaceflight. A modified formulation of growth medium, designed specifically for this investigation, allowed visualization of microbes trapped on the filter membrane of the MCD. Colony density results were converted to bacterial concentrations per unit of water. The results from the three sample volumes (10 ml, 50 ml, 100 ml) were inconclusive. Theoretically, the microbial count would be correspondingly higher in larger volumes of water. The results recorded by crewmembers did not hold to this pattern; in some cases, the MCDs processed with 10 ml of water had higher counts than the corresponding MCDs processed with 50 or 100 ml volumes. However, approximately half of the MCDs processed during the NASA 3 mission were processed incorrectly, as indicated by the presence of residual water in the MCDs. Proper processing required that all water be evacuated from the MCD before the growth medium was added. Failure to remove all of the water produced an aqueous suspension of organisms, which made accurate quantitation with this device impossible. Improved procedures and training techniques for subsequent missions seem to have corrected the incorrect processing of samples. None of the MCDs processed during the NASA 4 mission contained residual water. Human factors were another probable influence on the accuracy of results. The NASA 4 crewmember reported difficulty in interpreting what was or was not bacterial growth. Samples were not collected during the NASA 5 mission as scheduled, because the water experiment kit was lost when the Spektr module depressurized and was sealed off after Mir collided with a Progress resupply vehicle. This experiment also provided insight into the microbial characterization of a reclaimed water system. Analyses of the hot water samples indicated that the treatment train and final heating step of the Mir system was able to maintain the microbial quality of water from this source at standards well below the proposed US level of 100 colony forming units (CFU)/100 ml set for the International Space Station. The bacterial content of the cold reclaimed water supply did not exceed 125 CFU/100 ml; this count was within the Russian acceptability limit. The SVO-ZV ground-water supply contained the highest bacterial levels, but did not exceed 300 CFU/100 ml. Both the cold and SVO-ZV counts were slightly above the proposed US acceptability limit for the International Space Station, 100 CFU/100ml. The types of organisms recovered were consistent with those seen in previous analyses of Shuttle water and those seen in typical ground-water supplies. All water supplies were judged safe to drink. Although the full configuration of hardware needed to process the samples was somewhat awkward to handle, the goal of limited in-flight water analysis was achieved. Only minor problems were encountered with a small number of MCDs. The method of attaching Luer-lok fittings proved to be inadequate. These fittings occasionally became detached from the MCD during sample processing. A modification of this attachment method has been initiated.

title: Water Chemistry Monitoring
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: A major goal of the Advanced Life Support Program was to develop and validate technologies for regenerative life support systems for long-duration space missions (lunar, Mars, and orbital). One regenerative system needed to achieve this goal is the water recovery system to produce potable water from various wastewaters. During the course of the chamber project, four separate and distinct test phases with human test subjects were conducted, each progressively more complex in terms of the water recovery system. Recovered water was not used for human consumption during Phase I. However, water sampling was performed because the crewmember commented on a distinct iodine odor and taste. During Phase II, the main objective was to verify the performance of the integrated physicochemical air revitalization, water recovery, and thermal control systems for a four-person crew for 30 days. Similarly, life support systems specific for use on the International Space Station (ISS) were analyzed for the ability to provide a habitable environment for 60 days for four crewmembers during Phase IIa. Phase III was the first test to incorporate biological wastewater processing. The overall objective of this test was to conduct a 90-day test of integrated physicochemical and biological life support systems for air revitalization, water recovery, thermal control, and solid waste management.
approach: Water quality standards and monitoring requirements for the chamber studies were based on U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) standards and NASA Man-Systems Integration Standards (MSIS), a set of standards specifically developed by NASA for recycled water. For each chamber study, potable water samples were collected and analyzed during pretest, test, and post-test operations. Samples were collected using sampling equipment provided by the medical operations Water and Food Analytical Laboratory (WAFAL). This equipment consisted of benzalkonium chloride disinfectant wipes, cleaned Teflon® sample bottles, and labels. To collect a sample, the sample port was disinfected using a wipe. Next, approximately 250 ml of fluid was purged from the sample port and discarded. Then, 1000 ml of fluid was collected into a prelabeled sample bottle. After collection, samples were transferred from the test facility to WAFAL for chemical analysis and to the Johnson Space Center (JSC) Microbiology laboratory for microbial analysis. Chemical
results: only are reported in this experiment. Samples of recycled water collected from the potable water storage tanks during the chamber studies were analyzed for pH, turbidity, iodine, color, conductivity, anions, cations, trace metals, total organic carbon (TOC), volatile organics, semivolatile organics, alcohols, formaldehyde, amines, carboxylates, organic acids, diols (glycols), and urea. These samples were analyzed in an attempt to characterize at least 80% of the organic components of the recycled water. Other samples, such as the shower, galley, handwash sink, wastewater feed to the Water Recovery System (WRS), and effluent samples from many of the WRS subsystem components were also collected at various stages in the water treatment process. These samples were analyzed for a number of inorganic and organic parameters to verify system performance at various stages of water recovery and to collect data for future reference. Phase I: In preparation for Phase I, a system checkout pretest was conducted in April 1995 using a human metabolic simulator (HMS) in place of the human test subject. During this pretest, the HMS was sealed inside the airlock compartment of the VPGC while a crop of wheat was grown in the plant chamber. Two samples of plant atmospheric moisture (condensate) were collected from the condensate collection tanks located on the outside of the VPGC, one from each side of the chamber (sides A and B). For the actual Phase I test, a human test subject lived in the airlock compartment for 15 days while a crop of wheat grew in the plant chamber. Water recycling was limited to condensation of humidity from the air (human respired air, evaporation, plant transpiration). This recovered water, known as humidity condensate, was used to rehumidify the airlock and Variable Pressure Growth Chamber (VPGC), and was used to provide water for the plant nutrient solutions. Recovered water from humidity condensate was not used for human consumption during Phase 1. Potable water was not recycled during Phase I. Drinking water for the crewmember consisted of water from the NASA Johnson Space Center (JSC) public water supply that was deionized, filtered using a 0.2 µm microbial filter, and iodinated using a microbial check valve (MCV) to simulate spacecraft water supplies with iodine as the disinfectant. Two potable water samples were taken from the faucet at the sink in the airlock compartment of the VPGC, one before the start of the test and one at the end of the test. Four additional samples were collected in response to crewmember comments concerning a distinct iodine taste and odor. One of these samples was taken at the inlet of the MCV and another at the outlet of the MCV. Two more were taken at the sink outlet. Phase II: For Phases II and IIa, potable water was generated from the recycle of wastewater using physicochemical methods. A series of system verification tests were conducted before the start of Phase II. A viral challenge test was also conducted to verify the capability of the water recovery system to remove viruses and provide potable water that met the NASA MSIS. One water sample was collected for chemical analysis during the viral challenge test. Once samples were collected, the product water was discarded. No water produced from these tests was consumed. Three WRS donor mode tests and an integrated air revitalization system/water recovery system test were performed to validate the ability of the WRS to produce potable water from wastewater. During these tests, actual wastewater from human donors was processed. Although the final product water was not consumed by the donors, it was sampled and analyzed. The first donor mode test was initiated in March 1996 with a water recovery system consisting of a vapor compression and distillation subsystem (VCD), an ultrafiltration/ reverse osmosis subsystem (UF/RO), and an Aqueous Phase Catalytic Oxidation Subsystem (APCOS) for post treatment. On June 12, 1996, the actual Phase II test began with three of four potable water storage tanks filled with about 211 kg (465 lbs) of water from the JSC public water supply that had been deionized, filtered with a 0.2 µm microbial filter, and iodinated with a MCV. Samples were collected from the storage tanks once they were filled completely with recycled water processed from humidity condensate and wastewater from the shower, handwash, galley, laundry, and urinal. This normally occurred every two days. During the test, one of the four tanks would be "in use," one tank would be "on hold" awaiting completion of analytical tests, one tank would be a "spare," and one tank would be "filling" with processed water. The tanks were configured such that they were sequentially cycled from the fill, hold, spare, and use modes. Each tank also had the capability of being heated to disinfect, if required. Processing of wastewater for reuse began on day 1. The crew began using of one of the water tanks containing deionized water, while wastewater from hygiene activities was collected in one of two wastewater tanks. Crewmembers continued to consume deionized water during this period. Phase IIa: Similar to the Phase II WRS, the Phase IIa WRS was designed to accept wastewaters from the urinal, shower, handwash, and air revitalization system condensing heat exchangers (humidity condensate). In addition, the Phase IIa WRS was required to process simulated wastewaters expected on the ISS, such as condensate from animal experiments, wastewater from the Crew Health Care System (CHeCS) water quality monitors used for offline water quality monitoring, and condensate from the off-gassing of equipment and new materials introduced into the ISS environment. The amount of water to be processed was reduced from 211 kg (465 lbs) to 52 kg (115 lbs) to reflect the water usage rates expected. For process control, an in-line process control water quality monitor (PCWQM) was added for continuous monitoring of the processed water's conductivity, TOC, and iodine (I2) levels. If any of the three parameters were out of specification, the product water was rejected and returned to the inlet of the system for reprocessing. After processing, the water was stored in one of three potable water storage tanks containing a 0.2 µm microbial filter and a MCV at the inlet of each of the tanks. As with previous tests, several pretest verification tests were performed prior to the 60-day test including a subsystem check, an integrated wet functional test, and a WRS demonstration test. During subsystem checks, each subsystem was operated individually using deionized water. Next, the subsystems were plumbed together for the integrated wet functional test and deionized water was processed through the entire integrated system. Then, actual wastewater from human donors was processed by the integrated system during the WRS demonstration test. The processed water was not consumed by the donors, but instead was sampled and discarded. Six potable water samples were collected during the Phase IIa WRS demonstration test. The Phase IIa test began in January 1997 with water from the JSC public water supply that was deionized, filtered with a 0.2 µm filter, iodinated using a MCV, and filled in two of the three potable water storage tanks. Phase III: Phase III water recycling systems were based on a combination of physicochemical and biological recovery systems. In preparation for Phase III, a demonstration test was performed from March through June 1997. This test processed urine and hygiene water generated by human donors but the water was not consumed. The recovered water was analyzed during the final two weeks of the test to evaluate the system's capability to produce potable water. The Phase III test began on September 19, 1997. In terms of waste-water processing, biologically based systems were used to initially process the wastewaters collected during Phase III, and physicochemical systems were used for polishing and post-processing. After processing, the recovered water was stored in one of four potable water tanks. A 0.2 µm microbial filter and a MCV were positioned at the inlet of each of the tanks for microbial control and for adding iodine to the product water. As in the previous tests, each tank and its contents had the capability of being heated to disinfect the tank if microbial water quality requirements were not met. The Phase III WRS was required to process laundry, shower, handwash, and oral hygiene wastewaters, along with urine, humidity condensate, and incinerator condensate from the processing of human solid wastes. RESULTS: WAFAL analyzed about 160 water samples throughout the course of the Lunar-Mars Life Support Test Project. This project was the first time since the late 1960s that water recycling with human consumption was performed and the first time systems developed for the ISS were tested in this manner. Results from the analysis of samples show that the water recycling systems developed during Phases II, IIa, and III were capable of producing potable water which met NASA and U.S. EPA requirements after the water was treated using a commercial system. All recovered water samples analyzed met U.S. EPA standards. Generally, the majority of samples also met NASA potability standards. On several occasions the organic and inorganic content of the water exceeded the NASA specifications and required the water to be reprocessed prior to consumption. Parameters of most importance where requirements were not met included total organic carbon, total bacteria, copper, lead, and nickel. During Phase II, the water was reprocessed seven times because total organic carbon requirements were not met. During Phase IIa, problems with the water recovery system required the recycled water to be reprocessed eleven times for TOC excursions and ten times for excessive microbial levels. While Phase III did not require reprocessing because a commercial Milli-Q® was used as a post processor, high microbial levels did require the potable water tanks to be heat sterilized three times. Thus, systems for polishing and disinfecting the potable water tanks appear necessary. As out of specification results were detected that required reprocessing of the water for potablity, the need for onboard water analytical capabilities was clearly demonstrated. Similarly, on several occasions microbial contamination in the potable water was detected and required heat disinfection to assure microbial safety. Other standards outlined in the MSIS appear to be adequate. However, future work should concentrate on the development of short-term and long-term exposure requirements for the most critical water quality parameters. The sampling and monitoring plan performed during these studies proved to be adequate. However, analytical methods for identifying organic constituents in recovered water at low levels should be improved. More work should be done to increase the organic carbon recovery of the potable water samples by either developing more sensitive methods of analysis and/or by testing a wider array of organic compounds, especially those of a biological nature such as proteins and biomolecules.

title: Dietary Fat Consumption of U.S. General Population and LSAH Participants
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Nationwide, heart disease is the leading cause of death in both men and women. Many clinical studies have shown a correlation between nutrition and cardiovascular health. Much of this research has been focused on dietary fats and oils, which can promote either good health or disease depending on their quality and quantity. So choosing quality fats and oils should help improve personal cardiovascular disease risk and help decrease national cardiovascular disease rates. The three main types of fats are called saturated, monounsaturated, and polyunsaturated. Excessive consumption of saturated fats is one of the major risk factors for heart disease. Substituting either monounsaturated or polyunsaturated fats for saturated fats may help lower the blood cholesterol level and has been shown to have a protective effect on the cardiovascular system. This investigation compared the quality and quantity of dietary fat intake of the Longitudinal Study of Astronaut Health (LSAH) participants (astronauts and a group of comparison participants) with the U.S. general population.
approach: Dietary fat consumption data was taken from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey, 1988-94 (NHANES III) and compared with data from the 1998 LSAH Food Frequency Questionnaire (FFQ).
results: According to the NHANES data, the average adult consumes approximately 33.6% of total calories from dietary fats, 11.6% from saturated fat, 12.5% from monounsaturated fat, and 6.9% from polyunsaturated fat. These data show that Americans are consuming an excessive amount of the most harmful fats and a deficient amount of the most beneficial fats. On average, comparison participants (N=512) consumed the same percentage of dietary fats as the general population, while astronauts (N=134) reported a slightly lower figure (33.6% and 31.9% respectively). Both groups showed lower saturated fat consumption as compared to the general population, but neither group consumed enough of the beneficial fats. LSAH participants also reported more frequent use of polyunsaturated and monounsaturated fats and oils.

title: Motorized and Non-Motorized Treadmill Evaluation: Physiologic Responses and Biomechanical Aspects
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Treadmill exercise is currently employed as a countermeasure to space flight de-conditioning during long duration missions aboard the International Space Station (ISS). The primary treadmill currently in use, a space flight treadmill with vibration isolation and stabilization (TVIS), can be operated in either motorized (TVIS-M) or non-motorized (TVIS-NM) modes. Although nominal treadmill exercise is performed in the motorized mode, non-motorized treadmill exercise has been utilized as a contingency situation in case of treadmill motor failure or low power availability for treadmill operation. Additionally, a Russian non-motorized treadmill (BD-1) has been proposed as a contingency exercise device in the event of a TVIS failure. Although previous studies have demonstrated differences between motorized and non-motorized treadmill exercise, there has been no direct comparisons made between exercise hardware designed for space flight. Little is known about any differences in metabolic demand, muscle work, gait kinematics, and ground reaction forces between motorized and non-motorized treadmill exercise. The purpose of this study is to compare the acute metabolic and cardiovascular responses, as well as the kinetic and kinematic aspects of short-duration TVIS-M, TVIS-NM, and BD-1 treadmill exercise in relation to a standard laboratory treadmill (LAB-TM) exercise. The findings from this study provide valuable information regarding ongoing use of treadmill exercise as a countermeasure to musculoskeletal and cardiovascular de-conditioning associated with space flight and assist in the development of future treadmill exercise prescriptions.
approach: Twenty-four subjects (males and females) were recruited by the Human Test Subject Facility at NASA-Johnson Space Center. Cardiovascular functional capacity of the subjects was screened using a graded exercise test on a motorized treadmill. The investigator team predetermined that the minimal level of aerobic fitness for test subjects, as assessed by peak oxygen consumption (VO 2pk ), was 35 ml/kg/min. Previous experience in our laboratory suggests that this is the lower limit of fitness among US astronauts. Of the 24 volunteers, only 21 achieved the desired level of fitness, and one subject later withdrew from the study. Twenty subjects completed the study. Following the VO 2pk test, subjects reported for testing on at least ten different occasions: two familiarization and eight data collection sessions. During the familiarization sessions, subjects practiced walking and running on the motorized and non-motorized treadmills at each of the study speeds (3.2-11.3 km/hr; 2-7 mph). Subjects exercised on the LAB-TM and BD-1 treadmills during one familiarization session and exercised on the TVIS-M and TVIS-NM treadmills during the other session. During data collection subjects performed two exercise sessions in each of the four treadmill conditions. For each treadmill, the speeds were grouped as 3.2, 6.4, and 9.7 km/hr (2, 4, and 6 mph) for one session and 4.8, 8.0, and 11.3 km/hr (3, 5, and 7 mph) for the other session. Subjects attempted to complete five minutes of exercise at each speed, in order of increasing intensity, to acquire metabolic and cardiovascular measurements.
results: All but one subject completed five minutes of walking and running at each running speed in the motorized conditions, LAB-TM and TVIS-M. This subject could not complete the entire five minutes at 11.3 km/hr (7 mph). Not all subjects were able to complete walking or running during the non-motorized conditions on the TVIS-NM and BD-1. Subjects were successful at non-motorized treadmill speeds of 3.2 and 4.8 km/hr (2 and 3 mph), but the ability to complete the trials decreased precipitously as the speed increased from 6.4 to 11.3 km/hr (4 to 7 mph). All subjects completed the five minute walk at 3.2 km/hr (2 mph) in each of the treadmill conditions. Therefore, no comparisons were possible across treadmills for this speed. All subjects completed the five minute walk at 4.8 km/hr (3 mph) in the motorized conditions, and 19 of the 20 subjects completed five minutes of walking during the non-motorized conditions. At 4.8 km/hr (3 mph), there was no significant difference in completion times between the treadmill conditions. At speeds 6.4 km/hr (4 mph) and greater, subjects completed significantly longer exercise periods during the motorized treadmill exercise than during the non-motorized conditions. However, there was no difference in completion times between the LAB-TM and TVIS-M or between the BD-1 and TVIS-NM. Comprehensive kinematic and kinetic data were collected to determine the differences between treadmill locomotion on motorized and non-motorized treadmills. The results suggest: Subjects take shorter and more frequent steps to obtain a given speed on a non-motorized treadmill. Subjects will transition to a run at lower speeds on non-motorized treadmills (typically between 4.8 and 6.4 km/hr; 3 and 4 mph) than on motorized treadmills at the same speed. Peak ground reaction forces are not different between motorized and non-motorized treadmills. However, distinct impact peaks do not occur during running on non-motorized treadmills, and loading rates were much larger on the motorized treadmills, suggesting that motorized treadmill locomotion may provide a superior osteogenic stimulus. The greater forward lean and lack of heel strike during non-motorized locomotion suggest that gait on the non-motorized device should not be considered equivalent to gait on a level motorized treadmill at a similar speed. Hip range of motion was greater on the non-motorized treadmills, and knee range of motion was greater on the motorized treadmills, suggesting the emphasis upon different musculature depending on the device. Subjects exhibit different joint positions at heel strike, but similar positions at toe-off, suggesting that the physiological effects of locomotive exercise due to impact forces may differ between devices. Non-motorized treadmill locomotion on a level treadmill resembles motorized treadmill locomotion on an inclined treadmill. Long-term training on a non-motorized treadmill will probably result in different physiological effects than on a motorized treadmill.

title: Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) after Exposure to Microgravity
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: In microgravity, bones and muscles are not used as they are on Earth. As many studies have shown, this altered use
approach: All crewmembers of the NASA 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7 missions, as well as the Mir 21, 22, 23, 24 and 25 missions participated as subjects in this study. MRI scans were performed 30 and 60 days before launch, on the day of landing (U.S. crewmembers only), and 4, 14 and 30 days after landing on all crewmembers. Imaging was performed using a 1.5 Tesla Siemens Magnetom MRI system (1.5 Tesla denotes the strength of the magnet used for the test) with various coils, including spine, Helmholz neck and whole body coils. These coils are the antenna of the MRI system that broadcast the radio frequency signal to the patient and/or receive the return signal to form an image. Specific coils are used to image different parts of the body; for example, Helmholz coils are used to image the cervical spine and muscles in the neck. To begin the test, crewmembers were to lie down on a padded table, which would enter the magnet. Crewmembers were recumbent for approximately 10-15 minutes before beginning the test to minimize the effects of fluid shifts caused by lying down after standing. The order in which the measurements were made was kept the same for each crewmember from one imaging session to the next. The normal order was L3 spectroscopy, and then imaging of the intervertebral discs, then differential muscle volume measurements of the back muscles, neck muscles, thigh muscles and calf muscles. A number of variables are used to acquire MRI images, including echo time, echo sequence, repetition time and matrix size. The echo time is the amount of time between magnetic pulses. Echo sequences are the number of magnetic pulses used to create an image. The repetition time is the amount of time between repetitions of the echo sequence, and the matrix size determines the resolution quality, or clearness, of the image. Muscle volume of calf, thigh, lower back and neck: For imaging of the calf and thigh muscles, the feet of the subject were positioned in a holder during the test to minimize movement and insure repositioning. The portion of the leg being imaged was suspended, while the non-imaged portion was supported with foam supports. A radio frequency (RF) shield was positioned caudally to the imaged portion of the leg to remove artifacts in the image, which arise from parts of the body outside the imaging region but near the edge of the gradient coils. For the thigh and calf muscles of NASA 2, 3, 4 and 7 and Mir 21, 22, and 23 crewmembers, 32, 1 centimeter slices (0.8 centimeter slices for NASA 5, NASA 6, Mir 24, and Mir 25) with a 0.2 millimeter gap between slices were obtained using an echo time equal to 10 milliseconds (msec), a repetition time of 800 msec and a 256 x 512 matrix. Every tissue in the human body has its own spin-spin relaxation time (T2) value. Therefore, it can be used to differentiate between different tissue types (e.g. fat and muscle) and changes due to tissue changes (e.g. edema in sore muscles). Calf muscle spin-spin relaxation time (T2) was measured by rescanning the calf region using the same receiver gain at an echo time of 50 msec. Spin-spin relaxation times for each muscle pixel were calculated by comparing the image intensity between the echo times of 10 msec and 50 msec. T2 for a particular muscle was obtained by averaging the T2 for all pixels within that muscle. For the back muscles, 20, 0.5 centimeter slices centered on the third lumbar vertebra were obtained using a spine coil and a 10 msec echo time, an 800 msec repetition time and a 256 x 512 matrix. For the neck muscles, a similar protocol was used with 32, 3 millimeter thick slices, and a Helmholtz neck coil in place of the spine coil. Lumbar spine disc size and lumbar spine length: To measure lumbar spine intervertebral disc size and lumbar spine length, subjects were positioned within the MRI machine so that the imaging area was centered within the third lumbar vertebra, determined from a sagittal scout view. A coronal scout image was used to position a 1 centimeter slice of interest down the center of the spinal column. Imaging sequences of the lumbar spine varied between missions. During NASA 2 and 3 and Mir 21 and 22, two acquisitions of a four echo, spin echo sequence were obtained using echo times of 20, 45, 72 and 106 msec and a repetition time of 1 second. For NASA 4, 5, 6 and 7 and Mir 23, 24 and 25, two different sequences were performed. First, one gradient echo sequence was obtained with an echo time of 7 msec and a repetition time of 400 msec. Second, two single echo, spin echo sequences were obtained using echo times of 10 and 25 msec and a repetition time of 400 msec. The matrix size for spinal images of all NASA-Mir crewmembers was 256 x 256. Disc area was obtained for intervertebral discs in the lower back (T12-L1, L1-2, L2-3, L3-4 and L4-5) from the number of pixels in each image. A phantom was also imaged during each imaging session to correct for any changes in pixel size. To measure spine length, templates (small sub-images) were taken from the first preflight images, each containing a spinal disc. Each of these was registered (a mathematical best fit of position) for each subsequent measurement. The change in separation from the preflight positions to postflight positions was the change in spine length. Bone marrow content (L3 spectroscopy): To measure the fat to water ratio in vertebral bone marrow, volume selective proton spectroscopy was performed on a 15mm x 15mm cubic volume of interest in the third lumbar vertebra (L3) using a surface receive coil. Spectroscopy uses absorption, emission or scattering of electromagnetic radiation by atoms or molecules to qualitatively or quantitatively study the atoms or molecules. The Gradient Inversion Spectroscopy (GIS) technique was used to acquire spectra at echo times equal to 12, 18, 24 and 30 msec with a repetition time of 2 sec. Images were corrected for T2 weighting by exponential extrapolation of the spectra obtained at various echo times. Non-linear peak fitting was performed on the final spectrum to separate the water peak and different fat peaks from the background and to calculate their relative intensities. Bone marrow cellularity was determined from the fat to water ratio. T2 of the fat and water component was determined by fitting the decay of fat and water peaks with an exponential function. Back pain questionnaire: The crew also filled out questionnaires to document the frequency, severity and location of back pain or discomfort during the first 10 days of flight and the first 10 days after flight.
results: in calcium loss, degeneration of the skeleton, lengthening of the spine by expansion of the intervertebral discs, change in spinal bone marrow composition and muscle atrophy. Bedrest patients on earth show this same musculo-skeletal response with the exception of bone marrow alterations. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is one method that can be used to measure the resulting muscular and skeletal changes. MRI is a safe, non-invasive scanning technique that uses a large magnet and low frequency radio waves to form an image by reading the amount of hydrogen in an area of the body. These images can be used to examine soft tissues in the body, as well as determine muscle volume, spinal bone marrow mass and cross-sectional area of intervertebral discs. The objectives of this investigation were to use MRI procedures (1) to measure the muscle volumes of the calf, thigh, back and neck of the Mir astronauts and cosmonauts before and after flight; (2) to determine and compare muscle volume changes on the day of landing and four days after landing; (3) to determine the change in intervertebral disc size in the lumbar spine after flight, and determine the rate of recovery after return to gravity; and (4) to determine the bone marrow cellularity of the third lumbar vertebra (L3) before and after flight. RESULTS: Muscle volume: The muscle volume changes as a percentage of the mean baseline volume in 16 crewmembers after long-duration flight were determined. To calculate percent change from baseline, the first postflight measurement at 0 to 4 days after landing was used. These flights ranged from 115 to197 days in duration. Paired t-tests of the average preflight volume to the first postflight measurement showed significant decreases for all regions except the neck muscles. The values, expressed as a percent of baseline (%±SD), for the 16 subjects were: anterior leg, 85.5±2.9%; gastrocnemius, 83.1±4.4%; soleus, 83.2±4.4%; quadriceps, 89.9±4.4%; hamstrings, 87.3±3.4%; intrinsic back, 84.1±5.8%; psoas, 95.6±6.1%; neck, 100.9±8.3%. A linear regression of the percent loss against flight duration showed no significant slope for any of the regions suggesting that the volume changes reached a new steady state by or before about four months of flight. After landing, each of the flight crew were measured at multiple time points. Results indicate that muscle volume recovers at variable rates depending on the region, but generally have returned to baseline by 30-60 days postflight. A comparison of percent change in muscle volume versus the size of the muscle before flight showed poor or no correlation for any of the muscle groups except the hamstrings, r=0.71. This was also true for when change in muscle volume was correlated with total weight or total body lean mass. This indicates that the suggestion that the percentage loss might be greater in those individuals with greatest mass before flight is not supported by the results in this study. There was no significant correlation between the percentage loss in spinal bone mineral content and intrinsic back muscle volume during flight (n=12). However, when 12 bed rest subjects, half who performed an exercise countermeasure and the remaining who served as controls, were added to the flight data, the correlation was significant (r=0.61, p Comparison of flight results with bed rest data shows that the changes in the leg muscles during flight were generally less than bed rest. This is likely a consequence of the exercise countermeasure employed during flight since the bed rest data did not include exercise. The back muscles, however, showed greater loss during flight compared to bed rest, which may be reasonable, considering that the back muscles are active to a substantial degree in bed rest. Muscle T2: No muscle T2 measurements were possible on landing day. Therefore, the initial postflight measurements were obtained several days after landing which would obviously include significant ambulation prior to the first T2 measurement. The general pattern, however, is that T2 tends to be increased relative to baseline at the first postflight measurement and was almost always elevated at R+14 compared to the initial postflight measurement or baseline. By 30-70 days postflight the T2 decreased toward baseline in all cases where these measurements were available. The general response pattern is consistent with postflight muscle swelling associated with muscle damage. Muscle Swelling: Results show that muscle swelling can occur during the early reambulation period after landing. A similar pattern is seen following reambulation after bed rest. The largest changes were in the calf, particularly the gastrocnemius. The explanation for this swelling could represent rehydration of the muscle following dehydration of the muscle in microgravity. However, the muscle T2 postflight were invariably elevated above baseline, increased further for several weeks after flight and then returned toward the original baseline. These changes along with the reported sore muscles postflight would suggest muscle damage. The large change in the intrinsic back muscles of one crewmember has not been seen previously and may represent postflight swelling. Intervertebral Disc: Data indicate only minor spine lengthening and disc expansion by the time measurements were obtained on landing day. Measurements were made within 2-4 hours after landing with some walking and sitting up on a stretcher by the crewmember before testing. By 2-4 days postflight, slight residual expansion remained which by 2 weeks was back to baseline. Importantly, no long-term residual changes in disc size were found following these flights. Proton Spectroscopy: Comparison of NASA-Mir data to the LMS 17-day mission suggests that although the postflight T2 tends to increase as in the shorter LMS flight followed by a gradual return to baseline levels, there appears to be some differences. The first postflight T2 values were significantly reduced relative to preflight values; this was not detected after the shorter LMS flight. There is some evidence that the degree of decrease in the cellular bone marrow T2 is correlated with the percent change in spinal bone mineral density. Two distinct patterns exist. Postflight, some individuals begin below baseline and simply return to values close to baseline, while others like the LMS crew increase above baseline and gradually return to baseline over a period of several months. Back Pain: Out of 17 crewmembers (including one German guest cosmonaut on the Mir 97 mission), 9 (53%) indicated that they experienced back pain or discomfort during the flight. Generally, this occurred in the lower lumbar region during the first week or two of flight. The pain was typically described as "can be ignored," lasted a few hours to several days in duration and was most noticeable during or after resting. In one crewmember, it was most noticeable during exercise or applying bungies. Some crewmembers indicated that bending or application of massage seemed to relieve the pain. Postflight 8 of 17 (47%) crewmembers reported significant discomfort for some or all 10 days that monitoring was reported following flight. There were a number of cases where written reports were not available or were not filled out. Whenever possible, the crew were asked about their experience during and after flight. When no information was available these were treated as being negative reports and therefore, the incidence rates above may underestimate actual rates. Conclusion: There are measurable decreases in muscle volume during flight, which presumably represents muscle atrophy. These changes appear to be maximized within the first 4 months of flight. This degree of atrophy may indicate that bone loss may also reach a maximum probably at or around this same point, i.e., the rates of loss are different, but it seems reasonable that the degree of loss may be similar at the equilibrium point. If this turns out to be the case, muscle atrophy might be used as an early indicator of bone loss. Compared to bed rest without exercise, the inflight muscle changes are less, except in the back muscles. Recovery in all muscle groups is complete within the first 30-60 days after return to Earth, similar to recovery after bed rest. There are muscle volume and T2 changes during the first days and weeks after return from space flight compatible with muscle damage. We did observe small, but no long-term changes in disc size following these flights. There was a significant decrease in the T2 of the cellular component of the bone marrow of L3 which either increases to baseline during the first few weeks after landing or increases above baseline and subsequently returns to baseline over several months. No significant changes in the T2 of the lipid fraction of the same bone marrow or in the cellular to lipid fraction was seen. About 50% of the crewmembers reported some back pain during flight, however, the duration and magnitude of this problem seems not to be of major concern for long-duration flight. A more important consideration may be the potential for significant injury/pain after flight since about 47% reported significant postflight discomfort lasting for a number of days to weeks. This may be an important consideration after lengthy flights in microgravity followed by a visit to a planet that has significant gravity.

title: Precise Assessment of Prevalence and Progression Rates of Lens Opacities in Astronauts as a Function of Radiation Exposure during Space Flight and Development of Improved Routine Clinical Assessment of Ocular Lens Status
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Astronauts appear to suffer from cataracts more than the general population. The onset of cataracts tends to happen at a younger age in those who have flown in space, and the tendency to develop cataracts is increased for astronauts who have been exposed to relatively higher doses of radiation throughout their flight careers. It has also been shown that there is an association between the development of cataracts and exposure to the high linear energy transfer (LET) radiation (including heavy ions and neutrons) that occurs in space, or within a higher orbital plane of Earth's atmosphere. The objective of this study was to modify the current medical protocol used to assess the health of the eye's lens, as well as visual function, and then incorporate these modifications into a new periodic routine for vision assessment. The long term goal of this project was to improve ocular safety for astronauts during space flight.
approach: In an effort to more precisely define the magnitude of this risk and the relationship of space radiation to cataract progression, NASA funded this five year study to compare progression of cataract formation/development. The five institutions collaborating on this study were: Harvard University (Brigham and Women’s Hospital), NASA, Baylor College of Medicine, Space Center Eye Associates, and Wyle Laboratories. The study was designed to measure the effect of deep space radiation on the lens of the eye, and to measure the changes in lens clarity that might develop as a
results: of exposure to radiation in deep space. The study measured the status of the lens and visual function in the astronaut population (active and retired) and two control groups: military aviators (active and retired), and people without any military aviation background. The two control groups allowed comparison of cataract risks among space radiation-exposed astronauts and non-astronauts with and without controlling for a military aviator lifestyle. Included in this study are measurements of nutritional intake, ocular exposure to sunlight, and radiation exposure. This investigation was designed to add validated measures of visual function to NASA’s Johnson Space Center’s (JSC's) current protocol, including a measure of visual acuity (logMAR) and cataract severity using a Nidek EAS 1000 Imaging System. Pupils were be dilated to maximal size using topical medications: 2.5% phenylephrine and 1.0% tropicamide. Imaging of the anterior and posterior lens and slit imaging of the nucleus were performed. The modified drop procedure currently used at JSC was evaluated for its performance in achieving maximum pupil dilation. Reverse dilation drops were used after the images were obtained. From this digital lens data, a profile of the severity of each type of existing cataract was related to the type and duration of the astronaut's radiation exposure. These measurements will make it possible to predict the probability of cataract formation in astronauts if the anticipated radiation dose for a particular mission can be determined. RESULTS: A review of the evolution of methods of cataract documentation and classification, and a review of the current state-of-the-art digital measurements of early changes in cataract development, were conducted. A review of protocols used at the JSC for routine clinical assessment of the eye and lens has been conducted. Participants included 171 consenting astronauts who flew at least one mission in space and a comparison group made up of three components: (a) 53 astronauts who had not flown in space, (b) 95 military aircrew personnel, and (c) 99 non-aircrew ground-based comparison subjects. Continuous measures of nuclear, cortical and PSC lens opacities were derived from Nidek EAS 1000 digitized images. Age, demographics, general health, nutritional intake and solar ocular exposure were measured at baseline. Astronauts who flew at least one mission were matched to comparison subjects using propensity scores based on demographic characteristics and medical history stratified by gender and smoking (ever/never). The variability and median of cortical cataracts were significantly higher for exposed astronauts than for non-exposed astronauts and comparison subjects with similar ages (P=0.015). Galactic cosmic space radiation (GCR) may be linked to increased PSC area (P=0.056) and the number of PSC centers (P=0.095). Within the astronaut group, PSC size was greater in subjects with higher space radiation doses (P=0.016). No association was found between space radiation and nuclear cataracts. Cross-sectional data analysis revealed a small deleterious effect of space radiation for cortical cataracts and possibly for PSC cataracts. These results suggest increased cataract risks at smaller radiation doses than have been reported previously. Because of high variability and skewness of opacity measures, nonparametric methods were used to test for association between rates of opacification and space radiation exposure. First, median regression was used to collapse longitudinal data into robust estimates of progression rates (opacity severity compare to time for each eye of each subject). To quantify and test for a radiation effect, median regression with the dependent variable being the maximum of the two slopes (OD and OS) per subject was then used, adjusting for the confounding variables of age, nutritional, and sun-exposure histories. Median regression showed evidence of an association between the rate of cortical progression in the worse eye with radiation dose and age. The estimated median progression rate from space radiation being 0.25 ± 0.13% lens area/Sv/year (P = 0.062). The investigators found no relationship between radiation exposure and progression of aggregate area of posterior subcapsular cataract or nuclear progression rates. However, longer follow-up may be needed to further understand any impact of space radiation on progression rates for posterior subcapsular cataracts and nuclear cataracts, and to characterize changes to visual acuity.

approach: Experiment samples included blood, saliva, crew microflora and spacecraft microflora.
