title: Microbiological Investigations of the Mir Space Station and Flight Crew (Phase 1A)
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Microorganisms are ubiquitous in spacecraft environments, as they are on Earth. Microbes pose several risks to humans in space including: infectious diseases, allergies, degradation of air quality (e.g., release of volatiles), release of toxins, degradation of critical materials, and systems failure (e.g., water reclamation system). Maintaining the health and performance of humans in closed microgravity environments while reusing reclaimed air and water is a daunting task. Determining medical and technological risks that are dependent on microbiological factors during long-term space flight is a vital problem in theory, as well as practice. In such a closed environment, humans will be a major source of microbes released into the spacecraft. Animals and plants, when present, will also be significant contributors to the overall bioburden, and suitable containment and purification technologies are essential. Studies of microbial ecology in spacecraft have been mostly limited to short ( The success of long-duration space missions will depend on our ability to mitigate the adverse effects of microorganisms. This will require a much better understanding of the microbiology of closed environments and the human-microbe-environment interactions than are currently available. This joint US-Russian investigation was an important first step in gaining this understanding. The investigators hypothesized that during long-term space flight (>30 days) human microbiota and the microbial ecology of the Mir station will undergo quantitative and qualitative changes. The objectives of this study were to 1) characterize microbiota of crewmembers, air, surface, and water before, during, and after a long-duration mission aboard the Mir Space Station, 2) determine the exchange and distribution of microbes among crewmembers, and 3) assess the distribution and dynamics of crew microbiota throughout the Mir Space Station.
approach: Protocols for the collection and analysis of specimens from the crew, air, surface, and water were designed to provide the data necessary for a thorough characterization of their microbial populations. The protocols and sample collection schedules for the first Shuttle-Mir mission were developed to obtain the maximum possible data despite the limitations of space flight. Crew Microbiology Microbial samples from the throat, nose, ear, hand, axilla, scapula, groin, and urine, were collected, before and after flight, and examined for bacteria and fungi. Stool samples were also collected before and after flight and examined for bacteria, fungi, ova and parasites. Samples from the Mir 18 crew were collected on L-149 (149 days before launch), L-117, L-79, L-44, R+0 (landing day), R+9 (9 days after landing), R+14, and R+19. Samples from the Mir-19 crew were collected on L-254, L-221, L-148, L-112, L-14, R+0, R+7, R+14, and R+22. Each throat, nasal, ear and skin site was sampled using Culturette devices moistened with phosphate buffer. Throat samples were collected by swabbing the surfaces of the tonsils and posterior pharyngeal vault of the crewmember. Nasal samples were collected by swabbing the nares. Ear swabs were collected by swabbing the external ear canal. Skin surface samples from the hand, axilla and groin regions were collected by swabbing the skin surface of the area. Clean-catch midstream urine samples were collected in 4-ounce sterile specimen containers. Stool specimens were collected in commode collection kits and transferred to bacterial transport medium for culture and to SAF fixative for ova and parasite examination. Throat cultures were examined for the presence of pneumococci, beta-hemolytic streptococci, staphylococci, yeast, filamentous fungi and other microbes of medical significance. Fecal examination was performed to establish the obligate and facultatively aerobic microbes, including yeast and molds and anaerobic microbes, including bacteriods, bifidobacteria, lactobacilli and sporiferous bacilli (Clostridium). Enterobacteriaciae, pseudomonads, enterococci, staphylococci, hemolytic streptococci, yeast, molds and other microbes of medical significance were identified to the species level. Quantitative estimates were made in terms of Colony Forming Units (CFU). Species identification was conducted using either a Vitek Automated Identification System or a Biolog Automated Identification System. Species that were not identified by these means were sent to a microbial reference laboratory for identification by fatty acid analysis, or by other means of microbial classification as needed. Air Microbiology Air samples were collected inflight using a Russian supplied impaction air sampler (SAS), in which a small fan unit draws a known volume of air through the sampler and airborne particles are impacted onto growth media. Trypticase soy agar (TSA) and rose bengal agar (RB) were used for collection of bacteria and fungi, respectively. Mir samples were collected in the area of the Control Panel Post #1 in the Core Module (CM), the dining table, the Captain's cabin, and the Kristall module. Mir 18 samples were collected on FD 98 (Flight Day 98) and FD 107 (while docked with STS-71). Upon arrival of the Shuttle (STS-71), all inflight samples were transferred to refrigerated storage space aboard the Shuttle until landing. Mir 19 samples were collected on FD 19 and FD 55. Pre-, in- and postflight samples were also collected from the STS-71 middeck and Spacelab using the US supplied microbial air sampler (MAS) on L-57, L-1, launch day and FD 3. The number of colonies found on the surface of the collection media was used to determine the total bacteria and fungi present in the volume of air sampled. Airborne microorganisms were measured in CFU per cubic meter of air. Identification of isolated colonies was performed as described in the crew microbiology section. Surface Microbiology Surface samples were collected inflight using the Surface Sampler Kit (SSK) that contained Biotest Hycon Contact Slides. The slides consisted of a flexible plastic tray containing a microbial growth medium. The medium was pressed into contact with the surface area being sampled. The slides provided a nutrient surface on which microorganisms could adhere and grow. Bacterial and fungal samples were collected using trypticase soy agar and rose bengal agar, respectively. Microbial samples were collected from the Mir spacecraft surfaces on the control panel #1, the dining table, the mission commander's cabin wall, the treadmill trainer handles and the Kristall Module Hatch. Mir 18 samples were collected on FD 97 and FD 107. Upon arrival of the STS-71, all inflight samples were transferred to refrigerated storage space aboard the Shuttle until landing. Mir-19 samples were collected on FD 23 and FD 55. Pre- and postflight samples were collected from the STS-71 half-moon vent near the toilet, the Left-most Air Return in Crawl through between Middeck and Flight Deck, and the Spacelab Workbench Handle on L-77, L-57, L-1, FD 0, FD 3 and R+0. Total bacterial and fungal counts were determined by the number of colonies found on the surface of the collection media. Surface microorganisms were measured in CFU per squared centimeter. Identification of isolated colonies were performed as described in the crew microbiology section. Water Microbiology Water samples were collected and processed using the Water Microbiology Kit (WMK). The kit contained a microbial capture device through which a water sample volume was processed. An ampoule containing R2A medium was introduced into the microbial capture device to cultivate any microorganisms trapped on the filter. A preflight sample was collected from the ground water source of Mitischi, Moscow, that was supplied on a Progress resupply ship. Mir-18 samples were collected from the Rodnick tank and the galley hot water tap. The Rodnick tank, which holds water transferred from the Progress and Shuttle supplied stored water, was sampled on FD 107. The Mir galley hot water tap, which consisted of recycled potable water, was sampled on FD 13, 97, and 107. Upon arrival of STS-71, all inflight samples were transferred to refrigerated storage space aboard the Shuttle. STS-71 water samples were collected from the galley water tap on L-1 and R+2. Mir 19 samples were collected on FD 23, FD 42 and FD 55. Unprocessed water samples were collected using the water sampler/archiver. These archived samples and the processed water sample filters were returned for ground based examination. Total bacterial counts were determined by the number of colonies found on the surface of the collection media. Water microorganisms were measured in CFU per 100 milliliters. Identification of isolated colonies was performed as described in the crew microbiology section.
results: Crew Microbiology Mir 18: Staphylococcus aureus was chosen as the bacterial species to follow microbial dissemination from crewmember to crewmember and throughout the Mir environment. S. aureus was recovered from the throat swab of crewmember #1 three months before flight. It was also recovered from the hand of crewmember #2 eight days before flight and in substantial numbers in six of nine samples collected on landing day. S. aureus was recovered from crewmember #3 in six of nine samples collected at most sampling sessions. S. aureus was not recovered from backup crewmembers #4 and #6 but was recovered from backup crewmember #5 in seven of the nine samples during most of the preflight sampling periods (backup crewmembers did not participate in postflight sampling). Fungi were very rarely isolated from the crew. Fungal isolates, when present, represented common environmental contaminants, such as Aspergillus niger . Aerobic bacteria recovered from the fecal specimens were consistent with that of healthy individuals. Significant changes were not apparent in the aerobic bacteria isolated from the various specimens before and after flight. The anaerobic bacteria recovered from the feces included bacteroides, bifidobacterium, clostridium, and lactobacillus. No ova or parasites were seen from any crewmember. Although not a part of this experiment, Russian microbiological specialists used the data to assess flight readiness of the crew. The specialist identified a dysbacteriosis in all three crewmembers at 45 days prior to launch. This resulted in a course of bacteriotherapy to normalize and stabilize the crew's microflora prior to the mission. Re-examination at 7 days prior to launch showed marked improvement. Dysbacteriosis was again observed in one crewmember on landing day; again, bacteriotherapy was administered to normalize his microflora. Mir 19: Staphylococcus aureus was isolated from the throat, ear and hand of crewmember #1 before flight, and from his nasal, scapula and groin at pre- and postflight. It was also recovered from the throat of crewmember #2 pre- and postflight. Enterobacter aerogenes was isolated from the nasal swab of crewmember #2 at all sampling periods except L-254 but was isolated from his ear at L-254. Fungi were rarely isolated from crewmember #1, but were frequently isolated from crewmember #2. Aspergillus niger , a common environmental fungus, was not found on crewmember #2 preflight, but was found on his scapula, nose and throat postflight. Candida albicans , an endogenous yeast, was isolated from crewmember #2 fecal samples preflight. The yeast was also recovered from the postflight throat swab of crewmember #2. Urine samples were received in unsterile containers and all data was lost, which impacted science objectives. Fecal samples were collected improperly postflight. Air Microbiology STS-71: Air samples were collected from the middeck of the Space Shuttle and in the Spacelab. The bacterial levels were low in both locations on launch day and flight day 3. The levels were 38 CFU per cubic meter or less. However, the fungi tended to be much higher than usual. Levels reached a high of 930 CFU per cubic meter on the middeck and were over 100 for three of the four sampling periods. Aspergillus, Penicillium , and Cladosporium , common environmental taxa, were the frequently isolated fungi. Fungi were not detected on the Shuttle middeck during two preflight sampling sessions. Mir 18: Air samples were collected on flight days 98 and 107 from four locations in the Mir. Bacteria were not recovered in four of the eight bacterial samples. The levels in the other four samples never exceeded 22 CFU per cubic meter. These levels were exceptionally low and comparable with the levels found on the Shuttle. Fungi were not recovered from five of the eight samples. Fungal levels were generally low, but reached 220 CFU per cubic meter in the Kristall module on FD 97. Aspergillus and Penicillium were the predominant fungal genera isolated. The levels of both fungi and bacteria were clearly below the 1000 CFU per cubic meter acceptability limit for the International Space Station (ISS). Mir 19: Air samples were collected on flight days 19 and 55 from four locations in the Mir. Bacteria were not recovered from any of the sampling sites. Aspergillus niger was found in all four sampling sites. It was isolated in low levels in two sampling sites and in high levels in the two other sites. Control panel #1 revealed the highest counts of 1290 CFU/cubic meter on day 55, which is above the acceptability limit (1000 CFU/cubic meter) for the ISS. Surface Microbiology STS-71 and Mir 18: Surface data were collected from two areas in the Shuttle and one site in the Spacelab before, during and after the mission. The levels and species of bacteria and fungi were comparable to previous Shuttle data. Surface data were collected from five locations inside the Mir on FD 97 and 107. The level of bacteria and fungi were low and generally less than found in the Shuttle. The exception was the Kristall module, in which the highest bacterial levels of >300 CFU/cubic meter were found on FD 97. Unlike the air samples, surface fungal levels in the Kristall were low when detected. Mir 19: Surface data were collected from five locations inside the Mir on FD 23, 28 and 55. This data is from both contact slides and archived swabs. The levels of bacteria and fungi on the contact slides were low and generally less than found in the Shuttle. The microorganisms isolated are similar to those isolated from the Shuttle, with the exception of a larger number of Bacillus species recovered. Aspergillus niger was found on four of the five surfaces sampled. Only qualitative data was obtained from the archived swabs because the tubes were not maintained in a frozen state. Water Microbiology STS-71, Mir 18 and Mir 19: The only bacterial contaminant found in the Shuttle potable water system was Burkholderia cepacia . This common contaminant was recovered at L-1 (23 CFU/100 ml) and at R+2 (1 CFU per 100 ml). The Mir recycled potable water supply (galley hot water) was analyzed three times during the Mir-18 and Mir-19 missions. During Mir-18, there were problems associated with water collection. The bags leaked causing a decrease in the amount of water received postflight. The impact of this was minor. The cold water sample that was to be collected from Mir and archived was not collected. The total bacterial count for Mir-18 was: 60 CFU/100 ml on FD 13; 5 CFU/100 ml on FD 97, and 23 CFU/100 ml on FD 107. The total bacterial count for Mir-19 was: 3 CFU/100 ml on FD 23; 6 CFU/100 ml on FD 42; and 6 CFU/100 ml on FD 55. All of these values are within the International Space Station acceptability limits of 100 CFU/100 ml. The microbes recovered from the Mir recycled water was much different from those recovered from the Shuttle water system. The rigorous filter treatment and final heat step of the Mir system appeared to have eliminated many of the more fragile organisms. Bacillus and Staphylococcus , two robust gram positive bacteria, were the only organisms recovered from this source. Technical difficulties during Mir 18 made analysis and interpretation of the archived water samples difficult. Due to contamination, there were no quantitative results from the Mir 19 archived water samples. In conclusion, the aerobic microbiota of the three Mir 18 crewmembers was characteristic of healthy individuals and medically significant changes were not found after return to Earth. One crewmember was clearly a carrier of S. aureus and dissemination of this species in the environment and colonization of other crewmembers was probable. Levels of bacteria and fungi from the air, surface and water samples were within the ISS acceptability limits. The species recovered from the air and surfaces were similar to those found on the Shuttle. However, conclusions are difficult until the database for long-duration flight is expanded. Detection of Aspergillus and Penicillium fungal isolates from selected air and surface samples is a basis for further observations of their quantitative dynamics and distribution in the orbital station, as it is evident that these microorganisms are growing on different polymeric materials, causing biological harm and destruction. Microbial water analysis was successfully performed for the first time aboard a spacecraft. The bacterial content of the Mir water supply was much different from bacterial species isolated from the Shuttle water system. The aerobic microbiota of the two Mir 19 crewmembers was characteristic of healthy individuals. Remarkable change in the body-bioburden was not apparent upon return to earth with the exception of the presence of A. niger on the skin and throat swabs of crewmember #2. This fungus is commonly present in the terrestrial environment and was also isolated, in rather large numbers, from Mir surfaces and air samples. It is obvious, therefore, that the fungus was a "carry over" from Mir; no undesirable health effects were noticed. One crewmember was clearly a carrier of S. aureus , and completion of DNA fingerprinting will verify the suspected colonization of the other crew member. The surface and water borne bacterial and fungal loads were mostly within the limits set for the ISS. However, the fungal counts in the air tended to be higher. In general, the microbiological profile of the Mir was comparable to that of the Shuttle and Spacelab.

title: Bioassays of Body Fluids
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Orthostatic hypotension and weight loss were observed in the crewmembers of Gemini 3, 4, 5, and 6 immediately after flight. Scientists were concerned that space flight might affect the balance of body fluid and electrolytes since fluid losses can contribute to both of these symptoms. This led to a series of ground-based studies to simulate some of the conditions of space flight. An attempt was made to define the physiological parameters that would be affected by the condition of microgravity. These studies utilized bed rest and water immersion as a means of simulating microgravity. Both the cardiovascular and musculoskeletal systems experienced changes during the ground-based studies. Changes in body fluid chemistry were found to be reflective of the status of these systems. This experiment was designed to obtain objective data concerning the effects of space flight on the human body by examining alterations in the body fluid chemistry.
approach: Preflight plasma samples were collected from all crewmembers of Gemini 7, Gemini 8, and Gemini 9 approximately 10 days and 3 days before launch. Plasma samples were not collected in flight. Gemini 7 postflight plasma samples were collected immediately after recovery, and 6 hours, 24 hours and 72 hours after flight. Gemini 9 postflight plasma specimens were collected after recovery, and 6 hours and 72 hours after flight. The Gemini 8 mission was terminated after 11 hours and no postflight data was collected for this experiment. Urine sampling was scheduled preflight, inflight, and postflight for Gemini 7, 8, and 9. Preflight, two 48-hour urine samples were collected approximately 10 days and 3 days before launch. Inflight urine collection on Gemini 7 and 9 was accomplished by utilizing a specially designed urine transport system. The urine transport system permitted researchers to calculate the total urine volume for each void by means of tritium dilution. A 75 ml aliquot of each void was collected into a plastic sample bag and stored for return to Earth. No refrigeration was used, but benzoic acid was added as a preservative. Urine was collected continuously for 48 hours after landing. Inflight and postflight urine samples were not collected for the Gemini 8 crewmembers. Water and fluid electrolytes were examined to determine the mechanisms associated with weight loss during flight. The concentrations of plasma sodium, potassium, and chloride ions were measured preflight and postflight, and the rates of urinary excretion of these electrolytes were determined pre-, in-, and postflight. Total plasma protein concentrations, measured preflight and postflight, were used to indicate dehydration. Fluid intake and output were measured to determine whether weight loss was caused by sweat and insensible losses or by changes in renal function. Fluid intake was ad lib, but the quantities ingested during the pre- and postflight phases were recorded. The majority of the fluid intake was obtained with the diet. Inflight intake was estimated from a water dispensing device on board the space craft. The information was not sufficiently precise to perform calculation of fluid balance data. To complement the water measurements and electrolyte-balance measurements, both urinary antidiuretic hormone (ADH) and aldosterone were measured. The production of ADH is responsive to thoracic blood volume changes, and it was postulated that microgravity would decrease ADH secretion and
results: in an increase in urinary volume. Aldosterone was measured to study the mechanisms associated with sodium excretion. Increases in aldosterone secretion would result in decreased urinary excretion of sodium, and vice versa. Researchers hypothesized that aldosterone secretion would be decreased in space flight, resulting in an increased urinary excretion of sodium. To measure the effects of stress in space, two groups of hormones were assayed. The first group assayed, 17-hydroxycorticosteroids, was indicative of long-term stress responses. The second group assayed, catecholamines, was indicative of short-term or emergency responses. These parameters provided an objective, long-term evaluation of the physiologic cost of space flight. Bone demineralization was evaluated by measuring calcium, magnesium, phosphate, and hydroxyproline in plasma and urine both preflight and postflight and in urine collected in flight. Changes in bone mineralization were studied by calculating the ratio of bound to unbound calcium in the plasma. This ratio was approximated from an estimate of plasma protein and calcium. Hydroxyproline, an amino acid unique to collagen, was measured in urine to study bone and collagen breakdown. It was presumed that an increased excretion of hydroxyproline accompanying bone demineralization resulted from dissolution of bone matrix. Urinary urea concentration was measured to study protein intake and tissue metabolism. Creatinine excretion was measured to study muscle protein metabolism. Decreases of creatinine excretion are associated with loss of muscle tone and activity. RESULTS: When the preflight and postflight plasma samples were analyzed for Gemini 7, by far the longest Gemini flight, electrophoretic patterns were normal. All values were in the normal range, except for an anticipated increase in 17-hydroxycorticosteroids in the first sample taken after recovery. These values decreased to preflight values within 6 hours following recovery. Hydroxyproline did not change significantly. Plasma uric acid was reduced. The cause of the reduction was unknown, but presumed to be dietary. Plasma ADH was significantly elevated in the first postflight plasma sample of one subject of Gemini 7, but returned within normal range as urine output returned to normal. It was concluded that 14 days of orbital space flight did not result in any gross aberrations of plasma electrolytes. During the first 24-hours after Gemini 7, there was marked water retention for both subjects. The output for each subject was approximately 1 liter less than the preflight 24-hour volume. In addition, there was marked retention of chloride, sodium, and potassium. The water retention and the rapid weight gain after flight were consistent with the hypothesis that weight loss during flight was the result of fluid loss. Electrolyte and water retentions observed immediately postflight in the Gemini 7 subjects were consistent with bed rest studies that showed an increased ADH secretion contributed to decreased urinary volume. During Gemini 9, inflight urine volumes based on the tritium dilution were as great as 12 liters per urination. This great variation in urine volumes was indicative of an anomaly. Therefore, no further attempt was made to analyze or interpret the urine samples collected in flight. The Gemini 9 subjects experienced significant postflight retention of water. This was accompanied by retention of sodium, potassium, and chloride. Urinary calcium decreased slightly immediately postflight. The excretion of 17-hydroxycorticosteroids was increased immediately postflight. This was probably caused by the stress of re-entry. Postflight, the increase of plasma protein and a slightly smaller increase of plasma electrolytes were consistent with an inflight water and electrolyte loss that resulted in dehydration followed by the retention of water and electrolytes. It was not known whether the losses resulted from diuresis during flight or from sweat.

title: Toxicological Assessment of Airborne Volatile Organic Compounds
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Astronauts living for an extended period of time in a closed environment, such as the Mir Space Station, are continuously exposed to pollutants in respirable air. Pollutants originate from material off-gassing, human metabolism, systems and payload leaks, and utility chemicals. If pollutant concentrations reach high levels, crewmembers may experience health problems and scientific experiments could be confounded. This experiment was designed to sample the Mir Space Station air at various locations and times in order to estimate the effects of airborne pollutants on crew health. The following were objectives of this experiment: Determine if Mir air meets U.S. standards for crew health during long-term exposure to trace contaminants Sample air using several types of hardware to compare similarity of sampling methods Sample Mir Space Station air at multiple locations simultaneously to assess spatial variations in the Mir complex Measure ethylene concentrations to determine if plant growth experiments could be affected. Assess the rate of pollutant mixing after hatch opening between shuttle and Mir.
approach: In-flight air sampling was performed on NASA-Mir 2-7. Instantaneous air samples were obtained using grab sample containers (GSCs), and 24 hour time-averaged air samples were obtained using solid sorbent air samplers (SSASs). Formaldehyde badges were used to measure formaldehyde concentrations throughout Mir. The GSCs and SSASs were tested preflight at the Johnson Space Center (JSC) Toxicology Laboratory to ensure that each sampler was clean and could perform as expected. Formaldehyde badges were tested, reconfigured to fit the NASA flight configuration, and packaged for use during flight. During flight, GSC and SSAS samples were taken approximately every thirty days. After each sampling session, the date, time, and location were recorded. Once during each mission, a spatial variation assessment was performed by sampling multiple modules simultaneously. The formaldehyde badges were worn by the crewmembers and also placed in the individual modules. Upon return to Earth, the GSC samples were analyzed by gas chromatography (GC) and a modified EPA TO-14 gas chromatography/mass spectrometry (GC/MS) method. The GC analysis was used to estimate ethylene concentrations. The SSAS samples were analyzed only via the GC/MS method. The filters were removed from the formaldehyde badges and extracted with formaldehyde-free water. The aqueous extracts were then analyzed for formaldehyde using a chromotropic acid-spectrophotometric method.
results: The air quality on NASA-Mir 2-7 met, and exceeded, U.S. standards for human-rated spacecraft. However, the irritant group was slightly above a toxicity index of 1 during NASA-Mir 2, 6, and 7, and the carbon dioxide toxicity index was above 1 during NASA-Mir 2 and 3. The toxicity index was calculated for each toxicological group by summing the ratios of the measured concentrations to the space maximum allowable concentrations for each contaminant in a toxicological group. The high toxicity index of the irritant group was due in part to high concentrations of formaldehyde. As hypothesized, spatial variations of contaminants were small within the Mir complex for both SSAS and GSC samples. The variations were most likely caused by contaminants localized in the different modules. The rate of pollutant mixing after hatch opening between Shuttle and Mir could not be established because of too few samples. A comparison of the U.S. and Russian air sampling methods showed that the Russian AK-1 sorbent system samplers, on average, measured higher concentrations than did the U.S. samplers. During the course of this experiment, several opportunities arose that allowed scientists to study situations that had previously been unexamined. During NASA-Mir 4, a fire was caused by the solid fuel oxygen generator (SFOG); this presented an opportunity to study the contaminants released into the Mir atmosphere due to the fire, and also assess how well the life support system scrubs contaminants from the air. The life support system worked excellent and brought the pollutants associated with the fire back to baseline concentrations within 32 hours. During NASA-Mir 4 the investigators also had the opportunity to compare the results of the formaldehyde badges to those of the formaldehyde active sampler (FAS). Because of the difficulties involved with collecting inflight formaldehyde samples, conclusive results were not obtained. However, another opportunity arose to compare these two methods during the second phase of the Lunar Mars Life Support Test Project (LMLSTP). The results of this test verified the validity of the badges when compared to other methods. During NASA-Mir 5, all sampling hardware was lost due to the decompression of the Spektr module. The focus of the experiment then changed to analyzing how well the humidity control system would scrub a large concentration of ethylene glycol from the air. It was hypothesized that ethylene glycol present in Mir air due to a leak would be removed quickly. However, ethylene glycol detector tubes were used to measure ethylene concentrations, and it took one month for the concentration to drop below the 180-day SMAC level. Additionally, ethylene concentrations measured by the GSCs during the other NASA-Mir missions were determined to be high enough to affect plant growth experiments. The final unscheduled event occurred during a low temperature catalytic oxidizer (LTCO) burn. Improper operation of the LTCO caused dangerously high levels of carbon monoxide (CO) to be released into the Mir atmosphere. The combustion products analyzer (CPA) recorded high levels of CO, but because the crew appeared to be doing well after the incident, the high levels were thought to have been caused by hydrogen interference. Because this was such a serious toxicological incident, many steps have been taken to prevent a reoccurrence. One step, which will be used on the International Space Station (ISS), is the use of a new CPA that has much less cross sensitivity to hydrogen.

title: Efficacy of Vitamin D Supplementation in an Antarctic Ground Analog of Space Flight
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Vitamin D is critical for space travelers because they lack ultraviolet light exposure and have an insufficient dietary supply of vitamin D. Despite the provision of vitamin D supplements to International Space Station (ISS) crewmembers, vitamin D status is consistently lower after flight than before flight, and in several crewmembers, levels have decreased to concentrations considered clinically significant. Vitamin D has long been known to play a role in calcium metabolism, and more recently its non-calcitropic functions (functions not related to calcium metabolism, e.g., effects related to the incidence of cancer or diabetes) have been recognized. According to the
approach: This was a five month prospective, randomized, double-blind study of vitamin D supplementation. It was conducted during winter in Antarctica at the McMurdo Station, when ultraviolet B radiation levels are essentially zero. The 55 subjects (41 men and 14 women, all white) were randomly divided into three groups for vitamin D supplementation: 2000 IU/d (n=18), 1000 IU/d (n=19), and 400 IU/d (n=18). Seven additional subjects (three men and four women) agreed to participate in the blood draws and diet logging, but they either did not want to take study supplements or were taking supplements of their own choosing. Those taking supplements of vitamin D >400 IU/d or of calcium >500 mg/d were excluded. The study consisted of three data collection sessions, each including a seven-day diet record, an 8-hour fasting blood draw, and body weight determination. Height was recorded at the beginning of the study. Baseline data (session 1) were collected at week five of the South Polar winter (the end of March and beginning of April); session 2 was at week 18 (the end of June and beginning of July), and session 3 was at week 25 (the middle of August). During each blood collection session, two 5-mL blood tubes were filled for each subject. The tubes were centrifuged and frozen at -80 degrees Celsius until delivered to the Johnson Space Center in Houston, Texas for analysis. The subjects were given two bottles, each with a known number of pills, and were instructed to take 1 pill from each bottle daily. Each bottle was labeled with a single letter code; there were 12 possible combinations (four possible combinations for each study dose) to ensure blinding of both the subjects and the on-site medical staff who conducted the study. The two bottles provided either one placebo and one 400-IU pill (the 400-IU dose group), one placebo and one 1000-IU pill (the 1000-IU dose group), or two 1000-IU pills (the 2000-IU dose group). The subjects were asked to return the bottles at the end of the study so that pill counts could be conducted to estimate compliance. Thirty-one of the 55 subjects returned the pill bottles at the end of the study.
results: of several recent studies, functionally relevant measures indicate that the lower limit of serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D (a marker of vitamin D status) should be raised from the current standard of 25 nmol/L to 80 nmol/L. The mean preflight serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D for U.S. ISS crewmembers to date is 63 ± 16 nmol/L, and after a four- to six-month space flight mission it typically decreases 25-30% despite a supplementation of 400 International Units per day (IU/d). The suboptimal pre- and postflight vitamin D status is an issue that needs to be addressed so NASA can better define the appropriate amount of supplemental vitamin D to serve as a countermeasure against vitamin D deficiency in crewmembers. This is very important for long-duration crewmembers, and is critical for exploration class missions. Providing a recommendation for vitamin D supplementation to maintain serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D at optimal concentrations (±75–80 nmol/L) is important for long duration crew members on the ISS (six month flights) and is critical for exploration-class missions on the Moon or Mars that could be years in duration. Ground-based models of space flight in which subjects receive limited sunlight exposure are valuable for performing vitamin D supplementation trials. One of these models is subjects spending the winter in Antarctica, where ultraviolet B light (UVB) radiation is essentially zero during the winter months. The main objective of this study was to determine the effectiveness of three different doses of supplemental vitamin D 3 in enabling subjects with no sunlight exposure to reach and maintain optimal vitamin D status (serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D concentration of 80 nmol/L). Specific Aims: (1) Determine the time course and magnitude of changes in vitamin D status during winter in Antarctica, with or without vitamin D supplementation. (2) Determine other markers of bone and calcium metabolism (such as serum calcium, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, parathyroid hormone, and vitamin D-binding protein) before and after vitamin D supplementation to determine the effectiveness of supplementation. APPROACH: This was a five month prospective, randomized, double-blind study of vitamin D supplementation. It was conducted during winter in Antarctica at the McMurdo Station, when ultraviolet B radiation levels are essentially zero. The 55 subjects (41 men and 14 women, all white) were randomly divided into three groups for vitamin D supplementation: 2000 IU/d (n=18), 1000 IU/d (n=19), and 400 IU/d (n=18). Seven additional subjects (three men and four women) agreed to participate in the blood draws and diet logging, but they either did not want to take study supplements or were taking supplements of their own choosing. Those taking supplements of vitamin D >400 IU/d or of calcium >500 mg/d were excluded. The study consisted of three data collection sessions, each including a seven-day diet record, an 8-hour fasting blood draw, and body weight determination. Height was recorded at the beginning of the study. Baseline data (session 1) were collected at week five of the South Polar winter (the end of March and beginning of April); session 2 was at week 18 (the end of June and beginning of July), and session 3 was at week 25 (the middle of August). During each blood collection session, two 5-mL blood tubes were filled for each subject. The tubes were centrifuged and frozen at -80 degrees Celsius until delivered to the Johnson Space Center in Houston, Texas for analysis. The subjects were given two bottles, each with a known number of pills, and were instructed to take 1 pill from each bottle daily. Each bottle was labeled with a single letter code; there were 12 possible combinations (four possible combinations for each study dose) to ensure blinding of both the subjects and the on-site medical staff who conducted the study. The two bottles provided either one placebo and one 400-IU pill (the 400-IU dose group), one placebo and one 1000-IU pill (the 1000-IU dose group), or two 1000-IU pills (the 2000-IU dose group). The subjects were asked to return the bottles at the end of the study so that pill counts could be conducted to estimate compliance. Thirty-one of the 55 subjects returned the pill bottles at the end of the study. RESULTS: Upon receipt of the blood tubes in Houston, it was found that some tubes had inadvertently not been centrifuged before they were frozen. This affected 27-29 data points, depending on whether one or both of the tubes were affected and whether hemolysis affected the tests. The average dietary intake of vitamin D during the study was 295 ± 224 IU/d (average for all subjects except one outlier). There were no significant differences between the supplementation groups at baseline (session 1) for any of the serum analytes measured. About five months after supplementation started (session 3), 25-hydroxyvitamin D increased to 71 ± 23 nmol/L in the 2000-IU/d group, 63 ± 25 nmol/L in the 1000-IU/d group, and 57 ± 15 nmol/L in the 400-IU/d group and decreased to 34 ± 12 nmol/L in the group not taking supplements. In both sessions 2 and 3, the serum concentration of 25-hydroxyvitamin D was higher in the 2000-IU/d group than in the group that did not take study supplements. When hemolyzed samples were excluded, similar results were obtained, except that 25-hydroxyvitamin D was higher in the 1000-IU/d group and in the 2000-IU/d group than in the group not taking supplements in session 3. In all groups that took study supplements, serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D was greater in sessions 2 and 3 than in session 1. Likewise, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D was greater in sessions 2 and 3 than in session 1, showing a significant difference between data collection sessions but not between supplementation groups. Similar results were obtained when hemolyzed samples were excluded from the analysis. Vitamin D supplementation did not affect 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D or calcium status (as expected); however, both 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D and serum calcium increased in sessions 2 and 3 in all subjects. Bone specific alkaline phosphatase was greater in session 3 than in session 1, showing a significant effect between data collection sessions but not between supplementation groups. Serum parathyroid hormone (PTH) was not significantly affected between data collection sessions or between the groups. Vitamin D-binding protein showed no significant difference between the groups. Body weight did not change over the course of the study, but serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D status did change. When body weight was graphed against 25-hydroxyvitamin D, there was a negative correlation in both session 1 (baseline) and session 3 (after 5 months supplementation) suggesting that increased body weight is related to a decrease in circulating vitamin D.

title: SCALE: Shared Cognitive Architectures for Long-term Exploration
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Among the remarkable team challenges NASA faces in long-duration space exploration (LDSE) missions is the need to maintain team shared mental models (SMMs). Maintaining team SMMs requires the ability to detect shifts in cognition that will likely occur during the mission that could lead to ineffective crew functioning and performance. Maintaining team SMMs also requires validated countermeasures for bringing team members' cognitive understanding back into alignment. Leaving low Earth orbit requires extreme teamwork. Team SMMs need to be maintained within teams operating close up (the crew), and between teams operating at an unprecedented distance (i.e., the crew and ground; 33 million miles in the case of a mission to Mars).
approach: A multidisciplinary research team leveraged expertise in psychology, industrial engineering, and anthropology to understand the emergence and outcomes of critical shifts in team cognition over long duration missions. This project utilized a novel conceptual framework of shared cognitive architecture (SCA) to understand the patterns of SMMs that dynamically link members of teams, and teams to other teams, as they go beyond low Earth orbit. Investigators used semantic analysis to identify cognitive shifts, and relational event network analysis to understand the antecedents and consequences of these shifts. Using this framework alongside an agent-based model (ABM) on LDSE analog data, investigators explored an exhaustive set of potential triggering conditions over the course of three Human Exploration Research Analog (HERA) campaigns.  The investigative team focused their data collection strategies into three distinct phases: Index of Cognitive Efficiency (ICE), leadership relations, and task and team mental modeling. The ICE Index of Cognitive Efficiency (overall score) was collected using Spaceflight Cognitive Assessment Tool for Windows (WinSCAT) which is a BHP Behavioral Medicine “surveillance” tool. For leadership relations in phase 2, the crew members completed a network survey asking about their leadership relations (i.e., “Who do you rely on for leadership?”) every five days. For phase 3, each individual’s task and team mental model was collected every day except Sundays, using the elicitation method. Crew members were asked, on a scale of 1 (totally unrelated) to 7 (very strongly related), to report their perceptions of the relationships between a list of 8 task elements, which produced 28 dyadic values for each crew member for each day.
results: Phase 1 The research team developed a computational model that  successfully predicted crew shared mental models based on personal, task, social, and situational  factors. This model can be used in future mission planning and mission support. C omprehensive meta-analysis of prior research established that shared mental  models are a robust predictor of team performance. Though moderators were found, the  relationship between shared mental models and performance was always positive. The implication  being that long distance missions should monitor and promote shared mental models among the  crew, among mission support, and between the crew and mission support. Leveraging research previously conducted on  Skylab missions demonstrated that crew shared mental models, and shared mental  models between the crew and ground can be assessed using text analysis of unstructured text; in  this case mission transcripts of spoken communication were used. Phase 2 The development of the computational model operationalizing shared mental models as network ties among crew members was finalized, followed by running “whatif” computational experiments to explicate how leadership network structures affect mental model development in teams over time. Fitting the empirical data to the computational model showed that crew relations (e.g., leadership), crew composition (e.g., cognitive ability, agreeableness diversity), and mission task design (e.g., workload, task importance) are consistent predictors that could be targeted for SMM countermeasure development. Results of computational experiments suggest that shared leadership results in the most shared mental models, followed by hierarchical leadership, and then connected leadership; factionalized and disenfranchised leadership structures result in the least shared mental models. These findings suggest informal leadership is a useful crew property to monitor, and that the formation of factions, or occurrence of disenfranchised crew members should trigger crew support countermeasures as these structures in the crew pose a threat to mental models and, by extension, performance. When evaluating how crew and ground schemas about communication networks affect information sharing, this experiment found crew members often overestimated the presence of communication links between members who are part of the same formal group and underestimated the presence of links between people who are in different groups. This underscores the importance of accurate relational schema as a precursor to effective information sharing and performance. Phase 3 In the first portion of this phase, the research team developed a prototype dashboard for the detection of shared cognitive architecture and explored the correlation between shared mental model and team performance in HERA. Investigators found substantial positive correlations of shared mental models and both dimensions of team performance. Though shared mental models are a strong predictor of team performance across mission stages, some nuanced shifts were observed: (1) shared mental models are the most strongly predictive of performance on creative thinking tasks before and after communication delay; (2) on problem solving tasks, shared mental models increase in predictive power continuously throughout the mission; (3) of all the outcomes, fluency is the most predicted by shared mental models. The second portion of Phase 3 evaluated isolation, confinement, and network position affect network routing accuracy. Using a network routing task, network acuity among HERA crews was significantly higher than mission control members in Campaign 4 and Campaign 5, but not Campaign 3. Additionally, communication delays did not impact network acuity among HERA crews, but reduced acuity among mission control members. Further, crew members who scored lower on the personality characteristic of conscientiousness had higher network acuity in both Campaign 3 and Campaign 4. Finally, crews’ network acuity was associated with personality characteristics of openness to experience, agreeableness, and neuroticism in Campaign 4 but not Campaign 3. Overall, the findings suggest that selecting crews with high network acuity will play a key role in alleviating the risk of information-sharing failures within a multiteam system under conditions of communication delays.

title: Predicting Vulnerability to Performance Impairment from Sleep Loss
variables: Performance evaluation and effort rating scales
Psychomotor vigilance test pre- and post-assessment mode scales
Repeated acquisition of response sequences task
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Studies by NASA have shown that astronauts obtain only approximately 6 hours of sleep per day on average during space flight missions. Laboratory experiments have revealed that within a few days, such reduction of sleep can
approach: In this study, n=21 subjects served as their own controls through a design in which extensive neurobehavioral and physiological assessments were made during three replications of extended, 36-hour waking performance, as part of three 69-hour in-laboratory experimental sessions. The amount of sleep allowed during the week prior to each laboratory session was varied in counterbalanced order between a satiated condition (i.e., 12 hours time in bed) and a restricted condition (i.e., 6 hours time in bed). Research subjects also underwent two screening sessions and a 29-hour adaptation session in the laboratory before entering the experimental phase of the study, and a follow-up session to conclude the experiment. The study was designed with the following considerations: 1. title: Frames of Reference for Sensorimotor Transformations
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: This experiment addresses the fundamental question of reference frames used by the central nervous system (CNS) to interpret sensory information and to control movements. By studying the perception and coordination of visual and haptic stimuli in space, researchers can better understand the role of gravity in interpreting and calibrating these two sensory modalities on earth. Gravity plays a potential role in calibrating different essential reference frames. The CNS can sense the gravitational force, and thus define a vertical direction, in a variety of ways. Mechanisms in the inner ear permit the measurement of gravity in a head-centered reference frame. The force of gravity acting on an outstretched limb permits the perception of vertical in an arm-centered coordinate frame, while visual cues in the environment (walls, falling objects) can be used to define vertical in retinotopic coordinates. The constant direction of gravity can potentially be used to align these different reference frames. This experiment is composed of a series of psychophysical tests specifically addressing the role of gravity in defining, calibrating, and aligning different sensory and motor reference frames. A. Hypotheses Gravity provides a potential reference direction for the interpretation of sensory information. In microgravity, we might expect to see a shift from allocentric interpretations of visual and kinesthetic information to an egocentric reference frame: head/retinal for visual data and body/joint for motor and kinesthetic information. Gravity serves to align visual, kinesthetic, and haptic reference frames. In microgravity we might expect to see a reduction in the capacity to coordinate visual and haptic information. Interpretation of kinesthetic sensation is based on internal models of the limb and of the environment, including a model of the constant force of gravity acting on the body. We can expect that initially in orbit, the discrepancy between the internal models appropriate for a 1-G environment and the actual 0-G conditions will introduce specific biases in the perception of proprioceptive and haptic stimuli. We might further find that these biases disappear as the internal models are adapted to novel conditions. B. Specific Objectives Test the hypothesis that gravity can be used to align visual and motor frames of reference. Identify the role of gravity in defining the reference frames used to code visual, proprioceptive, and haptic information. By extension, measure the adaptation of the perceptual system to an environment lacking gravity. Collect fundamental baseline data on the capacities of the human visual, proprioceptive, and haptic perceptual systems under conditions of microgravity. C. Functional Objectives This experiment consists of a series of psychophysical tests designed to measure the subject's ability to measure and align visual and haptic stimuli. Visual Orientation – Test the accuracy of alignment of two visual stimuli (lines). Haptic Orientation – Test the ability to discriminate between two directions of hand displacements in the fronto-parallel plane. Haptic/Visual Coordination – Test the ability to align a visual line with the orientation of the haptically presented axis. Visual Magnitude – Test for perceptual differences between the lengths of visually presented horizontal and vertical lines. Haptic Magnitude – Test for perceptual differences between the length and width of a haptically presented rectangular "hole".
approach: The subject was seated in a body restraint chair, and secured with belts around the shoulders and hips. The feet were placed in foot restraints installed in front of the chair. The subject observed a flat video screen through a 60 cm long, cylindrical tunnel. The face was placed inside a mask at one end of the tunnel, and secured lightly with a Velcro strap that passed behind the head. The subjects manipulated the ROBOTOP joystick mounted below and to the right (right-handed subject) or left (left-handed subject) of the video monitor. The subject was required to adjust the length or the orientation of a ‘variable’ stimulus to match the length or orientation of a fixed ‘reference’ stimulus. Preflight, inflight, and postflight psychophysical test sessions were identical. Subjects were presented with two stimuli (such as lines on the screen) sequentially. One of these stimuli, the reference, was fixed for the duration of a single trial. The second, the variable stimulus, was under the control of the subject via the ROBOTOP joystick and a control knob. The task for the subject was to adjust the variable stimulus such that it matched the reference. The characteristic of the reference stimuli was randomly varied, as was the starting value for the variable parameter. Different starting points were used for trials with the same reference value. Using this technique, two effects were measured. Differences between the reference stimulus and the average final value of the variable stimulus, for a given reference, indicated a bias in the sensing of the desired parameter and/or a bias in the mapping from one direction/modality to another. The standard deviation of values for a given reference will indicate the accuracy with which the subject can control and reproduce the desired output. To effectively measure the biases in perception, it was important that the subject not know about eventual errors that he or she might make. Feedback about errors would give an instant clue as to how the response should be corrected. However, it was very difficult to remain focused on the experiment task if there was no feedback about performance. To this end a "score" was devised for the subjects. This score represented the variability of responses to a given reference stimulus. If the subject was alert and performing well, he or she would produce approximately the same response for a given reference stimulus, and the score would be small. If, on the other hand, the subject was distracted or not concentrating well, it was expected that responses to a given stimulus would be more variable, thus producing a larger score. It was, therefore, desirable to have as low a score as possible. This score measured precision and not accuracy. The score was intended purely for the use of each individual subject in order to provide feedback about the work that they were performing. These scores were not reported to anyone, nor were they used in any way to rank subjects.
results: Data was collected on flight days 25, 27, 28, 53, and 54, but the sessions scheduled for flight day 120 and 121 was canceled due to equipment failure. The experiment was not performed on NASA 5. Data from the NASA 4 study have been drawn from a single subject, so care must be taken in interpreting these results. Nevertheless, the following observations can be made from the performance of these tasks by this subject. Some of the results have been confirmed by the Russian experiment "Orientation", which followed the same protocol as this experiment and was performed on two subjects from the Mir 23 crew. Visual Orientation The oblique effect for the comparison of visual orientation is apparent in the plots of response variability. The variability of responses is lower for vertical (90°) and horizontal (0°) stimuli, compared to the other orientations. The data suggest that variability may increase more in microgravity for the oblique angles than for the canonical horizontal and vertical references. This observation is confirmed in the average of the NASA 4 and Mir 23 subjects, particularly around the horizontal direction. Note that an anomaly in the onboard hardware created a vertical reference line on the video monitor that may have aided the subjects in aligning the vertical stimuli. This may explain why variability at +115.5 degrees was not increased in microgravity. If confirmed, these results suggest that in the absence of the gravitational reference frame, visual perception of orientation is perturbed, with a greater bias towards a body-aligned reference frame for ‘vertical’ and ‘horizontal’ lines. Haptic Orientation Responses are somewhat more variable for the haptic perception of orientation. There is no clear evidence for an oblique effect in this test of the human haptic system, nor is there an obvious effect of microgravity on either the biases or the variability of responses. This latter observation is confirmed in the average across the 3 subjects which shows no clear preference for 0° or 90° stimuli nor an obvious effect of microgravity on the average variability. Haptic-Visual Coordination Subjects are understandably less precise in matching the orientation of a visual stimulus to the direction of a haptically-perceived reference, due to the sensorimotor transformations involved. Both bias and variable error are significantly greater for the haptic-visual coordination task. A strong oblique effect can be observed in the measures of variable error, with significantly less variability for horizontal and vertical stimuli. These observations are confirmed in the average across the 3 subjects. Note that the effect is much stronger in the haptic-visual task than would be expected from the results of either the visual or haptic perception tasks alone. Thus, it is in the transformation of orientation from visual to haptic space that the horizontal and vertical directions become particularly salient. The lack of a systematic change in the patterns of responses due to weightlessness suggests that it is a body-centered coordinate system that mediates transformations between the two sensory modalities. Visual Magnitude When adjusting the length of visually presented lines, the subject consistently produced a vertical response length that was shorter than the horizontal reference. These responses are consistent with the well-known visual illusion for horizontal and vertical lines. The comparison of 0-G versus 1-G data does not show systematic increases in either the magnitude of the illusion or in the variability of responses. These results support the hypothesis that the visual illusion arises from differences in retinal receptive fields as opposed to differences in a gravitationally-linked reference frame. Haptic Magnitude The NASA4 subject showed similar differences for haptic perception of lengths as is normally seen for visually perceived lines. When asked to produce a square hole, the subject systematically responded with a rectangle that was shorter than it was wide. Furthermore, the magnitude of the illusion increased in microgravity, with no consistent change in variability. Thus, haptic perception of form appears to be affected by the gravitational environment or background levels of force applied to the limb. This interesting observation is confirmed by the results of the Mir 23 study. Subjects do not consistently produce short or tall rectangles in the place of squares for stimuli presented in this posture and workspace region. Nevertheless, all subjects produced rectangles that were shorter in microgravity than on the ground. Furthermore, one can observe a ‘rebound’ effect in the post-flight data. Early post-flight responses are even taller than those produced pre-flight, while in 2 out of 3 subjects, later post-flight tests produce results closer to pre-flight values. The time-course of these effects tends to indicate a gradual adaptation of haptic perception that is influenced by changes in the gravitational environment. Discussion From the haptic magnitude experiment, it appears that the action of gravity on the arm influences the perception of hand displacements in a way that is different for horizontal vs. vertical movements. In related experiments, the researchers have observed that gravity affects both the haptic perception of applied forces and the control of arm movements. Results from these three experiments suggest that haptic perception involves mechanisms that include information about the intended action, as opposed to a passive interpretation of sensory information. The human nervous system requires knowledge about the effects of gravity on the sensory and motor apparatus to correctly interpret and coordinate sensorimotor information. Gravity plays a role in the interpretation of visual stimuli and in the perception of limb position. It was therefore hypothesized that gravity might play a role in aligning visual and proprioceptive or haptic reference frames. Despite the observed effects of gravity on haptic perception, one can see that a gravitational reference is not essential to the alignment of visual and haptic reference frames. The oblique effect seen for the transformation of information between these two modalities persists in microgravity. Thus, the reference frame used to coordinate these two modalities appears to be linked to the axis of the trunk or head. The coordination of visual and haptic sensory modalities might nevertheless be aided by the presence of gravity's pull. In these initial experiments, the body axis was fixed with respect to the head and with respect to the floor of the Mir station. Cognitive information about the subject's orientation with respect to these reference frames may allow the subject to substitute the body axis for a gravitational reference frame when the gravitational reference is removed. However, much of the work to be performed in 0-G is not carried out with the body fixed in such a rigid fashion, most notably during extra-vehicular activity (EVA). This experiment was designed to test the hypothesis that gravity is the unique or dominant reference frame for visuo-haptic coordination, and the results tend to reject this hypothesis. It is well known, nevertheless, that the nervous system can adapt and substitute alternate reference frames when adequate sensory cues are not available. Indeed, the cognitive perception of ‘vertical’ combines sensory information from visual, vestibular, and haptic cues, and the effects of gravity on this perception are most easily observed when these cues are no longer aligned. Additional experiments involving head and whole-body tilt are planned, both on the ground and in microgravity, to distinguish between the different possible body reference frames for visuo-haptic coordination and to see if gravity influences the interpretation of visual and/or haptic sensation when the egocentric and allocentric reference frames are no longer aligned. These data, interpreted in the context of current theories on sensorimotor integration, should be useful for understanding the basic operating principles of the human nervous system. Such understanding is crucial for developing diagnostic tools and eventual therapies for those afflicted with deficits for sensorimotor function. Information about difficulties in sensorimotor coordination imposed by the microgravity environment may also aid in the design of more effective tools and interfaces for the astronaut community.

title: Evaluation of the Kentavr as a Countermeasure to Orthostatic Intolerance
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: One of the most important physiological changes that negatively impact flight operations and crew safety is postflight orthostatic intolerance. Orthostatic intolerance is commonly experienced by astronauts when they return to Earth and can lead to hypotension and syncope (temporary loss of consciousness, fainting, or dizziness). This problem affects about 30% of crewmembers who fly short-duration missions (4-18 days), and 83% of astronauts who fly long-duration missions. This condition creates a potential hazard for the returning crew by impairing their ability to exit the vehicle after landing. A major driver for orthostatic intolerance is plasma volume loss. Despite the use of a mandatory fluid load before re-entry, astronauts return from space with plasma volume deficits ranging from 7-20%. To provide additional protection against space flight induced orthostatic intolerance during re-entry and landing, both NASA and the Russian Federal Space Agency use compression garments, or antigravity suits. NASA astronauts use an inflatable antigravity suit (AGS) that is worn under the Advanced Crew Escape Suit. It has five interconnected air bladders that cover the abdomen, thighs, and calves. The AGS can be inflated to pressures ranging from 0.5 per square inch (psi), which is equivalent to 25.9 mmHg, to 2.5 psi (129.3 mmHg) in increments of 0.5 psi. When inflated, the AGS provides mechanical protection that reduces venous pooling and maintains arterial pressure. Russian cosmonauts wear a non-inflatable compression garment, called the Kentavr, which is made of an elastic fabric. It is composed of shorts that extend from the waist to the knee and a pair of gaiters that cover the calves. Each component of the Kentavr has lacings to allow for an individualized fit. The nominal pressure provided by the Kentavr is 0.6 ± 0.1 psi (30 ± 5 mmHg). The purpose of this study was to evaluate the ability of NASA’s AGS and the Russian Kentavr garment, to prevent hypovolemia-related orthostatic intolerance.
approach: Prior to participation, 19 healthy volunteers, ages 32 – 54 years, passed a modified Air Force Class III physical. Subjects were randomly assigned to one of two groups: AGS (six men and three women) or Kentavr (six men and four women). A separate group of 16 subjects (11 men and 5 women) from a related study participated in the same protocols and served as controls (no countermeasure group). Data collection was completed in two visits to the cardiovascular laboratory. For the first session, subjects reported to the laboratory following voluntary reduction of their dietary salt intake for 24 hours. Subjects provided a urine sample to confirm that urinary sodium was less than 100 mEq/gm -1 creatinine. Those meeting the selection criteria participated in a carbon monoxide re-breathing protocol to measure plasma volume. Subjects then received a single dose of furosemide (a loop diuretic commonly marketed under the brand name Lasix) and consumed a low salt diet provided by the investigators. Subjects returned to the laboratory 36 hours later, when the plasma volume measurement was repeated and subjects underwent a tilt test protocol to assess orthostatic tolerance with (AGS inflated to 1.5 per square inch or Kentavr) or without a compression garment (separate study). Subjects did not consume any caffeine, nicotine, or alcohol for 12 hours and did not participate in maximal exercise or take any medications for 24 hours prior to testing.
results: Hypovolemia Control subjects experienced a mean loss of plasma volume of 17.1 ± 1.7%. AGS and Kentavr groups had a plasma volume loss of 16.9 ± 4.0% and 18.4 ± 2.6%, respectively. All subjects wearing a compression garment (either AGS or Kentavr) during the tilt test completed the test without symptoms of orthostatic hypotension or presyncope (0% incidence). In contrast, only nine control subjects (56%) were able to complete the tilt test without signs or symptoms of orthostatic hypotension or presyncope. The change in systolic blood pressure of control subjects was significantly greater than in the AGS and Kentavr subjects, but no differences were found between countermeasure groups. title: Constellation Program (CxP) EVA Systems Test 2 - Metabolic Costs and Biomechanics of Exploration Tasks in a Planetary Suit
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: The Constellation Program (CxP) extravehicular activity (EVA) Systems Project Office (ESPO), which is developing design requirements for the next-generation lunar EVA suit, initiated a series of tests, working with the EVA Physiology, Systems, and Performance (EPSP) Project and the Anthropometry and Biomechanics Facility (ABF) aimed at understanding human performance and suit kinematics under a variety of simulated lunar EVA conditions. These studies included matched unsuited controls in an attempt to identify the specific metabolic costs and biomechanics of the prototype Mark III Advanced Spacesuit Technology Demonstrator (MKIII). A primary goal of the overall test series is to provide evidence-based recommendations for suit mass, center of gravity (CG), pressure, and suit kinematic constraints that optimize human performance in partial gravity environments.
approach: Subjects were recruited from two different pools of personnel – those who typically perform EVA suited studies for the JSC Engineering Directorate and a group of astronauts, many of whom have previous in-space EVA experience, selected to support exploration EVA studies. Suit fit-checks in the MKIII suit were performed on a range of subjects, and only those who had good suit fit were considered for inclusion in this study due to potential medical and safety issues. From this list, six male astronaut subjects participated in the data collection phases of the study. All subjects had also participated in IST-1 and had significant experience with both the MKIII and the POGO. At this time, no available female astronauts properly fit in the MKIII suit. For suited testing, the MKIII suit was used as it represents a suit concept that provides the dynamic ranges of motion considered necessary for a wide variety of planetary EVA tasks within today’s technology level given other constraints that must be considered in pressure garment design. The MKIII also had an existing method to integrate with the POGO and allowed for varied pressure testing. Thus, the MKIII provides a valid test bed from which attainable requirements for future suit development can be derived. Each subject performed a battery of tasks representing typical activities expected during lunar EVA performance. Tasks included, in the order of performance, are small rock pickup, large rock pick up, shoveling (biomechanics emphasis), shoveling (metabolic emphasis), kneel and recover, rock transfer, hammering, ladder placement, and busy board. This testing protocol was performed during all suited and shirtsleeve configurations except for the two suited conditions at 34.5 kPa (5.0 psi) and 44.8 kPa (6.5 psi). These higher-pressure conditions were not tested because subjects used the Phase VI gloves with the MKIII suit, which were believed to provide better manual dexterity but were only rated to 29.6 kPa (4.3 psi). Each subject walked on a level treadmill for three minutes at his lowest walking speed while carrying a weighted load in front of him. Each subject completed three different loads of 4.5, 9.1, and 13.6 kg (10, 20, and 30 lb) for three minutes each. The 4.5- and 13.6-kg loads were round rubber medicine balls, and the 9.1-kg load was a rectangular sandbag. This testing protocol was performed at the POGO suited configuration of 29.6 kPa (4.3 psi), 121-kg suit mass, and lunar gravity. It was also completed during the shirtsleeve configuration at lunar gravity.
results: of this test series will also be combined with studies in other lunar analogs to evaluate the effectiveness and limitations of these environments. The MKIII also has the most variable operational pressure range of the available prototype suits. POGO configuration, including the mass of the Portable Life Support System (PLSS) mock-up and gimbal, which is 29.6 kPa (4.3 psi) during inclined ambulation and exploration tasks in 1/6-g. Quantify the effects of the following factors on suited and/or unsuited metabolic rate, biomechanics, and subjective ratings during exploration tasks and inclined ambulation: a. Suited – varied suit pressure at constant offload, mass, and CG b. Suited – varied suit offload (weight) at constant pressure, mass, and CG c. Unsuited – varied offload (weight) at constant mass and CG d. Understand specific human performance limitations of the suit compared to matched shirtsleeve controls. Collect metabolic and ground-reaction force data to develop an EVA simulator for use on future prebreathe protocol verification tests.
