archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Although some portions of the musculoskeletal system have been examined as part of other astronaut examinations (doctor’s physical, stress test, X-rays, et cetera) there has been no specific integrated examination for this largest system of the human body. Conversely, the musculoskeletal system plays a primary role in space operations and research. The state of muscles and the subject’s use of them determines, not only their condition and potential performance, but also condition of the cardiovascular and respiratory system on Earth and in space. Defects or limitations of this system can make it impossible for a subject to perform essential functions in operation and thus are disqualifying. A number of such limitations are specified in the physical requirements, but measurement of them requires equipment and techniques not usually available to the flight surgeon. Anthropometric measurements are urgently required by many man-machine designers in the space program. Anthropometric data have also become increasingly important as a research tool for investigation of effects of weightlessness of the body. Such information is particularly important for Shuttle, which is accepting an entirely new space-flight population.
approach: In 1978, approximately 207 astronaut candidates were examined during a NASA astronaut selection for the first Space Shuttle missions. Of this number, 80% were men and 20% were women. The crew positions to be assigned included male pilots, and both male and female mission specialists. Basic physical examinations were conducted in addition to numerous specialty exams. The tests included a treadmill stress test and musculoskeletal examinations of each candidate. The treadmill test used the standard Balke-Ware protocol. The musculoskeletal exam consisted of a detailed history and physical examination, a large series of anthropometric measurements, and strength testing of major muscle groups by means of an isokinetic ergometer.
results: The results of the examinations were immediately supplied to the medical examination board to use in the selection process. As expected from historical and general experience, the females were significantly weaker than the males, especially in the upper extremities. Also, as in general experience, there were one or two exceptionally strong females well outside the normal range in the entire group of females. This difference was most marked in the upper extremities when absolute comparisons were made. If strength relative to body weight in pilot candidates, male mission specialist candidates, and female mission specialist candidates were compared, the difference was less but marked. Since body fat was so different in males versus females (15 percent versus 25 percent in this case), the question was raised as to what happens if the female singly loses weight. This was indicated by calculating strength per lean body mass. In this case, back and leg differences in strength were much less, but arm and shoulder strength remained significantly different. Some minor surprises were the differences in shoulder and back strength in pilots and mission specialists. Mission specialists were stronger in both areas even when they were normalized for body weight and lean body mass. As a matter of fact, the females had greater back strength on the basis of lean body mass than the pilots.

title: Endocrine, Electrolyte, and Fluid Volume Changes Associated with Apollo Missions
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: The objective of this study was to evaluate the biochemical changes in Apollo crewmembers. The areas studied were balance of fluid and electrolytes, regulation of calcium metabolism, adaptation to the environment, and regulation of metabolic processes. Although these studies, like others of the Apollo program, were designed mainly for crew health maintenance and well-being, the
approach: The same general protocol described below was used for the Apollo 7-10 and 15-17 missions. It has been reported that deviations from this procedure were necessary during the Apollo 11-14 missions due to the constraints imposed by the lunar quarantine program. The general protocol was as follows: with the crewmembers reclining for 30 minutes, a 45 ml sample of venous blood was drawn 30, 15, and 5 days before flight. Blood samples were also drawn approximately 2 hours, and 1, 7 and 14 days postflight. All preflight blood samples were drawn after a fasting period from midnight to 7:00 a.m., approximately one hour after waking up. Postflight samples were drawn regardless of time of day and food intake. The sample drawn two hours after recovery was taken approximately six hours after the crew's last meal and eight hours after waking up. Pre- and postflight 24-hour urine samples were collected from each crewman on the same days as the blood samples. Additionally, urine samples were collected in flight during the Apollo 16 and 17 missions only. Samples were collected using the Biomedical Urine Sampling System (BUSS), which contained a large 4-liter pooling bag in which the urine was collected. Each pooling bag also contained 10 g of boric acid for stabilizing certain organic constituents. The pooled urine was collected without additive, aliquoted, stabilized with boric acid, and frozen for analysis. One entire 24-hour urine sample was returned for each Apollo 16 crewman. For Apollo 17 collections, a sampling bag was used which could store as much as 120 cc of urine for later analysis. The Apollo 17 collection bags contained 30 ml of lithium chloride. The final lithium concentration was used to estimate total urine volume. Blood samples were analyzed for osmolality, sodium, potassium, chloride, adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), angiotensin I, cortisol, growth hormone (GH), insulin, parathormone, thyroxine, and tri-iodothyronine. The 24-hour urine samples were analyzed for electrolytes, osmolality, volume, aldosterone, cortisol, antidiuretic hormone (ADH), total and fractionated ketosteroids, and amino acids. Prolonged exposure to increased temperature and to the boric acid preservative made the urine samples collected inflight unsuitable for catecholamine or ADH analysis.
results: of these studies provided an idea of the nature and the extent of the endocrine responses by the crewmen who flew the Apollo missions. APPROACH: The same general protocol described below was used for the Apollo 7-10 and 15-17 missions. It has been reported that deviations from this procedure were necessary during the Apollo 11-14 missions due to the constraints imposed by the lunar quarantine program. The general protocol was as follows: with the crewmembers reclining for 30 minutes, a 45 ml sample of venous blood was drawn 30, 15, and 5 days before flight. Blood samples were also drawn approximately 2 hours, and 1, 7 and 14 days postflight. All preflight blood samples were drawn after a fasting period from midnight to 7:00 a.m., approximately one hour after waking up. Postflight samples were drawn regardless of time of day and food intake. The sample drawn two hours after recovery was taken approximately six hours after the crew's last meal and eight hours after waking up. Pre- and postflight 24-hour urine samples were collected from each crewman on the same days as the blood samples. Additionally, urine samples were collected in flight during the Apollo 16 and 17 missions only. Samples were collected using the Biomedical Urine Sampling System (BUSS), which contained a large 4-liter pooling bag in which the urine was collected. Each pooling bag also contained 10 g of boric acid for stabilizing certain organic constituents. The pooled urine was collected without additive, aliquoted, stabilized with boric acid, and frozen for analysis. One entire 24-hour urine sample was returned for each Apollo 16 crewman. For Apollo 17 collections, a sampling bag was used which could store as much as 120 cc of urine for later analysis. The Apollo 17 collection bags contained 30 ml of lithium chloride. The final lithium concentration was used to estimate total urine volume. Blood samples were analyzed for osmolality, sodium, potassium, chloride, adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), angiotensin I, cortisol, growth hormone (GH), insulin, parathormone, thyroxine, and tri-iodothyronine. The 24-hour urine samples were analyzed for electrolytes, osmolality, volume, aldosterone, cortisol, antidiuretic hormone (ADH), total and fractionated ketosteroids, and amino acids. Prolonged exposure to increased temperature and to the boric acid preservative made the urine samples collected inflight unsuitable for catecholamine or ADH analysis. RESULTS: Apollo crewmen showed an average of 5% decrease in body weight after flight when the mean of the preflight results was compared to the individual postflight values. One-third of this weight was regained within 24 hours after recovery. Significant differences were observed in a 7.3 % decrease in potassium and a 4.5% decrease in magnesium immediately postflight. No significant changes in serum sodium or chloride accompanied these changes. The 24-hour urine electrolyte results exhibited significant decreases in sodium, potassium, chloride and magnesium values. Renin activity, measured as angiotensin I in blood samples, and aldosterone levels, measured in urine, were aids in the understanding of water and electrolyte balance and renal function. Plasma angiotensin I values showed a 488 % increase in the crewmen tested on the day of recovery. This elevation was followed by a significant increase (57%) in urinary aldosterone during the first day following recovery. A postflight 32% decrease in urine volume was detected along with significant increases in osmolality (20%) and ADH (152%). The creatinine clearance results showed no significant change in renal function after flight. A slight but significant increase in blood urea nitrogen (BUN) was found. Urinary calcium, phosphorus, and parathormone (PTH) results reflect normal bone metabolism and seem to reflect normal renal function, as well. Plasma cortisol and ACTH results showed no significant changes, but a mean decrease was found for each hormone. Urinary cortisol demonstrated a 24% increase, whereas the total 17-hydroxycorticosteriod excretion was decreased by 30%. Both catecholamine compounds showed decreases after flight when the data from all crewmen were grouped for analysis. Results of total and fractionated ketosteroid demonstrated a 30% decrease in the total component, which is spread over four fractions: androsterone, etiocholanolone, dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA), and 11=OH etiocholanolone. A slight increase was observed in pregnanediol and 11=O etiocholanolone. Glucose showed a 10% increase after flight and insulin showed an increase of 32% after flight. Human growth hormone demonstrated a 304% increase after flight. The postflight increase in thyroxine was statistically significant, whereas slight change was noted in percentage of tri-iodothyronine binding. Variable results were obtained when pre- and postflight levels of six urinary acids were compared. These amino acids were phosphoethanolamine, taurine, glycine, alanine, tyrosine, and ß-alanine. Taurine, however, was consistently elevated after flight by 140%. After considering all of the previously mentioned data, together with the clinical condition of the returning Apollo crewmen, the following hypothesis was proposed to explain the changes: in a weightless environment, there is a tendency for plasma volume to shift from occupying the gravity-dependent extremities to occupying a more even distribution throughout the vascular system. Receptors, possibly in the right atrium, interpret this shift as an increase in vascular volume. This increased volume is counteracted by an increased water loss, followed by a compensatory, adrenal-pituitary-mediated retention of water and sodium and by a continued loss of potassium. Other hormone changes observed are tentatively ascribed to the stresses associated with the condition of the Apollo space flights, to the well known consequences of hypokinesis, and to the metabolic effects of hypocaloric nutritional intake. The crewmembers' in-flight diet of low-residue, high-fat and high-carbohydrate foods may have been the cause of decreased levels of cholesterol, triglycerides and uric acid. However, these values did not return to preflight levels in two weeks after the mission, even though the crew began eating a conventional diet immediately after recovery. This fact suggested possibly that other metabolic consequences were involved. Adrenal steroids have been shown to be elevated during flight which may have accounted for the decrease in the stores of precursor cholesterol, particularly if not replaced by the diet. The decreased cholesterol was in agreement with elevated thyroxine levels, and contributed to the evidence of increased thyroid function during flight.

title: Apollo Flight Crew Vestibular Assessment
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: The United States manned space flight program addressed the potential problems that could arise during flight due to vestibular disturbances, particularly motion sickness. Concern was expressed because of the highly unusual microgravity environment encountered during space flight. Interestingly, astronauts from the early Mercury and Gemini programs reported no significant vestibular problems. However, the Apollo program presented several significant changes from previous programs, including increases in the size of the spacecraft's interior and differences in the activities being performed during the mission. Due to the larger habitable volume of the Apollo Command Module (CM), as compared to the Mercury and Gemini modules, crewmen were able to move about freely within the spacecraft. In addition, inflight docking procedures allowed the crewmen to move back and forth between the Lunar Module (LM) and the Command Module. It was also noted that crewmen would make the transition from zero-g (0-G) to the one sixth-G environment on the lunar surface and then back to 0-G numerous times during the six Apollo lunar-landing missions. With these changes, particularly the greater mobility permitted by the larger volume of the CM and the LM, the potential for the first serious vestibular problems became evident. Therefore, a set of qualitative assessment procedures was developed for the Apollo series of missions in order to document the vestibular disturbances experienced by the astronauts. Opportunities for inflight quantitative monitoring of the vestibular system were severely limited because of the principal mission objectives and the technical nature of the tasks that were performed on each mission. The objective of the vestibular investigations performed during the Apollo program was to obtain definitive information regarding the effects of microgravity on the vestibular system while using primarily qualitative data collection procedures.
approach: Qualitative assessment procedures: The qualitative information used in the study was gathered from a variety of sources. An attempt was made to compile detailed information on the history of the astronauts' motion sickness experiences. These histories indicated whether an individual astronaut had ever experienced motion sickness in automobiles, boats, during 0-G parabolic flight, or during spacecraft egress exercises. In addition, heavy emphasis was placed on subjective reporting by astronauts regarding the type and magnitude of vestibular disturbances experienced during and following their missions. The inflight subjective reports documented whether the astronauts experienced stomach awareness, nausea, vomiting, or illusions while performing tumbling exercises. Special preflight and postflight laboratory measurements: To accomplish a comprehensive evaluation of vestibular function, two types of pre- and postflight tests were performed on the Apollo 16 and 17 astronauts. Postural equilibrium tests were selected as a means of providing an assessment of a behavioral skill that is sensitive to altered vestibular inputs
results: ing from prolonged exposure to weightlessness. The second test, caloric irrigation, complemented the tests of balance by monitoring changes in semicircular canal activity as a possible cause of postflight equilibrium disturbances. For the postural equilibrium test, each astronaut was fitted with military-type shoes to rule out differences in footwear as a variable in subject comparisons. Duration of time was the parameter designated as the performance measure of the balancing tasks. The subject was instructed to stand on the prescribed support with eyes open and his feet in a tandem heel-to-toe arrangement and then to fold his arms and maintain his balance. Timing began when the subject folded his arms. In the second series of tests, the time measurement was initiated after the subject attained a balanced position and closed his eyes. Rails of four widths (1.90, 3.17, 4.45, and 5.72 cm) and the floor provided the foot support for the standing subject. A strip of tape 10.16 cm wide and 68.5 cm long served as a foot-guide alignment for the floor portion of the test. The caloric irrigation test required electrodes for recording nystagmic eye movements. The silver chloride electrodes (Beckman) were placed at the outer canthus of each eye and the reference electrode was placed in the center of the forehead. A Tracor RN-243 electronystagmograph system was used throughout the caloric test to record potential changes across the cornea and the retina. Eye movement calibration and all subsequent caloric testing were done in a dark room. Electronystagmographic calibration of eye movements in degrees per centimeter was obtained with the subject sitting in an upright position and fixating on two alternately flashing red lights placed at a distance from the center of eye rotation, providing a separation of 20 degrees of arc. The subject was then reclined in a Tracor torsion swing chair so that his head was approximately 60 degrees from upright. Baseline measurements were taken for 40 seconds to determine the presence of spontaneous nystagmus. Two separate water baths were maintained at temperatures that ensured irrigating temperatures of 35.5 degrees Celsius (C) and 34.0 degrees C. Calorization of each subject proceeded according to the following schedule: right ear (RE), 35.5 degrees C; left ear (LE), 35.5 degrees C; RE, 34.0 degrees C; and LE, 34.0 degrees C. In each case, approximately 160 ml of water was directed onto the tympanic membrane for a period of 40 seconds. To maintain mental alertness, the subject silently solved arithmetic problems during the response period. Following irrigation of each ear at 35.5 degrees C and a period of continuous recording that indicated the disappearance of all nystagmic response, an additional period (140 seconds) of rest was started; this rest period was increased to 260 seconds following the 34.0 degree C irrigation. After all caloric testing, eye movement calibrations again were made in accordance with the pretest procedure. Nystagmus parameters measured during the caloric irrigation test included direction of eye movement, lag time, average velocity, maximum velocity, maximum frequency, duration of nystagmus, and right-left asymmetry. Lag time is defined as the time between the onset of irrigation and the first measurable nystagmus. Maximum velocity was obtained by selecting the 10-second time frame of a given record that contained the greatest preponderance of high-velocity, slow-phase nystagmus, and by calculating the average slow-phase velocity value for that time frame. Maximum frequency was obtained by a similar calculation. The duration of nystagmus was the interval between onset and complete cessation of nystagmus. Right-left asymmetry was a measurement which compared right and left ear nystagmus responses and documented which ear elicited the greater response. Preflight data were collected on the Apollo 16 prime and backup astronauts 30 days before launch (L-30). Postflight data were collected on all three prime astronauts three days following recovery; two of the three crewmen were tested again four days later. Preflight data on the Apollo 17 prime and backup crewmen were collected at L-30 and at L-15. No postflight data were collected on the Apollo 17 crewmen. RESULTS: Motion sickness (MS) history and inflight MS: The results of the MS history examination indicated that twenty-seven of the thirty-three Apollo crewmen had a positive MS history. However, only nine of those twenty-seven crewmen experienced inflight MS symptoms. Of the six crewmen who had a negative MS history, only two experienced MS symptoms during flight. Therefore, the total number of Apollo astronauts who experienced inflight MS symptoms was eleven. Severity of inflight symptoms: The total number of occurrences of mild MS (stomach awareness) was six. Moderate MS symptoms (stomach awareness, nausea) occurred only twice throughout the entire series of Apollo missions. However, severe MS symptoms (stomach awareness, nausea, vomiting) occurred three times. Previous space flight experience: Of the thirty-three Apollo crewmen, fifteen were classified as inexperienced astronauts (first space flight). Six of the fifteen inexperienced crewmen experienced MS symptoms during flight. Of the eighteen veteran crewmen (one or more space flights), only five experienced inflight MS symptoms. Special pre- and postflight laboratory measurements: Postflight data were not collected on the Apollo 17 crew. Therefore, a complete data analysis was completed only for the Apollo 16 crew. Preflight results for the postural equilibrium test indicated that all three crewmen were within the range of performance typically exhibited by young, healthy, pilot-type subjects. Postflight results indicated that during the first and second test periods, 3 (denoted as R+3) and 7 (denoted as R+7) days after landing, respectively, postural equilibrium with eyes open was nearly identical to preflight performance in all crewmen. However, at R+3, the Commander (CDR) and the Command Module Pilot (CMP) showed a marked decrease during the eyes-closed test. When these two individuals were tested again at R+7, there was a definite improvement in postural stability with eyes closed compared to their R+3 results. The preflight results for the caloric irrigation test indicated that all Apollo 16 crewmen possessed normally functioning vestibular canals. The nystagmus produced was always in the expected direction. Spontaneous nystagmus was present in all three crewmen, but no meaningful trends were observed. All of the crewmen exhibited an asymmetry in right and left ear nystagmus responses which generally remained unchanged through the R+7 test date.

title: Printed Electrochemical Sensor Strip for Quantifying Bone Density Loss in Microgravity
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Without the load-bearing forces of gravity experienced on earth, astronauts have an increased risk of bone-related injuries
approach: Aim 1: Develop conductive, telopeptide selective and dielectric inks for printed sensor. a) Develop conductive and dielectric inks Both commercial and home-made inks were evaluated for this study. JS-B40G silver nanoparticle (AgNP) ink, XP PriElex SU-8 1.0, and 7500 Series carbon nanotube (CNT) were used without modification as inkjet conductive and dielectric inks. BQ242 carbon, FE3124 silver, and 5880 silver|silver chloride (Ag|AgCl) were used without modification. Home-made carboxylic acid functionalized multiwalled carbon nanotube (MWCNT-COOH) ink was modified in house by refluxing commercial MWCNT-COOH in 56% nitric acid for 8 hours, sonicating by probe sonication for 3 hours, and finally resuspending in water. Home-made gold nanoparticle (AuNP) ink was synthesized using the Tukevich method and then resuspending in water. Homemade inks were evaluated by dynamic light scattering and zeta potential (ζ-potential) analysis to measure particle size and surface charge. b) Develop telopeptide selective ink and conjugation reactant Telopeptide selective inks of AuNP functionalized with NTx were prepared. A solution of 10 nM citrate capped AuNP (AuNP@citrate), 0.028% SDS in water and 0.015 mg/mL of HS-PEG-COOH was incubated overnight at room temperature. The solution was washed with DI water, centrifuged at 14000xg for 30 minutes at 4°C, and resuspended in 25 mM MES pH 5.5 to remove excess PEG, yielding pegylated AuNP (AuNP@PEG-COOH). To 20 mL of 1 nM AuNP@PEG-COOH 250 μL of EDC (0.2M) and 500 μL of NHS (0.2M) were added. The solution was allowed to incubate for 30 minutes at room temperature, centrifuged at 14000xg for 30 minutes at 4°C, and suspended in 10 mM phosphate buffer pH 7.4, yielding EDC/NHS activated AuNP@PEG-COOH. 100 μL of NTx (1 mg/mL) was added to the EDC/NHS activated AuNP@PEG-COOH solution and incubated overnight at room temperature. The
results: ing from changes in bone mineral density. Microgravity disrupts the balance between bone formation and bone resorption which can lead to the development of space osteopenia/osteoporosis after extended exposure to microgravity, which can manifest in a reduction of bone density by 1 to 1.6%. Development of a sensor that monitors reliable biomarkers of bone loss is a critically important step to help mitigate this specific risk. This experiment aimed to develop a flight suitable sensor that evaluated the change in bone mass indirectly through an excreted biomarker of bone remodeling, amino-terminal collagen crosslinks (NTX). NTX, a degradation by-product of Type I collagen, is widely measured in clinical bone resorption studies and is considered a biomarker of interest when evaluating bone health. Bone density loss is currently evaluated through the measurement of bone mineral density by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) of flight crew before and after spaceflight. However, DXA only provides partial information regarding bone strength and cannot detect the early shift of bone metabolism. Several bone remodeling biomarkers have been identified and used to provide an early assessment of bone loss, when DXA data is insufficient to make a diagnosis. Moreover, the equipment necessary for DXA is bulky, heavy, and energy inefficient, making it incompatible for flight. The proposed printed bone health sensor would be more suitable for spaceflight due to its versatility, size, and ease of use. Not only is the necessary hardware more compact than DXA equipment, but the sensor is also conducive to potential in-flight manufacturing using commercially available materials for inkjet printing. This study had the following specific aims: Develop conductive, telopeptide selective and dielectric inks for printed sensor. Print and electrochemically characterize 3-electrode device for NTX detection. Integrate sensor with urine collection device and handheld potentiostat hardware. APPROACH: Aim 1: Develop conductive, telopeptide selective and dielectric inks for printed sensor. a) Develop conductive and dielectric inks Both commercial and home-made inks were evaluated for this study. JS-B40G silver nanoparticle (AgNP) ink, XP PriElex SU-8 1.0, and 7500 Series carbon nanotube (CNT) were used without modification as inkjet conductive and dielectric inks. BQ242 carbon, FE3124 silver, and 5880 silver|silver chloride (Ag|AgCl) were used without modification. Home-made carboxylic acid functionalized multiwalled carbon nanotube (MWCNT-COOH) ink was modified in house by refluxing commercial MWCNT-COOH in 56% nitric acid for 8 hours, sonicating by probe sonication for 3 hours, and finally resuspending in water. Home-made gold nanoparticle (AuNP) ink was synthesized using the Tukevich method and then resuspending in water. Homemade inks were evaluated by dynamic light scattering and zeta potential (ζ-potential) analysis to measure particle size and surface charge. b) Develop telopeptide selective ink and conjugation reactant Telopeptide selective inks of AuNP functionalized with NTx were prepared. A solution of 10 nM citrate capped AuNP (AuNP@citrate), 0.028% SDS in water and 0.015 mg/mL of HS-PEG-COOH was incubated overnight at room temperature. The solution was washed with DI water, centrifuged at 14000xg for 30 minutes at 4°C, and resuspended in 25 mM MES pH 5.5 to remove excess PEG, yielding pegylated AuNP (AuNP@PEG-COOH). To 20 mL of 1 nM AuNP@PEG-COOH 250 μL of EDC (0.2M) and 500 μL of NHS (0.2M) were added. The solution was allowed to incubate for 30 minutes at room temperature, centrifuged at 14000xg for 30 minutes at 4°C, and suspended in 10 mM phosphate buffer pH 7.4, yielding EDC/NHS activated AuNP@PEG-COOH. 100 μL of NTx (1 mg/mL) was added to the EDC/NHS activated AuNP@PEG-COOH solution and incubated overnight at room temperature. The resulting AuNP@PEG-NTx solution was centrifuged twice at 14000 xg for 30 minutes at 4°C and finally suspended in DI water as the telopeptide selective ink. The telopeptide ink was evaluated at each step of preparation, AuNP@citrate, AuNP@PEG-COOH, and AuNP@PEG-NTx, by UV-Vis, dynamic light scattering and zeta potential (ζ-potential) analysis (ZetaSizer Nano, Malvern PANanalytical, Westborough, MA) to measure particle size and surface charge. The AuNP@PEG-NTx will be referred to as AuNPNTx for simplicity. c) Develop Anti-NTx conjugate Conjugate antibody was prepared for the sensor’s competitive assay. Methylene blue-NHS was covalently bound to Anti-NTx using EDC/NHS coupling chemistry to form Anti-NTx-MB. 100 μl of antibody (0.4 mg/ml) were incubated with 10 μL of methylene blue (1 mM) for 1 hour. The labeling reaction was dialyzed using a 10 kDa molecular weight cut off dialysis membrane against PBS. The PBS was substituted with fresh PBS twice (every 2 hours) and left to dialyze overnight. Aim 2: Print and electrochemically characterize 3-electrode device for NTx detection. a) Print sensor 3-electrode electrochemical sensors, containing a working electrode (WE), counter electrode (CE) and reference electrode (RE), have been prepared by the following two methods: 1) precision microdispense printing by an nScrypt 3Dn-Series printer and 2) dropcast method. All sensors were print onto Kapton 500HN as the substrate material. To generate the base architecture of the electrochemical sensors, precision microdispense printing was performed. A nScrypt 3Dn-Series printer was used to laser cut 3 holes through a Kapton substrate. Next, FE3124 silver ink was microdispense printed inside the 3 holes to create a via structure and around the holes on one side of the Kapton to form the contact pads. Finally, the substrate was flipped over to expose the front side of the device. 5880 Ag|AgCl ink was microdispensed to form the RE and BQ242 ink was microdispensed to form the WE and CE. All prints were performed at the NextFlex Research Institute in San Jose, CA and delivered to the NASA ARC team for evaluation, electrochemical characterization, and further modification with 7500 Series CNT and AuNP-NTx inks. To generate the telopeptide sensing surface, modification of the WE were performed first by a drop cast method and finally by inkjet printing. For the drop cast method, 0.5 μL of 7500 Series CNT ink was pipet on the WE surface and annealed at 125°C on a hotplate for 15 min. Finally, 1 μL of AuNP-NTx (37 nM) ink was pipet on the CNT modified WE surface and dried at 42°C for 10 min. The resulting electrochemical sensors were characterized immediately or stored in a petri dish at 4°C. For inkjet printing, the 45 layers of the 7500 Series CNT ink were deposited on the surface of the WE. The printing bed was heated to 60 °C and the print head was heated to 42°C. The CNTs were then dried at 125 °C in a convection oven at 125 °C for 15 min. The electrodes sheet was then loaded and aligned in the inkjet printer. 10 layers of the AuNP-NTx selective ink were then deposited on top of the CNT modified WE. For this deposition the print bed temperature was lowered to 40 °C and the printhead was kept at 42 °C. The resulting electrochemical sensors were characterized immediately or stored in a petri dish at 4°C. b) Develop fluidics Fluid delivery was accomplished using a lateral flow assay assembly. A lateral flow assay’s fluid handling components consist of various layered wicking materials that are assembled in a plastic cartridge. A sample pad consisting of bound glass fiber was placed under the sample inlet port of the top of the cartridge. A conjugation pad consisting of glass fiber and containing the dried anti-NTx conjugate was placed overlapping and underneath the sample pad. A membrane of nitrocellulose served as the fluid delivery layer and contacted the printed sensor, the conjugate pad and a waste pad consisting of high purity cotton fibers. All the layered wicking materials and the printed sensor were arranged in a clamshell configured plastic cartridge with top and bottom components that snap closed for a tight fit. The lateral flow’s fluid delivery was evaluated by assembling and running an optical assay through the assembled fluid handling layers. The conjugate pad was cut to size and saturated with 1× PBS pH 7.4, 1% BSA, 2% sucrose, 0.25% Tween 20 and dried in a convection oven at 37 °C for 2 hours. 2 μl of 70 μg/mL Anti-NTx-HRP were diluted in 18 μL of PBS and these 20 μL were pipet onto the conjugate pad and dried in a convection oven at 37 °C for 1 hour. The conjugate pads were used immediately or stored in a sealed microcentrifuge tube at room temperature. For the lateral flow fluid delivery experiment, 100 μL PBS was introduced and let flow for 10 min. It was then dried at 42 °C for 1 hour. Next, 100 μL of 3,3’5,5’-Tetramethylbenzidine (TMB) solution was placed in the sample inlet and allowed to flow for 15 minutes. Finally, the cassette was disassembled and the TMB colorimetric product was observed on the waste pad. c) Validate sensor performance The sensor was designed as a competitive assay. Briefly, AuNP-NTx on the WE surface served as a recognition element. If NTx is present from the specimen, it binds to the Anti-NTx-MB from the conjugate pad and thus eliminates the Anti-NTx-MB ability to bind to the NTx on the AuNP-NTx on the WE. To optimize the assay and demonstrate electrochemical readout, incubation steps were first performed without the nitrocellulose fluidics. 20 μL of Anti-NTx-MB (128 μg/mL) with various amounts of NTx specimen (0 to 100 nM) and allowed to incubate 30 minutes. The resulting mixture was incubated for 30 min on the AuNP-NTx WE surface. The sensor was washed with PBS and electrochemical measurements were performed in K4Fe(CN)6/K3Fe(CN)6 in PBS. Electrochemical measurements of cyclic voltammetry, differential pulse voltammetry and electrochemical impedance were acquired using an EmSTAT Pico Development Kit. Cyclic voltammograms were performed sweeping potentials of -0.2 to 0.6 V at 50 mV/sec. Cathodic and Anodic peak heights and peak-to-peak separation were recorded. Differential pulse voltammetry was performed from -0.2 to 0.6 V with step size of 0.005 V. Electrochemical impedance spectra were acquired from 100 kHz to 0.1 Hz. Resulting Nyquist plots were analyzed by NOVA software and charge transfer resistance (RCT) were recorded. Aim 3: Integrate sensor with urine collection device and handheld potentiostat hardware. d) Package the sensor The printed sensor was packaged in a lateral flow cassette with lateral flow materials. The lateral flow cassette was cut to allow the electrical contact pads of the electrochemical sensor to extend outside of the lateral flow device. An EmSTAT Pico Development Kit was used as the potentiostat to drive and read the sensor. The electrical contact pads of the packaged sensor were interfaced with the EmSTAT Pico by a screen printed electrode (SPE) adapter/connector for simple and reproducible measurement setup. Lastly, the lateral flow design of the packaged sensor was chosen to easily interface with the urine collection vessel. The urine collection vessel has a spigot at the bottom, used to evacuate the vessel. The lateral flow sensor can be placed in direct contact with the spigot of the urine collection vessel to deliver 1 drop of urine to the inlet port of the lateral flow sensor. RESULTS: The NTx printed sensor strip was successfully prototyped using an In-Space Manufacturing approach. A combination of CNT and AuNP inks were used to improve the sensors electrochemical response and provide a simple method of manufacturing the telopeptide selective ink. Sensor manufacturing proved to be very reproducible with sensor devices achieving a suitable variance for real testing applications. The lateral flow fluid delivery provided a simple method of delivering liquid specimens to the sensor surface without the need for more complex microfluidics and/or crew provided laboratory operations. The packaged sensor design provided a reliable interface between the urine collection device and handheld potentiostat reader. Lastly, detection of NTx was accomplished in low concentrations, down to 0.1 nM NTx, for a sensitive measurement.

title: Metabolic Assessment of Suited Mobility Using Functional Tasks
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Existing methods for evaluating extravehicular activity (EVA) suit mobility and verifying requirements have typically relied on measurement techniques such as motion capture and joint torque measurements looking at several isolated joint range of motions. These methods are straightforward and can be clearly defined, but they have little to do with how well a crewmember can actually perform in an EVA suit. EVA tasks often rely on the movement of several joints concurrently to complete the task. This study evaluated alternate methods of evaluating suited mobility through measurement of metabolic rate and time to completion of functional tasks. This study had the following specific aims: Determine the feasibility of assessing suited mobility requirements using functional tasks. Determine a task battery and effective execution methods of the selected tasks. Determine the metabolic variability in repeated measures for the same task in the same suit by the same subject. Determine the metabolic variability for the same task in the same suit by different subjects.
approach: Traditional joint torque and isolated joint range of motion measurements may be quantifiable and measurable, but they do not provide information that describes how the EVA suit as a whole allows the crewmember to function. Investigators proposed that by focusing on crewmember physiological performance of functional tasks, they can define metrics that verify that a suit is meeting suit mobility requirements. Six male subjects completed two-three trials of five functional tasks (walk, side step, stair climb, and upper body and full body object relocations) in each of three different space suits including two prototype planetary EVA suits, the Mark III (64 kg) and Rear Entry I-suit (REI, 43 kg), and a modified intravehicular activity suit (Demonstrator, 27 kg) with enhanced mobility for contingency EVA. All tasks were performed in 1g. Rate of carbon dioxide (CO2) production was determined by measuring suit inlet flow and outlet CO2 concentration. Respiratory exchange rate was assumed to be 0.85 for the conversion to kilocalorie (kcal). Mixed-effects regression methods were used to compare metabolic cost across the three different space suits, incorporating random intercept terms to accommodate the within-subjects experimental design, and random variance terms to accommodate the observed heterogeneity of variance among the three suits. Five separate models were evaluated; one per functional task.
results: The metabolic cost (MC) of all functional tasks was significantly higher in the Demonstrator suit, averaging 33-62% more depending on task. The Mark III and REI suits elicited similar MC, except in response to the side step and stair climb tasks. In these tasks, MC was significantly lower in the REI relative to the Mark III. Although the Demonstrator is the lightest space suit evaluated here, it required the highest MC to complete functional tasks, suggesting poor relative functional mobility. Differences between the Mark III and REI were evident on tasks that required vertical travel, with REI suit having lower MC for side step and stair climb. When normalizing MC results to system mass (subject + suit), then MC per kg favors the Mark III; therefore, these small differences in MC at 1g may not be as evident on the moon or Mars.

title: Cardiovascular Regulation in Microgravity
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: The D-2 experiment, Cardiovascular Regulation in Microgravity , flown on Spacelab, was designed to test the general hypothesis that human cardiovascular adaptation to microgravity is rapid and effective but associated with significant dysfunction on return to Earth. The principal specific objectives were to (1) contribute to better understanding of the control of body fluid volumes at microgravity by characterizing the responses to rapid expansion of intravascular volume before, during, and after space flight, and (2) to define the mechanisms underlying post-flight orthostatic hypotension.
approach: Responses to rapid intravenous fluid loading Preflight measurements were obtained, supine and sitting, in the four D-2 payload crewmembers at six and nine months before flight and in-flight on mission day 5. A system for warming saline to 37 degrees Celsius and an air-free intravenous infusion system was developed through a collaborative effort involving the University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center and NASA Johnson Space Center. The isotonic saline solution, 22 ml/kg, was delivered over 20 minutes by air pressure from two inflatable bladders compressing a plastic saline bag. The driving pressure was generated by a hand-held inflation bulb and displayed by an aneroid manometer. Mean delivery in microgravity was 95.9% of the intended volume which ranged from 1595 to 1919 ml. Finger arterial pressure was monitored. Cardiac output was measured by the foreign gas rebreathing technique. Mechanisms of post-flight orthostatic intolerance The stand test had a scheduled duration of 10 minutes with detailed cardiovascular measurements at rest supine, after five minutes standing, and during the last minute of the test. An electrocardiogram and Finapres arterial pressure were recorded continuously. Cardiac output was measured with the acetylene rebreathing technique. Leg volume was measured at rest and during standing using a stocking plethysmograph.
results: Studies of the four D-2 payload crewmembers before and immediately after flight were an essential part of a detailed study of orthostatic intolerance that also involved crewmembers from the flights of the Spacelab life sciences missions SLS-1 and SLS-2, in 1991 and 1993 respectively. Combined, 14 crewmembers, 11 men and 3 women, were examined preflight and within four hours of landing after flights of 9 to 14 days. Preflight, all crewmembers were able to complete the ten-minute stand test. Post-flight, nine of the fourteen (64%) were unable to finish. Pre- and post-flight supine haemodynamics were similar in both groups except slightly (p The cardiovascular effects of fluid load on-orbit were significantly different from the preflight supine data and closely approached, but did not consistently reach, the preflight sitting response levels. The stroke volume data from microgravity were virtually identical to preflight measurements in the sitting position. At the time of this experiment, the exact mechanism(s) underlying the inadequate vasoconstrictor response early after return to 1-G were yet to be defined. Maximal oxygen uptake was reduced post-flight but maintained at preflight levels after five to eight days in space, which was consistent with grossly intact cardiovascular regulatory mechanisms at microgravity. Responses to a graded intravenous infusion of the alpha-adrenergic agonist phenylephrine were measured as changes in leg and total peripheral resistance; responses noted two days after return to 1-G were not different from preflight. However, a series of stand tests performed early after return from space demonstrated lower plasma norepinephrine levels in non-finishers than in finishers. The results from D-2, SLS-1, and SLS-2 provided the base for a new series of detailed and specific studies of cardiovascular control mechanisms planned for Neurolab, a Spacelab flight, flown in 1998, and for a series of long duration flights in the Russian space station Mir.

title: Vitamin D Metabolites and Bone Demineralization
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Research data from previous calcium imbalance studies have shown that exposure to microgravity during space flight may cause bone mineral loss, increased plasma calcium, increased urinary calcium excretion, and an overall negative calcium balance. The objective of this experiment was to determine whether plasma levels of vitamin D metabolites, and parathyroid hormone (PTH) were altered in the crew of the 8 day Spacelab 2 mission. Significant changes in these hormones during space flight may indicate that the calcium homeostatic mechanism is adversely affected by exposure to microgravity. The calcium homeostatic mechanism operates through the integration of intestinal calcium absorption, calcium deposition and resorption from bone, and calcium excretion. The mechanism is regulated by the interaction of several hormonal factors, including PTH, calcitonin, and vitamin D. Vitamin D plays a key role because one of its metabolites, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (1,25(OH)2D), regulates intestinal calcium absorption and, in conjunction with PTH, induces bone mineral resorption to maintain normal blood calcium levels. An increase in circulating levels of these two hormones could be responsible for initiating changes in the calcium homeostatic mechanism by activating bone remodeling sites and by regulating calcium transport in the intestine, kidneys, and in bone. Long term space flight may cause hormonal imbalances in this mechanism which can lead to detrimental effects such as bone demineralization and kidney stone formation.
approach: During the preflight testing phase, investigators studied hormone levels in blood samples from both humans and animals to devise new and better methods for metabolite analysis. The
results: of the tests helped investigators choose the best methods for analysis of the in flight samples and provided them with a broad range of data to use for comparative analysis. Four crewmembers participated in the study and were divided equally into two teams, the red team and the blue team. The protocol called for samples to be collected at 24, 18, and 3 days prelaunch, immediately after landing, and at days 3 and 10 postlanding. The in flight protocol required each subject to collect two blood samples during the mission. One sample was collected early in the mission while the other was collected toward the end of the mission. The blue team collected their early samples at 18 hours into the mission while the red team collected samples at 31 hours. The late samples were collected at 6 days, 19 hours and 7 days, 7 hours for the blue and red teams, respectively. Two tubes of blood were taken during each sample session; one tube was used for the vitamin D metabolite analysis while the other tube was used for measurements of PTH, albumin, calcium, and phosphorus. All samples were collected in glass tubes, centrifuged to separate the plasma from the blood cells, and frozen until the analysis was performed. The volume collected for all samples was 25 ml and each sample yielded 4 to 5 ml of plasma. The vitamin D metabolite analysis included measurements for 24,25(OH)2D, 25 OHD, and 1,25(OH)2D. RESULTS: The results of the plasma analyses showed no significant difference between preflight and postflight mean values for any parameter measured. However, the early in flight samples indicated that levels of 25 OHD did increase significantly when compared to preflight means but the in flight value was within the normal range. The level of 24,25(OH)2D increased markedly in one crewmember late in the mission, however, this increase was within the normal range and not significant when compared to preflight values. Essentially, the levels of two biologically active vitamin D metabolites, 25OHD and 24,25(OH)2D, remained unchanged at all time points. In contrast, levels of the key biologically active vitamin D metabolite, 1,25(OH)2D, did change. title: Cardiovascular Deconditioning Countermeasure Assessment
experiment_type: Shuttle Extended Duration Orbiter Medical Project (EDOMP)
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Early in the manned space flight program it was noted that the cardiovascular system undergoes several adaptive changes when subjected to the microgravity environment. Experimentation during NASA's Skylab missions demonstrated that fluid was shifted from the lower extremities to the more central and cephalad portions of the circulation. The
approach: On the day prior to Shuttle landing, all 26 crewmembers were to consume at least three quarts (2.7 L) of fluids as part of their usual meal and snack routine. This was intended to offset any dehydration due to low intake during the period of adaptation to weightlessness, or to high insensible loss; it was not expected that this consumption would alter the physiological adaptation to microgravity. Preliminary testing revealed that Shuttle crewmembers found isotonic saline unpalatable even in bouillon form. Therefore, the crews were provided with salt (sodium chloride) tablets (1 g each) and advised to take one tablet with each four ounces (114 ml) of water consumed, to a total of eight tablets and 912 ml of water. This concentration approximated isotonic saline. On the day of landing, starting two hours before entry into the earth's atmosphere, the participating crewmember was to begin oral intake of fluid and salt at a rate dictated by personal comfort. It was stressed that regardless of the total fluid volume consumed, the tablet-to-volume ratio be kept constant as prescribed. During the interval between one and two hours after landing, each crewmember's heart rate and blood pressure responses to a Passive Stand Test were recorded, for comparison with their preflight values. During the Stand Test, the electrocardiogram was recorded continuously, and blood pressures were measured each minute for five minutes while the crewmember was in the supine position and for five additional minutes immediately thereafter while the crewmember was standing. The individual stood with his/her feet six inches (15 cm) apart and nine inches (23 cm) from a wall, and leaned slightly backwards against the wall for support. Heart rate was determined from the electrocardiographic record as the number of QRS complexes occurring during each one-minute interval. Mean blood pressure was calculated as one-third the sum of the systolic blood pressure plus two times the diastolic blood pressure. The average heart rate, systolic blood pressure, and diastolic blood pressure during the equilibrated portion of each five-minute segment of this stand test were used in all calculations. In addition, the minute-by-minute group mean values for heart rate and mean blood pressure were plotted to illustrate the differences in the dynamic adjustments of cardiovascular function before and after space flight, and with and without the countermeasure.
results: of this redistribution and of other alterations in the controlling mechanisms of the circulation which were not well defined were termed "cardiovascular deconditioning." The term deconditioning was felt to be appropriate because those individuals who were tested during or immediately after space flight demonstrated less orthostatic tolerance when provoked with lower body negative pressure (LBNP), higher submaximal oxygen consumptions at equivalent workloads, and higher resting heart rates when compared to their responses preflight. With the advent of the Space Shuttle, it was known that astronauts would receive the effects of reentry deceleration in the + Gz axis (head-to-toe), compared to earlier space flights in which these forces were directed + Gx (chest-to-back). The combination of this more stressful acceleration loading with the deconditioned state of the human cardiovascular system following space flights increased efforts directed at developing suitable countermeasures. Most were rejected for actual use in the Space Shuttle due to either complex hardware requirements or objections by flight crews. Even the anti-G suit, considered by many as the only acceptable alternative at the inception of the Shuttle program, was not regarded favorably. Therefore, the development of other, more suitable countermeasures to post-space flight orthostatic intolerance took on greater importance. Earlier bedrest studies had revealed the usefulness of oral rehydration using normal saline in the more palatable form of bouillon, in providing a degree of protection against the loss of LBNP and acceleration tolerance by expanding the circulating plasma volume. In one study, six male volunteers underwent 15 days of bed rest to "decondition" their cardiovascular systems in a physiological simulation of weightlessness. On each of the last three days of bed rest, each subject was stressed by LBNP at -50 mm Hg in one of three randomly assigned conditions: employing no candidate countermeasures; having ingested 1 L of bouillon alone as a countermeasure; or following ingestion of the bouillon during three hours of LBNP at -30 mm Hg, as a combined countermeasure. The results showed that the combination of oral rehydration and prolonged LBNP provided a more sustained increase in plasma volume and reduction in stressed heart rate response. APPROACH: On the day prior to Shuttle landing, all 26 crewmembers were to consume at least three quarts (2.7 L) of fluids as part of their usual meal and snack routine. This was intended to offset any dehydration due to low intake during the period of adaptation to weightlessness, or to high insensible loss; it was not expected that this consumption would alter the physiological adaptation to microgravity. Preliminary testing revealed that Shuttle crewmembers found isotonic saline unpalatable even in bouillon form. Therefore, the crews were provided with salt (sodium chloride) tablets (1 g each) and advised to take one tablet with each four ounces (114 ml) of water consumed, to a total of eight tablets and 912 ml of water. This concentration approximated isotonic saline. On the day of landing, starting two hours before entry into the earth's atmosphere, the participating crewmember was to begin oral intake of fluid and salt at a rate dictated by personal comfort. It was stressed that regardless of the total fluid volume consumed, the tablet-to-volume ratio be kept constant as prescribed. During the interval between one and two hours after landing, each crewmember's heart rate and blood pressure responses to a Passive Stand Test were recorded, for comparison with their preflight values. During the Stand Test, the electrocardiogram was recorded continuously, and blood pressures were measured each minute for five minutes while the crewmember was in the supine position and for five additional minutes immediately thereafter while the crewmember was standing. The individual stood with his/her feet six inches (15 cm) apart and nine inches (23 cm) from a wall, and leaned slightly backwards against the wall for support. Heart rate was determined from the electrocardiographic record as the number of QRS complexes occurring during each one-minute interval. Mean blood pressure was calculated as one-third the sum of the systolic blood pressure plus two times the diastolic blood pressure. The average heart rate, systolic blood pressure, and diastolic blood pressure during the equilibrated portion of each five-minute segment of this stand test were used in all calculations. In addition, the minute-by-minute group mean values for heart rate and mean blood pressure were plotted to illustrate the differences in the dynamic adjustments of cardiovascular function before and after space flight, and with and without the countermeasure. RESULTS: All crewmembers from the first eight Space Shuttle flights were considered as the subjects of this investigation, for a total of 26 data sets from 24 individuals (two individuals flew twice). Of these subjects, 17 utilized the countermeasure and 9 did not. The space flights lasted from 54 hours to 192 hours, and flight length did not appear to correlate with the deconditioning parameters examined in this study. Crewmembers participated in the study on a voluntary basis. Those that did not take the countermeasure did not use other countermeasures for the Stand Test and were considered the control population. The astronauts using the countermeasure consumed fluid and salt according to personal preference. Some drank water while others preferred various on-board beverages, especially fruit juices. Salt tablets were taken as prescribed or less than directed but not in excess. As a result, the amount of fluid consumed ranged from 0.5 L of hypotonic solution to 1 L of isotonic solution. Occasionally, crewmembers who had used the countermeasure prior to reentry consumed additional fluids postflight before the Stand Test was performed. Because of this pattern of compliance, any attempt at volume loading with salt and fluids prior to reentry was considered a use of the countermeasure. Preflight, both groups had mean supine heart rates of 57 bpm, which upon standing increased to 70 bpm in the control group and 71 bpm in the countermeasure group. These changes in heart rate were statistically significant (p The preflight response to assuming the upright posture was a 6 to 10 mm Hg rise in mean blood pressure. Postflight, the control group's mean blood pressure dropped 7 mm Hg when the astronaut assumed the standing position. In the group which utilized the countermeasure, the mean blood pressure rose 2 mm Hg when changing from supine to upright posture. In both the control and experimental groups, the supine mean blood pressure was significantly higher (p The Cardiovascular Index of Deconditioning (CID) was calculated for each crewmember. For those who did not use the countermeasure, the average CID was 49.4 ± 9.6 S.D. For those crewmembers utilizing the countermeasure, the average ClD was 21.4 ± 15.9 S.D., a significantly (p Of the 26 crewmembers on the first eight Shuttle flights, one suffered an episode of outright postflight orthostatic syncope, and two had episodes of presyncope. None of these three individuals had utilized either the fluid loading or any other countermeasures for the Stand Test. This experiment became a standard medical operating procedure beginning with the STS-51A flight. The preflight and postflight echocardiogram was not included as part of the standard medical procedure.

title: Hyperosmotic Fluid Countermeasure
experiment_type: Shuttle Extended Duration Orbiter Medical Project (EDOMP)
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Space flight is known to cause a shift in fluid away from the lower body and a
approach: Twenty-three astronauts on 5 Shuttle flights were assigned to consume one of the following 1 to 2 hours before landing: a hypertonic combination of salt tablets and water, isotonic saline, or an isotonic combination of salt tablets and water. Each astronaut performed stand tests before the flight, on landing day and 3 days after landing.
results: ant decrease in body fluid. Hypovolemia may be one cause of the orthostatic intolerance that is common after space flight. Drinking a salt-water solution (or ingesting an equivalent combination of salt tablets and water) may help to restore plasma volume, but the effectiveness of such a countermeasure may depend upon whether the ingested solution is isotonic (its concentration is the same as the concentration of substances dissolved in the blood) or hypertonic (its concentration is higher than that of the blood). The objective of this study was to test the ingestion of 3 salt and water combinations during flight, comparing the efficacy of isotonic and hypertonic combinations for maintaining orthostatic function after space flight. APPROACH: Twenty-three astronauts on 5 Shuttle flights were assigned to consume one of the following 1 to 2 hours before landing: a hypertonic combination of salt tablets and water, isotonic saline, or an isotonic combination of salt tablets and water. Each astronaut performed stand tests before the flight, on landing day and 3 days after landing. RESULTS: The ingested volumes of the test solutions and of other fluids were too variable for any conclusions to be made. Evaluation of the relative efficacy of the different candidate fluid loading solutions was difficult due to the existence of several factors that compromised data quality. These factors were: (1) a flight rule requiring crew members to repeat half of the fluid load protocol in the event of a one revolution wave-off of landing, (2) variations in the amount of solution ingested, (3) subsequent uncontrolled fluid ingestion after completion of the fluid loading protocol, which, in effect, diluted the prescribed solutions,and (4) use of fluids other than water, as prescribed, which altered not only the conditions of the investigation but also the efficacy of the countermeasure. Evaluation of the candidate fluid loading countermeasure solutions and their ability to maintain orthostatic function after spaceflight was terminated without providing a conclusive answer to the question of the efficacy of a hypertonic solution as an end-of-mission rehydration countermeasure.

title: Dosimetric Mapping
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Radiation constitutes one of the most important hazards for humans in long-duration space missions. Leaving the earth's surface, humans are exposed to a wide spectrum of particles and energies of galactic and solar origin. The intensity, energy, and elemental composition of the radiation field changes considerably with orbital parameters, shielding thickness and solar activity.
approach: Several components of the DOSMAP dosimetry package (dosimetry telescopes [DOSTELS], computer interface unit [CIU], and the thermoluminescent dosimeter [TLD] reader and bulbs) were brought to the International Space Station (ISS) aboard A Shuttle flight. These components were unstowed and set-up in the Retention Net of the Human Research Facility (HRF). Another shuttle brought the remaining DOSMAP hardware (mobile dosimetry units [MDUs] and nuclear track detector packages [NTDP] to the ISS. The MDUs were charged, and an initial read-out was performed for the MDUs and the TLD bulbs prior to their installation throughout the U.S. Lab and Node 1. The NTDPs were also placed at the required locations. All placements were photo documented. Data collected from the TLD bulbs by the TLD Reader were downloaded to the HRF PC every 7-10 days, and data collected from the MDUs were downloaded through the CIU to the HRF PC every 5 days. During the same time intervals the MDUs were recharged. The DOSTELs were activated and data downloads to the HRF PC were performed every 10 days. All data of the active instruments were downlinked during the mission. All of the dosimetry hardware was returned to Earth on A shuttle flight.
results: from numerous space probes demonstrate heightened radiation levels compared to the earth's surface and a change in the nature of the radiation field, particularly the heavy ion component. Although considerable data has been accumulated from several spaceflights, it is not yet possible to provide a quantitative description of the radiation field, especially at the edge of the radiation belt, because of its highly complex composition regarding the particles present and their energy spectra. Data comparison is hampered by uncertain angular distribution of the single radiation components, by missing knowledge on the angular response of instruments and missing information about shielding distributions at the instrument locations. Current models either under- or overestimate the contribution of different radiation components. Due to the variety of particles and energies present in Low Earth Orbit (LEO), no single detector system is capable of providing sufficient information. Therefore, the DOSMAP (Dosimetric Mapping) dosimetry package consisted of several types of detectors to allow for measurement of different particle types and energies. The DOSMAP dosimetry package was further supplemented with instruments contributed by NASA (Phantom Torso) and NASDA (Bonner Ball). The different systems allowed for the first time inflight cross-calibration of measurements at the same shielding configurations. This is absolute necessary when recognizing that the comparison of currently available data is often not possible due to not well known angular response of the detector systems combined with unknown angular incidence of radiations and only approximate knowledge of shielding distributions. APPROACH: Several components of the DOSMAP dosimetry package (dosimetry telescopes [DOSTELS], computer interface unit [CIU], and the thermoluminescent dosimeter [TLD] reader and bulbs) were brought to the International Space Station (ISS) aboard A Shuttle flight. These components were unstowed and set-up in the Retention Net of the Human Research Facility (HRF). Another shuttle brought the remaining DOSMAP hardware (mobile dosimetry units [MDUs] and nuclear track detector packages [NTDP] to the ISS. The MDUs were charged, and an initial read-out was performed for the MDUs and the TLD bulbs prior to their installation throughout the U.S. Lab and Node 1. The NTDPs were also placed at the required locations. All placements were photo documented. Data collected from the TLD bulbs by the TLD Reader were downloaded to the HRF PC every 7-10 days, and data collected from the MDUs were downloaded through the CIU to the HRF PC every 5 days. During the same time intervals the MDUs were recharged. The DOSTELs were activated and data downloads to the HRF PC were performed every 10 days. All data of the active instruments were downlinked during the mission. All of the dosimetry hardware was returned to Earth on A shuttle flight. RESULTS: All data received by the investigators was of good quality. Several hardware issues resulted in small amounts of data loss. Due to the retirement of Prof. W. Heinrich the evaluation of the CR39 NTDP detectors by the group of the University of Siegen could not be completed. The science return may be roughly quoted at about 95%. TLD Results: Based on the characterization of the different detector systems, the following can be concluded. The data for all the different applied TLD systems agree very well taking into account the different Linear Energy Transfer (LET) efficiency of the detector types used as well as the different neutron sensitivity of 6Li doped and 7Li doped TLD materials. The higher dose values for TLD600 and TLD700 dosimeters are due to the higher LET efficiency of these dosimeter materials compared to Cu, P doped LiF crystals. Neutron Dose Results: The determination of neutron dose equivalent using chiefly recoil protons can give too high of a dose value depending on the amount of primary protons contributing to the signal. For this reason, two methods of neutron dose equivalent determination were used. However, both methods still have their limitations and uncertainties. On the other hand, the neutron dose values determined by the two different methods are almost comparable within the standard deviations determined by uncertainty propagation, which indicates that the assumptions made are not too wrong. Measurements with converters with even higher sensitivity to thermal neutrons may improve the standard deviation and better spectral knowledge of the neutron spectra in space may improve the uncertainty of the calibration factor for Albedo dosimeters. Passive Dosimetry System (PDS) Results: The use of the Pille reader in automatic mode permitted dose to be measured as a function of orbit number by TLD A0101. Orbits that passed through the SAA received doses of 30 to >50 µGy/orbit. During these particular orbits, the spacecraft received a substantially larger exposure to trapped protons than during orbits that did not pass through the SAA. For orbits that did not traverse the SAA, the absorbed dose was ~10 µGy/orbit. All orbits that passed through the SAA do not receive the same dose because each orbit passed through only a fraction of the SAA and the size of this fraction changed as the ISS orbit precessed around the Earth. Generally, the ISS passed through the SAA twice during each twenty-four hour period. Following exposure and return to the laboratory, each PDS detector was disassembled and the individual CR-39 PNTD layers were selected for chemical processing (etching). The combined LET spectrum for the x-, y- and z-oriented short-etch CR-39 PNTDs was generated following readout of the 3 detectors. Similarly, the combined LET spectrum was generated for the x-, y- and z-oriented long-etch detectors. There is fairly close agreement between the three mutually orthogonal spectra measured in the long-etch detectors. Similarly, for LET The relative contribution to the LET spectrum from neutron- and proton-induced target fragments tend to increase with increasing LET. The reduced efficiency with which tracks are detected in the short-etch detectors below ~30 keV/µm is apparent, as is the increased signal due to target fragmentation in the LET region above 100 keV/µm in the short-etch detectors. There is fairly close agreement between the detectors for the 2 etch regimes in the LET interval between 30 and 100 keV/µm. The crossover point of the short-etch and long-etch spectra, 35 keV/µm for PDS A0103, was located in the plot differential LET fluence spectra and used in combining the short-etch and long-etch curves into one total LET spectrum. During the DOSMAP experiment, mean total dose rate measured in the PDS dosimeters ranged from 6.88 ± 0.42 µGy/hr in Node 1, above the forward hatch leading to the FGB module, to 10.36 ± 0.54 µGy/hr above the aft hatch of Node 1. The mean total dose equivalent rate varied from 14.06 ± 0.93 µSv/hr to 18.81 ± 1.11 µSv/hr at these same respective locations. The average quality factor varied from 1.82 ± 0.13 above the aft hatch of Node 1 to 2.11 ± 0.16 on the starboard side of the US Lab near the aft hatch. DOSTEL Results: By chance a significant solar particle event occurred during the active phase of DOSTEL on April 15, 2001. Thanks to the action of the crew, DOSTEL 1 was switched into a special mode while DOSTEL 2 remained in the mode for article and dose rate measurement. In the special mode, the 2 detector signals of DOSTEL 1 were stored for each individual particle. Stopping protons impinging from the top and bottom of the telescope were clearly seen, along with some stopping He-particles that were also identified. A plot of dose rates during the mission clearly shows the dependence of dose rates from the altitude, which ranged from 404 km to 386 km. Based on the mean quality factor derived from the LET spectra by applying the LET dependence of the quality factor as defined in ICRP Report No. 60 equivalent doses can be calculated. Mobile Dosimetry Unit (MDU) Results: Approximately 4.5 MB of rough compressed information was received by each MDU. After decompression, the volume of data increases by an approximate factor of 30. The values of the mean doses per day was 180.7, 189.9, 166.1, 126.3 µGy/day in MDU#1 to MDU#4, respectively. When graphed these doses lie on the AP8MAX prediction line. Comparison of fluxes by 4 different MDUs shows that large differences are produced by the differences in the position of MDU and shielding distributions for them. In the time span 27 June-4 July 2001 four MDUs were placed at fixed locations: one unit (MDU#4) in the ISS "Unity" Node-1 and three (MDU #1-3) units were located at different locations in the US Laboratory module. MDU #2 results showed that the spectra inside the ISS has a maximum energy of 300 MeV and that the place of the maximum of the spectra moves from about 100 MeV at low L values toward 50-60 MeV at higher L values. The agreement of the data received by active and passive detectors is in the range of ±10%. Comparisons of the passive devices yield even a smaller range, when corrected by the efficiency function of the different materials. Dose equivalents were calculated from the measurements using the quality factor (Q) as defined in ICRP Report No. 60. Conclusion: In comparison to other spaceflight missions, the lower dose equivalents seen for ISS are due to less solar activity during the measurement period and due to higher shielding of the ISS. The dose equivalents received by the combination of nuclear track detectors with TLDs show values close to the DOSTEL dose equivalents. The error in the determination of the dose equivalent from passive detectors is about 6%. The combined CR39 NTDP/TLD dose equivalent appears too low compared to the DOSTEL dose equivalents. Since the low let measurements of the TLDs are in good agreement with DOSTEL and the CR39 NTDP LET spectra as well, further investigations are needed to close this gap of knowledge. Adding the neutron dose from the personal dosimeter would increase the dose equivalent measurements by about 33 µSv/day. The DOSMAP experiment was the first effort to map dose and dose equivalent as function of the location in the US lab and in Node 1 of the ISS. Having a fully developed 3-D ray tracing model the obtained data can be used to validate the Model. A quite impressive set of data has been produced by the "Dosimetric Mapping" experiment from which only a part could be presented in this summary. Since the radiation field is both complex and dynamic, measurements across the ISS need to be continued in future missions to study the radiation field and its modification by mass shielding, leading to attenuation, build up and/or activation. There is a continuous need for information on absorbed dose, particle and linear energy transfer spectra in real time.

title: Immunological Assessment of Crewmembers
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: The assessment of crew immunocompetence was required for the determination of space flight infectious disease risk. This is of significant importance for longer duration missions and particularly, orbital station environments.
approach: Data was collected from 54 crewmembers during six shuttle flights. White blood cells were collected after removal of the serum for use in the nominal Medical Operations physical. These cells were resuspended in isotonic saline and divided into two aliquots. One sample was used for flow cytometric analysis to determine cellular subpopulations and the other was further processed for functional assay of different immune cells (neutrophils, monocytes, and T-cells).
results: Phenotypic Analysis Flow cytometric analysis indicates that crewmembers exhibited a statistically significant decrease in total T cells with alterations in specific T cell subsets. In addition, a statistically significant increase in B cells as well as variable alterations in circulating monocytes was observed. Neutrophil Functional Testing Neutrophils exhibited a variable effect following space flight in response to a chemotactic factor.

title: Inflight Radiation Dose Distribution
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Manned interplanetary space travel involves long periods away from the protective cover of the Earth's magnetosphere to the regions where there exists the possibility of serious biological injury from galactic cosmic rays (GCR) and energetic solar panicle events (SPE). For an SPE, the major concerns are acute effects arising from sudden exposure to very large radiation doses of solar protons. The severity of these effects can be reduced when adequate storm shelters are provided. The high-energy heavy-ion transport code (HZETRN) developed at NASA Langley Research Center is a computationally efficient tool suitable for space mission shielding design use in the protection of crewmembers and microelectronics. It has been known for some time that terrestrial surface features of the geomagnetic field experience a secular westward drift at a rate of about 0.3° longitude per year. A prominent surface feature of the magnetic field is a local intensity minimum, currently located in the southern Atlantic Ocean near the coast of Brazil. Since the Inner Van Allen Belt particle population is governed by the Earth's magnetic field, it
approach: es closest to the Earth at that location. The positions of the field minimum and the South Atlantic field and the trapped radiation, one should expect that the South Atlantic Anomaly (SAA) would also participate in some fashion in the secular drift of the magnetic field. Thus, a change of location of the SAA over a period of several decades should provide positive evidence for this process. It is important for this study to use data obtained from a quiet magnetosphere, since following a large magnetic storm a disturbed magnetosphere is known to form additional belts and may temporarily change the location of the Inner Belt. To study the secular drift of the anomaly, the investigators averaged the dose rate in all the passes through the SAA as a function of longitude and determined the center of the distribution by fitting it to a gaussian. Similarly, they created a set of "synthetic" passes through the SAA by calculating the dose rate as a function of longitude for the same orbit using the AP-8 Max proton flux model and the IGRF 1965 field, epoch 1970. The investigators chose to use the AP-8 model rather than any single observation of the SAA because this model represents the observational
results: of a multitude of satellites and thus statistically probably provides a better measure of the particle distribution than any arbitrarily chosen individual measurement. These passes were also averaged in the same manner. The purpose of this joint NASA/DOD investigation was to establish, evaluate, and verify analytical and measurement methods for assessing and managing health risks from exposure to space radiation.
