APPROACH: A generalized analytic model was used to describe the energy deposition of direct ion interaction events in a micron-size detector. The transport calculation accounting for the Space Shuttle configuration was accomplished by using a new version of HZETRN that was extensively verified with laboratory and flight data. During STS-31 the tissue equivalent proportional counter (TEPC) was located on the starboard bulkhead of the crew compartment. Consequently, with respect to the TEPC, the mass distribution of the spacecraft and the associated systems was quite anisotropic and the high energy proton flux had predominant access from the starboard side while from the opposite direction additional shielding set the energy cutoff at a higher value. Since the investigators had information on the spacecraft altitude with respect to the magnetic field, they chose three passes through the SAA during which the spacecraft sampled either predominantly westward or eastward directed proton fluxes. When comparing passes it is very important that the same region of the SAA is covered. Thus, the investigators chose two passes whose longitude-latitude traces were close though not identical during which the TEPC saw a predominantly westward flux and one pass which fell between the other two during which the TEPC measured predominantly an eastward flux. The objectives of this experiment were accomplished using two hardware configurations. Configuration 1 consisted of a Passive Proton Spectrometer, a TEPC system, Bonner Spheres, and Activation foils. Preflight, a 15-minute introduction to the equipment for the flight crew occurred followed by the installation of the loop fastener (Velcro Pile) to the middeeck right wall near DLOC #2 (MR85B) in the orbiter. Within the first 4.5 hours after attaining orbit (FD1), a crewmember destowed the hardware. The deployments of elements on Velcro pads attached to the right wall near DLOC #2 (MR85B) occurred. The TEPC system was activated, noting mission elapsed time (MET). Near the conclusion of the flight, at any time after the completion of the last set of passes through the SAA, the TEPC was deactivated and the hardware restowed. There weren’t any postflight requirements by the crewmembers. However, Bonner Spheres and foils were returned to the Johnson Space Center (JSC) within 24 hours of landing. Configuration 2 consisted of a Charged Particle Spectrometer. Flights with an altitude of ~200 nmi were preferred. Preflight training involved a 30-minute introduction to the equipment for the flight crewmembers. Within the first 4.5 hours after attaining orbit (FD1), the pre-routed DC power cable was connected to the utility outlet and to the spectrometer, the power to the spectrometer was turned on, and MET was recorded to the nearest second. Prior to deorbit preparations, preferably after the completion of the last set of passes through the SAA, the instrument was deactivated and the DC power cable was disconnected and secured for landing. There weren’t any postflight requirements by the crewmembers. However, the data disks had to be returned to JSC within seven days of the landing. RESULTS: The lineal energy transfer (LET) spectrum of both the trapped and galactic cosmic radiation was measured using a TEPC. The overall physical dose is in fairly good agreement with measurements using thermoluminescent detectors in the least shielded location. A comparison of the trapped proton LET spectra from STS-31, STS-40, and STS-42 showed that shapes are rather similar. The measured galactic cosmic radiation LET spectra, however, yielded dose rates that were higher by 1.39 and quality factor lowered by 0.79 in model calculations. There were significant differences between the model calculated LET spectra and the observed spectrum. DSOs 31, 37, 40, and 48 The observations made both with the TEPC and proton and heavy ion detector telescope (PHIDE) show clearly that over the last 20 years a significant change has occurred in the location of the SAA. The average position of the SAA has moved westward by about 6.7° in longitude over a period of the past 20 years. While the westward drift in itself does not change, it does affect the planning for astronaut extravehicular activities (EVAs). Operationally, EVAs are scheduled to avoid the SAA as much as possible. The data obtained on STS-31 also allows investigators to observe the east-west effect whose magnitude is in qualitative agreement with both old and recent observations. The analysis of four shuttle flights which occurred between April 1990 and January 1992 preceding and following a large magnetic storm indicated that the location of the SAA in B-L space was at L = 1.3 and did not vary over that period. However, following the geomagnetic storm of March 24, 1991, the investigators clearly saw the emergence of a second radiation belt at L = 2 two and a half months later, and observed it moving to L = 1.8 six months after the storm. While it is reasonable to assume and independent evidence suggests that the second belt was produced during that storm, the investigators are unable to prove this because neither STS-31 nor STS-37 sampled the L = 2 drift shell. It is useful to point out that the second belt was detected not only by means of conventional particle detectors, but also through single event upsets (SEU) in proton sensitive devices. DSO 51 and 56 The predicted spectra and flight data are in good agreement for the range from 2 to 400 keV/µm to within 70% with the remaining region below2 keV/µm underpredicted. This trend is consistent for these two flights but with systematic differences in their flux level which suggests possible problems in the geomagnetic transmission function used. The underprediction below 2 keV/µm could be due to neglecting secondary pion, kaons, and electrons in the HZETRN. But the importance of the contributions from these secondaries can only be assessed after the indirect delta ray events are included in the TEPC response model.

title: Functional Fitness Assessment (Flight Analog)
archive_status: Data preservation is complete.  All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Physical fitness was assessed pre- and post- bed rest to guide individual physical training and to determine individual responses to training countermeasures. Functional Fitness pre- and post- bed rest testing captured a subject’s flexibility, endurance, and strength in absolute numbers.
approach: Functional fitness evaluations were performed by each subject before and after bed rest. Lower back and hamstring flexibility were tested by a sit and reach exercise immediately following a brief warm up and stretching exercises. Upper body strength was measured using a Smith Bench Press and lower body strength was measured using a leg press. Both measures used the 1 repetition maximum (RM) protocol. The 1 RM is typically achieved within 3 to 5 trials. The 1-RM value was recorded as the maximum weight lifted for the last successful trial. Endurance of the latissimus dorsi, elbow flexors, and pectorals was assessed by the number of pull-ups the subject was able to complete. Endurance of the pectoral and shoulder muscles was assessed by the number of push-ups the subject was able to complete in 2 minutes, and abdominal muscle endurance was assessed by the number of sliding crunches the subject was able to complete in 2 minutes.
results: This experiment has concluded in ground-based studies sponsored by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration's (NASAs) Human Adaptation and Countermeasures Division. This experiment was conducted during Bed Rest Campaigns 1 and 3, 5, Artificial Gravity (AG), and Head Down Tilt - 30 day (HDT30). There was no significant change in flexibility when comparing pre- bed rest day 2 to post- bed rest day 1. This may be due to the fact that subjects followed a daily stretching routine during the bed rest. Both genders had reduced endurance after bed rest. Both male and female subjects showed a significant reduction in strength between pre- and post- bed rest scores. The biceps and muscles of the back are used very little during bed rest, which leads to a reduction in muscular endurance. The tests of the leg press show a significant change from the pre- and post. During bed rest the subjects are not permitted to use their lower bodies; this provides the best representation to space flight that the investigators could record with Functional Fitness testing. Subjects lost substantial percentages of lower body strength from pre- bed rest day 2 to post- bed rest day 1. Strength returned to nearly the original pre- bed rest score on the final day of post-testing.

title: Physiologic Monitoring
experiment_type: NASA Extreme Environment Mission Operations (NEEMO) Project
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: The objective of the Physiologic Monitoring experiment was to test wireless medical monitoring devices and their accompanying procedures in a metal-walled habitat similar to the International Space Station (ISS). Specifically, crewmembers assessed ease of use, assessed the ability to transmit/receive data over a period of several days in an isolated/busy environment, assessed hardware for robustness, and observed potential problems in microgravity.
approach: During the experiment, crewmembers wore devices, which consisted of electrode leads attached to wireless transmitting devices, to record cardiac activity and respiration while inside the habitat. These devices were tested in two different scenarios: exercise and simulated injured crewmember. Prior to the first scenario, one crewmember began by testing signal coverage in the habitat (radiofrequency mapping). A wireless connection was established between a laptop or tablet PC and a wearable device, called a Crew Physiological Observation Device (CPOD). The crewmember determined if the signal was maintained at each of ten locations in the habitat and recorded the information on the data sheet. Once the radiofrequency mapping was complete, the crewmembers prepared for the exercise and simulated ill/injured crewmember scenarios. This involved unstowing the needed equipment and preparing the skin for the Nexan sensor. When the set-up was complete, the crewmember wearing the monitoring system engaged in 10 minutes of physical activity (such as push-ups, jumping jacks, sit-ups, etc.) while the second crewmember monitored the data transmission and download. During the injured crewmember scenario, the monitoring system was attached to an electrocardiograph (ECG) simulator. One crewmember set the ECG rhythms (simulating changes in heart rhythm), while the second monitored that data transmission and download.
results: For the purpose of testing our device, the Aquarius facility was a good space analog in that it is a metal walled habitat. The increased air pressure did affect the computer disk, but not any of the solid-state devices. Exercise Data Set with Nexan Sensor This exercise data set started at 4:36:35 and ended at 4:50:03 for a duration of 14:28. However the subject marked the exercise as beginning at 37:50. The Accelerometer data records vigorous activity from 37.58 to 44:25. The ECG II lead had 18 dropouts of less than one second and one of 1-2 seconds. The ECG V lead had the same number of dropouts. The R-Raw began at 2800 and varied smoothly between a high of 2825 and a low of 2700, spending a majority of the time around 2750. The AccX, AccY, AccZ have nice sine waves from the event at 37:55 to the end of exercise at 44:25. The temperature was mostly steady at 28 degrees Celsius but jumped for three seconds to 132 degrees Celsius, later for four seconds to 130 degrees Celsius, later one second to 131 degrees Celsius. The SPO2 numbers began at 92 and varied smoothly from a high of 99 to a low of 84, spending most time around 95. Exercise Data Set with Button Sensor This exercise data set began at 59:07 and ended at 12:57. The AccX values indicate that vigorous exercise began with the Event mark at 01:11 and ended at 8:33. The ECG II signal had approximately 42 dropouts of less than one second, one for 30 seconds, one for two seconds and one for 12 seconds. About 30 of the dropouts were before exercise began. The ECG V5 signal had the same dropouts. Noise was present in EV5 from 5:09 to 5:19. The AccX, AccY, AccZ values were valid looking sine waves. The temperature was steady at 30 degrees Celsius except for a three second jump to 126 degrees Celsius. The SPO2 varied smoothly between 84 and 99. The heart rate (HR) is a reasonable 97 average, but often jumped suddenly for two seconds at a time to an impossible 190 or 200. Ill or Injured Crew Simulated Data The ill or injured crew simulated data is ECG simulator data. One investigator reported that this was easily recognizable. That fact implies that the lines, the CPOD, and the transmission of data were good. The problem appears to arise in the sensors or their attachment to the subject or their sensitivity to movement rather than electro-magnetic flux.

title: Metabolism and Heat Dissipation During Apollo EVA Periods
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: During the zero-G extravehicular activities (EVAs) performed during the five Gemini missions, considerable difficulty was experienced by the crewmembers. In a space environment which imposed several life support requirements during EVA (the maintenance of a minimum oxygen pressure, the removal of expired carbon dioxide, the provision for useful mobility, and the maintenance of body temperature), the crewmen experienced high work rates and apparent overheating during the Gemini 4, 9, and 11 EVAs. The crewmen also encountered unexpected difficulty performing specific tasks on each of these missions. Events such as these prompted several researchers to evaluate the effects of one-sixth (or lunar) gravity on the cost of work in a pressure suit.
approach: Since it was desirable to measure metabolic rate during EVA on the lunar surface and in free space, several measurement approaches were evaluated. Standard laboratory methods would have required breaking pressure suit integrity if used in space or during vacuum chamber training on the ground; this was undesirable. The operational data available from the crewman and from his life support system were assessed to determine their usefulness in approximating metabolic rate. This consisted of voice and electrocardiogram (ECG) data from each crewmember, oxygen bottle pressure, Liquid Cooling Garment (LCG) coolant-water entry and exit temperatures, and suit-gas entry temperature. In addition, the sublimator water usage data was available after the majority of the EVAs; sublimator water usage provided a measure of the total heat loss from the suit. All of the heat removed from the pressure suit was first transferred to a heat sink maintained by the sublimator which rejected heat by the change of state involved in sublimating ice to water vapor in the vacuum of space.
results: , however, were inconclusive. Predictions were made that metabolic costs would decrease with subgravity walking. Other researchers predicted metabolic increases would accompany low traction exercise. Other uncertainties arose from the considerations of lunar terrain and surface composition and their effect on mobility and metabolic rate. In response to these uncertainties, conservative biomedical estimates of the life support requirements were defined on the basis of available data. Although metabolic rates were not measured during the Gemini EVAs, it was clear in several instances that crewmen worked at levels above the heat removal capability of the gas cooled life support system. The Metabolism and Heat Dissipation experiment was therefore performed to determine life support requirements during Apollo EVAs. APPROACH: Since it was desirable to measure metabolic rate during EVA on the lunar surface and in free space, several measurement approaches were evaluated. Standard laboratory methods would have required breaking pressure suit integrity if used in space or during vacuum chamber training on the ground; this was undesirable. The operational data available from the crewman and from his life support system were assessed to determine their usefulness in approximating metabolic rate. This consisted of voice and electrocardiogram (ECG) data from each crewmember, oxygen bottle pressure, Liquid Cooling Garment (LCG) coolant-water entry and exit temperatures, and suit-gas entry temperature. In addition, the sublimator water usage data was available after the majority of the EVAs; sublimator water usage provided a measure of the total heat loss from the suit. All of the heat removed from the pressure suit was first transferred to a heat sink maintained by the sublimator which rejected heat by the change of state involved in sublimating ice to water vapor in the vacuum of space. RESULTS: Two types of task identification methods were used for separating the activities performed during EVA periods. For the first method, the metabolic rate monitors divided the operational tasks into four types of activities of importance to mission planners: overhead activities (those tasks required for each EVA, such as egressing and ingressing the vehicle), deploying the Apollo lunar surface experiment package (ALSEP), making geological surveys, and riding in the lunar roving vehicle. The oxygen and LCG measurement methods could be used to obtain accurate metabolic rates for these activities. The second method of task separation was based on a time and motion study which required dividing the tasks into as many definable activities as possible. However, this method resulted in some activities of such short duration that metabolic rates could only be assigned using the postflight heart rate method. Metabolic rate measurements were determined for both lunar surface EVAs (Apollo missions 11, 12, and 14 through 17) as well as zero-G EVAs (Apollo missions 9, 15, 16, 17). Metabolic rates were lower than predicted before the Apollo missions for lunar surface EVAs. Overhead activities consumed the most energy, while driving or riding in the lunar roving vehicle consumed the least. This was comparable to shirt sleeve riding in an automobile. The highest average metabolic rate was experienced by one Apollo 11 subject who was very active in evaluating modes of locomotion. For discrete activities, the highest metabolic rates were associated with his transport of the ALSEP pallet, ingress to the Lunar Module (LM) with lunar samples, and drilling and removal of drill bits. For the Apollo 14 mission, which included some of the most extensive walking traverses, a specific effort was made to correlate metabolic rate and traverse rate. However, data obtained showed poor correlation. The crewmen apparently maintained a comfortable walking effort and, to a large extent, the rate of traverse at this level of effort varied with the terrain and the operational requirements of each traverse. In general, both the speed and efficiency of lunar walking were greater than could be achieved while wearing a pressure suit in a 1-G environment, but neither speed nor efficiency was equivalent to that of a shirt sleeve operation in 1-G. Operational film and kinescope were used in performing a time and motion study of Apollo 15 and 16 activities. Results from observations of Apollo 15 and 16 time and motion studies indicated that tasks were completed more rapidly at 1-G wearing space suits than at one-sixth-G, but at higher metabolic rates. The zero-G EVA activities were measured using the heart rate method. This method tended to yield higher estimates of metabolic rates therefore results ranging from 150 to 500 kcal /hr were considered maximum values. Voice data did not indicate that the crewmen were performing strenuously. In some cases, the actual metabolic rates were much lower than the values obtained by means of heart rate calibration data. Excitement, rather than physical exertion, was considered the cause of elevation of heart rates. The crewmen were able to perform planned EVAs and to extend them to the maximum time allowable without medical problems. The manually controlled Liquid Cooling Garment was effective in minimizing fatigue and water loss from sweating during EVA. Gas cooling was adequate during the short zero-G EVA performed from the Command Module. It was found that adequate body restraints, realistic zero-G preflight training in a water immersion simulator, and detailed planning of activities were essential to ensure completion of tasks and reduce fatigue.

title: Vestibular Modulation of Autonomic Responses to Orthostasis
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Orthostatic intolerance and related functional impairment remain a common problem for astronauts upon return from space. Despite considerable effort to develop countermeasures for this problem, a fundamental question remains unanswered: What is the cause of orthostatic intolerance? Post flight symptoms vary widely and include both vestibular and orthostatic intolerance manifestations. The role of vestibular disturbances in orthostatic intolerance is unknown. Although it is known that vestibular signals project to the vasomotor centers of the brainstem in cats, there has been no prospective study of vestibular system effects on blood pressure control during orthostasis or on orthostatic tolerance in humans. Most fundamental, it remains unknown whether otolith inputs play an important role in the cardiovascular adjustments to the upright position in humans. The altered vestibular function after space flight may influence orthostatic tolerance indirectly (producing intolerable symptoms requiring recumbent posture) and/or directly (by affecting autonomic responses to orthostasis). Post flight vestibular disturbances are complex and probably include some involvement of otolith inputs, semicircular canal inputs and related inputs. The purpose of this study was three-fold: 1) to determine the otolith contribution to the cardiovascular adjustments to the upright position; 2) to determine whether altering otolith or semicircular canal inputs affect blood pressure regulation during orthostasis; 3) to determine whether altering otolith or semicircular canal inputs affect orthostatic tolerance. The specific aims of the study were as follows: 1. To determine the role of otolith input in mediating the cardiovascular adjustments to the upright position. 2. To determine how otolith orientation affects the occurrence of pre-syncopal symptoms during an orthostatic stress. 3. To determine the effect of semicircular canal stimulation (with caloric testing) on the cardiovascular adjustments to orthostasis. 4. To determine the effect of semicircular canal stimulation (with caloric testing) on orthostatic tolerance.
approach: Study 1 : This study was performed to address specific aim 1. The response to seven perturbations involving combinations of head-up tilt (0, 30 and 60 degree) and neck position to affect otolith orientation. (30 degree flexion or extension) were obtained in random order. Study 2 : This study addressed specific aim 2 by assessing the heart rate, arterial pressure, sympathetic nerve activity, heart rate and blood pressure variances, respiration, responses to sustained orthostasis (30 degree head-up tilt plus lower body negative pressure at 10, 20 and 30 mmHg) with and without otolith input (0 degrees versus 60 degrees otolith orientation). Study 3 : This study addressed specific aims 3 and 4 by assessing the heart rate, arterial pressure, SNA. heart rate and blood pressure variances, responses to graded orthostasis (lower body negative pressure at -30, -40, -50 and -60 mmHg) with and without semicircular canal stimulation (caloric ear canal irrigation).
results: Study 1 : Within the first 20 seconds of tilt, arterial pressure increased most obviously in the 0 to 1 Gz otolith condition. Thoracic impedance tended to increase more in otolith-constant conditions. But no dependent variable differed significantly between tilt conditions, and no significant time x tilt interactions emerged. Study 2 : There was a trend for greater increases in heart rate, but not for differences in arterial pressure or vascular resistance during the graded orthostasis. In addition, changes in low frequency and high frequency spectral power trended toward significance,, but did not achieve significance. In some subjects, this effect suggests that autonomic control was modestly affected by the otolith stimulus during graded orthostasis. Study 3 : Significant nystagmus was provoked by the caloric stimulus in each subject with insignificant effects on baseline heart rate, mean arterial pressure, or sympathetic nerve activity consistent with previous pilot data and previous findings. The cold caloric stimulation performed during LBNP resulted in similar changes as the thermoneutral stimulus in heart rate and blood pressure suggesting that there was not a significant effect of semicircular canal stimulation.

title: Physiological Effects of Iodinated Water on Thyroid Function
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Iodine has been used as a potable water treatment and storage bactericidal agent by NASA for over three decades beginning with the Apollo program, and was a critical factor for the achievement of human space flight. Iodine is currently used for Space Shuttle potable water microbial control and the U.S. component of the International Space Station (ISS). The ISS U.S. water system recycles water from urine and other wastewaters for human consumption and requires long-term storage. With the proposed iodine exposure levels and the crewmembers originating from many countries including regions of low iodine intake, concerns have been raised regarding the use of iodine in ISS potable water. Iodine is a component of the two major thyroid hormones, thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3). These hormones regulate many key biochemical processes. Major target organs are the developing brain, muscle, heart, pituitary, and kidney. Most ingested iodine is reduced in the gut to iodide, which is absorbed almost completely. Once in circulation, iodide is removed primarily by the thyroid gland and kidney. The thyroid selectively concentrates iodide with the excess excreted into the urine. Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), produced in the anterior lobe of the pituitary gland, regulates the release of thyroid hormones from the thyroid gland into the blood. TSH secretion from the pituitary gland increases when the levels of circulating thyroid hormones decrease. The thyroid responds to the ingestion of elevated quantities of iodine by a transient decrease in thyroid hormone synthesis, termed the acute Wolff-Chaikoff effect. An investigation was undertaken during three ground-based, closed-chamber tests to examine thyroid function and hormone levels in chamber subjects who consumed potable water containing iodine. The purpose of this study was to document the thyroid functional biochemical measurements (n=12), urine iodine levels (n=8), and any clinical signs or symptoms of thyroid dysfunction in the 12 crewmembers who participated in the chamber studies.
approach: The chamber tests, in order of occurrence, were 30 days, Phase II; 60 days, Phase IIa; and 91 days, Phase III. Each chamber test had four crewmembers. Each crewmember was considered to be in good health and had normal thyroid function. In all three chamber tests, after the water recycling process was completed, 3.5 to 5.2 mg iodine/L was added to the water as the disinfectant. In Phase II (30 days) and Phase IIa (60 days), thyroid hormonal status (TSH and thyroid hormone levels) was assessed both in the pre- and postchamber period. In Phase III, the 91-day study, TSH, thyroid hormones, and urinary iodine levels were measured before and several times in chamber (first measurement at the 30-day mark). These were followed up with several more measurements in the postchamber period upon the subjects' exit from the chamber at the completion of the study. Subjects were monitored until all indices of iodine/thyroid status had returned to prechamber levels. For the Phase III study (91 days), due to changes in TSH levels at the 30-day mark, iodine was removed from the potable water before consumption. This was accomplished by installing an iodine-removal device and a microbial filter (0.2 µm) at the point of use of the water on chamber day 35. This device removed the iodine (I 2 and I - ) from the drinking water but did not affect the iodine levels in the remainder of the water used, i.e., for hygiene activities. Urinary iodine levels were spot-checked to determine iodine exposure.
results: While individual water consumption was not determined for Phases II and IIa crewmembers, analysis of diet records and the systematic evaluation of water usage indicates the crewmembers consumed from 4 to 10 mg total iodine/day. For Phase IIa (60 days), drinking water contained approximately 2 to 4 mg I/L and subjects excreted approximately 4.5 to 14 mg/day. Intake measurements were only completed twice during the study. The actual individual water iodine intakes and urinary losses were quantified for the Phase III, 91-day test. The total iodine in the water varied from approximately 3 to 8 mg/L with an average level for the first 35 days around 5 mg total iodine/L. Urinary iodine levels reflect recent iodine consumption. In all subjects, urinary iodine levels increased about 10-fold during the first 30 days of the Phase III chamber study, with iodine consumption levels ranging from 8 to 20 mg/day. Urinary excretion means for subjects ranged from 9.4 to 16.9 mg I/day. The variation in iodine intake between crewmembers was related to the individual volume of potable water consumed. Following installation of the iodine removal device at the galley sink, the total iodine levels measured less than 0.05 mg/L in the drinking water but remained in full concentration in the shower and wash water. Urinary iodine levels decreased 5- to 10-fold after cessation of the water iodine exposure but remained above baseline values. By the end of the 91-day study, 56 days after cessation of drinking water iodine, the urinary values continued to remain above baseline values in three of the four subjects. In three of the crewmembers, urine iodine levels fell to an average of 0.283 mg/24 hrs by three days after test completion. Although mean TSH levels remained within normal range throughout the studies, there was a statistically significant increase in TSH levels in the Phase II and III studies. For the Phase II study, the values returned to baseline levels in all subjects within two weeks after the subjects exited the chamber. In the 60-day Phase IIa study, although not a statistically significant change, serum TSH in three of the four subjects had increased by the end of the study. One subject, who had a baseline TSH value close to the upper limit, had a decreased TSH value below the baseline value at the end of the chamber study. This subject had the highest iodine consumption and urinary levels of the four subjects in the Phase IIa test. At day 62 postchamber, this subject had a very high TSH level and was referred for medical evaluation by an endocrinologist. There were no other biochemical or clinical signs of thyroid disease, and the TSH returned to near baseline value several months later. In the 91-day study, the mean serum TSH level in the four test subjects increased significantly above baseline values 30 days after entering the chamber. After the iodine was removed from the drinking water on day 35 (concentration For one subject in the Phase III study, the TSH remained higher than the baseline value but within the normal reference range throughout the chamber study period, with no decrease in the level after removal of iodine from the drinking water. After one year, the TSH levels returned to prechamber baseline levels. All other measures of thyroid function remained within normal ranges. The consulting endocrinologist diagnosed the crewmember with iodine-induced subclinical hyperthyroidism. During the Phase III study, urinary iodine levels remained at approximately 1 mg/day after iodine removal from drinking water at day 35, but returned to baseline levels within three days of exiting the chamber. One potential source of iodine contamination involved the methods for urine collection and measurement. A study was completed and found that this was not the cause of the persistence of urinary iodine levels above baseline. Other potential sources of iodine contamination were discussed and considered, however, no plausible explanation was identified. The results from the three chamber tests demonstrated that the levels of iodine in the potable water system proposed for the ISS were too high. Since these studies were concluded, the Food and Nutrition Board has established an upper limit for iodine intakes from all sources as 1.1 mg/day. The subjects in the chamber studies exceeded this level and consequently, for two subjects, TSH levels were significantly changed by the end of the chamber test. Since food consumption provides about 0.25 mg/day, the requirement was set at a maximum of 0.25 mg of iodine/L in ISS water supplied by the United States. This would limit water consumption to a maximum of 3 L/day to maintain daily intake levels from all sources at less than the limit established by NASA of less than 1.0 mg/day of iodine. Consequently, there remains concern that the maximum level of 0.25 mg/L of iodine in the spacecraft water will not provide sufficient microbial control, thus increasing the risk to ISS crewmembers.

title: Autonomic Mechanisms During Prolonged Weightlessness
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: The microgravity environment present during low-earth orbit (LEO) spaceflight may contribute to changes in autonomic cardiovascular regulation experienced by long-duration spaceflight crewmembers when they return to Earth's gravity. Theses changes manifest themselves as increased heart rates when standing, decline in arterial blood pressure, and even frank syncope. Several factors likely contribute to these changes, blood volume reductions, impaired baroreceptor-cardiac reflex responses, and inadequate increases in total peripheral resistance during standing. This experiment explored the probability that the disordered arterial baroreflex malfunction, documented during weightlessness or after simulated or actual weightlessness, is part of and a contributor to a broad range of autonomic abnormalities. The researchers developed this experiment using the following hypotheses as a guide: Vagal baroreflex impairment progresses during long-duration space missions, and plateaus to reach some asymptotic limit. Weightlessness impairs aortic as well as carotid baroreceptor reflexes, and that therefore, the baroreflex malfunction that develops in space may be due to central nervous system factors, rather than local changes in the wall of carotid arteries. Progressive impairment of integrated vagal baroreflexes in astronauts is expressed in reduced levels of vagal-cardiac nerve traffic, as reflected in fluctuations of R-R intervals during rigorously-controlled breathing. The progressive reduction of minimum R-R interval during baroreflex testing observed in previous space flight missions reflected increased sympathetic-cardiac neural activity. Diminished vagal-cardiac nerve traffic is associated with a reduced prevalence of atrial, and an increased prevalence of ventricular dysrhythmias in space. Low-frequency diastolic pressure power reflects quantitatively, levels of efferent human muscle sympathetic nerve activity. Reductions of baroreflex gain are related directly and significantly to impairment of vasoconstrictor responses to lower body negative pressure in space. Hypocapnia leads to a greater reduction of R-R interval power at respiratory frequencies, and carotid baroreceptor-cardiac reflex gain in space than on Earth. The researchers used the data obtained from this experiment to determine the adaptive changes that occurred in the autonomic nervous system of the flight subjects and to obtain insight into the various mechanisms that caused the observed integrated autonomic output.
approach: The design of this experiment was built around a battery of tests that activated different afferent nerve fibers, evoking different patterns of neural and cardiovascular responses through both separate and common mechanisms. These tests included: Controlled frequency breathing - a predetermined breathing protocol carried out using the Medikro Laptop Computer as an instructional guide. Valsalva’s Maneuver - performed by attempting to forcibly exhale with the nose closed and the mouth blowing into a pressurized breathing apparatus in order to increase blood pressure. Isometric Handgrip Exercise> - required the subject to sustain a muscular contraction, using a handgrip balloon assembly, to raise arterial blood pressure. Cold Pressor Test - involved rapid, sustained, severe cooling of a crewmember’s hand using the Cold Glove Assembly in order to elicit an increase in the subject's blood pressure and heart rate. Graded Lower Body Negative Pressure - provided a controlled, measured orthostatic stress to the cardiovascular system using the Chibis Lower Body Negative Pressure (LBNP) Device.
results: The data obtained from this experiment showed a decrease in RR-interval standard deviations for all subjects and a decrease in respiratory frequency RR-interval spectral power for two subjects while in microgravity. RR-interval spectral power was decreased and systolic pressure spectral power was increased in all subjects two weeks after returning to Earth. The data also showed that while in microgravity the transfer function between systolic blood pressures and RR-intervals was reduced. The transfer function showed a further reduction the day after the subjects returned to Earth, and had not returned to preflight levels by 14 days after landing. These results suggested that long-duration spaceflight decreased vagal-cardiac control (reduced R-R interval oscillations at a given respiratory frequency) and baroreflex gain (reduced systolic to R-R interval transfer function magnitude), and that after returning to Earth, the effects of weightlessness may persist for at least 2 weeks. This experiment did not come to any conclusions about the cause of the decreased vagal-cardiac nerve traffic; however, the well documented reduction of blood volume that occurs while in microgravity is a probable explanation. The researchers attempted to document the time-course of in-flight adaptations, however, they were unable to adequately record directional trends. It is not yet clear whether changes in autonomic cardiovascular regulation progress or stabilize as a function of the duration of exposure to microgravity. Although the data obtained from this experiment was limited, the researchers hope the information obtained from this experiment can help to guide future research onboard the International Space Station.

title: Otolith Tilt-Translation Reinterpretation
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: The Otolith Tilt-Translation Reinterpretation hypothesized that adaptation to space flight is a function of sensory rearrangement and that signals from the otolith organs during orbital flight are reinterpreted as linear displacements. An important question relating to this concept concerns the maintenance or substitution by other sensory systems of information to the central nervous system which will replace missing or altered vestibular inputs. Specifically, this study investigated the possibility of neck receptors as substitutes for otolith receptor inputs to maintaining ocular torsion during space flight. The measurement of ocular torsion is difficult under the best of circumstances. When coupled with the additional constraints imposed by orbital flight, very careful consideration had to be given to the mechanism and procedures that were to be used. The device and procedures had to be simple enough that the experiment could be performed by one crewperson at a time, while meeting size, weight, and safety requirements. To meet these criteria, a method of measuring ocular torsion first used about 140 years ago was selected. In this method an after-image of a target is formed on the retina. Any eye torsion occurring while the after-image is visible produces a tilting of the after-image relative to an objective reference target.
approach: An ocular counter-rolling measurement device was used to obtain ocular torsion with the after-image method. This device is a goggle arrangement housing an electronic flash to place the after image on the retina, and a digital read out to indicate angular position of the target. A small voice-activated tape recorder was attached to the goggle so that the subjects could verbally report the position of the target as well as their head position. A neck brace was used to eliminate proprioceptive cues from the neck as a control measurement during the flight. During pre- and postflight data collection, the subject set the target to the gravitational vertical with the thumbwheel. The vertical position corresponded to a value of 1000 on the digital display. Then, while following a checklist, the subject tilted his head and the goggles to a predetermined and randomized angle. Once the subject achieved the tilt angle, that position was maintained for approximately 30 seconds. Following the 30 second period the electronic flash was enabled and triggered to place an after-image on the retina. With the after-image in place, the subject returned the goggles to the upright position. The subject shut his eyes and displaced the target slightly with a thumbwheel in either the clock wise or counterclockwise direction. Once the target was displaced from the vertical, the subject opened his eyes, set the target reticle with the thumbwheel so that it matched the angular position of the after-image, and read a displacement value from the LED’s. The subject repeated this procedure in the upright position twice more for that angle, always displacing the target in the opposite direction between each measurement. This entire procedure was then repeated for each of the remaining eight angles of head tilt.
results: Based on the data obtained, the eyes show a compensatory torsional movement to head tilt. This compensatory torsional eye movement appears to be elicited by the neck receptors. These findings support a concept of sensory substitution, in this case the substitution of neck receptors for missing otolith information. If these findings are replicated on future flights, the Otolith Tilt-Translation Reinterpretation hypothesis may be modified to incorporate these results. As one might expect, adaptation to space flight is a complex process that is just beginning to be understood.

title: Influence of Weightlessness on Baroreflex Function
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Exposure to weightlessness alters postflight cardiovascular responses to exercise and standing. Although these changes are probably initiated during flight, they are not known to impair cardiovascular performance in space. However, functional problems become apparent upon landing, when most astronauts have reduced exercise capacity and orthostatic intolerance. Loss of plasma volume during weightlessness may be partially responsible for orthostatic intolerance. Orthostatic intolerance is a predictable, but a poorly understood consequence of space travel. Because arterial baroreceptors modulate abrupt pressure transients, including those provoked by standing, the hypothesis that space flight impairs baroreflex mechanisms was tested.
approach: Vagally-medicated carotid baroreceptor-cardiac reflex responses (provoked by neck pressure changes) in the supine position and heart rate and blood pressure in the supine and standing positions were studied in 16 U.S. astronauts (15 male and one female) before and after four to five day Space Shuttle missions. Preflight studies were performed nominally 10 and five days before launch; in practice, preflight data were collected between 13 and seven days, and again between seven and five days before launch. Postflight data were collected on landing (R+0), on R+3, and again on R+8. The electrocardiogram, respiration (abdominal bellows connected to a strain-gauge pressure transducer), and neck chamber pressure were recorded by FM tape and strip chart recorders. The electrocardiogram and respiration were recorded during the last five minutes of a 20-minute rest period prior to any intervention. Resting vagal-cardiac activity was estimated from average R-R intervals and their standard deviations. Blood pressure was measured manually with a sphygmomanometer before barorector testing.
results: On landing day, astronauts’ resting R-R intervals and standard deviations, and the slope, range, and position of their resting R-R intervals on the carotid transmural pressure-sinus mode response relation (operational point) were reduced relative to preflight values. Reductions of operational points (indicating reduced hypotensive buffering capacity) were related directly and significantly to reductions of postflight systolic pressure responses to standing. After landing day, baroreflex slopes and ranges were subnormal and remained so for the duration of the study (eight to 10 days). These results suggest that short-duration space flight leads to significant, functionally relevant impairment of human baroreflex mechanisms.

title: In-flight Evaluation of a Portable Clinical Blood Analyzer
experiment_type: Shuttle Extended Duration Orbiter Medical Project (EDOMP)
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Research on human adaptation to microgravity often involves storing blood samples for later analysis on Earth. Immediate, inflight analysis would make
approach: The Portable Clinical Blood Analyzer (PCBA) is a hand-held, battery-powered device that measures electrolytes by ion-selective electrode potentiometry, glucose by amperometry, hematocrit by conductometrics, and pH by direct potentiometry. It does not measure hemoglobin. The analyzer was tested on the ground against traditional laboratory methods, using capillary blood, venous blood and control solutions. It was then tested for inflight use on 5 Shuttle missions. Control solutions were analyzed before and during the flights. Twice during flight, 21 astronauts performed finger sticks on each other, collected capillary blood using heparinized capillary tubes, and transferred the blood to the analyzer. Blood samples were also collected and analyzed before and after flights.
results: available during a mission and would avoid the need for refrigeration or freezing and the possibility of deterioration of the samples. The objective of this hardware study was to test a portable device for inflight analysis of blood samples. APPROACH: The Portable Clinical Blood Analyzer (PCBA) is a hand-held, battery-powered device that measures electrolytes by ion-selective electrode potentiometry, glucose by amperometry, hematocrit by conductometrics, and pH by direct potentiometry. It does not measure hemoglobin. The analyzer was tested on the ground against traditional laboratory methods, using capillary blood, venous blood and control solutions. It was then tested for inflight use on 5 Shuttle missions. Control solutions were analyzed before and during the flights. Twice during flight, 21 astronauts performed finger sticks on each other, collected capillary blood using heparinized capillary tubes, and transferred the blood to the analyzer. Blood samples were also collected and analyzed before and after flights. RESULTS: The performance of the analyzer in microgravity was similar to its performance on the ground for all the control solutions except sodium, and the small difference in sodium levels was within clinical laboratory performance standards. The astronauts were able to collect and analyze blood samples in flight. Some changes were noted in pH and levels of potassium and ionized calcium during flight or on landing day, but the values returned to preflight levels within 3 to 6 days. The analyzer was found to be very reliable for immediate analysis of sodium, potassium, ionized calcium, pH and glucose on the ground and during space flight. It is being flown routinely to help flight surgeons evaluate the health of the astronauts, and it will be especially useful for following calcium levels and evaluating bone changes during long spaceflights. The device may also prove useful in remote areas on Earth.

title: Evoked Potentials
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: The objective of this experiment was to document changes in neurological system transducer signals and system processing of these signals in a space environment by utilizing a noninvasive investigating procedure. Time synchronized signals were applied to sensory areas and recordings were made from electrodes near associated nerve pathways. This included audio, visual, and somatosensory pathways.
approach: Tests primarily involved only the physician-crewmember (self-test), however, it was desirable to make recordings of opportunity on other crewmembers on a time available basis. Discrete repetitive stimuli such as clicks, optical patterns, or tactile stimuli were generated and presented to the individual. The signal time was recorded on one of two channels of the tape recorder, and after amplification the
results: ing signal from the nervous system was recorded on a second channel. The recording was processed by synchronously averaging the signals and displaying the period of interest. The physician-crewmember's notes and test correlation data were obtained for analysis. RESULTS: Five subjects participated in this experiment. Auditory evoked potentials were studied pre- and postflight on STS-8. All crew members received the pre- and postflight tests, and inflight studies were performed on two normal subjects and two subjects before and after developing space motion sickness. No change in short and mid-latency audio-evoked potentials was found, with or without SMS. Visual evoked potential studies were also done preflight and inflight. No significant changes were noted in visual evoked potentials.

title: Stability and Precision of Human Performance During a Spaceflight Mission
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: The success of long-term space flights with humans depends in part on harmonious individual and group behavior. The development of a technology that can effectively predict and provide behavioral support for individuals during prolonged exposure to confined environments is of primary importance. Performance studies of small groups over the past two decades have demonstrated that the consequence of any single individual's behavior is a critical determinant of both individual and group behavior under conditions of prolonged social and cultural isolation. Computerized procedures have been developed during ground-based studies for engendering and maintaining stable measures of complex human behaviors, including cognitive and psychomotor performances. In studies involving continuous performance monitoring, human participants were able to work productively and energetically over extended time intervals. The stability and sensitivity of the measures generated made it possible to assess both decrements and enhancements of performances affected by such things as sleep deprivation, medications, and other stressful conditions. The sensitivity and utility of these computerized tests allowed crewmember performance to be evaluated during space flight.
approach: Four subjects participated in this study. A computerized task battery was administered preflight, inflight and postflight. The task battery required approximately 20 minutes to complete and consisted of the following components: A 72 item research version of the Profile of Mood States (POMS) questionnaire requiring a 1 (not at all) to 5 (extremely) keypad rating of adjectives associated with eight empirically derived mood scales. An 11 item Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) requiring the use of a computer tracking ball to move an indicator to a location on a line between the labels titled "not at all" (on the left) and "extremely" (on the right). The action was in response to words on the computer display screen representing the subject's feeling at the time of presentation. A Time Estimation Task (timing measure) requiring that repeated presses on the keypad be spaced by a fixed time interval. The action would advance a point counter and increase the monitoring gauge on the computer display screen. A Repeated Acquisition Task (learning measure) requiring that the subjects learn to press four designated keys on the keypad to complete a sequence of 10 responses. Feedback for correct and incorrect responses was provided on the computer display screen. A new order for pressing the four designated keys was learned each time the task was presented. A Number Recognition Task (measure of short-term memory performance) requiring the subject to hold down two keys simultaneously on the key pad, one of which was designated a "yes" key and the other a "no" key. An array of numbers presented on the computer display screen disappeared after a brief exposure and a single test number appeared. If the test number was presented in the previous array, the finger was lifted from the "yes" key and if not, the "no" key finger was lifted. A Digit Symbol Substitution Task (psychomotor performance measure) requiring presses on a 9 digit keypad corresponding to the location of filled squares in signaled boxes in 3x3 patterns of boxes that appeared on the computer display screen. The location of the filled squares and the 3x3 signaled boxes on the computer display screen were changed frequently to prevent memorization of the patterns. daily log was also completed during each phase of the study, which provided information on sleep, diet, exercise and medication usage. In addition, debriefing reports were obtained during postflight interviews conducted with each individual. Performances during the computerized task battery were recorded on separate individualized computer diskettes. The time and duration of each data collection session were recorded along with rating scale responses and the number of correct and incorrect responses to each of the programmed tasks. The number of data collection sessions during each phase of the study varied between subjects. Each subject had 6 or more training sessions followed by 5 or more preflight baseline sessions, 5 or more inflight sessions, and 6 or more postflight sessions.
results: All four subjects learned the computerized task battery without difficulty and maintained stable levels of performance during preflight baseline data collection. Results obtained with the self-report mood (POMS) and feelings (VAS) scales reliably reflected changes in selected items during each study phase. For example, on measures of fatigue from both the POMS and the VAS, increased ratings obtained inflight (relative to preflight baselines) were significantly decreased postflight. POMS and VAS data obtained from individual subjects also showed consistency in the relationship between scale items, reflecting progressive changes inflight. Timing performances for all four subjects, as measured by the Time Estimation Task, remained stable and accurate throughout the study with no evident perturbations during any phase of the investigation. Learning performances as measured by the Repeated Acquisition Task were also found to hold up well throughout the study with no identifiable changes. Within each data collection session, all four subjects rapidly learned the correct 10-response sequence. There was evidence of increased efficiency of the learning performance across preflight, inflight, and postflight phases of the study. Across sessions, the efficiency with which these sequences were learned remained stable in the absence of any conditions that affected learning ability. Results obtained with the Number Recognition Task were consistent with the outcome of preliminary studies showing differences in information processing response times, specifically the times associated with determining whether the matching stimulus number was a "yes" or "no" response and whether the number of digits in the sample display was large (4 to 6) or small (1 to 3). In addition, evident increases in the response times were recorded inflight. A significant three-way interaction between the yes/no response times, the number of digits in the sample display array and the phase of the study was also recorded. A selective and significant (p Psychomotor performances as measured by the Digit Symbol Substitution Task showed selective inflight changes. While the performance rate increased modestly during the preflight and postflight testing phases, significant decreases in performance rates were observed inflight. Preliminary examination of daily log sheets and debriefing reports has been undertaken to identify factors of potential relevance to the outcome of the study. The results of this study show clearly that the stability and precision of human performance during spaceflight can be reliably and sensitively assessed with a computerized battery of cognitive and psychomotor tasks requiring only minimal training. Although the research findings identified significant changes in the performances of subjects inflight, no mission-impairing decrements were apparent. However, the nature of the changes during the inflight phase of the study do suggest that some elements of performance are sensitive to microgravity environments. Additional research is needed to further delineate the nature of these effects, and to assess the potential value of such measures as an index of other mission-critical dimensions of behavior over more extended space flight intervals.

title: Blood Pressure Monitoring During Reentry
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Postflight orthostatic hypotension has been noted since the Mercury flights and can be expected after exposures to weightlessness. Orthostatic hypotension arises from fluid shifts, fluid loss, decreased peak physical loads, and from neurological adaptation. Due to concerns related to hypotension during Space Shuttle reentry, crewmembers were provided with antigravity suits (AGSs). Concerns were expressed over orthostatic problems directly affecting the astronauts during and immediately following reentry.
approach: Blood pressure and heart rate were the standards by which orthostatic status was determined. A commercial blood pressure-heart rate recorder was used in space motion sickness (SMS) studies on several missions, and by one crewmember during reentry with AGS activation and deactivation. After several near-syncopal (fainting) episodes on Shuttle missions following seat egress, presumed to be orthostatic hypotension, this experiment was designed to make a series of blood pressure (BP) and heart rate (HR) records during entry and egress. The BP-HR recorder was an extensively tested and used, commercially available, ambulatory unit. More information is provided in the hardware description below. For preflight tests, the subject had a 30 minute briefing session on the recorder use and then made two recordings during simulations. For in-flight and postflight tests, 30 minutes was required for installation of the recorder; it was a one person effort, except for the wrapping of the arm cuff, which involved a second crewmember for less than one minute. The recorder was installed and started at least 30 minutes prior to strapping in for reentry. The recorder was carried on an elastic waist belt and did not interfere with other hardware. The recorder was worn through reentry without any restrictions on the crewmember. Inflation of the AGS was done as desired.
results: Ambulatory blood pressures (BP) and heart rates (HR) were recorded on a series of early Shuttle flights during preflight and pre-entry, entry, landing and egress. There were no significant differences between flight and preflight values during routine activity. Systolic blood pressure was slightly elevated in the deorbit period and systolic and diastolic blood pressure and heart rates were all elevated with onset of gravitoinertial loads and remained so through egress. Two of seven subjects had orthostatic problems in egress but their data did not show significant differences from others, except in heart rate. Comparison of this data to data from recent studies show even larger increase in HR/BP values during current deorbit and entry phases, which is consistent with increased heat and weight loads imposed by added survival gear. Both value and limitations of ambulatory heart rate/blood pressure data in this situation are demonstrated.

title: Evaluation of Samples Obtained from the Urine Monitoring System
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: The Urine Monitoring System (UMS) provides for collection, volume measurement, and sampling of void-by-void urine in 0-g or 1-g environments. However, UMS data gathered from STS-40 (SLS-1) indicated that verification of in-flight sample dilution from residual fluids was required along with volume measurement. This DSO was flown on two missions, STS-47 and STS-55, with the objective to determine if the in-flight sample dilution and volume measurement by the UMS was comparable to the method used in ground-based testing.
approach: Evaluation of the UMS sample dilution was performed by first comparing lithium solution concentrations before and after dispensing into the UMS, then determining the lithium recovery, thus the dilution effect of remaining fluids. One mL of lithium chloride solution (250 mmol/L lithium), used as a volume marker, was added to Shuttle beverage pouches then diluted with different volumes of water. These solutions were poured into the UMS, then samples were obtained for lithium analysis. Electrolytes and specific gravity were determined on these samples, and recoveries were also calculated for each analyte. Volume measurement evaluation was performed by comparing UMS mass readouts to known volumes either measured during ground-based testing or calculated from lithium concentrations of in-flight samples collected before dispensing into the UMS. Three sample configurations were used for STS-47 UMS testing: (1) 24 Shuttle beverage pouches containing lithium chloride marker, (2) three Shuttle beverage pouches containing 240 or 360 mL of saline solution, and (3) three urine voids each collected into Contingency Urine Collection Assemblies CUCAs. Preflight lithium-filled pouches were diluted with 120, 240, or 360 mL of milliQ water and dispensed into the UMS. Water (180 mL) was decanted into the UMS between some of the lithium samples to determine the amount of residual lithium remaining after the flush cycle. Saline and urine void configurations were not included, but were later added for in-flight and postflight testing. In-flight and postflight lithium-filled pouches were diluted with 4, 8, 12, or 16 ounces of galley water, while postflight pouches were diluted with 120, 240, 360, or 480 mL. Each sample was dispensed into the UMS. Second syringe aliquots were collected on some of the UMS samples. Saline and urine void configurations were included for testing. Two sample configurations were used for STS-55 UMS testing (saline solution samples were not configured for testing): 15-18 Shuttle beverage pouches containing lithium chloride marker, and 14-15 urine voids each collected into CUCAs. Lithium-filled pouches were diluted preflight and postflight with 120, 250, 360, or 480 mL of milliQ water (postflight also included 700 mL volume). In-flight samples were filled with 4, 8, 12, or 16 ounces of galley water. During the flight, some bags were not filled to specified volumes which
results: ed from low water pressure. Lithium-filled pouches were diluted preflight and postflight with 120, 250, 360, or 480 mL of milliQ water (postflight also included 700 mL volume). In-flight samples were filled with 4, 8, 12, or 16 ounces of galley water. During the flight, some bags were not filled to specified volumes which resulted from low water pressure. RESULTS: STS-47: The UMS performance on STS-47 (SL-J) was considered nominal until postflight inspection of the UMS flush water showed the presence of urine instead of clean water. It was later confirmed that the UMS flush water line was improperly connected in flight to the waste quick disconnect (QD). Postflight analysis of in-flight DSO 323 lithium samples confirmed the presence of urine constituents. It was expected that the dilution evaluation portion of this DSO would not result in reliable data due to lithium contamination from the waste water. Percent lithium recoveries were generally higher than STS-55 data, indicating probable lithium contamination, although postflight lithium testing of the in-flight waste water samples confirmed negligible lithium concentrations. In general, in-flight lithium recoveries were lower than pre- or postflight data, with greater dilution present in the smallest volume category (120 mL). In-flight volume calculations (calculated UMS volume dispensed) derived from lithium concentration of diluted samples dispensed into the UMS were not affected by urine contamination from the flush water. These calculated volumes were slightly higher than corresponding UMS mass readings. In-flight mass readings were slightly lower than ground-based mass readings of similar volumes. Comparison of saline and urine void data for in-flight and postflight testing periods was inconclusive due to in-flight urine contamination from the waste water and also inconsistent and insufficient postflight data. STS-55 Lithium data showed decreased percent recoveries with lower volumes. Second syringe samples of urine and lithium were less dilute than first syringe samples. Higher percent recoveries were noted in preflight samples versus in-flight and postflight samples. Calculated UMS volumes dispensed were slightly higher than adjusted UMS mass readings. Mass readings were adjusted according to in-flight calibration data and appeared to be more linear as compared to ST8-47 data (in-flight calibration not performed). Conclusions In-flight and ground study comparisons of UMS samples show that dilution of samples is more pronounced and is more varied with lower sample volumes, as expected. In general, in-flight samples were more diluted and had lower mass readings than ground samples with similar volumes.

approach: Eight Space Shuttle crewmembers, five from a 7-day flight and three from a 9-day flight, participated in this study. title: Cellular Immune Response
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: The functional capacity of lymphocytes (phytohemagglutinin (PHA) responsiveness only) was found to be depressed for studies conducted during Apollo missions 7 through 13 and Skylab missions 3 and 4. T-lymphocyte numbers were also suppressed in Skylab. The objective of this study was to examine the effects of space flight on the cellular immune response in Apollo-Soyuz Test Project (ASTP) crewmembers.
approach: Samples of heparinized peripheral venous blood (10cc) were obtained preflight and postflight on days L-30 (30 days before liftoff), L-15, L-5, R+0 (day of recovery), R+1 (recovery +1 day), R+8 and R+13. Samples were processed within 1 to 24 hours of collection. Parameters measured for this study included: 1) white blood cell concentrations, 2) lymphocyte numbers, 3) B-lymphocyte and T-lymphocyte distributions in peripheral blood and 4) lymphocyte responsiveness to PHA, pokeweed mitogen (PWM), Concanavalin A (Con A) and influenza virus antigen. Before separation, total leukocyte counts were performed using a hemacytometer and/or a Coulter Counter. Differential counts were determined using slide preparations stained with Wright’s stain. Lymphocytes were separated by Ficoll-Hypaque centrifugation, which uses a special liquid that provides a density gradient. Higher density blood cells are pulled far down into the liquid by centrifugal action, while the more buoyant lymphocytes remain near the center. The supernatant was removed by pipette, and the
results: ing mononuclear cells were washed three times in minimum essential medium (MEM). B-lymphocyte distributions were determined by calculating the percentage of 200 mononuclear cells with surface immunoglobulins, which were detected by the immunofluorescent antibody technique. The presence of E-rosette-forming lymphocytes (T-cells) was determined using a concentration of one million lymphocytes in 0.25 ml of 0.5% sheep red blood cell (SRBC) suspension. After mixing, the tubes were incubated at 37 degrees Celsius for 5 minutes, and then placed in ice water for 2 hours. Approximately half of the supernatant was removed, and the top cell layer was gently resuspended. Two hundred lymphocytes were counted with 3 or more adhering SRBC’s, which were used as criteria for E-rosetted lymphocytes. Purified lymphocytes (one million cells) in MEM containing 40% fetal calf serum were placed in culture plates. The antigens were diluted in MEM (containing Pen-Strep and L-glutamine) in the following concentrations: 0.01 ml PHA/ml MEM; 0.01 and 0.05 ml PWM/ml MEM; and 25 and 50 micrograms Con A/ml MEM. These diluted antigens were placed in the appropriate wells of the tissue culture plates in 0.1 ml aliquots (in duplicate). The cultures were incubated in a humidified carbon dioxide atmosphere at 37 degrees Celsius (3 days for PHA and 5 days for Con A and PWM). On the day of harvest, samples were treated as described in the following section for influenza virus antigen cultures. An inactivated monovalent type A influenza virus vaccine containing 1600 chick cell agglutinating units/ml of a Hong Kong strain was dialyzed against phosphate-buffered saline and stored at -70 degrees Celsius until used for tests. Separated lymphocytes were added in 0.1 ml aliquots for each influenza antigen dilution, and the cultures were incubated in a humidified carbon dioxide incubator at 37 degrees Celsius for periods of either 2 or 3 days. On the day of harvest, cells were pulsed for 2 hours with 1 microcurie of methyl(tritium)-thymidine, a radioactive marker. Cells were then harvested with an automated harvester onto glass-fiber filter strips and counted in a liquid scintillation counter. Data were expressed as counts per minute (CPM)/one million lymphocytes, and the stimulation index (SI) was calculated by dividing the mean result for stimulated cultures by that for unstimulated cultures. Allantoic fluid was used separately as a control of each crewman’s reactivity to chick embryo proteins. RESULTS: Preflight (L-30) white blood cell (WBC) counts for ASTP and Skylab were 6640±1830 WBC/mm3 and 6013±254 WBC/ mm3, respectively. The ASTP crew had significant increases in WBC numbers noted on R+0 (11,110±4210 WBC/mm3) and R+1 (13,530±610 WBC/mm3). Individual variation in WBC values was noted among the three Skylab crewmembers at R+0 (8980±5560 WBC/mm3), which is reflected in the large standard deviation. However, all values were within clinically normal ranges (7110±2400 WBC/mm3). Less variation overall was noted for total lymphocyte values; however, values at R+0 for ASTP (1950±490 lymphocyte count/mm3) and Skylab 4 (1177±381 lymphocyte count/mm3) were decreased below their previous baseline values (ASTP L-30=2820±480 lymphocyte count/mm3 and Skylab L-30=1940±670 lymphocyte count/mm3). Fluctuations in the individual values of T-lymphocytes, B-lymphocytes and nonreactive lymphocytes of ASTP crewmembers were indicated, but values remain within one standard deviation for normal laboratory values. T-cell values ranged from 1.29 million +/- 490,000 to 2.53 million +/- 440,000 lymphocytes/ml (normal=1.59 million +/- 630,000 lymphocytes/ml), B-lymphocytes from 470,000 +/- 20,000 to 710,000 +/- 40,000 lymphocytes/ml (normal=510,000 +/- 300,000 lymphocytes/ml) and nonreactive lymphocytes from 120,000 +/- 120,000 to 710,000 +/- 370,000 lymphocytes/ml (normal=850,000 +/- 560,000 lymphocytes/ml). In contrast, highly significant changes were noted in B and T cell distributions of the Skylab 4 crewmen. Results from culture studies show a definite decrease in the ability of lymphocytes to react with PHA at R+0 (SI=20±15) and R+1 (SI=12±8) for all three Apollo astronauts. Baseline SI mean at L-30 was 36±4. By R+8, all were back within normal ranges (SI range=10 to 282). Crewmembers began and remained at low-level SI ranges for Con A (3 to 49) throughout the preflight and postflight periods, except for one subject, who had a strengthened Con A stimulation of 151 at splashdown. Considerable individual variation was noted in the PWM data and no consistent trend was obtained. Variation of antigen stimulation indexes may be expected, due to the rapid exchange of cells between different compartments in the body. The entire Apollo crew responded to influenza virus England strain preflight in cultures, and one of the three astronauts responded postflight to influenza virus Hong Kong strain. Total lack of reactivity may reflect influenza susceptibility. ASTP crewmembers experienced contact with toxic gases upon splashdown. Depressions observed at R+0 were caused by either space flight or gas exposure a few hours prior to sample analysis. Similar depressions in lymphocytic responsiveness were observed in Skylab 3 and 4 data, although both of these missions were of much longer duration than ASTP. However, in comparable missions of similar lengths (i.e., the Apollo series) no changes in lymphocytic responsiveness were reported. The toxic gas exposure was severe enough to create concern for lung inflammation, which resulted in a corticosteroid treatment on R+1. Most cortisone preparations are known to cause a lymphocytic reaction. Consequently, it is likely that the increased immunosuppressions noted by cultural responses on R+1 for all mitogens and on R+8 for Con A were attributable to the steroid therapy.

title: Exercise Response

objectives: The success of the Apollo program overall, and the lunar landing missions specifically, was dependent upon the ability of the astronauts to engage in long and strenuous hours of extravehicular activity (EVA). Although it was expected that reduced gravity would make some tasks less difficult, it was noted that reduced suit mobility and the complexity of the mission timeline indicated that metabolic activity would exceed resting levels for extended periods of time. Because the type and extent of physiological dysfunction that could
approach: A bicycle ergometer and graded stress protocol were used to conduct the exercise stress tests. Heart rate (beats per minute) was used in determining stress levels. The bicycle ergometer was the only device capable of enabling quantitation of the work level. The graded exercise test permitted a progressive evaluation of physiological control system response and provided a better understanding of safe stress limits. By maintaining the same heart rate levels before and after flight, the same relative cardiovascular stresses were imposed. The tests were conducted 30, 14 and 4 days before flight, on recovery day (R+0), and 24 and 36 hours postflight. The same equipment was utilized before and after flight to conduct the stress tests. The protocol was comprised of exercise levels at heart rates of 120 ( for 6 minutes), 140 ( for 3 minutes), and 160 ( for 3 minutes). Samples of expired gas were obtained at appropriate times during each test. The Apollo 9 and 10 crewmen were also evaluated at stress level of 180 beats per minute (bpm). During each test, workload, heart rate, blood pressure, and respiratory gas exchange (oxygen consumption, carbon dioxide production, and minute volume) were measured every minute. For Apollo 15 to 17, cardiac output measurements were obtained by single-breath technique. Arteriovenous oxygen differences were calculated from the measured oxygen consumption and cardiac output.
