approach: The subjects' jugular flow was monitored via a pocket Doppler device, which provided an audio Doppler signal. The character of the jugular flow was assessed, and after a verification trial, the target pressure was accepted as the CVP estimate. A total of 9 astronauts, 4 women and 5 men, were subjects for this investigation. They flew on 4 Shuttle flights with flight durations of 5, 5, 6, and 8 days. Preflight data were collected one or more times from all 9 subjects while they were supine, and inflight data were collected as often as possible.
results: For the 9 subjects, absolute data, as well as data normalized using the preflight average, showed a significant decrease in CVP from early in the mission (day 1) to late in the mission (day 6). After inspection of the data, subjects were grouped according to whether or not the last in-flight data point was greater than their preflight average. The 2 groups (n=4 and n=5) were compared with respect to the relationship between CVP response and the subjects' sex, age, severity of motion sickness, body weight, and changes in body weight. The results for these factors were equivocal because of the small number of cases. The decrease in CVP agrees with earlier studies, but this study showed a different time course for the changes.

title: Leg Plethysmography
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Signs and symptoms secondary to fluid shifts in weightlessness were among the first physiologic effects noted in the manned space flight program. These effects included puffy faces, nasal congestion, in-flight and postflight weight loss, orthostatic hypotension, and cardiovascular changes. The headward shift of body fluids, both intravascular and extravascular,
approach: The stocking plethysmograph, first used on STS-5, 7 and 8, continued to be used for determination of direct girth-length measurements. From a series of circumferential measurements, volume was calculated under the assumption that a truncated cone represents a reasonable approximation of a leg volume segment. On these later Shuttle flights, the original leg volume protocol was modified to study the time course of leg volume changes; a sequence of measurements were made as early as possible in flight. Furthermore, leg volumes were obtained pre- and postflight during the routine medical stand tests.
results: from the absence of the 1-g hydrostatic gradient. The purpose of this study was to measure leg volume changes during space flight. APPROACH: The stocking plethysmograph, first used on STS-5, 7 and 8, continued to be used for determination of direct girth-length measurements. From a series of circumferential measurements, volume was calculated under the assumption that a truncated cone represents a reasonable approximation of a leg volume segment. On these later Shuttle flights, the original leg volume protocol was modified to study the time course of leg volume changes; a sequence of measurements were made as early as possible in flight. Furthermore, leg volumes were obtained pre- and postflight during the routine medical stand tests. RESULTS: Time course of the fluid shift was determined to be exponential with a time constant of 6-8 hours. A second result seen was the relatively small amount of fluid which is pooled in the legs postflight and the disproportionately large signs of orthostatic stress this induced. Either the blood volume remains small or there is a large pooling elsewhere in the body. There was also a suggestion that a blunting of normal heart rate response may have occurred. The volume change and percentage change were all compared with the preflight volume determinations. The landing measurements were made within 1.5 hours of touchdown. The postflight measurements were made during the first week post-landing. It should be noted that the 1-g leg volume measurements for Skylab and ASTP were made with the crewmembers in the supine position, whereas the measurements in the Shuttle program were made with the crewmembers standing. When going from standing to supine, there is a shift of approximately 300ml of blood out of the legs. The in-flight volume changes found in the 11 subjects from the Shuttle program demonstrated a mean volume change of 1026 ml or 11.6% with a range from 1790 ml or 16.9% to 685 ml or 8.3%. The majority of the subjects had a 10% to 12% volume change. This compares with the 12.2% from Skylab and 10.0% from ASTP. The source of this leg volume change is a relatively rapid shift of blood followed by interstitial fluid and probably intercellular fluid, with some tissue loss secondary to muscle atrophy.

title: In-flight Pharmacokinetics of Acetaminophen in Saliva
experiment_type: Shuttle Extended Duration Orbiter Medical Project (EDOMP)
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Evidence exists that the therapeutic effectiveness of some drugs may change in space. The objective of this study was to determine whether acetaminophen, a drug used frequently for pain relief by astronauts in space, actually reaches its site of action at concentrations sufficient to elicit a therapeutic response. The absorption and distribution of acetaminophen were examined to monitor potential changes in drug pharmacokinetics during spaceflight.
approach: A noninvasive saliva sampling technique was used. Tablets of acetaminophen were administered orally to 1 or 2 crew members on each of 7 missions (total of 13 subjects) twice before and at least once during space flight (ideally on flight day 3 or 4). Using the Saliva Collection Kit, saliva samples were collected 10 times, from 0 to 8 hours, after each drug administration. The concentration of acetaminophen in the samples, determined by high-performance liquid chromatography, was used to calculate parameters for pharmacokinetic evaluation.
results: Salivary acetaminophen concentration profiles during space flight were different from those obtained on the ground. Changes were more pronounced in the absorption phase than in the elimination phase. The time needed to reach maximum concentration of acetaminophen increased during flight, indicating that absorption time was prolonged. Changes in the maximum acetaminophen concentration depended on mission length. Results of this study supported predictions that drug dynamics change during flight and suggested that these changes depend upon mission length and individual physiologic responses to space flight. The limited in-flight data accumulated for this study were insufficient to characterize the degree and magnitude of pharmacokinetic changes and the mechanisms underlying them.

title: In vivo Testing Confirms a Blunting of the Human Cell-Mediated Immune Mechanism During Space Flight
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Changes in cellular immune potential during or following space flight have been reported in both the U.S. and Russian space programs. These changes were usually discovered using in vitro testing performed after flight, with various findings related to alterations in cellular responses. Direct in-flight, in vivo testing was used in this study to demonstrate the cell-mediated immune (CMI) system response during space flight.
approach: The delayed-type hypersensitivity (DTH) response of 10 Space Shuttle astronauts to 7 common recall antigens was measured using the Multitest CMI test system to administer antigens of tetanus, diphtheria, Streptococcus , Proteus , old tuberculin, Candida , and Trichophyton to the forearm after 2, 4, or 8 days of flight. This approach was used because DTH accompanies many manifestations of CMI and because skin reactions have often provided a model for the elucidation of effector mechanisms in CMI. Readings were conducted 48 hours after antigen administration. Data were evaluated in three ways: (a) the number of positive responses of the 7 possible, (b) the individual mean diameter (mm) of the positive response, and (c) the total sum, in mm, of all the positive reactions (reaction score).
results: The mean number of reactions was reduced from 4.5 before flight to 3.0 during flight, and the mean reaction score was reduced from 21.4 mm before flight to 13.7 mm during flight. The data suggest the CMI system was still being degraded by space flight conditions on day 4 of flight, and between day 5 and day 10 the depression maximized and the system began to stabilize at the new level.

title: Prevalence of Hypertension in LSAH Participants
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Blood pressure is the force of the blood pushing against the walls of arteries. It is measured in millimeters of mercury (mmHg), and given in two numbers. The higher number indicates systolic pressure, which is the amount of force exerted on the walls of arteries within and leading from the heart when it contracts (i.e., during systole). The lower number is the diastolic pressure, which is the force existing between contractions (i.e., during diastole). Normal blood pressure is usually considered to be 120/80 mmHg; measurements above 140/90 mmHg are considered to be hypertensive. Hypertension, or high blood pressure, simply refers to the increased tension or pressure in the arteries. Hypertension is a major risk factor for heart attack, heart failure, stroke, and kidney failure. Most hypertensive people have no symptoms. For most people, there is no single known cause of high blood pressure. This type of high blood pressure is called primary or essential hypertension. Essential hypertension can't be cured, although in most cases it can be controlled. In some cases, high blood pressure can be traced to a known cause like tumors of the adrenal gland, chronic kidney disease, hormone abnormalities, use of birth control pills, or pregnancy. This is called secondary hypertension, and is usually cured if the underlying cause passes or is corrected. The goal of this study was to examine hypertension among the astronaut and comparison populations.
approach: According to data from the third National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey conducted from 1988-1991 (NHANES III), 20.4% of the US adult population is hypertensive (defined as systolic pressure of at least 140 mmHg or diastolic pressure of at least 90 mmHg).
results: Annual examination data for active and inactive NASA astronauts between 1959-1999 show 5.5% of them (21 of 291) have been diagnosed with hypertension. In comparison, data from the annual examinations of comparison participants over a similar time period show 13.9% (121 of 870) had corresponding hypertension diagnoses. As physical fitness is a requirement for astronauts, they are expected to show a lower rate of hypertension as compared to the general population. The comparison participants had more than double the hypertension rate of the astronauts, but still had a lower rate than the general population. This lower rate of hypertension may be an effect of being a healthy working population. Cross-sectional data of LSAH participants by age group show that most of them have average systolic pressure around or below 120 mmHg. Up to age 49, male comparisons show the same trend of systolic pressure measurements, although with slightly higher values, with that of the male astronauts. Male comparison participants aged 50 and older showed a higher increase of their systolic pressure as compared to male astronauts aged 50 and older. The diastolic pressure measurements for the male comparisons do not show a corresponding upward trend. Although the highest average measurement from the oldest age group of male comparisons is still below the hypertensive value of 140 mm Hg, this trend follows one observed in the general population. Data from NHANES III show that the highest increase in hypertension prevalence occurs between the 40-49 and 50-59 years age group for men. The small sample size of female participants does not allow for age group comparisons beyond the 40-44 age group.

title: Viral Reactivation
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Seven or more herpesviruses commonly establish infections in humans. Herpes simplex type-1 (HSV-1), herpes simplex type-2 (HSV-2), cytomegalovirus (CMV), Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), varicella-zoster virus (VZV), human herpesvirus-6 (HHV-6) and human herpesvirus-7 (HHV-7) are some examples of the double stranded DNA viruses that may establish a life-long latent infection in a host organism. Latent viruses are subject to intermittent reactivation. For example, replication of the reactivated herpesvirus genome may give rise to both infectious and noninfectious (defective) virus particles. Since one or more of the herpesviruses infects nearly 100% of the adult population, they are prime candidates for studying the effects of space flight on latent viral reactivation in astronauts. Latent virus reactivation may be an important threat to crew health during extended space missions where crewmembers live and work in a closed environment for 3 months or more. Exposure to infectious agents such as bacteria, fungi, viruses and parasites can be controlled by preflight quarantine as opposed to latent virus reactivation, an infection that originates inside the host organism. The establishment of viral latency and the subsequent reactivation are not well understood, but changes in the immune system are known to increase the incidence and duration of viral reactivation and shedding. Increasing scientific data indicates that the physical and psychological stressors associated with space flight cause alterations in the human immune response. Therefore, the objectives of this experiment were to evaluate the effects of long-duration habitation in space on latent virus reactivation, indicative of perturbations to the intricate host-parasite relationships. In this experiment, scientists tested the hypothesis that stressors associated with space flight will alter the host-parasite relationship in crewmembers inhabiting the Mir space station during extended stays, increasing both the incidence and the duration of herpesvirus reactivation and shedding.
approach: The approach to this experiment was to assess viral reactivation by the collection of serum and saliva samples. The original plan for sample collection included both the Mir 18 and 19 crew. The inflight and postflight sampling sessions on Mir 18 were not completed due to a cancellation of this experiment. Preflight saliva samples were obtained, but no blood samples were collected. However, contingency saliva sampling was performed on one crewmember during the flight. Preflight, inflight, and postflight saliva samples were collected from two crewmembers of the Mir 19 mission. Detection of the herpesvirus reactivation and shedding was conducted by saliva sample collection, DNA extraction from saliva, Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) amplification of herpesvirus DNA, and analysis of PCR products by gel electrophoresis. DNA extraction from saliva Saliva was collected and transferred to microcentrifuge tubes for extraction. DNA was extracted using a modification of the RNAzol method. Genomic/viral DNA was isolated simultaneously by adding 0.75 ml of Tris-saturated phenol (pH 6.6) RNAzol solution to 250 microliters saliva and briefly vortexing. After incubating on ice for 15 minutes, the tubes were centrifuged for 15 minutes at 12,000 x g and stored at -20 degrees Celsius overnight. The tubes were then centrifuged for 30 minutes at 16,000 x g and the supernatant removed. The DNA was then washed once with 7% ethanol and resuspended in 20 microliters DEPC-treated water. The suitability of extraction was evaluated by gel electrophoresis without nucleic acid quantitation. PCR Amplification of Herpesvirus DNA The oligonucleotide primers selected for this investigation amplified a highly conserved region of the DNA polymerase gene from the herpesvirus group. These primers allowed amplification of DNA to be directed to selected nucleotide fragments of the DNA polymerase genes for HSV-1, HSV-2, CMV and EBV . DNA was amplified in a total volume of 25 ml or a reaction mixture consisting of 50 mM KCl, 10mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.3), 1.5 mM MgCl2, 0.01% gelatin, 5% dimethylsulfoxide, 200 micromolar deoxynucleoside triphosphates, 20 pmol of each oligonucleotide primer, 0.625 U Taq polymerase, and 2 ml purified DNA solution. The reactions were performed in an automated thermocycler. The cycle, repeated 40 times, consisted of 15 seconds of denaturation at 96 degrees Celsius, 15 seconds of annealing at 60 degrees Celsius, and 15 seconds of elongation at 72 degrees Celsius. All samples were run with simultaneous positive control and negative (reagent) control. Measures to control contamination included the use of latex gloves, aerosol-resistant pipette tips, and two separate laboratories for preamplification and postamplification procedures. Analysis of PCR Products Ten microliters of the reaction mixture was run on a 2% Nusieve GTG agarose gel containing 1 microgram of ethidium bromide per ml in 1x TBE buffer. The gels were then placed under UV light for visualization of the amplified products and photographed.
results: The cancellation of this experiment on Mir 18 resulted in a limited sample collection. Inflight and postflight samples were not collected from the Mir 18 crewmembers. Preflight samples were collected from three crewmembers and five inflight samples were collected from one crewmember as contingency samples. Therefore, the only samples analyzed were those collected from the crewmember that participated in the inflight collection. The samples collected from the other crewmembers are archived for future analysis. All of the preflight samples were negative for the presence of herpesvirus DNA. However, two of the five inflight samples were positive for the presence of herpesvirus DNA. Since these data were very limited, no conclusions were made concerning the effects of microgravity on the host-parasite relationship. However, the methodology and sample handling logistics were successful. Two cosmonauts, both backup crewmembers for Mir 18, participated in the viral reactivation study on the Mir 19 mission. Thus, the preflight saliva specimens collected to establish baseline shedding patterns were collected prior to the Mir 18 mission. Saliva specimens were collected before, during, and after the flight. The samples were analyzed for the presence of Herpes simplex type-1 (HSV 1) and Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). All specimens were negative for HSV 1. Unfortunately, preflight saliva specimens were insufficient in number and frequency to establish a sound baseline for either crewmember. However, preflight shedding of EBV in the saliva was detected in over half of the total specimens. EBV DNA were detected in the saliva of crewmember A before, during, and after the flight. At least six episodes of shedding of EBV were observed during the mission. Inflight saliva specimens were collected beginning at about FD 25 and ending on FD 75. Shedding was also observed on R+14 and R+24. Crewmember B shedded EBV much less frequently during the mission than crewmember A. EBV DNA was observed in saliva from crewmember B on only two occasions during the mission. The conclusions made from this experiment were: (1) PCR methodology was capable of detecting latent viral DNA in saliva specimens collected and stored on the ground and on Mir, (2) neither crewmember appeared to be shedding HSV 1, (3) both crewmembers shed EBV before, during and after the mission, (4) shedding patterns of EBV of the two crewmembers were highly different during the inflight phase, (5) the technical feasibility of the approach was clearly demonstrated. The low number of subjects prevented any major conclusions from being drawn related to host-parasite relationships during space flight.

title: Association Between Aging and Specific Physiological Measurements
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: As part of the process of examining data to separate the effects of space flight from the background effects of aging, a comparison is made of the age-specific values for certain physiological measurements among both the astronauts and the comparison participants. In the general population, aging is associated with weight gain and increased serum lipids, increased blood pressure, and hearing loss. Similar associations were found among the LSAH population and the differences between the astronauts and the comparison participants, in general, were not dramatic.
approach: The current mean age of the study population is slightly lower for the females (41 years) than for the males (49 years). The age range is from the late 20s to the middle 70s. The cumulative follow-up time is 4,057 person years for the astronauts and 12,874 person years for the comparison participants. For the purposes of looking at the association of aging, cross-sectional data for specific age groups were examined. The data were organized by age of examination for all annual examinations for all study participants. The first examination was selected for each participant when he/she entered a new age group. An individual is included in every age group that he/she has achieved but is represented only once in any age group.
results: Low-density-lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol is the component of cholesterol that is most closely associated with risk of heart disease. The ratio of LDL to high-density-lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol appears to be more important than the raw values of either type of cholesterol. The trend frequently observed in the general population is an increase in LDL and a decrease in HDL as aging occurs. The trend among the LSAH population for LDL is also an increase with age. However, the trend for HDL is relatively flat. HDL is associated with exercise and it can be speculated that the LSAH population is more active than the general population. As the numbers of individuals in the upper age groups increase, this flat trend for HDL may or may not continue. The values for both of these variables are noticeably different for the females compared to the males. This difference is consistent with the lower risk of heart disease for women during pre-menopausal years than for men of the same ages. The sharp increase seen in LDL for women at age 40-44 is associated with an increase in risk that is more like the risk men have for heart disease. Relatively small increases in blood pressure result in increased risk of circulatory diseases such as stroke and heart disease. Analyses show an upward trend in blood pressure with age for both the comparison participants and the astronauts. Again, the number of females included in 40 and above age groups is small and results in somewhat erratic trend lines. Hearing loss is associated with aging as well as with occupational exposures to noise. It would not be unexpected to see greater hearing loss among the astronauts than among the comparison participants. However, that is not evident in the current data. The results of one of the high frequency (6000 Hertz) tests completed in the standard audiometric test are shown. The patterns were similar for all frequencies from 500 through 8000 Hertz. A hearing loss is seen in association with age, especially for males, but the difference between the comparison participants and the astronauts is negligible. There are some differences between the astronauts and the comparison participants in the many physiological measures recently examined but the patterns seem to be very much alike for the two groups. The astronauts started this study from a point of selection based on a high standard of well being, whereas the comparison participants started from a point of being a generally healthy working population. The occupational exposures of the astronauts have some high risks and are different from the comparison participants. However, the current data suggests that both groups are affected by age in the same ways.

title: Surveillance of Health Risks Among Older Adults
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Advances in medical technology, research, and health education have helped individuals aged 65 years and older become the fastest growing segment of the U.S. population, with a predicted increase from 13% in 1999 to 22% in 2030. In addition, the National Cancer for Health Statistics reports and increase in the U.S. estimated life expectancy from 57.1 years in 1929 to 76.9 years in 2000. These are amazing public health feats. As many diseases and health conditions are more prevalent among older adults, the public health community wants to ensure that not only do adults live longer lives but also maintain good health, independence, and a good quality of life. Factors leading to morbidity and mortality among older adults include overweight, inadequate fruit and vegetable consumption, physical inactivity, and cigarette smoking. Healthy People 2010 (HP) is a comprehensive set of health objectives that identify public health priorities and quantifiable objectives for the nation by the year 2010. Relevant HP goals include a decrease in underweight and overweight to 40% of the adult U.S. population greater than 20 years of age, an increase in the percentage who consume a minimum of 2 fruits and 3 vegetables per day to 75% and 50%, respectively, a decrease in the number who participate in no leisure-time physical activity to 20%, and a decrease in the number of cigarette smokers to 12%.
approach: These factors have been evaluated within the Longitudinal Study of Astronaut Health (LSAH) populations in comparison with the general public through LSAH data and the Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS), 1994-97. The BRFSS is an ongoing, state-based surveillance system maintained by the Centers for Disease Control. The survey is administered annually to a random sample of the noninstituionalized U.S. civilian population 18 years of age and older. Body mass index (BMI) data for LSAH participants were extracted from medical records in both the JSC Flight Medicine Clinic and Occupational Medicine Clinic. Nutritional data were taken from the Food Frequency Questionnaire (FFQ), and smoking and physical activity data were obtained from the Lifestyle Questionnaire (LSQ). Both the LSQ (1995) and the FFQ (1998) were designed to collect essential data on study participants that were not otherwise collected. There were no responding female LSAH survey participants over the age of 55. Consequently, these data have been excluded for all populations. With the exception of BMI for LSAH populations, all data collected are self-reported; therefore, the estimates may be misreported. However, the skew may be in the same direction for all three populations and may still give a general trend for the health risks being assessed.
results: Overweight : Overweight and obesity account for an estimated 300,000 deaths per year in the U.S. with an economic burden of $117 billion in 2000. Associated health problems include, but are not limited to, heart disease, diabetes, cancer, arthritis, reproductive complications, and psychological disorders. Here, the term 'over weight' includes two individual public health terms: overweight, a BMI of 25.0-29.9 kg/m2, and obesity, a BMI greater than or equal to 30.0 kg/m2. BMI is a measure of obesity, which is obtained by dividing the weight in kilograms by the height in meters squared. Individuals are considered overweight if they reported a BMI of greater than 25 kg/m2. The median values by state (for 50 U.S. states, the District of Columbia, and Puerto Rico) of overweight persons aged 55 years or older were gathered from 81,137 BRFSS respondents. The corresponding values were gathered from 55 astronauts and 257 comparison participants, and the resulting values are summarized. The prevalence of overweight tends to decrease with increasing age for both the astronaut and BRFSS populations, but increases in the comparison participants. Nevertheless, as all three groups show more than 50% overweight prevalence in both age groups, they fall far short of the desired HP 2010 goal. Inadequate Fruit and Vegetable Consumption: Diets rich in fruits and vegetables have been associated with a reduction in cardiovascular disease, some cancers, and diseases of the gastrointestinal tract. This led to the establishment of 5 A Day for Better Health, a comprehensive health promotion program designed to increase the consumption of fruits and vegetables to five or more servings per day by 2010. This program is sponsored by the National Cancer Institute in conjunction with the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services and the Produce for Better Health Foundation. Since the program's inception in 1991, the U.S. Department of Agriculture reports that the average daily consumption of fruits and vegetables by adults aged 18 years and older increased from 3.9 to 4.4, which is only about half a serving less than the recommended 5 servings per day. Subjects in the LSAH and BRFSS populations were asked about their general dietary habits, including the frequency of fruit and vegetable consumption. Excluded is the consumption of fruits and vegetables served as mixed dishes. The eligible participants for this portion of the surveys are 29 Astronauts, 207 comparisons, and 71,517 BRFSS participants. The data were then analyzed to determine the percent of participants who consumed at least five servings of fruits and vegetables per day. The prevalence of individuals who reported eating at least 5 servings of fruits and vegetables per day tends to increase with increasing age for each of the populations. Overall, both groups of LSAH participants have a higher prevalence of those eating at least five servings of fruits and vegetables as compared to the U.S. population, and are well on their way to meeting the HP 2010 goals. Physical Inactivity Physical activity has been shown to contribute to overall health and wellness. Although benefits include disease risk reduction, increased musculoskeletal strength and function, and increased psychological well-being, over 60% of adults do not engage in the recommended amount of physical activity, and 25% are not active at all. Strenuous physical activity is not required to achieve health related benefits. Sessions can be as simple as 30 minutes of brisk walking or 15-20 minutes of jogging on most days of the week, depending on the fitness level of the individual. Thus, it is imperative for older adults to consult a medical professional before beginning a new program of physical activity. LSAH and BRFSS survey participants were asked if they participated in any leisure-time physical activity regardless of frequency, duration, and intensity. Of 52 Astronauts, 266 comparisons, and 71,517 BRFSS participants, the percentage of those reporting physical inactivity is presented. The prevalence of LSAH participants who reported participating in no leisure-time physical activity tends to decrease with increasing age for each of the populations. All astronauts in the 65-74 stratum reported participation in physical activities. In contrast, BRFSS respondents show a significantly higher prevalence of physical inactivity in both age groups. In this category, all LSAH participants surpassed the HP 2010 goal. Smoking Cigarette smoking has been called the single most preventable cause of premature death in the U.S., with over 400,000 attributable deaths per year and a 1998 excess of $75.5 billion in healthcare costs. Though the number of adult cigarette smokers has decreased significantly, a 2000 survey indicated that there are still 46.5 million current smokers. Older adults are particularly at risk of developing a smoking-related disease such as cardiovascular disease, because they generally have smoked longer and are heavier smokers. The eligible participants for this portion of the surveys are 52 astronauts, 266 comparisons, and 116,690 BRFSS participants. Present smokers, along with those who have smoked at least 100 cigarettes in their lifetime, are classified as current smokers. Those who do not currently smoke but have smoked at least 100 cigarettes in their lifetime, are classified as current smokers but have smoked at least 100 cigarettes in their lifetime are classified as former smokers. Smoking history data were collected differently for each of the surveys. The LSQ combined data for both current and former smokers, i.e., as ever smokers, whereas the BRFSS distinguished between the two. Consequently, results for the 3 populations cannot be directly compared as with the other health factors. For LSAH populations the prevalence of ever smoker increases with increasing age. For BRFSS participants, the prevalence of current smokers decreases with increasing age, while the prevalence of former smokers increasing age. Summary In general, LSAH participants are performing as well as or better than the general U.S. population with regards to the four health indicators examined here. Note that the results are based on self-reporting of respondents, which are subject to misreporting and recall bias. This review is also limited by the use of BMI because this weight-to height ratio does not distinguish between fat and muscle weight, so that a physically fit, muscular individual could inappropriately be classified as overweight. Also, this report only includes individuals aged 55 and older. Consequently it is also limited by survivor bias, i.e., survey participants may live healthier lifestyles, which have allowed them to outlive those with less healthy lifestyles.

title: Aging and Cardiopulmonary Function
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Previous analyses have compared age-specific values for certain physiological measurements among both the astronauts and comparison participants as part of the process to separate the effects of space flight from the background effects of aging. In this article, we examine the changes in cardiovascular and pulmonary functions of participants as they age. In the general population, cardiopulmonary function decreases with aging. Similar associations were found among the LSAH population.
approach: For the purpose of looking at the association of aging, cross-sectional data for specific age groups were examined. The data were organized by age of examination for all annual examinations for all study participants. The first examination was selected for each participant when he/she entered a new age group. An individual is included in every age group that he/she has achieved but is represented only once in any age group. Due to small sample size, female astronauts and comparisons over 40 years of age were grouped together into one age group represented as 40-59. VO 2 max, the maximum volume of oxygen consumed by the body during exercise, is a measure of an individual's cardiovascular function. It indicates one's maximal capacity to do aerobic work, and is commonly measured in units of milliliter per kilogram of body weight per minute. Dividing the oxygen volume by body weight accounts for differences in body size. LSAH comparisons show values similar to those observed for the general population, whereas the astronauts have almost 20% higher VO 2 max value than the corresponding comparison groups. These higher VO 2 max levels may be a reflection of the higher fitness level of astronauts as compared to the comparison participants. However, both groups show about the same rate of decline in VO 2 max with aging. Pulmonary function was assessed through two measurements, FEV 1 and FVC. FEV 1 . stands for forced expiratory volume 1, the volume of air that is forcefully exhaled in one second, in liters (L). FVC, or forced vital capacity, is the volume of air that can be maximally forcefully exhaled, in liters, so that FEV 1 is actually a subset of FVC. Values of 3.0 L and 4.0 L are considered average FEV 1 and FVC levels in the general population.
results: For FEV 1 , male astronauts younger than 35 years of age show a higher level than the corresponding comparison group. This advantage was virtually gone by the next age group, as both male astronauts and comparisons show almost identical FEV 1 values for ages 35-64 years. Only in the oldest age group did male astronauts have higher FEV 1 levels than the comparisons again. Female astronauts younger than 35 years of age have a lower mean FEV 1 value than the female comparisons. However, their FEV 1 values decline less steeply with age as compared to those of the comparisons, so that female astronauts of the 40-59 years age group show a slightly higher value of FEV as compared to female comparisons in the same age group. Similar aging trends are also observed for the astronauts and comparisons for their FVC values, though the decline rates for all male participants are less steep as compared to their decline of FEV 1 values with age. Male astronauts show higher FVC volumes than male comparisons in the younger age groups, but this advantage evens out in the ages between 40 and 60 years, before reappearing in the oldest age groups. Female comparisons show a decline in FVC volumes as they age. However, the FVC values for female astronauts hold steady across the age groups instead of showing the expected aging trend, which may be a function of the small sample size or retention of better physical fitness of this participant group. In general, higher values of cardiopulmonary function obtained for the astronauts are expected. The somewhat unusual trends shown by female astronauts may result from the small sample size of the group. These current observations suggest that cardiopulmonary function in both groups is affected by age in the same ways; further observations will continue, and will be shared with study participants.

title: Effective Dose Measurement during EVA
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: One of the many risks of long-duration space flights is the dose burden from cosmic radiation, especially at times of maximum solar activity. At such times, for instance during an extravehicular activity (EVA) when the wall of the spacecraft is not there to protect the astronauts, cosmic radiation poses a potentially serious health threat. Accurate dose measurement as well as the measurements of the ratio of low to high linear energy transfer (LET) dose components will become increasingly important in forthcoming years during the assembly of large orbital stations. Therefore an onboard thermoluminescent dosimeter (TLD) system capable of providing such measurements offers a solution for EVA dosimetry.
approach: The TLD system used during the NASA 4 mission (Pille '96 system), was a modified version of the Pille '95 TLD system used by the European Space Agency (ESA) during the Euromir '95 mission. The difference between the units was that the sensitivity of the reader was enhanced, due to the short duration of most EVAs. Also, the LiF TLD with a linear heating profile was introduced with this system to ensure effective LET measurement using the high temperature region (HTR) method. The TLD system was brought to Mir aboard STS-81 and recorded environmental space radiation measurements until May 6, 1997. The TLD system consisted of a portable TLD reader (Pille '96) and eight individual dosimeters. Seven TLDs were mounted at locations throughout the base block, two of which were used on one occasion to record radiation dose during an EVA. TLDs were removed from their respective locations and analyzed using the TLD reader at eight separate times during the mission. The memory card from the TLD reader was returned to the ground at the end of the mission for further analysis. This experiment was also scheduled to be performed during NASA 5. However, the TLD reader was located in the Spektr module which was damaged on June 25, 1997, and thus became inaccessible. This incident
results: ed in no data being collected for the NASA 5 mission. RESULTS: The dose rate (10.0 mGy/h) measured by an individual dosimeter on the astronaut was significantly lower than the mean value of the other three dosimeters (15.0 mGy/h) located at the working area and sleeping cabin. This result must have been caused by the unilateral shielding effect of the body of the astronaut. Justification of the results requires either model calculations or onboard phantom measurements. Three of the dosimeters (1A, 2A and 3A) were located at the same place as Area Passive Dosimeters (APDs) exposed during the NASA 2 mission (NMA-1, NMA-2 and NMA-3). The dose rate ratios (TLDs/APD) are: For dosimeter 1A: 15.1/13.6=1.11 For dosimeter 2A: 11.6/12.0=0.96 For dosimeter 3A: 18.3/17.0=1.08 The mean ratio is 1.05. These results show that the radiation situation remained virtually unchanged. The extra dose due to EVA was compared to the dose measured inside, and showed that the mean ratio, EVA/inside, without any correction is 4.2. Results from the Euromir '95 mission have been used for correcting the effect of higher background radiation inside the space station due to the South Atlantic Anomaly (SAA). The corrected EVA/inside dose rate ratio is 3.15. The glow curves from LiF-TLDs exposed on Mir Space Station show significantly enhanced high temperature TL-emission compared to glowcurves after 137Cs irradiation. According to the calibrations the estimated mean LET value was 7.5 ± 1 keV/mm.

title: Anticipatory Postural Activity
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: This investigation assessed the impact of microgravity on anticipatory postural activity during and after space flight. The goal of this investigation was to understand the underlying sensorimotor adaptations made by the body in microgravity, which are still present postflight. These adaptations were monitored by investigating posture control during voluntary arm movements, thus providing a better understanding of balance and locomotion in humans. The purpose of the inflight portion of the investigation was to determine whether foot pressure could be used to enhance neuromuscular activation during upper limb movements while free floating. Determining whether foot sensory input enhances lower limb and trunk neuromuscular activity could
approach: During the pre- and postflight data collection sessions, the subject wore a t-shirt and knee-high socks with electrodes and accelerometer leads attached to the upper body, legs and arms with adhesive tape. A wrist splint with an attached accelerometer was also worn. For testing, the subject stepped onto a force plate, assumed an upright position with feet shoulder-width apart and arms resting comfortably at the sides. With eyes closed, the subject performed 15 rapid, 90-degree shoulder flexions, keeping the arm and wrist locked throughout the movement. The movements were self-initiated, and the subject regained stability before performing the next movement. Inflight, the subject wore the Belt Pack Amplifier System (BPAS) vest assembly, which supported the collection of EMG and acceleration data during a series of arm raises. The inflight test protocol involved four test conditions: (1) 15 arm raises while free floating, (2) 15 arm raises while free floating with the addition of foot pressure, (3) 15 arm raises while attached to the Mir support surface with the addition of foot pressure, and (4) 15 arm raises while bungeed to the Mir treadmill (without foot pressure). To apply foot pressure during test conditions 2 and 3, the astronauts wore a specially designed boot with an integrated pneumatic bladder that allowed variable levels of pressure.
results: in a relatively inexpensive, yet highly effective countermeasure against muscle atrophy. In addition, foot pressure may eliminate inflight spatial orientation disturbances. The postflight component of the experiment addressed postural control problems reported by many astronauts. These difficulties include increased sway while standing, difficulty in rounding corners, and increased body segment movements during locomotion. The postflight postural stability was assessed using subject-initiated limb movements. The objectives of this experiment were: To determine how long-duration space flight alters the anticipatory neuromuscular activity associated with arm movement, To perform proof-of-concept research to determine whether foot sensory input modifies neuromuscular responses during space flight, To determine the time course of adaptation during long-duration space flight to foot sensory input as measured by patterns of neuromuscular activation, To determine whether long-duration space flight modifies anticipatory neuromuscular postural activity in the immediate postflight period, and To determine whether modifications in anticipatory neuromuscular postural activity associated with long-duration space flight are correlated with postural instability immediately after landing and during the recovery period. APPROACH: During the pre- and postflight data collection sessions, the subject wore a t-shirt and knee-high socks with electrodes and accelerometer leads attached to the upper body, legs and arms with adhesive tape. A wrist splint with an attached accelerometer was also worn. For testing, the subject stepped onto a force plate, assumed an upright position with feet shoulder-width apart and arms resting comfortably at the sides. With eyes closed, the subject performed 15 rapid, 90-degree shoulder flexions, keeping the arm and wrist locked throughout the movement. The movements were self-initiated, and the subject regained stability before performing the next movement. Inflight, the subject wore the Belt Pack Amplifier System (BPAS) vest assembly, which supported the collection of EMG and acceleration data during a series of arm raises. The inflight test protocol involved four test conditions: (1) 15 arm raises while free floating, (2) 15 arm raises while free floating with the addition of foot pressure, (3) 15 arm raises while attached to the Mir support surface with the addition of foot pressure, and (4) 15 arm raises while bungeed to the Mir treadmill (without foot pressure). To apply foot pressure during test conditions 2 and 3, the astronauts wore a specially designed boot with an integrated pneumatic bladder that allowed variable levels of pressure. RESULTS: The results from this investigation have confirmed previous findings that an increase in somatosensory input using the foot pressure boots results in enhanced neuromuscular activation. This increased neuromuscular activation during space flight may serve to maintain the operating characteristics of the reflex loops and motor units that would otherwise remain generally inactive during much of the flight. Failure to keep the reflex loops and motor units active during flight may result in the inability to properly activate muscle fibers upon return to Earth. These results suggest that the application of foot pressure may be used as a countermeasure to retard muscle atrophy and maintain the health of neuromuscular reflex loops. The addition of foot pressure during flight resulted in increased muscle co-contraction relative to movement conditions without the pressure boots. This measure is a further reflection of the increase in muscle activation caused by the addition of foot pressure. Free-floating arm movements performed without foot pressure resulted in the elimination or severe reduction of the lower limb muscle activation always observed prior to arm movements made while upright in unit gravity. Free-floating arm movements performed with the addition of foot pressure (provided by the pressure boots) resulted in the lower limb muscle activation always observed prior to arm movements made while upright in unit gravity. Postflight tests indicated that the subject displayed an increase in anterior-posterior postural sway and changes in muscle activation latencies after long-duration space flight. The subject also demonstrated decrements in postural control associated with voluntary arm movements. The magnitude of center of pressure (COP) motion was increased despite decreased arm acceleration features. This increased COP motion brought the subject closer to the limits of the base of support, which jeopardized postural stability. Thus, the subject was unable to optimally perform the arm raise task and demonstrated less postural control during the arm motion after space flight. The data indicate that the precise neuromuscular activation patterns necessary for optimal arm movement were not produced after space flight. The ground-based component of the study demonstrated that postural control during voluntary movement is disrupted after space flight. As such, this experiment was complementary to previous studies, which have investigated postflight postural control during altered sensory environments, and/or during support surface perturbations. This project also demonstrated that inappropriate neuromuscular activation patterns are likely to be a contributing factor in the loss of postflight postural control. The knowledge gained from this investigation has important implications in the area of rehabilitative medicine. Many patient populations suffer from poor postural control, and the demonstration that somatosensory input from the feet can enhance postural muscle activation suggests that various forms of foot pressure may be used to increase postural control with these patients.

title: Acoustic Noise During the Phase III Chamber Test
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: During the Lunar-Mars Life Support Test Project (LMLSTP), four test subjects participated in the 91-day experiment. As part of the acoustic study, they measured sound decibels in different life support areas of the test chamber. The LMLSTP enclosed test chamber was divided into three levels. The first level contained general living quarters with a dining/work table, communications, test and video equipment. The first level also contained a kitchen, bathroom and laundry facilities. The second level contained the mechanical equipment for air revitalization, storage and stationary bicycle. This level was the noisiest, and due to the location of the stairs, the subjects had to pass through this level while traveling between the first and third levels. The third level contained primary living quarters with bedrooms, partial bath and entertainment equipment. This level was the quietest. The goal of the acoustic noise study was to monitor and describe the noise environment of the 20-foot chamber during its extended 91-day operation. Noise levels were measured at multiple locations and subjects performed hearing threshold tests called audiograms at various frequencies before and after the chamber experience. The hearing threshold is the softest sound a person is able to hear. It is not clear what level of hearing threshold shift is cause for concern, but it is certain that larger changes in threshold are more serious. Monitoring acoustic noise in the chamber enabled recommendations to be formulated for hearing protection, if necessary. These measurements also established a baseline measure of the noise environment for comparison with other Earth-bound analog test facilities. In acoustic studies, noise is defined as undesirable sounds in the air in the hearing range of approximately 20 to 20,000 Hz. A certain level of noise can be tolerated over an eight-hour workday without long-term hearing detriment, but this same noise level may not be acceptable if it is continuous over a 24-hour period, such as in the closed environment of a space vehicle. During periods of loud noise, the blood vessels in the ear involuntarily constrict and reduce blood flow to protect the hair cells responsible for hearing. Outer hair cells respond to low intensity sound and become continuously stimulated or "saturated", by loud noise. The inner hair cells remain functional because they respond only to high intensity sounds. A temporary hearing threshold shift may thus occur due to chronic noise. An upward shift of hearing threshold can become permanent, since the outer hair cells that respond to low intensity sound would not have a chance to recover their normal function and would eventually die. Government regulations developed by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) set the maximum background noise level that an individual may be exposed to during an eight-hour day at 90 dB. Exposure to levels over 85 dB requires routine monitoring for hearing loss and the institution of hearing conservation programs. The EPA suggests that an eight-hour average noise level over 75 dB presents a reasonable risk for hearing loss.
approach: LMLSTP test subjects collected sound level measurements in various locations throughout the chamber module starting with entry day ceremonies, continuing regularly during the 91-day operation and ending with the welcome home celebrations. In total, 283 sample measurements of acoustic noise were collected from the chamber during the experiment. Noise levels were measured using an audio dosimeter and a more accurate sound level meter to obtain an A-weighted overall sound pressure level measurement at each location. The A-weighting represents the ear sensitivity by combining all frequencies together and averaging them to give a decibel value. Sample measurement locations were determined using two methods. In one method, each subject was asked to subjectively identify the noise sources and noisier locations in the chamber. Following discussion, the subjects jointly decided upon 25 locations to measure noise, including quiet locations that served as controls. The other method of determining measurement locations was the use of predetermined, geographically-spaced areas on each chamber level. Four different heights above the floor were monitored based on locations where a hypothetical fiftieth-percentile person's ear would be located during various activities. Measurements were taken at 10 cm above the surface of the floor to represent a person lying down, at 75 cm above the floor to represent a person sitting on the floor, at 120 cm above the floor to monitor a person sitting in a chair, and at 150 cm above the floor to represent a person standing. The locations were spaced at 30-degree increments about 60 cm from the wall, space permitting, and at the center axis of each level. Locations where the subjects were likely to spend more time were also chosen, such as a computer workstation, bed, stove, table, exercise machine, etc. A measurement was taken within 60 to 100 cm of the middle of any large area not already measured by other methods. Since this was a screening procedure, most data were rounded off to the nearest unit. Noise loudness is measured using sound level meters. Total noise exposure over a period of time is measured with a noise dosimeter. To determine how acoustic noise levels varied throughout a typical 24-hour day for each subject, an Ametek Audio Dosimeter (Model MK-3) was used in the dosimeter mode. An average was determined each minute as loudness equivalent (Leq 1 min) of a 24-hr period. This method produced 1440 samples each day. Data was downloaded to a desktop computer and graphed as noise level versus time, creating a histogram for each selected noise level interval. Each test subject wore the dosimeter over two 24-hour periods. Additionally, one subject wore the dosimeter for approximately one hour before, and one hour after, entering the chamber on the first day and an hour before and after exiting the chamber on the last day. On each of three other days, the dosimeter was placed in a central location in a bedroom, left among equipment on the second level, and attached to the ceiling in the middle of the first level. The exact days that the subjects wore the dosimeter, and the exact days and locations that the dosimeter was placed in a room were up to the subjects' discretion. Investigators wanted to know whether or not the noise levels inside the chamber would affect the threshold hearing levels of the subjects over the course of the 91-day stay in chamber. Hearing tests, called pure-tone air conduction audiometry, were conducted under standard conditions at the health clinic at NASA's Johnson Space Center (JSC) in a sound-insulated booth. A microprocessor-controlled audiometer presented pure tone stimuli to the subject and recorded his or her responses. The subject wore a headset through which the sounds were transmitted to each ear. When the subject heard a sound, he or she pushed a button, and the monitoring computer recorded the response. The computer presented sounds at predetermined frequencies and at incremental amplitudes, getting softer until there was no subject response, and then louder until there was a response, to double-check the person's threshold. Each ear was tested independently starting with frequencies of 1000 cycles per second (Hz). This first measurement at 1000 Hz was a training run. Then, the test was conducted at frequencies of 500 Hz, 1000 Hz, 2000 Hz, 3000 Hz, 4000 Hz, 6000 Hz and 8000 Hz for a total of seven data collection sessions and 42 audiogram measurements per subject. In an audiometry test, the hearing level is quantified based on what the normal ear detects, and a score of zero indicates normal hearing. Scores above zero indicate hearing loss. A 100 dB hearing loss at any frequency is nearly equivalent to complete deafness at that particular frequency tested. The four chamber test subjects were each given three audiograms. The first, conducted at the time of medical examination for eligibility, established a baseline measure. The second audiogram was performed within two hours after the subject left the chamber to determine whether there was any shift in hearing threshold after 91 days in the chamber. The third audiogram occurred between six and fourteen weeks after chamber egress to determine whether the hearing threshold had returned to baseline. It was expected that there would be a hearing threshold shift on egress day, but that no permanent shift would occur.
results: On the first chamber level, the acoustic noise from 105 measurements averaged 63.2 dB(A). The noisiest general area was the airlock, which averaged 63.7 dB(A), and where major noise contributors included exercise machines and ventilation fans. The only measurements that equaled or exceeded 70 dB(A) were from intermittent noise sources. The television was the loudest measured equipment noise source (average 75.2 dB(A)). The second level was much noisier, and the subjects reportedly avoided the area. The average noise level over 94 measurements was 74.6 dB(A). Only two of the samples were measured at less than 70 dB(A). Twelve measurements were in excess of 80 dB(A). On the third level, which was quieter than the others, noise levels were similar to those in a typical single-family residence. The average noise level over 84 measurements was 51.5 dB(A). Measurements in the immediate proximity of the beds averaged 42.4 dB(A). The noisiest area on the third level was in the hallway, averaging 59.8 dB(A), especially near the ladder that led to the noisier second level. Data from the dosimeter attached to a subject for a 24-hour period was consistent with that obtained by the sound level meter. It was possible to discern where the subject was in the chamber by analyzing the readings from the dosimeter. The first level's background noise was measured in the mid-60 dB(A) range, with an occasional spike attributed to human voices during conversation. Periods of time where noise measured above 70 dB(A) represented transitions through, or short visits to, the louder second level. Rest or quiet work on the third level could be assumed from the periods of time that measured 60 dB(A). When the subjects exited the chamber at egress, the dosimeters measured above 90 dB(A) during the first 10 minutes and above 80 dB(A) for most of the first hour. Audiogram measurements of the subjects on the pre-test ranged from 0 to 50 dB. A measure of 0 indicates that the threshold of hearing is the same as that for an average person without hearing loss, while larger numbers indicate hearing loss. Shifts of 5 dB or less are not considered problematic because they are within the range of expected test errors. On egress-day, audiogram measurements were 0 to 50 dB. Post-test measurements were 0 to 45 dB. For two subjects, all measurements were at or below 20 db; for another subject, all were at or below 25 dB. The final subject gave readings at or below 10 dB in one ear, while the other ear measured hearing loss in the 45 to 50 dB range for all three-test administrations. Audiometry data graphs indicate no clear distinction among pre-test, egress day and post-test audiometry measurements. A modified sign test was performed on the data as an indication of the overall tendency of the measured hearing threshold. Arithmetic differences between the egress day and pre-test measures were obtained for each data pair. There was no significant difference between the two measurements for hearing loss or improvement. However, a similar comparison showed that the hearing threshold measured at the post-test was better than either the pre-test or egress day tests. Yet, of the 56 comparisons among the pre-test, egress day and post-test, there were five for which the egress day measurements suggested hearing threshold loss that did not return to pre-test baseline level. Some interesting factors may explain the audiogram results. Upon egress, cheering crowds generated more noise than that found in the living areas of the chamber. This can be observed from the dosimeter readings. The loud celebration noise may have confounded the results of the egress day measures that were taken within two hours after egress. Another confounding factor may have been the subjects' environment during the pre-test baseline measures. During this timeframe, the subjects were involved in the development, assembly and testing of the mechanical equipment for the chamber. All pre-test hearing measurements were taken during the afternoon, after at least a half-day of work in a noisy environment. The subjects were also involved in the operation and maintenance of this equipment during the 91 days of the chamber test. About a week after egress day, the subjects took vacations, and the equipment was turned off. So the post-test measures were obtained after the subjects had been in a different noise environment, and under different stress conditions that were not monitored. After the first data were analyzed and reported to the subjects in the chamber, steps were taken to reduce the noise. Noise insulation barriers were constructed and redundant equipment was turned off. Schedules were changed so that the noisiest equipment was not operated when the subjects were in that area. The results of this study will be used to provide motivation to reduce the noise levels of the air and water revitalization equipment. A continuing benefit for habitation study crews is an increased understanding and awareness of the noise levels in a closed environment.

title: The Response of Single Human Cells to Zero Gravity
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Studies with centrifuges demonstrated that gravitational acceleration has a significant influence on cell biology systems. The purpose of this experiment was to determine the effects of zero-gravity on living human cells during and subsequent to the Skylab 3 mission. A strain of diploid human embryonic lung cells, WI-38, was chosen for this purpose. In general, this experiment was designed to detect the effects of zero-gravity on cell growth rates and on cell structure as observed by light microscopy, transmission electron microscopy and scanning electron microscopy, and histochemistry. Studies of the effects of zero-gravity on the cell function and the cell cycle were performed by time lapse motion picture photography and microspectrophotometry. Subsequent study of the returned living cells included karotyping, G- and C- banding, and analyses of the culture media. Some of the living cells returned were stored by deep freeze techniques for possible future experiments.
approach: The Woodlawn Wanderer 9 was used inflight to support the growth of human embryonic lung cells. Cell cultures were maintained with the proper replacement of media with new fresh media. The cells were kept at a constant temperature of 36 degrees Celsius and at a constant pressure of one atmosphere in a hermetically sealed compartment. Two phase-contrast time-lapse motion pictures of living cells for 28 days was used to collect data on the cell cycle and mitosis. An automated system fixed the cells at predetermined intervals for postflight examination under the light microscope, scanning electron microscope, and transmission electron microscope. Cultures were maintained at approximately 22 degrees Celsius after the first 12 days of the mission for the return of intact cells for subsequent subculture. The cell cultures brought back to ground for subculture were analyzed for chromosomal aberrations, and the cell culture media was analyzed to determine chemical composition. Cellular growth rates were determined by cell counting procedures accomplished with the aid of a phase-contrast contrast microscope using a grid reticle in a 10X magnification eyepiece. Postflight, cell counting was performed with the 15X eyepiece due to the fact that the high density of the cell population made it difficult to determine single cells. Time lapse films were analyzed with a projector which permitted projection 1-8, 16, and 24 frames/second. Cells were counted every 3 hours. Cell multiplication was determined by adding the number of observed mitoses and mitotic activity, which was calculated from the average cell density. The rate of cell migration was determined by covering the projection screen with paper and tracing the location of the nucleus of individual cells every hour. Whole coverslips with attached cell monolayers in 4 percent glutaraldehyde fixative with cacodylate buffer were processed for transmission electron microscopy, scanning electron microscopy, and phase contrast microscopy. Scanning microspectrophotometry was performed on selected areas of the nuclei using a scanning microscope photometer having a 1-micron measuring at 1 micron intervals at 540 nanometers. Subcultures were incubated overnight with fresh growth medium, then harvested with standard colchimid arrest and hypotonic treatment procedures. Banding analysis was performed on air dried slides. Five cells from control cultures were analyzed for G-band pattern and 10 cells were analyzed for C-band pattern. At least 10 cells of the flight culture were analyzed for G-band pattern and 20 cells were analyzed for C-band pattern.
results: Ten cultures were fixed during the first 12 days of flight. Growth curves, DNA microspectrophometery, phase microscopy, and ultrastructural studies of the fixed cells revealed no effects of a zero-gravity environment on the ten cultures. Two cultures were photographed by means of phase time-lapse cinematography during the first 27 days of the flight. Analysis of the films revealed no differences in mitotic index, cell cycle, and migration between the flight and control cells. No differences between the flight and control cell cultures were observed in the karotype and chromosome banding. Minor unexplained differences have been found in the biochemical constituents of the used flight and control media.

title: Women Astronaut Health
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: In October 1997, the Longitudinal Study of Astronaut Health (LSAH) reported on some variables concerning astronauts and their first flights. These data, valid through 1996, detailed various laboratory measurements including the mean differences in blood pressure and pulse values for pre- and postflight examinations. In 1996, there were 135 active astronauts: 30 women and 105 men. There were only 6 inactive women and 129 inactive men. The average age for active women astronauts is 39.9 years while the same average for active men is 41.9 years. For inactive corps members, men have a mean age of 50.9 years while women have a mean age of 46.5 years. At first flight, women average 39 years of age. Approximately 59 percent of men and 29 percent of women received a Master's degree as their highest degree earned. Fifty-one percent of women astronauts received a doctoral degree (M.D. or Ph.D.) while 28 percent of the men hold a doctoral degree in medicine, philosophy, or veterinary medicine. Racial makeup for the astronaut corps includes five groups: White, Black, Hispanic, Asian, and Native American. Eighty-eight percent (30) of female astronauts and 89.2 percent (141) of male astronauts are White. The next largest racial group is Blacks with 9 percent (8) of men and 5 percent (3) of women. From 1978 through 1996, women have been eligible to participate in 82 different missions. Of all flights: Women were crewmembers on 42 of those missions (51%) A woman was a pilot on 1 mission (1.2%) There were at least 2 women on 13 of those missions (15.9%) The purpose of this study was to examine the differences between male and female astronaut physiological parameters.
approach: Blood Pressure: The preflight (L-10) and postflight (R+0) examinations were used to calculate the differences in blood pressures for all astronauts. Pulse: Again, these values were obtained from L-10 and R+0 examinations, with the subjects in the sitting position.
results: Blood pressure: In particular, women had a mean difference in sitting diastolic BP: 10 mmHg for flights of six days or less (N=5) 8.2 mmHg for flights of 7 through 10 days (N=11) 0 mmHg for flights of 11 through 17 days (N=3) The mean differences in sitting systolic BP are: 14 mmHg for flights of six days or less (N=5) 12.7 mmHg for flights of 7 through 10 days (N=11) 14 mmHg for flights of 11 through 17 days (N=3) The mean differences for men were less than the mean differences for women on all flights except those 11 to 17 days in length. For those flights, men had a mean difference of 11.9 and 16.8 mmHg for diastolic and systolic BP, respectively. Sitting Pulse Values for Women: The average mean differences in sitting pulses for women are: 17 beats per minute (bpm) for flights of six days or less (N=4) 11.2 bpm for flights of 7 through 10 days (N=6) 1.3 bpm for flights of 11 though 17 days (N=3) The average mean differences in sitting pulses for men are: 7.7 bpm for flights of six days or less (N=22) 16.2 bpm for flights of 7 through 10 days in length (N=23) 8.0 bpm for flights of 11 through 17 days (N=17) Physiological differences between men and women will continue to be investigated.

title: Aging and Blood Pressure in Astronauts
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: A decline in cardiovascular function is expected with aging in the general population. Systolic and diastolic blood pressure measurements were examined to describe the effects of aging on the cardiovascular function of the LSAH population.
approach: Astronauts and comparison participants who were selected before 1992 were included in these analyses. Blood pressures were taken while the participant was seated and were a part of routine physical examinations. Ages were divided into five-year groupings beginning with less than 30 and up to 69 years. Data for men and women are combined for these analyses. An individual is included once in each of the five-year age group for which he/she is eligible, using the first examination for the participant after he/she entered that age group. There are small numbers of participants in the age groups above 55 and the
results: ing statistics for the older groups may not be stable. RESULTS: The mean systolic and diastolic blood pressures are shown in the data. Although the means for some of the age groups are not statistically different, overall the comparison participants have higher mean blood pressures than the astronauts. These differences may be due to differences in physical activity. The lower mean blood pressures are an indicator of better cardiac conditioning among the astronauts than among the comparison participants as a group. The ranges of individual measurements among the two groups do, however, overlap. These values also indicate that both the astronauts and the comparison participants may have experienced some decline in cardiac function with age. The rate of decline is similar in both groups even though the mean values for the astronauts are lower than the mean values for the comparison participants. These are crude analyses that have not been adjusted for any other variables. Exercise, weight gain, other illnesses, life style activities, and use of medications to control hypertension all make an impact on cardiac function and might have been included as confounding variables. However, the intention of this examination was to look at the simple association of age and cardiac function. The results indicate that this association is an inverse one, and that the rate of decline may be similar for a range of initial blood pressure values.

title: Crew Height Measurement
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Gross effects of zero-g on man's anthropometry were observed during and after extended orbital flights of the Skylab missions. In weightlessness, crewmen "grew taller" and the one-g erect posture was altered at several skeletal joints, namely the neck, shoulder, elbow, hip, knee and ankle. Quantification of these effects was important for optimizing the physical interfaces between the crewman and his workstation and flight clothing, particularly the space suit. The Apollo-Soyuz Test Project (ASTP) provided an opportunity to quantify the effects of zero-g on crewman height and to determine the change as a function of time over mission length.
approach: Data on ASTP crewmen were obtained during routine physical examinations conducted on L-45 (45 days before flight), L-30, L-15 and R+0 (day of recovery). Data requirements for all height measurements consisted of maximum stature, seated height, and eye-level height. Inflight data requirements were completed during three mission phases: 1. In the Command Module (CM), before docking module (DM) transfer, seated height and eye-level height were measured immediately after weightlessness was attained. 2. In the DM, stature and eye-level heights were measured periodically. 3. In the CM after DM jettison, seated height and eye-level height were measured immediately prior to reentry. Measurements in the CM were made with the crewman on the center couch. Seated height was measured with the seat in the 90-degree seat-to-backpan position. Eye-level height was measured with the seat in the 180-degree (flat) position. The crewman relaxed to the neutral, zero-g posture, his back parallel to the couch back and his feet touching the lower equipment bay (LEB) bulkhead. Measurements were made from the top of the couch support frame, parallel to the back of the couch, down to the top of the head and then to eye-level height. The measuring tape from the Leg Volume Measuring Kit was used for these measurements. Stature measurements were made as the crewman assumed a fully extended posture on the control and display (C&D) panel with his feet touching the DM hatch (Soyuz end). For eye-level height, the crewman assumed the neutral, zero-g posture, with his back to the C&D panel and feet touching the hatch. Measurements were read from a measuring tape decal affixed to the C&D panel.
results: Because of scheduling problems and the limited number of data points completed, only the stature measurements were quantified. In addition, only R+0 measurements were obtained due to crew health concerns. An increase in stature was noted for each ASTP crewman. This increase was attributed to the absence of g-loading on the spine, which resulted in loss of normal spinal curvature and an expansion of the intervertebral discs. A slight increase (less than 1.3 cm (0.5 in)) occurred between launch and mission day 6, which was the first measurement opportunity in the DM. The next larger increase, as much as 6.6 cm (2.6 in), occurred between mission days 6 and 9. This data, in conjunction with Skylab height data, indicated a two-step height increase. The smaller initial change may result from removing g-loads on the body and thus permitting loss of thoracolumbar curvature. A similar expansion is observed on Earth when stature is compared between standing and supine body positions. The second larger change may be accounted for from the expansion of the now unloaded intervertebral discs. When the muscles relax in weightlessness, the vertebral discs are unloaded and absorb water from the vertebral bodies. This expansion may be further affected by the headward fluid shifts in zero-g. Application of this data was used to develop workstation interface designs for future missions.

title: Bone Health and Physical Activity in LSAH Participants
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Physical activity, primarily weight bearing exercise, is an important factor in the development and maintenance of bone health. Weight bearing exercise is defined as any physical activity in which someone supports their weight (e.g., running, walking) or moves weights using their muscles (e.g., weightlifting, resistance training). For this study, weight bearing exercise was represented by the specific physical activities of walking, running, and weightlifting. This study compared the amount of participation in these activities between the Longitudinal Study of Astronaut Health (LSAH) participants, a group of comparisons, and the U.S. general population.
approach: The data were obtained through the Lifestyle Questionnaire, where respondents were asked to select the types of exercises they usually performed. A total of 1080 participants responded to the questionnaire (238 astronauts and 842 comparisons).
results: of a national survey, the 1998 National Health Interview Survey, were used to compare the LSAH participants to the U.S. general population (N=32,440). The survey had values for the U.S. general adult population’s participation in walking, running, and weightlifting. RESULTS: Astronauts reported the highest participation in running and weightlifting as compared to comparison participants and the general population.
