The most striking difference between the astronauts and the other two groups was in running, where about two thirds of the astronauts reported participating, whereas more than one third of the comparison participants and only about a tenth of the general population did. Astronauts reported higher participation in the more vigorous activities of running and weightlifting than the comparison participants or the general population. The comparison participants appeared to have a similar pattern with the general population in the types of exercise they participated in, albeit with higher participation percentages. Female astronauts (N=31) participated more in running and weightlifting than in walking. The female comparison participants (N=117) and the female general population (N=18,238) respondents showed a clear preference for walking over the other two activities. Overall, LSAH participants reported higher participation in weight bearing exercises as compared to the general population, with astronauts having the highest rates. The difference between astronauts and comparison participants is to be expected as astronauts by definition need to maintain their health for mission readiness. Both astronauts and comparison participants therefore have a better chance of maintaining their bone density as they age as compared to the general population.

title: Human Cerebral Cortex Plasticity in Response to Long-term Bedrest as an Analog to Microgravity
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: This investigation assesses the effects of weightlessness on the central nervous system and specifically the sensorimotor system by inducing cortical reorganization through altered cortical excitability. The measures of cortical excitability will be evaluated for correlation with measures of lower limb functional recovery.
approach: Transcranial magnetic stimulation was used to evaluate motor cortex plasticity through the acquisition of recruitment curves. The location for application of the magnetic stimulation was determined by functional and structural brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Data collected from these control subjects included resting motor threshold, paired pulse sequences and cortical silent periods, The compound motor action potential and Hoffman reflex (H-reflex) response were collected as measures of peripheral stimulation.
results: Significant leg RC slope decreases were observed on post-bed rest day 1 (P1) (t(2805) = -4.14, P Results of this research include a better understanding of the cortical plasticity associated with leg disuse and may lead to applications in patient and astronaut rehabilitation.

title: The Influence of Environmental Stress on Cell-Mediated Immune Function
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: The human immune system is composed of multiple interacting elements including contributions from both the humoral and cell-mediated arms. These elements play unique roles and interact in various ways with each other in maintaining the optimum immune status and health of humans. Cell-mediated immunity (CMI) involving sensitized T-lymphocytes is important in defense against certain infectious agents (e.g., viruses and fungi), in surveillance against neoplastic cells, and in regulation of immune function. CMI function testing has traditionally been done by skin testing with cutaneous placement of recall antigens (delayed cutaneous hypersensitivity). By introducing an antigen to which an individual has been previously exposed, the capacity of T-lymphocytes to respond to an antigen in memory can be assessed. Measurement of cutaneous delayed-type hypersensitivity (DTH) responses to a battery of commonly encountered antigens is a generally accepted and preferred means of assessing CMI function. In the past, such DTH testing suffered from lack of standardized testing techniques, number and characterization of reactions, doses employed, and interpretation of reactions and
approach: In this investigation, repeated skin testing was utilized in order to determine the functional state of the chamber crews' CMI systems over time and compare to a control group of subjects not exposed to the environmental stress of isolation within the closed chamber. There were two subject groups in this study: (1) the experimental (chamber) group, which consisted of the four chamber occupants, and (2) the control group, which consisted of four sex- and age-matched volunteers. All individuals completed a training session on the proper application of the skin test device and measurement of the
results: . A commercially available system has solved these problems by providing simultaneous and reproducible application of seven standardized recall antigens as a means of measuring DTH in assessment of CMI. Because of its properties, widespread clinical acceptance, and ease of use, this system was adopted for this study. This process of skin testing and evaluation of cell-mediated immune function has been used in other extreme environments such as Antarctic expeditions, tours of duty in submarines, and during both short- and long-duration space flights. All of these studies have shown that stress can have a negative impact on CMI function. The exact mechanisms underlying these changes are not yet fully understood. APPROACH In this investigation, repeated skin testing was utilized in order to determine the functional state of the chamber crews' CMI systems over time and compare to a control group of subjects not exposed to the environmental stress of isolation within the closed chamber. There were two subject groups in this study: (1) the experimental (chamber) group, which consisted of the four chamber occupants, and (2) the control group, which consisted of four sex- and age-matched volunteers. All individuals completed a training session on the proper application of the skin test device and measurement of the results. The following procedure was used for application of the testing device at each time point:   The volar surface of a forearm was cleansed with an alcohol pad and allowed to dry. The test device was then placed against the forearm and firmly pressed into the skin. The prongs at the tip of each arm entered the skin and delivered the antigen. A rocking motion was used to ensure adequate delivery of the antigens and control. The test device was removed, and the area was allowed to dry for 5 minutes. A permanent marker was used to outline the skin area tested to allow later observation of the proper sites. After 48 hours, each antigen site was evaluated for induration, and calipers were used to measure the diameter of the induration along the vertical and horizontal axes. The number of antigens that reach at least 2 mm in diameter were considered positive. The sum total millimeters of induration and the number of positive antigens were recorded and used to determine a CMI score according to the formula: CMI Score = Sum of Mean Indurations/Number of Positive Antigens. RESULTS The chamber subjects had fewer responses to the seven antigens at the C-30 time point compared to the control subjects. By chamber day 45 (C+45), the chamber subjects showed hypoergic responses, and by chamber day 90 (C+90) all chamber subjects exhibited anergy to the seven challenge antigens. The chamber subjects had returned nearly to their prechamber baselines within 30 days of exiting the chamber. The control group subjects responded to more antigens at the C-30 time point and showed variable responses, but only minor changes throughout the study period. Since the chamber subjects responded initially (C-30) to fewer antigens, the baseline value for the sum of the indurations in the chamber subjects is less than that for the control group. The chamber subjects showed a loss of reactivity to most of the antigens by chamber day C+45 and had no response to any of the antigens and thus no measurable indurations at chamber day C+90. By 30 days after exit from the chamber (E+30), the measured sum of indurations had returned to near baseline level in the chamber subjects. The control subjects showed a variable response throughout the study. One control subject exhibited a slightly attenuated response on chamber day C+45 while another showed increased responses at chamber days C+45 and C+90. On day E+30, all control subjects had values similar to pre-chamber baseline measurements. The most interesting and meaningful results for both the control and chamber groups involved their average CMI scores. The average CMI score for the control subjects varied little throughout the entire study period (range 4.05 to 4.23). However, the chamber subjects as a group showed a profound decrement in their average CMI scores on chamber days C+45 and C+90 with no response to any of the seven challenge antigens noted in any of the four chamber subjects on chamber day C+90. The average CMI score of the chamber group had returned to near the baseline level at 30 days postchamber (E+30). The chamber subjects had a nearly 49% decrease in their CMI scores during the chamber stay which was statistically different from the control data set at p = 0.002. The CMI scores of the chamber subjects were still decreased from control values by approximately 13% at time point E+30 (30 days after exiting the chamber), but the difference was not significant. The primary aim of this study was to determine if isolation of human subjects within a closed chamber over a period of 91 days would adversely affect function of the cell-mediated arm of the immune system. The CMI scores were significantly decreased (-48.7% ± 10.1 SEM; p= 0.002; n = 8) for the chamber subjects during chamber isolation. The CMI scores were decreased below the control level (-13.1% ± 13.05 SEM) for the isolated chamber subjects at 30 days after exit from the chamber, but were not statistically different from the control values at this time point. The short-term and long-term effects of decreased CMI in isolated human subjects are not known. Since CMI plays important roles in combating infectious agents (e.g., viruses and fungi), in surveillance against neoplastic cells, and in regulation of immune function, possible consequences include increased susceptibility to acute and chronic infections, increased cancer risk, and immune dysregulation. The level of these increased risks associated with decreased CMI function in conjunction with isolation and other still poorly understood environmental, physiological, and psychological factors is not known. Additional prospective and retrospective longitudinal studies are required to better understand underlying mechanisms and the level of risks associated with decreased CMI function in persons living in isolated environments. The role of exercise and the specific types, intensity levels, and duration in modulating the immune response during isolation requires further investigation.

title: Monitoring of Sweat Calcium Using Skin Patches
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Bone loss can occur during bed rest due to lack of limb use, and exercise has been researched as a potential countermeasure. Calcium loss in sweat from this normal exercise program has been a concern, especially if the exercise occurs at normal room temperature. In previous bed rest studies, early changes in bone mass have been detected by measuring calcium. Past subjects have undergone a negative calcium balance due to a rapid increase in calcium excretion through the urine and feces. Most studies did not measure calcium loss in sweat, because researchers assumed that the loss had a negligible effect on calcium balance. This assumption was not tested often, partly because an accurate measurement of sweat calcium was difficult. However, one previous study showed that calcium loss through sweat was much greater during one hour of running on a treadmill at room temperature than for the entire remainder of the day. The mean value of the calcium loss was 47 mg per hour while running and 0.8 mg per hour for the rest of the day. Another earlier study also supported the conclusion that sweat calcium loss was greater during strenuous exercise than for sedentary activities. Thus, loss of calcium in sweat could indeed prove to be a significant factor in total body calcium loss, especially when the countermeasures for bone density loss are applied. Since bone density and calcium balance are important factors in health, countermeasures against their degradation need to be optimized and a simple, reliable method of calcium sweat detection should be determined. This bed rest study had two main purposes. First, researchers tested a non-invasive sweat collection method for its ability to monitor sweat calcium loss. Second, changes in skin calcium loss were measured with and without a resistive exercise countermeasure performed at a lower environmental temperature.
approach: The subjects of this bed rest study consisted of six females (five white and 1 black) and ten males (nine white and one black). The subjects ages ranged from 22 to 48 years, and weight ranged from 60 to 97 kg. Heights ranged from 157 to 185 cm. Subjects were divided into three groups. One group was assigned resistive exercise with a workload that increased progressively throughout the bed rest study. A second group did not exercise, but ingested a drug called alendronate (brand name of Fosamax®), which is used to strengthen bone. The third group did not exercise or ingest a drug; these subjects served as controls. To collect sweat from the subjects, skin patches (Osteopatch®), were attached to the skin on the back, lower chest, and upper part of the arm. Initial studies involved placing two patches, one on each side of the body, on each area for a total of six patches. Later the number was reduced from two patches to one per body region. Data from the patches were collected from four different time periods: a baseline ambulatory time before bed rest and at 6, 12 and 17 weeks of bed rest. Patches were worn for 24 hours on two consecutive days. The subjects that were assigned resistive exercise performed the exercise six days a week with no exercise performed on Sunday. The two consecutive days for exercise sweat collection occurred within this six-day period so that both days contained exercise. For this group of subjects, sweat was collected on rest days, as well as exercise days. Since there were not two consecutive days without exercise, this sweat collection occurred on two successive Sundays. The bed rest room temperature was 23 to 26°C. The room temperature during exercise was 18°C or less to minimize sweat loss. The skin patch used to collect sweat had an absorbing area of 14 cm 2 and absorbed the solid components of sweat while the fluid evaporated out. The skin was cleaned with an alcohol swab and allowed to dry before the patch was applied. After 24 hours of wear, the patch was removed and the absorption pad portion was refrigerated until analysis. During elution, the pad was placed at the top of a tube and dried for 30 minutes to remove all fluid. One milliliter of distilled water was then added to the pad. After an hour, the tube was centrifuged for ten minutes at 3000 rpm to collect the liquid at the bottom of the tube while the patch remained secured at the top. Calcium concentration was determined from the collected liquid.
results: Baseline data, which were taken from 12 subjects, each with six different patches duplicating the three body areas, show no differences between the duplicate body measurements. Significant differences in calcium excretion were found between back versus arm sweat and back versus chest sweat. However no significant differences were found between chest versus arm calcium excretion in sweat. No significant differences were found between the two different but consecutive days. In addition, no interaction or change in the relationships between the three regions was found over the consecutive days. The most variability in the results, 58%, was attributed to body region site with only 0.3% variability attributed to the day and 10% to site by day interaction. The range of inter-individual variability during the baseline collection varied from 18 to 32% for the three regions, with arms at 20% variability, chest at 18% variability and back at 24% variability combined over the days. The inter-individual variability for the two days combined over sites was 20% and 29%. For seven subjects who did not exercise, data collection occurred over the four time periods. No significant differences were observed between their baseline and the other collections, which occurred at 6, 12 and 17 weeks of bed rest. Some of these subjects ingested the alendronate and others were in the control group. During the bed rest timeframe, data from five exercise subjects were taken on exercise days and on rest days. No significant differences were observed between the rest days and the exercise days or between the two consecutive exercise days for the same subject. Total body sweat calcium for the twelve subjects during baseline data collection was averaged for the three sites and was 35 ± 4 mg/day. The mean value for the arm was 33 mg/day. The chest mean value was 35 mg/day and the back was 37 mg/day. The patch collection method was shown to be reliable for the measurement of sweat calcium loss. This conclusion was supported by the lack of large variations among repeated measurements by day and by site. The small difference between the back calcium excretion and the arm and chest excretion agreed with another published study that found a higher evaporation rate from the back. In this investigation, dermal calcium excretion was not studied during profuse sweating, so no conclusions could be drawn about the use of the skin patch in that circumstance. No significant differences were found between exercise and rest day values of sweat calcium loss for bed rest subjects that performed resistive exercise with a lower room temperature. In addition, no significant differences were found between baseline and bed rest calcium loss values; this room temperature was also controlled, but was not kept as low as it was during the exercise condition. Calcium excretion in sweat has been shown in other studies to increase significantly when aerobic exercise was performed at standard room temperature. In this study, no effect was observed on sweat calcium due to exercise. This observation was due to the cool environment in which the exercise was performed and also, possibly, to the fact that the exercise in this study was resistive rather than aerobic. This bed rest study showed that the skin patch could be used to determine the amount of calcium excreted in human sweat for up to 24 hours in normal sweating conditions. Any changes in sweat calcium from bed rest, with or without exercise in a cool environment, did not significantly affect total body calcium balance.

title: Overweight and Obesity in the LSAH Population
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: The rising prevalence of overweight and obese Americans has been the frequent topic of recent media articles. Various national surveys show that the majority of Americans are overweight. According to data obtained from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES), the percentage of overweight adults (ages 20-74) in the general population has increased from 45% in 1960-1962, to 64% in 1999-2000. The percentage of obese individuals has increased from 13% to 31% within the same time period. The terms overweight and obesity are defined using the Body Mass Index (BMI), a measure that expresses the relationship of weight to height. BMI is calculated by dividing weight in kilograms by the squared height in meters. This study compared the BMI of the Longitudinal Study of Astronaut Health (LSAH) participants with that of the general population.
approach: Data for astronaut participants and a group of comparison participants were obtained from the Longitudinal Study of Astronaut Health (LSAH) database. The BMI calculations for LSAH participants used weight and height data obtained from annual physical exams. Data for the general population were obtained from the NHANES database.
results: When compared to the general population, LSAH participants showed a similar trend of rising overweight and obesity over time (1967-2003). A graph of the data showed that a smaller percentage of astronauts and comparison participants were likely to be overweight, as compared to the general population. Astronauts were the least likely of the groups studied to be overweight. Over time however, a higher percentage of astronauts and comparison participants were likely to become overweight than the general population. Some of this rising trend may have been a function of the small sample sizes of LSAH participants, and may have reflected their propensity to gain weight as they age. As indicated by their R-squared value, all trend lines showed good representation of their respective data points and their trend over time (compared to an R-squared maximum value of one.) The obesity comparison showed both astronauts and comparison participants maintaining much lower obesity prevalence as compared to the general population. The trend lines suggested that LSAH participants become obese at a lower rate than the general population, with astronauts maintaining lower obesity than the comparison participants. However, R-squared values for the astronauts’ and comparison participants’ obesity trend lines indicated a higher variability for their obesity data than their overweight data. Taken together, these comparisons suggest that although LSAH participants maintain much lower obesity as compared to the general population, their overweight trends show a rapid rise that may result in prevalences similar to that of the general population. Aging is certainly a factor in the rapid rise of their overweight prevalence. However, they may do well to take action to decrease their overweight prevalences for the sake of their health.

title: Motor Adaptation to Coriolis and Contact Forces
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: A rotating space vehicle could be used to generate 'artificial gravity' during long-duration missions, however this would have side effects. Movements made during body rotation would generate transient Coriolis forces that act perpendicular to both the rotation axis and the movement direction. Such Coriolis forces initially deviate the trajectories and endpoints of reaching movements, but adaptation occurs to restore accuracy if exposure continues. The patterns of movement deviation generated by Coriolis forces differ from those observed when movements are perturbed by external, mechanical contact forces of comparable timing and magnitude. This implies that cutaneous contact cues are critical in the control and monitoring of movement endpoint, trajectory, and adaptation. The goal of this research was to investigate the conjoint influence on reaching and adaptation of cutaneous sensory signals, proprioceptors, and efferent commands. The effect on reaching movements of exposure to contact force perturbations, non-contact Coriolis forces, and combinations of the two were measured. Acquisition, retention, and transfer of adaptation was also studied.
approach: Experiments were conducted using the Slow Rotation Room Facility located at the Ashton Graybiel Spatial Orientation Laboratory, Brandeis University, Waltham, MA.
results: The results of these experiments have shown the following: 1) reaching movements to targets are deviated by Coriolis forces and mechanical contact forces; 2) both contact and non-contact perturbations generate errors in reaching paths and endpoints in the direction of the perturbing forces; 3) adaptation of movement endpoint and movement path are dissociable; 4) endpoint adaptation occurs rapidly with additional movements even in the absence of visual error feedback so long as the hand makes contact with a surface at the end of the movement; 5) there are no aftereffects from adaptation to mechanically induced errors when the subjects' arms are no longer attached to the apparatus, however, after adaptation to Coriolis force perturbations when the slow rotation room was again at rest subjects showed large after-effects in pointing to targets; 6) there is partial cross-transfer between inertial Coriolis force perturbations and mechanical contact force perturbations, this indicates that adaptation to mechanical contact forces is context specific; and 7) If the hand is maintained in contact with a surface while moving to point to a target during rotation, adaptation to the Coriolis force will occur for movement trajectory but not movement endpoint if visual feedback is denied. This research has enlightened the scientific community about the presence of Coriolis and other inertial accelerations on the arms and legs during self-generated, voluntary movements in a normal terrestrial environment. This research has also helped to provide a basis for anticipating and solving potential performance problems in a rotating artificial gravity environment.

title: Thyroid Disease Investigated Among LSAH Population
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Iodine is used for microbial disinfection in the potable water systems of U.S. spacecraft. Because iodine is metabolically active within the body, there is concern about chronic exposure to iodine in drinking water aboard U.S. spacecraft. Iodine is an essential micronutrient. It is present in food and water predominantly as iodide. It is rapidly and almost completely absorbed, with the excess excreted in urine. Iodide is transported to the thyroid gland where it is used to synthesize and secrete the thyroid hormones thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3), which act at multiple sites throughout the body and help to regulate metabolic processes. The activity of the thyroid is regulated by a negative feedback mechanism involving the pituitary gland and the hypothalamus. Thyrotropin releasing hormone (TRH) is released by the hypothalamus and provokes the pituitary to secrete the thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH), which is also known as thyrotropin. TSH stimulates the thyroid gland to release its hormones and to trap iodide. The thyroid hormones in turn inhibit the release of both TRH from the hypothalamus and TSH by the pituitary, in this way maintaining normal plasma levels of the thyroid hormones. A deficiency of iodine can lead to a wide spectrum of diseases ranging from severe cretinism with mental retardation to barely visible enlargement of the thyroid. Endemic goiter and the more severe forms of iodine deficiency disorders are a worldwide issue. Providing an adequate iodine intake can prevent iodine deficiency disorders. The recommended daily allowance of total iodine is 0.15 mg/day. Dietary sources of iodine include seafood, water from coastal areas, and iodized salt. Plant and animal sources vary depending on the soil, fertilization, feeding of animals, and food processing. The iodine intake by the majority of the US population is considered to be adequate and safe. The potential chronic toxic effects of excessive iodine are of current concern with respect to the astronaut population. Goiter and thyrotoxicosis have been documented in areas of Japan and Tasmania where dietary intake of iodine was exceptionally high. In populations where the drinking water has been disinfected with iodine, reported associations of iodine and thyroid disease are mixed. Some studies have reported weak, but significant, associations and other studies have reported no associations. Generally, iodine intakes of up to 2 mg/day have caused no adverse physiological reactions in healthy adults, but that level may be too high to sustain over long periods of time.
approach: To assist in decision making regarding this issue, the LSAH has examined the incidence of thyroid disease among the astronauts and the LSAH comparison population and the association of thyroid disease with exposure to iodinated drinking water.
results: An investigation into the incidence of thyroid disorders among the LSAH population revealed 12 cases (4.4%) among the astronauts and 27 cases (3.2%) among the comparison population. Six of the 12 cases among the astronauts were diagnosed before exposure to the iodinated water used on spacecraft. A comparison of the incidence of thyroid disorders among the astronaut population with the incidence among the LSAH comparison population resulted in no statistical evidence that the incidence rates are different between the two groups. However, transient elevations of TSH have been identified on landing day for astronauts in the shuttle program. The TSH levels have returned to preflight levels during the postflight period. While there is no evidence of an association between the use of iodinated water during shuttle flights and postexposure thyroid disorders in the current astronaut population, the effects of longer-term exposures are unknown. In addition, the susceptibility of individuals to iodine exposure appears to vary and methods for identifying susceptible individuals are not well defined. Consequently, intensive efforts are underway to lower the iodine concentration in the water aboard spacecraft to an optimal level.

title: Ocular Blood Flow Measured Noninvasively in Zero Gravity
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: In spaceflight or a reduced-gravity environment, bodily fluids shift to the upper extremities of the body. The pressure inside the eye, or intraocular pressure, changes significantly. A significant number of astronauts report changes in visual acuity during orbital flight. Perfused blood flow in the dense meshwork of capillaries of the choroidal tissue provides necessary nutrients to the outer layers of the retina (photoreceptors) to keep it healthy and maintain good vision. Unlike the vascular system, the choroid has no baroreceptors to autoregulate fluid shifts, so it can remain engorged, pushing the macula forward and causing a hyperopic (farsighted) shift of the eye. This investigation studies the effects of zero gravity on the choroidal blood flow of volunteer subjects. This pilot project is designed to determine if choroidal blood flow is autoregulated in a reduced-gravity environment, to help ascertain in future experiments if there is a relationship between changing intraocular pressure and a systemic blood pressure with the choroidal flow.
approach: These experiments were conducted aboard a wide-body aircraft (KC-135) during parabolic flight trajectories (which produce environments varying from low to high gravity). A low-power (~100 mW) continuous-wave (CW) solid-state laser operating at a wavelength of ~780 nm was used to measure frequency shift in a head-mounted miniature laser Doppler flowmeter. The Doppler shift
results: from red blood cells flowing through the choroids. This yields parametric measurements of blood volume, speed, and flow. Each measurement takes approximately 15 seconds to complete. The incident laser light shifts in frequency after it interacts with the red blood cells flowing in the choroidal tissue. This frequency shift is proportional to the speed of the moving red blood cells: Df = 1/2p(Ks - Ki)VRBC, where Ks and Ki are the wave vectors of the scattered and incident light, respectively, with magnitude 2pn/l, where n is the refractive index of the medium, l is the wavelength of light in vacuum, and VRBC is the velocity of the red blood cells. The experimental scheme uses heterodyne detection, in which the light scattered from red blood cells is mixed with light reflected from the nonmoving tissue at an avalanche photodiode (APD) photodetector. After the electronic processing of these signals, a power spectrum is obtained and parameters such as blood volume, speed, and red blood cell flux are calculated. RESULTS: Both the velocity of the red blood cells flowing in the choroid and the arterial BP changed as gravity levels were varied during the parabolic flight of the KC-135. The red blood cell velocity increased consistently in reduced gravity and decreased in high gravity. The BP (both systolic and dystolic) decreased in low gravity and increased in high gravity.

title: Evaluation of the Space Therapeutics Assessment Recorder (STARx) and the Automated Neuropsychological Assessment Metric (ANAM) Readiness Evaluation System (ARES) on the Palm PDA Platform:  A Device for Real-Time Monitoring of Drug Effectiveness
experiment_type: NASA Extreme Environment Mission Operations (NEEMO) Project
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: The purpose of the STARx study performed during the NEEMO missions was three-fold. First, the relative efficacies of medications taken by each NEEMO 4 and 5 crewmember were evaluated. Second, the effect of medications on NEEMO 5 crewmembers' neuro-cognitive performance was evaluated. The third objective was to evaluate the functionality of the device used to collect drug effectiveness and neuro-cognitive data during both NEEMO 4 and 5 missions.
approach: A hand-held Palm Personal Data Assistant (PDA) preloaded with both the Space Therapeutics Assessment Recorder (STARx) application and the ANAM (Automated Neuropsychological Assessment Metrics) Readiness Evaluation System (ARES) was provided to each crewmember. The STARx software application allowed crewmembers to record drug effectiveness data in real time using a severity of symptoms scale specific for each class of medications, as well as information about the clinical status. Each time a crewmember took a medication, they entered that information into the Palm PDA. The crewmember then decided when to be notified by the PDA to enter in data regarding the drug’s effectiveness. At the specified time, an alarm sounded on the PDA, and the crewmember entered in the requested data. In addition to the effectiveness data, crewmembers completed a sleepiness score loaded as part of the STARx application, which recorded the ability of medications to induce drowsiness. Any additional information was entered as notes using the "Memo Pad" application also loaded on the Palm PDA. The ARES software application consisted of two short-term memory tests known as the Match to Sample (MTS) and Continuous Processing Task (CPT) for neuro-cognitive analysis. The crew completed the ARES test two times a day, once in the morning and once before retiring to bed.
results: The STARx software application was not used during the mission due to the fact that no medications were taken during the 14-day NEEMO 5 mission. All four NEEMO 5 aquanauts completed the pre-mission training sessions and daily ARES data collection during the 14-day mission. A total of 26 sessions were completed in the Aquarius habitat. However, changes in cognitive performance could not be correlated with medication use, because no medications were taken. A comparison between early morning and late evening ARES scores was performed with the following results: Evening MTS response times were 10 to 22% less than morning response times. The decrease in two of the four aquanauts was statistically significant (p Evening CPT response times were 2 to 8% less than morning response times. The decrease in one of the four aquanauts was statistically significant (p Aquanaut accuracy scores during all test sessions for the MTS and CPT tests were very high regardless of morning or evening conditions, i.e., greater than 80% and 88%, respectively.

title: Sociokinetic Analysis as a Tool for Optimization of Environmental Design
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: The Lunar-Mars Life Support Test Project (LMLSTP) Phase III testing experiment was designed to develop a practical application to the design of enclosed environments, such as those for long-duration space missions. Social interaction in a built environment is a dynamic constant that expresses itself as a type of kinesis, or a choreographic pattern, by which the members of a group occupy a given place. The force and effectors to any given interaction lie partly in the realm of personal and group psychology. Behavioral psychology demonstrates many ways of viewing the inherent relationships in a group. Personal or subjective studies alone are insufficient to explain the behavior described as social interaction, because the environment in which these interactions occur contains elements that tend to stimulate or suppress specific behavior. In general, these cues seem to complex to identify, isolate, or characterize in terms of their behavioral impact. The design of enclosed or hermetic habitats for long-duration human life support in extreme situations, such as Arctic or Antarctic research, space exploration, or lunar-Mars bases, is of extreme importance. Under such circumstances, the habitat itself takes on a uniquely influential role as the primary or sole environment and is thus critical in either supporting or undermining the mental health, productivity, and interactions of its inhabitants. Therefore, the conscious control of environmental cues such as programming, acoustics, and orientation, becomes fundamental to the facility's design and, by extension, to the success of the mission. Sociokinetic analysis, or the study of the patterns in which a group of individuals within a given environment make use of that environment, was developed at NASAs Johnson Space Center (JSC) in 1997. This method involves: (1) capturing hard data regarding the use of volume within a hermetic habitat, and (2) applying statistical analyses from this data to the resident group. Strict documentation of the habitat is then weighed against the
approach: Cameras were placed throughout the three-level facility to monitor the environment; two were mounted on level one, one on level two, and one in the corridor area of level three. Level one was a multifunctional area consisting of a galley and wardroom, science workstations for advanced life support studies, principal personal hygiene and waste compartments (shower and toilet), and a dedicated exercise area in the airlock. The airlock was smaller than other rooms and was loud when in use. In addition, the airlock was the only location in the chamber from which the crew could be observed by anyone walking through the Building 7 high bay. The common room housed the entertainment center (TV and VCR), as well as the only table large enough for communal activities or large work tasks. Despite the room's cramped and intermingled location, it housed all of the equipment most desired for group functions. Level two housed all principal equipment that supported the basic functions of the chamber, including bioreactors and gauges. The average noise intensity on level two was 70 decibels. Fluorescent fixtures arrayed vertically along the walls so that the occupants experienced a combination of glare and reflection at all locations on that level. A generous workstation table was provided on this floor, the same size as the wardroom table on level one but without the crowding and intermingled location. Level three was the uppermost and most private level of the chamber, housing four identical crew quarters and a toilet. This level had one opening from a central landing at the head of the stairs. To establish the desired habitable living quarters for the four-person crew, it was essential to find a quantitative, nonintrusive method of studying their use patterns in the 20-foot chamber facility over a three-month time span. The approach utilized the four cameras already present in the chamber, because the intrusiveness of any measurement system would have inherently affected the data collected. The cameras recorded the chamber 24 hours a day, seven days a week, over a three-week span. The question of adaptation or change was also a consideration. Therefore, data was taken during the early, middle, and late stages of the LMLSTP, specifically, weeks 3, 7, and 11. Investigators were able to document when the crewmembers were enjoying the privacy of their personal quarters without invading that privacy, because the camera on level three recorded the public segment of that floor off of which all four crew quarters were located. Thus, the advantage gained was having complete and reasonable access to the crew's activities in a manner that was nonintrusive. For instance, the crew was alerted that taping would begin at a certain time on the evening before each week that was observed. By week three (the first week studied), this alert was of negligible impact to the data, because by this time the crew had become accustomed to the constant vigilance of the control room staff and had begun to ignore the presence of the cameras, or to accept them as a simple fact of daily life. An onscreen video time stamp was used, which permitted the researchers to verify the actual recording time against the time marked on the cassette. At the completion of the test, a total of 512 hours of video was tracked using statistical analysis software, and the period of each crewmember's tenure on each floor was quantified in seconds. These units were then tracked against time, total duration, and the simultaneous activity of other crewmembers. The principal questions under consideration were:     Did the crew's preference for group versus private areas or other use patterns change over the duration of their confinement? Did the crew prefer more private locations or more public/shared locations, with all things being equal (i.e., specific site-related activities aside)? Were any marked social patterns or behaviors anomalous to non-confined groups? Did any marked behaviors reflect in an unambiguous fashion to known conditions of the crew's environment?
results: in order to force certain environmental design cues to the forefront. The first run of this method involved an objective study using patterns of JSC's 20-foot chamber during Phase III of the Lunar Mars Life Support Test Project (LMLSTP) over the 91-day time span from September through December 1997. APPROACH: Cameras were placed throughout the three-level facility to monitor the environment; two were mounted on level one, one on level two, and one in the corridor area of level three. Level one was a multifunctional area consisting of a galley and wardroom, science workstations for advanced life support studies, principal personal hygiene and waste compartments (shower and toilet), and a dedicated exercise area in the airlock. The airlock was smaller than other rooms and was loud when in use. In addition, the airlock was the only location in the chamber from which the crew could be observed by anyone walking through the Building 7 high bay. The common room housed the entertainment center (TV and VCR), as well as the only table large enough for communal activities or large work tasks. Despite the room's cramped and intermingled location, it housed all of the equipment most desired for group functions. Level two housed all principal equipment that supported the basic functions of the chamber, including bioreactors and gauges. The average noise intensity on level two was 70 decibels. Fluorescent fixtures arrayed vertically along the walls so that the occupants experienced a combination of glare and reflection at all locations on that level. A generous workstation table was provided on this floor, the same size as the wardroom table on level one but without the crowding and intermingled location. Therefore, data was taken during the early, middle, and late stages of the LMLSTP, specifically, weeks 3, 7, and 11. Investigators were able to document when the crewmembers were enjoying the privacy of their personal quarters without invading that privacy, because the camera on level three recorded the public segment of that floor off of which all four crew quarters were located. Thus, the advantage gained was having complete and reasonable access to the crew's activities in a manner that was nonintrusive. For instance, the crew was alerted that taping would begin at a certain time on the evening before each week that was observed. By week three (the first week studied), this alert was of negligible impact to the data, because by this time the crew had become accustomed to the constant vigilance of the control room staff and had begun to ignore the presence of the cameras, or to accept them as a simple fact of daily life. An onscreen video time stamp was used, which permitted the researchers to verify the actual recording time against the time marked on the cassette. At the completion of the test, a total of 512 hours of video was tracked using statistical analysis software, and the period of each crewmember's tenure on each floor was quantified in seconds. These units were then tracked against time, total duration, and the simultaneous activity of other crewmembers. The principal questions under consideration were:     Did the crew's preference for group versus private areas or other use patterns change over the duration of their confinement? Did the crew prefer more private locations or more public/shared locations, with all things being equal (i.e., specific site-related activities aside)? Were any marked social patterns or behaviors anomalous to non-confined groups? Did any marked behaviors reflect in an unambiguous fashion to known conditions of the crew's environment? RESULTS: First, an analysis was made of the percentage of time the crew spent on each floor during each week of the test. Although there was less variation from week to week than had been anticipated, a slight but steady trend was seen toward less use of the airlock and level one (the group areas) in favor of level three (private zones). Although this difference is not considered statistically significant, a significant trend was detected in the comparison of individual room usage within each week. Furthermore, this trend held true across all three weeks of testing. This trend was identified after the project using Tukey's analysis. Of greatest interest for future refinements of this test was the analysis of use patterns against the time of day during the study period. While the rates of use for the airlock and level two appear to be similar, the incidence of that use is different. Because of the exercise function in the airlock, its use by only a single crewmember at a time was extended throughout the waking day with small peaks between 08:00 and 10:00 and between 18:00 and 20:00 as personnel exercised. Level two usage, however, was almost exclusively in 20-second increments steadily throughout the day - in other words, the amount of time it took for a person to traverse the level two landing on the stair while in transit between levels one and three. Occasionally, crewmembers would spend slightly larger blocks of time on level two to check or maintain equipment, but the greatest percentage of use stemmed from the transit function, which was more or less constant throughout the day. Another important (although less marked) data point was the set of locales for socialization. While level one-group interactions included any number of crewmembers up to four, the group interactions on Level Three were never more than three and predominantly of only two persons at one time. Moreover, crewmembers were never seen entering one another's private quarters. The group appeared from very early on to have established an unofficial protocol whereby people talking would stand just outside or in the doorway of another person's room, thus establishing a territorial boundary between the semiprivate realm of the corridor/landing and the private realm of the crew quarters. Mutual-boundary interactions also took place as crewmembers stood in their own doorways and conversed with one another across the landing. Use of level one was almost perfectly mirrored by the use of level three; in other words, when personnel were not on level one , the chances were very high that they were on level three and vice versa (rather than in the airlock or level two). In many instances this use at specific times of day was unsurprising. Level three, for example, was the area of choice between 24:00 and 08:00, while the crew was sleeping; and level one was most popular around 12:00 and 20:00, at lunch and dinnertime. However, this mirroring was also unaccompanied by anything but a static, constant baseline in the airlock and level two areas, suggesting that the use or disuse of levels one and three had bearing on one another but no bearing on the occupancy of level two and the airlock. Thus two of the four areas of the habitat (some 35-40% of its total available area for habitable use) went virtually unused except by necessity, while the other two areas became in essence the whole inhabited volume of the test chamber. By separate use of these terms a distinction has been established between "habitable" volume and "inhabited" volume. The difference between the former and the latter is that "habitable" volume can be occupied by humans, whereas "inhabited" volume will be occupied and used by humans. This is tremendously useful data because it identifies which environments the crew found acceptable, and which they did not. The evidence is nearly overwhelming that the crew preferred levels one and three of the 20-foot chamber over the airlock and level two. This is true to such a degree that these areas almost constitute wasted volume in that, despite the expressed needs of the crewmembers for greater privacy and flexibility within the habitat, they largely rejected the use of two semiprivate areas, which could have been, utilized as offline workstations and/or relaxation areas. In addition, the semiprivate landing area of level three could have become less of a public site for mutual-boundary interactions had it been possible for the crew to interact "offline" in some non-private room other than the level one common area. Thanks to this pattern of nonuse, environmental factors were identified that people clearly found unacceptable to the point of rejecting their use. The airlock was a small, cylindrical area that was not comfortably outfitted but rather housed only the exercise and other mechanical equipment. Furthermore, it was the only part of the habitat exposed to the exterior, resembled a"goldfish bowl" and sensibility may have swayed inhabitants. Other than exercise, there was no other activity associated with the room, and it was not very welcoming. Level two, on the other hand, had a pleasant level of illumination, carpeting, and a cozy corner or two to offer. Only two factors were less than optimal in it's outfitting, yet these appear to have had a decisive effect on the usability of the room: the very loud acoustic environment and the direct-glare lighting. While the room appeared calm, it was extremely difficult to make oneself heard for the noise generated by the equipment. Also, although the lighting levels were acceptable for tasks, the angle of lighting was extremely unpleasant. Thus a few important rules for design of inhabitable built environments have been derived from this experiment:   Finishing's, dimensions, and privacy affect the usability of an area High-glare illumination can render an area unusable to the resident population An unacceptably loud acoustical environment can render an area unusable to the resident population. The private/semiprivate/public boundary issues raised by interpersonal communications on level three also suggest some useful rules of programming (i.e., functional allocation of volume) for future hermetic habitats In a restricted habitat, private rooms are considered inviolable territory and will not be invaded unless by explicit invitation The territory immediately adjacent to private rooms may/will be annexed as a semiprivate social center (unless other areas specifically intended for offline socializing are provided). In conclusion, environmental conditions have been found to affect the efficiency and usability of a closed environment facility.

title: Environmental Radiation Measurements on Mir Station
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: This experiment attempted to expand the knowledge of environmental radiation at the 51.6 degree orbit, the location of the Mir station and future location of the International Space Station. Information on the shielding effects of the station and different methods of radiation dosimetry was also gathered. The data and associated analysis contributed to the establishment of a reliable database for the radiation environment in space.
approach: Two types of spectra were measured and compared: linear energy transfer (LET) and absorbed dose. The measurements for both spectra occurred inside six area passive dosimeters (APDs) that were flown to Mir via Shuttle mission STS-76 and placed at six different locations on Mir. LET spectra was measured using CR-39 PNTDs that were placed on the APDs. The CR-39 plates were etched with a NaOH solution and read out on an image digitizer system and analyzed. The absorbed spectra was measured using thermoluminescent detectors (TLDs) attached to the APDs. The flight data was compared with data read from background and calibration TLDs.
results: By using identical APDs in the exact locations on Mir, changes in radiation levels over time were recorded and analyzed. The measured dose rates in the APDs ranged from 268 to 422 mGy/d, yielding an average of 324 mGy/d. The differences in the high and low values were most likely caused by shielding differences due to the individual APD placements on Mir. Also, secondary target fragments, generated by inelastic scattering of protons and alpha particles within the detector medium, contributed to the spread of values. The dose and dose equivalent rates were used to calculate the effective quality factor, which was determined to be about 9 for LETs 25 keV/mm. This value shows the significance of short-range high LET target fragments to dose equivalent. The shielding data is currently being used to model the APD measurements made in the Mir Core.

title: Habitability Assessment:  Habitat Utilization Analysis from Human Factors Perspective
experiment_type: NASA Extreme Environment Mission Operations (NEEMO) Project
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: The purpose of the habitability assessment project is to evaluate the Aquarius from the human factors and habitability perspective as an isolated, confined analog for the International Space Station (ISS), determine the human factors and habitability requirements for such an isolated and confined analog, and identify potential enhancement for the next generation habitat via use of naturalistic data capture, habitability questionnaire, and Space Operations Issues Reporting Tool (SOIRT). By identifying how participants use the Aquarius habitat, conclusions can be drawn about which habitability attributes cause specific interactions and behaviors facilitating a systematic design to achieve desired human performance. In addition, the inclusion of objective data may provide inputs to other analysis of work/rest schedules. Finally, naturalistic data collection has been under investigation as a means to opportunistically gather data during NASA training and actual International Space Station (ISS) missions. Inclusion of this method of data collection served as a test case to identify pros and cons and associated technological challenges.
approach: Crewmembers filled out a habitability survey, including questions regarding acceptability of the Aquarius habitat such as its interior layout, physical environment (e.g., noise, humidity), tasks, and individual experience/comments. This survey was required to be completed only once for the duration of each mission. Crewmembers also filled out an issue reporting form, called SOIRT, to note any design or activity based issues and/or enhancements. This form was filled out on an as-needed basis throughout each mission. The NEEMO 5 project also involved taping live feed from cameras, positioned with a view to the central common areas in the Aquarius. Taping took place during pre-defined periods of the 14-day mission. A heads-up signal was given at bedtime the night prior to taping, to remind the crewmember of the taped monitoring the following day. A second heads-up was given upon wake-up the following day, and a third at the end of the taping. The videos, which showed how crewmembers chose to use common spaces in Aquarius during the course of the day, were analyzed by computer to extract
results: in conclusions of certain features that cause certain behaviors. Finally, questionnaire data was analyzed to look for common pros and cons of the habitat across NEEMO/Aquarius crews, as well as consistency across different analogs used for space missions. This will help identify the functional needs and human factors requirements for living and working in an isolated, confined environment. RESULTS: From analysis of the video, several habitability issues related to the Aquarius habitat became apparent: Workstations were poorly placed and interfered with the flow of traffic in and out of the Main Lock. Particularly, the two workstations located near the entrances were problematic both for people trying to pass through, as well as for people working at them who were interrupted in their work. When more than one person was at either of the two workstations, sitting on the step ladder or standing and looking over the shoulder of the other person, traffic flow was obstructed even more. In at least one instance, the stepladder was left behind after two crewmembers were working together, and another crewmember passing through had to step over it. Another habitability issue revealed by the video analysis was the inappropriate size of the table. Used for eating, working, meetings, and group teleconferences with ground, the table sometimes needed to accommodate up to six people at once. Even for four people, as was more often the case, the table was far too small and it was obvious from the video that the crewmembers were uncomfortable. Often during group meetings some of them would have to sit on the step ladder or stand. Given its frequency of use, the table should be larger to comfortably seat all members of the crew to improve comfort, work, and social interaction. From the videos it also became evident that the food storage was poorly sited. Multiple instances were recorded where crewmembers were seen reaching across the small galley, blocking traffic or standing precariously on the stepladder to reach the storage areas. This also occurred frequently near and during meal times when most of the crewmembers were in and moving about the Main Lock. Also noted during these periods was the fact that the refrigerator and microwave/storage areas were located too far from each other, as lots of back and forth traffic occurred between them. Given the narrow passage, it was readily apparent that traffic within the Main Lock could be much ameliorated simply by moving these two areas closer together. In conclusion, video analysis provided useful ideas as to how an enclosed habitat might be improved. As with the common human factors method of link analysis (e.g. Thelwell, 2004), simply noting which areas are accessed frequently together can provided insight into how to rearrange the habitat to improve efficiency and even reduce risk of injury. While web cast video had its technological problems, such as erratic skips, lags, graininess, blocked views, and lighting inconsistencies, it did provide useful overall information for practical recommendations. Systematic research, however, would require a higher standard of data collection. Perhaps in the future, notes regarding crew activity could be added by those recording the video to aid those tasked to analyze it later. This feature was sometimes present in the NEEMO 5 video; however, it was not present often enough to prove useful to the researchers. Also, video size and quality should be closely monitored to ensure that a larger percent of the captured video is analyzable. Naturalistic data capture by webcast video was found to be effective for getting the broad picture of habitat use by the NEEMO 5 crew. While there is obviously room for improvement, predominantly with the technology, there are some major benefits to be taken from this type of effort, as Adams (2002) reported previously. This type of work is crucial for designing and optimizing a habitat to support crew behavior as it will occur, especially since many of the findings were not captured in crew debriefings. This may be due to the unconscious influence of environmental performance shaping factors; however, more research is needed to support this claim. The inclusion of automation, such as sensors and location tracking, in future studies would make recording and analyzing certain metrics far easier and improve accuracy (e.g., entries and exits, frequency of use). The significant input that this type of research provides for generating optimal habitat designs and guidelines should not be neglected in any future long duration spaceflight effort.

title: Colorectal Cancer in LSAH Participants and a Comparison Population
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: The incidence of colorectal cancer and colonic polyps is monitored in the Longitudinal Study of Astronaut Health (LSAH) participants. It is believed that astronauts could be at increased risk for colorectal cancer because if their unique exposures, particularly radiation exposure.
approach: Data for the astronaut participants and a group of comparison participants were obtained from the LSAH database.
results: No increased incidence in colorectal cancer or colonic polyps has been observed in astronaut participants when compared to the comparison population.

title: Body Mass Index (BMI) in LSAH Participants
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Body mass index is a measurement of weight adjusted for height, calculated as: weight (kg)/height (m)2. LSAH reported body mass index measurements for LSAH participants at baseline. The mean values for the study group at baseline were 23.28 for the astronaut group and 23.34 for the comparison group.
approach: The most recent physical examination for each study participant has been reviewed, and the group
results: show a slight increase in body mass index because of weight gain as study participants age. For this assessment, weight and height for each study participant, as reported on the last physical examination completed in the JSC Clinics, were used. RESULTS: The mean body mass index for the most recent visit was 24.71 for the astronaut group and 24.37 for the comparison group. The change in weight over time for the comparison group is very similar to the change in weight for the astronaut group. Both groups show a small increase in mean weight since baseline.

title: Inflight Lower Limb Volume Measurement
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: During space flight, the body's fluids tend to shift from the lower body toward the head and chest. This fluid redistribution is clear from observations and confirmed in data collected from the Apollo and Skylab crews. These changes and their effects were described by crewmembers: fullness of the head, puffy faces, stuffy noses, distended veins in the neck and forehead and a noticeable shrinking of muscles. First measured inflight on the Skylab 4 crewmembers; leg volume measurements were also performed on the Apollo-Soyuz Test Project (ASTP) crewmembers. The objectives of this study were to substantiate the volume reduction that occurs inflight, to obtain inflight leg volume determinations earlier than those obtained on Skylab 4 and to document the time course of fluid shifts by frequent leg volume measurements.
approach: Leg volume was determined by multiple serial circumference measurements using the Limb Volume Measuring Kit. The kit included a leg template, a measuring tape, and a stowage pouch. The template was marked at 12 positions for circumference measurements. During measurement, the template was attached to the leg with straps at the ankle, knee, and thigh. With the subject supine (leg fully extended) and relaxed, circumferences were measured with the measuring tape at each position. Measurements were conducted preflight, inflight, and postflight on each crewmember (both legs preflight and postflight; left leg only inflight).
results: The earliest inflight determinations were obtained approximately 6 hours into flight. Leg volume decreased 0.26 liters below the preflight volume and was statistically significant. After 32 hours of space flight, all three crewmembers evidenced substantial leg volume reductions of 5 to 10 percent. This decrease was observed earlier than in previous leg volume measurements obtained on Skylab 4 (taken on flight day 3). Subsequent measurements showed moderate variability with a definite downward trend. Most variations were parallel in all three crewmembers, although different crewmembers contributed to measurement variance. Earliest postflight determinations were taken between 1.5 and 2 hours after splashdown. Leg volumes on all three crewmembers had increased well above their last inflight values. Second measurements taken on recovery day, 2 to 5 hours after splashdown, evidenced even greater leg volumes. This was in accordance with the reversing effects of re-adaption to the 1-G environment. Leg volumes measurements one day after landing were achieved before arising that morning and clearly show the established diurnal pattern of minimal volume at the end of the sleep period, with the subjects in a supine position. The last postflight measurements taken four days after landing exhibited increasing trends toward preflight values. Because of circumstances associated with a problem during landing, leg volumes were not obtained beyond four days after landing. In conclusion, it appeared that the major fluid volume shift from the legs does not occur within the first few hours in orbit. The trend seems to have assumed an exponential form with maximum decrease within the first 24 hours. A distant plateau was evident by 3 to 5 days inflight, with little significant additional decrease occurring after the first week in weightlessness. These fluid volume shifts coincided with the occurrence of crew symptomatology, such as a feeling of fullness in the face, and the plateau with relative adaptive stability.

title: Development of a Flash X-ray Radiography and Tomography System to Measure Bone Mineral Density
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: This project addressed NASA's need for a relatively compact and portable x-ray system to perform bone mineral density studies on the International Space Station. The use of a 60 ns x-ray pulse to image biological specimens has been successfully demonstrated. With the dual-energy flash source, there is no need to change the anode-cathode (AK) voltage since the applied voltage across the AK gap is effectively swept during operation. The x-ray energy is high early in the pulse and lower later in the pulse. Utilizing the dual energy properties of the x-ray source to perform x-ray absorptometry without changing the applied voltage across the AK gap or changing filters simplifies the implementation of the source. A computer simulation model was developed for the x-ray source, which permitted the distribution of radiated energy in a plane normal to the symmetry axis of the x-ray anode to be determined as well as its spectrum. The use of two amorphous silicon (aSi) imaging panels stacked in tandem with a metal x-ray filter yielded both hard and soft x-ray images. X-ray assays of bone mineral density (BMD) to accuracies of 2% percent are possible when the attenuation of the soft tissue is removed by means of a subtraction algorithm and by using a calibration phantom. The dual-energy x-ray absorptometry (DEXA) project implemented a complete system that integrates the dual energy pulsed x-ray source with the aSi digital imaging panels. Experiments were performed to determine the distribution of radiation over the image plane and the sensitivity or modulation transfer function of the imaging panels. Based on the imaging experiments and the ability of the software to generate computed tomographic (CT) images, a decision was made to add CT capability to DEXA imaging so that a 3-D map of the site bone mineral density could be obtained. The addition of the CT capability increases the patient radiation dose; so image-based reconstruction was planned for the purpose of reducing the dose. In this process a limited number (3 to 5) images of a target site are processed using a priori knowledge of the site architecture to construct a CT image. The following questions were examined and answered during this project. Is the fluence, forward distribution, repeatability, and energy spectrum of the pulsed x-ray source sufficient? Will the sensitivity of the aSi digital imaging panels and the choice of conversion phosphor produce an image suitable for DEXA analysis? Will the DEXA software operate correctly, and is it capable of generating a 3D map of bone mineral density?
approach: System tests were run to evaluate the CT image capability of the software. The DEXA system was configured to examine a Lamb femur. The specimen was frozen to prevent motion during the periods between image collection. The images were recorded on two stacked aSi digital panels and processed. The front panel was designed to be sensitive to 25-45 keV photons. Each image was processed using pixels located within a slice equivalent to a fan-beam. The set of all slices was processed to generate a volume view of the object capable of full 360 degree rotation about the x,y,z axis. Since hard and soft x-ray CT image data were available, the DEXA could be used to extract both the density and composition of the scanned object. Specifically, the DEXA software used a plastic-aluminum calibration phantom to create a raster of all possible values scanned, then correlated this data to the correct attenuation value, generated a surface polynomial to approximate the surface, and used the surface to correct a complete dataset by simulating a monochromatic source. When the corrected dataset was passed through a CT 3D reconstruction, the
results: ing reconstruction contained calibrated data that could be used to determine the volumetric density. To further evaluate the DEXA's imaging capabilities, the denser bone-mineral was extracted from the surrounding tissue by applying a cubic volume opacity filter followed by an isosurface reconstruction of the digitized x-ray image. By using both soft (25-45 keV) and hard (67-150 keV) images, the bone mineral density in the CT volume reconstruction could be determined. RESULTS: Understanding the process of charge flow in Marx-driven x-ray tubes was one of the goals of this research. The SCL flow in x-ray tubes with conical anodes and coaxial cathodes was successfully modeled using Langmuir's analytic solution for charge flow between coaxial cylinders, provided that the width of the plasma cathode was treated as a free parameter and that magnetic field effects were neglected. The use of simulated cathode current and AK voltage in a calculation of the x-ray emission spectrum confirmed that the x-ray tube was operating as a SCL diode and that the model could accurately simulate the emission spectrum and total radiated energy in the x-ray pulse. Moreover it was shown that when the filtered hard x-ray pulse was subtracted from the unfiltered x-ray pulse, the residual pulse was the expected soft x-ray pulse with the correct temporal shape. This work experimentally verified the dual energy nature of the x-ray pulse. The second research goal was to develop a digital imaging system with radiography and computed tomography (CT) capabilities. The ability of the present system to deliver detailed CT volume reconstructions was dependent on the number of views in the sampling set. title: Chromosome Analyses of Gemini Astronauts
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Exposure to ionizing radiation was a known hazard during the Gemini program. Although the U.S. Mercury and Gemini crews, as well as Soviet crews, received only small doses of radiation during their missions, scientists were certain that future high altitude orbital flights and ultimately the lunar missions would subject crews to appreciable exposures. In the 1960s, relatively little was known about the radiation response of man, and therefore much less was known about flight crews and what their responses would be if exposed to various doses under various circumstances. It was assumed that radiation responses on the ground would be identical to radiation exposure in spaceflight. In earlier suborbital and orbital flights, biological materials were flown, and had
approach: This study was first conducted on Gemini 3. Preflight and postflight peripheral leukocyte chromosome analyses were made of blood samples obtained from the Gemini 3 crew. These measurements had two purposes: first, to serve as a control of the experiment entitled "Synergistic Effect of Zero-g and Radiation on White Blood Cells" (experiment ID S004), and secondly, to examine the effect of spaceflight on human chromosomes. Subsequently, preflight and postflight chromosome analyses were made on all other Gemini flight crews (except Gemini 8, where postflight samples could not be taken because of the mission''s early termination). Leukocyte samples were obtained from blood drawn during the last preflight medical exam and the first postflight medical exam. For most flights, postflight samples were flown to and processed at Cape Kennedy; the samples for Gemini 3 and 11 were processed aboard the recovery vessel along with the samples for the S004 experiment. Short term leukocyte cultures were prepared, and the leukocytes were then separated from the heparinized blood by centrifugation. The cells were then placed in culture medium: 10 ml of Medium 199 with 30% AB+ inactivated human serum, 5000 units penicillin, 5mg streptomycin, and 0.5 ml phytohemagglutinin M (Difco) per culture. The cultures were then incubated at approximately 36 degrees Celsius in an atmosphere of 5% CO2 in air. Colchicine was added after 60 hours of incubation to a final concentration of 10 to the -4 M, and cells were fixed after 66 hours. Cells then suitable for chromosome analysis were scored for chromatid- and chromosome-type aberrations. It should be mentioned that on the Gemini 4, 5 and 7 flights, small quantities of various radioisotopes were injected into the crewmen preflight and postflight for other studies of plasma volume and red cell mass: RISA (125I-iodinated human serum albumin) was used on Gemini 4 and 5 51Cr-labeled red cells were used on Gemini 5 and 7 DFP (tritiated di-isopropyl fluorophosphonate) was used on Gemini 7. Preflight and postflight blood samples for this chromosome study were obtained before any of these isotopes were injected; on Gemini 4, however, one postflight sample from one crewman did not produce satisfactory cultures, so a second sample had to be obtained 1 week after recovery (after postflight isotopes had been injected.) While the estimated total-body radiation doses from the decay of these isotopes was very small (less than 88 mrem per man for the Gemini 5 flight, for instance), even minute radiation doses like these could cause some chromosome breakage. More complete details can be found in the experiment "Bioassay of Body Fluid" (experiment ID M005). Furthermore, for the missions where RISA was used, a control subject was injected with 2.5 micro-c of RISA and blood samples were taken for chromosomal analysis at times corresponding to the flight crew sampling times. No controls were done for the 51 chromium or DFP procedures.
results: of radiation exposure several magnitudes higher than expected, given the relatively low doses they were exposed to during flight. This led to the hypotheses that (1) a synergism might exist between radiation and some other parameter of spaceflight, such as weightlessness or vibration, or (2) that weightlessness itself might induce effects more commonly associated with radiation exposure. In an attempt to answer these hypotheses, several inflight experiments were carried out during the Gemini program. Chromosomal aberration production in human peripheral leukocytes irradiated in vitro during the flights was studied. This measurement had been demonstrated to be a sensitive method of biological radiation dose estimation, and had been successfully used in a number of cases of accidental whold body irradiation. Subsequently, preflight and postflight chromosome analyses were made on all other Gemini flight crews (except Gemini 8, where postflight samples could not be taken because of the mission''s early termination).
