It should be mentioned that on the Gemini 4, 5 and 7 flights, small quantities of various radioisotopes were injected into the crewmen preflight and postflight for other studies of plasma volume and red cell mass: RISA (125I-iodinated human serum albumin) was used on Gemini 4 and 5 51Cr-labeled red cells were used on Gemini 5 and 7 DFP (tritiated di-isopropyl fluorophosphonate) was used on Gemini 7. Preflight and postflight blood samples for this chromosome study were obtained before any of these isotopes were injected; on Gemini 4, however, one postflight sample from one crewman did not produce satisfactory cultures, so a second sample had to be obtained 1 week after recovery (after postflight isotopes had been injected.) While the estimated total-body radiation doses from the decay of these isotopes was very small (less than 88 mrem per man for the Gemini 5 flight, for instance), even minute radiation doses like these could cause some chromosome breakage. More complete details can be found in the experiment "Bioassay of Body Fluid" (experiment ID M005). Furthermore, for the missions where RISA was used, a control subject was injected with 2.5 micro-c of RISA and blood samples were taken for chromosomal analysis at times corresponding to the flight crew sampling times. No controls were done for the 51 chromium or DFP procedures. RESULTS: No large chromosomal effects of spaceflight were demonstrated. Postflight effects of the magnitude seen in biological materials flown on pre-Gemini flights were not seen on any of the Gemini flights. Some classes of aberrations did show a slight increase after some of the flights, but could not be correlated with flight duration, isotope injection or extravehicular activity (EVA). In particular, postflight increases of chromatid- and chromosome-type deletions are significant by a simple Chi-square test. The results were quite puzzling, in that chromatid-type aberrations occurred; these aberrations are only induced in cells that have already started DNA synthesis. However, the researchers used phytohemagglutinin-stimulated cultures, which were in the pre-DNA-synthesis stage. Only chromosome-type aberrations can be induced in such cells. The investigators offered a possible explanation for the origin of the chromatid-types: either the cells or the serum, some of which is always carried over into the culture with the cells, contain some chemical substance capable of breaking chromosomes during or after DNA synthesis. This, however, does not explain why only some crewmembers showed the increases. These experiments correlated with the results of the Gemini 3 and 11 in vitro experiments, in that investigators were unable to demonstrate any dramatic spaceflight effects on chromosome aberrations. None of the observations with the leukocyte chromosome system suggested any special genetic hazards associated with spaceflight. The leukocyte system was recommended to be a feasible biological dosimeter for future missions.

title: Physical Activity Profiles of LSAH Participants
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: The physical activity profile of LSAH participants can be gleaned from their responses in the Lifestyle Questionnaire (LSQ).
approach: The questionnaire has been used to collect lifestyle data from each class of astronauts and comparison participants since 1993, with an update in 1997.
results: Of 223 astronaut and 820 comparison participant respondents, the most recent data show that 58.8% of the former and 72.4% of the latter report 2 or fewer types of exercise (as defined in the LSQ) performed in their usual routine. When broken down into exercise types, the data show that 69.8% of astronauts and 58.7% of comparison participants report running or jogging as their usual form of exercise (exercise types are not mutually exclusive). More astronauts report weight lifting as an activity than comparison participants, while fewer astronauts report walking as an activity than comparison participants (56.5% to 28.5%, and 29.2% to 48.9%, respectively). Note that the LSQ question on exercise type does not specify any flexibility exercise in its list of possible answers. In terms of frequency, a higher percentage of astronauts reported more frequent exercise per week than comparison participants. Almost 29% of the astronauts reported exercising from five to seven days a week compared to 18% of comparison participants. Conversely, a higher percentage of comparison participants reported rarely exercising (occasionally to not at all) as compared to astronauts (31.8% to 11.2%, respectively). These data suggest that both astronauts and comparison participants may benefit from incorporating additional modes of exercise into their usual routine, as well as varying activities. A well-rounded fitness program has three main components: cardiovascular exercise (e.g., running, walking, swimming), strength training (e.g., weight training, plyometrics), and flexibility (e.g., yoga, Pilates).

title: Association Between Age and PSA Values in LSAH Participants
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Male participants in the LSAH have been offered prostate-specific antigen (PSA) screening since 1993. The
approach: Age-specific ranges have been suggested for improved sensitivity and specificity. The sensitivity of a screening test is the probability of correctly identifying a person as disease free. Prostate cancer generally progresses slowly and is more likely to make a major health impact when it occurs at a young age than when it occurs in old age. The sensitivity of the screening test is, therefore, among younger men and the specificity is more important to older men. To determine the association between age and PSA values, a study was conducted among 422 healthy men age 40 to 79 years in Olmsted County, Minnesota. These men were determined to be free of prostate cancer, based on detailed clinical examinations that included a digital rectal examination, PSA testing, and a transrectal ultrasound.
results: of these tests are used, on an individual basis, to assess the need for more extensive screening for prostate cancer. The LSAH now has enough group data to provide population information about the normal ranges of the test values and the variation in values associated with age. The normal range of values is generally considered to be 0 to 4 ng/mL (nanograms per milliliter of serum), with higher values prompting further investigation and testing. However, questions have been raised about the upper level of this standard because a significant number of older men in the general population, whose values exceed the range, may have received more extensive testing than necessary. APPROACH: Age-specific ranges have been suggested for improved sensitivity and specificity. The sensitivity of a screening test is the probability of correctly identifying a person as disease free. Prostate cancer generally progresses slowly and is more likely to make a major health impact when it occurs at a young age than when it occurs in old age. The sensitivity of the screening test is, therefore, among younger men and the specificity is more important to older men. To determine the association between age and PSA values, a study was conducted among 422 healthy men age 40 to 79 years in Olmsted County, Minnesota. These men were determined to be free of prostate cancer, based on detailed clinical examinations that included a digital rectal examination, PSA testing, and a transrectal ultrasound. RESULTS: The values of the PSA testing correlated directly with age. The distribution of the values was examined and the 95th percentile was identified for each age decade. The use of the 95th percentile value in the disease-free portion of a population would, conceptually, result in 95 percent of disease free men being correctly identified as disease free and 5 percent of disease free men at all ages would be subject to further testing. This study did not address the converse; that is, they did not examine diseased men to determine what percent of that population would have PSA values within the normal range and, therefore, might not be referred for further testing. The experiment identified the age-specific distribution of PSA values among the LSAH participants, both astronaut and comparison, and identified what percent of this population would not be routinely referred for further testing using the age-specific-range of values recommended by the Olmsted County study. For the purposes of this report, only PSA values were used. Therefore, the comparison is between a disease-free (Olmsted County study) population and the LSAH population without any prior assumption being made about the disease status of the LSAH population. The most recent test for each individual was included in these analyses. A total of 428 men (295 comparisons and 133 astronauts) have PSA results from their most recent physical examination.

title: Biomechanics of Movement During Locomotion
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: During space flight, adaptive processes recalibrate the central nervous system to permit new sensorimotor strategies to emerge in microgravity. However, the adaptive state achieved on orbit is inappropriate for a 1-G environment, which leads to postural and gait instabilities upon return to Earth. These instabilities have been reported by both U.S. astronauts and Russian cosmonauts even after short duration (5-10 days) space flights. Subjects experienced a turning sensation while attempting to walk a straight path, encountered sudden loss of postural stability especially when rounding corners, perceived exaggerated pitch and rolling head movements while walking, and experienced sudden loss of orientation in unstructured visual environments. In addition, oscillopsia and disorienting illusions of self-motion and surround-motion occurred during head movement induced by locomotion. The objectives of this study were to (1) determine whether eye-head-trunk coordination strategies, which occur during terrestrial locomotion, were modified following long-duration space flight and (2) ascertain whether these changes were associated with disturbances in gaze control, lower limb kinematics and muscle activity patterns of the leg during locomotion. This information will aid in the design and evaluation of sensorimotor countermeasures against the deleterious effects of long-duration space flight.
approach: During each test session, subjects were required to walk and run on a motorized treadmill while visually fixating on a centrally located Earth-fixed target (light-emitting diode, LED) positioned either 2 meters (FAR target) or 30 centimeters (NEAR target) from the subject, and at the height of subject perceived eye level. Both FAR and NEAR visual targets were placed on stands and viewed within the context of a full-field visual scene consisting of the laboratory surroundings. During fixation of the FAR target, a wall was visible approximately 0.5 meters behind the LED. For the NEAR target, the wall was 2.2 meters behind the LED. This task was designed to investigate postflight alterations in eye-head-trunk coordination of gaze stabilization during locomotion and determine whether these changes induced commensurate alterations in muscle activity patterns of the legs and lower limb kinematics. Three trials were performed by the subjects while walking/running on the treadmill. The trials, which lasted 20 seconds each, included slow walking (4 km/hr), fast walking (6.4 km/hr), and running (9.6 km/hr). All trials were repeated three times while fixating on a FAR target. Fast walking was also repeated three additional times while focusing on a NEAR target. These trials were scheduled for 120, 45 and 10 days preflight and 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 9 and 12 days postflight. Before beginning the test, the subject straddled the treadmill track while the treadmill speed was increased. When the treadmill track reached the required speed, the subject was free to begin walking. A few strides were permitted for the subject to become comfortable with the speed of the treadmill and to attain a steady gait. After a verbal "ready" indication from the subject, data collection began, and the subject continued to walk/run while visually fixating on the target. The subject was instructed to fixate on the target for the full duration of the trial. To prevent falling, each subject wore a torso harness that was attached to an overhead frame. During nominal treadmill performance, this harness provided no support and did not interfere with the natural movement of the head or limbs. To measure head and trunk movements, passive retro-reflective markers, which served as tracking guides, were affixed to the vertex, occipital, and right temporal positions of the head, on the seventh cervical vertebrae (C7) of the neck, and on the sacrum. Leg movements were measured by placing markers on the feet, ankles, knees and hips. The movements of these markers were simultaneously recorded with four video cameras that sampled concurrent video images at 60 Hz. The position of each marker was uniquely determined using a video-based motion analysis system. Subjects were outfitted with shorts, sleeveless shirts, athletic socks, and running shoes with electronic force sensors attached to the heels and toes so that times of heel strike and toe off could be determined. Marker trajectories were low-pass filtered at 10 Hz using a finite impulse response filter with a Hamming window. Movement of the head in the sagittal plane (pitch) was characterized by the angle between the horizontal and the line connecting the vertex and occipital markers. Vertical (z-axis) trunk translation was determined from the displacement of the marker placed on the C7 vertebrae. Surface electrodes were applied above and below the left eye, and behind the left ear to measure compensatory vertical eye movements using standard DC electro-oculographic (EOG) methods. To measure muscle activity patterns of the legs, preamplifier surface electromyogram (EMG) electrodes were placed on the subject's rectus femoris, biceps femoris, tibialis anterior and gastrocnemius in parallel to the muscle fibers. The electrodes were attached with hypoallergenic tape and then covered with elastic leg wraps to prevent movement on the skin. The analog EMG data were bandpassed at 30-300 Hz before being digitized at 752 Hz. Foot-switch information, also sampled at 752 Hz, was stored within the EMG data files. Compensatory pitch head movement waveforms were subjected to Fourier Analysis, and the amplitude of the predominant frequency was determined. Each 20-second trial was divided into 4 epochs of 4 seconds duration. The frequency spectra of each 4-second epoch was then calculated separately. Thus, for each subject in three walking sessions, twelve individual epochs were analyzed and the predominant peak determined, which allowed a mean peak amplitude to be determined for each subject.
results: In general, results were consistent throughout the Mir 18 and Mir 19 studies. Crewmembers showed significant alterations in head-trunk coordination following long-duration space flight. This change in head-trunk coordination disrupted gaze stabilization during locomotion and may have led to disorganization and descending control of locomotor function. Crewmembers also showed some disruption in lower limb muscle activation patterns during locomotion that exceeded the disruption seen in Shuttle crewmembers. In addition, microgravity induced alterations in head-trunk coordination during locomotion may play a central role in astronaut locomotor dysfunction which occurs following space flight. During preflight testing, pitch head movements acted in a compensatory fashion to oppose vertical trunk translation during locomotion: as the trunk translated upward, the head pitched forward/downward, thereby maintaining target fixation. Following space flight, Fourier Spectral Analysis indicated a significant increase in pitch head amplitude during locomotion. Test subjects B, D and E showed a significant reduction in the predominant frequency amplitude while fast walking (6.4 km/hr) that persisted through the postflight data collection period. However, subjects B and D demonstrated a recovery trend during the postflight testing period. Alternatively, subject A showed an increase in amplitude across all walking/target conditions. Subject C exhibited no discernible pre/post change; however, it should be noted that his first postflight data session occurred five days after landing, possibly after most of the recovery had occurred. Mir crewmembers exhibited a higher incidence and a longer lasting modification in head movement control after long-duration flight than did crewmembers of relatively shorter duration Shuttle flights. Pearson correlation coefficients, used to compare preflight and postflight muscle activation patterns, were generally very high. Similarly high correlations were observed for the left lower limb musculature. These high correlations indicated that by the time postflight testing was conducted, the sensorimotor system was able to generate the lower limb neuromusculature activation waveforms, which permitted effective treadmill locomotion. Moreover, the subjects were able to maintain the preflight levels of activation symmetry between the right and left lower limb musculature, which was required to continue movement on the treadmill. Despite great similarity in the phasic features of the muscle activation wave forms, analysis of the relative activation amplitudes indicated definite changes in motor control characteristics. Investigators have focused their analysis of relative activation amplitude around the behavioral events of heel strike and toe off because these events involve large transfers of energy, which if not controlled properly could result in the loss of locomotor stability. Although patterns of change were not consistent across subjects A, B and C, all displayed changes in the relative amplitude relationships among the lower limb musculature. Two Mir 18 subjects displayed greater postflight increases in the relative amplitude of the biceps femoris (BF) around heel strike relative to changes observed in the rectus femoris (RF). This pattern of postflight change indicated that the knee extensor/hip flexor musculature must generate more musculature tension relative to the RF compared to preflight patterns. Another example was the increase in relative activation of the gastrocnemius (GA) and tibialis anterior (TA) around toe-off. This increase in both antagonists suggested a generalized relative increase in ankle joint stiffness. Given that effective toe-off involves rapid changes from a large plantar flexor moment (GA activation and TA inhibition) to a large dorsiflexor moment (TA activation and GA inhibition), a generalized increase in ankle stiffness was not an optimal control strategy. Subjects D and E showed the greatest postflight changes in the activity pattern of the RF while fast walking. The findings observed in the Mir 18 and Mir 19 subjects are consistent with those found after short-duration Shuttle missions. In general, the consistent findings of alterations in the relative amplitude relationships across the lower limb musculature indicate the precise neuromusculature control necessary for maximally efficient locomotion was disrupted after long-duration space flight. Analysis of lower limb kinematics during locomotion indicated altered coordination patterns during the load acceptance phase of the gait cycle. The implication of this finding was that the normal energy modulation occurring during heel strike may be altered leading to increased energy transmission to the head causing postflight visual-vestibular disturbances. Concerns regarding postflight walking and head control include management of the shock wave created at the moment of foot contact, and the transmission of this shock wave to the head. Evidence suggests that inappropriate shock wave transmission to the head while walking could interfere with head and gaze control, resulting in a compromise of dynamic visual acuity and possibly a disruption in descending vestibular control of locomotion. To address this issue in crewmember performance, analyses were focused on the lower limb joint kinematic data on the load acceptance phase of each stride as defined by the time period calculated from right heel strike to the following maximum of knee angle flexion. For this functionally defined time period, the total joint angular displacement for the ankle, knee and hip joints were calculated, as well as the average joint angular velocity for the knee and hip joints.

title: Risk of Cancer Mortality Among LSAH Participants
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: A significant health concern associated with space travel is the potential exposure to radiation. NASA has addressed this concern with medical projects that monitor exposures and maintain lifelong exposure records. Early detection of precancerous conditions is a primary effort of the occupational physical examinations provided to astronauts and to the LSAH comparison population. A task of LSAH is to monitor the incidence of medical events and to provide data to NASA Medical Operations management to aid program decision-making.
approach: Recently, reviews have been implemented on cancer mortality rates and the news is promising for the LSAH population as a whole. The cancer mortality rates among LSAH participants have been compared with the cancer mortality rates for the general population of the Texas Gulf Coast area residing in Public Health Region 6. Public Region 6 includes Harris County and the surrounding counties of Austin, Colorado, Montgomery, Wharton, Brazoria, Fort Bend, Liberty, Walker, Chambers, Galveston, Matagorda, and Waller. The age-specific average annual cancer mortality rates for the years of 1987 through 1993 were obtained for this area from the Texas Cancer Data Center. The rate of the astronauts has also been compared with the rate of the LSAH comparison participants. All cancer deaths among the LSAH population have been among males; therefore only males were included in these analyses. This is a conservative analysis approach since the denominator used in the rate calculation is based on the total population being examined. Given a consistent numerator (the number of cancer cases) the smaller denominator obtained by including only males
results: in a higher rate. All males selected as astronauts between 1959 and 1995 (210) and male comparisons for the same time period selected from the JSC employee population (618), as participants in LSAH were included in this cancer mortality investigation. Person years of follow-up time for each of the two study groups were calculated for the same age-specific groupings identified in the reference population of Public Health Region 6. The expected rates of cancer mortality are obtained by applying the age-specific rates of the reference population to the study population. The results are those rates that would be expected if the study population had experienced the same cancer mortality as the reference population. The observed rates of cancer mortality in each of the two LSAH study groups were compared with the expected rates. The ratio of the observed rate to the expected rate is known as the Standardized Mortality Ratio (SMR). An SMR of 100 indicates that identical rates exist for two groups. Confidence intervals (CI) around the SMRs (CI, 95%) were calculated. RESULTS: Both the astronauts and the comparison group currently have lower age-specific rates of total cancer mortality than that seen in the general population residing in the Texas Gulf Coast area. The rate among the astronauts is somewhat higher than the comparison participants but not significantly higher. The difference may be from chance alone. There have been three cancer deaths among the astronaut population. The SMR of 47 indicates that the observed cancer deaths among the astronaut population are 53 percent less than the 6.25 expected deaths. The confidence intervals indicate that, even though the observed rate of cancer mortality is noticeably lower than expected, it is not statistically different from the general population. There have also been three cancer mortalities among the LSAH comparison population versus an expected 17.3 cases. The resulting SMR of 17 (CI = 3.5, 37.9) is significantly lower than expected. The particular types of cancers experienced among the LSAH population are relatively rare among the general population. Conversely, the more common cancers among the general population (lung, colorectal, prostate) have not been identified as causes of mortality among the LSAH population. Comparisons made between astronaut health data and general population health data should be viewed with some skepticism because of the differences between the astronauts and the general public. Risk factors associated with many cancers are also associated with life-styles and education. The astronauts are highly educated and receive routine preventive medical care. They are, in general, physically fit and nonsmokers. Because of the difficulties associated with making comparisons between the astronauts and the general population, the comparison population was selected from the JSC employees. Age, sex, and body mass index were used as matching criteria, and all JSC employees have access to preventive medical care through the Occupational Medicine Clinic. A comparison of cancer rates between these two groups is much more statistically sound than comparisons made with the general public. If the astronauts experienced the same age-specific rates of cancer as the comparison participants, 0.87 deaths would have been expected compared with the three observed deaths. This results in an SMR of 345 (CI = 69.5 to 756.2). The rate of total cancer mortality among the astronauts is elevated when compared with the LSAH comparison participants, but not significantly different.

title: Serum CPK Reported in LSAH Participants
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Creatinine phosphokinase (CPK) is an enzyme found in skeletal muscle, cardiac muscle, and the brain. All of these areas have elevated serum levels of CPK when stressed, therefore, monitoring the serum level of CPK is important because elevated levels may indicate a serious health disorder, such as heart attack, stroke, or brain tumor. However, other factors such as age, sex, and exercise also affect CPK levels. In fact, elevated CPK is common in adults who exercise regularly. Normal levels of serum CPK vary from 0 to approximately 188 micrograms per liter. Different laboratories may report slightly different upper limits as within the normal range because of differences in test procedures and population differences. During exercise, especially of the highintensity burst type, considerable amounts of CPK leak into the extracellular fluid and plasma as a
approach: Serum CPK is used as an indicator of muscle integrity with the level of specific isoenzymes aiding in the diagnoses regarding which type of muscle (cardiac, skeletal, or brain) has been stressed. There are two isoenzymes, i.e., chemically different but functionally identical forms of CPK. The isoenzyme produced in the brain is identified as CPK B and the isoenzyme produced in muscle is identified as CPK M. As a rule of thumb, cardiac muscle stress produces CPK MB, and skeletal muscle stress produces CPK MM. CPK BB is an indicator of stress of brain tissue and is not usually examined in routine physical examinations unless there is a suspicion of stroke, tumor, etc. There are divergent opinions about the proportion of CPK MB in skeletal muscle as well as about the proportion of total CPK in association with acute myocardial infarction. Studies have shown large elevations in CPK MB in some women after step exercise and in highly trained female endurance runners. In the absence of symptoms and other positive physical examination information, elevated CPK MB is not usually considered sufficient evidence of a heart attack. Identification of these isoenzymes requires laboratory testing procedures not routinely completed for LSAH.
results: of changes in membrane activity. The type of exercise and the duration affect the elevation of serum CPK. Non-weight-bearing activities such as rowing and swimming cause less pronounced CPK elevations than comparable weightbearing events. CPK elevations have been found to be linear with the duration of exercise up to 5.5 hours. Longer durations of exercise are associated with an accelerated increase in CPK. Exercise-induced increases in the level of serum CPK are temporary. Resting levels of CPK changes generally become elevated during exercise days and then return to normal levels during rest days. Peaks in serum CPK have been reported to occur at 5 minutes, 11 hours, 24 hours, 25 hours, and even 4-6 days following exercise. With continued physical activity, CPK levels remained elevated. Resting levels of serum CPK are higher in exercised trained individuals than in untrained ones. CPK elevations vary with age and sex. Older individuals are less likely to have elevations after exercise than are middle-aged or young adults. Women are more likely to have exercise induced elevations than are men. Some researchers suggest that muscle cell permeability increases during exercise and others think that muscle degeneration and necrosis occurs. Muscular soreness has been reported to accompany elevated CPK levels. While increases in serum CPK are common in adults who exercise, there are also pathological states, such as myocardial infarction or heart attack, which may be accompanied by an increase in serum levels of CPK. APPROACH: Serum CPK is used as an indicator of muscle integrity with the level of specific isoenzymes aiding in the diagnoses regarding which type of muscle (cardiac, skeletal, or brain) has been stressed. There are two isoenzymes, i.e., chemically different but functionally identical forms of CPK. The isoenzyme produced in the brain is identified as CPK B and the isoenzyme produced in muscle is identified as CPK M. As a rule of thumb, cardiac muscle stress produces CPK MB, and skeletal muscle stress produces CPK MM. CPK BB is an indicator of stress of brain tissue and is not usually examined in routine physical examinations unless there is a suspicion of stroke, tumor, etc. There are divergent opinions about the proportion of CPK MB in skeletal muscle as well as about the proportion of total CPK in association with acute myocardial infarction. Studies have shown large elevations in CPK MB in some women after step exercise and in highly trained female endurance runners. In the absence of symptoms and other positive physical examination information, elevated CPK MB is not usually considered sufficient evidence of a heart attack. Identification of these isoenzymes requires laboratory testing procedures not routinely completed for LSAH. RESULTS: Approximately 16 percent of the 211 CPK tests completed for the LSAH participants during 1992-94 reported elevated serum levels. During this time period, about half of that 16 percent of laboratory tests were also examined for the isoenzymes. The isoenzymes identified in these tests have consistently been CPK MM. These data suggest that study participants are exercising prior to physical examinations. Questions regarding type and frequency of exercise routinely asked during the examination aid the physician in assessing the relationship between elevated CPK values and recent exercise.

title: Reported Levels of Physical Activity by LSAH Participants
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Physical activity has long been regarded as a key component of a healthy lifestyle. Medical benefits of physical activity include increased mental health and health-related quality of life as well as a decreased risk of cardiovascular diseases, cancer of the colon, diabetes, musculoskeletal related conditions, and obesity. Physical inactivity is second only to tobacco use in causing the most preventable deaths in the United States with at least 300,000 annual attributable deaths. Contrary to the mounting evidence of the positive effects of physical activity, over 60% of U.S. adults do not attain the recommended level of physical activity, while 25% are not active at all. Inactivity is more prevalent among women, minorities, older adults, and the less affluent.
approach: The first national effort to encourage physical activity in young Americans took place in the 1950's. This movement was the first of its kind in the world. In the 1970's, another health education effort enlightened Americans on the cardiovascular benefits of vigorous activity. In the 1980's and 1990's, new information on the benefits of moderate intensity activities was brought forward. Traditional beliefs toward exercise and fitness may have led most Americans to believe that an effective exercise program must be rigorous and strenuous; however, scientific studies have dispelled this belief. This idea has now been expanded even further. In a 1994 report issued by the Surgeon General, a public health recommendation was made for a moderate-intensity physical activity schedule to be carried out on most, if not all, days of the week. It is hoped that this revised public health recommendation will start a new movement that will save lives and allow the maintenance of a high quality of life. The term physical activity is used loosely when compared to the terms exercise and physical fitness. It refers to a lifestyle of casual activities that
results: in the expenditure of energy. The term moderate refers to an intensity of activities that utilizes 3 to 6 metabolic equivalents (METs). One MET is defined as the amount of oxygen utilized while the body is at rest, which is 3.5 ml/kg of body weight/minute. Intermittent activities performed throughout the day are also beneficial to one's health. Individuals who are currently physically active will reap additional benefits by increasing the duration or intensity of their current activities. To assess the activity level within the LSAH population, information from the LSAH Health Lifestyle Questionnaire (LSQ) was compiled and compared with data from the 1990 National Health Interview Survey (NHIS). Information from the NHIS was gathered from 22,760 noninstitutionalized U.S. civilians at least 18 years of age. NHIS participants were divided into four basic categories based on the intensity, frequency, and duration of physical activity: Sedentary, Irregular, Moderate, and Vigorous. Sedentary indicates no leisure activity, Irregular indicates leisure activity that does not meet the current public health recommendation. Moderate refers to activities with an intensity of 3 to 6 METs performed a minimum of 30 minutes at least five days per week. Vigorous refers to activities with an intensity of greater than 6 METs performed a minimum of 20 minutes at least 3 days per week. The LSQ was developed in 1993 to collect essential data on NASA astronauts and LSAH comparisons. Two hundred twenty out of 272 astronauts and 780 out of 889 comparisons have completed this questionnaire. The physical activities of LSAH participants were categorized according to the NHIS definitions; however, their data were gathered using different time intervals, so both Moderate and Vigorous categories refer to activities performed a minimum of 20 minutes. Walking was categorized as a Moderate activity. Since the number of METs of an activity refers to the intensity with which it is performed, the assumption is made that the remaining activities listed on the LSQ were performed in a vigorous, energetic manner. These activities are running, swimming, bicycling, weight lifting, skating, aerobics/ dancing, racquet sports, rowing, and other organized sports. RESULTS: About one third of the NHIS participants reported a level of physical activity that meets the current public health recommendation. This is compared with nearly half of the comparisons and two-thirds of the astronauts. The higher degree of physical activity of LSAH comparisons, as compared to the NHIS population, may be a manifestation of the healthy worker effect. The latter simply describes the phenomenon in which an employed population exhibits healthier characteristics than the general population. This effect is even more pronounced in the astronaut corps because it is in their interest to remain physically active in order to perform their duties effectively. A higher percentage of male NHIS respondents reported participation in the recommended level of physical activity as compared to female respondents; this trend is also observed to a lesser extent in the LSAH comparisons. However, female astronauts reported a greater percentage of participation in physical activity than male astronauts. This increase may be due to the younger average age of female astronauts as compared with the older average age of male astronauts. The results may also be affected by the smaller number of female astronauts. When the results are broken down by age, older NHIS respondents reported less physical activity than younger respondents, while LSAH comparisons reported about the same level of physical activity across the age groups. The decrease in physical activity with age was also seen in the astronauts, though in the 25-44 years age group this cohort reported more than double the participation in physical activity as compared to the corresponding age group of NHIS respondents. The higher relative participation of astronauts in moderate and vigorous physical activity was further displayed as more than half of the astronauts in the oldest age group reported participating in such activity. However, one must keep in mind that the number of astronauts in the oldest age group is much smaller than that of the NHIS respondents.

title: Achilles Tendon Reflex
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Muscle motor control studies have investigated changes in the Achilles tendon reflex as affected by exposure to microgravity. Scientists have noted that the length and tension properties of muscle, as well as its structure, seem to play important roles in the changes in motor control induced by microgravity. Generalized hyperreflexia of the Achilles tendon was reported following the long-duration Skylab missions. It was hypothesized that short-duration missions would produce same
approach: Measurement of Achilles tendon reflex time was performed during the physical examination on all three prime astronauts at F-30 (30 days prior to launch), F-15, and on recovery day (R+0) using a Burdick FM-1 photomotograph. A technique using a photoelectric cell was employed to time the Achilles tendon reflex by measuring the displacement of the foot. The subject was instructed to kneel on a specially designed chair and the unit was positioned so that the light beam was partially intercepted by the metatarsal region of the foot. The observer then tapped the Achilles tendon with a percussion hammer and thereby caused the foot to move in the light beam and generate a change in photocell voltage. The change in voltage was recorded to give a time-position plot of the reflex action. To determine the duration of the reflex response in milliseconds, measurements were made from the beginning of the hammer tap to the middle of the relaxation period.
results: . The objective of this investigation was to test for changes in the neuromuscular function of the Achilles tendon reflex after the short-duration Apollo-Soyuz Test Project mission. APPROACH: Measurement of Achilles tendon reflex time was performed during the physical examination on all three prime astronauts at F-30 (30 days prior to launch), F-15, and on recovery day (R+0) using a Burdick FM-1 photomotograph. A technique using a photoelectric cell was employed to time the Achilles tendon reflex by measuring the displacement of the foot. The subject was instructed to kneel on a specially designed chair and the unit was positioned so that the light beam was partially intercepted by the metatarsal region of the foot. The observer then tapped the Achilles tendon with a percussion hammer and thereby caused the foot to move in the light beam and generate a change in photocell voltage. The change in voltage was recorded to give a time-position plot of the reflex action. To determine the duration of the reflex response in milliseconds, measurements were made from the beginning of the hammer tap to the middle of the relaxation period. RESULTS: Four preflight baseline sets of data were obtained on the command module pilot (CMP) because he had previous tests conducted while serving as a backup crewmember for Skylab missions three and 4. However, the commander (CDR) and the docking module pilot (DMP) only performed the test on F-30, F-15, and R+0. The reflex was measured within 2 hours after recovery on R+0. The CDR and the DMP exhibited a shorter reflex duration time, whereas the CMP showed a longer reflex time when the data was compared with the preflight results. In addition to the noted changes in reflex time, all three crewmembers showed significant fine tremors, which could reflect the effects of the nitrogen tetroxide vapor, which was accidentally inhaled. In general, the data showed the predicted postflight change in the Achilles tendon reflex time.

title: Correlation of Disconjugate Eye Torsion with the Time Course of the Space Adaptation Syndrome
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Space motion sickness (SMS) during space flight is very similar to motion sickness on Earth. SMS can be predicted during parabolic flights on Earth by observing characteristic eye movements. By identifying these same characteristic eye movements, particularly rotary eye movements during the course of space flight, researchers hope to obtain information on SMS, which will have a direct impact on Earth-based motion sickness. This study documented the correlation of eye torsional changes with the development and recovery over time of SMS.
approach: Three astronauts underwent preflight, inflight, and postflight testing of spontaneous ocular torsion and ocular counterrolling (OCR) reflexes governed by the gravity-responsive otolith organs in the inner ear. Subject A flew a 30-day space mission during Euromir '94 and was examined with a monocular video-oculography (VOG) system. Subjects B and C were studied with a binocular VOG during the 180-day Euromir '95 mission. VOG is a technique used to examine the function of the human balance system located in the inner ear (vestibular system) and the visuo-oculomotor interactions of the vestibular organ. The subjects’ eye movements were measured, recorded, and evaluated by state-of-the-art video techniques. Preflight and postflight measurements were performed with the subject in a head-upright position. Inflight measurements required only that the subject remain stationary. To record images from both eyes simultaneously during Euromir ‘95, the monocular VOG used during Euromir '94 was augmented by one additional camera and recorder unit. The binocular system videotaped both eyes simultaneously providing 25 synchronized images of each per second. The torsional eye position was derived from surface landmarks of the iris. First, a circular ring segment or arc was selected and defined by its radius from the center of the pupil, the thickness of the ring segment, and the angle swept by the arc. A geometric assumption was made that the visible borders of the pupil were part of a circle or an ellipse. For each line of the video image that passed through the pupil, the threshold for entering and leaving the pupil was determined. If a line passing through the pupil was interrupted by reflections or other artifacts, that line was rejected. The accepted lines were calculated to form a circle. In this manner, reliable pupil center could be determined even though up to 50% of the pupil was not visible. A reference iris profile was calculated and stored in computer memory. Using this reference, subsequent iris profiles could be compared to determine any changes in ocular torsion, e.g. the reference iris profile obtained preflight was compared with other profiles obtained preflight, during flight, and postflight. In the preflight and postflight experiments, the astronauts were strapped into a special chair. An individual bitebar was made and fitted to a mask-headband assembly containing two small video cameras, one in front of each eye. The bitebar was also rigidly attached to the chair. The astronaut’s eyes were adjusted to Earth-horizontal. Once the bitebar-to-mask and bitebar-to-chair attachments were satisfactory, the joints were tightened and sealed in position. The bitebar could fit only one way to the mask and chair. This meant the relation of the mask and its cameras in front of the eyes could be precisely replicated for all other preflight and postflight experiments. In the earth-based studies, subjects were seated in the special chair, the bitebar-mask-head apparatus donned, and the eye position verified to be Earth-horizontal. The subjects maintained their eyes in the primary position by gazing at a target one meter away. The heights of the cameras were adjusted so that the iris images were equidistant from the lower edge of the video monitor. In each of these Earth-based experiments, the eye positions were recorded for two minutes as the subject sat quietly upright. Following the upright position, eye positions were recorded for two minutes with the subject tilted and maintained at a 30º right-ear-down tilt and two minutes with the subject in a 30º left-ear-down tilt. For space-flight experiments, an identical individual bitebar-to-camera apparatus was made for each subject and taken to the Mir Space Station. These masks maintained the same head-to-eye-to-camera relation as the ground experiments. The astronauts were adept at donning the apparatus and making sure the iris images were equidistant from the bottom of the video monitor. A two-minute videotape was made with the head “upright” in six to eight experiments during the six-month space flight. As required, all three subjects had vestibular “deconditioning” training for several weeks before space flight and again toward the end of flight. This consisted of vigorous head rotation in the pitch and yaw modes. During each experimental session in flight, each subject marked a detailed questionnaire of SMS symptoms as being absent, mild, moderate, or severe.
results: Five to six preflight baseline data collections (BDCs) were obtained for each subject. In the upright position while seated quietly, spontaneous torsional eye movements were approximately ±0.75º, consistent with earlier studies of normal subjects. The eyes were mostly conjugate. When held for two minutes in a static tipped position, mean ocular counterrolling (OCR) in the three subjects was –5.94º and +5.54º in response to the 30º right and left tilts, respectively. All inflight and postflight analyses were based on a preflight external reference image enabling comparison of eye positions relative to the preflight baseline. In all three subjects, the torsional position of each eye was substantially changed from its preflight setting. A torsional reset was manifested during the entire inflight and postflight testing period, although each eye position might vary considerably throughout the study. The SMS evaluation forms on two subjects indicated no SMS symptoms during space flight. One had moderate nausea in the Soyuz transport vehicle on the way to Mir and on flight day 4. This subject was symptom-free at all other times. Upon return to Earth, two subjects were grossly ataxic immediately after landing. Seven hours after landing, both subjects could walk slowly with support. Turning caused them to lurch to one side. Both were pale and weak with marked atrophy of the legs. Both were nauseated and had headaches. One subject became nauseated by repeated head rotation, while the other felt too ill to be tested at all. The day after landing (R+1), both could slowly walk independently with no further nausea, even with head rotation maneuvers. After several more days, their overall behavior seemed normal. The leg atrophy was improved by R+10. Postflight testing repeated the preflight protocol with two minutes in each upright position, 30º right and 30º left. In all three subjects, OCR amplitude differed from that observed preflight. Subject B showed increased OCR to both sides of tilt, especially to 30º left, even considering the torsional reset of the eyes in the upright position. Subject C also showed increased OCR to the left and approximately the same OCR to the right as preflight. Subject A had decreased OCR on the day of landing, increasing daily until postflight day 10 (R+10), at which time it exceeded the baseline OCR in both directions of tilt. At day 150, however, this subject’s torsional eye position had returned to its preflight baseline. No tests were performed between day 10 and 150, and therefore the time course of recovery cannot be ascertained. By R+10, subject B’s right eye had approached its preflight baseline; however, with the head in the upright position, the left eye remained about 2.5º torted counterclockwise. Subject C had likewise not returned to his baseline settings by R+10. As two of the three subjects did not have SMS and the third had none or marginal SMS, none of the changes in ocular torsion found during this study can be related to SMS. However, analysis of parabolic flight disconjugacy in two of the present subjects correctly predicted absence of SMS.

title: Influence of Center of Gravity on Human Performance in Partial Gravity
experiment_type: NASA Extreme Environment Mission Operations (NEEMO) Project
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: The Apollo program demonstrated that suit center of gravity (CG) is an important variable affecting human performance in Lunar Extravehicular Activities (EVAs). This study assessed crew performance of representative planetary exploration tasks with a single EVA suit weight with six different CG locations.
approach: A reconfigurable back pack with repositionable weight modules was used to simulate Perfect, Low, Forward, High, Aft and NASA Baseline CG locations. All CG locations were based on the assumption of a 60 pound suit, a 135 pound Portable Life Support System (PLSS), and a standardized 6 foot 180 pound subject. These tests were conducted in NASA´s Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory and during underwater missions in the NOAA Aquarius Habitat. Subjects were weighed out for lunar gravity. Twenty-one subjects performed a task-battery that included ambulation, kneel and recovery, fall and recovery, rock pick-up, rock transfer, inclined ambulation from 10-30 degrees, shoveling, and ladder climb. Subject performance was assessed using a modified Cooper- Harper scale to assess operator compensation required to achieve desired performance.
results: Results suggest that CG location affects human performance. Subjects preferred Perfect, Low and Forward CG over High, Aft or Baseline (both High and Aft), which suggests that a conventional back pack PLSS may not be optimal and that alternative configurations should be considered.

title: Hearing Loss Among LSAH Participants
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Noise is one of the most common causes of hearing loss, and noise-induced hearing loss (NIHL) is the most common occupational illness in the United States. The effects of noise on hearing are often underestimated because the damage takes place so gradually, without pain, and cannot be visibly detected because the delicate inner ear is buried deep in the skull. Audiometric testing, using pure tone stimuli, has been the traditional method of monitoring hearing loss. Hearing tests have always been part of NASA’s hearing conservation program for personnel exposed to hazardous noise from aircraft and other equipment. Audiometric data from the Longitudinal Study of Astronaut Health (LSAH) database was reviewed in order to assess trends and compare data with other population studies.
approach: Audiometric data of LSAH astronaut participants, a group of comparison participants, and Air Force subjects (during 1975-1976) were reviewed. The mean of the audiometric hearing thresholds at 3000, 4000, and 6000 Hz were compared for the LSAH participants and other populations.
results: Formal hearing conservation efforts (e.g., training in hearing protection and effects of noise, enforcement of hearing protection use) have been aimed at all astronauts, but only those comparison participants who worked in noise-hazardous jobs at the NASA Johnson Space Center (JSC). Consequently, it would be logical to assume that the astronauts, as the target population of the conservation efforts, were more at risk for and would show more NIHL as compared to the comparison participants. However, the analysis of the data yielded surprising results. A hearing threshold is the lowest sound level that is detected from a specific percentage of presentations during a hearing test, so a higher value indicates less acute hearing. While hearing loss data in the comparison participants closely matched the average high frequency hearing loss for similar age groups reported for the general population (International Organization for Standardization, 1999), astronauts showed less hearing loss (in the 50 and 60 year-old age groups) than the comparison participants. When compared to a study of Air Force personnel for the years 1975-1976, astronauts also had better hearing sensitivity, suggesting that close vigilance and high motivation in NASA hearing conservation programs among astronauts may have yielded more effective hearing loss prevention. In the 70 and 80 year-old age groups, astronauts had more hearing loss than the comparison participants. One possible explanation is that hearing conservation programs did not exist or were very primitive prior to 1970. As a result, the current hearing losses among these individuals may have been accelerated by early NIHL, when hearing conservation efforts, now more rigidly enforced, were not effective. Whatever the basis for the audiometric results, it is clear that hearing loss prevention is vital to protecting remaining hearing function.

title: Intraocular Pressure in the LSAH Population
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Glaucoma is one of the leading causes of blindness in the United States. A common threat to good vision in midlife, it affects two out of every 100 people over the age of 40. Glaucoma is a degenerative disease of the optic nerve. In glaucoma, some of the nerve fibers become damaged and fail to transmit signals to the brain. As a
approach: Intraocular pressure is measured with a tonometer. Although several slightly different types of tonometers are used, the basic principle is the same. This test uses air pressure (in mmHg) against the outside of the eyeball to measure the resistant pressure inside the eyeball. This painless and non-invasive test is performed on both astronauts and comparison participants as part of the routine physical examination. Normal intraocular pressure is typically between 10 and 20 mmHg. If elevated intraocular pressure is detected, an in-depth evaluation of the eye is warranted before a diagnosis of glaucoma can be made.
results: , there may be blind spots, which usually occur at the outer edges of the field of vision. This gradual loss of peripheral vision often goes unnoticed until significant optic nerve damage has occurred. If not treated, glaucoma may affect an increasing number of nerve fibers, causing continued shrinking of the visual field. The cause of the nerve damage in glaucoma is not known precisely. In most patients, it is associated with increased fluid pressure inside the eye known as intraocular pressure. The eye constantly produces and drains fluids. If the drainage mechanism in the eye is blocked or restricted, the buildup of fluid will result in an increase in intraocular pressure. It is important, however, to understand that high intraocular pressure (i.e. ocular hypertension) does not necessarily result in glaucoma. There are individual tolerances for eye pressure and it can be higher than average in some individuals without resulting in optic nerve damage or subsequent loss of vision. Most individuals with ocular hypertension go for years without developing nerve damage and may never have damage to the optic nerve. However, people with ocular hypertension have a higher risk of developing optic nerve damage. The goal of this study was to compare intraocular pressures between astronauts and comparison subjects. APPROACH: Intraocular pressure is measured with a tonometer. Although several slightly different types of tonometers are used, the basic principle is the same. This test uses air pressure (in mmHg) against the outside of the eyeball to measure the resistant pressure inside the eyeball. RESULTS: There is no significant difference in the distribution of intraocular pressures between the astronauts and the comparison population. Mean values of the right eye intraocular pressure were 13.5 mmHg for the astronauts and 13.2 mmHg for the comparisons. Left eye values were 13.7 mmHg for the astronauts and 13.5 for the comparisons.

title: A Speech-Based Artificial Intelligence System for Predicting Team Functioning Degradation in HERA Missions
archive_status: Data preservation is complete.  Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request.  Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: NASA’s priority on the Artemis missions as a preliminary phase for Mars exploration, it is expected that long-distance space exploration will propose various challenges due to the prolonged constraint of small teams living and working together in an intense environment and the absence of real-time communication with Earth, broadening the risk of inadequate team cooperation and coordination. This proposed study aims tested the hypothesis, that a minimal set of speech-based measures, potentially different depending on the structured or unstructured nature of the focal tasks, will be indicative of team functioning degradation, and that the various parts of the mission will contribute differently to this outcome, by building a speech-based artificial intelligence system that unobtrusively predicts degradation in team functioning, including performance and cohesion, during HERA Campaign 4 (C4) and Campaign 5 (C5). The AI system conducted automated analysis of prosodic and linguistic of speech, modeled their interaction among team members, and extracted influence and turn-taking statistics among speakers, without requiring additional human coding, thus
approach: The PI team investigated the broad picture of team functioning throughout the whole duration of focal parts of the mission via observing structured and unstructured team interactions. Audio data were pre-processed via removing stationary and short burst noise, followed by voice activity detection and speaker identification. Speaker excerpts were transcribed via automatic speech recognition (ASR), where speaker adaptation was applied to improve ASR performance. The following acoustic and linguistic features were extracted: degree of speech periodicity (e.g., fundamental frequency-F0, jitter, shimmer); shape of the speech spectrum (e.g., cepstrum, Mel-frequency spectral coefficients); patterns of vocal intensity (e.g., loudness); grammatic features (e.g., I/you/we pronouns); and lexicon-based features capturing cognitive, affective, and social processes. Interaction measures included the degree of similarity in acoustic and linguistic features among interlocutors; the degree of connectivity of a graph, team member nodes and edges; and turn-taking measures modeling the conversation progress (e.g., alternating turns, pauses, speech overlap). Interpretable machine learning (ML) models were trained based on the interaction measures to predict self- reported team performance and coherence. Ablation studies were conducted to identify the subset of features, potentially different depending on the structured or unstructured nature of the focal tasks, and parts of the mission that are most predictive of team functioning, degradation, and feasible prediction horizon windows. Investigators used previously collected self-reports, audio, and team task performances from structured and unstructured tasks from the HERA Campaigns 4 and 5. Acoustic and linguistic measurements were used for the outputs of team functioning variables when training ML models. To better understand data and feasible system configurations, various trainings and testing occurred. Team-independent evaluation was conducted via a leave-one-team-out cross-validation, where data from 8 teams was used for training and data from the remaining team were used for testing. Team-dependent evaluation was conducted such that a subset of data from a target team was included in the training set and the remaining were in the test set. To increase the model’s robustness and generalizability investigators included data from other teams. Longitudinal data was used for multiple horizons prediction (1-5 days in advance). Once investigators aggregate the data at the day level, employ were implemented for multi-level models for hypothesis testing.
results: ing in an automated method that relies on unobtrusive passive monitoring for predicting team outcomes. The proposed research had three specific aims: 1.
