title: Smoking Prevalence of LSAH Participants
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Smoking is the leading cause of preventable mortality in the United States. Since the release of the first Surgeon General's Report on Smoking and Health in 1964, about 10 million people in the United States have died from smoking related illnesses such as heart disease, lung cancer, or emphysema. Another estimated 25 million Americans will die prematurely from a smoking-related disease if current smoking trends continue. Over the years, as the connection between cigarette smoking and serious diseases has become indisputably clear, there has been an overall decline in the smoking rate within the general population. This change can be traced back to the first Surgeon General's Report in 1964, which officially reported cigarette smoking as the cause of cancer and other serious diseases. Subsequent acts to reduce the health hazard of smoking on society include the 1965 Federal Cigarette Labeling and Advertising Act requiring warning labels on cigarette packaging, and the prohibition of cigarette advertising on television and radio in 1969. Consequently, the smoking prevalence of adults (18 years and older) in the U.S. has declined over the years from 42.4% in 1965 to 24.1% in 1998. However, this rate seems to have reached a plateau in the 1990's, where it has hovered around the mid-20's percentage mark.
approach: Some data on the smoking prevalence of LSAH participants have been obtained through the Lifestyle Questionnaire. This survey was developed in 1995 and sent to all astronauts and comparison participants enrolled in the study; the questionnaire has also been sent to subsequent classes upon their selection into the study. The data gathered from 1995 to 1999 include smoking data on 217 astronauts and 776 comparison participants (from a total of 271 astronauts and 915 comparisons at that time). The survey asks whether the respondent has ever smoked, and whether the respondent is currently smoking.
results: Of the astronauts who responded, 16.1% of them ever smoked, and 1.4% were still smoking, while the values for the comparison participants are 20.1% and 6.4%, respectively. For comparison purposes, smoking data among the U.S. general population were obtained from the National Health Interview Surveys (NHIS). The smoking prevalence among U.S. adults 25 years and older from 1995 to 1999 ranged between 24.5% and 23.4%. These numbers show that compared to the general population not only did a lower percentage of astronauts start smoking, but also that a much lower percentage of them continued to smoke. This behavior is expected because of their higher health awareness as compared to that of the general population. More surprising are the low prevalences of ever smoked and currently smoking comparison participants. The smoking trend of LSAH participants can be estimated by breaking down the prevalence of participants who ever smoked into their selection year cohorts. This serves as an approximation of the LSAH participants' general attitude towards smoking within that time, and is compared against the smoking prevalence in the adult general population of the same period. The astronauts parallel the smoking trend of the general population, while comparison participants show a steeper decline compared to the other groups. Note that the measure of goodness of fit (R2) for the astronauts' and comparison participants' trendlines are 0.63 and 0.74, respectively. The trendline for the general population has an R2 of 0.97, very close to the maximum value of 1. A maximum goodness of fit is achieved when the line is a precise representation of the data points and their trend over time. The values obtained for the LSAH participants indicate that their trendlines are not as precise a representation of smoking prevalence over time as that of the general population. This is probably a function of the small sample sizes of the LSAH cohorts, which subjects the resulting prevalence to high variability. In general the smoking prevalence of LSAH participants is much lower than that of the adult general population within the same time period. The lower smoking prevalence for astronauts as compared to the general population is expected, as by definition astronauts must be highly aware of activities affecting their health and fitness. However, the difference in smoking prevalence between the general population and the comparison participants is much greater than anticipated. When the data for LSAH participants ever smoked are broken down into cohorts, the results suggest that more comparison participants never started smoking at a higher rate as compared to the astronauts and general population.

title: Simulated Space Radiation Studies for the Assessment of Chromosomal Damage: An Integrated Experimental and Theoretical Approach
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Outside of the protection of Earth's atmosphere humans are exposed to increased radiation, even inside the shielded walls of their spacecraft. Significant aberrations in the chromosomes of humans who stay in space for long-durations have been measured. The blood cells of several Mir crewmembers showed such abnormalities. This is of great concern since these aberrations lead to the death of cells, mutation of genes and, eventually, cancer. This study investigated the frequency of several classes of chromosomal aberrations (lethal, non-lethal, carcinogenic and complex) that occur in human cells irradiated by protons and high-energy HZE particles through various types of shielding. p> As high-energy radioactive particles penetrate the hull of a spacecraft, some of them are fragmented into a mixture of component particles. Understanding what comprises this mixed beam of radiation is imperative for predicting the overall effect on chromosomes. The experimental portion of this study was complemented by the development of an effective theoretical model to predict radiation-induced aberrations. This research will help design future spacecraft shielding so that radiation risks are minimized. The ultimate goal is to lower the radiation risk to astronauts during long-duration missions.
approach: Cultured human fibroblasts and epithelial cells were irradiated within realistic shielding types. The studies were conducted using proton beams, and later, heavy nuclei and protons, including energetic protons, neon and iron particles. Shielding material will vary in material and thickness. These measurements were designed to lead to development of a chromosome model and calculation of the frequency of radiation-caused aberrations. It is not feasible or cost-effective to lab-test all variations or types of shielding. The product of this research study was an algorithm made into a user-friendly software that allows NASA to predict shielding effectiveness before designing and building spacecraft. In addition, the orientation of cells during irradiation were altered randomly to test the hypothesis that, to be realistic to actual conditions of the body during space flight, cell orientation needs to be altered during radiation exposure.
results: The theoretical model developed in this project can be used to predict biological effects such as chromosome aberrations for incident mixed beam combined with mixed beam due to nuclear disintegration caused by shielding materials. The effectiveness of the HZE iron ions for induction of acentric fragment producing chromosome-type aberrations at the first mitosis after irradiation of human GM2149 cells in G0 was not measurably different for incident iron ion energies of 0.3, 0.6, or 1GeV/n. Furthermore, the filtration of 1 GeV/n or 0.6 GeV/n Fe ions with 1.8cm or 5.4 cm of aluminum or 5.5cm or 11.0cm of polyethylene did not measurably alter the effectiveness of the emerging beam. One of the most important conclusions derived from the successful completion of this study is that, based on the current estimate of thicknesses of shielding materials, the biological effects of a mixed beam due to fragmentation processes will not be much different than the un-fragmented and pure beam.

title: Body Mass Changes in NASA/Mir Astronauts
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: International Space Station (ISS) Phase I, more commonly known as Phase I, served as a precursor to the ISS experience. In this program, the existing resources of the US Shuttle orbiters and the Russian Space Station Mir were used to test the challenges facing the international partners in the areas of cooperation, data gathering, and logistics. As part of Phase I, seven NASA astronauts served as Mir crewmembers between March 1995 and June 1998. Physiological data gathered on these NASA astronauts can give insight on the effects of long-term weightlessness on individuals, which in turn is important for future ISS considerations.
approach: Changes in body weight during periods of prolonged weightlessness were examined for six of the seven US astronauts who have flown on Mir. The data present mean body weight and standard deviations (SD) at four intervals: the annual examination in the year prior to flight (Preflight Annual), inflight on approximately Flight Day 90 (FD 90), the third day after return to Earth (R+3), and the annual examination in the year after flight (Postflight Annual).
results: Mean weight was 77.2 kg at the preflight annual examination, 73.8 kg at FD 90, 77.3 kg at R+3, and 78.1 kg at the postflight annual examination. There was a downward shift in mean weight inflight, with return to preflight mean weight occurring by R+3. However, inflight mean weight was not statistically significantly different from the preflight and postflight mean weights. Another way to look at this type of data is to calculate and examine the percent change between preflight and inflight values. Data are inflight data, comparing weight on FD 30, FD 60, and FD 90 to weight at preflight annual examination. Percent of change is calculated by the difference between the preflight annual examination weight and the inflight weight divided by the preflight weight multiplied by 100. The resulting negative value indicates that weight decreased early in the mission (-3.5% by FD 30) and then remained relatively constant at the next two inflight intervals (-4.0% by FD 60 and -4.25% by FD 90). The method of measurement is different for inflight and on ground, which may contribute to the differences in weight reported here. These results suggest that during periods of prolonged weightlessness, astronauts may experience weight loss early in the mission. Inflight weight appears to stabilize at the new level, and return to preflight levels after return to Earth. Further research into nutritional status during long duration spaceflight may reveal the causes and consequences of this temporal weight loss.

title: Magic Window System:  Habitability and Recreational Applications of Innovative Imagery Systems
experiment_type: NASA Extreme Environment Mission Operations (NEEMO) Project
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: The objective of the Magic Windows study was to determine the functional requirements of innovative imagery systems for possible use on long-duration missions such as the International Space Station (ISS) and beyond. An imagery system could be used to display preferred information or images (work or entertainment), such as pictures, movies, and operational procedures like a "Magic Window" on the ISS. A magic window for exercise, such as a virtual reality display, could show a moving scene that changes as the user advances on a treadmill. In order to determine the best technology and facilitate its effective use, the desired functionality and needs for these types of systems were investigated.
approach: Each aquanaut was asked to fill out individually the one-page Imagery System Technology Usability Matrix toward the end of the mission while still in the habitat. Completing the survey took less than an hour. The matrix addressed the usability of the Ipaq, Palm, and Comm System (e.g. useful for the task, usable interface, improvements, or different equipment better suited for task). The Imagery System Technology Usability Matrix was set up with Technology (split into applications, if applicable) by Usability categories (interface usability, technical issues, and wearability). Usability categories contained questions which participants were asked to provide a rating on the scale of 1 (completely unacceptable) to 7 (completely acceptable). The last column of the matrix included suggested alternate uses for each technology and general comments. Paper and electronic copies of the matrix were both available.
results: Usability matrix survey was collected on the current display interfaces to determine additional needs and identify user interface issues. The investigators had a complete dataset. All crewmembers filled out the survey (in paper-and-pencil format). A post mission debrief was attended to obtain additional comments and inputs. The issues that rated the lowest and the aquanaut comments have been focused on. Each usability category has been discussed separately pointing out the specific technologies that received low ratings. Interface Usability The ease of use and input controls and displays were highly acceptable with ratings ranging from 5.5 to 6.5 (with a scale of 1 being completely unacceptable, to 7 being completely acceptable). Therefore, the personal digital assistant (PDA) is a reasonable tool for implementing tasks. Aquanauts commented that using an Ipaq and a Palm seemed to be unnecessary, and it would be beneficial to use one PDA for all tasks requiring the small interface. Technical Issues Data transfer was consistently rated moderately unacceptable for Ipaq tasks (average rating of 3.0 for timeline viewing and e-mail and average rating of 3.8 for journal writing). A problem of synching with the computer could be due to the laptop rather than the Ipaq. However, in terms of getting crewmembers to use a PDA for tasks, it is important to reduce frustration of data transfer. General comments were made that additional training and familiarity with PDA interfaces prior to the mission would be helpful. Wearability Wearability information was only applicable to a subset of technologies. Of those technologies, the In-suit Doppler Device received low ratings for personal comfort (average 3.5), don/doff ease (average 4.0), and adjustability and good fit (average rating 4.3). The application of the probes with the adhesive to the skin was reported to be difficult to remove resulting in discomfort and some skin damage. It would be beneficial to look into alternatives that have less discomfort if this is to be used in future missions. Additional Observations One of the concurrent efforts in the Usability Testing and Analysis Facility (UTAF) conducted by a summer intern was packaging of a personal entertainment system. The NEEMO 5 crew attempted to set up an entertainment system for watching a Digital Video Disc (DVD) as a group by hanging towels from bunk to bunk to hold the speakers and using a stepladder for the monitor display. Through the imagery system project, investigators hope to provide an integrated concept to provide a better set up. The information gathered from this Imagery System Technology Usability Matrix was valuable to gain a better understanding of the uses of technologies for life sciences missions. If similar research is to be done on future NEEMO missions, it might be beneficial to expand the matrix to elicit more specific comments above and beyond rating scores. Specifically, during the NEEMO 5 mission debrief, some communication technology issues were presented that warrant further investigation for future missions. Some additional research ideas were also generated that might be valuable for future missions, such as aquanaut comments about combining multiple activities on the same technology (e.g. need for only one type of PDA. Overall, Aquarius is an appropriate space flight analog for the habitability and human factors discipline to evaluate usability and user interface issues in a confined setting.

title: Dietary Calcium Intake in LSAH Participants and U.S. General Population
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Dietary calcium intake was measured to determine if Longitudinal Study of Astronaut Health (LSAH) participants meet the recommendations of the National Osteoporosis Foundation for prevention of osteoporosis and promotion of bone health.
approach: The data were obtained through a Food Frequency Questionnaire sent out in the fall of 1998. A total of 651 participants responded to the questionnaire (116 male astronauts, 21 female astronauts, 448 male comparisons, and 66 female comparisons).
results: of a national survey, the 1996 Continuing Survey of Food Intakes by Individuals (CSFII), were used to compare the LSAH participants to the U.S. general population. The findings for respondents over 20 years of age (1704 males and 1532 females) were used as comparison to those of LSAH participants. RESULTS: All respondents reported dietary calcium intake below the recommended amount of 1000 mg per day, with the exception of female astronauts. Female comparison participants also reported higher calcium intake than the female general population. The male comparison participants reported the lowest calcium intake as compared to male astronauts and the male general population.

title: Visual Light Flash Phenomena
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: The first reporting of flashes of light, visible primarily when the eyes were closed, was from Apollo 11 astronauts and occurred during transearth-coast (TEC) travel. Subsequent light flashes were reported by astronauts on the remaining Apollo missions, during both translunar-coast (TLC) and transearth-coast (TEC) travel. Although it had been generally accepted that the observed light flashes were caused by cosmic ray particles passing through the eye, the exact mechanism of particle interaction was still unknown. Some investigations supported the premise that the visual flashes were caused by direct cosmic ray particle and retina interaction, while others tended to favor Cerenkov radiation from relativistic particles as the etiology. While both mechanisms probably contributed, the consensus was that most of the flashes
approach: Two periods of observation by one observer were planned for the Skylab 4 mission. These observation sessions were accomplished on orbits selected to provide the best data on both latitude and SAA effects. The first observation session occurred on mission day 74 and was 70 minutes in duration. The second occurred on mission day 81 and was 15 minutes shorter because of very critical time limitations during the last few days of the mission. At the start of each session, the observer got into his sleep restraint, set a timer for the prescribed period (either 70 or 55 minutes), donned a blindfold, and began observing for light flashes. The subject allocated the first 10 minutes of each session for dark adaptation. During the first session, no particular position in the sleep restraint was specified. The spacecraft was in Solar Inertial Mode during both periods and local noon occurred very close to the equator in both cases. For the second session, directions were given for head positioning that placed the anterior-posterior axis of the head parallel to the Earth’s magnetic field lines in the SAA. The astronaut described each light flash event on a voice tape recorder and a transcript was obtained after flight for analysis.
results: ed from direct ionization energy loss as the particle traversed retinal cells. In either case, if cosmic particles were the cause, a strong latitude effect of the light flash rate would exist for an observer in Earth orbit, due to the Van Allen Radiation Belts. Near the equator, only cosmic particles with very high energy can reach orbital altitudes, while near the magnetic poles, particles of much lower energy can reach comparable altitudes. The primary objective of the study was to investigate the frequency and character of visual light flashes in low-Earth orbit as the Skylab trajectory passed from northern to southern latitudes. Because the trajectory periodically passed through the South Atlantic Anomaly (SAA), another objective was to investigate possible visual flashes during passage through this region. APPROACH: Two periods of observation by one observer were planned for the Skylab 4 mission. These observation sessions were accomplished on orbits selected to provide the best data on both latitude and SAA effects. The first observation session occurred on mission day 74 and was 70 minutes in duration. The second occurred on mission day 81 and was 15 minutes shorter because of very critical time limitations during the last few days of the mission. At the start of each session, the observer got into his sleep restraint, set a timer for the prescribed period (either 70 or 55 minutes), donned a blindfold, and began observing for light flashes. The subject allocated the first 10 minutes of each session for dark adaptation. During the first session, no particular position in the sleep restraint was specified. The spacecraft was in Solar Inertial Mode during both periods and local noon occurred very close to the equator in both cases. For the second session, directions were given for head positioning that placed the anterior-posterior axis of the head parallel to the Earth’s magnetic field lines in the SAA. The astronaut described each light flash event on a voice tape recorder and a transcript was obtained after flight for analysis. RESULTS: Unfortunately, no single orbit possessed ideal geomagnetic latitude and SAA conditions. The first session provided the best latitude conditions, but Skylab passed through the edge of the SAA region. The second session passed through the center of the SAA but did not achieve geomagnetic latitudes as high as in the first session. A total of 168 flashes were reported. During the second session, there were 144 reported flashes while the spacecraft was in the center of the SAA, greatly outnumbering the 24 flashes observed when Skylab passed through the edge of the SAA in the first session. The relationship between flash occurrence and geomagnetic latitude of High Mass Energy (HZE) particle flux was difficult to determine because of the few flashes observed and the varying lengths of time spent at different latitudes. It was known, however, that the time from equator passage was directly related to latitude. When the cosmic ray flux was plotted against time from equator passing, and the number of light flashes observed inside and outside the SAA was added, a correlation of flash occurrence with cosmic ray flux (or geomagnetic latitude) appeared. Dosimeter data from the Van Allen radiation belts indicated increased radiation levels in the SAA, and the flash rate coincided well with the increased radiation levels. Although light flashes were reported as casual observations by the crews of Skylab 2 and Skylab 3, the events reported during Skylab 4 represented the first dedicated observations made in Earth orbit. No flashes were observed during the Mercury and Gemini flights or during Apollo missions prior to Apollo 11. One explanation as to why no flashes were observed prior to Apollo 11 was that the eye must be dark-adapted. Furthermore, it was thought that the observer must be reasonably relaxed and free from most distracting activities to observe light flashes. This was not the case on earlier flights. Also, without a precedent for their observation, there would probably be the tendency to discount minor flashes as nothing unusual and simply a harmless event in an environment where there were more important observations to be made. Once the phenomenon was known to occur, astronauts could observe and record these events. The following conclusions were drawn from the data: Dark-Dark adaptation of at least 10 minutes was required to begin observing the flashes. There was a strong correlation of very high flash rates with passage through the SAA. From physical arguments and event descriptions, it appeared certain that these flashes were due to radiation trapped inside the Van Allen Radiation Belts. There was evidence for the predicted latitude effect, although existing data were insufficient for a thorough statistical evaluation. A greater particle flux in the trajectory through the SAA during the second observation period probably explained the increased number of flashes observed at that time. However, there were also more flashes observed outside the anomaly during the second period where the cosmic particle environment should have been comparable. Researchers were unable to explain the phenomena. It was suggested from the event rates and description of flashes during the SAA passes that particles heavier than protons may have been in the inner belt of trapped radiation. Existing knowledge of the inner belt included an upper limit of approximately one heavy nucleus per 1000 protons. The Skylab 4 light flash data were compatible with this limit, but suggested the existence of a significant flux of energy particles with atomic number (Z) > 2. This provided strong motivation for making detailed and accurate measurements of the SAA (inner belt) heavy component during the Apollo-Soyuz Test Project mission.

title: Asthma in the LSAH Population
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Asthma is a chronic respiratory condition characterized by the inability to breathe properly. Asthma affects 5% to 10% of the world's population, and more than 17 million Americans have asthma. The elderly and urban poor are at the highest risk for severe asthma and death. Highly trained athletes such as long-distance runners and swimmers are more susceptible to asthma. For example, 10% of U.S. athletes in the 1996 Olympics had asthma. Occupational exposures to a wide range of chemicals and other substances may increase the risk of asthma. Obesity and asthma have been associated, but it is not clear if one causes the other. The objective of this experiment was to compare asthma occurrence in LSAH participants with the general population.
results: In a 2000 survey of the U.S. general population, 7.2% of the respondents reported having asthma. In comparison, the prevalence rate among LSAH participants as documented in their medical records is lower: less than 4% of comparison participants were diagnosed with asthma. For the astronauts, the diagnosis rate was even lower, with less than one percent diagnosed with asthma.

title: Pulmonary Function and Aging in LSAH Participants
variables: Forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1)
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Reduced pulmonary function has been reported by a number of investigators as an important contributor to all-cause mortality independent of cigarette smoking. Specifically, forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) has been identified as a predictor of mortality. The pathobiology underlying this association is unclear. A reduced level of pulmonary function may be a proxy variable for other risk factors such as decreased physical activity, smoking-related injury, or leukocyte activity (increase in white blood cells).
approach: LSAH participants undergo pulmonary testing as a part of the routine physical examinations, at which time FEV1 is measured. Because age and height are associated with the actual measure of FEV1, an adjusted value is also calculated. This adjusted value, reported as FEV1%, is a percentage of the expected value, given the standard population normal FEV1 values for age and height. The LSAH database currently contains values for FEV1% from the pulmonary function tests completed at the baseline examination for 36 astronauts and 161 comparisons. There are values for FEV1% from the most recent visit for 170 astronauts and 310 comparisons. Both a baseline and a most recent measurement are available for 34 astronauts and 113 comparisons. The mean number of years between these specific baseline measurements and most recent visit measurements is 4.4 years for astronauts and 9.8 years for comparisons. All available data have not yet been data entered; therefore this look at the data is an interim analysis and not a final report.
results: Baseline FEV1% for both astronauts and comparisons were recorded. The mean values of 104.3 for astronauts and 106.4 for comparisons are not statistically different. It is interesting however that the distribution of values is much wider for comparisons than for astronauts. The FEV1% values measured at the most recent visit were also reported. The mean values are similar to the means at baseline and again are not statistically different. The range of values at the most recent visit is somewhat smaller than the range at baseline, and the range between the two groups is more similar at the most recent visit than at baseline. This difference at baseline may be a function of change in testing procedures over time, but it may also be a function of partial data entry. Whether an association will be seen between forced expiratory volume and mortality in this population remains to be seen. Because of the theory that FEV1 may be a proxy measure for physical activity, we also looked at the association between FEV1% and volume of oxygen consumed per kilogram of body weight per minute measured during exercise testing. The volume of oxygen consumed during exercise testing is an indicator of physical fitness. We found no association between these two variables in this small data set. These data will be reevaluated when all data have been entered to the data base.

title: Sleep-Wake Actigraphy and Light Exposure During Spaceflight
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: The success and effectiveness of manned space flight depends on the ability of crewmembers to maintain a high level of cognitive performance and vigilance while operating and monitoring sophisticated instrumentation. Astronauts, however, commonly experience sleep disruption and may experience misalignment of circadian phase during space flight. Both of these conditions are associated with insomnia and impairment of alertness and cognitive performance. Relatively little is known of the prevalence or cause of space flight-induced insomnia in short-duration missions, and less is known about the effect of long-duration space flight on sleep and circadian rhythm organization. This experiment used state-of-the-art ambulatory technology to monitor sleep-wake activity patterns and light exposure in crewmembers aboard the Space Shuttle and International Space Station (ISS). In this investigation, test subjects wore a small light-weight activity and light recording device (Actiwatch) for the entire duration of their mission. The sleep-wake activity and light exposure patterns obtained during flight are compared with data collected before and after space flight. The study also evaluated the effects of space flight on crewmembers' subjective evaluation of the amount and quality of their sleep.
approach: Baseline Data Collection : Baseline Data Collection (BDC) occurred twice before launch. The first session was two weeks in duration and occured in the window between 120 days before launch (L-120) and L-75. Crewmembers either wore the Actiwatch continuously for two weeks or they wore the watch for two one-week periods. Along with wearing the watch, crewmembers also completed a short paper sleep log every morning. The log consisted of questions relevant to the quantity and quality of the crewmembers’ sleep for the previous night. This allowed the investigator to compare watch data with written data and analyze the crewmember's sleep patterns and any disruptions they experienced. The second BDC session was from L-11 to L-0. The Actiwatch was again worn continuously for the eleven days before launch and paper sleep logs were again completed in the mornings. The two sessions were designed to document the differences in sleep quality and quantity of crewmembers in their regular routines right before a launch. After the mission is over, recovery from space flight was assessed from the day of landing (R+0) through R+7. The watches were worn continuously for the eight days upon arriving back on Earth. The paper sleep logs were again completed in the mornings. Inflight Operations : Each crewmember participating in the experiment donned the Actiwatch as soon as possible upon entry into orbit on flight day 1 (FD1) and wore the watch continuously throughout the flight. Sleep logs were completed each day within 15 minutes of awakening. On the last day of the mission, the crewmember removed and stowed the Actiwatch.
results: Investigators collected data from astronauts on space shuttle missions and ISS missions with ground-based data from all astronauts. Crewmembers attempted and obtained significantly less sleep per night as estimated by actigraphy during space shuttle missions, 11 days before space flight, and about 3 months before space flight compared with the first week post-mission. Crewmembers on ISS missions obtained significantly less sleep during space flight, in the 11 days before space flight, and during the 2-week interval scheduled about 3 months before space flight compared with in the first week post-mission. 61 of 78 shuttle-mission crewmembers reported taking a dose of sleep-promoting drug on 500 of 963 nights while 12 of 16 ISS crewmembers reported using sleep-promoting drugs.

title: In-Flight LBNP: Countermeasure to Reduce Post-Space Flight Orthostatic Intolerance
experiment_type: Shuttle Extended Duration Orbiter Medical Project (EDOMP)
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Space flight is known to cause a shift in fluid away from the lower body and a
approach: Thirteen astronauts were studied before and during space flights of 7 to 14 days. Two months or more before a flight, the astronauts' tolerance of LBNP was checked by applying LBNP in steps of 10 millimeters of mercury (mm Hg) until the astronaut showed signs of presyncope (impending fainting). Ramp tests were carried out before the flight as well as during the flight at three-day intervals before, and one or two days after, the LBNP countermeasure protocol, which was called a "soak." A stepwise decompression (ramp) to -50 mm Hg was followed by 3.5 hours at 30 mm Hg below ambient pressure. During the first hour at -30 mm Hg, the astronauts ingested one liter of water or artificially sweetened fruit drink and eight grams of sodium chloride to provide isotonic saline. The effect of the soak treatment was evaluated by comparing heart rate and blood pressure responses to ramp tests before and after the treatment. A LBNP chamber that could be collapsed and stowed was used aboard the Shuttle. Negative pressure was provided by connecting it to a vacuum source (the Waste Collection System or the Spacelab Vacuum Vent).

However, countermeasures like oral fluid and salt loading or the use of an anti-gravity suit have not succeeded in preventing postflight orthostatic intolerance. It may be that orthostatic intolerance could be counteracted by the ingestion of isotonic saline while negative pressure is applied to the legs and abdomen to allow the plasma volume to increase. The objective of this study was to evaluate this lower body negative pressure (LBNP) and fluid loading countermeasure for use in flight. APPROACH: Thirteen astronauts were studied before and during space flights of 7 to 14 days. Two months or more before a flight, the astronauts' tolerance of LBNP was checked by applying LBNP in steps of 10 millimeters of mercury (mm Hg) until the astronaut showed signs of presyncope (impending fainting). Orthostatic tolerance was assessed independently of gravity in LBNP ramp tests, in which blood pressure and heart rate were monitored while the astronauts spent five minutes at each 10-mm Hg drop of pressure down to -40 to -60 mm Hg. Ramp tests were carried out before the flight as well as during the flight at three-day intervals before, and one or two days after, the LBNP countermeasure protocol, which was called a "soak." A stepwise decompression (ramp) to -50 mm Hg was followed by 3.5 hours at 30 mm Hg below ambient pressure. The effect of the soak treatment was evaluated by comparing heart rate and blood pressure responses to ramp tests before and after the treatment. A LBNP chamber that could be collapsed and stowed was used aboard the Shuttle. Negative pressure was provided by connecting it to a vacuum source (the Waste Collection System or the Spacelab Vacuum Vent). RESULTS: Evaluable data were obtained from only four astronauts. The heart rate at maximum LBNP increased significantly between preflight and early in-flight ramp tests. RESULTS: Most bulk leukocyte subsets (WBC, differential, lymphocyte subsets) were unaltered during space flight, but were altered following landing. title: Integrated Resistance and Aerobic Training Study
variables: Muscle fiber, peak rate of tension development
Rate of elimination of carbon dioxide (VCO2)
Upper body rate of force development
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Current exercise countermeasures are insufficient to prevent muscle atrophy, cardiovascular deconditioning and bone loss associated with long-duration space flight. A known limitation has been the inability of the International Space Station (ISS) exercise hardware to provide sufficient loads to the human body that are required for maintaining physiological function. New flight exercise hardware, including the advanced resistance exercise device (ARED) and second generation treadmill (T2) are designed to provide astronauts with the ability to exercise at higher intensity. This opens an array of new possibilities for exercise programming in long-duration space flight. While the ability to do resistance exercises at heavier loads and the ability to run faster and potentially with more body loading are obvious improvements in exercise capabilities, the details of how this new equipment should be used are not so obvious. Towards this end, two workshops were held, the NASA Muscle Workshop in June 2008 and the NASA International Space Station Exercise Prescription Workshop in October 2008. Intramural and extramural experts concluded that using higher intensity resistance exercises and interval aerobic exercise would help to maintain physiological function while simultaneously decreasing total exercise time and volume. Therefore, the purpose of this research is to evaluate the efficacy of a new Integrated Resistance and Aerobic Training (Sprint) program designed to minimize loss of muscle, bone and cardiovascular function during ISS missions. Highlights of the Sprint program include an increase in the intensity and a reduction in the volume of resistance exercises, inclusion of very short, but high intensity interval-type aerobic exercises, and starting the exercise countermeasures as early as possible in the flight, preferably in the first week. Pre-, in- and postflight testing, and data sharing with selected on-going medical assessment tests, will be used to assess the effectiveness of this candidate prescription (active group) versus normal in-flight exercise (the control group).
approach: Subjects will be tested pre-and post-flight for a thorough analysis of muscle, bone and cardiovascular fitness. Muscle Performance Measures include: maximal strength, maximal power, power endurance, and force steadiness for upper and lower body, as well as central activation for the lower body. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) scans along the entire leg to characterize space flight-induced change in muscle Cross-Sectional Area (CSA) will be completed pre- and postflight. Ultrasound scans of the thigh and calf will be obtained and compared to the MRI
results: in an attempt to validate the use of ultrasound in evaluating muscle CSA. Pre-and postflight maximal aerobic capacity (VO2max) will also be evaluated. A muscle biopsy of the thigh and calf will be collected pre- and postflight to determine: single fiber size and contractile function, single muscle fiber type identification, and biomarkers for aerobic and glycolytic enzyme markers. Muscle biopsy is optional and not required to be considered a participant in the study. Bone testing will include the current standard Dual X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) medical requirement and Quantitative Computed Tomography (QCT). Crewmembers will use the ARED and T2 during their normal gym time for several weeks prior to launch to become familiar with the hardware and Sprint exercise prescription. In-flight monitoring of training loads on ARED and T2 will be evaluated as assessment of muscle function. Cardiovascular fitness will include a monthly measurement of VO2max, heart rate (HR) response to submaximal exercise, ventilatory threshold, left ventricular (LV) mass, and contractility. Subjects will perform the new Sprint exercise prescription six days per week in-flight, beginning as early as possible, preferably on the first full in flight day. The first two weeks in flight will be an acclimation period of reduced training intensity and volume; after week two the full training will begin. The early onset of training is an important evidence-based aspect of the Sprint exercise prescription for prevention of the initial deconditioning that can occur in the first 30 days of unloading in the absence of any exercise program. RESULTS: Upon completion of this study, investigators expect to provide an integrated resistance and aerobic exercise training protocol capable of maintaining muscle, bone and cardiovascular health while reducing total exercise time over 180 days of space flight. This will provide invaluable information in support of the long-term goal of protecting human fitness for even longer space exploration missions.

title: Space Flight and Immune Function
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: As astronauts work and live in crowded and confined conditions on board spacecraft for longer periods of time, the risk of infectious disease increases. They experience a unique set of stressors that contribute to a diminishment of many immune responses. Exploration class human space flight missions will require astronauts with robust immune systems. Innate immunity will be an essential element for the healthcare maintenance of astronauts during these lengthy expeditions. This investigation was designed to determine the functional status of important elements of the immune response, and will provide valuable data to help in the assessment of infectious disease risks associated with long-duration space flight. Astronauts live and work in relatively crowded, confined environments on the Space Shuttle. They experience a unique set of stressors that contribute to a diminishment of many immune responses. Exploration class human space flight missions will require astronauts with robust immune systems. Innate immunity will be an essential element for the healthcare maintenance of astronauts during these lengthy expeditions. The investigators studied the innate arm of immunity. Specifically, the natural-killer (NK)-cells, neutrophils, and monocytes were identified to be studied. The goal was to measure the cellular functions of these three immune cells. This study will complement ongoing and previous investigations in space immunology. The hypothesis being tested for this experiment is that essential functions of neutrophils, monocytes, and cytotoxic cells (lymphokine-activated (LAK) and natural killer (NK) cells) will be altered during space flight. The specific aims were 1) Conduct functional analysis of neutrophils and monocytes before and after space flight and 2) Assess cytotoxic cells and cytokine production before and after space flight
approach: To understand the effects of space flight on innate immunity, a 10 ml blood specimen and a 10 ml urine specimen were collected during the astronaut's physical examination at 10 days prior to launch (L-10), at landing (R+0), R+15, and at the crewmember's annual medical exam (AME). The samples collected at the AME served as a low-stress baseline and were collected either preflight or postflight, whichever was furthest from the participant's mission. Neutrophils: Changes in leukocyte subpopulations and function after space flight have been observed but the mechanisms underlying these changes are not well defined. This first study of 16 astronauts from three shuttle flights investigated the effects of short-term spaceflight (8 –14 days) on circulating leukocyte subsets, stress hormones, immunoglobulin levels, and neutrophil function. A second study investigated neutrophil phagocytosis, oxidative burst, and degranulation of 25 astronauts after four space shuttle missions and in nine healthy control subjects. Space flight duration ranged from five to eleven days. Blood specimens were obtained 10 days before launch, immediately after landing, and three days after landing. Monocytes: The study included four space shuttle missions and 25 astronauts. Nine non-astronauts served as controls. Blood specimens were collected 10 days before launch, within three hours after landing, and again three days after landing. This study also investigated the ability of the shuttle crewmembers’ monocytes to respond to Gram-negative endotoxin that they could encounter during infections. Blood specimens were collected from 20 crew members and 15 control subjects 10 days before launch, three to four hours after landing, and 15 days after landing and from crewmembers during their annual medical examination (AME) at six to twelve months after landing. NK-cells: Cytotoxic activity of non-major histocompatibility complex-restricted (CD561) (NMHC) killer cells and cell surface marker expression of peripheral blood mononuclear cells were determined before and after space flight. Ten astronauts (nine males, one female) from two space shuttle missions (nine- and 10-day duration) participated in the study. Blood samples were collected 10 days before launch, within three hours after landing, and three days after landing. All peripheral blood mononuclear cell preparations were cryopreserved and analyzed simultaneously in a four-hour cytotoxicity 51Cr release assay using K562 target cells. NMHC killer cell lytic activity was normalized per 1,000 CD561 cells.
results: Neutrophils: At landing, a 1.5-fold increase in neutrophils was observed compared with preflight values; lymphocytes were slightly decreased, whereas the results were variable for monocytes. The magnitude of increase in neutrophils varied across individual studies, but a significant increase in neutrophils following space flight was a very consistent finding. Even though neutrophil bands were observed in nine of sixteen astronauts, demargination of neutrophils from the vascular was thought to be the major contributor to the very consistent finding of increased circulating neutrophils following space flight. A second study found the number of neutrophils increased by 85% at landing compared to preflight levels. The mean values for phagocytosis of Escherichia coli and oxidative burst capacity in neutrophils from astronauts on the five-day mission were not significantly different from those observed in neutrophils from the control subjects. Before and after nine- to eleven-day missions, however, phagocytosis and oxidative burst capacities were significantly lower than control mean values. No consistent changes in degranulation or expression of surface markers were observed before or after any of the space missions. This study indicates that neutrophil phagocytic and oxidative functions are affected by factors associated with space flight and this relationship may depend on mission duration. Monocytes: The number of monocytes did not differ significantly over the interval sampled in both the astronaut or control groups. However, following five to eleven days of space flight, the astronauts’ monocytes exhibited reductions in ability to engulf Escherichia coli , elicit an oxidative burst, and degranulate. The phagocytic index was significantly reduced following space flight when compared to control values. When challenged with Gram-negative endotoxin, the crewmember’s monocytes collected at all three time points produced lower levels of interleukin-6 (and IL-1 and higher levels of IL-1ra and IL-8 compared to those of control subjects. There were also increased levels of the lipopolysaccharide binding protein in the plasma of the crewmembers three to four hours and 15 days after landing. This study shows that space flight-associated factors (in-flight and preflight) modulate the response of monocytes to Gram-negative endotoxins. NK-cells: When all 10 subjects were considered as one study group, NMHC killer cell numbers did not change significantly during the three sampling periods, but at landing lytic activity had decreased by 40% from preflight values. Nine of ten astronauts had decreased lytic activity immediately after flight. NMHC killer cell cytotoxicity of only three astronauts returned toward preflight values by three days after landing. No correlation of changes in NMHC killer cell function or hormone levels with factors such as age, gender, mission, or space flight experience was found.

objectives: Weightlessness during space flight induces a wide range of physiological and biochemical changes in crewmembers, such as disruption of gastrointestinal (GI) function and physiology, changes in liver function, alterations in organ blood flow, and hormonal and metabolic perturbations. approach: This investigation was comprised of three tests: lactulose and acetaminophen test, glucose breath hydrogen test, and 3-C Urea Helicobacter test. Each of these tests was to be conducted both before and after flight; no data collection was scheduled during flight. During pre- and postflight sessions, a specified breakfast was to be provided, followed by an oral ingestion of acetaminophen. Timed breath and saliva samples were collected, as were void-by-void urine samples. Food, fluid, exercise and medications were monitored during the urine and saliva collections. The rate of acetaminophen absorption and metabolism would be determined by analysis of the urine samples and timed saliva samples. Lactulose and Acetaminophen Tests: Participants were asked to avoid eating foods that are likely to generate hydrogen (such as cabbage, beans, dairy products) for twenty-four hours before the test. After approximately an 8-hour fast (sleep period), a saliva sample, a urine sample, and two consecutive breath samples, 5 minutes apart, were collected from the subjects. The subjects then ate a low fiber breakfast, followed by ingestion of 650 mg of acetaminophen (650 mg). After acetaminophen ingestion, participants drank orange juice (or an agreed-upon fluid) containing 20 g of lactulose. Subjects were to record intake of food, fluids, medications, and exercise during the 24-hour protocol period. They were not to eat or exercise for 4 hours following ingestion of medication; however, drinking water was allowed. H. pylori is a bacterial pathogen suspected to promote incidence of gastric and duodenal ulcer disease. The

These effects must be countered in order to maintain optimum health and performance during flight, as well as to initiate re-adaptation to gravity upon return to Earth. Medication uptake may also improve in a fed state during which a low fiber breakfast was ingested, than during a fasted state, lasting 8 to 10 hours, as a means of compensating for the expected GI decrements during space flight. Additionally, unusually high breath levels of hydrogen (Shuttle data) and methane (Mir data) were observed, in addition to the reported regular use of countermeasure (lactobacillus) by the Russian program, which indicated changes in GI microbes. This warranted the need to examine the microbial physiology of the GI tract. Decreased GI motility--as indicated from the limited results from the Extended Duration Orbiter Medical Project and the Shuttle-Mir Science Program experiment "Gastrointestinal Function During Extended Duration Space Flight (DSO 622)"--will affect drug absorption and bioavailability of oral medications and thus compromise therapeutic effectiveness during space flights. This effect will be compounded by anticipated changes in the hepatic metabolism of drugs and other xenobiotics. The purpose of this experiment was to determine changes in the GI function and physiology and examine the pharmacokinetics of orally administered pharmaceutical probe acetaminophen. Estimating clinically significant organ functional changes and resultant pharmacokinetic consequences will lead to the design and development of effective pharmacologic countermeasures and therapeutic adjustments. After ingesting the acetaminophen and drinking the lactulose/orange juice mixture, the following samples were collected from the subjects: 1) 12 additional saliva samples 2) 16 additional breath samples (per the prescribe schedule) 3) Urine voids for 24 hours (as separate samples) Glucose Breath Hydrogen Test: After an overnight fast, a breath sample was collected. Participants then consumed a dose of glucose dissolved in water. Breath samples were collected every 15 minutes for 120 minutes after dose consumption. Urea Helicobacter Test: After overnight fasting, a baseline breath sample was obtained. Subjects then consumed a liquid test meal containing 13-C urea. Breath samples were collected every 10 minutes for 30 minutes post-ingestion. A ground-based protocol of DSO 632 was also performed. Recent data collected on GI function (DSO 632) in astronauts indicates five out of the six subjects tested exhibited active colonization of H. pylori in their stomach. H. pylori is a bacterial pathogen suspected to promote incidence of gastric and duodenal ulcer disease. The objective of this addendum was to screen and establish population data for the incidence of H. pylori in the local Johnson Space Center (JSC) population in reference to the astronaut population. The investigators aimed to screen a total of 50 subjects from ground support personnel and from astronaut core (about 30 and 20 each, respectively). The investigators wanted to screen astronauts that have flown before and those who have not flown. Crewmembers from international partners were also encouraged to participate in the screening. Subjects could self administer at their convenience. This simple, safe and noninvasive breath test known as Breath Tek -UBiT, is a clinical test administered by health care providers to diagnose pathology associated with H. pylori incidence. The test was administered in the morning after an overnight fast. The total time required for the implementation of this protocol was 30 minutes for briefing before the test (at subjects' convenience) and approximately 20 minutes for the test itself. Test protocol includes collection of two breath samples, one before and another 15 minutes after consumption of a test beverage provided by the vendor. Samples were analyzed using vendor-provided instrumentation. A GI symptoms checklist was provided to subjects having results in the positive range to assess any incidence of pathology associated with H. pylori . A copy of the test results was provided to the subjects along with instructions for action if positive test results were observed. RESULTS: Results indicated significant changes in GI motility and absorption of APAP during both short and long-duration space flights; difference between early, mid and late flight days (n=2) was not significant suggesting that the GI functional changes manifest early in flight and remain consistent throughout the mission. Results for the ground-based portion of this study aren't available.

title: Cardiovascular and Cerebrovascular Responses to Standing Before and After Space Flight
experiment_type: Shuttle Extended Duration Orbiter Medical Project (EDOMP)
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: On landing day, some astronauts become presyncopal, which means that their blood pressure drops, their heart rate increases, and they feel faint. These responses may occur because some of their physiological responses for maintaining blood pressure, such as releases of norepinephrine, epinephrine, and renin are inadequate in some way. The objective of this study was to define differences in the physiological responses to space flight of astronauts who did or did not become presyncopal on landing day.
approach: Studies were performed on 40 astronauts at (although only 29 were included in the analysis) L-30 and L-10, on R+0 after space flights of up to 16 days, and R+3 and R+10. An enhanced stand test was performed that included an echocardiographic measurement of the aortic cross-sectional area, ultrasonic (continuous-wave Doppler) measurement of aortic flow, beat-to-beat measurement of arterial pressure, and an electrocardiogram while the astronauts were lying supine and then while they were standing. During the supine and the standing parts of the stand test, the astronauts gave blood samples for analyses of plasma norepinephrine and epinephrine levels and renin activity. The cerebral vascular resistance and the mean flow velocity in the middle cerebral artery were also measured in the supine and standing positions with a transcranial Doppler device. Plasma volume was measured by the carbon monoxide re-breathing technique.
results: Eight astronauts could not complete their stand tests on landing day because they became presyncopal. These astronauts had significantly lower norepinephrine levels when standing than the astronauts who did not become presyncopal. The increase in their norepinephrine levels during the stand test was smaller than it had been before the flight, and smaller than the increase produced by the stand test in the nonpresyncopal astronauts. These results indicate that the sympathetic nerves failed to release sufficient norepinephrine to increase the peripheral vascular resistance and avoid presyncopal symptoms. Three days after landing, the presyncopal group had recovered their ability to raise norepinephrine levels when standing. The astronauts who became presyncopal on landing day showed significant differences before the flight from those who did not become presyncopal. They had lower blood pressures, lower peripheral vascular resistance, and higher heart rates, although all values were within normal limits. Most of these differences were still present three days after landing. The results suggest that adaptation to microgravity alters the reflexes that maintain blood pressure so that about one-fourth of astronauts have inadequate norepinephrine responses to orthostatic drops in blood pressure. It appears that these astronauts may have some difference in venous compliance or vascular responsiveness even before the flight. It may therefore be possible to identify before launch a subset of astronauts who are more susceptible to postflight presyncope and are more likely to benefit from countermeasures.

title: Analyzing Interferometer for Ambient Air
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: For crew safety and health, the spacecraft atmosphere needs to be continuously monitored for harmful trace gases. In case of accidental release of harmful gaseous contaminants, extreme offgassing of materials, or malfunctions of the air revitalization system, fast response by the crew is mandatory. The longer the mission duration, the more vital is the monitoring implementation. The ANITA flight experiment tested the accuracy and reliability of Fourier Transform Infrared (FTIR) technology as a potential next generation atmospheric trace gas monitoring system for the International Space Station (ISS). After completion of flight experiment activities, ANITA; remained powered to continuously collect data and to aid in further developmental activities. In its initial calibration, ANITA allowed for the monitoring of 32 contaminants in the cabin atmosphere with fast-time resolution for immediate trend analyses to determine if the initialization of countermeasures;would be required. ANITA was designed to monitor the cabin air for contaminants at concentrations down to the low parts per million (ppm) or high parts per billion (ppb) with high precision. Its fast measurement cycle allowed the trend in air quality to be analyzed in near real-time. The instrument has two modes of operation: local cabin air sampling and non-local cabin air sampling. In summary, the objectives of this experiment were to: Demonstrate that FTIR based trace gas monitoring was an effective (accurate and precise) technology for quasi-online local and non-local measurements, Measure 32 in-situ gases, 23 of which could only be detected offline in gas samples brought down to Earth prior to ANITA, Prove that modified commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) hardware meets flight quality standards, Demonstrate the use of the ANITA trace gas monitoring system in a real space environment, and Monitor quasi-online simultaneously 32 gaseous air contaminants at low parts per million (ppm) in the crew cabin atmosphere.
approach: In the local cabin air-sampling mode, the instrument operated continuously and;automatically after initiation by the crew. The cabin air directly surrounding the ANITA inlet was monitored by filling the gas cell, analyzing the air sample, and storing the data on the hard drive of a dedicated experiment laptop. After this sequence, the gas cell was flushed back into the cabin and refilled for the next monitoring cycle. Each cycle took only six minutes. This process was possible since the physical and chemical properties of the gas sample were not changed. On day one of the experimental protocol, the crew initiated the 10-day Local Sampling sequence. The Local Sampling sequence ran automatically until manually stopped to perform the Non-Local Sampling or any off-nominal activities. A data downlink of the measurements occured daily during this protocol. After the 10-day protocol, ANITA continued to function in local sampling mode under the ownership of the NASA Environmental Factors Division. In the non-local cabin air-sampling mode, the instrument operation;was semi-automatic. Since ANITA was in a fixed location, a crewmember;went to a place of interest; on the ISS and filled an ANITA Sample Bag with air by means of a hand pump. The bag was flushed three times with local air before the air sample was taken. After collecting the sample, the crewmember connected the ANITA Sample Bag to the Air Flushing Unit. The crewmember started the pump via control software, allowing the sample to be drawn into the gas cell. The analysis of the Non-Local air sample was automatic. The data was downlinked to the ground team for analysis. This process was repeated to allow multiple non-local samples to be analyzed in this manner. ANITA is an European Space Agency (ESA)-NASA cooperative program. The flight experiment has been developed under ESA contract by Kayser-Threde GmbH in Germany (the instrument Prime Contractor and hardware developer) and SINTEF in Norway (responsible for the gas analysis software and instrument calibration). In normal operational mode, ANITA automatically monitors the local air by filling its gas cell, measuring the sample and storing the analysis data. The gas cell is then flushed back into the cabin and refilled for the next measurement cycle, each of which takes six minutes. This process is possible since the air sample is physically and chemically unchanged by the measurement. If so desired, the crew can also collect air samples at remote locations using a hand pump and sample bags. The sample bags are then manually connected to ANITA’s inlet for analysis. Considering the experimental character of the gas analyses, the
results: , contaminants identification, and concentrations are not visible to the crew. Only the ground support team is able to access the data. The identification and quantification objectives cover the background gases - water, carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide and methane - currently measured on ISS using NASA's Major Constituent Analyzer (MCA). In addition it covered numerous organic and inorganic trace contaminants including formaldehyde, perfluoropropane, ammonia, and three siloxanes, which are currently not measured onboard. RESULTS: ANITA was installed in the International Space Station (ISS) module Destiny, and was in operation from September 2007 through August 2008. The core ANITA hardware consisted of two locker drawers/inserts, which were integrated in the EXPRESS Rack on Destiny. One drawer contained the FTIR instrument with the gas cell; whereas, the power supply, main electronics and the pumping unit were integrated in the second drawer. ANITA was controlled by a laptop (data unit). Every six minutes new measurement results (spectra, concentrations) were obtained. In total, 20,430 spectra were received from ANITA whilst on-board the ISS. Local Air Sampling Quantitative air quality results were generated. The feasibility of the ANITA analysis method was fully demonstrated. The mission clearly revealed the technological maturity of the ANITA hardware, although specific deficits in the instrument performance (“spectral ghosts”, line shape variations) were recorded. ANITA provided continuous air quality information on the cabin atmosphere on the ISS. This is particularly highlighted by the detection of the PFP release when ANITA unexpectedly detected a sudden increase of PFP from a few ppms to more than a 100 ppm. The source of the gas was traced to a PFP leakage on board ISS. ANITA also detected a high concentration of the trace gas SF6 - a compound not in the gas list. Non-local Sampling Results The non-local sampling was a well working procedure. Also, the crew was satisfied with the easy handling of the gas bag and the hand pump. The big advantage of the procedure was that it can be used everywhere on the ISS and therefore it is not restricted to a certain place in only one module. In general, the instrument worked well and produced a large number of valuable results about the gas contents on the ISS. Positive highlights of the ANITA mission were: - ANITA generated on-line measurements results throughout almost the entire mission. Only on a limited number of days the instrument did not operate - The instrument could be operated by the ANITA control software in a very stable manner with no major errors - The automatic (with no crew interaction) alignment of the instrument on-board was successfully performed each time, the only exception being the very first day of activation, when a second trial was necessary - No failure of hardware items was observed The ANITA project was considered a technology demonstrator phase for future manned space monitoring systems e. g. onboard ISS. The development of a permanent instrument (ANITA second generation) requires several improvements and implementation of specific requirements for long lasting missions.

title: Lower Body Negative Pressure - Countermeasure Against Postflight Orthostatic Intolerance
variables: Lower body negative pressure (LBNP) device pressure
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: During space flight, astronauts experience a headward fluid shift due to the absence of gravity. This fluid redistribution is associated with many physiological changes, such as cardiovascular deconditioning and reduced blood volume. These changes have the potential to cause problems when astronauts return to Earth's 1-G environment, such as orthostatic hypotension when standing, which may
approach: Four crewmembers participated in the study; they were divided into two groups, countermeasure and control. Preflight and postflight collection sessions were performed in the Johnson Space Center (JSC) Cardiovascular Laboratory, and landing day collection occurred at Edwards Air Force Base. Medical monitoring and sample collection were provided by members of the investigative team. Flight simulation baseline data collection sessions, at 6 and 3 months preflight, consisted of two 3-day repetitive sessions in which inflight LBNP procedures were followed. During these sessions, subjects performed the complete inflight experiment. No blood or urine collection occurred during these sessions. The preflight supplemental baseline data collection occurs at L-30, L-10, and L-5. This required all participating subjects to undergo a single response test on each specified day. For each test, subjects provided a 24-hour urine specimen for analysis of electrolytes (Na, K, Cl) and hormones (ADH, aldosterone, epinephrine, norepinephrine) important in fluid regulation. Additionally, a blood sample was drawn, pre- and post- ramp for blood volume (hematocrit, hemoglobin), electrolyte, and hormone level determinations. Inflight, LBNP permitted both testing and countermeasure protocols to be employed. A collapsible LBNP device (LBNPD) was used for all inflight decompressions. The American Flight Echocardiograph (AFE) was used to obtain and electrocardiogram (ECG) and generate a 2-dimensional image of the heart using ultrasound. The Automatic Blood Pressure System (ABPS) measured heart rate and blood pressure and provided output consisting of ECG, Korotoff sounds, cuff pressure, and the vacuum signal from the LBNP controller. The Central Venous Pressure Device (CVPD), an ultrasound probe which is pressed lightly over the jugular vein, was used to document blood flow and estimate central venous pressure. Calf measurements were obtained during LBNP using the Ultrasonic Limb Plethysmograph in which electrodes are attached to the crewmember's leg. The Stocking (Leg) Plethysmograph was used to determine leg circumference that was later calculated into leg volume. LBNP response tests or "ramps", were conducted three times inflight over four flight days (4,5,6, and 7) for each subject. The control subjects performed a single ramp (flight day 4). During this test, 6 minutes of baseline data were collected, after which the pressure was decreased in 10 mmHg steps every 3 minutes until a pressure of -50 mmHg was attained. After 3 minutes at -50 mmHg, the vacuum was released and 3 minutes of recovery data were collected. ECG, cardiac dimensions, and calf dimensions were monitored continuously, and BP was taken every minute of the ramp. Leg volume was measured immediately before and after each ramp. The LBNP countermeasure protocol, called "soak", was conducted once inflight ( on either flight day 4 or 5) for each participating crewmember. After 6 minutes of baseline data collection, the pressure was decreased in 10 mmHg steps every 3 minutes until -50 mmHg was attained. The vacuum was then reduced to -30 mmHg for the soak period and maintained for 225 minutes. During the first hour, the subjects ingested salt tablets (8 grams total) and four beverage containers of water (128 ounces total). ECG and BP were continuously monitored for 10 minutes at scheduled times every hour. In addition, one BP measurement was taken every 15 minutes throughout the soak. After the 4-hour treatment, the pressure was reduced in 10 mmHg steps every 3 minutes until -50 mmHg was attained. After 3 minutes at this pressure, the vacuum was released and 6 minutes of recovery data was collected. ECG, cardiac dimensions and calf dimensions were monitored continuously; BP measurements were made every minute. Postflight data collection occurred at R+0 (landing day), R+1, R+3, and R+5 days. Each collection session included one ramp test on both inflight countermeasure subjects and the two control subjects. Urine and blood sample collection on participating subjects followed the same protocol as the preflight supplemental data collection.
results: in presyncopal or syncopal symptoms. Previous studies have shown that after 1-2 weeks of bed rest, ingestion of a 1-liter salt water solution during 4 hours of continuous exposure to 30 mmHg lower body negative pressure (LBNP) will protect orthostatic function and blood volume for up to 24 hours. It was hypothesized that a similar countermeasure would reduce the effects of fluid loss induced by headward fluid shift during space flight. The inflight countermeasure, LBNP combined with salt and fluid ingestion, is intended as a single application, end-of-mission treatment to pre-adapt the cardiovascular system to orthostatic stress exposure during and after reentry, landing and cabin egress. The objective of this experiment was to evaluate the efficacy of the proposed countermeasure in reversing the effects of microgravity in the cardiovascular system. This investigation also documented additional cardiovascular responses to graded simulated orthostasis in space flight, including leg volume and total peripheral resistance changes. APPROACH: Four crewmembers participated in the study; they were divided into two groups, countermeasure and control. Preflight and postflight collection sessions were performed in the Johnson Space Center (JSC) Cardiovascular Laboratory, and landing day collection occurred at Edwards Air Force Base. Medical monitoring and sample collection were provided by members of the investigative team. Flight simulation baseline data collection sessions, at 6 and 3 months preflight, consisted of two 3-day repetitive sessions in which inflight LBNP procedures were followed. During these sessions, subjects performed the complete inflight experiment. No blood or urine collection occurred during these sessions. The preflight supplemental baseline data collection occurs at L-30, L-10, and L-5. This required all participating subjects to undergo a single response test on each specified day. For each test, subjects provided a 24-hour urine specimen for analysis of electrolytes (Na, K, Cl) and hormones (ADH, aldosterone, epinephrine, norepinephrine) important in fluid regulation. Additionally, a blood sample was drawn, pre- and post- ramp for blood volume (hematocrit, hemoglobin), electrolyte, and hormone level determinations.
