title: Effects of Space Flight on Aerobic and Anaerobic Metabolism During Exercise
experiment_type: Shuttle Extended Duration Orbiter Medical Project (EDOMP)
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Microgravity may have a deconditioning effect on the capacity to perform aerobic exercise. Regular aerobic exercise during space flight might help to maintain aerobic capacity. Changes in the body's protein, mineral, and water content might occur during space flight and could contribute to a decline in aerobic performance. The objectives of this study were: (1) to measure aerobic exercise capacity before and after space flight (2) to investigate the use of aerobic exercise during flight to reduce the severity of postflight aerobic deconditioning (3) to test a new method for monitoring changes in the protein, mineral, and water content of the body before and after space flight (4) to determine how decreases in aerobic capacity are related to changes in body composition.
approach: The exercise tests were performed on a treadmill by four astronauts, on a rower by three astronauts, and on a cycle ergometer by 10 astronauts. The astronauts were instructed to exercise to the point of fatigue. Heart rate, heart rhythm, and blood pressure were monitored during the tests. Aerobic capacity was defined as the peak oxygen consumption during the tests and was measured with a Q-Plex system. The Q-Plex system is a computer driven device for cardiac, respiratory, and rehabilitation stress test (similar to an EKG stress monitor). The composition of exhaled air was analyzed either with a mass spectrometer preflight or with zirconium oxide and infrared sensors postflight. Twenty astronauts on missions of 5 to 17 days' duration completed one or two exercise tests before space flight and another test on landing day. Seventeen of the astronauts exercised during the flight, using a rower (three astronauts), a cycle ergometer (10) or a treadmill (four) that had a harness and tether to simulate gravity. They followed continuous (one) or interval (16) exercise protocols with target heart rates intended to correspond to 65 to 85% of preflight maximum oxygen consumption. Some subjects had difficulty achieving these heart rates on the treadmill. A monitor displayed and recorded the heart rate. The total exercise performed during flight was quantified by multiplying the percentage of the maximal heart rate by the number of minutes per exercise session and by the number of sessions per week. The body composition of 10 of the astronauts was analyzed preflight and on R+2 after flights lasting seven to 16 days. Extracellular water, intracellular water, total body fat, percent fat, and fat-free mass were derived from body weight, body density, and body water. Body density was determined by weighing the astronauts under water and correcting for residual lung volume. Body water was determined from a previously validated bioelectrical response spectroscopy model to avoid taking the multiple blood samples and using the radioactive tracers or other tracers that are usual for this purpose. Total body protein and mineral contents were derived from total body water and body density by using a mathematical model that assumes the body is made up of three compartments (fat, water, and dry lean mass). The effects of changes in body composition on aerobic capacity were studied in eight astronauts from 7- to 16-day missions. Preflight and R+0 or R+2, their body composition was analyzed by the methods described above, and their aerobic capacity was determined in treadmill exercise tests on the same day, after the body composition measurements.
results: Postflight peak oxygen consumption during the exercise tests was 13% lower than that of the astronauts who did not exercise preflight. The exercise test results from this DSO were analyzed together with those from DSO 476, and the combined results indicated that the capacity to perform aerobic exercise was reduced after space flight, but that aerobic exercise during flight attenuated this effect. The results did not indicate the optimal exercise device or protocol for maintaining aerobic capacity. Results of the analysis of body composition showed that the astronauts lost about two percent of their fat-free mass, about three percent of their intracellular water and about four percent of their total body protein and minerals from preflight to postflight. Little change occurred in extracellular water or in fat. The decrease in intracellular water may have been largely due to the loss of proteins and minerals, because differences in the concentrations of dissolved proteins and minerals cause water to move by osmosis. These losses could affect the performance or health of the astronauts during or after space flight. The eight astronauts who underwent both body composition analysis and exercise testing lost 12% of their aerobic capacity from preflight to postflight. Statistical analysis of covariance, which was performed to separate the effects of the various body composition variables, showed that the decreases in aerobic capacity were due at least in part to decreases in total body protein. The protein loss most likely represented a loss of muscle mass.

title: Sleep and Respiration in Microgravity
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: There is evidence that sleep is often impaired in microgravity. Some crewmembers state that arousals are common and sleep quality is poor. As a
approach: Sleep Studies Respiration was measured during sleep by instrumenting the subject with the Respiratory Inductance Plethysmograph (RIP) Suit and pulse oximeter, allowing continuous measurement of both the rib cage and abdominal motion, as well as arterial oxygen saturation. In addition, subjects were fitted with an electrocardiograph (ECG), an electroencephalograph (EEG), an electrooculograph (EOG), a nasal airflow temperature sensor and an ingestible body temperature sensor. From these sensors, measurements were taken of changes in ventilation, relative rib cage and abdominal contribution to ventilation, thoraco-abdominal asynchrony, sympathetic and parasympathetic contributions to heart rate variability, and the coupling between respiration and heart rate, all as a function of sleep stage. Measurements were taken with and without the administration of melatonin preflight and inflight. Awake Studies Pulmonary Function Test (PFT): The preflight and postflight Pulmonary Function Test (PFT) sequences deviated from the inflight protocol in that the subject performed the sequence in the standing and supine positions. The subject also underwent a hypoxic ventilatory depression (HVD) test with two levels of hypoxia (10% inspired oxygen and 12% inspired oxygen). The HVD test was not part of the PFT sequence; it was a stand alone test with a separate set of hardware and data systems. The HVD test required the subject to rebreathe a low oxygen gas mixture from a bag in which carbon dioxide was actively removed to maintain isocapnia in the face of increased ventilation and decreasing oxygen. The subject was instrumented with ECG electrodes, RIP Suit and pulse oximeter. RIP signals were continuously recorded for ventilation, ventilatory timing, and relative rib cage and abdominal contributions to breathing throughout the PFT sequence. The hardware system centers around a bag-in-box system. Gases are dispensed into the bags within the box, and the subject controls the breathing path based on prompts presented on a microcomputer display. Flow was measured with a Fleisch #2 pneumotachograph in the wall of the bag-in-box which was coupled to a Validyne MP-45 differential pressure transducer. Gas concentrations were measured at the lips of the subject with a quadrupole mass spectrometer (GASMAP). The subject performed a rebreathing (REB) maneuver from a gas mixture containing 10% argon, 0.6% acetylene, 0.3% carbon monoxide, 21% oxygen and balance nitrogen. From the insoluble argon, lung volume was determined; from the soluble acetylene, the cardiac output and pulmonary tissue volume were determined; and from the highly absorbed carbon monoxide, the pulmonary diffusing capacity was determined. A resting gas exchange (RGE) maneuver was then performed. The subject breathed air for 5 minutes during which time gas exchange and ventilatory timing were determined. ECG and blood pressure were recorded, allowing determination of the coupling between heart rate, respiration and blood pressure. At the end of the test, a vital capacity slow exhalation was performed and the range of ventilation-perfusion ratios in the lung was determined. Several determinations of the inspiratory occlusion pressure at 100 milliseconds (P100) were also made during the quiet breathing phase. P100 was measured during resting tidal breathing, and during the hypercapnic and hypoxic response tests. At the beginning of an inspiration, the breathing path was briefly occluded to measure the inspiration airway pressure. The P100 was determined from this pressure. To determine control of ventilation (hypercapnic ventilatory response), the subject breathed room air for one minute then switched to the rebreathing bag containing 5% carbon dioxide, 60% oxygen and balance nitrogen. The subject rebreathed for approximately 4 minutes, or until the carbon dioxide level reached 10%, or until the subject voluntarily terminated the test. During this period, carbon dioxide and oxygen were monitored, establishing the carbon dioxide stimulus to breathe on a breath-by-breath basis. To determine hypoxic ventilatory response (HVR), the rebreathing bag was filled with a volume of test gas (1 to 2% carbon dioxide, 23% oxygen, balance nitrogen) equal to the subject's vital capacity plus 1 liter. The subject breathed normally for 3 minutes, providing baseline resting gas exchange data to determine average end-tidal carbon dioxide values. The subject then took three deep breaths to ensure adequate mixing with the gas in the rebreathing bag, and then breathed normally. As isocapnia is maintained, the oxygen concentration in the rebreathing gas mixture decreases proportionally to the subject's oxygen consumption. Termination of the HVR test occurred when either the end-tidal oxygen reached 40 torr, arterial oxygen saturation decreased to 65-70% (this is subject dependent), or when the subject evidenced any distress. Several determinations of the P100 were also made during the test, providing a measure of respiratory drive.

RESULTS: Microgravity exposure greatly reduces the number of sleep related apneas and hypopneas, significantly reduces snoring, and reduces the number of respiratory arousals in normal, healthy individuals. These changes were probably due to the elimination of the gravitationally induced changes in the upper airway anatomical structures. Indeed, the reduction in the total number of arousals in microgravity resulted almost entirely from the large reduction in respiratory-related arousals. From these data investigators can infer that gravity plays a dominant role in the increase in upper airway resistance and obstruction that occurs after the transition to the supine posture and during all stages of sleep. It has long been recognized that gravity might play a role in some forms of sleep-disordered breathing (especially obstructive sleep apnea (OSA)). However, these data provide the first direct evidence that the effect of gravity on the upper airways is dominant in causing obstruction. As such, the results may prove useful increasing the emphasis on postural treatments for OSA. The simple expedient of decreasing the rearward gravitational effect on the upper airways by encouraging sleep in a semi-upright posture may prove more acceptable to some patients than other treatments such as continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP). Microgravity also resulted in a significant reduction in the hypoxic ventilatory response; however, the change that occurred was no different to that seen in the supine position. In contrast to the hypoxic response there was no change in the response to inhaled CO2 caused by either the supine position or by microgravity. Thus the ventilatory control mechanisms in microgravity in these healthy subjects were much the same as they were in the supine position on the ground. The similarity is borne out by the similar numbers of central apneas and hypopneas observed in microgravity and on the ground, since central events result primarily from the ventilatory control system. In conclusion, our data suggest that any sleep disruption caused by spaceflight or by microgravity has origins unrelated to the respiratory system.

title: Assessing the Impact of Communication Delay on Behavioral Health and Performance: An Examination of Autonomous Operations Utilizing the International Space Station
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Space crews of exploration missions in the future will need to be more autonomous from mission control and act and operate independently, in part, due to the expectation that communication quality between the ground and exploration crews will be more limited by communication delays and other quality factors than on any mission to date. Communication delays and the impact these delays have on the quality of communications to the crew will create performance decrements if crews are not given adequate training and tools to support more autonomous operations. This study examined the impact of implementing a communication delay on the International Space Station (ISS) on individual and team factors and outcomes, including performance and related perceptions of autonomy. Specifically, this study examined how interdependent teams interacted and performed tasks with and without delays in communications between the team elements. The tasks performed by the teams varied along two dimensions: 1) those that were either critical or not critical (“criticality”) and 2) those that were either novel or familiar (“novelty”). Tasks included variations in both dimensions as it is assumed that highly novel and highly critical tasks are similar to those that a team may encounter during a long-duration mission in which they have no prior training but must address. This study provided a preliminary understanding of the impact of communication delays on individual and team performance as well as insight into how teams perform and interact under autonomous conditions in the analog environment most comparable to deep space. The overall aim of the study was to determine whether the communications delays (as an indicator of communication quality) likely to be experienced on a long-duration mission to an asteroid or to Mars will
approach: The study included three astronauts on the ISS. Participants also included 18 mission control support personnel. Participants performed 16 tasks, 8 under conditions of no delay in communications, and 8 under conditions of a 10 minute one-way delay. Tasks were designated by subject matter experts (SMEs) in collaboration with the Mission Operations Directorate (MOD) for monitoring based on their level of novelty (high/low) and criticality (high/low). Individual semi-structured interviews were conducted with each of the astronaut participants approximately four months prior to mission launch. Participants were asked open-ended questions as to prior experience in working on a team. After each task, participating ISS crewmembers and mission support personnel were asked to complete post-task questionnaires that included questions about individual and team behavior, performance and mood. Individual semi-structured interviews were conducted with each of the astronaut participants less than 21 days post-mission to obtain their opinions about feasibility of data collection, importance of delays in communications, and communication delay factors that influenced their well-being.
results: in clinically or operationally significant decrements in crew performance and well-being on the ISS. Specifically, the investigators aimed to accomplish the following: Determine the feasibility and acceptability of conducting a study of communication delays on the ISS. Determine if there is an association between delays in communication (like those expected to be experienced during a Mars mission), individual and crew performance, and well-being. Determine whether this association is affected by task complexity (criticality and novelty), social support, perceived stress, and task autonomy. APPROACH: The study included three astronauts on the ISS. Participants also included 18 mission control support personnel. Participants performed 16 tasks, 8 under conditions of no delay in communications, and 8 under conditions of a 10 minute one-way delay. Tasks were designated by subject matter experts (SMEs) in collaboration with the Mission Operations Directorate (MOD) for monitoring based on their level of novelty (high/low) and criticality (high/low). Individual semi-structured interviews were conducted with each of the astronaut participants approximately four months prior to mission launch. Participants were asked open-ended questions as to prior experience in working on a team. After each task, participating ISS crewmembers and mission support personnel were asked to complete post-task questionnaires that included questions about individual and team behavior, performance and mood. Individual semi-structured interviews were conducted with each of the astronaut participants less than 21 days post-mission to obtain their opinions about feasibility of data collection, importance of delays in communications, and communication delay factors that influenced their well-being. RESULTS: The quantitative results suggest crew morale and the quality of communications were significantly reduced in communication delay tasks compared to control tasks. In addition, both quantitative and qualitative data suggest communication delays increased stress and frustration. However, no significant differences in individual, crew or team performance or autonomy were observed across control and delay tasks. The qualitative data expanded on these findings. The astronauts reported the quality of support from the ground support team was good regardless of whether or not there were communication delays. Furthermore, the performance-related challenges that were reported under situations of communication delays were not explicitly linked to individual or team failures, but rather involved operational outcomes and teamwork processes, such as reduced task efficiency and decreased situational awareness. Given these findings, future studies should consider including post-task questions that assess efficiency and team/task coordination issues. Qualitative data from post-mission interviews also identified factors that contributed to performance and mood-related challenges of communication delays, including task-specific factors such as high task-related communication demands (either due to low crew autonomy or poor communication strategies), complex tasks, and time-critical tasks. The astronauts reported communication delays interfered with the crewmembers ability to receive the support they needed in a timely fashion, which in turn made it difficult to move forward with the task procedures, and importantly these challenges were amplified in tasks that involved high levels of back-and-forth communications. Given these findings, and the limited availability of crewmember time on the ISS, future studies should prioritize research time on the ISS to include tasks that are most likely to negatively impact individual and team outcomes.

title: Autonomic Neurophysiology in Microgravity
variables: Blood pressure, mean, power spectral density
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: The Autonomic Neurophysiology in Microgravity experiment was one of four autonomic nervous system experiments performed during the 1998 Neurolab mission. This experiment focused on how microgravity affects the overall function of the autonomic nervous system. The autonomic nervous system (ANS) is the part of the nervous system that supplies stimulation to the involuntary muscles, like the smooth and cardiac muscles, and to the glands. The autonomic nervous system is controlled principally by parts of the brain stem and the hypothalamus. For the first time in space flight history, direct measurement of muscle sympathetic nerve activity (MSNA) was made via microneurography. Microneurography is a procedure in which a small needle (the size of an acupuncture needle) is placed in an accessible nerve just below the knee. With the needle, the nerve signals traveling from the brain to the blood vessels can be measured directly. The investigators were particularly interested in the effect of microgravity on the sympathetic limb of the baroreflex through spillover of norepinephrine (NE). Norepinephrine is a hormone produced by the adrenal glands and also secreted from nerve endings in the sympathetic nervous system as a chemical transmitter of nerve impulses. Also known as noradrenaline, many of its general actions are similar to those of adrenaline, but it mainly functions to maintain normal body activity, rather than to prepare the body for emergencies. This hormone is of interest because one suggested reason for change in the blood pressure control system is that it is underactive in space. The ANS releases chemical messengers (e.g., norepinephrine) when it operates. There has been some evidence from previous space flights that NE levels are lowered in space, indicating a low level of activity in blood pressure control. However, looking at NE levels alone can lead to false conclusions, since the blood level of a hormone depends not only on how much is released, but also on how fast it is removed from circulation. For that reason, on Neurolab, norepinephrine was measured as spillover rate to clue into ANS changes.
approach: To provide clear insight into how ANS is functioning, a microneurography needle was placed above the peroneal nerve just below the knee; the nerve signals traveling from the brain to blood vessels were measured. Subjects infused radioactively-labeled NE into the blood stream and collected blood samples to show how fast NE is released into and removed from circulation, thereby allowing investigators to assess whether blood press control system is really underactive. To monitor physiological changes, serum and urine catecholamines were collected. After cooling to +4 degrees Celsius, the tubes were centrifuged into separate blood components. Both the blood tubes and urine samples were stored at -22 degrees Celsius until landing. To obtain baseline data, these procedures were also performed before and after flight.
results: All three scheduled sessions were performed by four crewmembers, one session early (Flight Day 2), the second session mid (Flight Days 7 and 8), and the third session late (Flight Days 12 and 13) in flight. Additional sessions were performed on Flight Days 2 and 8 by one subject on the early mission session. Data appear to be of good quality based on the initial evaluation. In this study, the hypothesis that space flight impairs cerebral autoregulation was studied in six astronauts approximately 72 and 23 days before, after 1 and 2 weeks in space (n = 4), on landing day, and 1 day after the 16-day Neurolab space shuttle mission. Beat-by-beat changes of photoplethysmographic mean arterial pressure and transcranial Doppler middle cerebral artery blood flow velocity were measured during 5 minutes of spontaneous breathing, 30 mmHg lower body suction to simulate standing in space, and 10 minutes of 60 degree passive upright tilt on Earth. Dynamic cerebral autoregulation was quantified by analysis of the transfer function between spontaneous changes of mean arterial pressure and cerebral artery blood flow velocity, in the very low- (0.02-0.07 Hz), low- (0.07-0.20 Hz) and high-frequency (0.20-0.35 Hz) ranges. Resting middle cerebral artery blood flow velocity did not change significantly from preflight values during or after space flight. Reductions of cerebral blood flow velocity during lower body suction were significant before space flight (P Results indicate that: (1) reductions of cerebral blood flow velocity during lower body suction are similar before, during and after spaceflight; (2) reductions of cerebral blood flow velocity during upright tilt are smaller after than before space travel; and (3) dynamic fluctuations of cerebral blood flow velocity in response to changes of arterial pressure, as reflected by transfer function gain, phase and coherence, are significantly less in the low-frequency range during and after than before spaceflight. These results reject the hypothesis that exposure to microgravity impairs cerebral autoregulation and suggest rather that microgravity improves it.

title: Study of the Impact of Long-term Space Travel on the Astronaut's Microbiome
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: The human microbiome, the collection of microbes that live in and on the human body, plays an important role in human health contributing to the processing and absorption of nutrients in the human body, and plays a protective role by competing for resources with pathogenic organisms. Changes in the dynamic or composition of the human microbiome may lead to altered human metabolic function or pave the way for the colonization of the human body by opportunistic pathogenic microorganisms. It is known that factors such as stress, diet, and an impaired immune system can trigger changes in the human microbiota, increasing the risk of contracting a disease. The goal of the experiment was to determine how the composition of the human microbiome changes during long-term space exploration and to evaluate its potential impact on a crewmember’s health. This is a retrospective study using data from Functional Immune Alterations, Latent Herpesvirus Reactivation, Physiological Stress and Clinical Incidence Onboard the International Space Station (Functional_Immune) and The Effects of Long-Term Exposure to Microgravity on Salivary Markers of Innate Immunity (Salivary_Markers). Some microbial species from the human microbiome have a beneficial or protective effect on health; the loss of these species can lead to an altered metabolic function and, in conjunction with reduced immune response, may increase the chance of infection by opportunistic pathogens. By sampling the microbiome of astronauts on earth while in peak physical health and during subsequent times of stress, including long-term exposure to microgravity, g-forces, radiation and changes in health status, the investigators aimed to define signatures of human response to a variety of relevant aspects of space travel. This study had the following objectives: Characterize and investigate the changes occurring in the prokaryotic and viral microbiome of astronauts from key body sites before, during, and after a space mission. Assess astronaut immune function before, during, and after the space mission. Identify associations between changes in the astronaut’s microbiome and relevant metadata.
approach: A total of 23 International Space Station (ISS) crewmembers (15 from Integrated Immune and 8 from Salivary Markers), were enrolled in this study. Data were collected over 18 separate ISS missions. Additionally, six ground-based controls were enrolled in this study, as part of Salivary Markers, to ensure assay validity. To assess the composition and dynamic of the subjects microbiome, Microbiome Sampling of the forehead skin, left and right forearm, left and right nares, oral cavity, and saliva was collected preflight, inflight, and postflight. Blood was collected prior to launch and again on landing day to assess the subject’s immune function. Stool gauze samples were also collected during this timeframe. In conjunction with the subject swab/gauze sampling, environmental microbiome sample swabs were taken from ISS module locations used throughout a normal crew day. Environmental surface swab samples were collected from the crewmembers sleeping quarters, exercise equipment, and two air vents located within frequently used ISS modules. Whole body perspiration collection took place on flight day 7 and R-14.
results: Characterization of the overall spatial patterns of microbial community structure demonstrated that the factor that most contributed to variation among all samples was sampling site, in agreement with previous studies showing that the skin and nose microbiomes are more similar to each other than to those from feces or the mouth. In addition, samples collected from the same body site tended to cluster by crewmember. Interestingly, ISS environmental samples overlapped with specimens from the two skin sites and the nose microbiota. Further analysis showed that there was no significant difference among bacterial species that were present/absent in ISS microbial communities and inflight forehead and forearm skin microbiomes.

title: Sleep-Wake Actigraphy and Light Exposure During Spaceflight
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: The success and effectiveness of manned space flight depends on the ability of crewmembers to maintain a high level of cognitive performance and vigilance while operating and monitoring sophisticated instrumentation. Astronauts, however, commonly experience sleep disruption and may experience misalignment of circadian phase during space flight. Both of these conditions are associated with insomnia and impairment of alertness and cognitive performance. Relatively little is known of the prevalence or cause of space flight-induced insomnia in short-duration missions, and less is known about the effect of long-duration space flight on sleep and circadian rhythm organization. This experiment uses state-of-the-art ambulatory technology to monitor sleep-wake activity patterns and light exposure in crewmembers aboard the International Space Station (ISS). Crewmembers wear a small light-weight activity and light recording device (Actiwatch) for the entire duration of their mission. The sleep-wake activity and light exposure patterns obtained in flight will be compared with baseline data collection collected for two weeks between 120 days before launch (L-120) and L-75 and from L-11 through L-0. Recovery from space flight was assessed from the day of landing (R+0) through R+7. These data should help researchers better understand the effects of space flight on sleep, as well as aid in the development of effective countermeasures for both short- and long-duration space flight. The primary objective of this experiment was to document the effects of long-duration space flight on sleep-wake activity patterns using a wrist-worn Actiwatch. Additional objectives were to measure the ambulatory light exposure of individual crewmembers and to evaluate the effects of space flight on crewmembers' subjective evaluation of the amount and quality of their sleep. The information derived from this study will help to better understand the effects of space flight on sleep, as well as aid in the development of effective countermeasures for long-duration space flight. Moreover, a better understanding of the etiology of insomnia is relevant to the millions of people on Earth who suffer nightly from insomnia. Finally, the advancement of state-of-the-art technology for monitoring, diagnosing, and assessing treatment effectiveness is vital to the continued treatment of insomnia on Earth and in space.
approach: Baseline Data Collection Baseline Data Collection (BDC) occurred twice before launch. The first session was fourteen days in duration and occurred in the window of L-120 to L-75. The participating crewmembers must either wear the Actiwatch continuously for two weeks or wear the watch in two separate one-week sessions. Along with wearing the watch, crewmembers also completed a short paper sleep log every morning. The log consists of questions relevant to the quantity and quality of the crewmember's sleep for the previous night. This allowed the investigators to compare watch data with written data and analyze the crewmember's sleep patterns and any disruptions they may experience. The second BDC session was from L-11 to L-0. The Actiwatch was again worn continuously for the eleven days before launch, and paper sleep logs were again completed in the mornings. The two sessions were designed to document the differences in sleep quality and quantity of crewmembers in their regular routines and right before a launch. After the mission is over, additional BDC data was taken. The last session is from R+0 to R+7. The watches were worn continuously for the eight days upon landing back on Earth. The paper sleep logs were again completed in the mornings. Inflight Operations The crewmembers donned the Actiwatch as soon as possible (within 48-hours of docking to ISS) and wore the watch continuously (day and night) throughout the mission with the exception of extravehicular activities (EVA) and showers. The crewmembers accessed an electronic sleep log on a Station Support Computer. Sleep logs were completed within 15 minutes of awakening/getting out of bed seven consecutive days every three weeks for the duration of the mission. The data from the Actiwatch was downlinked at least once per month to the investigators at the Johnson Space Center (JSC). This downlinking activity required no crew time. After each data download, the Actiwatch was re-initialized and donned for continued data collection. Within one week of arrival of the next Expedition crew, the current crew replaced the Actiwatch lithium battery with a fresh one and performed a final data download.
results: Investigators collected data from astronauts on space shuttle missions and ISS missions with ground-based data from all astronauts. Crewmembers attempted and obtained significantly less sleep per night as estimated by actigraphy during space shuttle missions, 11 days before space flight, and about 3 months before space flight compared with the first week post-mission. Crewmembers on ISS missions obtained significantly less sleep during space flight, in the 11 days before space flight, and during the 2-week interval scheduled about 3 months before space flight compared with in the first week post-mission. 61 of 78 shuttle-mission crewmembers reported taking a dose of sleep-promoting drug on 500 of 963 nights while 12 of 16 ISS crewmembers reported using sleep-promoting drugs.

title: The Influence of Space Flight on Erythrokinetics in Man
variables: Band neutrophils, percentage of white blood cells
Stage 1-3 echinocytes, red blood cell percentage
Red blood cells, percentage reticulocytes, flow cytometry test
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Data from previous studies of the influence of space flight on hematologic functions have consistently shown that exposure to microgravity significantly reduces the circulating red blood cell mass (RCM). These
approach: The mission specialists (MS1 and MS2) and payload specialists (PS1 and PS2) who flew on the Spacelab 1 mission served as the subjects for the experiment. As a control for the blood draw protocol and a comparison of inflight
results: have been noted in numerous American astronauts and Russian cosmonauts. The RCM is a measure of the number of erythrocytes (red blood cells) circulating in the blood stream. The objective of this experiment was to measure factors involved in the control of erythrocyte turnover that might be altered during weightlessness. Many of these biochemical and hematological parameters had not been previously measured during space flight. APPROACH: The mission specialists (MS1 and MS2) and payload specialists (PS1 and PS2) who flew on the Spacelab 1 mission served as the subjects for the experiment. As a control for the blood draw protocol and a comparison of inflight results to bed rest results, the mission was simulated on the ground with a group of five subjects selected from a human test-subject pool. In order to simulate the inflight period, control subjects were placed at -6 degrees head-down bed rest for 10 days (mission duration). Blood samples were obtained from each crewmember and bed-rest subject three or four times (depending on the subject) during the preflight (pre-bed rest) period, two or three times inflight (during bed rest) and four times during the postflight (post-bed rest) period. Inflight samples were taken on flight days (FD) 1 and 7. Radionucleotide measurements of red cell mass and plasma volume were made 65 days before flight (L-65), on landing day (R+0), and 8 days postflight (R+8). Preflight and postflight blood samples and all samples from the bed-rest subjects were collected by venipuncture with the use of standard clinical materials and procedures. Inflight blood samples were collected with the Inflight Blood Collection System (IBCS). Samples were collected in plain tubes for serum and in heparin / EDTA tubes for plasma. The samples were immediately separated by centrifugation into fluid and cellular phases. The centrifuged samples were then stored in an on-board cryogenic freezer (-195 degrees C). After landing, the samples were stored frozen in the laboratory until analysis was performed. Slides for reticulocyte count, white cell differential, and reticulocyte age classification were prepared inflight. Hematocrit was also determined during the inflight period. Postflight hematology analyses were performed on whole blood that had been stored at the spacecraft ambient temperature during the flight. The effect of space flight on erythrocyte survival time was measured by injecting 51Cr-labeled red blood cells immediately after landing and determining the percentage of labeled cells that remained after 8 days. Reticulocytes were counted by the standard manual method and by flow cytometry using stained cells. Erythropoietin was measured with fetal mouse liver cell cultures; when a radioimmunoassay became available later, it was used to assay frozen samples. Histogram contouring of stained blood cells was used to measure the amount of RNA in reticulocyte cytoplasm. Data were analyzed using a multi-way analysis of variance with repeated measures and the Student-Newman-Keuls multiple comparison test. The pre- and postflight diet of the crewmembers was not controlled or monitored. Bed rest subjects consumed the standard hospital diet. Two weeks before launch, the sleep-wake cycle of MS1 and PS1 was shifted by 12 hours to prepare them for a sleep-wake cycle that would permit a continuous 24-hour operation cycle of the Spacelab. To attempt to monitor any shift in metabolic functions, urine specimens were collected from MS1 and PS1 throughout several 24-hour periods 6 months before the flight, when they were on their normal daytime work schedule, and during the preflight period, when they were adapting to their new work-rest schedule. These samples were analyzed for calcium, potassium, and cortisol and compared to samples taken immediately postflight to determine if the individuals had adapted to the imposed time change. Two hours before landing, MS1 and MS2 consumed salt tablets with water as a countermeasure to postflight gravity stress on the cardiovascular system. During the first three days of the mission, all crewmembers ingested anti-motion sickness medication. RESULTS: Circadian Rhythms: Cortisol, calcium, and potassium had statistically significant circadian rhythms 6 months before flight, and the peak time of these rhythms did not change while crewmembers were on a shifted schedule. Preflight Period: Changes in some variables occurred during the preflight period, most of them between L-7 and L-1. For this reason, the mean of the values for the first two preflight days was compared with the other days on which samples were taken. No consistent preflight changes occurred in bed-rest subjects. Erythrocyte Production and Destruction: Red cell mass (ml/kg) was decreased on landing in all four crewmen, with a significant mean decrease of 9.3 percent from preflight. By R+8, only 3.3 percent had been replaced and the decrease was still significant. Neither hyperoxia nor an increase in blood phosphate, nor a lack of iron, was a cause of the decrease in RCM, and a decrease in erythrocyte production could not be the sole cause of such a large, rapid change. Although the number of erythrocytes with abnormal shapes was elevated on R+8, erythrocyte survival time on R+8 had not changed significantly from preflight survival time. Erythropoietin decreases found with the fetal mouse liver assay were not significant, but radioimmunoassay results showed significant decreases on FD1 and FD7. Since serum haptoglobin did not decrease, intravascular hemolysis was not thought to contribute substantially to the RCM decrease. Leukocytes and Platelets: The total white blood cell (WBC) count and the percentage and number of segmented neutrophils, lymphocytes, eosinophils and basophils remained unchanged during and after flight. The percentage and number of band neutrophils were significantly increased on the first inflight sampling day, and the percentage and number of monocytes were significantly increased on the last postflight sampling day. The number of platelets did not change significantly during or after the flight. Data from the bed-rest experiment showed that on R+0, the number of neutrophils was significantly higher than during the preflight period. Plasma and Blood Volume: A 6 percent decrease in plasma volume (ml/kg) at landing was not significant compared to preflight, and recovery was complete by R+8, at least a week before RCM recovered. Blood volume (ml/kg) was significantly decreased (10.5 percent) on landing, but was close to its preflight level a week later. Serum Chemistry: Sodium was significantly decreased during flight, on R+1, and on R+12/13. Osmolality was significantly lower than its preflight level on R+8 and R+12/13 . Proteins: Total serum protein was decreased from the preflight value by 3.8 percent on FD7. The decrease in serum protein was significant (7.6 percent) on R+8, when albumin, alpha-2 globulin, beta globulin, and gamma globulin were decreased. On R+12/13 alpha-l and alpha-2 globulin were significantly increased. From the second inflight measurement (FD7) through at least 12 hours after landing, ferritin in crewmembers increased significantly over its preflight level. Simulation: Red cell mass decreased significantly in all bed-rest subjects, with a greater decrease (8.4 percent) on R+8 than on R+0 (4.6 percent). Ferritin was significantly decreased on R+8 and R+12/13. Potassium was significantly increased in simulation subjects on FD1. Red cell shape classification was not performed for this part of the experiment. Conclusions: The most likely causes of RCM decrease resulting from space flight are a premature loss of erythrocytes and a failure of erythropoiesis to make up for the loss. The number of subjects in this study was small and they were not a homogeneous group in several respects. Moreover, changes in some of the measured variables occurred during the preflight period. These results must be considered preliminary until more experiments can be done.

title: Validation of On-Orbit Methodology for the Assessment of Cardiac Function and Changes in the Circulating Volume Using Ultrasound and Braslet-M Occlusion Cuffs

archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: The Braslet experiment was a collaborative effort between the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) and the Russian Federal Space Agency (FSA) for which each organization acted as a portion of the co-investigator team. The objective of this study was the development and validation of an in-flight methodology to assess a number of cardiac and vascular parameters associated with circulating volume and its manipulation in long-duration space flight. Responses to modified Valsalva and Mueller maneuvers were measured by cardiac and vascular ultrasound (US provided) before, during, and after temporary volume reduction by means of Braslet-M thigh occlusion cuffs (Russia provided). This study had the following specific aims: Establish and validate non-invasive ultrasound measurement techniques for comprehensive cardiac and vascular evaluation Develop and validate methodology to assess the circulating volume changes and cardiac function in space flight conditions, through short-term hemodynamic modification using Braslet-M occlusion cuffs. Determine the utility of Valsalva and Mueller respiratory maneuvers as means of auxiliary physiological modification to obtain additional functional information of clinical and scientific significance. The Braslet SDTO used multiple modes of ultrasound imaging and measurements, in combination with short-term application of Braslet-M occlusive cuffs and cardiopulmonary maneuvers using both Valsalva and Mueller techniques to demonstrate and to evaluate the degree of changes in the circulating volume on orbit. This was accomplished by performing echocardiographic examinations in multiple modes, including tissue Doppler mode and ultrasound measurements of jugular and lower extremity venous vasculature. Responses to Braslet-M device under nominal conditions and also during cardiopulmonary Mueller and Valsalva maneuvers were recorded and analyzed. Identical measurements were repeated without and with Braslet-M applied and a subset of data were collected during release of the occlusion device.
approach: The study protocol was conducted in 14 sessions on nine International Space Station (ISS) crewmembers, with an average exposure to microgravity of 122 days. All data were collected by ISS crewmembers with remote guidance. Baseline cardiovascular measurements were taken by echocardiography in multiple modes, including tissue Doppler of both ventricles and femoral and jugular vein imaging. The Braslet devices were then applied and measurements were repeated after greater than 10 minutes. The cuffs were then released and the hemodynamic “recovery” process was monitored. Actual experiments varied slightly to accommodate communication dropouts, hardware-related delays, and other operational nuances. Remotely guided examinations for the entire protocol were usually completed within a sixty minute time frame. Responses to Braslet-M device under nominal conditions and also during cardiopulmonary Mueller and Valsalva maneuvers were recorded and analyzed. Identical measurements were repeated without and with Braslet-M applied and a subset of data were collected during release of the occlusion device. The real time ultrasound video image and cabin video recorded the crew activity and displayed it to the experiment team in mission control. Data was recorded and stored on the ground during the scanning session, and selected higher resolution images were down linked from the ISS ultrasound following the experiment. All digital images were collected using Digital Imaging and Communications in the Medicine (DICOM) format. Complete analysis of the ultrasound measurements were performed following each scanning session. The real time ultrasound video was further reduced to individual video frames to analyze the dynamic changes seen in function, area, volume and flow during dynamic respiratory maneuvers, and at rest before and after the Braslet-M device. The DICOM imagery provided views to calculate changes in cardiac function after the application of the Braslet-M with and without respiratory maneuvers. Still images were analyzed using ProSolv CardioVascular analysis software. Data was analyzed at the same point in the cardiac cycle for three heart beats for each parameter and condition. These three data points were averaged to arrive at the value for that particular parameter and condition for each subject. These values were then averaged and reported as described in the
results: section of this report. A directed cardiac examination was performed to acquire the four chamber view of the heart. The primary cardiac window used for volume and Doppler was the apical four-chamber; when this view did not yield satisfactory images, the subcostal four chamber window was used. The remote guidance team made real-time decisions on what view should be used based on the limitations from each subject‘s physiology. The window that yielded the best view of all four chambers of the heart was eventually chosen. The probe was remotely guided by voice commands to achieve the desired images. Examination completeness was evaluated initially by the ground-based Braslet team consisting of two expert sonographers by viewing the real-time downlinked ultrasound video stream. Modified Valsalva and Mueller maneuvers were performed to initiate responses throughout the protocol. These maneuvers induced increased and decreased intrathoracic pressure, and initiated physiological changes as demonstrated by changes in the cross section areas of the veins, chamber sizes of the heart, and blood flow patterns. Respiratory maneuvers were performed using an ISS drinking straw to limit extreme pressures that might be caused by exerting against a closed glottis; this approach was taken as a safety measure. The straw effectively metered the air and allowed the crewmember to time the inhalation or expiration of air across the maneuver to roughly gauge the extent of the maneuver. Participants were asked to inhale or exhale through the straw for approximately 10 seconds, starting from a moderate lung volume. These respiratory maneuvers altered the cardiac loading in manner similar to changing posture in a gravity environment. RESULTS: Findings conclude that the Braslet device acutely reduced the effective circulating volume by sequestering fluid in the lower extremities, as directly observed by vascular ultrasound and supported by the reduced preload indexes measured by echocardiography. Vascular ultrasound confirmed reduced distention of the jugular venous system and increased sensitivity of the jugular vein area to thoracic maneuvers. These findings combined with subjective comments from crewmembers, suggest that the relative cranial venous insufficiency caused by microgravity is partially alleviated by the Braslet device. These respiratory maneuvers were shown to cause statistically significant hemodynamic effects. A statistically significant reduction in jugular venous (IJV) filling was also observed during Braslet application, which coupled with negative airway pressure to consistently collapse the IJV. Remotely guided ultrasound provided an effective and objective means of measuring the physiological effects of the Braslet and produced data quality that was superior to previous investigations in space. Fourteen of eighty-one conditions (27 parameters measured at baseline, Valsalva, and Mueller maneuver) were significantly different when the Braslet-M cuff was applied. Seven of twenty-seven parameters were found to respond differently to respiratory maneuvers depending on the presence or absence of thigh compression. The Valsalva and Mueller maneuvers appeared to enhance the ability at the microgravity bedside to determine volume status.

title: Vestibular Experiments
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: The Vestibular Experiments were planned by a team of researchers from the US and Canada to study the causes of space motion sickness (SMS) and associated sensory-motor adaptations to weightlessness. SMS symptoms have been consistently reported in the Soviet space program and were also seen in the Apollo and Skylab crews. In addition, incidence among Shuttle crews has exceeded 50 percent. Space motion sickness is now recognized as a significant problem affecting astronaut performance, safety, and well-being. Symptoms generally appear soon after insertion into orbit and range from malaise and irritability to nausea and severe vomiting. Many hypotheses attempt to explain the underlying causes of SMS and the majority of them focus on how the vestibular system is affected by microgravity. The vestibular system is responsible for our ability to sense changes in the speed and direction of bodily movement, even when our eyes are closed. We use information from the vestibular organs to walk, maintain an upright posture, and to see clearly as our head moves. The vestibular system consists of two similar vestibular organs located on either side of the head in the inner ear and it functions to maintain the body's balance by detecting the position and motion of the head. Each organ is made up of three semicircular canals and two otolithic organs which detect angular and linear accelerations, respectively. The otolithic organs depend on gravity to function properly; therefore, they are especially sensitive to microgravity conditions. The vestibular organs and the eyes work in conjunction to send signals to the brain, which then activates the appropriate muscles to keep the body balanced. According to the sensory-motor conflict theory, motion sickness
approach: Visual-Vestibular Interaction: The "Rotating Dome" experiment was designed to test the hypothesis that with increasing adaptation to weightlessness, crewmembers become increasingly dependent on visual and tactile cues as opposed to vestibular cues. The experiment hardware consists of a motor-driven rotating "dome" (drum) into which the subject’s head is placed. The visible surface of the dome was white and covered with randomly positioned colored dots. When the drum rotates, a sensation of self rotation in the direction opposite to that of drum rotation is felt. This tilting sensation causes a muscle reflex which attempts to turn the head back to a vertical position. Since the head is actually held stationary by a biteboard assembly, the neck torque produces counter rotation forces in the body. On Earth, the onset and strength of this sensation are thought to be inhibited by the lack of confirming motion signals from the vestibular organs. In microgravity, this inhibition should be reduced and thus researchers expected the crewmembers to feel a stronger sensation of self rotation. Each experimental run consisted of a series of six trials. For each trial, the dome rotated at a constant angular velocity of 30, 45, or 60 deg/s clockwise or counterclockwise for a period of 50 seconds (s) followed by a 10 s stationary pause separating the trials. Two separate sequences of trials, each with randomized speed and direction, were utilized in the study. Crewmembers were instructed to deflect a rotary knob "joystick" to indicate the speed and direction of their own perceived self-motion. Ocular torsion was measured with a video camera installed in the center of the rotating dome. Body sway data was recorded using a video camera with a back view of the subject and the rotating dome. Inflight, the above experiment procedure was also performed with the crewmember constrained in a bungee-cord harness. The harness was employed to produce tactile and proprioceptive forces on the legs, trunk and feet that the subject would feel in a 1-G environment. The "Rod and Frame" experiments also investigated visual-vestibular interaction by measuring static visual field dependence. The experiment tested the subject's ability to indicate the direction of the vertical as influenced by a tilted visual framework. The experiment was only performed pre- and postflight, since it's purpose was to determine if the increased dependence on static visual cues for orientation in space would carry over after flight. Subjects were seated in a chair in a dark room and viewed a dimly lit frame with sides 107 cm long by 2.5 cm wide surrounding a rod 99 cm long and 2.5 cm wide, located 180 cm from the subject. This frame was tilted to 28 degrees in either direction from the upright position. The subject told the experimenter to rotate the rod about a central axis until the subject judged it to be vertical. Angular deviation of the rod was measured by a potentiometer, and constituted the determination of field dependence. During each experimental session, four measurements were taken in each direction, as well as two control measurements without the frame. Otolith-Spinal Reflex: These experiments focused on the neural link between the otolith organs and the motor neurons of the spinal cord which control limb muscle activity. These neural pathways control the otolith-spinal reflex which is responsible for preparing the leg muscles for a landing from a fall. The experiments were set up to assess changes in the otolith-spinal system during and after prolonged exposure to microgravity. Researchers wanted to investigate how the otolith-spinal system adapts to a new sensory-motor environment, and how it readapts to gravity after landing. The protocol for the "Hop and Drop" experiments was designed to examine calf muscle responses during unexpected "falls" to see if the otolith contribution is altered and determine if the time course of this alteration correlates with other otolith response measures. Pre- and postflight falls were produced as the subject grasped a handle above his head, raised his feet, and then dropped to the floor as the handle was released. In the absence of gravity, the downward acceleration toward the Spacelab floor was provided by adjustable elastic cords which connected a torso harness to the Spacelab floor. A total of nine cords, grouped into 3 sets of 3, ran from the harness attachment points to the floor. When properly adjusted, they provided a downward force approximately equal to the subject's weight as he hung by his arms from the handle. By removing one elastic cord from each set the acceleration was reduced to 0.67 g, and by removing another from each set it was reduced further to 0.33 g. All data were collected in the first 150 milliseconds (ms) after release. The electromyographic (EMG) response was recorded from 2 surface electrodes located over the lower ends of the lateral and medial heads of the gastrocnemius of the left leg. A ground electrode was placed on the midline over the soleus 5-10 cm below the others. During inflight testing, head longitudinal acceleration was recorded using an accelerometer strapped to the subject's head and an electronics package worn at the waist. This signal was used to confirm both the times of onset of fall and of landing, and the magnitude of acceleration stimulus. Contact with the floor was detected by means of a ribbon switch attached under the subject's left foot. During pre- and postflight testing sessions, the onset of fall was detected by a microswitch located in the releasing device. Contact with the ground was determined using a series of ribbon switches located under a section of carpet upon which the subject landed. All test sessions included 45 falls, with a stimulus of 0.2 g for the first 15, 0.5 g for the next 15 and 1.0 g for the final 15. To achieve stimuli of less than 1.0 g during pre- and postflight testing, the subject wore a parachute harness which was attached to counterweights via a cable and pulley system. Awareness of Orientation and Limb Position: Many astronauts have reported that they lose their sense of "up" and "down" orientation with respect to the vehicle when their eyes are closed or when the lights are turned off. Researchers wanted to investigate this problem further by examining the role of limb position awareness in this orientation disturbance. On Earth, the central nervous system uses tactile and proprioceptive cues from the limbs to factor in the effect of gravity on the "up" and "down" orientation process. However, in microgravity the tactile and proprioceptive cues from the limbs may be altered, and researchers wanted to investigate the origins of the loss of spatial orientation. More specifically, they examined whether the disorientation occurs immediately after closing the eyes or whether it requires some time for the memory of orientation to "wash out". They also examined whether the loss of limb position awareness is caused by microgravity or sleep periods. Experiments were conducted in the Spacelab module in both a loosely and tightly tethered condition to control for the effects of tactile forces. Experiments were also conducted in the Orbiter middeck bunk area in order to make observations after sleep. Subjects were instructed to view the location of several different target objects placed on nearby walls, were blindfolded, and were then asked to describe the position of their limbs and to point accurately to the targets. Different intervals of time were measured between the time of blindfolding and the time of describing the position of their limbs. Posture Control: Researchers have found that exposure to microgravity causes postural difficulties both during microgravity and for several days postflight. The difficulties may be due to the changes in central processing of vestibular information that occur during prolonged exposure to microgravity. This study was designed to identify changes in electromyographic (EMG) latency and amplitudes that might explain the postural instabilities observed postflight. These experiments were only conducted before and after the 10 day Spacelab 1 mission. The "Posture Platform" experiments used a pneumatically driven platform to initiate changes in standing posture. Subjects wore hard soled shoes and were instructed to stand on the platform with their eyes open (or closed) facing a wall with head erect and legs straight. As the platform is suddenly tilted proprioceptive reflexes that normally stabilize posture are inappropriate to maintain stability. Therefore, the body relies on other sensory systems such as the vestibular organs to compensate for the disturbance in posture. Prior to testing, surface electrodes were placed over the tibialis anterior (TA) and the gastrocnemius-soleus (G-S) muscles of the left leg. The raw EMG signals from the ankle flexors (TA) and ankle extensors (G-S) were sampled for 10 s at 200 samples per second by a microcomputer that also controlled the movement of the platform. Six trials were performed consisting of a randomized set of three up and three down tilts of the platform with the eyes open, followed by a different randomized set of six trials with eyes closed. The EMG signals were later analyzed for latency, amplitude, and frequency of oscillation of the late, post 500 millisecond, response. The "Sharpened Romberg" test is a standardized procedure for measuring standing stability and posture. This test was also used as a method of evaluating the postflight postural instabilities of the Spacelab 1 crew. The experiments used two long rails (one narrow and one wide) mounted on wooden beams to conduct four different tests. (1) Narrow rail walking: The subject walked with arms folded in front, heel to toe, along the narrow rail for a maximum of six steps. (2) Narrow rail standing: The subject stood, eyes open, with arms folded, in the heel to toe position on the narrow rail for a maximum of 60 s per trial. (3) Wide rail standing/eyes closed: The subject stood heel to toe on the wide rail and when stable, closed his eyes. The position was maintained for a maximum of 60 s. (4) Wide rail standing/eyes open: The subject stood heel to toe on the wide rail for a maximum of 60 s with eyes open. All trials were terminated if the subject unfolded his arms or placed a foot on the floor. The operator measured the duration of the test or, in the case of the narrow rail walking test, the number of steps. Individual scores for each subject were the sum of the best three out of five trials for that test. Motion Sickness Susceptibility: The motion sickness susceptibility investigation involved a head movement/symptom monitoring experiment and pre- and postflight susceptibility tests which were designed to systematically collect data on the origins, prediction, symptoms, and prevention of the disorder. results: when incoming sensory signals to the brain no longer match expected patterns learned during previous sensory/motor experience. Exposure to microgravity affects the function of vestibular organs causing a mismatch in visual and vestibular signals which results in a sensory-motor conflict in the central nervous system (CNS). A good example of this occurs when a crewmember is floating weightless and upright in reference to the Shuttle's floor, but in reality he or she may be completely upside down due to microgravity. Accordingly, visual inputs in this situation would indicate the correct "up" and "down" orientation but the vestibular organs would not sense the correct orientation because they rely on gravity to function properly. Researchers believe that this sensory-motor conflict is the underlying mechanism responsible for SMS, illusions of motion, and spatial-orientation disturbances. These investigations were aimed at assessing human vestibular function and visual responses in space during the 10 day Spacelab 1 mission. Each experiment examined a different motor output to reveal some aspect of the way the CNS adapts to the altered vestibular inputs resulting from exposure to microgravity. The sensory reinterpretation hypothesis which served as a basis for all the experiments was divided into three working hypotheses as follows: (1) that as a result of sensory-motor experience in microgravity, otolith afferent signals are centrally inhibited or reinterpreted as indicating head translation rather than tilt, (2) that longitudinal (z-axis) reflex sensitivity to "falling" is decreased, (3) that visual and tactile cues should play an increasing role in spatial orientation. APPROACH: Visual-Vestibular Interaction: The "Rotating Dome" experiment was designed to test the hypothesis that with increasing adaptation to weightlessness, crewmembers become increasingly dependent on visual and tactile cues as opposed to vestibular cues. The experiment hardware consists of a motor-driven rotating "dome" (drum) into which the subject’s head is placed. The visible surface of the dome was white and covered with randomly positioned colored dots. When the drum rotates, a sensation of self rotation in the direction opposite to that of drum rotation is felt. This tilting sensation causes a muscle reflex which attempts to turn the head back to a vertical position. Since the head is actually held stationary by a biteboard assembly, the neck torque produces counter rotation forces in the body. On Earth, the onset and strength of this sensation are thought to be inhibited by the lack of confirming motion signals from the vestibular organs. In microgravity, this inhibition should be reduced and thus researchers expected the crewmembers to feel a stronger sensation of self rotation. Each experimental run consisted of a series of six trials. For each trial, the dome rotated at a constant angular velocity of 30, 45, or 60 deg/s clockwise or counterclockwise for a period of 50 seconds (s) followed by a 10 s stationary pause separating the trials. Two separate sequences of trials, each with randomized speed and direction, were utilized in the study. Crewmembers were instructed to deflect a rotary knob "joystick" to indicate the speed and direction of their own perceived self-motion. Ocular torsion was measured with a video camera installed in the center of the rotating dome. Body sway data was recorded using a video camera with a back view of the subject and the rotating dome. Inflight, the above experiment procedure was also performed with the crewmember constrained in a bungee-cord harness. The harness was employed to produce tactile and proprioceptive forces on the legs, trunk and feet that the subject would feel in a 1-G environment. The "Rod and Frame" experiments also investigated visual-vestibular interaction by measuring static visual field dependence. The experiment tested the subject's ability to indicate the direction of the vertical as influenced by a tilted visual framework. The experiment was only performed pre- and postflight, since it's purpose was to determine if the increased dependence on static visual cues for orientation in space would carry over after flight. Subjects were seated in a chair in a dark room and viewed a dimly lit frame with sides 107 cm long by 2.5 cm wide surrounding a rod 99 cm long and 2.5 cm wide, located 180 cm from the subject. This frame was tilted to 28 degrees in either direction from the upright position. The subject told the experimenter to rotate the rod about a central axis until the subject judged it to be vertical. Angular deviation of the rod was measured by a potentiometer, and constituted the determination of field dependence. During each experimental session, four measurements were taken in each direction, as well as two control measurements without the frame. Otolith-Spinal Reflex: These experiments focused on the neural link between the otolith organs and the motor neurons of the spinal cord which control limb muscle activity. These neural pathways control the otolith-spinal reflex which is responsible for preparing the leg muscles for a landing from a fall. The experiments were set up to assess changes in the otolith-spinal system during and after prolonged exposure to microgravity. Researchers wanted to investigate how the otolith-spinal system adapts to a new sensory-motor environment, and how it readapts to gravity after landing. The protocol for the "Hop and Drop" experiments was designed to examine calf muscle responses during unexpected "falls" to see if the otolith contribution is altered and determine if the time course of this alteration correlates with other otolith response measures. Pre- and postflight falls were produced as the subject grasped a handle above his head, raised his feet, and then dropped to the floor as the handle was released. In the absence of gravity, the downward acceleration toward the Spacelab floor was provided by adjustable elastic cords which connected a torso harness to the Spacelab floor. A total of nine cords, grouped into 3 sets of 3, ran from the harness attachment points to the floor. When properly adjusted, they provided a downward force approximately equal to the subject's weight as he hung by his arms from the handle. By removing one elastic cord from each set the acceleration was reduced to 0.67 g, and by removing another from each set it was reduced further to 0.33 g. All data were collected in the first 150 milliseconds (ms) after release. The electromyographic (EMG) response was recorded from 2 surface electrodes located over the lower ends of the lateral and medial heads of the gastrocnemius of the left leg. A ground electrode was placed on the midline over the soleus 5-10 cm below the others. During inflight testing, head longitudinal acceleration was recorded using an accelerometer strapped to the subject's head and an electronics package worn at the waist. This signal was used to confirm both the times of onset of fall and of landing, and the magnitude of acceleration stimulus. Contact with the floor was detected by means of a ribbon switch attached under the subject's left foot. During pre- and postflight testing sessions, the onset of fall was detected by a microswitch located in the releasing device. Contact with the ground was determined using a series of ribbon switches located under a section of carpet upon which the subject landed. All test sessions included 45 falls, with a stimulus of 0.2 g for the first 15, 0.5 g for the next 15 and 1.0 g for the final 15. To achieve stimuli of less than 1.0 g during pre- and postflight testing, the subject wore a parachute harness which was attached to counterweights via a cable and pulley system. Awareness of Orientation and Limb Position: Many astronauts have reported that they lose their sense of "up" and "down" orientation with respect to the vehicle when their eyes are closed or when the lights are turned off. Researchers wanted to investigate this problem further by examining the role of limb position awareness in this orientation disturbance. On Earth, the central nervous system uses tactile and proprioceptive cues from the limbs to factor in the effect of gravity on the "up" and "down" orientation process. However, in microgravity the tactile and proprioceptive cues from the limbs may be altered, and researchers wanted to investigate the origins of the loss of spatial orientation. More specifically, they examined whether the disorientation occurs immediately after closing the eyes or whether it requires some time for the memory of orientation to "wash out". They also examined whether the loss of limb position awareness is caused by microgravity or sleep periods. Experiments were conducted in the Spacelab module in both a loosely and tightly tethered condition to control for the effects of tactile forces. Experiments were also conducted in the Orbiter middeck bunk area in order to make observations after sleep. Subjects were instructed to view the location of several different target objects placed on nearby walls, were blindfolded, and were then asked to describe the position of their limbs and to point accurately to the targets. Different intervals of time were measured between the time of blindfolding and the time of describing the position of their limbs. Posture Control: Researchers have found that exposure to microgravity causes postural difficulties both during microgravity and for several days postflight. The difficulties may be due to the changes in central processing of vestibular information that occur during prolonged exposure to microgravity. This study was designed to identify changes in electromyographic (EMG) latency and amplitudes that might explain the postural instabilities observed postflight. These experiments were only conducted before and after the 10 day Spacelab 1 mission. The "Posture Platform" experiments used a pneumatically driven platform to initiate changes in standing posture. Subjects wore hard soled shoes and were instructed to stand on the platform with their eyes open (or closed) facing a wall with head erect and legs straight. As the platform is suddenly tilted proprioceptive reflexes that normally stabilize posture are inappropriate to maintain stability. Therefore, the body relies on other sensory systems such as the vestibular organs to compensate for the disturbance in posture. Prior to testing, surface electrodes were placed over the tibialis anterior (TA) and the gastrocnemius-soleus (G-S) muscles of the left leg. The raw EMG signals from the ankle flexors (TA) and ankle extensors (G-S) were sampled for 10 s at 200 samples per second by a microcomputer that also controlled the movement of the platform. Six trials were performed consisting of a randomized set of three up and three down tilts of the platform with the eyes open, followed by a different randomized set of six trials with eyes closed. The EMG signals were later analyzed for latency, amplitude, and frequency of oscillation of the late, post 500 millisecond, response. The "Sharpened Romberg" test is a standardized procedure for measuring standing stability and posture. This test was also used as a method of evaluating the postflight postural instabilities of the Spacelab 1 crew. The experiments used two long rails (one narrow and one wide) mounted on wooden beams to conduct four different tests. (1) Narrow rail walking: The subject walked with arms folded in front, heel to toe, along the narrow rail for a maximum of six steps. (2) Narrow rail standing: The subject stood, eyes open, with arms folded, in the heel to toe position on the narrow rail for a maximum of 60 s per trial. (3) Wide rail standing/eyes closed: The subject stood heel to toe on the wide rail and when stable, closed his eyes. The position was maintained for a maximum of 60 s. (4) Wide rail standing/eyes open: The subject stood heel to toe on the wide rail for a maximum of 60 s with eyes open. All trials were terminated if the subject unfolded his arms or placed a foot on the floor. The operator measured the duration of the test or, in the case of the narrow rail walking test, the number of steps. Individual scores for each subject were the sum of the best three out of five trials for that test. The cart was positioned at the center or end of the track and a step acceleration was then applied to the cart. A step deceleration was applied after the cart had traveled one quarter of the track. (2) CLOAT: This test measured the subject's ability to use linear acceleration cues to perform a manual control task. During CLOAT the subject made use of otolith sensory information in a closed loop sensorimotor nulling task where the motor function (hand manipulation of a joystick) was presumed relatively unaffected by exposure to microgravity. The subject was in control of sled velocity using a joystick. A disturbance motion was generated by the computer and combined with the subject's control. The disturbance consisted of a random appearing velocity profile made up of 12 logarithmically spaced sinusoids added together lasting 82 s. The subject's task was to try to nullify the disturbance motion by holding the cart still, thereby closing the loop. CLOAT was performed once in the light and three times in the dark for each test session. The resultant sled velocity profiles in the dark were averaged in the frequency domain before further analysis was performed. (3) Dynamic ocular torsion: This test isolated the gravitoinertial contribution to dynamic ocular counterrolling. The inability to distinguish between gravitational and inertial forces results in an ocular torsion response to lateral acceleration with the head upright. In this case, the gravitoinertial force vector, rather than the pure gravitational force vector, is rotated with respect to the head. The orientation of the head remains fixed and no rotational accelerations impinge on the head. Sinusoidal oscillation of amplitude 0.61 g was used at two frequencies, 0.42 Hz and 0.83 Hz, for 12 and 15 cycles, respectively. Torsional eye position was obtained by correlation and trigonometric analysis of eye and head position in photographs obtained with a camera. Photographs were taken at a rate of 2.5 frames per second. Eye torsional position was derived from two landmarks obtained from either naturally occurring landmarks in the iris or marked contact lenses adhered to the eye by a drop of distilled water.
