During a simulated extra-vehicular exploration on planetary surface, performance was compared with different types of displays for aiding navigation (NavAid): a 3D spatial auditory navigation aid (NavAid), a 2D North-Up visual map, and the combination of the two in a bimodal NavAid. Four different environmental conditions were tested combining high and low levels of visibility and ambiguity. To facilitate comparison with the previous work, performance was analyzed separately for the Single Task and Dual Task studies, and then compared between the two tasks for all the independent variables (factors). For both studies, the quantitative dependent variables were: percent correct orientation, left/right decision time, localization accuracy, and localization time. Qualitative measures (subjective ratings) were also collected after the experiment. Study 2 Docking Task Method: In the second study, a single-task paradigm was used that involved performing a docking task associated with telerobotic planetary exploration on Mars (linkage of a remotely controlled vehicle to a surface habitat). Three different types of docking aids (DockAid) analogous to the NavAids of the previous studies were evaluated: a 2D visual DockAid, an auditory DockAid, and a combined bimodal DockAid. The experiment investigated the impact of display modality of the docking aids on operator performance (docking accuracy and response time) with increased workload introduced via additional control latencies ranging from 0 to 1000 msec. Performance was also assessed under high and low visibility conditions. The quantitative dependent measures were docking accuracy (radial distance between the centers of the targeting reticle and the docking target) and the docking response time. Qualitative measures (subjective ratings) were also collected after the experiment. RESULTS: Study 1 Dual Task Results: Overall for Single Task and Dual Task, the bimodal NavAid was associated with the best performance, both in terms of correct orientation and response times. For orientation, the auditory information channel proved to be an efficient countermeasure to the conflict generated by the difference between egocentric and allocentric reference frames in the displays tested. For localization, an “audio locator” display also greatly facilitated accuracy and response time in localization. Taken together, the observations made for Single Task were corroborated in Dual Task and, in fact, the bimodal advantage was more pronounced under high visual workload. Study 2 Docking Task Results: On-time docking accuracy was greater in the bimodal condition than in the best unimodal condition, again supporting some form of positive multisensory effect. The apparent difficulty of a purely auditory docking evidenced by longer docking times was contradicted by the high rate of accurate docking (94% total, 54% on-time) and shows that the learning curve for processing of spatialized auditory sonification is very quick. As expected, the introduction of latencies was associated with performance degradation. However, this effect was shown to be modality specific, and the presence of auditory cues provided some degree of protection against the negative impact of latencies of 500 ms or less. This performance inflection point may be related to the limits of a “cognitive horizon” for teleoperation in space, i.e., a latency limit of ~500 ms beyond which performance degrades, as described by Lester & Thronson (2011). Conclusions: Overall, the results of both studies support the idea of integrating 3D audio into displays to aid extravehicular activity on planetary surfaces for tasks as diverse as orientation, localization, or docking. Spatial auditory displays can aid situational awareness, navigation, and way finding by reducing the risk of errors and response latencies. Alone, the auditory system provides a reliable alternate channel of information in cases where the visual information is degraded or unavailable. In particular, it may mitigate the deleterious effects of the relatively small latencies present during lunar telerobotic control from Lagrange points or from Mars orbit during future surface exploration and control missions. When auditory information is provided in synergy with the visual channel, bimodal performance usually exceeds that of the best unimodal display. This multisensory enhancement proved to be inversely proportional to the reliability of the individual sensory inputs (inverse effectiveness effect, Meredith and Stein, 1986). Recommendations for Guidelines: The results presented here demonstrate that spatial audio displays, both alone and in combination with a visual display, enhance performance and situational awareness, mitigate the impact of visual environment degradation and increased workload, and add to the intuitiveness of the information display: User acceptability for 3D audio is very high. 3D audio provides an intuitive, ecological, and low-workload solution for the presentation of spatial information. 3D audio can be used to efficiently substitute for visual information that is missing or degraded, when workload is increased, and as an effective countermeasure for mental remapping. In the orientation/localization task, bimodal presentation of the auditory DockAid and the visual DockAid spatial information leads to a significant reduction of incorrect orientation responses and a reduction in decision times. The use of an auditory localizer, a type of dynamic sonification display, has proved its efficacy, particularly under degraded visual conditions. The results of the docking task study indicate that bimodal displays can also mitigate the negative impact of workload in the form of moderate (= 500 msec) control latencies. The docking study represents a proof of concept for a purely auditory docking aid. While the auditory aid took longer compared to the visual aid, the fact that accurate auditory docking only required ~30 sec suggests that a purely auditory DockAid is a viable display solution. Thus, it is recommended that bimodal and/or multimodal displays be used for EVA missions. It is increasingly evident that the auditory channel will need to convey spatial information about localization and navigation in an environment where the visual channel is already saturated by the display of symbology and checklists. The ecological validity of using sound for localization, combined with the possibility of learning to use virtual auditory signals to navigate between virtual waypoints, support their integration in advanced EVA display systems. Similarly, the viability of auditory and/or bimodal aids for tasks such as docking argue for their application to closed-loop tasks involving moderate control latencies. The integration of alternative ways to present information brings up additional questions such as the best methods for switching between different modes within and/or between the different sensory channels that have been made available to the operator. Issues that must be investigated include that: the use of each sensory channel must be prescribed for a given type of activity; the different functions available cannot overlap; and the sensory channels must combine appropriately to contribute to a reduction of the overall workload while increasing the sense of presence and situation awareness. For example, 3D audio could provide a higher level of immersion and improved perception of the 6 degree of freedom operational space. The combination of spatial and/or moving sound images with visual stimuli may increase vection and improve the sense of spatial presence as well as mitigating spatial disorientation. Two potential benefits may be of particular interest: (1) providing immediate feedback on operator location as well as the actions performed in space, and (2) providing an auditory “frame of reference” such as an artificial auditory horizon combined with “auditory security boundaries” that define the crew’s position in space in relation to the external features of the environment. Further, during training, the use of spatial audio could provide an additional countermeasure against cyber-sickness (nausea, disorientation, and oculomotor disturbances) induced by scene oscillation along the different axes of motion (pitch, roll, and yaw). Finally, future investigation of multimodal displays for surface exploration should be extended to the use of tactile displays, for example, in emergency situations requiring coordinated communications between multiple personnel where both the visual and auditory channels may be overloaded.

title: Spacesuit Trauma Countermeasure System for Intravehicular and Extravehicular Activities
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Extravehicular Activity (EVA) is a critical component of human space flight. Working in gas-pressurized space suits, however,
approach: Investigators analyzed data for correlations between anthropometry, space suit components, and shoulder injury. They also analyzed human-space suit interaction during EVAs. The musculoskeletal analysis developed provided new insights into the human musculoskeletal performance inside the space suit, and contributed to the assessment of astronaut health and safety during EVA.
results: in numerous challenges, causing fatigue, unnecessary energy expenditure, and injury. These problems are exacerbated with the additional hours astronauts spend training inside the suit, especially underwater in the Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory (NBL). Although the U.S. has studied space suit performance and improved upon system designs, relatively little is known about how the astronaut moves and interacts with the space suit, what factors lead to injury, and how to prevent injury. The objective of this research is to develop an understanding of how the person interacts with the space suit, and use that information to design personalized solutions to mitigate injury. This will be achieved through the following specific aims. Specific Aim 1: Analyze data for correlations between anthropometry, space suit components, and injury. The investigators’ work compiles all known open source injury information from the literature to create an EVA specific database. They then focus on analyzing the most up to date EVA injury database currently used by NASA. The database currently includes information regarding each subject and their selected space suit components. Anthropometric dimensions, spacesuit components, and all recorded EVA injuries will be included in an updated database because a mismatch between body dimensions and suit sizes is hypothesized as a causal mechanism for injury. Data mining techniques will be used to find correlations between anthropometry, suit components, and injury. Specific Aim 2: Develop a pressure-sensing garment. The investigators will develop a pressure- or force-sensing garment worn by astronauts inside the space suit. The pressure-sensing garment will be worn to quantify the locations on the body where the person impacts the space suit to move it. This suit is beneficial to many stakeholders, such as spacesuit designers, engineers, researchers, flight surgeons, and exercise and rehabilitation specialists. In our project, the data will be used to determine areas of discomfort and impingement, which are prone to injury. Additionally, the sensing capability can be used determine the effectiveness of protective devices (Specific Aim 4). Specific Aim 3: Model human-spacesuit interaction. A human-space suit model will be used to understand the biomechanics of movement in a spacesuit. It will be used to quantify changes between unsuited and suited conditions leading to injury. In addition, the human-space suit model will elucidate the differences in the astronaut biomechanics once suit modifications and protective devices (Specific Aim 4) have been implemented. Specific Aim 4: Develop modular protective devices. The ultimate objective of this work is to develop solutions to mitigate injury. The protective devices will alleviate injury prone areas and adjust the person’s placement within the suit to improve suit fit. They will be integrated to the space suit and protective garments can be personalized for each crewmember. APPROACH: Investigators analyzed data for correlations between anthropometry, space suit components, and shoulder injury. They also analyzed human-space suit interaction during EVAs. The musculoskeletal analysis developed provided new insights into the human musculoskeletal performance inside the space suit, and contributed to the assessment of astronaut health and safety during EVA. RESULTS: Specific Aim 1: Statistical Shoulder Injury Analysis. The first specific aim is to analyze data for correlations between anthropometry, space suit components, and shoulder injury. Four hypotheses were proposed to relate injury to 1) body morphologies, 2) space suit HUT components, 3) training variables, and 4) previous injury. Each hypothesis was confirmed, since for both models variables for each of the first three hypotheses were identified and record of previous injury was associated with the Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory (NBL) model. The major contributions of this work are to: 1) Add quantitative statistical analysis to the causal mechanisms of injury found in the literature. 2) Provide a framework for identifying relevant predictor variables related to injury given the small number of data points, large number of predictor variables, and the differences in their distributions. 3) Identify variables related to injury which can be addressed and resolved through operational changes to training, suit design and accommodation, and identification of higher risk subjects given previous medical history. 4) Propose future areas of study for which additional data may continue to be collected and analyzed, such as HUT sizing information as related to clearance anthropometry. Specific Aim 2: Experimental Evaluation of Human-space Suit Interaction. Development of a wearable pressure sensing garment. The novel Polipo low-pressure sensing system for extreme environments achieved here has many advantages. With the Polipo human-suit interaction can be measured for the first time through dynamic movement. It can accurately measure low-pressures against the body over underneath the soft-goods. The system of 12 sensors is transferrable between many different people, creating an independent stand-alone pressure-sensing system. Sensors can easily be changed to allow for improved designs or to accommodate different target pressures. The wiring was intentionally designed to achieve the best trade-off between flexibility, resistance, and stretch ability. The system achieves near shirt-sleeve mobility as sensors are moved to accommodate users. It can also be used in conjunction with a high-pressure sensing mat placed over the shoulder to measure loading between the person and HUT. The electronics architecture allows for low power onboard or real-time data collection. The entire system has been designed with extreme environments in mind, where considerations of shock, battery hazards, and material properties in mixed gas environments were minimized to ensure user safety. Finally, it has a cover shirt to slide easily over the system and prevent catching and ensure proper placement. Nearly all requirements were met and those that were not were evaluated for extent of their impact on the system performance. Therefore, this work confirms Design Requirement 1 “A pressure sensing tool will achieve both high wearability and high utility in a space suit environment.” This system could easily be extrapolated to other environments where biomechanics and comfort under load needs to be evaluated, for example, soldier pack accommodation or wearable protective devices for the elderly where discomfort substantially decreases compliance. Specific Aim 3: Human-Space Suit Interaction Modeling. A new framework has been developed to analyze human-space suit interaction during EVA. The musculoskeletal analysis being developed will provide new insights into the human musculoskeletal performance inside the space suit, and will contribute to the assessment of astronaut health and safety during EVA. Ongoing research includes analysis of data in the MarkIII-suited conditions, together with knee flexion/extension motion capture data from subjects wearing the EMU and MKIII collected at Johnson Space Center. Future work includes refining the space suit model by incorporating EMU torques in other joints, and using a more accurate human musculoskeletal model that contains musculotendon actuators in the upper torso and arms. Specific Aim 4: Prototype Design. The present injury of astronauts during training and space operations are significant. Some injuries are mild, such as skin being chafed or irritated; others are more severe, such as sprains, torn muscles or ligaments. The preventive protecting system being used today provides the astronaut with foam pads sometimes layered with a rigid Teflon sheet. These vary in thickness depending on the size of the astronauts, and their physical relationship to the space suit. Although this system has proved to be effective, astronauts still report pain, and are getting injured.

title: Morphological, Histochemical and Ultrastructural Characteristics of Skeletal Muscle
variables: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), intrinsic back muscles
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: When crewmembers make the transition from Earth's gravity to the weightlessness of space, they have to adapt to moving around in space and be able to determine their orientation as they move. Normal activities on Earth require the brain to interpret and integrate information coming from all the body's senses. This information is used to give feedback to the body on how the limbs are positioned, how the entire body is oriented, and which muscles need to be moved if reorientation or repositioning is desired. Loss of muscle mass and strength in the lower extremities was noted as a consequence of exposure to microgravity in reports from Gemini, Apollo, and Skylab programs. Indirect evidence of increased muscle catabolism in humans during space flight has included elevated urinary amino acids, nitrogen, phosphorus and negative potassium balance. At the gross level, decreased circumferential size of the lower extremities has been recorded in American astronauts and Soviet cosmonauts. Preflight and inflight countermeasures have not been completely effective in ameliorating the loss of muscle tissue and development of associated muscle weakness in all crewmembers. While it appears to date that the decrease in muscular function has not compromised the performance of astronauts except possibly during extravehicular activity, longer duration exposure to microgravity including extended (>14 day) Shuttle missions, Space Station habitation, and manned interplanetary flights are anticipated to induce significant muscle atrophy. This will require the development and implementation of appropriate and effective countermeasures to prevent or ameliorate muscle atrophy in order to assure crew health and safety. approach: MRI was performed on a Siemens 1.5 Tesla Magnetom either in Houston, Texas, at the Texas Medical Center/Methodist Hospital or in Moscow, Russia at the Cardiology Research Center. Computer software was used to produce preflight- and postflight-acquired 2-D images that were volume representations of the muscles and intervertebral discs. Phantoms were used judiciously to allow for corrections in pixel sizes between measurement sessions at both locations. In order to minimize fluid shifts caused by assumption of a recumbent position after being upright, the subject was required to lie down for 6-10 minutes before the start of data acquisition, and the order of measurements was consistent during each session. The feet were held static by strapping them to a Lean holder during image acquisition. The portion of the lower limb under analysis was suspended by placing supporting materials on either side of the imaged area. This allows the anatomical area of interest to assume a natural and reproducible shape rather than being distorted by its own weight. A radio frequency (RF) shield was positioned caudally to the imaged portions of the leg. For the thigh and calf muscles, thirty-two one-millimeter slice images were obtained using a Te=10 milliseconds, Tr=0.8 seconds and a 256 x 512 matrix. For the back muscles, a similar protocol was used, except twenty 0.5-centimeter image slices were obtained. For images of the cervical neck muscles, a Helmholtz neck coil was used in place of the spine coil. Biochemical assessment of muscle dysfunction and damage were obtained before, during and after flight by venous blood samples taken by standard venipuncture technique or via indwelling venous catheters. Total creatine phosphokinase activity was determined on a Beckman CX5 clinical chemistry instrument using a commercially available assay based upon the conversion of NADP to NADPH. Myoglobin concentrations in venous serum samples were determined with a commercially available system (OPUS) utilizing a 2 site or "sandwich" fluorogenic enzyme linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). Preflight and postflight comparison of dry lean mass was done using a 3-component model of body composition: 1) total body water (TBW) 2) lean body mass (hydrostatic densitometry) 3) fat mass (hydrostatic densitometry) Hydrostatic weighing was performed in a water tank and weight measurements were made during maximal pulmonary exhalation; lung residual volume was determined by a standard oxygen dilution technique. TBW values determined by the doubly labeled water (DLW) technique were obtained from the Fluid and Electrolyte experiment on Mir 18 and details of the assay can be found in that report. An exercise log recorded the type and amount of exercise performed 120 days before, during, and 30 days after flight, as well as exercise performance data, and any other countermeasures that were used (required for correlation with morphological and biochemical studies).

Myoglobin concentrations in venous serum samples were determined with a commercially available system (OPUS) utilizing a 2 site or "sandwich" fluorogenic enzyme linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). Preflight and postflight comparison of dry lean mass was done using a 3-component model of body composition: 1) total body water (TBW) 2) lean body mass (hydrostatic densitometry) 3) fat mass (hydrostatic densitometry) Hydrostatic weighing was performed in a water tank and weight measurements were made during maximal pulmonary exhalation; lung residual volume was determined by a standard oxygen dilution technique. TBW values determined by the doubly labeled water (DLW) technique were obtained from the Fluid and Electrolyte experiment on Mir 18 and details of the assay can be found in that report. An exercise log recorded the type and amount of exercise performed 120 days before, during, and 30 days after flight, as well as exercise performance data, and any other countermeasures that were used (required for correlation with morphological and biochemical studies). RESULTS: Preflight measurements originally scheduled for the L-60 (60 days before launch) to L-45 timeframe were delayed until L-30. This actually improves the value of the science since the analyses were performed closer to the launch date. Postflight measurements were not performed until R+2 (2 days after landing) or R+3. Although measurements taken as close to R+0 are optimal, this should have little effect on the value of the science. It was not possible to schedule both R+0 and R+14 postflight hydrostatic weighing sessions because of intense postflight science and crew rehabilitation activities. It was elected to schedule one session between the two requested postflight days. Subject 1 declined to participate in the hydrostatic weighing session and the data collection from Subject 2 was suboptimal. Subject 3 did complete the session. Since Subject 1 declined to participate, this portion of the science was extremely compromised and it was elected not to conduct further sessions on other crewmembers. Only a partial data set for Subject 3 was obtained and that was analyzed for comparison to muscle losses demonstrated by MRI. Additionally, Subjects 1 and 2 both declined to participate in the recovery MRI studies at R+56. This was extremely unfortunate as little is known about the recovery rate of muscle loss after long-duration space flight. With the exception of the above stated preflight and postflight anomalies, all data collection was completed. Inflight blood samples for creatine phosphokinase and myoglobin were originally withdrawn from the protocol because of concern about total inflight blood volumes. It was possible to perform these analyses on serum remaining after all other blood analyses were completed for other experiments. These data compliment the preflight and postflight blood data. Averages of two preflight measurements were compared to postflight measurements made 2 to 3 days after landing. Significance of comparisons was determined with student's t-test, p Anterolateral compartment -15 + 3 Gastrocnemius -18 + 1 Soleus -18 + 4 Quadriceps -11 + 3 Intrinsic lower back -18 + 4 Psoas -7 + 4 (not significant) Venous blood data did not support the presence of significant ongoing muscle damage in the inflight and immediate postflight period. With data from only three subjects, it is perilous to draw more than preliminary conclusions. However, the collective data reasonably supports loss of muscle mass during long-duration space flight even though participation in a highly structured inflight exercise protocol was a crew requirement. In this particular flight, the amount of exercise that was completed by each crewmember evidently was quite variable but the muscle losses in all three crewmembers were similar. Certainly, one of the most important conclusions that can be drawn is that the loss of muscle mass during microgravity exposure does not appear to be purely a linear response with respect to time. Short flights (5-11 days) have resulted in up to a 10% loss in some muscles, while the amount of loss nearly doubled that in this 115-day flight. The precise impact of the exercise program on countering muscle atrophy is not known as no studies of long-duration space missions have been performed on crewmembers that have not exercised during their period of microgravity exposure. Venous blood samples collected at various periods during flight and analyzed for creative phosphokinase activity and myoglobin do not support muscle damage during flight as a contributing factor to loss of muscle volume and function. Body composition data obtained in one crewmember showed an approximate 20% reduction in dry lean mass. This correlated well with the volume losses measured in the muscles of the back and legs which collectively contribute the bulk of muscle mass and thus dry, lean weight. It was suspected that measurements of neck muscle volume would reveal a loss of muscle volume, particularly in the posterior cervical extensors, since head bobbing has been observed in motion analysis studies of crewmembers upon return and weakness of neck muscles has been described and measured. It appears that since the neck muscles are small by comparison to the other measured muscles, the sensitivity of volume measurements for these muscles may not be sufficiently sensitive and the reproducibility of measuring such small volume (50-60 cc) muscles is poor. Thus, although it was not possible to show loss of cervical neck muscle volume, there is still good reason to suspect that atrophy of these muscle groups occurs. Alternative protocols and perhaps methods may be required to make measurements that are sufficiently precise to allow statistically significant comparisons.

title: Reliability of the DAMEC Portable Pulmonary Function System (PPFS)
variables: Fractions of expired oxygen and carbon dioxide
Carbon dioxide, metabolic gas analyzer system
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: The National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Human Research Program’s Integrated Research Plan specifies that acquisition of data regarding the changes in maximum exercise oxygen consumption (VO2max) during and following space flight is a high priority to support future space exploration endeavors. In order to support such measurements, a metabolic gas analysis system capable of being used in a spacecraft is required. One such device, known as the Pulmonary Function System, was developed for International Space Station (ISS) use and was validated in the Exercise Physiology Laboratory at NASA-Johnson Space Center (JSC). The PFS is currently being used to support studies of resting metabolism and cardiac function on board the ISS, but is not portable and is confined to a relatively immobile rack location. The exercise equipment on board the ISS changed locations since earlier expeditions, and the cycle ergometer used for exercise testing was moved to a different module than the PFS. Thus, the need for a portable metabolic gas analysis device for ISS use arose. The Portable Pulmonary Function System (PPFS) was developed by a contractor to the European Space Agency (ESA) to fill this need. The PPFS is a sized-optimized variant of the PFS which is capable of being used in any location on board the ISS that has available power and data connections. A NASA sponsored validation study of the PPFS was conducted in 2009 (EORS_PPFS), prior to its delivery to the ISS. The general findings of that study were that the PPFS yielded metabolic gas analysis values fairly comparable to a well-validated clinical system, and where statistically significant differences did occur, they were not large enough to be of clinical relevance. However, the reproducibility of the PPFS remained untested. In addition, the validation findings suggested that expired carbon dioxide (FECO2) when measured with the PPFS may differ from that measured by the clinical reference system. Because the validation study design precluded simultaneous measurements of either expired oxygen (FEO2) or FECO2 from both devices, this finding was speculative. The purpose of the current study was to examine the reliability and intra-subject repeatability of PPFS obtained metabolic gas analysis and cardiovascular data during exercise tests which contained both steady-state submaximal stages and maximal exertion levels. In addition, a portion of the current study was designed to obtain PPFS and reference system values of FEO2 and FECO2 in a manner which would allow direct comparison of the data.
approach: Eight healthy subjects volunteered to participate in this study. Subjects passed a modified Air Force Class III physical exam prior to participation and received written and verbal explanations of test protocols before providing written informed consent. The NASA Johnson Space Center Committee for the Protection of Human Subjects reviewed and approved the test protocols and procedures. The cycle ergometer used for all testing was a LODE Excalibur Sport (Groningen, NL). Prior to the exercise test sessions, the subjects completed an overnight fast and consumed a standardized dietary supplement (Ensure ® ) approximately 2 hours prior to testing which was performed in the morning, typically between 0830 and 1000. The Ensure ® was given to insure that none of the subjects consumed either an extremely high fat or high carbohydrate meal prior to their tests as dietary extremes have been demonstrated to effect metabolic gas analysis
results: , particularly the respiratory exchange ratio (RER=VCO2/VO2). None of the subjects performed heavy exercise in the 24 hours prior to the testing sessions and refrained from caffeine consumption for 12 hours prior to testing. Subjects performed an initial peak cycle test protocol identical to that used by NASA to determine pre-flight VO2max of astronauts prior to participating in an ISS mission. Subjects with a body mass of > 65 kg were to cycle for 3 min at 50, 100 and 150 Watts (W) followed by stepwise increases of 25 W/min until peak exertion was reached. If the subject’s body mass was © (PM) system was used to perform metabolic gas analysis. For each subject, the VO2 and work rate data from this test was used to prescribe the protocol for PPFS reliability exercise testing. To obtain data regarding the reproducibility of PPFS metabolic gas measurements during exercise, each subject performed three repeated trials. The cycle exercise testing protocol, identical to that used for the current ISS VO2max study consisted of 3, 5-minute stages designed to elicit 25%, 50%, and 75% of the individual’s previously determined VO2max. These stages were followed by stepwise increases of 25W/min work rate until subjects reached volitional exhaustion. These tests were conducted within one month after the initial test, and were separated by at least a week in order to minimize the potential effects of residual soreness or fatigue. No more than 3 weeks elapsed between trials within a subject. Each subject was instructed not to substantially vary their physical activities between trials. For all the reliability trials, prior to the start of exercise the subjects rested quietly for 5 minutes in the seated position on the ergometer while resting measurements of heart rate (HR) and rhythm and blood pressure (BP) were taken. HR and rhythm were measured electrocardiographically using the PPFS, which has an ECG incorporated into the device. HR and metabolic expired gas were measured continuously throughout the exercise test protocol. During the last minute of seated rest, and the last minute of each of the first 3 exercise stages, a non-invasive measurement of cardiac output was obtained. RESULTS: The PPFS appears in practically all respects to yield highly reliable metabolic gas analysis data. The lower reliability of RER measurements are commonly reported in the literature and likely are not a function of the PPFS device per se. Further examination of PPFS CO2 versus PM CO2 data is warranted to precisely quantify this relationship. The PPFS should provide accurate data when utilized to study the adaptations and responses of humans to exposure to the space flight environment.

archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: The Short Radius Centrifuge (SRC) was a NASA developed system used for research into the effects of artificial gravity as a potential countermeasure to the deleterious effects of microgravity on the human body. The SRC was located at the University of Texas Medical Branch at Galveston (UTMB) along with the UTMB/NASA bed rest facility. The artificial gravity employed in this experiment was produced by spinning subjects on a short-radius, human rated centrifuge. The centrifuge radius was 3.0 m, and it contained two subject stations oriented 180 degrees apart from each. The subject stations were rigidly mounted to the centrifuge hub, which was capable of rotating on a bearing. The centrifuge motion was driven by a computer-controlled electric motor, and the rotation profiles were created and controlled via rotator controller software. Ramp-up and ramp-down accelerations were controlled via this software interface, enabling the rotator to come to a complete stop from maximum rotation speed in less than 10 seconds.
approach: For centrifuge protocols, subjects may spin on the centrifuge alone or with another test subject. The subjects were positioned on their backs in one of the two subject stations with their feet against the foot plate. The subject was secured to the centrifuge with a safety harness, but the subject station was unlocked so that it freely glided over a range of 10 cm on a set of bearings, allowing subjects to 'stand' against the footplate and ensuring the full load of the centrifugal force was borne by the subjects' feet. The centrifuge design allowed for a 6 degree head down tilt or horizontal orientation of the subject. The 6 degree head-down tilt orientation was used in the pilot study because control subjects were transported to the centrifuge each day, and were required this orientation to avoid fluid shifts that would likely occur if a horizontal orientation were used. The subject was positioned along the centrifuge arm so that his or her feet were 2.5 m away from the center of rotation. The centrifuge was accelerated at an angular acceleration of 5-10 degrees/sec2 to a maximum angular velocity of 180 degrees/sec (30 rpm), providing a 2.5 g centrifugal force at the feet. The centrifugal force varied along the body z-axis in direct proportion to the radial distance from the center of rotation. With the 2.5 g at the feet, the centrifugal force at the heart level ranged from approximately 1.0 g for the tallest subjects to approximately 1.4 g for the shortest subjects. Similarly, the centrifugal force at the top of the head ranged from approximately 0.6 g for the tallest subjects to approximately 1.0 g for the shortest subjects. The estimated body weight (total z-axis force) during centrifugation ranged from approximately 1.1 to 1.4 times the resting (1 g) body weight of the tallest and shortest subjects, respectively. All subjects (Treatment and Control) were prescreened during the Screening to ensure they could tolerate the AG exposure regimen planned for the study. For the Centrifuge Screening Test Protocol, each subject was tested to see if they were capable of tolerating a minimum of 75 minutes on the centrifuge under the planned treatment protocol conditions of 2.5 g at the feet and 30 rpm rotation rate. Subjects unable to tolerate the 75 minute centrifuge hop were excluded from the study; however, the data was retained for subsequent analysis of factors affecting AG tolerance. Additional tests were performed to assess whether significant decrements were observed after bed rest in the control group. Comparisons were observed in decrements with similar measurements from other bed rest studies and from short-duration space flight studies. To demonstrate the effectiveness of daily 1-hour doses of AG in ameliorating the physiological deconditioning, data was used from the treatment group to test whether the specific AG protocol protected that group from serious symptoms of physiological deconditioning. The treatment group was compared to the control group to test whether decrements observed in the control group subjects were significantly improved in the treatment group subjects.
results: Results indicate that subjects were able to tolerate the SRC protocol every day without any significant problems. Cardiovascular, muscular, and mechanical responses were consistent throughout the in test days. Motion sicknesses observed during this study were scores. The average motion score was 0.26 plus or minus 0.09, while the average peak motion sickness score for each subject was 0.70 plus or minus 0.21. The overall health scores were high, and the mean score was 9.7 plus or minus 0.08. The centrifuge protocol was very well tolerated by the subjects and less than 97 percent of the SRC test sessions were completed without incident. However the loading protocol was well tolerated by the males but the females has some tolerance issues with the protocol. Future studies would require fine tuning the loading protocol, as well as the addition of an exercise program to the centrifuge protocol, to assist in mitigating the deconditioning effects that are presented in bed rest. This experiment has concluded in ground-based studies sponsored by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration's Human Adaptation and Countermeasures Division. This experiment was conducted during the Artificial Gravity Bed Rest Study.

objectives: Space flight induces a host of physiological changes that have harmful effects on human function in normal gravity. Upon entry into a gravitational environment, astronauts must cope with impairments in strength, balance, and the ability to ambulate. Although scientific investigations have begun to explain the underlying physiological mechanisms of these changes; the corresponding impairments in functional performance have yet to be quantified. Therefore, an interdisciplinary team was formed to systematically evaluate the impact of space flight induced physiological changes on the performance of functional tasks (e.g. ladder climbing, hatch opening). This collective effort is referred to as the Functional Task Test (FTT) project. The Exercise Physiology and Countermeasures Project has been instrumental in supporting the development of the functional tasks as well as developing the battery of skeletal muscle performance tests for the FTT project. During space flight, astronauts experience alterations in muscle performance that may cause significant impairments in the performance of operational tasks immediately following landing on a planetary surface. The effects of reduced strength to body weight ratio on the performance of functional tests that are representative of critical mission tasks for lunar and Mars operations were examined. The investigators tested human subjects on an integrated suite of functional tests while wearing a special suit that allows external loads to be applied in order to manipulate subjects’ strength to body weight ratio. Ths study assisted investigators in 1) documenting the degree to which a reduction in strength to body weight ratio affects functional task performance, and 2) identifying critical strength to body weight thresholds that need to be protected in order to maintain task performance capability.
approach: Normal, healthy volunteers were recruited through the JSC Test Subject Facility. The subjects who exhibited a peak isokinetic knee extensor strength (60 degrees/sec) to body weight ratio of greater than 2.6 Nm/kg body weight during initial testing weren't included in the investigation. The rationale for this upper strength limit is two-fold; the investigators expected task performance to be noticeably reduced as the strength to body weight ratio approaches one. With a maximal loading of 100 or 120% body weight (depending on group), individuals who are particularly strong would be able to be loaded sufficiently to reduce the ratio to near one. Second, average preflight crewmember strength is 2.1 Nm/kg and there is a desire to roughly match the astronaut strength for this study. Subjects completed each of the exploration tasks without external load and with an external load equal to 20, 40, 60, 80, 100, 120% of body weight applied via a weighted suit. Task performance metrics were plotted against the subjects’ strength-to-body-weight (including the external load), power-to-body-weight, and total-work-to-body-weight ratios (upper and lower body muscle performance measures were analyzed). Best fit fractional polynomials were generated in order to understand the relationships between muscle-performance-to-body-weight measures and task performance capability. Relationships were task specific.
results: Spline regression was used to identify muscle function thresholds for each task. Upright seat egress and walk was the most difficult task according to the spline regression analysis thresholds. Thresholds normalized to body weight were 17.8 N/kg for leg press isometric force, 17.6 W/kg for leg press power, 78.8 J/kg for leg press work, 5.9 N/kg isometric knee extension and 1.9 Nm/kg isokinetic knee extension torque. Leg press maximal isometric force/body weight was the most reliable measure for modeling performance of ambulatory tasks. Laboratory-based manipulation of relative strength has promise as an analog for spaceflight-induced loss of muscle function. Muscle performance values normalized to body weight can be used to predict occupational task performance and to establish relevant strength thresholds.

title: Inflight Phonocardiogram
variables: Duration of electromechanical delay, cardiac cycle, T
Duration of electromechanical systole, cardiac cycle, S
Duration of the cardiac cycle, R
Interval between the first and second heart sounds, cardiac cycle, X
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: The objective of the Inflight Phonocardiogram (M004) experiment was to measure the duration of the electrical and mechanical phases of the cardiac cycle of the heart during orbital flight. The experiment was conducted in order to gain information on the functional cardiac status of flight crewmembers during prolonged space missions.
approach: Electrocardiogram (ECG) and phonocardiogram recordings were obtained on five astronauts: subjects A and B during Gemini 4 (4 day mission), subjects C and D during Gemini 5 (8 day mission), and subject E during Gemini 7 (14 day mission). ECG recordings of one additional subject, subject F of Gemini 7, were made at lift-off and reentry. The recording procedure was entirely automated and did not require active participation on the part of the flight crewmembers. The experiment equipment system consisted of: a) a phonocardiogram , b) the Gemini bioinstrumentation system, and c) an on board biomedical tape recorder. Both the ECG and phonocardiographic signal conditioners was housed within the Gemini pressure suit in pockets of the astronaut's undergarment. The phonocardiographic sensor was applied parasternally at the left-fourth intercostal space of each subject, and remained attached to the chest throughout the mission. The sensor was secured to the chest wall by means of a small disk of double-sided adhesive. ECG electrodes were applied at the top and bottom of the sternum. The analog data from the biomedical tape recording were played back after completion of the mission. The records were semi-automatically digitized with an analog-to-digital converter. Digital readings were then taken at each one of the following points: at the onset of a QRS complex or the beginning of the electrical systole at the onset of the first heart sound at the onset of the second heart sound (which indicated the end of the mechanical systole and the beginning of diastole) at the onset of the next QRS complex (which indicated the end of the cardiac cycle.) A computer program was used to process the digitized data and calculate the duration of systole and diastole, the interval between the onset of QRS and the first heart sound (electromechanical delay), and the interval between the first and second heart sounds. The same computer program allowed for computation of means and standard deviations of these variables after 15 consecutive beats. ECG and phonocardiogram data were obtained during the following periods for subjects A and B: continuously for 8 minutes from the time prior to lift-off until the spacecraft had reached orbit continuously from 5 minutes before the period of extravehicular activity (EVA) to 10 minutes following the EVA continuously from 5 minutes before reentry until splashdown, continuously for approximately 1 minute at 2-hour intervals for the first 24 hours and at 4-hour intervals for the second, third, and fourth flight days. Technical difficulties precluded recording of the phonocardiogram from the tenth through the eighteenth hour on subject B, throughout the EVA on subject A and from the ninety-third hour through splashdown on subject A. Data on subjects C and D were obtained during the following periods: continuously starting a few minutes before lift-off until the spacecraft had reached orbit continuously from 5 minutes before reentry until splashdown continuously for 1 minute at hourly intervals for the first 24 hours of the mission and at 4-hour intervals for the rest of the flight until 5 minutes before reentry. Data on subject E were obtained: continuously from 15 minutes before lift-off to 11 minutes into the mission continuously for 1 minute at 1, 3, and 4 hours inflight continuously for 1 minute at hourly intervals during periods assigned for rest from the fifth day through the fourteenth day of the mission. Limitations in the number of measurements in subject E were imposed by the recording capability of the biomedical tape recorder. No recordings were made during reentry. ECG recordings for Subject F on Gemini 7 were made on liftoff and reentry.
results: All astronauts had an increased heart rate (i.e., short cardiac cycle) at the time of lift-off. This was reflected in a very short cardiac cycle accompanied by a proportional shortening of the systole and electromechanical delay time intervals. There was a rapid deceleration of heart rate as soon as the spacecraft entered orbit, but a steady state was not reached until approximately 16 hours into the mission. Throughout the mission, the duration of the cardiac cycle varied considerably with concomitant changes in the duration of electromechanical systole and of the time interval between the first and second heart sounds. The electromechanical delay remained relatively constant, but usually there was a significant “anticipatory” shortening that began several hours before landing. In the instance of subject A, this phenomenon began 20 hours before reentry. Decreases in the duration of the cardiac cycle and its various components were always observed at reentry when peak heart rates were about 160 beats per minute. Electromechanical systole and the electromechanical delay reached their lowest values at reentry. Data analysis showed that the duration values of electromechanical systole (S), the time interval between the first and the second heart sounds (X), and the electromechanical delay (T) were longer when the total duration of the cardiac cycle was also longer (that is, when the heart rate was slower.) In the case of subject C, the relationships between S, X and T were normal in practically all instances. However, lower than-predicted values for systole were recorded at the time of reentry. In the case of subject B and to a lesser extent in the subjects A and E, observed values were slightly lower than normal. Subject E exhibited a very prolonged cardiac cycle (i.e. low heart rate) during periods of rest. The highest values (instantaneous heart rates of 37 to 45 beats per minute) for subject E were recorded during mid-mission night sleep periods. In general, shorter-than-predicted measurements of cycle components for a cardiac cycle of given duration were observed under the influence of adrenergic or stress factors, whereas longer-than-predicted measurements are indicative of the influence of cholinergic or vagal factors. A preponderance of adrenergic influences was thus uniformly noticed in all the astronauts at the time of lift-off and especially at the time of reentry. A remarkable quantitative difference was observed in subject D. In this individual, the durations of electromechanical systole and of electromechanical delay were significantly longer than predicted for normal healthy subjects. There was a relative shortening of these periods only at the time of lift-off and reentry. It was assumed that the longer duration of systole and of electromechanical delay of subject D was an expression of increased vagal tone except at lift-off and reentry. Increased vagal tone was further suggested by the marked sinus arrhythmia recorded during sleep and quiet periods.

title: Structural Chromosome Aberrations Formed in Response to Changes in Proton Energy and Dose Rate
variables: Chromosome aberrations, interstitial deletions and rings
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Risk uncertainties related to radiation exposure during space exploration are unacceptably large. These include the effects of sporadic solar particle events (SPEs) which can produce relatively high levels of radiation, principally from protons. The notion that dose rate effects from protons will be the same as for x- and gamma rays is widely held. However, not much direct experimental evidence to support this contention exists. In fact, the
approach: Energies and dose rates that were compatible with the investigation’s scientific
results: ant dose to personnel from an SPE can be high enough to warrant concerns of cancer induction. Because human epidemiological data in this area are not available, reduction in risk uncertainties will require data from meaningful surrogate endpoints. For this investigation, structural damage to chromosomes of human cells in culture has been chosen as a surrogate endpoint for cell death and cancer. An SPE will be simulated using proton emissions from the National Space Radiation Laboratory (NSRL) at Brookhaven National Laboratory (BNL). Owing to differences in ionization density that may translate to differences in biological effect, proton energies of 50 MeV and 250 MeV will be studied. These will be delivered at both high and low dose rates. Results will then be compared to those obtained for gamma rays from a 137-Cesium source. Objective 1 Construct quantitative dose responses for the induction of chromosome aberrations found in cells when they arrive at the first mitosis following exposure. For this and other objectives, multiplex fluorescence in situ hybridization (mFISH) will be used, which effectively paints each of the 23 pairs of human chromosomes a unique color. This allows even very complicated rearrangements among all chromosomes to be visualized simultaneously. Objective 2 Complete an analysis of chromosome damage in clonal descendants of single cells that survive exposure to radiation. Several such clones will be expanded in culture and examined by mFISH for transmissible chromosome aberrations. A subset of these clones will be further examined for structural aberrations that are too small to be seen under the microscope, by employing comparative genomic hybridization applied to DNA microarrays (aCGH). Genetic damage in cells surviving radiation may be diagnostic of the type of radiation encountered, and that such damage has more direct relevance to carcinogenesis. APPROACH: Energies and dose rates that were compatible with the investigation’s scientific objectives were determined on the basis of biophysical modeling, and constraints of NSRL facilities. Two runs were made at NSRL. For the first run, 150 MeV protons and 1 GeV protons were used. Both were delivered at high (30 cGy/min) and low (30 cGy/h) dose rates to telomerase-immortalized human fibroblasts to total absorbed doses of (not including the sham-irradiated zero-dose control) 100, 200, and 300 cGy. For the second run, 50 MeV protons became available, and this energy was used instead of the previous 150 MeV treatment group. As in the first run, 1 GeV protons were used again, serving as a repeat. For both NSRL runs, density-inhibited telomerase-positive BJ-1 human fibroblasts were re-fed with conditioned medium prior to shipment to NRSL. The morning following exposure, flasks were shipped back to UTMB (University of Texas Medical Branch) for immediate subculture. RESULTS: The expected diminution of chromosome damage per unit dose following reduction in dose rate was confirmed, as was the predicted attenuation in upward curvature. These results are consistent with the assumption that protons and photons elicit a qualitatively similar biological response. Curvature in the dose response following 150 MeV protons was effectively eliminated at the LDR of 0.05 cGy/min. This is evidence that the limiting low dose rate (LLDR) was reached, and is consistent with expectations based on gamma ray studies. Irrespective of energy, the preponderance of curvature in all responses derives from complex exchanges, which is also similar to the situation for photons. The above conclusions regarding similarity of effect between high energy protons and gamma rays need to be tempered by the following observations: The unexpected observation that higher energy protons were more effective at producing chromosome damage per unit dose. More data for the 50 MeV protons would be needed to establish whether this is a trend. The fact that curvature in the response was not altogether eliminated for the higher energy 1 GeV protons following LDR. It is unknown whether the LLDR hadn’t yet been reached for this radiation, or whether single track action is capable of producing such curvature. Additional work may eventually be needed to put hard numbers on quantitative differences regarding gamma photons versus protons in order to estimate meaningful RBEs. In particular this would include more dose points over the lower dose range. Regarding clones recovered from exposed cell populations, roughly 25% following 3 Gy of protons harbored transmissible chromosome rearrangements, most of which were simple reciprocal translocations; a significant number contained complex exchanges as well that involve simultaneously three or more chromosomes. These results are consistent with those observed following exposure to 4 Gy 137Cs gamma-rays. Because they are homogeneous for the particular rearrangements they carry, these clonal derivatives serve as ideal material for molecular analysis, as for example, analysis by array-based comparative genomic hybridization (aCGH) High-density CGH arrays (aCGH) were used to examine the distribution of large (megabase-sized) and small (tens of kilobase size) deletions in several of the surviving clones described above. The size-frequency distribution of such deletions, on both the megabase and kilobase scales suggest that the formation of smaller deletions are favored over larger ones, but that the distributions are characterized as having “long asymmetrical tails.” In at least one case, a clone had suffered a deletion in near proximity to an apparently simple reciprocal translocation, suggesting the rearrangements was “complex,” i.e., a co-deletion, as part of the translocation/exchange process.

title: Neurostructural, Cognitive, and Physiologic Changes During a 1-year Antarctic Winter-Over Mission
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: The proposed study concentrates on neurostructural, cognitive, physiologic, and social effects of prolonged confinement and isolation on subjects over-wintering in the space analog environment of the Antarctic Concordia station. Investigators also propose to investigate an age-, gender-, and education-matched and non-confined control group living in Cologne, Germany with identical methodology. The research encompasses the following specific aims: Perform structural and functional neuroimaging prior to, immediately after, and six months after the winter-over. This includes the administration of cognitive tests inside and outside of the scanner. Assess cognitive performance on a wide range of cognitive domains with the Cognition test battery during the period of confinement and isolation on a monthly basis. Investigate changes in sleep duration, sleep-wake rhythms and light exposure with continuously worn wrist actigraphy during the period of confinement and isolation. Investigate physiologic changes in heart rate, heart rate variability, and sleep structure with monthly 24-hour ECG measurements during the period of confinement and isolation. Investigate changes in psychomotor vigilance performance, mood, depressive symptoms, and subjective assessments of workload, stress, sleep quality, tiredness, sickness, and conflicts among crewmembers during the period of confinement and isolation on a weekly basis. Unobtrusively and continuously monitor crew cohesion and team structure with proximity sensors built into the wrist-worn actigraphs during the period of confinement and isolation.
approach: This study investigated neurostructural and functional changes in 25 crewmembers over-wintering in the Antarctic Concordia station and in 26 age- and sex-matched controls at the German Aerospace Center (DLR). Structural and functional neuroimaging was obtained prior to, immediately after, and six-months after the winter-over. Crewmembers and controls performed the Cognition test battery on a monthly basis in mission. They also wore a small device measuring heart rate for a 24-hour period on a monthly basis. Finally, the crew continuously wore wrist actigraphs to measure wake activity and sleep-wake rhythmicity. These watches also recorded proximity to watches worn by the other crewmembers and to devices strategically placed throughout the station as surrogate measures of crew cohesion and habitat use. Two Antarctic research stations (Neumayer and Halley) were added after the start of the study. The crews in these stations (N=17 at Neumayer and N=25 at Halley) only performed the Cognition test battery on a monthly basis. At Neumayer station, neuroimaging was also available before and three months after the mission.
results: For T1-weighted MRI, results indicate small, but robust volume reductions immediately post-mission in the Antarctic winter-over group. Volume generally normalized by the six-month follow-up, except for a small reduction in parietal volume. In contrast to volume, gray matter density (GMD) increased in the Antarctic winter-over group, and normalized at the six-month follow-up. These findings indicate that isolated, stressful environments are associated with transient brain volume reductions and by small increases in gray matter density. Increase in GMD may reflect experience-dependent structural plasticity and is also found in children who have experienced traumatic stressful events. Most hippocampal subfield measurements indicated little to no change in the Antarctic winter-over group. There was a nominal decline in the parahippocampal cortex (PHC) immediately upon return that completely normalized. Changes in the PHC are relevant as this region of the brain is critical for memory encoding and retrieval that could affect performance. Moreover, extant research has shown that this hippocampal region is sensitive to stress and other environmental stressor (e.g., radiation). As such, alterations in these brain structures should continue to be closely monitored, particularly in longer duration missions. For diffusion weighted imaging (DWI), functional anisotropy (FA) in white matter decreased in the winter-over group and returned to baseline at the six-month follow-up. There were no significant changes in brain mean diffusivity (MD). Alterations in brain white matter signify microstructural changes in neural communication that are critical for sustaining neurocognitive performance, in particular working memory and executive function, and may relate to the manifestation of clinical symptoms. As such, it is important to monitor changes in brain white matter, especially for longer missions. For functional MRI, Voxelwise regional homogeneity (ReHo) was nominally increased in fronto-dorsal and temporal lobes immediately upon return from winter-over that normalized at the six-month follow-up exam. Correlations between brain volume changes in the MRI and cognitive performance changes across the mission showed the strongest associations in subcortical brain regions. Individuals with larger reduction in brain volume in the nucleus accumbens (bilateral) and the right hippocampus after the winter-over mission showed larger performance deficits (less efficient) on Cognition over time. These data indicate significant individual differences in the relationship between alterations in brain structure and performance. Moreover, these data suggest that even small changes in brain subcortical volume can significantly impact cognitive performance in some individuals. Additional biologic and performance measures should be sought to identify individuals that may be vulnerable to small changes in brain volume given the effect that these changes have on cognitive performance. Paradoxically, volume change in the cerebral cortex showed the opposite pattern. More volume reduction during the winter-over was associated with improved performance on Cognition over time. Analyses in the Neumayer crew showed that dentate gyrus, CA1, and CA3 volumes were significantly decreased after the expedition. The strongest effects were observed for the dentate gyrus. All other subfields also showed a reduction, but these changes did not reach statistical significance. There were no statistically significant correlations between linear trends in cognitive accuracy, speed, and efficiency (across cognitive domains) with time in mission and change in dentate gyrus volume. Cognitive performance data suggest significant increases in cognitive speed and decreases in cognitive accuracy, with a net increase in cognitive efficiency, across study sites with increasing time in mission even after adjusting for practice effects. This suggests a change in response strategy (sacrificing accuracy for speed) rather than an isolated insult to cognitive accuracy. However, these changes were small and likely irrelevant. Except for a few cognitive domains, differences in accuracy and speed between sites were minor and statistically non-significant. The findings suggest no relevant negative effect on cognitive performance when spending prolonged periods of time (10-14 months) in Antarctic ICE environments on cognitive performance. The investigators found some differences in sympathovagal balance between the first and the second half of the mission in the Concordia crew, with higher vagal activity in the afternoon and evening in the second mission half compared to the first. There was no difference in average heart rate between the Concordia crew and DLR controls. However, sympathovagal balance was shifted towards sympathetic activity in the Concordia crew relative to DLR controls, which could have been caused by the chronic hypobaric hypoxia at Concordia station. Crews and controls subjectively reported low levels of stress, loneliness, depression, and conflict; high levels of happiness and health; and intermediate levels of workload, physical exhaustion, boredom, and monotony. Of note, the Halley crew scored highest on levels of boredom, monotony, loneliness, and depression. There were significant linear trends across mission quintiles for all of the studied outcomes, indicating a deterioration with increasing time in mission. Unobtrusive proximity measurements were found to provide useful information on who is spending time with whom as a proxy of crew cohesion, and how crew cohesion changed over time in mission.

title: Bed Rest Standard Measures: Vertical Jump
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: The objective of this test was to assess muscle power in the legs before and after bed rest.
approach: Muscle power was assessed twice before and twice after bed rest by performing the vertical jump test on a ground reaction force plate platform. Subjects performed countermovement vertical jumps. The subjects were instructed to jump as high as possible, with their hands on their hips. Attempts were made to obtain three maximal jumps; however, fewer jumps were performed in the post-bed rest phase. Body mass, reaction force, and jump height were recorded during data collection and jump power was calculated.
results: This experiment has concluded. Tabular results are available for the public. .

title: Testosterone Supplementation as a Countermeasure against Musculoskeletal Losses during Space Exploration
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: The long-term goal of this study was to determine the therapeutic efficacy of testosterone at preserving lean muscle mass, muscle strength, and bone mineral density in healthy humans during space flight. Investigators examined the interactive or additive effects of the combination of testosterone and exercise on lean body mass, muscle strength, and bone health. To achieve these goals investigators tested the following hypotheses before, during, and after 70 days of bed rest: Cycled testosterone replacement (weekly testosterone injections for two weeks, followed by two weeks off) in conjunction with exercise will have an additive effect in preventing loss of muscle mass and muscle strength in men representative of the astronaut population compared to exercise with placebo testosterone. Cycled testosterone replacement (weekly testosterone injections for two weeks, followed by two weeks off) in conjunction with exercise will have an additive effect in preventing loss of bone mass and alterations in markers of bone metabolism in men representative of the astronaut population compared to exercise with placebo testosterone. To address these hypotheses investigators studied the following specific aims before, during, and after 70 days of bed rest: To determine the effect of cycled testosterone replacement in conjunction with resistance exercise during bed rest on muscle mass, muscle strength, and fatigue in men aged 24-55 years. To determine the effect of cycled testosterone replacement in conjunction with resistance exercise during bed rest on markers of bone metabolism and bone mass in men aged 24-55 years.
approach: Male volunteers were randomly assigned to one of three bed rest groups 1) non-exercising + placebo (control group), 2) exercise + placebo (exercise A group) , and exercise + testosterone (exercise B group) using a standard of care approach with NASA space flight nutritional requirements and standard exercise protocols as the control condition. A total of 24 subjects completed the study. Eight subjects were in each bed rest group.
results: Results suggest that exercise groups A and B appear protected against the bed rest-induced loss of lean body mass (LBM, total and legs). The exercise B group, but not A, significantly increased LBM and prevented increases in fat mass during bed rest. Effects on bone for both exercise groups was not significant.

title: Vitamin D Supplement Evaluation of Dosing Requirements
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Vitamin D is critical for space travelers because they lack ultraviolet light exposure and have an insufficient dietary supply of vitamin D. Despite the provision of vitamin D supplements to International Space Station (ISS) crewmembers, vitamin D status is consistently lower after flight than before flight, and in several crewmembers, levels have decreased to concentrations considered clinically significant. Vitamin D has long been known to play a role in calcium metabolism, and more recently its non-calcitropic functions (functions not related to calcium metabolism, e.g., effects related to the incidence of cancer or diabetes) have been recognized. According to the
approach: This study was conducted at the Johnson Space Center in Houston, TX. Subject participation and sample collection occurred between June 2008 and September 2009. The protocol was approved by the Johnson Space Center Committee for the Protection of Human Subjects. The procedures followed were in accordance with the Helsinki Declaration of 1975 as revised in 1983. The subjects provided written informed consent before they participated in the study. Subjects were randomly assigned to one of 4 groups: no supplement (placebo), 2,000 IU per day, 10,000 IU per week, and 50,000 IU per week for 4 weeks and then monthly for the next 2 months. The placebo group consisted of 4 subjects taking a daily placebo, 4 subjects taking a weekly placebo, and 4 subjects taking a weekly placebo for 4 weeks and then monthly for the next 2 months. There was one exception to randomization: subjects whose screening serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D was greater than 85 nmol/L were assigned to the placebo group. Ultraviolet B (UVB) radiation exposure was recorded using polysulfone film badges. Subjects were asked to wear the badges the day before the 0-day and 60-day blood draws. Materials Vitamin D3 capsules (2,000 IU, 10,000 IU, 50,000 IU, and placebo) were manufactured by Tishon Corp. (Westbury, NY). All doses (and placebos) were identical in appearance. Three samples from each dose were analyzed for actual vitamin D3 content before the study began. The 2,000-IU and 10,000-IU capsules (and daily and weekly placebo doses) were repackaged into blister-sealed pouches to most efficiently track compliance. The 50,000-IU capsules (and corresponding placebo group) were administered in a supervised manner for each dose and therefore were not supplied to the subjects in blister packs. Ultraviolet B (UVB) radiation exposure was recorded using polysulfone film badges. Subjects were asked to wear the badges the day before the 0-day and 60-day blood draws. Study Design The supplementation period was 3 months. In the first week of each study month, subjects came to the Human Test Subject Facility at the Johnson Space Center for a fasted blood draw and 24-hour urine sample (baseline, 0 days). Immediately after the fasted blood draw, subjects were administered a placebo or a 2,000-, 10,000-, or 50,000-IU pill of vitamin D3. Blood was collected again 6, 12, 24, and 48 hours after this initial dose. A fasted blood draw and 24-hour urine sample was collected again from all subjects after 30, 60, and 90 days. On day 60, subjects came in for a fasted blood draw and were administered their respective vitamin D dose (or placebo) and blood was collected 6, 12, 24, and 48 hours later. Vitamin D Intake Assessment At the monthly blood draws (0, 30, 60, and 90 days), subjects completed a 7-day recall food questionnaire for the 6 days before the blood draw and supplement provision, and the 24 hours after supplement provision. The questionnaire was developed for this study, and was designed to include foods known to contain vitamin D. Supplement use was also recorded. Questionnaires were analyzed and vitamin D intake was calculated using the Nutrition Data System for Research developed by the Nutrition Coordinating Center, University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, MN. Sample Collection and Processing All baseline (time 0) blood samples were collected in the morning after an 8-hour fast. Blood was allowed to clot, and then it was centrifuged and serum was separated into individual aliquot cryotubes. Serum calcium, blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, and liver enzymes (aspartate aminotransferase and alanine aminotransferase) were measured within 4 days of collection for each blood draw. Other samples were frozen at minus 70 degrees?Celsius and batched until the end of the study so that all samples were analyzed together.
results: of several recent studies, functionally relevant measures indicate that the lower limit of serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D (a marker of vitamin D status) should be raised from the current standard of 25 nmol/L to 80 nmol/L. The mean preflight serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D for U.S. ISS crewmembers to date is 63 ± 16 nmol/L, and after a four to six-month space flight mission it typically decreases 25-30% despite a supplementation of 400 International Units per day (IU/d). The suboptimal pre- and postflight vitamin D status is an issue that needs to be addressed so NASA can better define the appropriate amount of supplemental vitamin D to serve as a countermeasure against vitamin D deficiency in crewmembers. This is very important for long-duration crewmembers, and is critical for exploration class missions. The investigators recently completed a ground-based investigation titled, "Efficacy of Vitamin D Supplementation in an Antarctic Ground Analog of Space Flight," which evaluated vitamin D supplementation efficacy during the winter months in Antarctica, when UV-B radiation levels are essentially zero. A supplement of 2,000 IU/d raised serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D to acceptable levels, but as with any time a daily supplement or change in routine is required, compliance can be an issue. In this study, investigators studied whether a weekly or monthly dose of vitamin D could be substituted for a daily dose. Data from this study will help investigators provide long-duration space flight crewmembers a safe, effective, and evidence-based recommendation for vitamin D supplementation to achieve and maintain optimal vitamin D status before, during, and after flight. RESULTS: The data provides evidence that vitamin D doses of 2,000 IU daily, 10,000 IU once weekly, or 50,000 IU (weekly then) monthly dosing regimens used in this study were similarly effective at raising circulating vitamin D status over the course of 90 days. Even though the mean urinary calcium response at 30, 60, and 90 days was not different between groups, more subjects in the 50,000-IU group had urinary calcium concentrations higher than the upper end of the normal range at some point during the study.
