archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Long-duration space flights are associated with increased levels of psychological stress, acute and chronic exposure to space radiation, and microgravity-induced changes which are known to detrimentally impact the immune system. Studies have evaluated the magnitude of immune alterations during space flight, however, due to logistical constraints unique to the space flight environment, they have either been limited to short-duration space flight missions or to basic pre- and postflight measures. The successful implementation of exploration-class missions to Mars or other near-Earth objects requires a better understanding of the impact of long-duration space flight on the immune system in order to evaluate the risks associated with immune dysregulations. In this regard, The Effects of Long-Term Exposure to Microgravity on Salivary Markers of Innate Immunity (Salivary_Markers) and Validation of Procedures for Monitoring Crewmember Immune Function (SMO 015) were conducted in order to assess immune function relating to cells of innate and adaptive immunity, as well as salivary immune parameters during a six-month mission on the International Space Station (ISS). These studies provided important data relating to innate immunity and immune cell changes during space flight, however it remains unknown whether astronauts become immunocompromised during space flight. The main goal of this study was to characterize acute and chronic changes in polyclonal Free Light Chains (FLC), and in Immunoglobulin (Ig) class switching, indicative of a state of chronic inflammation and overall B-cell function. Investigators also assessed if changes to these sensitive biomarkers are associated with altered risk of viral reactivation and subsequent inflammation.
approach: Using stored plasma samples collected during the two flight studies, investigators retrospectively evaluated B-cell function and humoral immunity during and following long-duration missions. Investigators analyzed archived plasma samples from two different flight studies as well as ground-based controls. The blood samples were collected from ISS crewmembers before, during, and after space flight. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays (ELISAs) to determine latent viral status, Ig, and cytokine levels were also conducted to measure other indices of immune activation and suppression.
results: There was no effect of space flight on kappa FLC concentrations and only a marginal reduction was observed in lambda FLC levels upon return to Earth. Furthermore, IgG and IgM remained unchanged during and after space flight, when compared to pre-flight values. These results indicate that B-cell homeostasis is maintained during long-duration space flight in astronauts, advocating for potential in-flight vaccination as viable countermeasures against viral reactivation during exploration-class missions.

title: A Mechanistic Investigation of Space Radiation-Induced Carcinogenesis
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: One of major concerns for manned space missions of NASA is exposure to galactic cosmic rays (GCRs) or highly charged energetic (HZE) particles, which carries distinct health risks. The major goal of the NASA Bioastroanautics Roadmap and NASA ground-based studies in radiation biology is to assess potential risks of human exposure to HZE particles and to generate knowledge that can be used to mitigate the health risks of HZE particle exposure eventually. In this project, investigators will address two specific aims to study HZE particle-induced mutagenesis and carcinogenesis in mammalian cells. These are: 1) to determine the potential interactions of reactive oxygen/nitrogen species and apoptosis in regulating HZE radiation-induced mutagenesis in mammalian cells and 2) to determine the roles of program cell death in HZE radiation induced mutagenesis/carcinogenesis.
approach: The methodology is embedded in the
results: below. RESULTS: The major goals of this project were to understand the roles of free radicals and programmed cell death in space radiation induced mutagenesis and carcinogenesis. Major achievements include: A) The development of a non-invasive bioluminescence-based imaging method to monitor gamma H2AX foci, a major indicator of DNA double strand breaks (DSBs). Using this reporter, investigators showed that space radiation induced DSBs came in two waves. The first wave occurs within minutes and lasted for hours while the second wave occurs after 24 hours and lasted for more than a week. The second wave of DNA damage has strong implications for space radiation induced DNA damage and carcinogenesis. This type of damage could be responsible for persistent genetic instability often observed after radiation exposure. B) The discovery of the “Phoenix Rising” pathway for wound healing and tissue regeneration. Investigators discovered that dying cells in damaged tissues play a key role in mediating wound healing and tissue regeneration. Surprisingly, caspase 3 and caspase 7, which are usually recognized as executioners of damaged or unwanted cells, play key facilitative roles regulating growth-promoting signals from dying cells. The elucidation of the counter-intuitive roles of apoptotic cells and apoptotic caspases significantly advanced the understanding of tissue homeostasis mechanisms in metazoan organisms. C) Investigators also found that the same “Phoenix Rising” pathway was hijacked by tumors during radiotherapy. Dying cells in tumors exposed to radiation release potent caspase 3-controlled growth signals that promote the growth of surviving tumor cells, which fuels the repopulation of damaged tumor. Most importantly, consistent with these findings, higher levels of activated caspase 3 in tumor samples from human patients correlated with worse prognosis. These results are counter-intuitive and significantly changed the way they view cell death during tumor radiotherapy. D) Another discovery that investigators made concerns with surprising roles of caspases 3 and 8 in epigenetic reprogramming. They show that during induction of induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells from human and mouse fibroblasts, caspases 3 and 8 are clearly activated. However, contrary to conventional wisdom, they found that blocking caspase activation did not increase the efficiency of iPSC induction. Instead, it significantly attenuated or completely blocked iPSC induction. These findings suggest that caspases played a facilitative role for epigenetic reprogramming, a role that has not been suggested before. E) Still another significant finding in this project involves the successful reprogramming of primary human fibroblasts into dopaminergic neurons. Investigators showed that a combination of 5 transcription factors (Mash1, Ngn2, Sox2, Nurr1, and Pitx3) can directly reprogram human primary fibroblasts into doparminergic neurons. These cells should stimulate research in providing a promising autologous source for cell replacement therapy for Parkinson’s disease.

title: Telomeric Proteins in the Radiation/DNA Damage Response
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Appropriate cellular response to natural chromosomal termini (telomeres) and to exogenously created double-strand breaks (DSBs) is critical to maintaining genomic stability. Incorrect handling of DSB ends leads to mutations, chromosomal rearrangements, instability, and carcinogenesis, and altered levels of telomeric proteins have been reported in some tumors. The intriguing interplay between telomeres and DSBs may be better understood not only by viewing the striking differences between them, but perhaps even more importantly by viewing the obvious similarity – they are both DNA ends, the very substrate both telomere and damage response/repair proteins specifically recognize. This leads to the hypothesis that telomeric proteins aren’t just for telomeres anymore. For example, Telomeric Repeat Factor (TRF1) and TRF2 have multiple interacting binding partners, including some that are telomere specific, like Protection of Telomeres (POT)1 and tankyrase1, and some involved in DNA repair. Telomerase is also known to interact with many telomeric, as well as non-telomeric proteins (including DNA repair proteins), and extra-curricular/pro-tumorigenic activities of telomerase independent of its classical role in telomere length maintenance, including enhanced repair, were proposed.
approach: The investigators approach was to knock down expression of critical telomeric proteins in human cell lines utilizing small interfering RNA (siRNA) strategies. DNA damage was induced via exposure to ionizing radiation (low LET gamma-rays or HZE 56Fe ions). They employed a powerful combination of mutational and molecular cytogenetic analyses to examine the phenotypic and genotypic consequences of telomeric deficiencies on DNA repair endpoints.
results: Investigators studied roles of the telomere associated Poly(ADP-ribose) Polymerase (PARP), tankyrase 1, in both telomere function and the DNA damage response following IR exposure. Tankyrase 1 knockdown significantly elevated recombination specifically within telomeres; i.e., telomere sister chromatid exchange (T-SCE), a phenotype with the potential of accelerating cellular senescence, and therefore aging. Most surprising however, was that depletion of tankyrase 1 resulted in concomitant and rapid reduction of the non-homologous end-joining (NHEJ) protein DNA-PKcs, while Ku86 and ATM protein levels remained unchanged; DNAPKcs mRNA levels were also unaffected. The investigators also evaluated telomerase activity following IR exposure to determine whether differences in radiation quality differentially influences telomerase activity, an important consideration for carcinogenesis with particular implications for stem cell compartments. They tracked telomerase activity and telomere length in a panel of cancer and non-cancer cell lines following both acute and low dose rate (LDR) exposures to gamma-rays. They observed elevations of telomerase activity in cancer, but not non-cancer, cell lines following acute exposures to IR. Further, telomere length was significantly reduced in both cancer and non-cancer cells postacute IR exposure. As IR induced enrichment of cancer stem cells (CSC) in established cancer cell lines was recently suggested to play a role in accelerated tumor repopulation following radiation therapy, the investigators studied a potential role for telomerase in the IR induced enrichment of CSCs. Consistent with previous reports, they detected a significant enrichment of breast CSCs in MCF-7 mammary carcinoma cells at five days post exposure, and demonstrated significant enrichment of CSCs in the non-tumorigenic MCF-10a, WTK1, and LCL15044 cell lines. Further, small molecule inhibition of telomerase activity effectively blocked CSC enrichment in both MCF-7 and MCF-10a cells. Together, these results suggest that telomerase is a significant player in the IR induced enrichment of CSCs in both cancer and non-cancer mammary epithelial cells, independent of its role in telomere length maintenance, supporting non-canonical roles of telomerase in the IR response. No datasets exist for this study. A final report was archived.

title: Bioavailability of Nutrients in Food
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: NASA is planning for long-duration missions beyond low Earth orbit. In order to ensure sustainment of crew health and performance, adequate nutrition must be delivered by the food system and efficiently absorbed by crewmembers to prevent micronutrient deficiency. No collective source of literature on nutrient bioavailability in processed foods is available. The purpose of this task is to conduct a literature review of nutrient bioavailability taking into account the form of food ingredient interactions and processing conditions. The review will identify where information is inadequate and be used to propose formulation and processing suggestions for the development of food products with improved bioavailability. The Specific Aims were: Review current scientific literature on bioavailability of nutrients and how it is affected by form, ingredient interactions and processing conditions. Characterize the conditions that reduce or improve bioavailability of nutrients for future food development.
approach: The methodology isn’t available.
results: Supplemental forms of vitamins and minerals generally are better absorbed by the body than the natural forms of the micronutrient though this phenomena is not always the case. The bioavailability of vitamin E and riboflavin is higher from natural sources as compared to their synthetic counterparts. Additionally, natural forms of vitamin C, biotin, calcium, magnesium, potassium, and zinc were shown to achieve equal serum concentrations as the supplements after consumption of like amounts in controlled test scenarios. Hence, as necessary, food fortification can occur with many of the micronutrients without adverse consequence to the physiological delivery provided that adequate stability of supplemental micronutrients can be achieved. Many ingredient interactions and matrix effects occur with micronutrients that impact nutrient absorption. One ingredient interaction which occurs during the absorption phase is the competitive absorption of similar compounds in the body. For example, beta-carotene competes with other carotenoids for intestinal absorption. Likewise, zinc limits iron absorption when the two are consumed simultaneously. Another interaction affecting bioavailability is the inhibitory nature of phytate and phytic acid, naturally occurring compounds in plants, with the mineral absorption of calcium, chromium, iron, magnesium, phosphorus, and zinc. Some vitamins, such as vitamins A and E, have increased bioavailability if some fat is consumed simultaneously. Vitamin A, riboflavin, and vitamin C show increased absorption if more dietary fiber is present at consumption so that the vitamins have a longer gastrointestinal residence time for absorption. Processing impacts to the bioavailability of micronutrients were very limited. Vitamin concentrations in foods are commonly affected by heat, water leaching, or oxidation. However only two vitamins actually had documentation of bioavailability differences that was dependent on the processing method. Vitamin A provitamins, because of their placement in the microstructure of plants, often become more bioavailable after cooking or pureeing. The niacin in grains must be released by acid or alkali extraction to allow significant absorption. Future work with regards to nutrient bioavailability in the space food system should focus on ensuring that micronutrients are provided in an optimal matrix within many food items. Both vitamin and mineral absorption in many instances was dose-dependent, meaning that percent absorption was higher at lower doses, up to a physiological nutrient saturation level, but overconsumption of micronutrients did not result in absorption at the same rate above saturation. Hence, micronutrients should be spread across many food items to ensure continued nutrient delivery at each meal occasion. Competing nutrients should be staggered in their consumption. Additionally, fortification efforts must take into account the data here in terms of surrounding food matrix and form of the supplemental micronutrient used.

objectives: The objective of the ocular tests was to monitor subjects’ ocular health during the study. Recent evidence from astronauts returning from long-duration missions on the International Space Station (ISS) indicated vision disturbances linked to intracranial pressure affecting the optic disk and optic nerve. A Data and Safety Monitoring Board (DSMB) was constituted to monitor ocular health of the bed rest subjects.
approach: A battery of ten tests was used to assess and monitor subjects’ ocular health during the bed rest study. The tests were designed to gather data on visual acuity, retinal health and structures, strabismus, ocular muscle function, peripheral vision, pupillary reflex, intra-ocular pressure, and eye refractive error. Review of Systems Questionnaire – This questionnaire was used to ask subjects if they experienced any physical symptoms in the past week. Questions regarding eye health were included. This questionnaire was administered weekly in all phases of the bed rest study. Best Corrected Visual Acuity (near and far) – Visual acuity is a measure of the spatial resolution of the visual processing system. Corrective lenses were used if needed by the subject to achieve their best performance. Cycloplegic Refraction – Refraction is the procedure by which the natural optical error is characterized and quantified. This procedure helps to distinguish between blurred vision caused by refractive error and medical abnormalities of the visual system. Cycloplegic refraction refers to refraction done with a cycloplegic agent to dilate the pupil. The cycloplegic agent was used to overcome accommodation by paralyzing the ciliary muscle so that the absolute refractive error can be measured. Modified Amsler grid testing – The Amsler grid is a grid of horizontal and vertical lines used to evaluate the central visual field for damage to the macula or optic nerve. In this test, the person looks with each eye separately at a small dot in the center of the grid composed by black lines on a white background. Wavy, blurred, distorted lines, or missing areas of the grid may be indicative of retinal disturbances. Red Dot test – The Red Dot test is used to evaluate visual fields. The person focuses their vision on a black dot centered within a circle of red dots located 14” (33cm) away. The person looks at the center black dot and indicates whether or not all the red dots can be seen. Each eye was examined separately by covering the opposite eye. Corrective lenses were worn if needed. Inability to see the black dot or any of the red dots suggested a visual field deficit. Confrontational Visual Field testing – This test is used to assess peripheral vision. The subject covers one eye while the other fixates a point straight ahead. A target is moved from the far periphery to the near periphery in each of the visual quadrants. Subjects were asked to indicate when the target appears in their field of view. Color Vision testing – For color vision testing, subjects identify shapes that vary in color and intensity and lie within a background of dots. The type and degree of color vision deficiency is then assessed based upon subject’s responses. Hardy-Rand-Rittler plates were used for this purpose. Tonometry – Applanation tonometry was used to assess Intracular Pressure (IOP). Using this method, IOP was determined by the amount of force required to flatten the cornea by a specified standard amount. Because the instrument is placed on the eye, a topical anesthetic was used to numb the eye prior to taking the measure. Non-mydriatic Fundus Photography - This test allows the examination of the posterior segment of the eye, mainly the retina and optic disc. The subject was directed to look straight ahead at a distant object. The ophthalmoscope illuminates the retina through the pupil. Structures that are observed lie in the innermost aspect of the globe: retina, retinal blood vessels, optic nerve head (disc), and to a limited degree, subjacent choroid. Optical coherence tomography - OCT is a noninvasive, noncontact, transpupillary imaging technology that can image retinal structures in vivo with a resolution of 10 - 17 microns. Cross-sectional images of the retina are produced using the optical backscattering of light. The anatomic layers within the retina can be differentiated and retinal thickness can be measured.
results: Subjects completed the 14- and 70-day head-down-tilt (HDT) bed rest studies. The magnitude of HDT bed rest–induced changes was not significantly different between the two studies for all outcomes, except the superior, nasal, and inferior peripapillary retinal thickness. IOP increase from baseline occurred during 14- and 70-day HDT bed rest. On November 20, 2012, the Data Safety Monitoring Board (DSMB) concluded after review of the subjects from the 14 day (C17) and subjets from the 70 day (C11) head-down tilt bed rest studies, that there were no significant safety issues based on the review of accumulated data. The members, therefore, have reached a consensus decision to conclude safety monitoring by the DSMB and to officially close-out the DSMB monitoring.

title: Bioavailability of Scopolamine Dosage Forms and of a Combination Dosage Form with Dextroamphetamine after Oral Administration to Human Subjects
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Space motion sickness (SMS) is one of the most common ailments experienced in space by astronauts. Although on ground, motion sickness is regarded as a nuisance or a discomfort, SMS occurs during mission-critical times in space and is suspected to hinder crew performance during launch and reentry. The National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Bioastronautics Critical Path document states that "the most overt change affecting an astronaut in space flight is the immediate response of the neurovestibular system to changes in gravity. Astronauts experience orientation illusions, posture and locomotion disturbances, vestibulo-occular function and gaze changes, space motion sickness, and possible structural changes affecting sensory-motor behavior and reorganization". SMS occurs most severely during gravity shifts (launch and reentry) and also during the first few days of (orbital) missions. Nearly 40% of in-flight medication use by US astronauts has been for the treatment of SMS. SMS symptoms include nausea and vomiting, both of which negatively affect drug concentration after oral administration and reaction time. Reaction time is a marker of cognitive performance. Scopolamine (SCOP) is an alkaloid which has been used historically for many years as an anti-emetic, a medicine that prevents or controls nausea and vomiting, and a sedative. It is a muscarinic (a type of receptor in the parasympathetic nervous system that releases acetylcholine as its neurotransmitter) anticholinergic (a substance that opposes or blocks the action of acetylcholine) agent with anti-emetic and anti-vertigo activity
approach: Study design overview The overall design consisted of 4 treatments administered separately in a randomized fashion to 12 healthy subjects. Treatments were separated by a minimum four-day washout period between doses. Serial biological samples were collected for 24 h post dose along with administration of the ANAM Readiness Evaluation System (ARES) test battery. ARES is a selection of Automated Neuropsychological Assessment Metric (ANAM) tasks presented on a handheld computer. Subjects Twelve healthy, non-smoking subjects of normal weight for body size between the ages of 21 and 48 years participated in the study. All subjects were screened and selected through the NASA Johnson Space Center (JSC) Human Test Subject facility. Subjects were excluded if they reported: drug allergies to scopolamine or amphetamines, use of prescription or over-the-counter medications within 3 days of starting the study, use of antibiotics (especially furazolidone) or mono-amine oxidase (MAO) inhibitors within 14 days of starting the study, use of an investigational drug within 30 days of starting the study, tobacco smoking within the past year, blood donation or significant blood loss within 30 days of starting the study, significant gastrointestinal disorder, asthma, seizure disorders, glaucoma, history of urinary retention, history of alcohol or other drug abuse, pregnancy or suspected pregnancy, or lactation, or packed cell volume (Hematocrit ® ) values less than 41% for males and 37% for females. Scopolamine dosage forms All formulations were supplied by the flight medicine clinic at the JSC. The tablet manufacturers were Hope Pharmaceuticals & Eli Lilly & Company. Treatments A 0.8 mg dose of SCOP and a combination dose with 0.8 mg SCOP and 10 mg DEX were administered as tablets or in a gel cap on the morning of the study day after 8-10 h of overnight fasting. Subject numbers were assigned randomly. Visual examination Visual testing was administered by a nurse or laboratory personnel. All vision measurements were taken in the same windowless briefing room after having no less than five minutes of accommodation to the ambient lighting. Subjects identified their dominant eye after being taught a simple cover-uncover test. All vision measurements were taken on subjects' dominant eye, with the non-dominant eye covered by an eye patch. Visual acuity was measured using a Snellen chart held 38 cm from the dominant eye. Visual accommodation was determined using a Prince Rule, consisting of text of known font size on a card mounted on a slide rule. Subjects were instructed to hold the Prince Rule to their dominant eye with the text card adjacent to the eye, and to slowly slide the card out until the text is legible, but not yet clear. All three tests were administered immediately prior to dosing and immediately after ARES had been completed by the subject at 0.5, 1, 2, 8, and 24 hours post dose. Sample collection Blood and saliva samples were collected at 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, and 24h post dose. Urine samples were collected pre-dose and as PRN ( pro re nata , a Latin term used in medicine that means "as necessary") voids for 24h post dose. Blood samples (7 ml) were collected into heparinized Vacutainer TM tubes from an indwelling catheter (Intracath ® , Becton and Dickinson) placed in the antecubital vein of the arm. Stimulated mixed saliva samples were collected using Salivettes ® (Sarstedt Inc.). Blood and saliva samples were centrifuged at 3000 rpm, samples transferred to cryotubes and stored frozen at -70°C until analyzed. Urine samples were collected into labeled polycarbonate bottles, volumes measured, aliquots (10 ml) stored frozen at -70°C for future analysis, and the remainder discarded. Sample analysis SCOP and DEX concentrations were quantitated using a modified liquid chromatography quadrupole mass spectrometry (LC-MSMS) method. Plasma and saliva samples were processed by solid phase extraction followed by analysis by positive ion electrospray LC-MSMS; urine samples were diluted 1/100 fold before solid phase extraction. Pharmacokinetic Analyses Plasma and saliva concentration versus time profiles were plotted and PK parameters were calculated by area moment estimation using WinNonlin (software for pharmacokinetic, pharmacodynamic, and noncompartmental analysis). Relevant parameters were compared using both paired t-tests and analysis of variance (ANOVA) to determine differences in PK parameters as a function of treatment.
results: ing from suppression of vestibular labyrinthine input to the central nervous system (CNS). Earlier reports indicate that SCOP is efficacious for countering space motion sickness symptoms. Several sources report SCOP as being the most effective drug for suppressing nausea and vomiting caused by motion sickness. Many motion sickness drugs, including SCOP, have been reported to negatively affect concentration, cognition, and other cognitive behavioral measures. SCOP has a shorter half-life compared to other SMS medications used at the present time and therefore, side effects caused by the drug may resolve more rapidly. Therapeutic effect of a drug is governed by its intrinsic activity and concentration at the site of action. Pharmacokinetics is the mathematical description of drug concentrations in the body (usually in blood or plasma) as a function of time after administration and the physiological variables that govern pharmacokinetic processes, absorption from the site of administration, distribution to the site of action and elimination from the body by metabolism and excretion. Pharmacodynamics, on the other hand, deals with the mathematical description of the onset, magnitude and duration of pharmacologic effect in relation to circulating drug concentration as a function of time. The therapeutic efficiency of a drug, therefore, is determined by the pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of a dosage form. Earlier reports on SCOP pharmacokinetics indicate that the drug is rapidly eliminated from the body after administration with a systemic clearance of 65 ± 5.2 L/h and a moderate volume of distribution of 1.4 ± 0.3 L/kg. Oral and intranasal bioavailability of the drug is 10.7-48.2% and 83% after oral and intranasal administration, respectively. There are no reports on the bioavailability or pharmacokinetics of the custom-dispensed combination dosage form of SCOP and dextroamphetamine (DEX), commonly referred to as SCOP-DEX. The KC-135 and currently the DC-9, affectionately referred to as the "vomit comet," are, or have been, operated by NASA's Reduced Gravity Office (RGO) as the primary simulation method of microgravity. They are flown in a series of parabolic maneuvers which cause brief periods of microgravity onboard and they are usually used for both astronaut reduced gravity training and equipment testing. Both the parabolic microgravity simulations of the KC-135/DC-9 and longer-term microgravity exposure, such as shuttle and International Space Station missions, induce SMS. Recent studies of SMS suppression on the KC-135 using SCOP-DEX have demonstrated an unexpected lack of efficacy prompting this investigation into the relative bioavailability of dosage forms of SCOP currently used by the NASA health care program. Further, KC-135 passengers who elect to take scopolamine to suppress or prevent motion sickness often have visual deficits which impede their performance. A recent study comparing the efficacy of existing motion sickness medications indicated that SCOP was the most efficacious treatment for suppression of both nausea and the vomit reflex. Of the medications tested in the study, only SCOP was able to affect a prolongation in mean duration of rotation time in a vertical rotation chair. Additionally, accuracy of Delayed Match-to-Sample (DMTS) test, a short term memory and attention test, was found to be unaffected by SCOP whereas other medications negatively affected DMTS; this finding illustrates SCOP's lesser negative impact on cognitive performance when compared to other motion sickness medications. Scopolamine pharmacokinetics Bioavailability of 0.4 mg SCOP tablets in normal, nonsmoking male volunteers was reported to be 26.8 ± 5.1%. Plasma and renal clearance estimates in this study were 65.3 ± 5.2 L/h and 4.2 ± 1.4 L/h. Approximately 6% of intravenous and 1% of oral dose was reported to be eliminated unchanged in the urine. SCOP is known to cross the blood-brain barrier and the placenta and to be reversibly bound to plasma proteins. SCOP is known to be metabolized in the liver mainly to conjugated forms. Oral bioavailability of SCOP has been shown to be increased by pretreatment with grapefruit juice due most likely to inhibition of gut metabolism and/or inhibition of gut transporter proteins caused by flavanoid-like compounds in grapefruit. No significant effect of grapefruit juice on elimination of SCOP was detected. Dextroamphetamine pharmacokinetics Dextroamphetamine is readily absorbed from the GI tract following oral administration with an onset of action generally within an hour of administration. Biological half-life of the drug was reported to be 11 h in adults with a systemic clearance of 0.31 L/h/kg. It is distributed throughout the body with high concentrations in the CNS. Elimination of the drug is affected by urinary pH: alkalinization of urine increases half-life and decreases clearance (18 h and 1.5 L/h/kg); acidification of urine decreases half-life and increases clearance (to 4 h and 2.6 L/h/kg). Significance Scopolamine is regularly used in the space program as a custom dispensed formulation, both by itself and in combination with dextroamphetamine, as a countermeasure for motion sickness; however, adequate pharmacotherapeutic evaluation of these formulations has not been conducted. It is important to characterize interactions between currently used countermeasures in order to optimize pharmacotherapeutics in space and on the ground. This study examines the pharmacotherapeutics of operational countermeasure formulations and interaction potential of two currently used medications for SMS; this study was conceived based on anecdotal reports of treatment failure by NASA RGO physicians. The results presented herein are also useful for the Space Medicine and Health Care Systems Office in selecting or optimizing treatment of SMS. All vision measurements were taken in the same windowless briefing room after having no less than five minutes of accommodation to the ambient lighting. Subjects identified their dominant eye after being taught a simple cover-uncover test. All vision measurements were taken on subjects' dominant eye, with the non-dominant eye covered by an eye patch. Visual acuity was measured using a Snellen chart held 38 cm from the dominant eye. Visual accommodation was determined using a Prince Rule, consisting of text of known font size on a card mounted on a slide rule. Subjects were instructed to hold the Prince Rule to their dominant eye with the text card adjacent to the eye, and to slowly slide the card out until the text is legible, but not yet clear. All three tests were administered immediately prior to dosing and immediately after ARES had been completed by the subject at 0.5, 1, 2, 8, and 24 hours post dose. Sample collection Blood and saliva samples were collected at 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, and 24h post dose. Urine samples were collected pre-dose and as PRN ( pro re nata , a Latin term used in medicine that means "as necessary") voids for 24h post dose. Blood samples (7 ml) were collected into heparinized Vacutainer TM tubes from an indwelling catheter (Intracath ® , Becton and Dickinson) placed in the antecubital vein of the arm. Stimulated mixed saliva samples were collected using Salivettes ® (Sarstedt Inc.). Blood and saliva samples were centrifuged at 3000 rpm, samples transferred to cryotubes and stored frozen at -70°C until analyzed. Urine samples were collected into labeled polycarbonate bottles, volumes measured, aliquots (10 ml) stored frozen at -70°C for future analysis, and the remainder discarded. Sample analysis SCOP and DEX concentrations were quantitated using a modified liquid chromatography quadrupole mass spectrometry (LC-MSMS) method. Plasma and saliva samples were processed by solid phase extraction followed by analysis by positive ion electrospray LC-MSMS; urine samples were diluted 1/100 fold before solid phase extraction. Pharmacokinetic Analyses Plasma and saliva concentration versus time profiles were plotted and PK parameters were calculated by area moment estimation using WinNonlin (software for pharmacokinetic, pharmacodynamic, and noncompartmental analysis). Relevant parameters were compared using both paired t-tests and analysis of variance (ANOVA) to determine differences in PK parameters as a function of treatment. SCOP Tablets (ST) The pharmacokinetic parameter estimates of SCOP given orally are similar to those reported in the literature. Maximum concentration was 0.26 ± 0.04 ng/mL with time for maximum concentration at 0.71 ± 0.02 h after dosing; these data indicate a fairly rapid absorption rate after oral administration. Volume of distribution and clearance after oral administration are 47.6 ± 4.72 L/kg and 23.0 ± 4.58 L/h/kg, respectively, both of which were lower than those from earlier reports. SCOP Gelcaps (SG) Time to maximum SCOP concentration was significantly longer when given as gelcap formulation (1.04 h) than when given as a tablet; however, maximum concentrations for both formulations were not statistically different. No other pharmacokinetic parameter estimates were different from ST. SCOP-DEX Tablets (SDT) The area under the (concentration vs. time) curve (AUC) of SCOP was significantly lower when given with DEX than when given as SCOP tablet; bioavailability of SCOP from SDT was 75% of that from ST. In addition, both SCOP volume of distribution and clearance were higher with SDT (60.9 L/kg and 25.5 L/h/kg, respectively) than with ST (47.6 L/kg and 23.0 L/h/kg, respectively); however, this could be a result of lower bioavailability from SDT which leads to overestimation of clearance and volume of distribution parameters. These results indicate that the effects of DEX on SCOP (SDT, SDG) pharmacokinetics and bioavailability are greater than those from gelcap (SG) formulation. For pharmacodynamic analysis, linear regression analysis was performed between scores from ARES tests and circulating SCOP concentrations using both pooled data from all subjects and individual subject data. Simple reaction time throughput, a parameter that incorporates both accuracy and reaction time, was significantly (p Visual acuity for some individuals, but not for all, was significantly affected by SCOP. Visual acuity for sensitive individuals was affected by even the lowest concentrations of SCOP. The relationship was sigmoidal, meaning that the effect of SCOP on visual acuity is linear, and therefore concentration dependent. In lower concentration ranges there is a minimal response, and in higher concentration ranges there is a maximum response.

In the Skylab program, blood samples were collected during all phases of the flight. The approach of Skylab experiment M114 was to analyze peroxidation of red blood cell lipids, enzymes of red blood cell metabolism, and levels of 2,3-diphosphoglyceric acid and adenosine triphosphate (ATP) to determine if changes in these variables could be related to hemolysis and subsequent decrease in red blood cell mass. APPROACH: During the Gemini and Apollo missions, blood samples were retrieved only during the pre- and postflight periods, limiting study of the red blood cell system. In the Skylab program, blood samples were collected during all phases of the flight. The approach of Skylab experiment M114 was to analyze peroxidation of red blood cell lipids, enzymes of red blood cell metabolism, and levels of 2,3-diphosphoglyceric acid and adenosine triphosphate (ATP) to determine if changes in these variables could be related to hemolysis and subsequent decrease in red blood cell mass. In addition, hemoglobin determination was made on blood samples by using the cyanmethemoglobin method. RESULTS: On Skylab 2, 3 and 4, no evidence of lipid peroxidation, a biochemical effect known to be associated with irreversible cell damage, was observed. In addition, changes in observed glycolytic intermediates and enzymes provided evidence of red blood cell damage. The mean data from Skylab 2 indicated an in-flight increase in hexokinase, pyruvate kinase, and glyceraldehyde phosphate dehydrogenase. Postflight there was a significant decrease of phosphofructokinase. Skylab 3 mean data indicated significant in-flight decreases of hexokinase, phosphoglyceric acid kinase, and acetylcholinesterase, and increases in pyruvate kinase. The Skylab 4 mean data indicated significant change only in phosphofructokinase during the early in-flight phase of the mission. The most consistent change noted was a decrease in phosphofructokinase, an enzyme susceptible to the effects of oxygen that is thought to be at the center of the Pasteur effect (the shift from anaerobic glycolysis to respiration, brought about by the presence of oxygen).

title: Retrospective Study of Serum Sclerostin Measurements in Bedrest Subjects
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Reduced mechanical loading, as in prolonged bed rest, immobilization or space flight, is invariably associated with bone loss. New investigations are needed to gain insight into the mechanisms underlying the musculoskeletal response to mechanical loading, thereby identifying novel targets for preventing musculoskeletal deterioration in situations of reduced mechanical loading, such as bed rest, immobilization, stroke, spinal cord injury, and age-related reductions in physical activity. Osteocytes are believed to play a key role in skeletal mechanosensing, modulating bone modeling, and remodeling by orchestrating the activity of osteoblasts and osteoclasts. However, little is known in humans as to how osteocytes respond to and regulate skeletal adaptation to mechanical unloading. In mice, exposure to hindlimb tail suspension leads to increased osteocyte apoptosis in both trabecular and cortical bone. It has been postulated that osteocyte cell death is an initiator signal for osteoclast remodeling activity or that loaded osteocytes release an osteoclast-inhibiting factor. Furthermore, mature osteocytes are one of the only cells that express, postnatally, the protein sclerostin, a product of the gene SOST. Sclerostin protein has been shown, in vitro and in vivo , to be a strong inhibitor of bone formation, acting in part through the Wnt/B-catenin pathway to reduce osteoblast proliferation and differentiation. Consistent with the negative effect of sclerostin on bone mass, transgenic mice over expressing SOST have low bone mass, whereas SOST-null animals have high bone mass in line with the human conditions of Van Buchem’s disease and sclerosteosis, which are due to inactivating mutations in the SOST gene. Furthermore, the SOST/Sclerostin pathway has been implicated in the bone’s response to mechanical loading, such that increased skeletal loading reduces SOST/Sclerostin levels, and decreased mechanical loading leads to higher SOST/Sclerostin levels. Specific Aims : 1. Determine whether skeletal unloading increases circulating levels of sclerostin by conducting assays in archived serum specimens of subjects exposed to 90 days of bed rest. 2. Determine association between serum sclerostin and standard measures of bone turnover markers (urine N-teleopeptide (NTX), serum osteocalcin and bone specific-alkaline phosphatase (BSAP). 3.Determine association between increase in serum sclerostin and BMD changes following bed rest (an analog for space flight).
approach: Seven healthy adult men underwent 90-day six-degree head down tilt bed rest at The University of Texas Medical Branch (UTMB) – NASA bed rest facility. Subjects were: a) between the ages of 25 and 55 years; b) required to pass a modified Air Force Class III flight physical within one year prior to the study; c) mentally fit for bed rest study as assessed by psychiatric interview and test; and d) not currently taking prescribed medication that would have interfered with physiological measurements, including bisphosphonate therapy. Serum and urine were collected prior to bed rest and during bed rest. The study protocol was approved by the NASA JSC Institutional Review Board, and all subjects gave informed consent prior to participation. Areal bone mineral density (BMD) was measured by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA, Hologic Discovery). BMD of the whole body, lumbar spine, left and right hips, heel, and forearm was assessed at baseline and repeated at BR-60 and 5 days after the end of the bed rest period (BR+5). Serum sclerostin levels were assayed using the APLCO/Biomedica human sclerostin kit per manufacturer’s recommendations. Measurements were made on two pre-bed rest measurements and during bed rest days 28, 60, and 90 (BR-28, B-60, and BR-90). Assays were run in duplicate. Markers of bone metabolism, formation and resorption were also assayed in urine and serum specimens, including serum parathyroid hormone (PTH), testosterone, leptin, 1,25 Vitamin D, markers of bone turnover (bone specific alkaline phosphatase, RANKL/OPG, and osteocalcin), and urinary calcium and phosphorus excretion normalized to creatinine, and 24 hour pooled urinary markers of bone turnover normalized to creatinine. All biochemical analyses were performed by personnel at the NASA Johnson Space Center Nutritional Biochemistry Laboratory with standard commercial techniques. For all serum and urine markers, the two pre-bed rest measurements samples were averaged to provide a single baseline value for each subject.
results: Serum sclerostin increased after bed rest in all subjects. Specifically, serum sclerostin levels increased above BL at BR-28 and appeared to plateau in most subjects at BR-60. Sclerostin levels remained mildly elevated at BR-90, although this result did not reach statistical significance. In contrast, serum PTH levels declined at BR-28 and BR-60, remained reduced at BR-90, but did not reach statistical significance. Urinary levels of bone resorption markers (NTX, DPD, PYD) increased significantly compared with BL at all time points. Urinary calcium excretion was also significantly increased throughout the study, whereas urinary phosphorus levels were elevated at BR-28 and BR-60, with a return to BL at BR-90. Serum bone formation markers (serum BSAP, osteocalcin), serum RANKL, OPG, and the RANKL/OPG ratio did not change. 25 (OH) vitamin D was above BL at all time points (P = 0.005), whereas 1,25 (OH)2 vitamin D was significantly lower than BL at BR-28 and tended also to be lower at BR-60 (P = 0.06) and BR-90 (P = 0.07). Subjects had normal BMD because BL Z-scores at the distal radius, lumbar spine, total hip, and femoral neck were 0.2 ± 0.7, 0.6 ± 1.0, 0.2 ± 1.0, and 0.0 ± 1.3, respectively. BMD declined significantly at BR-60 and BR+5 at all weight-bearing skeletal sites, including the lumbar spine, hip, femoral neck, and calcaneus. There was no change in forearm BMD.

title: Occupational Risk Surveillance for Bone: Pilot Study-Effects of In-flight Countermeasures on Sub-regions of the Hip Bone
variables: L1 Centr 3D bone mineral density BMD

archive_status: Data preservation is complete.  All datasets are privacy-protected.  Data is available via data request.
objectives: Measurement of areal bone mineral density (BMDa, g/cm2) by dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DXA) is required by NASA for assessing skeletal integrity in astronauts. Advantages of DXA include the facts that BMDa is a widely applied predictor of fractures in the aging population and that there are BMDa-based guidelines for identifying persons at high risk for osteoporotic fractures. In contrast to the 2-d imaging by DXA, quantitative computed tomography (QCT) is a 3D bone imaging technology that is used typically to scan the hip and spine. QCT is capable of measuring, volumetric BMD (BMD, mg/cm3) of separate cortical and trabecular sub-regions as well as of total (integral) bone. QCT is limited to research applications at this time because there is not enough medical evidence to determine how QCT data should be used in clinical practice. QCT however provides additional information on bone structure and increases the understanding of how bones respond to effectors of bone loss or gain. NASA recently convened a panel of clinical bone experts to review available medical and research information from astronauts who flew on long-duration space missions. As part of its charge, the panel identified a clinical trigger upon which the flight surgeon should have the astronaut evaluated further by a bone endocrinologist. Specifically, the Panel recommended that if restoration to preflight BMD is not observed for the hip trabecular compartment at two years after return to earth, then that astronaut should be evaluated for possible therapeutic intervention to prevent premature osteoporotic fractures. This pilot study used preflight and postflight QCT scanning of the hips in International Space Station (ISS) astronauts to evaluate the ability of in-flight countermeasures to prevent the occurrence of this clinical trigger. This study furthered hypothesized that QCT scanning could distinguish the effects of different categories of in-flight countermeasures/activities on distinct sub-regions of the hip bone. For example, this pilot study demonstrated that biochemically based countermeasures (e.g., dietary manipulation of acidic to basic amino acid intake or bisphosphonates medication) have a detectable prevention of BMD loss in the hip trabecular compartment while biomechanically based countermeasures (exercise regimens) have detectable expansion of cortical bone apposition -- increasing both bone cross-sectional area and integral BMD consequently. These different effects on hip morphology have subsequently translated to an effect on hip bone strength of the ISS astronaut. The combination of countermeasures that impact both compartments

results: ed in greater hip bone strength -- as estimated by analyzing QCT data by Finite Element Modeling (FEM) -- than of any singly applied countermeasure. This assertion was approached in this pilot study by addressing the following objectives in each ISS astronaut:   1) Characterize the response of i) trabecular and cortical BMDs of the hip and ii) cross-sectional areas of cortical bone, trabecular bone and integral bone, to countermeasures that are either based upon biochemistry or mechanical-loading – with QCT measures. 2) Translate the QCT-measured changes in hip bone morphology to hip bone fracture loads (aka, “hip bone strength”) using FEM. 3) Characterize QCT-measured changes in hip bone morphology following a 12-month postflight period on earth and, in addition, translate these changes to the percentage recovery of preflight hip bone strength determined by FEM.   APPROACH: QCT scanning of the hip was performed at a local hospital (e.g., Christus St. John Hospital, GE VCT 64-slice scanner) on approximately L-45, R+5, R+360 and R+720.  Cotton medical scrubs were provided for the crewmember to wear during scans. The technician was positioning the crewmember in the CT scanner prior to scanning.  The QCT scan were performed at the scanning facility as close as possible to the final departure to Russia.  QCT scanning of the hip were performed in the same hospital facility as the postflight scans to ensure that the same scanning QCT protocol would be performed on the same CT machine.  In addition, crewmembers were asked to keep an exercise and medication log pre, in, and postflight.  RESULTS: In this study, utility of data acquired by hip QCT scans has been demonstrated by the following: i) its delineation of concurrent mechanical and biochemical countermeasures both of which can attenuate or prevent previously-observed declines in hip aBMD after spaceflight and ii) its ability to be transformed to a functional index “bone fracture load” - which could enable NASA to assess the probability of overloading bones with physical activities (especially under atypical and possibly hazardous conditions) or to establish engineering requirements to prevent astronauts from hazardous loads. Finally, researchers conclude that QCT is an important adjunct technology to DXA testing which cannot detect the novel effects of spaceflight on the 3-dimensional measures of trabecular and cortical bones of the hip. In the end, a fuller and more accurate documentation of spaceflight effects on hip bones would be obtained to evaluate risk/benefit of various countermeasures, to inform the feasibility of in-flight mitigation strategies and to refine decision-making for the selection/deselection of countermeasures for specific spaceflight missions.

title: Man's Immunity In-vitro Aspects
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: During early manned space flights scientists were concerned that the immune system would be compromised from the lack of exposure to multiple immunological challenges. Astronauts could be repeatedly exposed to the same antigen. Therefore, the closed environment of the spacecraft module might increase the susceptibility to infections.
approach: Humoral and cellular immune parameters were determined from blood samples taken from the crew and control group during the preflight, in-flight and post flight phases. All of the samples were immediately separated by centrifugation into plasma and cellular phases by the in-flight sample processor, specially designed for operation in a weightless environment. Following separation, the samples were frozen at -20 degrees Celsius and cold-stored in the Skylab Orbital Workshop until recovery. Blood samples were analyzed by measuring total blood proteins and plasma protein fractions involved with the immune system. Protein concentrations and electrophoretic patterns were evaluated to study humoral immunity. Cellular immunity function was evaluated by lymphocyte response to in vitro mitogenic challenge with phytohemagglutinin (PHA). Lymphocytes were tested for DNA and RNA synthesis rates. The RNA synthesis rate after 24 hours in culture, and the DNA synthesis rate after 72 hours in culture, were determined from 3H-uridine and 3H-thymidine uptake, respectively. The higher the uptake of 3H-uridine and 3H-thymidine indicated a positive response to the PHA mitogen. In addition, on Skylab 4, T-lymphocyte counts, B-lymphocyte counts, and the mixed lymphocyte test were conducted, prompted by findings from Skylab 2 and Skylab 3. Furthermore, lymphocytes from Skylab 4 astronauts were examined by electron microscopy to study cell membrane characteristics.

Therefore, the immunological integrity of Skylab crewmembers was assessed for the medical risks of manned space flight. The functional objectives of this experiment were to (1) measure changes in humoral and cellular immunity as reflected by the concentrations of plasma and blood cell proteins, blastoid transformations, synthesis of ribonucleic acid (RNA) and deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) by the lymphocytes and (2) to acquire data that will add to the findings of other Skylab biomedical experiments to yield a greater comprehension of the affects that space travel has on man. RESULTS: The plasma protein profiles after Skylab 2 indicated that (1) no significant changes were observed in total proteins and electrophoretic patterns (2) no significant changes were observed for immunoglobulins (3) no significant changes were observed for protease inhibitors (4) a slight decrease in complement component, C3, was observed immediately post flight in all three crewmembers was, by 13 days post flight, within the normal levels and (5) post flight two crewmembers had increased levels of lysozyme that were elevated for 13 days. In addition, there were no significant plasma protein modifications during Skylab 3 or Skylab 4. Lymphocyte responsiveness was decreased in most Skylab astronauts on the day of recovery. However, this finding, characteristic of all three missions, did not appear to be related to the duration of the flight. Lymphocyte responsiveness recovered rapidly, and by 3 to 7 days post flight was within the established preflight limits. These changes prompted further studies conducted on Skylab 4 to observe the response of cells in a mixed lymphocyte culture and to quantitate preflight and post flight B- and T- lymphocyte distribution. It was found that the lymphocyte responsiveness was decreased temporarily on Skylab 4. However, lymphocyte function tested by the mixed lymphocyte reaction indicated that lymphocyte function was normal on landing day. The number of circulating T-cells on recovery day was decreased, but returned to normal levels by post flight day 3. In contrast, a transient elevation in the number of B-cells were observed on post flight day 1, with a rapid return to normal levels by post flight day 3. It was believed that hormones might be the cause for the temporary alterations of the mechanisms of lymphocyte functions. Absolute white cell count was elevated at recovery, but returned to preflight levels. Differential counts indicated that this elevation was due to an increase in the number of neutrophils without significant change in lymphocyte counts.

title: Treadmill with Vibration Isolation and Stabilization (TVIS) Harness Comfort Evaluation
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: The Treadmill with Vibration Isolation and Stabilization (TVIS) Harness Comfort Study which was designed as a pilot study was conducted on the Exercise Countermeasures Laboratory's enhanced Zero-g Locomotion Simulator (eZLS) at NASA Glenn Research Center. This experiment falls under the Exercise Countermeasure Project (ECP) and part of the ECP mission is to develop requirements for new exercise equipment designs. This study sought to develop a standardized test protocol for evaluating comfort and effectiveness of two harness designs when loading subjects during simulated zero-gravity treadmill exercise. The purpose of this pilot study was threefold; 1) to evaluate and compare the comfort of the current U.S. TVIS flight harness design with a prototype harness design (Cleveland Clinic) using the eZLS, 2) to provide recommendations for improvements to the harness/subject load device (SLD) system which increases comfort and effectiveness for both in-flight exercise systems and ground based zero-gravity exercise simulators, and 3) to identify measurements and data analysis
approach: Six test subjects (three male, three female) were approved for participation in the pilot TVIS Harness Comfort study, under approved Institutional Review Board (IRB) protocol from the NASA JSC Committee for the Protection of Human Subjects (CPHS). Test subjects exercised with a flight replica of the U.S. harness (currently in use on the International Space Station), and a custom-fit prototype harness (the Cleveland Clinic design), at 7 mph for 3-minute sessions on the eZLS at 50%, 75%, and 100% bodyweight (BW), using two subject load devices - the linear motor subject load device (LM-SLD) and flight replica ISS bungees. The LM-SLD applies a more constant force profile during running to the test subject than the bungees, in which the force fluctuates as a function of the amount of extension in the bungees. Subjects also ran for 20 minutes continuously, at 5 mph (slow jog), with each of the two harnesses and the LM-SLD set at 75% BW. Subjects' heart rate was monitored continuously throughout the exercise sessions with a heart monitor (Polar Electro Inc., Lake Success, NY) and wireless transmitter. The maximum allowable heart rate during this study, as dictated by the IRB panel, was 75% of age-predicted maximum, calculated by the formula 220 minus the subject's age in years. Subjective comfort data was obtained from the subjects using the visual analog scale (VAS) comfort rating system at six body locations (shoulders, neck, back, waist, hips, overall).

RESULTS: The Cleveland Clinic harness was subjectively rated as more comfortable in the shoulders and overall than the U.S. harness. The mean and maximum pressures under the shoulder straps were higher in the U.S harness. There was little difference in gait parameters, regardless of the harness condition.
