title: Effects of Isolation and Confinement on Hippocampal Volume and Visuo-Spatial Memory
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: While a large body of research has documented the effects of microgravity on the cardiovascular system, body fluids, skeletal muscle, and bone metabolism, there is a renewed interest in the understanding how long-term space flight affects cognitive functioning and in particular neuroplasticity. In spite of increasing knowledge on behavioral adaptations during space flight, these studies remain controversial and are not necessarily reliable predictors of changes in brain structure and function. Data from the investigators’ ground-based analog experiments (i.e. bed rest and isolation studies in Antarctica) indicate that the hippocampus will be particularly vulnerable to detrimental effects associated with the various stressors during long-duration space flight. The hippocampus is part of the limbic system and plays important roles in learning and memory formation, and specifically spatial learning and episodic memory. Any malfunction and/or structural changes of the hippocampus could have substantial consequences on learning and memory consolidation as well as general cognitive performance. In spite of ongoing research projects employing state-of-the-art imaging techniques, none of these experiments focused on the hippocampus. The primary objective of this project was to identify the changes in hippocampal subfield volume. Investigators hypothesize that hippocampal subfield volume will be reduced after 30 days of isolation and confinement in NASA’s Human Exploration Research Analog (HERA) facility. Moreover, investigators expect that these changes correlate with decrements in visuo-spatial navigation and memory. They also expect that these changes can be explained by changes in important neurotrophic key factors. This study aimed to assess the impact of human isolation and confinement on: The neuroplasticity of the brain. Cognitive performance and mood. Biomarkers of neuroplasticity. The proliferation and differentiation into hippocampal neurons and their underlying gene expression patterns of an immortalized multipotent, human hippocampal progenitor cell line.
approach: The study compared 16 participants living in the HERA facility for 30 days to 16 control subjects, matched for gender, age, and educational level, who continued their normal living conditions. Subjects completed the Cognition Test on their iPads. Cognition is a test battery that consists of 10 different cognitive tests that are administered with the Cognition software. The battery started with a brief questionnaire, followed by administration of the 10 cognitive tests. Subjects were asked to perform the Cognition battery (all 10 tests) three times pre-mission, once weekly in-mission, and three times post-mission. To assess visuo-spatial performance, working memory, and executive function visuospatial ability testing (10 computer-based tasks) were performed four times pre-mission, once weekly in-mission, and twice post-mission. Subjects also completed Visual Analog Scales (VAS) on their iPad. It is a standardized questionnaire of perceived mental and physical exhaustion, fatigue, stress, workload, conflict, depression, anxiety, personality, social desirability, and sleep quality. They performed this three times pre-mission, once weekly in-mission and up to three times post-mission. The investigators used an innovative, state-of-the art technique for high-resolution hippocampal neuroimaging as well as a unique human 3-D water maze task, which was used as a human analog model for the classical spatial learning task typically employed for laboratory rodents to assess spatial orientation. In addition, biomarkers were obtained from blood and plasma samples to determine key neurotrophic and inflammatory factors related to neuroplasticity. To further elucidate the effects of isolation on neuronal growth investigators assessed hippocampal plasticity in-vitro using an immortalized multipotent, hippocampal progenitor cell line.
results: NASA does not currently have an agreement to archive the hippocampal plasticity and biomarker data from this International investigation. However, the Co-Investigator, Dr. Mathias Basner, submitted the cognitive and behavioral data from all subjects.

title: Coordination of Turning and Reaching
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: How the neuromotor system controls the reactive forces that arise between moving segments of the arm has been studied for years, because several patient populations, including stroke patients and Parkinson’s patients have been shown to suffer from specific deficits in control of interaction forces among limb segments. Previous studies in a rotating artificial gravity environment opened a new perspective on the issue which was relevant for both astronauts and terrestrial patients. The new finding was that Coriolis forces generated between the arm and torso during every day turning and reaching movements are much larger than interaction forces between arm segments, yet we can adapt to them rapidly and completely. Investigators developed a turn and reach paradigm to assess post-flight disturbances of arm-trunk coordination. Their recent ground-based work has shown that simultaneous turn and reach movements involve high rotational velocities of the trunk that generate large, potentially disrupting Coriolis forces on the reaching arm and on balance. Nevertheless, reaching accuracy is preserved because the central nervous system programs compensation for the self-generated Coriolis forces. Failure to predict accurately Coriolis force magnitude produces disruption of coordination and potentially loss of balance. Specific Aims: 1. Parametrically evaluate Coriolis force influences on kinematics and dynamics of voluntary turning and reaching to targets under conditions of normal and increased body weight. 2. Measure reaching movements and postural control after motor adaptation to rearrangement of the relationship between voluntary torso rotation relative to the feet and inertial torso rotation in space. 3. Assess whether motor adaptation to Coriolis force perturbed reaching acquired in a rotating room transfers to turn and reach movements in a natural environment. These experiments will be of value in pinpointing factors contributing to post-flight postural and arm-trunk coordination deficits. They will also have significance for understanding potentially contributing factors in populations at risk for falling. The overall goal of this project was to study reaching movements made during simultaneous voluntary torso rotations, which investigators call turn and reach movements (T&R). These movements generate Coriolis forces which are large enough to cause substantial reaching errors, but such errors do not occur. Understanding the process of compensation for T&R is tantamount to understanding motor learning in novel force environments.
approach: The methodology for this study is embedded in the
results: section below. RESULTS: The first experiment was motivated to understand the process by which we compensate for Coriolis forces generated on the moving arm by simultaneous voluntary torso rotation. Investigators wanted to distinguish between two alternative mechanisms: either a predictive feed forward muscle activation profile is generated on the basis of an internal estimate of the forthcoming combination of torso angular velocity relative to space or arm linear velocity relative to the torso, or reactive feedback compensation is produced due to spinal stretch reflexes and vestibulospinal reflexes. The experimental rationale was to distort motor control of torso rotary movements and then measure whether arm movements would consequently be distorted. If arm movements were normal then accurate feedback about the abnormal torso rotation would have to be considered responsible for correcting it, but if the arm movements showed directional then an improper feed forward compensation based on planned but erroneously executed torso rotation would be the most likely mechanism. The investigators altered motor control of torso rotation movements by having subjects swivel their torso while standing on a platform programmed to swivel at a proportion of the angular speed of their torso (relative to their feet). If the floor turned in the same direction as their torso, it created a situation where the motion of the torso relative to space was larger than the angular rotation of the torso relative to the feet. Inertial motion governs the torque required to move, so in this situation subjects had to learn to increase their foot-to-torso rotary torques in order to achieve a constant rotary excursion of their torso relative to the feet. This was done in darkness, and subjects did not detect that their inertial motion had changed. After many leftward torso movements (without moving the arms) during progressively larger leftward floor rotations, investigators stopped the floor and had subjects make either additional torso movements without arm movements, arm movements without torso movements, or T&R movements. The post-adaptation spatial extent and speed of torso movements were amplified relative to baseline movements. After adaptive potentiation of leftward torso rotation the finger velocity relative to the torso was the same as pre-adaptation, so the rightward Coriolis force was increased. During post-adaptive T&R movements, there was a radial deviation of the arm final position and peak velocity relative to the torso, rightward of the pre-adaptation baseline. Arm movements made without torso rotation did not differ before and after adaptive recalibration of torso movements. The arm deviations seen in the T&R movements indicate subjects had pre-programmed their reaches to compensate for the rightward Coriolis force that would be present if they physically turned leftward the amount they intended rather than the actual larger amount. The second set of experiments investigators completed evaluated the effects of the background force environment and of hefted loads on compensation for Coriolis forces in T&R movements. One experiment examined T&R movements under conditions of normal, decreased and increased body weight, in parabolic flight. The experimental results demonstrate that under 1g conditions subjects when turning and reaching for a target are very accurate, regardless whether they reach slow or fast, or without visual feedback. Normal subjects show temporally overlapping arm and torso velocities, with the peak velocities occurring virtually simultaneously. As a consequence, very large Coriolis forces are generated on the reaching arm; nevertheless these forces do not disrupt movement accuracy. By contrast, reaching movements during passive body rotation have large trajectory deviations and endpoint errors. These results confirm that in natural turn and reach movements there is an anticipatory feed forward compensation for the impending Coriolis force which maintains straight and accurate reaches in external space coordinates. Subjects exposed to 0 g (feet anchored to the floor) and 1.8g force levels in parabolic flight initially exhibit disruptions of movement paths and endpoints. Within 40-50 turn and reach movements they achieve a great deal of compensation. This indicates that the T&R paradigm is useful for evaluating whole body performance in non-1g environments and for pre-adapting subjects who are about to undergo force transitions (e.g., re-entry to Earth gravity, transition from weightlessness to artificial gravity). Another experiment explored the effects of hefted loads on T&R movements. Subjects made T&R movements while grasping objects weighing 500g or 1000g. In addition to providing a static vertical load, the objects increased the dynamic Coriolis force which needed to be compensated during the T&R movements. Investigators found the compensation was optimal under both loads conditions as well as in unloaded conditions. This was true when subjects used their preferred or non-preferred hand. The results indicate the humans can generate automatic compensations for impending Coriolis forces based on estimates of their own body dynamics and the dynamics of a hefted object.

title: Automation Interface Design Tools Development
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: The addition of automation has greatly extended humans’ capability to accomplish tasks, including difficult, complex and safety critical tasks. The majority of Human - Automation Interaction (HAI)
approach: es may provide the type of analysis needed, but are not currently usable by designers without extensive cognitive science expertise. The automation design community needs methods that are usable by designers early in the design process to meet the demands for the development and testing of automation required for space exploration. The
results: in more efficient and safe operations; however, certain unexpected automation behaviours, or “automation surprises” can be frustrating and, in certain safety critical operations (e.g. transportation, spaceflight, medicine), may result in injuries or the loss of life. The next generation of space exploration systems will place an increased reliance on automation. Traditional techniques for the design and evaluation of automation interfaces rely on subject-matter-experts, human-in-the-loop testing (i.e. usability testing), guidelines, heuristics and rules-of-thumb. Given the volume and time-line for the development of new automation required for space exploration, the time and cost required to perform these evaluations by human factor experts will be prohibitive. Further, guidelines, heuristics, and rule-of-thumb have previously yielded sub-optimum designs (as they are focused on the interface, not on the process of interaction between human and automation interface. State of the art cognitive science and Human-Automation Interaction (HAI) approaches may provide the type of analysis needed, but are not currently usable by designers without extensive cognitive science expertise. The automation design community needs methods that are usable by designers early in the design process to meet the demands for the development and testing of automation required for space exploration. The objective of this research project is to develop a set of methodologies and tools to support the design and evaluation efficient, and robust interaction with automation. The research plan is to integrate existing foundational research results into HAI methods and tools usable by designers. APPROACH: This work is divided into three areas, with the ultimate goal of developing a suite of tools to support each area. It is important to note that the idea of the project is to develop and evaluate the tools in actual design processes, and the level and type of support and evaluation will be dependent upon the scope and maturity of each design domain. The three areas are organized around an abstraction of the primary focii of the design process. Analyze: The first set of methods and tools are intended to help designers to identify, describe and evaluate the different parts of the job. Depending on the stage of the design process, these methods are referred to as work domain analyses, task decompositions, task analyses, knowledge elicitation, and in the later stages, validation. Formulate: The second set of methods and tools is intended to bridge the gap from the analysis of the work domain. Specifically, once the structure of the work domain and tasks has been determined, methods and tools are needed to link the task structures to corresponding interface structures that can later be refined and evaluated. We will be drawing upon research from a number of different communities for this effort including ecological interface design and design patterns. Build: This set of methods and tools are intended to enable rapid development and evaluation of automation, including the user-interface and the underlying automation behavior. The specific focus of this effort is to develop methods and tools that are usable by designers who are expert in the design domain, but aren’t necessarily formally trained in computer programming, or human performance analysis. We will primarily be using research in formal methods to help support the Build effort. RESULTS: The outcomes of this research will be methods and tools for the automation of the design and evaluation of the automation interfaces. These tools will provide the means to: (i)meet the demand for analysis required for space exploration development time-line, (ii)enable increased iterative human factors testing of automation prototypes early in the design process (ii) reduce the cost of development by design and testing of proposed systems early in the development life-cycle (iii) reduce the cost of training and the maintenance of proficiency (iv)improve safety (and reduce the costs of inefficiency and unsafe operations) through significant reduction in failure to complete task metrics. This research makes contributions at two levels. At one level, the problems of interaction between humans and computers/automation in a particular application domain was addressed. The domain of application was the planning work done by Attitude Determination and Control Officers (ADCO), part of Mission Control for the International Space Station (ISS). At a second, higher level, it was abstracted from this case to suggest a more general method for needs analysis and this was the primary motivation for this research. A brief summary on the ADCO domain follows, before describing the methods and tools that emerged from working on this case. A core aspect of this research was a detailed study of the planning work done by ADCO and identification of the work needs that should be supported by software. As the analysis was carried out of the ADCO planning domain, the characterization of the problem was changed. It was realized that rather than focusing on the current tasks and practices, as in Task Analysis, the needs future software should meet were identified. One result of this work was support for ADCO by providing an analysis of ADCO needs. An illustrative prototype designed to better fit these needs was developed. An experimental study of this prototype, comparing performance to that with the legacy system was conducted. These products are of value to ADCO operators seeking the design of software that is more effective than their current legacy systems. The second, more general result was development of methods and tools for carrying out such analyses. The ADCO domain was used to develop Structure Identification, our approach to needs analysis. Structure Identification was developed to be particularly appropriate for rapid identification of needs for safety critical, technical, information work. Needs analysis based on Structure Identification finds the high-level structure in the work domain and uses this to design the structure of the interaction between the human and computer or automation. A combination of eliciting function information from expert users, identifying candidate structure from documents and functional descriptions, and vetting the developing characterization with experts was relied on. Structure Identification contrasts with conducting needs analysis based on Task Analysis; task analysis identifies current tasks, yet a change in the work applications naturally brings with it change in the tasks so that matching the old tasks is not a reliable design guide. Task Analysis can be a helpful approach to identifying structure, but we prioritize identifying the domain structure not the activities. This approach is related to both Work Domain Analysis (WDA) and Contextual Inquiry (CI), in that these also seek to identify stable aspects of work in order to guide design. WDA focuses on identifying constraints, particularly constraints in how a physical system, such as a chemical plant, operates; it is directly applicable to control tasks, but much less applicable to work consisting of finding, transforming, building, and distributing information products. CI methods focus on observing users, typically carrying out office work; this approach is less adequate in highly technical domains where critical aspects of work cannot be understood from watching users. The goal was to make needs analysis more efficient and effective. To this end the methods that were developed focused on gathering important information quickly. We consolidated what we learned to make the methods easier to reuse and to apply to another case, by building simple tools as we carried out the needs analysis for the ADCO planning domain and developed the SI approach. These include templates for gathering high-level function information from experts, templates for presenting the identified structure to experts for verification, and templates for comparing the contents of multiple product documents. An additional contribution of the research was a preliminary assessment of Structure Identification. Broadly, whether Structure Identification, followed by Structure Matching from the domain to an application structure, contributes to better design of the application was investigated. An illustrative study using the ADCO planning domain was conducted. The domain structure was used to guide the design of an experimental prototype for ADCO planning. An experiment was conducted comparing the experimental prototype, which closely matched the domain structure, versus the legacy system, which matched much more poorly. A variety of measures were included, from speed of performance to conceptual understanding and retention of periods of disuse. Differences in performance on a variety of planning tasks that are detailed analogs of simple ADCO planning tasks were predicted: overall faster performance by users of the new, well-matched system compared to that by users of the legacy, poorly-matching system; and particular performance advantage for the new system at points where the legacy system most mismatched domain structure. It was found that performance times were cut in half for the new prototype vs legacy system on some tasks, accompanied by much lower error rates as well. Further, it was also found the predicted pattern of poor performance at legacy points of mismatch. The whole design cycle was run through, from needs analysis through evaluation, in the ADCO domain. This process provided an illustrative case showing the feasibility of this approach. The results from this experiment suggest that capturing and matching domain structure may be an efficient, productive way to guide design of interaction between humans and computers/automation for technical information work.

title: A Comprehensive Fatigue Management Program and an Evaluation of a Photic Countermeasure for Mission Controllers
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: The success of a human space flight critically depends on the interaction between the crewmembers and the mission controllers. The ability of both the crew and the controllers to be alert and to maintain high levels of cognitive function while operating and/or monitoring complex, technical equipment is essential. Optimal human health, performance and safety during space flight operations requires sufficient sleep and synchrony between the circadian pacemaker—which regulates the timing of sleep, endocrine function, alertness and performance—and the timing of the imposed sleep-wake schedule. Flight mission controllers often work extended duration shifts, rotating shifts, including night shifts. Such schedules instigate significant acute and chronic sleep deprivation and consequently fatigue. Although the effects are often unrecognized, both the acute and chronic lack of sleep substantially degrades a federal air marshal’s ability to react and think quickly, to make good decisions, and to recognize when fatigue is impairing his or her own performance and safety. Further, both acute and chronic sleep deprivation adversely affects personal health, increasing the risk of gastrointestinal and heart disease, impairing glucose metabolism and immune function, and substantially increasing the risk of injury due to motor vehicle crashes. In addition, it is likely that a significant proportion of mission controllers suffer from undiagnosed sleep disorders which will further impair their sleep and exacerbate fatigue. The deleterious effects of fatigue are readily observed in a wide range of safety-sensitive professions, including law enforcement officers, and include increased risk of self-injury, higher rates of fatigue-related motor vehicle accidents, and greater incidence of serious errors. The investigators implemented a Fatigue Risk Management Program (FRMP) for the flight controllers. The goals of this program were to reduce the adverse consequences of fatigue on the flight controllers’ alertness, performance, health, and safety. The objectives of the program were to: 1) Evaluate the current flight controller schedules; 2) Develop an online education training program; 3) Offer an efficient online screening for common sleep disorders; and 4) Evaluate the acceptability, feasibility and efficacy of a combined fatigue countermeasure including shorter-wavelength light exposure during operational night shifts.
approach: Investigators enrolled 17 flight controllers and three flight directors selected from the seven International Space Station (ISS) mission control consoles regularly staffed for Orbit 1 operations (Flight, OPS Planning, ADCO, SPARTAN, ETHOS, CRONUS, Ground Control). Data were collected during one off-console week and each controller was scheduled to work two blocks (4-7 days each) of Orbit 1 shifts during the study. They randomized each block to either the control or experimental condition. During the experimental condition, controllers were encouraged to visit the Experimental Break Room (EBR) once before the shift, twice during the shift, as operations allowed, and following the Orbit 1 shift. The EBR provided subjects with passive exposure to blue-enriched fluorescent lamps installed in existing ceiling fixtures. In addition, subjects were encouraged to exercise on treadmills or stationary bikes located in the room (10 minute bouts, not to exceed more than 65% maximum heart rate). The controllers were instructed to continue their normal routines during the control block. The controllers completed Visual Analog Scales and a 5-minute Psychomotor Vigilance Task before, twice during, and following each Orbit1 shift. They also wore actigraphs to monitor sleep and completed daily work/sleep logs. All subjects completed drive diaries following each commute and a subset of the subjects wore Optalert drowsiness monitoring glasses on commutes to and from work to
results: The fatigue countermeasure proved feasible and acceptable as controllers reported taking 2.9 breaks per experimental shift and 90% of prescribed exercise sessions were completed. Flight controllers reported being significantly more alert and happy and had faster response times during Orbit 1 shifts with access to the EBR as compared to control Orbit 1 shifts.

title: Evaluation of Thermoregulation During Space Flight
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Impaired thermoregulation may have significant impact during space flight operations such as extravehicular activities (EVA), entry, landing and egress. Impaired thermoregulation, as represented by an increase in core (intestinal) temperature in response to a given thermal load, has been consistently observed in subjects confined to bed rest or immersed in water (Greenleaf, 1980; Greenleaf, 1985; Fortney, 1987). Further, these changes were observed during exercise following these simulated microgravity exposures (Greenleaf, 1980; Greenleaf, 1985; Fortney, 1987). Similar changes were expected to occur during space flight. This impairment of temperature regulation may be manifested as decreased exercise capacity and increased orthostatic intolerance; it may also be manifested as higher levels of core body temperature for a given level of work (oxygen consumption, Vo 2 ) both during and after space flight. The higher core temperatures may be due to altered cutaneous vasodilatory reflex (delayed onset of vasodilatation and decreased skin perfusion for a given level of core temperature), increased sweating threshold, and decreased sweating sensitivity, while heat production might not be altered. The purpose of this preliminary experiment was to assess human core (intestinal) temperature and thermoregulatory responses to exercise after adaptation to long-duration spaceflight. Specific objectives of this experiment were to: 1) Determine whether overall thermoregulation is impaired during space flight by comparing core temperature (T in ) during two submaximal levels of aerobic exercise preflight, inflight, and postflight; 2) Determine whether the elevated core temperature is caused by altered heat production, as calculated by indirect calorimetry; 3) Determine whether the elevated core temperature is caused by impaired heat loss, as assessed by the skin blood flow/core temperature relationship (where changes in skin blood flow are measured pre- and postflight by laser Doppler flowmetry, and estimated during all tests by calculations of tissue conductance) and by the sweating response. Local sweat response/core temperature relationship was measured pre- and postflight using a dew point hygrometer, and total body sweat loss is estimated during all tests by measuring body weight loss. It was anticipated that, for a given absolute level of work, body temperatures would increase to a greater degree due to (1) a smaller production and/or decreased efficiency of evaporation of sweat, and (2) decreased convective heat loss from the surface of the skin.
approach: This investigation examined body temperatures (skin and core), heat production (indirect calorimetry), and evaporative heat loss during 2 standard levels of exercise (40% and 65% of preflight VO 2peak ). Submaximal Cycle Exercise Test (before and after flight) - Graded maximal cycle exercise testing was first conducted to volitional fatigue on 2 crewmembers in the supine position. These sessions occurred 2-3 days before the preflight submaximal exercise tests, repeated during the last 5 days of the mission, and 6 days after landing (R+6). The graded maximal cycle exercise test protocol consisted of: 5 minutes of supine rest on the ergometer 2 minutes of warm-up at 50 Watts (W) 5 minutes of pedaling at 100 W 5 minutes of pedaling at 125 W 5 minutes of pedaling at 150 W After the 150-W segment of the protocol, exercise intensity was increased by 25 W-per-minute until the subject could no longer maintain the 75-rpm pedaling frequency. Cool down was conducted at 50 W for 3-5 minutes after maximal exercise. During each maximal test, oxygen (O 2 ) uptake and carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) production were measured and averaged over 30-s intervals using a gas analysis system. Heart rate was continuously monitored with a standard electrocardiogram (ECG). Blood pressure was measured during the last 30 seconds of each exercise level using manual sphygmomanometry. The highest level of O 2 uptake, averaged over a 60-s period, was designated peak oxygen consumption (VO 2peak ). Exercise intensities requiring 40% and 65% of the preflight peak value were used during the submaximal tests. The supine submaximal cycle tests were conducted 145-146 days before flight (L-145) and on R+5. All testing was performed at room temperature (22.6-23.3°C; 56-64% humidity) and at the same time of day to mitigate circadian effects. Postflight sessions occurred during the summer (July, 1995), but the crewmembers were almost exclusively confined to air-conditioned buildings. The submaximal exercise tests consisted of a continuous protocol of the following: 20 minutes of quiet rest 20 minutes of exercise at 40% preflight VO 2peak (50 or 60 W) 20 minutes of exercise at 65% preflight VO 2peak (100 or 110 W) 10 minutes of quiet resting recovery Heart rates during submaximal exercise were monitored with a heart watch. Blood pressure was measured twice before exercise and every 10 minutes during exercise with a manual sphygmomanometer. Skin temperatures were measured continuously with four external skin thermistors (forearm, calf, thigh, chest) and recorded with a data logger. Core temperature was measured using a small ingestible telemetry thermal sensor pill that was ingested 6 hours before exercise. Temperature data was sampled every 30 seconds and stored in a receiver. Skin blood flow velocity was measured continuously with a laser Doppler skin blood flow monitor using an integrated probe attached to the forearm with a local skin-heating (38°C) collar. Local sweating rate at the upper quadrant of the chest was measured continuously with a dew point hygrometer sweat system. The dew point sensor was ventilated (500-800 ml· min -1 ) with ambient air from the room. Subjects towel dried after each exercise session and were weighed in the same dry gym shorts before and after exercise. All measurement devices were calibrated before each exercise session. Submaximal Exercise Test (during flight): No submaximal data was collected during flight due to the late arrival of the Spektr module and scheduling problems after the module arrived.
results: These results should be viewed as preliminary results only, since the low number of subjects did not allow for statistical analysis of the data. However, the results do suggest that thermoregulation was impaired following long-duration space flight. Maximal Exercise: The preflight maximal exercise supine cycle VO2peak values for the subjects were 32.6 and 29.5 ml• kg-1• min-1 for Subjects 1 and 2, respectively. Due to the limited active muscle mass with this form of exercise, these supine cycle values were each approximately 20% lower than the measured upright treadmill VO2peak values. During flight, Subject 1 was reported to have performed approximately 70% of the standard prescribed Russian countermeasure program (which consists of approximately 2 hours each day of aerobic and resistive exercises), while Subject 2 was reported to have performed less than 70% of the prescribed countermeasures. Near the end of the mission, on flight day 112, Subject 1 had a cycle VO2peak of 27.2 ml• kg-1• min-1(reduced 17% from preflight); for Subject 2, the value was 20.8 ml• kg-1• min-1(reduced 29%). After flight, neither crewmember could complete the exercise protocol, stopping after 28-29 minutes. Postflight, cycle VO2peak on R+6 was further reduced to 23.5 ml• kg-1• min-1 for Subject 1 (reduced 28% from preflight). For Subject 2, no value was obtained because the medical monitor would not allow the postflight maximal exercise test to be performed because of the subject's delayed recovery from the mission. Submaximal Exercise: Both crewmembers were able to complete the preflight submaximal exercise protocol; final exercise heart rates were only 137 and 123 bpm for Subjects 1 and 2, respectively. On R+5, Subjects 1 and 2 could not complete 11 and 12 minutes of the 65% VO2peak level, respectively. In both cases, the medical monitor terminated the test shortly after the exercise heart rate exceeded the preflight response. In each case, the subject appeared fatigued and was having difficulty maintaining the pedaling frequency. Blood pressure responses to exercise were similar before and after flight. Oxygen uptake on R+5 was similar to preflight values, except at the last sampling time for Subject 1, where the lower value was most likely due to his difficulty maintaining the pedaling frequency. The Respiratory Exchange Ratio (RER) value was higher at most sampling times on R+5. A consistent difference was not seen between pre- and postflight supine resting skin temperatures at any measurement site. Resting intestinal temperature was similar preflight and at R+5. During postflight exercise, the core temperature, (Tin, ingestible telemetry pill) at test termination was similar (37.8 degrees C for both subjects despite a 29% shorter exercise time and a 40% reduction in the total cumulative work (W• min-1). The sweating and skin blood flow responses for the two subjects were altered postflight. The slope of the sweating/Tin relationship (mg• min-1• cm-2• °C-1) was reduced from 4.5 preflight to 2.1 postflight for Subject 1 and from 11 to 3.6 for Subject 2. The slope of the skin blood flow/Tin relationship (percent change Perfusion Unit• °C-1) was also reduced from 346 preflight to 214 postflight for Subject 1 and from 214 to 143 for Subject 2. Tin thresholds for the onset of sweating and vasodilation were not altered in a consistent manner after flight. For sweating, Tin thresholds (°C) were 37.4 preflight and 37.6 postflight for Subject 1 and 36.6 and 36.6 for Subject 2. For skin blood flow, Tin thresholds were 37.3 preflight and 37.5 postflight for Subject 1 and 37.6 preflight and 37.7 postflight for Subject 2. Total body sweat (weight) loss during preflight exercise was 636 g vs. 272 g postflight for Subject 1 and 455 g vs. 45 g postflight for Subject 2. Subject 2 had just reached the sweating threshold postflight when the session was terminated. Body weight on R+5 was reduced in both crewmembers from the preflight value--for Subject 1 by 0.8 kg and for Subject 2 by 2.3 kg. In conclusion, these preliminary findings suggest alteration of heat loss responses in two crewmembers following a 115-day space flight. The sensitivity of the heat loss responses was reduced after long-duration space flight, resulting in a faster rate of increase in core temperature.

title: Monitoring of Bone Loss Bio-Markers in Human Sweat: A Non-Invasive, Time Efficient Means of Monitoring Bone Resorption Markers under Micro and Partial Gravity Loading Conditions
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Loss of bone mass, density and structural integrity is a significant health risk in a variety of populations such as the elderly, post-menopausal women, young female athletes and astronauts. Such changes in overall bone quality lead to a greater risk of bone fracture and potentially a reduced rate of bone healing after injury. The ability to monitor biomarkers of bone remodeling (e.g. ionized calcium, collagen cross links) using sweat as an analytical sample provides an attractive alternative to the more invasive and costly measures presently employed, such as a bone density scans by DXA, 24-hour urine collection protocols or whole blood analyses. The development of a non-invasive, skin-mounted monitoring device which allows the quantitation of ionized calcium and/or collagen cross links in sweat will allow bone loss to be monitored in a wide variety of terrestrial populations that to date have not easily been monitored outside of a clinical setting. This particular project focuses on validating the concept that sweat analysis can be used as a non-invasive means of monitoring bone loss in crew members during periods of mechanical unloading under altered gravitational conditions. In addition, this project is also investigating the best technical
approach: to collecting a sweat sample, specifically applicable to the space-flight environment, while utilizing well-accepted, clinically validated analytical methods. Development of a technology capable of real-time monitoring of biomarkers of bone loss that satisfies the criteria required for use in the space-flight environment (i.e. non-invasive/non-intrusive, passive, small, light-weight, low power) has many direct applications in various populations here on Earth. APPROACH: The team was tasked with validating that the rate and extent of unloading-induced bone loss in humans can be assessed by monitoring the levels of two bone resorption markers in sweat, namely ionized calcium and collagen break-down products. Initial testing was carried out in a young healthy population (at rest and during activity) and then in a clinical population undergoing active bone loss, namely spinal cord injury patients. All groups included both male and female participants. Biomarker concentration was determined in contemporaneous samples of sweat, blood, and urine collected during both short (24 hour) and long-term studies (multiple sessions over a period of months) to define the relationship between biomarker levels in the respective biological samples. Several different sweat collection techniques were investigated to determine the most appropriate and efficient means of sample collection suitable for deployment during a space flight mission. These experiments also included investigation of the most appropriate biomarker analysis techniques that allow for future deployment in micro- or partial gravity environments. This near-real-time monitoring approach also provided the information required to justify modifying an ineffective bone loss countermeasure prescription during a mission. One of the approaches tested was a novel, micro-fabricated fluid collection capillary array, known as the micro-fabricated sweat patch (MSP) device, specifically developed for use in microgravity. The MSP technology was initially developed because of its potential to become an autonomous, solid-state collection/analysis device worn on the skin of an astronaut requiring little or no crew interaction to perform its monitoring function.
results: Initial studies indicate significant individual variation in the amount and rate of sweating observed between subjects based on: 1) the anatomical site sampled (i.e. forehead, shoulder, forearm); 2) level of activity (i.e. "active" sweating during exercise; and 3) the concentration of biomarkers relative to the onset of "active" sweating. In addition, the existing sweat collection technology previously employed to collect sweat (i.e. commercial absorptive pad) exhibited significant analytical issues based on sub-optimal analyte retention and analyte extraction efficiency. To overcome these difficulties investigators developed a standardized sweat collection protocol in which subjects performed a defined exercise protocol at a fixed level of intensity (i.e. 30 minutes of aerobic exercise at an intensity of 40 percent of their age-predicted VO2max) under similar environmental conditions and hydration status. Sweat samples were collected at the forehead using micro-fabricated polymer capillary arrays which collect sweat as an unadulterated liquid sample. This approach allows both determination of the volume of sweat produced and has the advantage of minimal residual analyte retention within the array due to its polymer construction, unlike the commercially available absorptive sweat collection technology. Sweat samples were initially collected at discrete time intervals to determine when during exercise-induced sweating did biomarker concentration reach "steady-state" levels. These experiments indicated that biomarker concentrations (i.e. Ca2+ and T-CCL) in "active" sweat reached a "steady state" after 15 minutes of exercise regardless of the volume of sweat produced by a particular individual. In addition, analyte concentration (i.e. T-CCL) in actively produced sweat was found to be highly correlated (R = 0.92) with plasma levels of the same analyte during the period sweat was being collected. However, comparison of analyte concentration produced during actively produced sweat and 24 hour urine voids in the same individual indicated, indicated that although related in a linear fashion (R = 0.61), sweat analyte excretion during the 15 min period of exercise was not predictive of total 24hr urine analyte excretion. As 24 hour urine void collection provides an integrated value for whole body biomarker excretion rates, comparison of the amount of biomarker excreted during a 15 minute period of “active” sweating from 7.5cm of skin surface at the fore-head appears inappropriate as a means of predicting total calcium and T-CCL excreted in a 24 hour urine void. The team investigated the accuracy of the existing commercially available absorptive patch sweat collection technology with regard to analyte concentration relative to unadulterated liquid sweat samples collected in a contemporaneous fashion at the same anatomical site. These data indicated that the cellulose matrix of the commercially available absorptive patch posed significant analytical problems. These issues were that the cellulose matrix: 1) contained significant amounts of endogenous calcium signal; 2) resulted in significant retention of sweat-derived T-CCL that could not be extracted from the matrix using the standard method (i.e. extraction in ddH2O); and 3) that extraction efficiency from the matrix was variable between identical samples. To address these analytical issues during Year 2 of these projects, investigators studied the use of two new absorptive materials, a glass fiber material and a polypropylene woven material, for the collection of sweat over a 24 hour period. Their initial experiments focused on the extraction efficiency of four bone loss biomarkers of interest, namely calcium, T-CCL, NTx and osteocalcin (OST). They also modified the extraction protocol to utilize acidified ddH2O (pH 5.0) or a Tris buffer (pH 5.0) to enhance the solubility of these biomarkers in the extraction buffer and reduce ionic interactions within the matrix of the absorptive material. Unlike the original commercially available cellulose absorptive pad technology, efficient recovery of known amounts of all analytes was achieved using our modified extraction method from both the glass fiber and woven polypropylene materials. Glass fiber absorptive pads (7.5cm2 in area) and the modified extraction protocol were used to collect sweat samples from a total of 18 normal healthy subjects over a period of 24 hours at three separate anatomical locations: shoulder, hip and forearm. 24 hour urine voids were also collected from these subjects during the same 24 hour period. When the total amount of calcium excreted in sweat over a 24 hour period into a 7.5cm2 glass fiber absorptive pad was compared to the total amount of calcium excreted in a 24 hour urine void obtained from the same individual, results indicated that there is a near linear correlation between the two values in sweat collected from the shoulder (R = 0.90) and forearm (R=0.86) and contemporaneous 24 hour urine voids. A similar relationship between 24 hour sweat T-CCL and 24 hour urine void T-CCL levels was observed at the shoulder (R = 0.99) in a subset of these subjects (N=6) for which this analysis has been completed. Data indicate that calcium and T-CCL levels detected in 24 hour sweat samples are highly correlated with levels detected in 24 hour urine voids from healthy individuals, suggesting that bone loss biomarker concentration in the criterion sample (i.e. 24 hour urine void) can be accurately predicted from that found in a sweat sample collected over the same 24 hour period using an absorptive pad technology. The project then focused on validating this approach to monitoring bone loss biomarkers in a terrestrial population undergoing active bone loss (a clinical population of spinal cord injured patients). In addition, the team also developed a new protocol suitable for deployment on-orbit for the extraction and collection of analytes from the absorptive sweat patch based on the Salivette technology previously validated for use on-orbit.

title: Influence of Exercise on Human Single Muscle Fiber Function with Long-Term Bedrest
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: The purpose of this investigation was to extend the previous space flight and ground-based studies that have examined the cellular mechanisms related to the loss of muscle mass and function with long-duration unloading. Investigators measured the contractile properties of individual slow- and fast-twitch muscle fibers from lower limb skeletal muscles and the concentration of the two main contractile proteins, myosin and actin, from single muscle fibers. These cellular physiology and molecular muscle studies were conducted on subjects before and after 90-days of bed rest with and without countermeasure activities (aerobic and resistance training). These studies will provide further insight into the mechanisms of muscle wasting associated with space flight and provide information on effective countermeasures to maintain skeletal muscle mass and function in male and female space travelers.
approach: Vastus lateralis and soleus muscle biopsies were analyzed for global protein fractions (mixed, sarcoplasmic, myofibrillar) and force-specific proteins (myosin, actin, collagen).
results: Significant Findings: 1. Upper Leg – Complete and viable exercise countermeasures for whole muscle and single muscle fiber contractile function/structure. The resistance plus aerobic exercise program was complimentary for unloaded skeletal muscle. 2. Lower Leg – Incomplete exercise prescription. The resistance plus aerobic exercise program was better than resistance exercise alone. 3. Nutrition – The nutrition countermeasure provided no benefit for the protection of skeletal muscle during long-term unloading. In fact, the nutrition intervention led to greater loss in thigh muscle mass as compared to control. 4. Potential gender-related issues for skeletal muscle. Women appear to loss more muscle mass in a shorter period of time compared to men. 5. The WISE 2005 exercise prescription protocol and hardware were as good as or better than what investigators have reported with the International Space Station (ISS) regimen. 6. The last decade of exercise countermeasure research has significantly reduced the time necessary to protect most muscle groups ( Vastus Lateralis This study shows that the concurrent training program of resistance (2-3 days per week) and aerobic (3-4 days per week) exercise was protective of the thigh muscle during 60-days of bed rest in women. This finding is supported by the maintenance of whole muscle and single muscle fiber parameters (MHC I and IIa) during the bed rest period. These data indicate that in light of the difficulty in protecting slow-twitch muscle fibers by resistance training alone during prolonged unloading, concurrent resistance and aerobic training protocols should be considered as a viable countermeasure for the upper leg of crewmembers during long-duration space travel. The nutrition countermeasure did not provide an ergogentic benefit for whole muscle or single muscle fiber size and function during bed rest. This information should be useful to the international space community and health care industry working with patients stricken with extended bed rest. Soleus While the addition of aerobic exercise to resistance exercise proved complimentary and completely protective for the vastus lateralis, whole muscle and single muscle fiber properties for the soleus, in particular the MHC I fibers, did not achieve the same level of protection. The fact that MHC I fibers from the vastus lateralis and soleus muscle atrophy to a similar extent with long-duration unloading, but respond differently to the same exercise loading program, was an interesting and novel finding. These data suggest that unique and specific exercise regimens for the upper (vastus lateralis) and lower leg (soleus) may be necessary to protect human skeletal muscle during extended unloading periods. The difference in the vastus lateralis and soleus muscle response to the concurrent exercise program is not a volume of exercise issue per se, but more related to the type of muscle contractions performed. All of the muscle contractions performed as part of this investigation (>100,000 per muscle group over 60-days) were dynamic in nature. However, given that the soleus is suited for postural support; static type contractions of longer duration to more closely mimic the typical load on Earth in a 1-g environment may be required. It is not recommended that static load contractions be performed in lieu of dynamic contractions. Rather, it is likely that a proper combination of static and dynamic contractions will be necessary to protect the quantitative (size) and qualitative (intrinsic speed and power) properties of the soleus muscle fibers.

title: Retrospective Analysis of Inflight Exercise Loading and Health Outcomes
variables: Areal bone mineral density (aBMD), femoral head
Areal bone mineral density (aBMD), left trochanter
Areal bone mineral density (aBMD), lumbar spine
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Astronauts perform treadmill exercise during long-duration space missions to counter the harmful effects of microgravity exposure upon bone, muscle, and cardiopulmonary health. When exercising in microgravity, astronauts wear a harness and bungee system that provides forces that maintain attachment to the treadmill. Typical applied forces are less than body weight. The current exercise devices on the International Space Station (ISS) allow astronauts to complete prescriptions at higher intensities which potentially allow for greater exercise benefits with increased efficiency. However, although overall health outcomes have improved, the specific factors related to increased benefits have yet to be determined. This study had the following specific aims: Quantify the exercise-related mechanical loading experienced by crewmembers during their mission on the ISS. Explore relationships between exercise loading variables, bone, and muscle health changes during the mission. Determine if specific mechanical loading variables are more critical than others in protecting health. Develop methodology for operational use in monitoring crew exercise programs.
approach: This retrospective analysis was conducted using data from seven crewmembers that were subjects in the Treadmill Kinematics study (Kinematics_T2). Crewmembers completed approximately six-month missions on the ISS and performed regular exercise on the T2 throughout their mission, although each subject’s specific prescription varied. Exercise logs and inflight ground reaction force data were summarized to quantify T2 mechanical loading occurring during flight. Mechanical loading variables were compared to bone mineral density changes to determine if relationships existed.
results: Results indicate that increased time and distance jogging related to improved bone health. Further investigation revealed that in the current subject pool, those who performed exercise sessions that include both running and jogging, such as during high intensity interval training, tended to have better bone-related outcomes. More study is necessary, including increasing subject size and inclusion of resistance exercise to better assess exercise relationships to bone health.

title: Oxidative Stress as a Mechanism for Altering Acute and Chronic Functional Changes in the CNS Exposed to Low Dose, Low Dose Rates, and Mixed Fields of Protons and HZE Nuclei
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: The space radiation environment poses unique hazards that include solar particle events and galactic cosmic rays. These types of radiations have been shown to cause acute and long-lasting chemical changes referred to as oxidative stress that can alter the normal physiology of the central nervous system (CNS). The chemical species produced can cause a wide range of effects in cells within the CNS that largely depend on the types of pathways they activate and the types of damage they produce. Proper functioning of the CNS depends on many factors, but is known to require subpopulations of neural stem and precursor cells that participate in the repair of CNS injury
approach: The methodology is embedded in the
results: ing from irradiation. This proposal focused on analyzing the effects of space radiation on these critical populations of multipotent neural stem and precursor cells. Investigators have developed the technology to isolate and grow these cells in culture and will use a variety of techniques to analyze how cells exposed to space radiation change. They planned to monitor the time course of oxidative stress in these cells and how that depends on the dose, the dose rate and type of radiation applied. They will determine how radiation-induced oxidative stress impacts cellular proliferation, signaling between cells, cell fate and survival. Collectively their studies using both rodent and human neural stem and precursor cells will help NASA understand the acute and longer-lasting sequelae associated with the exposure of the CNS to the space radiation environment. These studies will facilitate efforts to more appropriately establish estimates of risk for radiation exposure to the CNS in space. APPROACH: The methodology is embedded in the results below. RESULTS: Past data collected by the investigators has demonstrated that the radiation response of multipotent neural precursor cells to x-rays, protons, and HZE nuclei involves an acute and persistent oxidative stress that can last for months. The importance of neural precursor cells to the repair and remodeling of the irradiated CNS is underscored by the data showing that the radiation-induced depletion of these cells is linked to the inhibition of neurogenesis and the onset of cognitive impairment. Investigators believe oxidative injury is critical in this context, and plays a contributory if not causal role in determining neural precursor cell function, survival and fate. A summary of the study findings are listed below. 1. Mice genetically manipulated to overexpress human catalase in the mitochondria were found to exhibit higher basal levels of neurogenesis and after low dose exposure to 150 MeV protons. These data suggest that interventions targeted to reduce oxidative stress in the mitochondria are neuroprotective. 2. A great deal of work characterizing the response of cultured neural stem cells from both rodents and humans were performed. These data reveal a marked predisposition of neural stem cells to exhibit radiation-induced oxidative stress. The functional importance of radiation-induced oxidative stress in regulating adaptive responses was also shown, as treatment of cells with the antioxidant N-acetylcysteine eliminated the protective effect of prior exposure on cell survival following exposure to a subsequent higher dose of protons. Collectively, these data provide further evidence in support of the ides that space relevant fluences of charged particles elicit significant levels of oxidative stress that impact survival and proliferation. 3. Work characterizing the effect of HZE particle irradiation on cultured neural stem cells and the irradiated rodent brain was performed. There was a marked and persistent increases in oxidative stress found months after exposure to very low fluences of 600 MeV iron ions. Oxidative stress measurement made in vivo found that low dose exposure caused marked changes in the level and activity of several key antioxidant enzymes two weeks after exposure that returned to background one month after irradiation. Importantly, exposure to 5 or 30 cGy of 600 MeV oxygen or titanium ions was found to elicit significant deficits in novel object recognition 12 weeks after exposure. These data link key changes in redox metabolism to functional changes in cognition, changes that have important implications for astronauts exposed to the space radiation environment. 4. Investigators were able to assess the metabolic activity of neural stem cells after low dose irradiation using non-invasive 2-photon spectroscopy. 5. This is a comprehensive study that has defined the radiobiological response and consequences of human neural stem cells exposed to low LET radiation. 6. A review of the redox stress biology of irradiated neural stem cells and stem cells from other organ systems. In summary, investigators have obtained significant data over the course of their funding period demonstrating that low dose charged particle irradiation can elicit oxidative stress in multipotent neural stem and precursor cells, derived from both rodents and humans. Their data shows conclusively that prior exposure elicits adaptive responses that are capable of attenuating oxidative stress and survival. Collectively their data suggest that radiation-induced oxidative stress constitutes a biochemical mechanism of functional significance to neural stem cell biology and cognition.

title: Hypovolemia as a Model of Space Flight: Cardiovascular Exercise Effects and Countermeasures
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Reduced exercise capacity, orthostatic tolerance, and plasma volume are common observances following space flight and bed rest. The Johnson Space Center Cardiovascular Laboratory (CVL) investigated the relationship between orthostatic hypotension and plasma volume by pharmacologically inducing hypovolemia in normal subjects. The Exercise Physiology Laboratory (EXL) sought to extend this information to understanding the factors involved in decreased exercise capacity. Following orthostatic testing in normal and hypovolemic conditions, a subset of the subjects recruited performed a graded cycle exercise test to volitional fatigue to determine peak oxygen consumption (VO2pk). The CVL was responsible for the overall administration of the project, and the EXL was responsible for the additional measurements and analyses. Specifically, the CVL recruited and instructed subjects, scheduled the testing, and was responsible for measurement of plasma/blood volume and orthostatic tolerance. The EXL was responsible for administering the test of exercise capacity using a cycle ergometer protocol similar to that used for International Space Station (ISS) and Space Shuttle (STS) astronauts. In addition to the ISS and Flight Analog Project standard measures during the cycle ergometer test, the CVL obtained echocardiographic measures of cardiac function and plasma catecholamines, and the EXL measured blood lactate concentrations and peripheral muscle metabolism by near infrared spectroscopy (NIRS). Oxygen consumption, heart rate, rating of perceived exertion, and blood pressure were measured per standard laboratory protocols. Additionally, echocardiographic measures of stroke volume, systolic and diastolic function, blood lactate, plasma catecholamines, and peripheral muscle metabolism by NIRS was measured. Data from these testing sessions assist in understanding the factors associated with reduced exercise capacity after space flight; served as a basis of comparison for responses to similar tests after space flight and bed rest; and aided in the continued development of NIRS as a non-invasive metabolic measurement system for space flight and extravehicular activities. The primary purpose of this study was to determine the specific effects of decreased plasma volume, independent of deconditioning, on aerobic exercise capacity (VO2pk), cardiac function, and peripheral muscle metabolism. The investigators also sought to collect pilot data regarding two pharmacological interventions that are being considered for the treatment of post-flight orthostatic hypotension that may similarly protect VO2pk. The secondary purpose of this project was to validate the use of a National Space Biomedical Research Institute (NSBRI) funded sensor as a surrogate measure of oxygen consumption in an analogue of space flight and as non-invasive method to determine anaerobic threshold. Specific Aims were: (1) To determine whether central cardiac and peripheral skeletal indices of exercise performance are related to reduced VO2pk and anaerobic threshold in subjects whose plasma volume is reduced. (2) To determine whether near infrared spectroscopy can be used to non-invasively, unobtrusively measure oxygen consumption during cycle ergometer exercise in normal and hypovolemic conditions.
approach: Subjects gave written informed consent prior to participation. Twelve healthy subjects (8 men and 4 women), passed a modified Air Force Class III physical examination, and volunteered to participate in this study. Subjects received written and verbal explanations of the testing procedures and provided written documentation of informed consent prior to participation. Study protocols and procedures were reviewed and approved by the NASA Johnson Space Center Committee for the Protection of Human Subjects. Following a familiarization session, subjects participated in testing in both the normovolemic and hypovolemic conditions in cross-over design. For the seven days prior to the normovolemia testing day, subjects were encouraged to drink fluids ad libitum and consume a normal diet supplemented with 2 g of sodium each day. To induce hypovolemia, subjects received a single dose of furosemide and consumed a low salt diet provided by the investigators. The order of the conditions was not randomly assigned initially due to the constraints of a companion study, but the investigators attempted to balance the order of the test conditions. Seven of the 12 subjects completed testing in the normovolemic condition first. Hypovolemia Subjects received a single dose of furosemide through a catheter in an antecubital vein. Blood pressure and urine output were monitored during and after the infusion until they had stabilized, typically one to two hours. Following the infusion, the catheter was removed and subjects consumed a controlled, low-sodium, caffeine-free diet for 30 hours. The diet was developed by dieticians at Memorial Hermann Hospital General Clinical Research Center (Houston, TX), and the food was prepared by the Space Food Systems Laboratory at Johnson Space Center. The diet was limited to 600 calories and 250 mg sodium per day. Subjects were allowed to drink sodium-free bottled water ad libitum. Plasma Volume Plasma volume was measured using the carbon monoxide rebreathing technique, as previously described. In short, an intravenous catheter was inserted into an antecubital vein. After 20 minutes of supine rest, a 3 mL baseline blood sample was collected. Thereafter, subjects breathed 100% oxygen for two minutes using a closed breathing circuit with a two-way non-rebreathing valve. Sixty mL of carbon monoxide were then added to the system and rebreathed for 10 minutes, followed by the collections of a second blood sample. Graded Exercise Test Subjects reported to the laboratory in comfortable exercise clothes which allowed access to the chest for echocardiographic measures and 12-lead ECG and to the thigh for near infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) measurements. Subjects performed the exercise test in the upright posture to simulate orthostatic characteristics of normal gravity exercise following space flight exposure. Prior to the start of the test, subjects were instrumented with electrodes for the monitoring of 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) and heart rate. Also, a small non-invasive NIRS sensor was adhered to the skin overlying the mid-point of vastus lateralis , and a catheter was inserted into the antecubital vein by a registered nurse to obtain resting, exercise, and immediate post-exercise blood samples. During the cycle ergometer test, heart rate, metabolic rate, and NIRS were continuously measured. Stroke volume and cardiac output were measured halfway through each stage. Blood pressure, Rating of Perceive Exertion (Borg Scale, 6-20), and blood lactate were obtained near the end of each stage. Blood also was drawn from the catheter during exercise to determine plasma catecholamines, blood glucose, serum electrolytes, hemoglobin, hematocrit, and carboxy-hemoglobin at exercise stages corresponding to approximately 75% of VO2pk, estimated from RPE reported in the previous exercise stage. Based upon data previously collected in the investigator’s laboratory using the same testing protocol, the investigators estimated that the 75% VO2pk exercise stage would correspond to the exercise stage following that which a subject reported a RPE of 11 or greater. The exercise stage in which blood was drawn was determined in the first exercise test irrespective of whether the subject was normo- or hypovolemic.
results: The primary finding of this study was that plasma volume loss to levels similar to those reported following short-duration Space Shuttle missions does not result in a decrease in VO2pk as great as that previously observed following space flight. In this study, VO2pk during a graded exercise test on a cycle ergometer, using a protocol similar to that used in previous space flight investigation conducted at JSC, was eight percent lower during pharmacologically-induced hypovolemia, but this is only one half to one third that which has been reported after Space Shuttle missions. Additionally, submaximal stroke volume and cardiac output were lower during hypovolemia, as has been observed after space flight, but other symptoms of deconditioning such as elevated submaximal heart rate, respiratory exchange, and ventilation rate, were not evident.

The objective of this study was to identify the key underlying physiological factors that contribute to performance changes in functional tests that are representative of critical mission tasks for planetary operations. Subjects were tested on an integrated suite of functional and physiological tests before and after 70 days of bed rest. This study had the following specific aims: Identify the critical mission tasks that may be impacted by alterations in physiological responses. Map physiological changes to alterations in functional performance. Aid in the design of countermeasures that specifically target the physiological systems responsible for impaired functional performance. APPROACH: Functional task test (FTT) data samples were collected from 26 male subjects, including 10 bed rest controls and 16 bed rest exercisers. During each session, subjects were asked to complete the following physiological and functional task tests: Plasma Volume, Seat Egress and Walk, Recovery from Fall/Stand, Fine Motor Control, Dynamic Posturography, Rock Translation, Torque Generation, Construction Activity Board, Jump Down, Treadmill Locomotion, Ladder Climb, and Muscle Performance Measures. During testing, subjects were equipped with hardware that recorded heart rate, blood pressure, body position data, and electrical activity from the muscles. Body position measurement units were secured to the head and trunk. Surface electrodes were placed on the lower limbs to collect muscle electrical activity signals and on the upper body to collect electrical signals from the heart during each test session. Surface electrodes were placed on the thigh for stimulating the thigh muscles during each test session. During each test session, subjects were asked to complete seven functional tests in addition to a series of physiological tests. RESULTS: The muscle function data showed reductions in lower body muscle performance metrics in bed rest subjects who did not exercise. Bed rest subjects who performed an integrated high intensity interval-type resistance and aerobic training program while in bed showed significantly improved lower body muscle performance compared to bed rest control subjects. Bed rest subjects experienced deficits both in functional tests with balance challenges and in sensorimotor tests designed to evaluate postural and gait control indicating that body support unloading experienced during space flight plays a central role in post-flight alteration of functional task performance. Taken together the bed rest and in-flight exercise training data point to the importance of providing increased body loading during in-flight treadmill and lower body resistive exercise. Lastly, bed rest data indicate that an elevated heart rate was required to maintain arterial blood pressure during performance of multiple functional tasks.

title: Bed Rest as a Spaceflight Analog to Study Neurocognitive Changes: Extent, Longevity, and Neural Bases
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: : The objective of this experiment was to determine the effects of an analog of long-duration space flight on neural structural alterations and assess associated impacts on cognitive and behavioral performance. This experiment performed structural and functional MRI brain imaging (fMRI) to identify the relationship between changes in participants' neurocognitive function and neural structural alterations following 70 days of head-down tilt bed rest. The central hypotheses were that measures of brain structure, function, and network integrity would change from pre- to post- bed rest to a greater extent than that observed in matched control subjects, but to a lesser extent than what was observed in crewmembers under the NASA funded flight study, “Spaceflight Effects on Neurocognitive Performance: Extent, Longevity, and Neural Bases” ( NNX11AR02G) . This study had the following two specific aims: 1: Identify changes in brain structure, function, and network integrity as a function of 70 days head down tilt bed rest and characterize their time course. 2: Specify relationships between structural and functional brain changes and performance and characterize their time course.
approach: Specific Aim 1 The investigators acquired brain structural and functional images at two time points pre-, two time points during, and three time points post- bed rest in 18 individuals and 16 controls who were tested at 4 time points but otherwise went around their daily lives. The researchers hypothesized that bed rest participants would exhibit changes from pre- to post- the intervention that were significantly greater than those seen in control participants across the same time period. Scans conducted during and following bed rest characterized the time course of changes and recovery. Specific Aim 2 The investigators administered a broad ranging battery of sensory, motor, and cognitive assessments at the time points described for Aim 1 . The researchers hypothesized that bed rest participants would exhibit pre- to post-intervention decrements in sensorimotor performance. Additionally, for some measures and time points, the researchers expected that there might be no performance effects despite alterations in brain structure and function due to compensatory brain processes, which would be identifiable with neuroimaging approaches. The measures acquired can be categorized into behavioral assessments and brain imaging assessments. The behavioral tests measured outside of the scanner included: card and cube rotation tests of spatial working memory, digit symbol substitution test of processing speed, rod and frame test of visual bias, pegboard test of bimanual coordination, sensory organization test of vestibular-mediated balance, functional mobility test of obstacle course navigation, and vestibular evoked myogenic potential to assess vestibular function. The neuroimaging tests of brain structure and function included: structural MRI to measure regional brain volumes and relative gray matter density, diffusion weighted scans (often referred to as DTI) to measure structural connectivity integrity, resting state functional MRI to measure functional connectivity integrity, and functional MRI to measure brain networks engaged during the performance of various tasks. The latter tasks included: imaging of the functional vestibular cortex, brain regions engaged during single and dual tasking of cognitive and motor behaviors, brain regions engaged during adaptation of pointing movements to perturbed visual feedback, and brain regions engaged for spatial working memory and foot tapping.
results: : The investigators found robust changes with bed rest in balance and functional mobility, replicating other studies that have previously reported sensorimotor declines. They also observed changes in brain gray matter volume, functional connectivity, and task based activation that were specific to the time period of the bed rest intervention, many of which were associated with the magnitude of behavioral change. Some metrics exhibited complete recovery by the last time point 12 days post bed rest, while others were trending towards recovery but had not yet returned to baseline levels.
