RESULTS: During Skylab 2, one subject's forced expired volume in 1 second (FEV-1) was significantly reduced one day postflight (R+1). Based on the subject's normal forced vital capacity, it is possible that the decreased FEV-1 was due to less than maximal subject effort. No data were obtained postflight for one Skylab 2 subject due to orthostatic intolerance complicated by seasickness. During Skylab 3 one subject showed no changes in pulmonary function except for a slight increase in vital capacity 5 days post-recovery. Vital capacity of one Skylab 3 subject was slightly higher inflight but normal postflight, relative to preflight values. One Skylab 3 subject exhibited decreased vital capacity inflight but normal vital capacity postflight relative to preflight. Skylab 4 vital capacities were generally observed to be lower inflight relative to preflight. Vital capacity for one subject remained below preflight levels for the entire inflight period. Nitrogen washout curves for Skylab 4 crewmembers' pulmonary function tests showed no indications of trapping. All washout curves appeared to reflect the anticipated two time constants representing washout of pulmonary and total body nitrogen spaces. One subject had a pronounced vasovagal response following maximal oxygen inspiration during the first closing volume determination on recovery day, and further testing was curtailed until the next day. All other measurements on the first day following recovery, and all measurements on days 2 and 5 postflight were within normal ranges. Residual volume in one Skylab 4 subject was slightly increased immediately following recovery and on day 2, compared to preflight. Residual volume/total lung capacity percent indicated that these changes were probably insignificant. Ventilatory equivalents of this subject were variable and reflected the irregular respiratory pattern observed during washouts. Although vital capacity for the subject was slightly decreased on the second day following recovery relative to preflight, forced vital capacity was normal. Maximum midexpiratory flow rate (between 25 percent and 75 percent of the forced vital capacity) values for the subject were the highest ever recorded in the investigator's laboratory. Skylab 4 provided the first opportunity for extensive, noninvasive pulmonary function screening on astronauts before and following an extended zero-g exposure. No physiologically significant quantitative decrement in pulmonary function was shown by any crewman during examinations following this 84-day Earth-orbital mission. Postflight chest films for all crewmen were compared to preflight films to detect any changes in the pulmonary vessels, parenchyma, or heart size. No significant pulmonary vasculature or parenchymal changes were observed in any instance. Vital capacity, the only parameter measured preflight, in-flight, and postflight, showed inflight decreases approaching 10 percent in the case of one subject from Skylab 3 and all three crewmembers from Skylab 4. These decreases in vital capacity apparently resulted from one or a combination of the following factors: cephalad shift of the diaphragm in zero-g; body fluid redistribution into the thoracic cavity; or a direct result of decreased ambient pressure. In summary, the vital capacity changes observed inflight may be partially explained as a response to 34.5 kPa (5 psia) ambient pressure. However, the proportion of vital capacity decreases directly attributable to other factors such as body fluid shifts and a cephalad shift of the diaphragm cannot be determined from the present data. Regardless of the cause(s) of decreased inflight vital capacities, a review of postflight data shows that these changes revert to normal within 2 hours following recovery without significant impact on crew health status.

title: Training for Generalizable Skills and Knowledge: Integrating Principles and Procedures
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: of this investigation was to identify the characteristics of skills and knowledge that lead to better retention and transfer context to new situations. By identifying these the proposed research also will help identify how current training practices at NASA should be changed to acquire integrated skills and knowledge. This study had the following aims: Determine which skills and knowledge can be retained and generalized. Determine which skills and knowledge are needed for operating and supporting on-board life support systems. Determine how expertise and transferable skills and knowledge are interrelated
approach: Investigators conducted an opportunistic study on retention of learned skills. They contacted and arranged the return of previous participants, five returning from one experiment after a bit less than two years and seven from the second experiment returning after a bit less than one year. The investigators recruited 14 new matched participants. They provided all participants with very basic retraining on how to use the software, but with minimal explanation or practice. Individual variation was large and overall performance was broadly similar. One of the key transfer tasks showed a significantly higher completion rate by returning users and the number of action-fails triggered by users was lower for returning than new users. The training environment was a micro-world providing simulated habitat equipment from the International Space Station (ISS) and software for executing operational procedures. It modeled the Carbon Dioxide Removal System (CDRS), the Active Thermal Control System (ATCS) providing cooling water, and the Remote Power Control modules (RPCMs) distributing power. Users operated equipment through the procedure automation software and associated procedures activating and deactivating equipment.
results: The fourth study under this research grant compared a condition with integrated training of model and procedural knowledge to a condition only training procedural knowledge. The investigators found that after training participants in the integrated model condition produced better diagrammatic and text explanations of how the CDRS work than it did participants in the no-model condition. Thus, they did succeed in teaching the participants at least model information (whether or not integrated with procedural skill). A Monitoring Task asked participants to task discriminate and explain whether a statically presented situation is normal or problematic; participants in the Integrating Model Condition provided better explanations than did those in the No Model Condition. However, participants were similarly likely to produce appropriate, successful performance on procedure execution tasks that required recognition of a problem or potential problem. Across these studies investigators have also informally observed variety in behavior that seems to be influenced by a variety of other factors, both in training and in the transfer tasks. Identification and organization of these factors may be helpful in identifying factors limiting performance in a specific technical situation. They have investigated some of these factors but further understanding is needed.

title: Development of an Objective Behavioral Assay of Cohesion to Enhance Composition, Task Performance, and Psychosocial Adaptation in Long-Term Work Groups
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: The overarching goal of this study was to generate experimentally-derived insights on how crew composition and trait-like cooperative motivation predict task cohesion, social cohesion, and biopsychosocial adaptation in long-term work groups through systematic ground-based research and development of a simple, rapid, and objective behavioral assay of implicit propensity toward cooperation, productivity, and fairness. This study had the following specific aims: Investigate effects of group composition on voluntary cooperation. Investigate effects of crew composition on performance, task cohesion, social cohesion, and psychosocial adaptation in long-term work groups. Develop next-generation Task Performance Task (TPT) software. Extended long-term research of group cohesion, team performance, and biopsychosocial adaptation to several space analog environments; the Human Exploration Research Analog (HERA) facility, NASA's Extreme Environment Mission Operations (NEEMO) laboratory, and the investigator's laboratory using Planetary Exploration Simulation (PES).
approach: Investigators conducted ground-based experiments to systematically investigate the effects of group composition (gender and personality) on voluntary cooperative propensity in three-person teams. They also assessed the predictive validity of pre-mission TPT "social personality profiles" and the effects of group composition on performance, task cohesion, social cohesion, and biopsychosocial adaptation in mixed-gender "crews" participating in a long-term simulated space exploration task. In addition, investigators also developed next-generation software to advance the technology beyond their current prototype used for proof-of-concept/validation research into a broadly applicable tool with cross-platform networking and connectivity, enhanced usability/human factors features, extensive parameter manipulation/flexibility to maximize sensitivity, and integrated data collection and processing capabilities.
results: Results indicate that the TPT/COHESION objective social behavioral assay approach is sensitive to team composition factors and temporal dynamics in both laboratory and field settings. Laboratory experiments reveal a potential risk of decreased cooperation and reduced cooperative resilience in majority female teams and teams with whose members are all high in conscientiousness. The TPT/COHESION tool quantifies "individual differences" in social behavioral processes over time at both the person and team levels, which correlate with subjective ratings of team cohesion. A single pre-mission TPT/COHESION session can predict several objective in-mission team performance outcomes.

title: The Effect of Long-duration Spaceflight on the Biomechanics of the Proximal Femur
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Three-dimensional quantitative computed tomography (CT) was used to assess the biomechanics of the proximal femur where significant differences in the patterns of cortical and trabecular bone loss have been found in a group of astronauts. This research will provide insight into the physiological response of proximal femoral bone tissue to space flight and may
approach: for assessing muscles that are of key importance for protecting hip bone strength. If these muscles are identified, then it would be possible to reduce the time burden and injury risk associated with exercise programs by finding activities that are more efficient for protecting bone strength. APPROACH: The methodology for this study is embedded in the
results: in a more sensitive method for tracking the efficacy of countermeasures aimed at preserving skeletal strength. The overall objective of the task was to determine the extent to which hip strength is lost during space flight and whether it is recovered as the skeleton readapts to Earth gravity. The most important aspect of this task is the use of finite element analysis to analyze bone strength with respect to loads exerted by the hip in falls. The second objective was to combine the finite element analysis of the hip with inter-subject registration techniques so that it will be possible to visualize the overall response of the proximal femur at the organ level to changes in loading. The idea is to use the technique to identify regions of the hip that may be at highest risk for failure due to abnormal loading in falls or during excursion activities. The third objective was to develop an approach for assessing muscles that are of key importance for protecting hip bone strength. If these muscles are identified, then it would be possible to reduce the time burden and injury risk associated with exercise programs by finding activities that are more efficient for protecting bone strength. APPROACH: The methodology for this study is embedded in the Results section below. RESULTS: Finite element analyses The investigators installed finite element software developed by Dr Joyce Keyak in the laboratory at UCSF. The software, which creates biomechanical models of the hip from CT scans to estimate the whole bone strength of the proximal femur in loading conditions simulating normal ambulation and a fall to the side, has been applied to pre-flight, postflight, and a subset of one year scans from the astronauts of increment 2-8. Finite element modeling of pre- and postflight scans and one year are complete for 16 subjects, and 5 one-year scans are available for data reduction as they are computing FEM-specific corrections for a scanner change that took place during the study. After obtaining institutional review board approval and informed consent, pre- and post-flight CT scans were obtained of the hips of astronauts who participated in long-duration International Space Station (ISS) missions. Mission length ranged from 4.3 to 6.5 months. Demographic data cannot be provided due to HIPAA regulations. A four-sample calcium hydroxyapatite (CHA) calibration phantom (Image Analysis, Columbia, KY) was placed under the subjects’ hips during scanning and used to calibrate the CT scan data in terms of CHA concentration. From the CT scan data, a finite element (FE) model of each subject’s left proximal femur was generated using methods described previously. These models employed patient-specific geometries and material properties. Ash density (rho ash, g/cm3) of each element was computed from the calibrated CT scan data (rho QCT, g/cm3), rho ash=0.0633 + 0.887 rho QCT. Mechanical properties were calculated from as densities. These properties were calibrated to result in accurate predictions of FFE.4 The models were analyzed under loading simulating single-limb stance2, and impact from a fall onto the greater trochanter. For stance loading, force was applied to the femoral head at 20 degrees to the shaft axis, within the coronal plane. For fall loading, force was applied to the femoral head at 60 degrees to the shaft axis and 25 degrres to the coronal plane, as the opposing surface of the greater trochanter was restrained in the opposite direction. FE-computed hip strength (FFE) in each loading condition was determined. A paired t-test was used to evaluate differences between pre- and post-flight values of FFE. RESULTS: For stance loading, the average proximal femoral strength decreased significantly (p DISCUSSION: This study has shown that astronauts exposed to microgravity for 4.3 to 6.5 months lose hip strength at an average rate of 2.6 percent/mo under single-limb stance loading and 1.9 percent/mo under fall loading. Previous DXA measurements of astronauts returning from the ISS indicated that aBMD decreased by 1.4 percent/mo in the neck and 1.5 percent/mo in the total femur.1 Thus, estimates of bone strength loss that are based on DXA aBMD alone will understate the reduction in hip strength. The recovery data available thus far seem to be consistent with the investigators finding in their 2006 bone recovery paper that shows that the recovery of bone mass and areal density is nearly complete at one year, but that volumetric bone density, particularly the density of trabecular bone does not recover. This seems to be driven by periosteal expansion, which increases bone volume and mass, while the recovery of volumetric bone density lags. The larger bone may be optimized for the loads incurred in normal usage but may still be at risk for fracture in pathologic conditions such as falls. Thus, recovery of bone mass may not be sufficient to gauge the recovery of bone after space flight. Intersubject registration The investigators obtained the Montreal Neurological Institute Animal intersubject image registration program, installed it in their laboratory, and have applied it to successfully co-register CT scans of the hip from 16 subjects with pre- and postflight image data. They have carried out voxel by voxel statistical comparisons of those models for the pre- and postflight time points, and have demonstrated a focal pattern of accelerated bone loss in the compressive trabecular band in the femoral head region. Quantitation of muscle cross-sectional area and attenuation coefficient from Hip CT scans Acquisition of volumetric CT scans of the hip: Analysis of proximal femoral musculature was carried out using volumetric CT scans optimized to analyze the density and structure of the proximal femur. In these studies, the patient lied supine on the imaging table, and an anteroposterior scoutview was acquired which spans the iliac crest to the mid-thigh. The operator then defined a helical scan volume between the superior limit of the left femoral head and an inferior limit 3-5 mm inferior to the lesser trochanter. The muscle analyses was carried out on images obtained with 120/80 kVp, 150 mAs, 3 mm or 1-mm section thickness (pitch=1), 48 cm field of view, reconstructed with a soft tissue filter. Images in all studies were obtained with a QCT calibration phantom (Image Analysis, Columbia, KY) positioned below the patient’s hips. Analysis of images for muscle cross-sectional area and mean attenuation coefficient: Based on previous studies of gait, balance and muscle function, the investigators have selected four groups of muscles to quantify which are well-visualized within the field of view of the proximal femur QCT scan: these include the hip extensors (gluteus maximus), hip abductors (gluteus medius, gluteus minimus and piriformis), hip adductors (adductor magnus, adductor brevis, adductor longus, quadratus femoris, quadratus externus, pectineus) and hip flexors (rectus femoris and sartorius). These groups are easily distinguishable on almost all of the cross-sections in the field of view in CT scans of the proximal femur. Because the cross-sectional areas of these muscle groups vary differently as a function of slice location within the QCT scans, they developed a method to select individual cross-sections on which to quantify the areas and mean attenuation coefficients of these muscle groups. This involved two steps. First investigators examined annotated optical and CT images in the Visible Human data set to determine the locations in the CT scan field of view where the muscle groups are of maximal size and are optimally distinguished from the surrounding tissue, and second they developed a protocol for employing boney landmarks to calculate the locations of these cross-sections relative to the hip anatomy, so that the muscle measurements could be compared between individuals and reproduced within an individual over time. To select the slice location, a mid-coronal reformation of the image is employed to display the proximal femoral anatomy. The user marks the slice position of the superior aspect of the femoral head and the inferior aspect of the lesser trochanter to generate a metric by which the individual muscle cross-sections can be reliably located. SH is the slice position corresponding to the superior aspect of the left femoral head. D is the distance between SH and the inferior aspect of the lesser trochanter, which defines the inferior limit of the proximal femoral analysis. The cross-sections are chosen as the slice numbers corresponding to the nearest integer to the calculations. Thus three cross-sections are selected for display, one for the extensors, one for the abductors, and a third cross-section containing the adductors and flexors. Each slice is then displayed in an image window, and the user draws the boundary around the fasceal plane of the corresponding muscle group. Once the drawings have been completed, the program processes each cross-section according to the following steps: 1) The program finds the water equivalent cell of the calibration phantom. Based on the mean and standard deviation of the HU in the water equivalent cell, the program calculates HU intervals to be used for calculations of muscle and fat areas within defined tissue boundaries. 2) The program generates the outer body contour by performing a region growing operation, searching for the skin-air boundary on each section from a user-placed seed point inside one of the muscle groups. Following that, the program performs a region growing, starting from the same seed point, finding the cortical bone/muscle boundary. The region within the bone boundary is then excluded from subsequent soft tissue calculations. 3) The program then starts at the body contour, and grows inward, searching for the fat/muscle boundary. This provides mask of lean tissue. Findings: Astronaut study: Investigators have applied this methodology to pre- and post-flight scans of their astronaut data, including 16 subjects with pre- and postflight QCT scans. Comparison of pre- and post-flight scans showed 1-5 percent losses in total lean area and in the areas of the flexor, abductor, adductor and extensor muscle groups, with only a 5 percent loss in the adductor area being statistically significant (p=0.02) Small losses may reflect effect of inflight and postflight exercise protocols and the acquisition of CT data over 2-4 weeks post-return, allowing for some recovery of muscle area. Hip fracture study: To test the hypothesis that hip muscle size and attenuation are associated with hip fracture, investigators compared CT scans of the contralateral hip in 45 women (mean age 74.71±5.94) imaged within 48 hours of their hip fractures to 66 age-matched control subjects (mean age 70.70±4.66). A volumetric CT scan encompassing the proximal part of the femur was analyzed for total percentage of fat tissue in the in the CT field of view and for the CSA and lean tissue Hounsfield Unit (HU) values of the hip extensor, abductor, adductor and flexor muscles. The CT scan was also analyzed to compute areal bone mineral density (aBMD) of the hip bone. Logistic regression analyses were employed to determine differences between fracture subjects and controls in body composition measures after adjustment for age, height, and BMI. Receiver-operator curve (ROC) analyses were employed to determine if combinations of aBMD and body composition were better discriminators of hip fracture than aBMD alone. Investigators found that subjects with hip fractures were on average 5 years older (p

title: Bed Rest Standard Measures: Functional Neurological Status Exam
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: The objective of the Bed Rest Standard Measure (BRSM) Functional Neurological Status Exam (FNSE) was to perform functional neurological assessments that provide an objective test of neurosensory re-adaptation to the period following bedrest, as an analog to crewmember readaptation to Earth's normal gravity following prolonged weightlessness.
approach: Three neurological assessments were performed pre-bedrest on BR-8 and post-bedrest on BR+0 and BR+4: (1) Neurological Signs and Symptoms -- Headache Assessment (degree of headache the subject is experiencing: 1=none, 2=resolved, 3=intermittent, 4=persistent) -- Dizziness/Faintness(degree of dizziness/faintness the subject is experiencing: 1=none, 2=mild, occasional, does not interfere with activity; 3=moderate, frequent, interferes with some activity; 4=severe, persistent,interferes with most activity) -- Vertigo/Spinning (degree of vertigo/spinning the subject is experiencing: 1=none, 2=mild, occasional, does not interfere with activity; 3=moderate, frequent, interferes with some activity; 4=severe, persistent,interferes with most activity) (2) Motor Performance -- Gaze/Ocular Movements (degree of gaze/ocular movements the subject is exhibiting: 1=normal, 2=mild nystagmus, quickly remits in one direction; 3=moderate nystagmus, quickly remits in more than one direction; 4=severe nystagmus, sustained in one direction) -- Finger to Nose Movement (subject's performance on the finger to nose touch test: 1=normal, 2=touches nose on first attempt, misses finger first attempt; 3=misses nose, touches finger first attempt; 4=misses nose, misses finger first attempt) -- Drift (subject's performance on the drift test (close eyes, extend arms, palms up): 1=normal, 2=touches nose on first attempt, misses finger first attempt; 3=misses nose, touches finger first attempt; 4=misses nose, misses finger first attempt) (3) Gait and Station -- Rising from chair (subject's performance in rising from a chair, without the use of arms: 1=normal, 2=slow, 3=tends to fall back, uses arms; 4=uses arms to stand) -- Standing/Romberg (subject's performance on the standing/Romberg test [feet together, arms extended, close eyes]: 1=normal, 2=sway noted, 3=catches self with leg extension, 4=unable to perform with eyes closed) -- Leg lift - Hop (subject's performance on leg lift and hop test [close eyes, lift leg, hop 3 times, alternate]: 1=normal, 2=hops with eyes open, 3=cannot stand on one leg with eyes closed, 4=cannot perform) -- Tandem/Heel to toe walk (subject's performance on a tandem/heel to toe walk (5 meters): 1=normal, 2=performs with arms extended, sense of falling; 3=slips/leans to one side but recovers; 4=cannot perform) -- Dynamic equilibrium (subject's performance on a dynamic equilibrium test [close eyes, walk 9 meters, turn 180 degrees and return]: 1=normal; 2=walks straight, performs turn with difficulty; 3=walks straight, cannot perform turn; 4=cannot walk straight A total score is calculated by adding scores from the 3 part test: (1) Neurological Signs and Symptoms (2) Motor Performance (3) Gait and Station. A total score of 11-13 is normal, 14-15 suspect, and 15, consider referral.
results: This experiment has concluded in ground-based studies sponsored by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration's Human Adaptation and Countermeasures Division. Although the raw data are archived, there are no summarized results available for this investigation. This experiment was conducted during Bed Rest Campaigns 1. LSDA does not expect to receive results from this study.

title: Mechanism of Radiation-Induced Alteration of Astrocyte-Neuronal Coupling
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Neurons and astrocytes form an interconnected network; a syncytium in which an alteration in one cellular component inevitably affects the other. Disturbances in neuron-astrocyte interactions appear to be at the center of several neurological disorders such as cerebral ischemia and neurodegeneration. A significant portion of neuroglial coupling is mediated via glutamate uptake and metabolism, and involves the recycling of substrates between neurons and astrocytes (e.g. glutamate-glutamine shuttle and lactate shuttle). Thus, metabolic and functional cooperativity between astrocytes and neurons is dependent on glutamate. Preliminary data suggested that astrocytes and neurons have reciprocal functional responses to irradiation and very different recovery kinetics. The objective of this investigation was to better understand the mechanistic changes occurring in the astrocytes-neuron couple following exposure to radiation. It was hypothesized that ionizing radiation disrupts the metabolic coupling between neurons and astrocytes by altering glutamate transport and metabolism. It was proposed to investigate the mechanism for this uncoupling by measuring alterations in glutamate uptake and metabolism, and to determine how abnormal glutamate uptake affects intercellular signaling following irradiation. NTera2/D1 cells, which can be induced to differentiate into mature neurons and astrocytes, would be utilized first. Then findings would be confirmed using primary astrocytes and neurons. These differentiated cell types would be used to investigate the mechanism of neurometabolic uncoupling following acute exposure to 290 MeV carbon and 1 GeV iron ions. Specific aims of this investigation were to: Measure glutamate transport and metabolism in human astrocytes and neuronal cultures following acute exposure to 290 MeV carbon and 1GeV iron ions delivered as single fractions of 0, 10, 50 and 200 cGy. Also explore the physical and soluble dependency of homeostatic cooperativity between astrocytes and neurons. Measure the endogenous and temporal changes in expression of antioxidants and reactive oxygen species in astrocytes and neurons using the same radiation conditions described in aim 1. Examine alterations in inter-astrocytic and neuronal communication after exposure to ionizing radiation by analyzing essential elements of physical coupling and calcium signaling.
approach: Both cultured and primary human astrocytes and neurons were exposed to gamma rays and protons as well as 290 MeV carbon and 1 GeV iron ions. Harvest points were at 3 hours, 2 days, and 7 days post irradiation. Proton, carbon, and iron samples were stored frozen. In addition to conducting experiments with the isolated astrocytes and neurons, sets of astrocytes and neurons mixed at a 10 to 1 ratio and allowed to establish for 4 days prior to exposure to radiation were also studied. The glutamate transport and metabolism response of the astrocytes and neurons was measured. Standard assays were used to determine endogenous and irradiated antioxidant status of cultures of isolated neurons and astrocytes
results: Collectively, the glutamate data from the carbon and iron exposures showed similar results as the gamma ray experiments with the astrocytes having decreased glutamate uptake and the neurons having an increase in glutamate uptake. For gamma rays the response of the astrocytes was only significant at 3hrs post exposure, by the 2 day time point the cells returned to normal with respect to their glutamate uptake. The neurons which normally do not take up glutamate show a radiation induced increase that stays elevated throughout the 7 day time point, the last harvest point in these experiments. The results of the sustained glutamate uptake in the neurons showed some dose dependence with higher doses persisting through the 7 day point post irradiation. The difference with respect to high linear energy transfer (LET) radiation was that the duration of the change in the astrocytes persisted longer, with depressed glutamate uptake through the 2 day time point. The neurons response to LET was reduced magnitude of the increased glutamate uptake. In general the magnitude of the signal was inversely proportional to the LET. The results for glutamate function and apoptosis following gamma rays, protons, carbon, and iron ions were muted with respect to the same measurement taken from the isolated cell types. The oxidant/antioxidant levels measured for gamma rays were also muted in the mixed cultures. The LET effect on radiation-induced changes in glutamate uptake lead to the possibility that the change may be due to fluence differences which decreases as the LET increases. The other possibility is the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) which also decrease as the LET increases. The first measurements done in attempt to explain changes in function were to measure the levels of the transporters expressed on the respective cell types. The changes in glutamate uptake were not due to an overt change in the levels of the transporter’ protein levels as western blots and quantitative immunocytochemistry confirmed that the transporters did fluctuate with time but not with dose of radiation. The change in function was also not fully attributed to reactive oxygen species as the levels were mimicked using paraquat to stimulate super oxide levels and only a very slight change in the glutamate uptake was seen. To rule out ROS as a suspect in the radiation-induced changes in glutamate uptake measured in these experiments, significant investigation of oxidant/antioxidant activity following exposure to gamma radiation was undertaken. A complete set of oxidant/antioxidant studies have been conducted following carbon and iron exposure and the samples stored frozen.

title: Evaluation of an On-Astronaut Wireless Sensor System to Support Crew Health Monitoring for Exploration Class Missions
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Long-duration space flight requires a health monitoring system that is compact, interoperable with an integrated data management system, and requires limited consumables. Astroskin was the first prototype of this technology, consisting of a wired sensor system for continuous monitoring of electrocardiograph (ECG), heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, skin temperature, and body movement. NASA and the Canadian Space Agency (CSA) began collaborating in 2014 to validate this system in controlled tests at both Ames Research Center (ARC) and Human Exploration Research Analog (HERA) facilities at Johnson Space Center (JSC). Lessons learned from these test activities led the CSA to develop the capabilities of a wireless version of the Astroskin that, unlike the current shirt-based version, would use small, unobtrusive, stand-alone patch sensors. Wireless sensor capabilities could enhance comfort, improve movement and fit, and minimize interference in crewmember performance of tasks. The proposed On-Astronaut Wireless Sensor System (OAWSS) included sensors on the upper body, as well as a Sensor Interface Unit (SIU) located on- or off-body that communicates via Bluetooth Low Energy with the body sensors. The SIU was developed to interface with NASA’s Medical Data Architecture (MDA) system to accurately monitor and manage crew health and performance data. Monitoring multiple vital sign parameters over a prolonged period of time is not possible with other currently available wearable products. Compared to Astroskin, or other commercial products, the OAWSS offers a solution that allows exploration of a different operational mode. The dissemination, management and storage of data vary from other wearables created for space flight monitoring by: 1) the fully wireless nature of the technology; 2) the dynamic and flexible user interface; 3) the capability to acquire data continuously (up to one week without interruption); and 4) the possibility of adding additional sensors (plug-and-play) since there is no physical connection with the data acquisition module. Specific aims of this experiment included: Determine the efficacy of OAWSS measures under lab and field test conditions; Evaluate OAWSS system performance relative to standard laboratory measures; Conduct participant surveys to assess usability and wearability of the OAWSS; and Integrate and demonstrate compatibility of the OAWSS with the NASA Medical Data Architecture (MDA).
approach: To develop OAWSS integration, a ground-based studie was conducted in 2 phases with a total of 16 participants between the ages of 25 and 45. Prior to study selection, participants underwent a complete Class II physical to ensure acceptable health and fitness levels. Phase 1 of the research was carried out at ARC using 9 volunteer participants. These participants underwent 3 days of laboratory testing to assess the functionality of the OAWSS: submaximal ergometer and rowing exercise on days 1 and 2; and a standard rotating chair test designed to elicit motion sickness symptoms on day 3. Research subjects wore the OAWSS biosensors continuously for 48 hours off-site to collect biometric data and evaluate user comfort and functionality of the biosensors. In addition to OAWSS sensors, standard lab devices (Equivital harness and Empatica E4) were worn by participants to provide reference measures for comparison. Phase 2 of the study was conducted at JSC using another 8 male and female research participants. For these tests, participants wore the OAWSS, Equivital harness and Empatica E4 while they performed a flight-like cycle ergometer protocol, followed by a self-pacing treadmill test with various inclines to simulate climbing up a hill to deploy a communication device and then descending. During this task participants wore a weighted suit with an additional 40% of their body weight to simulate interference experienced by the space suit. The purpose of the data collection in these conditions was to evaluate functionality and interference of the OAWSS in response to physical exercise and a simulated Lunar or Mars exploration task.
results: This study evaluated the reliability and validity of the OAWSS for measuring heart rate (HR), respiration rate (RR), skin temperature (ST), and galvanic skin response (GSR) against criterion devices (e.g., EQ02 LifeMonitor, Equivital Inc. New York, NY and E4 wristband, Empatica, Boston, MA, respectively). In study 1, five male and four female volunteers (mean ± SD, 39.1 ± 5.1 yr) completed two days of testing in which HR, RR, ST, and GSR were collected from the OAWSS and criterion devices at the same time for approximately 90 minutes while engaged in low, medium, and high intensity activities which were repeated on two consecutive days. In study 2 four male and four female volunteers (mean ± SD, 35.1 ± 6.5 yr) completed one day of testing in which the above parameters were collected for approximately 3 hours while engaged in a flight-like aerobic exercise protocol and a simulated EVA task. Reliability was determined by calculating the change in measured parameters (i.e., error scores) between test activities on day 1 and day 2 (study 1 only). Validity was determined by calculating the change in measured parameters between OAWSS and criterion devices during test activities of both studies 1 and 2. Results demonstrated that only OAWSS ST was reliable during activities in study 1, and only OAWSS HR hill climb met the validity criteria in study 2. In conclusion, the OAWSS should not be evaluated further in its current configuration based on the poor reliability and validity of measurements from both studies. In addition, the low acceptability results strongly suggest the OAWSS will need a significant form factor improvement in order to be acceptable to flight crew as a health monitoring device. Future research should also examine other physiological variables such as body position, movement, SPO2, and blood pressure, to more accurately determine health status.

title: Microbiological Investigations of the Mir Space Station and Flight Crew
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Microorganisms are ubiquitous in spacecraft environments, as they are on Earth. Microbes pose several risks to humans in space including: infectious diseases, allergies, degradation of air quality (e.g., release of volatiles), release of toxins, degradation of critical materials, and systems failure (e.g., water reclamation system). Maintaining the health and performance of humans in closed microgravity environments while reusing reclaimed air and water is a daunting task. Determining medical and technological risks that are dependent on microbiological factors during long-term space flight is a vital problem in theory, as well as practice. In such a closed environment, humans will be a major source of microbes released into the spacecraft. Animals and plants, when present, will also be significant contributors to the overall bioburden. Suitable containment and purification technologies are essential. Studies of microbial ecology in spacecraft have been mostly limited to short ( The success of long-duration space missions will depend on our ability to mitigate the adverse effects of microorganisms. This will require a much better understanding of the microbiology of closed environments and the human-microbe-environment interactions than are currently available. This joint US-Russian investigation was an important first step in gaining this understanding. The investigators hypothesized that during long-term space flight (>30 days) human microbiota and the microbial ecology of the Mir station will undergo quantitative and qualitative changes. The objectives of this study were to 1) characterize microbiota of crewmembers, air, surface, and water before, during, and after a long-duration mission aboard the Mir Space Station, 2) determine the exchange and distribution of microbes among crewmembers, and 3) assess the distribution and dynamics of crew microbiota throughout the Mir Space Station.
approach: Crew microbiology Pre and postflight, microbial samples from the throat, nose, ear, hand, scapula, axilla, groin, feces, and urine were collected and examined for bacteria and fungi. Feces were also examined for ova and parasites. In-flight microbial samples from the throat, nose, ear, hand, scapula, axilla, and groin were collected with the Crew Microbiology Kit (CMK). Quantification and isolation of organisms was performed by, preparing serial dilutions of each sample and spread-plating those samples onto selective media. Any aerobic bacteria or fungi isolated were identified using a Vitek Automated Identification System, Biolog Automated Identification System, or classical means. Species that were not identified by these means were sent to a microbial reference laboratory for identification. Air microbiology Air samples were collected from the Shuttle middeck and flightdeck, pre, in, and postflight using the Microbial Air Sampler (MAS). In-flight air samples were also collected from and Mir with the MAS. Mir sampling locations included the area of the Commander's seat (Core Module), area of the dining table (Core Module), in the Commander's cabin (Core Module), and in the Kristall Module hatch. Organisms were isolated using selective media, and species were identified as described in the crew microbiology section. Surface microbiology Surface samples were collected from the Shuttle pre, in, and post flight. Shuttle sample areas included the half-moon shaped air vent above the Waste Control System in the middeck, the left-most air return in the port side crawl-through, and the half-moon shaped air vent for the Commander's chair in the flight deck. In-flight surface samples were collected from the Shuttle and Mir with the Surface Sampler Kit (SSK). Mir sampling locations included the Commander's seat post #1 (Core Module), the dining table (Core Module), the Commander's cabin wall (Core Module), the right handle of the treadmill (Core Module), and the wall above the hatch in the Kristall Module. Once during the NASA 3 mission, a sample from the galley water dispenser needle was collected. Organisms were isolated using selective media, and species were identified as described in the crew microbiology section. Water microbiology Water samples were collected from the Shuttle pre and postflight. Tank A was sampled preflight, and tanks A and B were sampled postflight. In-flight water samples from the Mir were collected and processed with the Water Experiment Kit (WEK). Mir sampling locations included the galley hot and coldwater ports, and the SVO-VZ port. Organisms were isolated using selective media, and species were identified as described in the crew microbiology section. Food packet microbiology During the NASA 4 mission, a food packet was contaminated due to a puncture in the packaging material. A sample was obtained and processed similar to the procedure used for the shuttle surface sample. 'Free' surface sample During NASA 6 and 7, crewmembers came in contact with 'free' surface condensate in various locations during housekeeping procedures. Representative samples were collected for evaluation of any potential risks that the crewmembers might be exposed to. The samples were collected using the Contingency Water Quality Kit (CWQK), this being assembled from hardware components contained within the Water Experiment Kit (WEK). The condensates were aspirated into a 60cc syringe, and then expelled into a 300 ml sample bag. These samples were returned to ground for complete analyses. Organisms were isolated using selective media, and species were identified as described in the crew microbiology section.
results: CREW MICROBIOLOGY NASA 3/Mir 22 6 subjects were sampled pre and post flight, three of which were also sampled in-flight. No significant changes were apparent in the aerobic bacteria isolated from the pre-, in-, and postflight specimens. Staphylococcus aureus was the bacterial species used to follow microbial dissemination from crewmember to crewmember and throughout the Mir environment. Crewmembers 1 and 2 were the prime crewmembers that were replaced one week before flight; S. aureus was recovered only once from the nose on each of these crewmembers. Candida albicans was also recovered once from the throat of Crewmember 2. S. aureus was recovered from the throat of Crewmember 3 twice preflight and once postflight. This bacterium was also recovered from the nose of this crewmember at all preflight sampling sessions, three of four in-flight sessions, and two of three postflight sessions; the organism was occasionally isolated from this person's skin, urine, and feces samples. Candida albicans , an endogenous yeast, was isolated from the feces of Crewmember 3 once postflight. S. aureus was recovered from the throat, nose, hand, and axilla of Crewmember 4 at L-2 days. Enterobacter cloacae , Aeromonas hydrophila , and Enterobacter hormaechei were isolated from the throat of Crewmember 4 at L-2 days; E. cloacae were also isolated from the nose at this sampling time. Yeast was present in 5 of 9 samples collected from Crewmember 4 at R+0; Serratia liquefaciens was isolated from the hand at this collection period. Specimens from Crewmember 5 frequently had S. aureus isolated; is was present in the nose at 6 of 11 sampling periods. Once during flight, the organism was present in 4 of 7 samples. At R+0, it was recovered from 4 of 9 specimens, from 5 of 9 at R+7, and from 5 of 9 at R+11. At L-59, Klebsiella pneumoniae was recovered from the throat of Crewmember 5; Pseudomonas aeruginosa was isolated from the throat at L-2. S. aureus was not recovered from Crewmember 6. NASA 4 One crewmember was sampled pre, in, and postflight. Opportunistic gram negative rods were recovered from the throat at several sampling times: Panteola agglomerans on FD19, Pastuerella multicoida , Serratia odifera , Serratia species , Enterobacter gergoviae on FD117, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa on landing day. Candida albicans , an endogenous yeast, was isolated from the throat 143 days before flight. Klebsiella pneumoniae was recovered from the nose at landing. Organisms recovered from the hand included Acinetobacter haemolyticus on L-9 and Enterococcus faecalis and Serratia marcescens on FD117. Candida albicans was recovered from the groin on FD117, and was present in the feces before and after flight. Enterococcus faecalis was present in low numbers in the urine on landing day and 5 days thereafter. NASA 5/Mir 24 3 crewmembers were scheduled to be sampled pre, in, and postflight. The in-flight monitoring that was to be performed on all crewmembers on FD15, FD55, FD85, FD115, and FD135, was cancelled due to the Spektr accident. The sample collection kits, as well as archived samples, were stowed within the Spektr module at the time of the accident. No further sampling or the return of samples was possible. A number of opportunistic gram negative rods were recovered from 5 of 9 samples collected from Crewmember 1 at the L-10 sampling period. Staphylococcus aureus , a potential pathogen, was recovered from the nose of Crewmember 1 at all postflight sampling periods; this organism was also recovered from the throat at R+0. Several opportunistic gram negative rods were recovered from 4 of 9 samples collected from Crewmember 2 at the L-11 day sampling period. Staphylococcus aureus was recovered from the nose of Crewmember 2 at all sampling periods; this organism was also recovered from the throat and groin at R+0. Candida species , an endogenous yeast, was isolated from the throat at all three postflight sampling periods. Opportunistic gram negative rods were only occasional recovered from Crewmember 3. Klebsiella pnuemoniae was isolated from the groin at R+0 and from the nose at R+14 days. Staphylococcus aureus was recovered from the nose of Crewmember 3 at L-28 days; this organism was recovered from the throat and hand at R+14 days. Candida species , was isolated from the throat and feces during both preflight and postflight sampling periods. NASA 6/Mir 25 3 subjects were sampled pre and postflight. The opportunistic bacteria Staphylococcus aureus as well as Candida albicans (a yeast) were recovered from the throat of Crewmember 1 during both of the preflight sampling times. Staphylococcus aureus was also recovered from the nose of this crewmember at all three sampling times. Enterobacter cloacae were isolated from the throat of Crewmember 1 at L-21; at L-14, Candida albicans was recovered from the feces. Staphylococcus aureus was recovered from the throat of Crewmember 2 on landing day and from the nose at the L-9 and R+0 sampling times; Candida albicans was isolated from the feces on L-9 and was too numerous to count in the throat at R+0. On landing day, Crewmember 2 exhibited a colony count of too numerous to count from the urine; the organism recover from this specimen was Staphylococcus species and was probably a contaminant. Enterobacter aerogenes was isolated from the throat and nose of Crewmember 3 on landing day. Candida albicans was recovered from this crewmember's throat at L-9 and R+0 (too numerous to count), and from the urine at R+0. Penicillium species (too numerous to count) and Candida parapsilosis were also present in the nose of Crewmember 3 on landing day. Staphylococcus aureus is frequently a resident of the nasal passages; Candida species are ubiquitous yeasts, being found as normal flora of the alimentary tract and mucocutaneous membranes. NASA 7 One crewmember was sampled pre and postflight. The opportunistic bacteria Staphylococcus aureus was recovered from the nose at all three sampling times. No clinical symptoms were experienced by the crewmember as a result of the presence of this organism. Staphylococcus aureus is frequently a resident of the nasal passages. AIR MICROBIOLOGY NASA 3 and STS-79 Fungal levels were often above the Russian standard of 100 CFU/m3. Mir bacterial levels occasionally exceeded the Russian standard of 500 CFU/m3. Enterococcus faecalis was isolated from the area of the dining table and in the Commander's cabin on FD52. On FD80, both bacterial and fungal levels in three of four Mir sampling locations greatly exceeded the US standard of 1000 CFU/m3 proposed for the International Space Station (ISS). The highest bacterial level observed during any of the Shuttle sampling sessions was 319 CFU/m3, found in the middeck of STS-79 at R+0. The highest fungal level observed on the Shuttle was 550 CFU/m3 in the flight deck of STS-79 at R+0. NASA 4 and STS-81 On board the Mir in the area near the commander's chair, the bacteria Aeromonas hydrophila and Comamonas testosteroni were recovered on FD53. Bacteria recovered from the area of the dining table included Staphylococcus aureus on FD80 and Pseudomonas putida on FD117; fungi isolated from this same area included Aspergillus niger and two species of the yeast Candida . The bacterium Aeromonas veronii biovar sobria was isolated from the commander's cabin on FD19 and FD80; Sphingobacterium spiritovorum and Chryseobacterium meningosepticum were also recovered on FD80. Candida guilliermondii was recovered in the Kristall Module hatch on FD117; Sphingomonas paucimobilis and Candida fumata were isolated during the Shuttle docked phase of STS-84. Mir bacterial levels occasionally exceeded the Russian standard of 500 CFU/m3. Fungal levels were above the Russian standard of 100 CFU/m3 in all sampling locations at all sampling times. The standard set by the US for the International Space Station (ISS) is a combined bacterial and fungal count of 1000 CFU/ m3 . This amount was only occasionally exceeded, e.g. in the area of the commander's seat on FD80, in the area of the dining table on FD117, and in the Kristall Module hatch on FD80 and FD117. Onboard the Shuttle, the fungal levels increased during the docked phases of STS-81. NASA 5 and STS-84 The in-flight monitoring that was to be performed on the Mir on FD55, FD85, FD115, and FD135, was cancelled due to the Spektr accident. The sample collection kits, as well as archived samples, were stowed within the Spektr module at the time of the accident. No further sampling or the return of samples was possible. The in-flight recording of data from Mir samples collected on FD19 was received. On board the Mir, Staphylococcus aureus was recovered from the area of the dining table during the docked phase of STS-84; Sphingomonas paucimobilis and Candida famata were isolated from the area of the Kristall module during this same sampling session. On FD19, Mir bacterial levels slightly exceeded the Russian standard of 500 CFU/m3 in 3 of the four sampling sites. Fungal levels were above the Russian standard of 100 CFU/m3 in all sampling locations at all sampling times. The standard set by the US for the International Space Station (ISS) is a combined bacterial and fungal count of 1000 CFU/ m3 . This amount was only occasionally exceeded, e.g. in the area of the commander's seat and in the Commander's cabin on FD19. Onboard the Shuttle, the fungal levels increased during the docked phase of STS-84. NASA 6 and STS-86 On board the Mir, in the area of the dining table, the fungi Aspergillus niger was isolated on FD29. Bacillus cereus was recovered from this location of FD 54 and FD100; Staphylococcus aureus recovered on FD100. Fungi recovered from the area of the commander's cabin included Aspergillus niger on FD54. This same fungi was also recovered in the Kristall Module hatch on FD54. Mir bacterial levels occasionally exceeded the Russian standard of 500 CFU/m3. Fungal levels were always above the Russian standard of 100 CFU/m3. The standard set by the US for the International Space Station (ISS) is a combined bacterial and fungal count of 1000 CFU/ m3 . This amount was only exceeded once in the area of the Commander's seat on FD54 and once in the area of the dining table on FD29. Onboard the Shuttle, the bacterial and fungal levels exceeded acceptability limits in the Middeck on FD5 of STS-86 during the docked phase. Aspergillus niger was recovered in low numbers from the Flight Deck during the pre-docked phase of STS-86. NASA 7, STS-89, and STS-91 On board the Mir in the area near the commander's chair, the fungi Aspergillus niger was isolated; yeast recovered from this location included Rhodotorula rubra on FD43, Candida guilliermondii on FD 119, and an unidentified yeast on FD 135. Bacteria recovered from the area of the dining table included Pseudomonas fluorescens on FD119. Bacteria isolated from the commander's cabin included Serratia marcescens on FD78, Stenotrophomonas maltophilia on FD119, and Pasteurella haemolytica on FD135. Aspergillus niger was recovered in the Kristall Module hatch on FD135; The bacterium Serratia liquefaciens was recovered from all of the locations during multiple sampling periods; these included site 4 on FD 43, sites 1,2, and 4 on FD78, and from all sampling sites on FD 119. Mir bacterial levels occasionally exceeded the Russian standard of 500 CFU/m3. Fungal levels were frequently above the Russian standard of 100 CFU/m3. The standard set by the US for the International Space Station (ISS) is a combined bacterial and fungal count of 1000 CFU/ m3. This amount was only exceeded once in the Kristall Module hatch on FD43. Onboard the shuttle, the fungus Aspergillus niger was isolated during the pre-docked phase of STS-89 in the Flight Deck. The yeast Candida guilliermondii was isolated during the docked phase of STS-91 in the Middeck; however, the bacterial and fungal levels never exceeded acceptability limits. SURFACE MICROBIOLOGY NASA 3 and STS-79 Mir bacterial levels occasionally exceeded both US and Russian standards; fungal levels exceeded the standards only once during the mission. S. aureus was isolated from the Commander's seat (post #1) on FD24. Yeasts were isolated from the dining table on FD24, FD52, and FD80 of the NASA 3 mission, as well as during the docked phase of STS-81. During the docked phase with STS-79 and on FD52, yeast was recovered from the wall in the Commander's cabin. In the Kristall Module hatch, yeast was isolated on FD109; Serratia liquefaciens was found during the docked phase of STS-81. Both bacterial and fungal levels during all of the sampling sessions for STS-79 were within the US limits proposed for ISS. The yeast Cryptococcus albidus was isolated from the half-moon shaped air vent above the Waste Control System in the middeck at both preflight sampling periods of STS-79; an unidentified yeast was isolated from the same location during the docked phase with Mir. No yeast was recovered from any location after landing. NASA 4 and STS-81 Mir bacterial levels frequently exceeded the Russian standard of 1000 CFU/100 cm2 as well as the US standard of 4000 CFU/100 cm2 set for ISS. Fungal levels were occasionally above the Russian standard of 100 CFU/100 cm2, but exceeded the US standard of 400 CFU/100 cm2 set for ISS only once. Bacteria recovered from the commander's seat post #1 included Sphingomonas paucimobilis on FD19, Aeromonas veronii biovar sobria , Pseudomonas putida , and an unidentified gram negative rod on FD53, as well as an unidentified gram negative rod on FD80. Aeromonas veronii biovar sobria was isolated at 4 of the 6 sampling periods from the dining table; other microorganisms recovered from this location were Rhodotorula rubra (a yeast) during the Shuttle docked phase of STS-81, Aspergillus niger on FD19, Aeromonas hydrophila on FD53, Candida parapsilosis on FD117, and Sphingomonas paucimobilis during the Shuttle docked phase of STS-84. From the commander's cabin wall, Aeromonas veronii biovar sobria was again isolated at 4 of the 6 sampling periods; other microorganisms recovered from this location were Aeromonas caviae , Sphingomonas paucimobilis , and Vibrio alganolyticus on FD19, Sphingomonas paucimobilis on FD80, Stenotrophomonas maltophilia and an unidentified gram negative rod on FD117, and Aspergillus niger during the Shuttle docked phase of STS-84. Bacteria isolated from the handle of the treadmill included Aeromonas veronii biovar sobria on FD53 and Chryseomonas luteola on FD80. Staphylococcus aureus was recovered from the Kristall Module hatch on FD117 and during the Shuttle docked phase of STS-84. Bacterium also recovered from this location were Serratia liquefaciens and Stenotrophomonas maltophilia during the during the Shuttle docked phase of STS-81, Aeromonas veronii biovar sobria on FD19, Aeromonas caviae on FD53, and Sphingomonas paucimobilis during the Shuttle docked phase of STS-84. On STS-81, both bacterial and fungal levels exceeded US limits at R+0 at the same air vent. The sample collection kits, as well as archived samples, were stowed within the Spektr module at the time of the accident. No further sampling or the return of samples was possible. The in-flight recording of data from Mir samples collected on FD19 was received. Mir bacterial levels frequently exceeded the Russian standard of 1000 CFU/100 cm2 as well as the US standard of 4000 CFU/100 cm2 set for ISS. Fungal levels were occasionally above the Russian standard of 100 CFU/100 cm2, but never exceeded the US standard of 400 CFU/100 cm2 set for ISS. On FD5, Sphingomonas paucimobilis was recovered from the dining table and Kristall module hatch; Aeromonas veronii biovar sobria was recovered from the dining table and the commander's cabin wall. Staphylococcus aureus was also isolated on FD5 from the dining table and Kristall module hatch. NASA 6 and STS-86 Mir bacterial levels occasionally exceeded the Russian standard of 1000 CFU/100 cm2 as well as the US standard of 4000 CFU/100 cm2 set for ISS. Fungal levels were occasionally above the Russian standard of 100 CFU/100 cm2 as well as above the US standard of 400 CFU/100 cm2 set for ISS once. Bacteria recovered from the commander's seat post #1 (site 1) included Vibrio alginolyticus on FD54. Stenotrophomonas maltophilia was isolated from the dining table (site 2) on FD28; an unidentified Gram negative rod was recovered from this location was on FD54. Rhodotorula glutinis , a yeast, was isolated from the handle of the treadmill (site 4) on FD100. The bacterium Pasteurella haemolytica was recovered from the Kristall Module hatch (site 5) on FD54. NASA 7, STS-89, and STS-91 Mir bacterial levels frequently exceeded the Russian standard of 1000 CFU/100 cm2 as well as the US standard of 4000 CFU/100 cm2 set for ISS. Fungal levels were occasionally above the Russian standard of 100 CFU/100 cm2 as well as the US standard of 400 CFU/100 cm2 set for ISS. Bacteria recovered from the commander's seat post #1 included Serratia marcescens and Stenotrophomonas maltophilia on FD78, and Pasteurella haemolytica on FD135. The fungi Aspergillus niger was isolated from this site on FD43; yeast recovered from this location included Candida parapsilosis on FD78 and an unidentified yeast on FD135. Pseudomonas stutzeri and Serratia marcescens were isolated from the dining table on FD43; other microorganisms recovered from this location were Klebsiella pneumoniae and Rhodotorula rubra on FD78, and Serratia fonticola on FD119. From the commander's cabin wall, Serratia liquefaciens was recovered on FD43 and Aspergillus niger on FD78. Bacteria isolated from the handle of the treadmill included Sphingomonas paucimobilis on FD43; Aspergillus niger was recovered on FD43. Serratia liquefaciens and Aspergillus niger were recovered again from the Kristall Module hatch on FD43. Onboard the Shuttle, Aspergillus niger , Candida parapsilosis , and Candida guilliermondii were recovered from the half-moon shaped air vent above the Waste Control System during the docked phase of STS-89. Yeast recovered from the left-most air return in the port side crawl-through included Candida guilliermondii during the docked phase of the STS-89. Acinetobacter lwofii was recovered from the half-moon shaped air vent above the Waste Control System during the sampling session performed 26 days before the launch of STS-91. Yeast recovered from the left-most air return in the port side crawl-through included Candida guilliermondii and Candida parapsilosis during the docked phase of STS-91. Acinetobacter lwofii was recovered from the half-moon shaped vent for the Commander's chair in the Flight Deck one day before the launch of STS-91. WATER MICROBIOLOGY NASA 3 and STS-79 All but one of the Mir hot water samples had no bacterial growth, indicating that the rigorous treatment train and final heat-pasteurization step of the Mir system is well able to maintain the quality of water from this source at standards well below the US and Russian maximum limits. Burkholderia cepacia was the only bacterial contaminant recovered from the Shuttle potable water system; this organism is frequently recovered from this system. Tank B represents pre-treated water, and predictably contained many bacteria. NASA 4 and STS-81 All Mir hot water samples were within the US acceptability limits set for the International Space Station. All but one of the Mir hot water samples had no bacterial growth, indicating that the treatment train and final heat-pasteurization step of the Mir system is able to maintain the microbial quality of water from this source at standards well below both the US (100 CFU/100 ml) and Russian (10,000 CFU/100 ml) limits. Cold and SVO-ZV samples predictably contained many bacteria. NASA 5 and STS-84 The in-flight monitoring that was to be performed on the Mir on FD15, FD55, FD85, FD115, and FD135 was cancelled due to the Spektr accident. The sample collection kits, as well as archived samples, were stowed within the Spektr module at the time of the accident. No further sampling or the return of samples was possible. Pre and postflight samples from STS-84 were analyzed. All Mir hot water samples were within the US acceptability limits set for the International Space Station. The one Mir hot water sample had a bacterial level of only 20 CFU/100 ml, indicating that the treatment train and final heat-pasteurization step of the Mir system is able to maintain the microbial quality of water from this source at standards well below both the US (100 CFU/100 ml) and Russian (10,000 CFU/100 ml) limits. Cold and SVO-ZV samples predictably contained many bacteria. NASA 6 and STS-86 None of the Mir hot water samples had bacterial growth, indicating that the treatment train and final heat-pasteurization step of the Mir system is able to maintain the microbial quality of water from this source at standards well below both the US (100 CFU/100 ml) and Russian (10,000 CFU/100 ml) limits. SVO-ZV samples predictably contained a moderate number of bacteria. NASA 7, STS-89, and STS-91 None of the Mir hot water samples had bacterial growth, indicating that the treatment train and final heat-pasteurization step of the Mir system is able to maintain the microbial quality of water from this source at standards well below both the US (100 CFU/100 ml) and Russian (10,000 CFU/100 ml) limits. Cold and SVO-ZV samples predictably contained many bacteria. During the first water sampling session of the mission, the NASA 7 crewmember reported the presence of "brown specks" in the unprocessed sample. The crewmember was instructed to proceed with the sample processing and retain the sample collection bag for return to ground. All of the samples that were collected during the mission were returned to Earth. Analysis was based on the descriptions given by the crewmember during debrief, by visual inspection of the sample collection bags which were returned to ground, and by chemical analysis of the discolored water. Upon inspection of the bags, laboratory personnel did not observe any type of particulate present. However, in four of five bags that were returned, there was a small amount of discolored water in one of the two valve stems present on the bags. Chemical analysis showed that the water was found to contain sodium thiosulfate. Each sample bag contains a small amount of sodium thiosulfate, a chemical that is added to the bags before flight to neutralize the biocide (silver) used in the Russian water reclamation system. The cause of this observation noted by the crewmember has not been conclusively determined. One possible cause could have been inadequate temperature control of the Water Experiment Kit. It is known that elevated temperatures will cause a yellowish-brown discoloration of this compound. FOOD PACKET The microorganisms present seem to be of environmental origin, rather than contamination of the food. 'FREE' SURFACE CONDENSATE NASA 6 A sample of 'free' surface condensate was collected on FD113 and returned to ground on STS-89 for complete analyses. Upon visual examination of the sample, the following observations were noted: the sample was cloudy with a brown particulate matter present. A wet mount preparation resulted in the rare observation of amoeba (Figure 1) and ciliated protozoa (Figure 2). Scanning Electron Microscopy revealed the presence of rod- and spirochete-form bacteria (Figure 3). Selected staining techniques resulted in no ova or parasites being observed. Culturing was performed using selective media for the detection of aerobes and fungi. A wide variety of bacteria were present in the samples. The bacteria isolated were of types that will grow in different environmental conditions and can tolerate a wide temperature range. Members of the Enterobacteriaceae family (organisms of enteric origin) that were isolated, such as the genera Serratia and Yersinia , can colonize sites in healthy hosts. The presence of these organisms is noteworthy in that they are opportunistic pathogens and can cause disease in immuno-compromised hosts. Other bacteria that were isolated, such as Flavobacterium meningosepticum , are rarely of clinical significance but may occasionally cause wound infections. NASA 7 Two samples of 'free' surface condensate were collected on FD127 and returned to ground on STS-91 for complete analyses. Upon visual examination of each sample, the following observations were noted: the "slimy" sample was cloudy with a brown particulate matter present; the "fresh" sample was slightly cloudy with a white particulate matter present. A wet mount preparation resulted in the rare observation of dust mites and showed the presence of a few ciliated protozoa. Scanning Electron Microscopy revealed the presence of rod- and spirochete-form bacteria. Selected staining techniques resulted in no ova or parasites being observed. Culturing was performed using selective media for the detection of aerobes, anaerobes, fungi, Legionella spp., and mycobacteria. A wide variety of bacteria were present in both samples. The bacteria isolated were of types that will grow in different environmental conditions and can tolerate a wide temperature range. Members of the Enterobacteriaceae family (organisms of enteric origin) that were isolated, such as the genera Enterobacter , Citrobacter , Serratia and Yersinia , can colonize sites in healthy hosts. The presence of these organisms is noteworthy in that they are opportunistic pathogens and can cause disease in immuno-compromised hosts. Although a presumptive identification of Legionella spp. was reported, final pneumophila species identification was not confirmed. Other bacteria that were isolated, such as Comamonas spp. , Flavobacterium meningosepticus and Pseudomonas fluorescens , are rarely of clinical significance but may occasionally cause wound infections. CONCLUSIONS: Overall, the microbiota of all crewmembers sampled was characteristic of healthy individuals. When present the fungal isolates recovered from specimens generally represented common environmental contaminants. No significant changes were found during spaceflight or upon return to earth relative to preflight results. Amounts of microorganisms observed in the air and on surfaces of the Shuttle and Mir station were mostly within the acceptability limits set by the US for the ISS. The types of organisms recovered were consistent with previous findings from both Shuttle and Mir missions. Fungal levels of the air samples collected on the Mir were often above the limits set for this station; however, no major adverse health effects were seen in the crewmembers. The temporal fluctuations in levels of organisms probably reflect changes in environmental characteristics, such as temperature and humidity, at the time of sample collection. The bacterial load of the Shuttle water samples were consistent with those seen on previous missions. All Mir galley hot water samples were within the standards set for both the Mir and the ISS. All isolates were consistent with findings from previous Shuttle and Mir missions. The hardware designed for in-flight microbial monitoring performed nominally. Collection and examination of 'free' surface condensate can prove to be a valuable tool in assessing the overall condition of the health of a closed environmental system such as a space station. Although many potential pathogens were isolated from the surfaces, air and "free" surface condensate, it is interesting to note that the microbial flora of the crewmembers remained that of healthy individuals and that these microorganisms imposed no adverse health effects.

title: Physiologic Alterations and Pharmacokinetic Changes During Space Flight
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Space flight induces a wide range of physiological and biochemical changes in crewmembers. Examples of these changes are disruption of gastrointestinal (GI) function and physiology, changes in liver function, fluid and electrolyte imbalances, alterations in circulatory dynamics and organ blood flow, and hormonal and metabolic perturbations. Any of these changes can influence the pharmacokinetic behavior and pharmacodynamic consequences of medications administered to crewmembers during space flight. Since the therapeutic effectiveness of medications is dependent upon their pharmacokinetics and bioavailability, determination of flight-induced changes of the characteristics for operationally critical medications is crucial for ensuring the effectiveness of inflight pharmacologic treatment. Saliva sampling techniques have been used to evaluate the pharmacokinetics of acetaminophen (a common pain-relief medication) during space flight. Preliminary
approach: This investigation consisted of two protocols. The first protocol, GI-Acetaminophen, was designed to evaluate pharmacokinetic changes during space flight using acetaminophen as a representative drug. GI function, an important contributing physiologic parameter to pharmacokinetic variability during flight, was estimated using a lactulose breath-hydrogen test, which is a noninvasive and reliable indirect measure of GI motility. The second protocol, Hepatic-antipyrine, was designed to estimate changes in hepatic metabolism by monitoring the clearance of orally administered antipyrine. This method provides an indirect determination of hepatic metabolizing-enzyme activity. GI Experiment Protocol: After 8 to 10 hours fasting, each crewmember collected a saliva, a urine sample and two consecutive breath samples; breath samples were collected in sample bags. The crewmembers then ate a prescribed low-fiber breakfast, followed by ingestion of a 650-mg dose of liquid acetaminophen. Next, orange juice containing 20 grams of lactulose was ingested. After drinking the mixture, the crew collected serial breath samples, saliva samples, and void-by-void urine samples as per a predetermined schedule. All in-flight samples were identified and collection times were recorded with a barcode reader (BCR). For each crewmember, eighteen breath samples were collected over a period of 6 hours and 12 saliva samples over an 8-hour period. Void-by-void urine samples were collected for 24 hours after dosage ingestion. With the extension of the Mir 18 mission, additional time was available to collect 4 additional breath samples from the Mir 18 crew. The data collected was helpful in examining the effects of cabin atmosphere on the breath sample components. The time of peak breath hydrogen concentration after ingestion of lactulose was used to determine gastrointestinal motility before, during, and after flight. Pharmacokinetic parameters and bioavailability were determined for pre-, in-, and postflight samples using concentration-time data of parent drug and metabolites. Hepatic Experiment Protocol: After 8-10 hours fasting, crewmembers collected a saliva and a urine sample then consumed a prescribed low fiber breakfast. A 1.2-gram antipyrine dose was then ingested. This was followed by the collection of 8 saliva samples and void-by-void urine samples for 48 hours after dosage ingestion. All in-flight samples were identified and collection times were recorded with a BCR. Hepatic metabolic activity was determined by calculating the total body clearance of orally administered antipyrine from concentration-time data of pre-, in- and postflight samples.
