The data show only minor variations in Ig concentration. In addition, no definite trends were noted when the preflight, inflight, and postflight results were analyzed as three separate groups. Only one crewmember had an IgG concentration which was significantly outside the normal range for all eight samples.

title: Microgravity Vestibular Investigations
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: The Microgravity Vestibular Investigations (MVI) studied the underlying perceptual and physiological mechanisms associated with sensori-motor adaptations to space flight. Human perception of orientation in space depends on the interaction of virtually every sensory system. Changes in the environment and the interaction with the new stimuli
approach: The MVI experiment used a rotator chair, which provided angular rotation stimuli about a single axis (subject’s yaw, pitch or roll). The drive rotators were computer controlled and provided three types of velocity profiles: pseudorandom, step, and sinusoid. The rotator axis was oriented for earth-vertical rotation for the ground tests, and perpendicular to the Spacelab floor for inflight testing. The chair utilized straps and padding to stabilize the subject and minimize pressure points. A helmet with inflatable bladders was used to fix the head in respect to the chair. The helmet also blocked any external light sources and integrated earphones masked any noises from other ongoing Spacelab activities. The helmet-mounted optokinetic stimulus (OKS) module provided visual stimuli, including targets for eye calibrations. The OKS module was mounted over the subjects right eye and a camera module was mounted over the left eye. The visual scene, visible for the subject when wearing the helmet was a black-red checkerboard pattern and illuminated by red Light Emission Diodes (LEDs). The speed, direction and pattern of the LED display were computer controlled. Eye measurements were recorded with both electro-oculographic (EOG) and video techniques. For EOG recordings, surface electrodes were placed at the outer canthi of both eyes to record horizontal eye movements, and above and below the right eye to record vertical eye movements. Video was used to analyze roll rotation of the eyeball. To record nystagmus, the subject wore a contact lens with reference markings in the left eye. The MVI experiments were integrated into eight different functional
results: in a different interpretation by the central nervous system (CNS) of the incoming sensory information. Because the human orientation system is adaptable and complex, it is difficult to trace a change in behavior to any one sensori-motor unit in the synergistic orientation system. In this investigation, the effects of different stimuli on the human sense of orientation was determined; thereby an interactive model for orientation was used. APPROACH: The MVI experiment used a rotator chair, which provided angular rotation stimuli about a single axis (subject’s yaw, pitch or roll). The drive rotators were computer controlled and provided three types of velocity profiles: pseudorandom, step, and sinusoid. The rotator axis was oriented for earth-vertical rotation for the ground tests, and perpendicular to the Spacelab floor for inflight testing. The chair utilized straps and padding to stabilize the subject and minimize pressure points. A helmet with inflatable bladders was used to fix the head in respect to the chair. The helmet also blocked any external light sources and integrated earphones masked any noises from other ongoing Spacelab activities. The helmet-mounted optokinetic stimulus (OKS) module provided visual stimuli, including targets for eye calibrations. The OKS module was mounted over the subjects right eye and a camera module was mounted over the left eye. The visual scene, visible for the subject when wearing the helmet was a black-red checkerboard pattern and illuminated by red Light Emission Diodes (LEDs). The speed, direction and pattern of the LED display were computer controlled. Eye measurements were recorded with both electro-oculographic (EOG) and video techniques. For EOG recordings, surface electrodes were placed at the outer canthi of both eyes to record horizontal eye movements, and above and below the right eye to record vertical eye movements. Video was used to analyze roll rotation of the eyeball. To record nystagmus, the subject wore a contact lens with reference markings in the left eye. The MVI experiments were integrated into eight different functional objectives to address: (1) semicircular canal dynamics, (2) vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR) suppression, (3) visual-vestibular interaction, (4) VOR responses to velocity steps, (5) optokinetic nystagmus, (6) sensory perception and motion sickness reports, (7) positional and spontaneous nystagmus and (8) changes in dynamic posture. The objectives (1) through (6) were performed pre-, post- and inflight, while objectives (7) and (8) were only tested pre- and postflight. (1) Semicircular canal dynamics. The vestibular system provides information of angular acceleration (semicircular canals) and linear acceleration (otoliths) to the central nervous system (CNS). There is evidence that under some circumstances one set of receptors can modulate the input of the other system. It was hypothesized that in the microgravity environment, which is defined by the absence of the gravity vector, the semicircular canals would continue to supply input about the direction and magnitude of any rotation, while the otoliths would not provide the expected information regarding linear acceleration. Thus, this sensory conflict would cause a change in the VOR. Sinusoidal and pseudorandom rotational stimuli, provided by the rotator chair, were used to study the dynamic response characteristics of the VOR. The selected frequencies covered a broad range to observe any changes in the interactions between the VOR and other visual tracking reflexes caused by different frequencies. Four single frequencies were tested during pitch rotation, including 0.05 Hertz (Hz) (for 100 seconds), 0.2 Hz (for 25 seconds), 0.8 Hz (for 20 seconds) and 1.25 Hz (for 20 seconds). The peak angular velocities of these profiles were maintained constant at 60 degrees per second (except for 1.25 Hz which was limited to 40 degrees per second). The test subjects had their vision occluded and were asked to fixate an imaginary wall target approximately 1 meter (1.1 yards) away. To evaluate the horizontal VOR, a pseudorandom (sum-of-sine) stimulus was used, and corresponding single sine measurements were obtained during 0.2 Hz and 0.8 Hz yaw rotations. The pseudorandom stimulus was comprised of seven frequencies ranging from 0.02 to 1.39 Hz. (2) Vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR) suppression. Turning the head produces a vestibular stimulus which activates the VOR and generates a compensatory eye movement in the opposite direction to hold the gaze stationary. When humans use head and eye movement to track a (moving) target the VOR is suppressed at low frequencies and diminishes slowly with increasing frequencies. During the MVI experiment, the vertical VOR was tested during pitch sinusoidal chair rotations at frequencies of 0.05 Hz (low frequency) and 1.25 Hz (high frequency). During the tests, the subjects were asked to fixate on the stationary checkerboard pattern displayed inside the OKS module. Yaw VOR suppression was tested by pseudorandom stimulus profiles utilizing the rotator chair. (3) Visual-vestibular interaction. The vestibular motion sensors detect transient head rotation, but during sustained rotation their signal becomes progressively less accurate. During head rotation in light, the optokinetic system compensates for the fading vestibular response, which leads to the conclusion that during light both systems are stimulated and the eye movement response, called the visual-vestibular nystagmic response (VVR), is the result of the combined response of both systems. The objective of this part of the experiment was to evaluate the relative role the vestibular and optokinetic systems encounter during adaptation to microgravity. The subjects were sinusoidally oscillated at 0.2 Hz and 0.8 Hz with the rotator chair while viewing a constant velocity optokinetic stimulation at + 35 degrees per second inside the OKS module. This procedure caused a nystagmic response of different quality when both stimuli were of same or opposite directions. The visual-vestibular interactions were tested both in the horizontal plane (rotation of subject in yaw combined with horizontal optokinetic stimulation), and in the vertical plane (rotation in pitch combined with vertical optokinetic stimulation). (4) VOR responses to velocity steps. When a human subject is rotated in the earth vertical axis and in darkness for an extended period of time, the nystagmus decays and after several minutes of rotation the nystagmus disappears and the subject is no longer aware of the rotation. If the rotation is suddenly stopped, the subject indicates rotation in the opposite direction. This phenomenon is called post-rotatory nystagmus. Previous experiments demonstrated that the duration and magnitude of post-rotary nystagmus is gravity dependent. During the MVI investigation, post-rotatory VOR was studied after chair rotations of one minute at a speed of 120 degrees/second clockwise with fast accelerations and an abrupt stop. During the test, the subject was instructed to gaze straight ahead. The eye movements were recorded for 1 minute after the chair was stopped. After a brief pause, the procedure was repeated with counter-clockwise rotation. (5) Optokinetic nystagmus. The objective of this experiment was to detect any changes in optokinetic nystagmus, which was induced by a rotating image inside the binocular OKS module. Horizontal and vertical optokinetic responses were recorded while the subjects were restrained into the rotator chair, positioned in yaw and pitch chair orientations, respectively. For each optokinetic stimulus run, three speeds of OKS-rotation were presented in succession (20, 60 and 40 degrees per second) in one direction for 15 seconds each. Immediately after the last image, the optokinetic nystagmus was recorded in darkness for 15 seconds. The same stimulus sequence was then presented with OKS-rotations in the opposite direction. Later during the IML-1 mission, the protocol was repeated while the test subjects were free-floating inside the Spacelab module. (6) Sensory perception and motion sickness reports. The IML-1 crewmembers were asked to report their perceptions of particular motions while in microgravity and define if those motions were (1) different than on earth and (2) more or less confusing (or disturbing) than on Earth. The subjects were also asked to describe, quantify, and record any changes in space motion sickness symptoms during the space flight. The occurrence of motion sickness and the nature and degree of symptoms were important to the interpretation of the collected data, as was the intake of anti-motion sickness medication. Motion sickness symptoms were reported using a special score (0=no symptoms to 20=vomiting) during other MVI experiments. To do so, the astronauts used a voice recorder during the experiments and a checklist for evaluations performed at the end of each test and at the end of their work shift. (7) Positional and spontaneous nystagmus. Positional or spontaneous nystagmus occurs when the vestibular receptors indicate that the head is accelerating. In microgravity, the presence of spontaneous nystagmus (positional nystagmus has no meaning in 0-g) suggests that the CNS is receiving a head acceleration signal and is forwarding motor signals to the eye muscles. During baseline data collection, eye movements to detect spontaneous nystagmus were recorded during the following tests: (1) gaze nystagmus test (at + 10 and 20 degrees), (2) sinusoidal pursuit tracking test, using a swinging pendulum over + 30 degrees, (3) Benign Paroxysmal nystagmus test (test for positional nystagmus), and (4) positional nystagmus testing with eyes open and occluded vision and with eyes closed using the following sequence: sitting, supine with head hanging, supine with head straight up, supine with head turned to the right, and then to the left, and finally with the right ear to the floor and repeated with the left ear to the floor. The subject was returned to an upright (sitting) position between each test position. Eye movements were recorded with electro-oculography (EOG). During the space flight, eye movements were recorded during all test sessions to enable observations of transient spontaneous nystagmus before and after each rotational test. (8) Changes in dynamic posture. Many astronauts returning from space exhibit some degree of postural dysfunction. To quantify these dysfunctions, a posture platform system (used for clinical diagnosis of disorders in balance control) was modified for postflight testing of movement coordination and sensory organization. For movement coordination tests, the foot plate was rapidly translated (maximum translation + 7 cm) or rotated (maximum tilt + 10 degrees) to provide stimuli to the subject’s posture control system. The postural responses to the sudden perturbations were monitored and recorded for a period of 2.5 seconds each. Sensory organization tests required the subjects to attempt a stable upright stance under different sensory input conditions. The conditions could be altered by a tilting foot-plate and a skipping visual surround which could be changed individually or both at the same time. The postural reaction to each sensory input was recorded for 20 seconds after each input. Preflight, the MVI testing was completed in six single test sessions which were conducted on L-130 (130 days prior to launch), L-68, L-30 and L-15. The inflight test schedule included tests on seven flight days of the 8-day IML-1 mission for the MVI. Each of the four test subjects followed an individual test schedule. Postflight sessions were conducted on landing day, and 1, 2, 5, 8, and 30 days after landing. RESULTS: (2) Vestibulo-ocular reflexes. There was a consistent increase in the VOR gain observed at the mid-to-high frequencies (0.2 Hz and 0.8 Hz) of chair rotation towards the end of the space flight. And the observed changes were greater in pitch than in yaw position of the chair. (5) Optokinetic nystagmus. Although not statistically different, there was a trend for the gain of the optokinetic nystagmus to be increased during the space flight and during early postflight testing. (6) Motion Sickness and perceptual reports. All four subjects reported some form of motion sickness symptoms. One subject reported severe malaise through most of the flight; the other three crewmembers reported significantly subsided symptoms by the third flight day prior to the majority of most MVI measurements. Three of the four crewmembers reported an increase in motion sickness symptoms while performing the MVI experiments. Reports from two subjects indicated that sensations of rotation, induced by both oscillatory and ramp stimuli, were somewhat more intense in orbit than on Earth. Also, during the pitch ramp stimuli, three of the four subjects tested inflight indicated that they felt they were tumbling “head-over-heals” rather than rotating in pitch (laying on their side). (7) Positional and spontaneous nystagmus. Before the flight, positional nystagmus was observed in all four subjects. During the inflight performance of the MVI experiments, transient spontaneous nystagmus was observed: all four subjects displayed some form of nystagmus, and one subject displayed vertical downbeat nystagmus, a form of nystagmus which exhibits all the characteristics of vestibular origin. (8) Changes in dynamic posture. Two subjects participated in postural equilibrium tests on landing day and several times during the recovery period. The other two subjects were tested for the first time at R+1 and several times during the slower, secondary phase of recovery. The two subjects tested for the first time on R+1 displayed signs of disturbed postural equilibrium control 24 and 27 hours after landing, recovered to preflight levels by 47 and 48.5 hours after landing, and overshot preflight levels by 120 and 122.5 hours post landing. The two subjects tested on landing day (R+0) showed little or no improvement in recovery on R+1 and R+2. At about 120 hours after landing, both subjects had recovered to preflight levels and by 190 hours after landing one subjects displayed hyperstability. This led to the conclusion, that some postflight tests (most likely the pitch axis rotation test) interfered with the readaptation process.

title: 3D Tissue Models for Study of Intercellular Signaling Stimulated by High Energy Particles
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: In space, astronauts are exposed to a complex, unique radiation environment including energetic protons and charged particles from galactic cosmic rays and solar particle events. Although these radiations can
approach: The Caco2 colon cancer cell line was chosen for initial studies since this line has been used as a model for colon epithelium in published literature, including one radiation study. The 3D colon model was established with the CaCo2 cells as the epithelium and AG01522 normal human fibroblasts as the stromal cells embedded in collagen. Cells were irradiated with X-rays, protons, and iron ions. With the cells in monolayer, a transwell insert co-culture system was used to assess DNA damage in both irradiated cells and unirradiated bystander cells sharing medium with the irradiated cells.
results: in significant cumulative doses to astronauts during long-duration space flights, most exposures occur at low fluences, so that particle traversals through an astronaut's body are well separated in tissue location and time. Under such conditions, bystander effects, where unirradiated cells express biological changes in response to signals from irradiated cells, have increased significance. The overall hypothesis of this investigation is that increased oxidative stress caused by charged particle-stimulated intercellular signaling-- bystander effects-- in cells and tissues creates a microenvironment conducive to altered carcinogenic processes; responses can be triggered at very low doses, with the lowest effective dose depending on radiation type, but the magnitude of the response being radiation quality-independent. Previous studies showed that bystander responses can be induced in unirradiated cells in a 3D skin model, including after low fluences of protons or iron ions, and that in 3D both irradiated and bystander cells are more resistant to induction of DNA damage than cells in monolayer. Different epithelial tissues can differ in their 3D architecture and, therefore, might be expected to have different radiation and bystander responses. This project proposes to compare bystander signaling in 3D models of colon with previous data for the skin epithelial model. The specific aims for this study are: Develop a 3D model of colonic epithelium for testing effects of low fluences of charged particles in comparison with the responses in our previously developed 3D skin model. Quantify DNA damage, apoptosis, differentiation and proliferation in the 3D model of colonic epithelium exposed to low fluences of charged-particles Determine whether the bystander response in the colon model has the same radiation dose and LET dependence as the skin model, and whether reactive oxygen species (ROS) play a role in the intercellular signaling. APPROACH: The Caco2 colon cancer cell line was chosen for initial studies since this line has been used as a model for colon epithelium in published literature, including one radiation study. The 3D colon model was established with the CaCo2 cells as the epithelium and AG01522 normal human fibroblasts as the stromal cells embedded in collagen. Cells were irradiated with X-rays, protons, and iron ions. With the cells in monolayer, a transwell insert co-culture system was used to assess DNA damage in both irradiated cells and unirradiated bystander cells sharing medium with the irradiated cells. RESULTS: Data show induction of micronuclei (MN; surrogate for chromosome aberrations) in Caco2 cells 72 h after irradiation with X-rays, 1 GeV protons or 1 GeV/n silicon or iron ions. In all cases, there is a large, radiation dose-dependent increase in MN in irradiated cells, but importantly, there is up to a 3-fold increase in the fraction of unirradiated bystander cells having MN after co-culture with irradiated cells. Additional studies using induction of foci of the DNA repair-related protein 53BP1, a surrogate for DNA double-strand breaks, as an endpoint have been done in irradiated and bystander Caco2 cells after exposure to X-rays, protons, and iron ions. With all radiation types, in the irradiated population, the fraction of cells with foci is substantially increased at 1 h, is maximum 5 h after irradiation, then decreases substantially by 24 h. In the bystander cell population, the increase in fraction of cells with foci is slower, not being maximal until 12 h after irradiation and the start of co-culture, and still being elevated at 24 h. The maximum fraction of bystander cells with increased level of foci is about 3-fold higher than in untreated cells, similar to the magnitude of bystander effect seen using MN as endpoint. This delayed development and removal of damage in bystander cells compared to irradiated cells is similar to the responses seen in the 3D skin model. Comparing the 2D and 3D data in the CaCo2 cells suggests several findings: First, in 3D there are fewer foci per cell, including in untreated samples, so a cut-off of only 1 focus per cell for analysis was used in 3D compared to 5 foci per cell minimum for scoring in 2D. If the 5 foci per cell cut-off had been used in the 3D samples, the fraction of cells with damage would be much lower in 3D, consistent with the finding with the skin model. Second, the time courses for development and disappearance of foci in 3D are similar to those in 2D, with cells in both architectures showing the delay in bystander responses compared to responses in irradiated cells. The model has been extended to use normal human colon epithelial cells (FHC cells) in both 2D and 3D studies. The early data had some scatter, but the trends show that in monolayer, 53BP1 foci appear to be maximal at 5 h after irradiation in both irradiated and bystander FHC cells, but replicate experiments are needed to confirm this finding. Furthermore, although these cells grow very slowly, 3D constructs in which the FHC cells form a single epithelial layer on the basement material containing fibroblasts, consistent with the single-layered colon epithelium have been successfully produced.

title: Interface Consistency (Phase II): Risk Assessment, Standards, and Guidelines
archive_status: Data preservation is complete.  All datasets are privacy-protected.  Data is available via data request.
objectives: To achieve mission objectives, future exploration missions depended on the design and development of vehicles and sophisticated technologies from both NASA and numerous outside commercial partners. NASA's current strategy to commercial spaceflight development is to give providers considerable flexibility and possibilities to innovate, notwithstanding the existence of consistency-related restrictions. Because inconsistent interface features and interactivity may affect crew performance and mission effectiveness, the level of standardization across Artemis vehicle interfaces is an issue. According to the Interface Consistency Phase I pilot study's findings, inconsistent interfaces are linked to greater workload, inefficiency (slower performance time, more actions needed), and decreased system satisfaction. Since there is no evidence regarding the differential impact of particular types of inconsistency related to complex systems, determining the amount of risk is challenging. The high levels of stress and unpredictability that come with more autonomous future missions may make these consequences worse. This study expanded on the research initiated in Phase 1: Characterization and Measurement, that addressed many of the shortcomings found in the literature by creating a definition for consistency, formulating a taxonomy of tangible interface characteristics, applying this framework as guidance for developing consistency assessment tools, and conducting an exploratory pilot study to assess performance of these tools. During Phase 2, the investigative team accomplished these objectives using the following specific aims: 1. Refine the assessment tools using feedback and
approach: During Phase 2, investigators focused on the feedback and
results: obtained during Phase I, including: item reduction, item phrasing, adding item descriptions and/or free-form responses, and weighting items or scales, if applicable 2. Refine tasks and prototype stimuli using feedback from Program human interface and Artemis training Subject Matter Experts. 3. Characterize risk by understanding differences in human performance and subjective feedback related to each specific type of inconsistency (i.e., interface characteristics and interaction) 4. Propose a set of standards and guidelines addressing aspects of inconsistent design that appear to have the most impact on performance Approach During Phase 2, investigators focused on the feedback and results obtained during Phase 1 to refine the assessment tools, bringing forward one tool intended for expert/practitioner use and one tool for crew use. Interviews were conducted with program human interface and training subject matter experts (SMEs) to identify tasks that were likely to be performed across exploration vehicles, to increase the fidelity of tasks conducted during the risk assessment research. These interviews identified interface attributes encountered across vehicles, which influenced updates to the prototype designs. Together, the inputs from SMEs helped create prototype designs that are more representative of exploration systems, more resilient supporting more practical tasks, compared to Phase 1. The prototypes demonstrate consistency changes between assessed pairings at each taxonomy level such as highly consistent (interfaces and interaction highly consistent), high interface consistency, low interaction consistency, low interface consistency, high interaction consistency, and highly inconsistent (interfaces and interaction highly inconsistent). This research gave insight into the kinds of consistency that have a greater influence on performance and subjective feedback. Participants completed a variety of tasks (e.g., monitoring telemetry, sending messages to ground control, configuring systems) on multiple prototypes. Performance (e.g., eye tracking, error rates, time on task), subjective data (e.g., workload, usability, Intersystem Consistency Scale consistency scores), and transfer of training were measured for participants working with different versions of the prototype. Results The results of this study convey the risk associated illustrates each consistency category and whether there might be interactions between categories. This will reveal the impact of different types of consistency and allow further refinement of the assessment tool(s). These results also suggest which consistency types should be subject to greater scrutiny when evaluating designs proposed by commercial providers. The team has developed a set of standards and guidelines from the research that will help ensure the most important types of consistency required for future programs.

title: Sweat Rates during Continuous and Interval Aerobic Exercise: Implications for NASA Multipurpose Crew Vehicle (MPCV) Missions
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Aerobic deconditioning is one of the effects of space flight. Missions longer than eight days will involve exercise countermeasures including those aimed at preventing the loss of aerobic capacity. The NASA Multipurpose Crew Vehicle (MPCV) will be NASA’s centerpiece architecture for human space exploration that targets destinations beyond low Earth orbit. Aerobic exercise within the small habitable volume of the MPCV is expected to challenge the ability of the environmental control systems, especially in terms of moisture control. The limitation of the environmental control system as it relates to dealing with exercise is currently humidity control as opposed to maintenance of oxygen or carbon dioxide content. In its current configuration the limitation to exercise protocols and intensities will be moisture production. Exercising humans contribute moisture to the environment by increased respiratory rate (exhaling air at 100% humidity) and sweat. Current acceptable values are based on theoretical models that rely on an “average” crewmember working continuously at 75% of their aerobic capacity. Evidence suggests that high intensity interval exercise for much shorter durations are equally effective or better in building and maintaining aerobic capacity. This investigation examined sweat and respiratory rates for operationally relevant continuous and interval aerobic exercise protocols using a variety of different individuals. This study had the following specific aims: Determine if aerobic exercise protocols involving different intensities and total workloads elicit different moisture loads during exercise and 30 minutes thereafter. Identify which aerobic exercise protocols are compatible with planned MPCV environmental control capabilities. Be able to provide MPCV project with real world exercise-induced moisture production numbers so that available options to optimize environmental controls can be made.
approach: Studies were performed at the NASA Johnson Space Center in the Biomedical Research and Environmental Sciences Division’s environmental chamber. Subjects reported to the laboratory for five total sessions, two of which are preliminary sessions and three experimental sessions. Trials were performed in an environmental chamber set to 21 degrees Celsius and 57% humidity, similar to environmental parameters of the MPCV vehicle. The environmental chamber had the required space and environmental control capabilities. Aerobic Capacity Session - Aerobic capacity (VO2max) was determined by indirect calorimetry for all participants. Workloads for the experimental sessions was be determined based on this value. Subjects were tested using a rowing cycle ergometer. The load on the ergometer was increased in a graded manner until volitional fatigue was reached. Familiarization Session - A linear relationship between Watts and O2 utilization was used to estimate workloads corresponding to 75%, 85%, and 170% of the VO2max load. During familiarization, subjects cycled for 10 minutes at the calculated 75% VO2max load while oxygen consumption was measured. Subjects continued to cycle until the desired O2 consumption range was reached and the workload was adjusted as necessary. Experimental Sessions – Three aerobic training protocols were implemented. All experimental sessions were conducted on the cycle ergometer used for the aerobic capacity and familiarization sessions. Respiratory gas measurements were collected throughout. Each protocol was followed by 30 minutes of resting recovery to capture post-exercise sweating and oxygen consumption. Total moisture was determined by the difference in protection difference between pre and post testing dry weight. An additional weighing occurred 30 minutes later to characterize post-exercise moisture production. Respiratory water production was calculated based the difference between expired and inspired water content assuming saturation of expired air. Sweat rate was calculated as the difference between total moisture production and respiratory water production. Oxygen consumption, CO2 production, and ventilatory rate and volume was calculated based on metabolic gas collection using the Parvo Medics software.
results: Results show that the 4 minute and 30 second interval protocols produce less sweat versus the continuous exercise protocol. Furthermore, sweat production correlated with work performed on the ergometer and energy expenditure during exercise. These results suggest that interval exercise is an alternative to continuous aerobic exercise for situations where moisture production must be carefully monitored to avoid condensation issues.

RESULTS: Of the several projects that this investigation has actively participated in (the Flight Analogs Project Bed Rest Study out of Johnson Space Center (JSC), future Mars surface missions, operations planning for the NASA Extreme Environment Mission Operations (NEEMO) analog, and for crew and ground operations onboard the International Space Station (ISS)), common challenges with planning tools, design and build solutions were identified. title: Bone Strain During 0G Exercise
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Considerable NASA resources have been devoted to a vibration-isolated treadmill (TVIS) that has been installed in the International Space Station (ISS). This device is attractive because programs may be designed to allow exercise countermeasures to be applied against bone, muscle, and cardiovascular adaptations. Despite the need for on-orbit exercise using the TVIS, almost no research has been conducted to determine the acceptability of the subject load device (SLD) and harness used to tether crewmembers to the treadmill. Data regarding the bone strains produced by exercise countermeasures, such as running in reduced gravity, are also unavailable, yet there is little doubt that bone strain plays an important intermediary role in the signal transduction pathway responsible for bone maintenance and functional adaptation. This study in simulated microgravity was designed to evaluate the comfort and function of a new SLD design applied to subjects running in a system that allows controlled distribution of the load between the waist and shoulders during treadmill running. The specific aims of this study were: 1.To define the parameters (load, load distribution, and exercise frequency) of a treadmill exercise program using the SLD harness system that would be acceptable to the crew during prolonged space flight. 2. To measure gravity replacement loads, kinematics, ground reaction forces, muscle activity, and subjective ratings of comfort during the exercises defined in specific aim #1. 3. To use data generated in specific aim #2 to extend the capabilities of a parallel robot (Rotopod R2000) that acts as a cadaveric dynamic gait simulator, which will enable measurement of bone strains generated during on-orbit treadmill running. 4. To determine bone strain at several sites on the distal tibia during walking in 1g, and during the simulated on-orbit conditions identified in specific aim #1.
approach: Using the Zero Gravity Locomotion Simulator (ZLS), twelve subjects completed nine, five minute running trials at a constant speed (3.35 ms-1) using 3 SLD loads (50%, 75% and 100% BW) presented at random while using a 50:50 shoulder-to-waist loading ratio. Subjective ratings of discomfort, ground reaction forces and SLD loads were collected. 100% BW in the ZLS
results: ed in similar ground reaction forces (GRF) profiles to those obtained from the literature for over ground running. The full body weight loading conditions were comfortably tolerated. The ZLS and its SLD system are promising methods of simulating over ground running in zero gravity as evidenced by the low discomfort levels of subjects and their ground reaction force profiles. Prior to the second phase of the study, a new pneumatic SLD system was implemented to increase comfort and reduce load variation. A new harness utilizing backpack technology was constructed to improve subject comfort while running on the ZLS. The second phase of this investigation examined the feasibility of the new system in a long-term exercise program, such as the three to six months that crewmembers are currently spending on the ISS. Subjects ran four times per week on the ZLS for three continuous weeks. During each session, the subjects ran for a total of 30 minutes at a pace of 2.68 - 3.49 ms-1 while loaded to 100% BW. Comfort data were collected relating to both harness and lower extremity discomfort. Both measures decreased from session 1 to session 12 and fell within acceptable levels, indicating that repeated long duration running under 100% BW is a feasible exercise option. During the third phase, data collected on various human subject experiments were incorporated into robotic cadaver simulations in order to directly measure bone strains in cadaver limbs moving through accurate kinematic and kinetic reconstructions of orbit-based locomotion. The simulations replicated walking in lunar, Martian, and Earth gravity, highlighting the relationship between gravitational load during locomotion and bone strain. Thus, these sequential experiments will provide the unique psychophysical and biomechanical information needed to design better exercise countermeasures to bone loss on the ISS. They will also provide fundamental new data on the relationship between external loading and strain in human bone. RESULTS: PHASE 2 Eight subjects (5 females and 3 males, 31.9 ± 9.2 years, 168.0 ± 12.1 cm, 62.6 ± 11.7 kg) completed the protocol for phase 2 of the experiment. Subjects were tested in the ZLS, and height and weight was measured at the first visit. Based on the desired outcome of astronauts eventually running on-orbit while loaded to full body weight, all subjects were loaded to 100% of their 1g weight (100% BW) during the 30-minute run portion of each session. GRFs were recorded from a force platform under the treadmill belt and SLD loads were measured with in-line SLD force transducers. Subjects wore an instrumented harness, which had force transducers mounted in-line between the shoulder straps and waist belt, allowing the loads applied to the shoulder and the waist to be calculated. All subject-controlled modifications of the shoulder to hip load distribution were captured for later correlation with comfort evaluation data. After a warm-up of a two-minute walk and three-minute jog, subjects ran for up to 30 minutes in the ZLS at a pace of 2.7-3.5 ms-1 (6.0-7.8 mph). Subjects were allowed to take breaks during the run if needed, and the durations of the breaks were recorded. Following the run, subjects cooled down by jogging for three minutes and walking for two minutes. Subjects were asked to rate their discomfort in various regions of the body (including the neck, shoulders, back, waist, hips, glutes, quadriceps, hamstrings, gastrocnemius, tibialis anterior, and overall) using the Visual Analog Scale (VAS). Discomfort was measured at the beginning and end of the exercise session as well as periodically during the session. The entire testing session was repeated at the same time of day, four times per week for a period of three consecutive weeks, for a total of 12 test sessions per subject. All subjects completed a 15-minute training session in the ZLS prior to the first data collection session. The discomfort ratings collected at the end of the 30-minute run were compared via reduced equations with gender, training level, day, speed variation above 6 mph, duration of time between final rest break and discomfort measurement, and total duration of rest breaks for both the harness and lower extremity regions. Over the course of the twelve sessions all the ratings of harness-related and lower extremity discomfort measured at the end of the 30-minute run decreased. PHASE 3 Data collected on various human subject experiments were incorporated into a cadaver model experiment using the 6 degree-of-freedom parallel robot. A kinematic trajectory was prescribed for the robot so that the final motion of the cadaveric lower extremity mimicked the kinematics seen in life. Walking was simulated with a stance phase duration of 2.8 seconds. Computer controlled actuators applied loads to the tendons of five major lower extremity muscles, the triceps surae, tibialis anterior, or in two cases, extensor digitorum longus, tibialis posterior, peroneous longus, and flexor hallucis longus, to generate appropriate muscle forces. The kinematic data were conformed via a force platform mounted vertically on the robot which doubled as the walking surface for the cadaveric foot. The muscle forces were confirmed via in-line force transducers. Data from the force platform and transducers was sampled at a rate of 1000 Hz. During the walking simulation, bone strain measurements were recorded at three locations on the tibia (Anterior/Lateral, Anterior/Medial and Posterior) approximately 7-9 cm superior to the lateral malleolus. A fourth rosette was placed on the flat portion of the lateral surface of the calcaneus. Data from all rosettes were collected simultaneously. The effective sampling rate of the system was 1000 Hz for the first three specimens and 400 Hz for subsequent specimens. Strain data from the individual rosette elements are averaged over four trials for each load condition and filtered using a Butterworth filter at a cutoff frequency of 0.5Hz. Data from individual rosette elements were used to calculate the principal strain components and strain directions at each site. Axial strains at each site on the tibia were collected as the strain measured in the gage of the rosette oriented with the long axis of the bone. The robot and muscle actuators were directed to simulate walking with a 2.8-second stance phase at lunar (1/6 g), Martian (3/8 g), and Earth (1 g) gravities based on the donor weight associated with each specimen. In order to be included in the study, a specimen needed to have at least two successful trials for each gravity condition. A total of 16 specimens were tested, but eight had to be removed from analysis. Six of those specimens failed during testing and did not have an adequate number of trials to be included. One specimen had broken foot bones, and one had a faulty strain gage. Of the eight remaining specimens, six were right lower extremities (3 male, 3 female) and two were left lower extremities (2 male). All specimens were from different donors (79.8 ± 8.0 years, 65.7 ± 13.7 kg) to maintain sample independence. All strain parameters at each site, as well as kinematic and muscle force data, were collected for all trials.

title: Individualized Real-Time Neurocognitive Assessment Toolkit for Space Flight Fatigue
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: This study addressed the goal of developing tools to assess crew performance in real-time and evaluate countermeasures to mitigate the effects of fatigue, circadian misalignment, and work-overload. It is responsive to the critical need to identify how a range of cognitive functions of astronauts can be affected in space flight by fatigue alone, and its interaction with other risk factors and conditions such as elevated carbon dioxide, intracranial pressure, space fog, and countermeasures. This study aimed to deliver a comprehensive, software-based, neurocognitive toolkit (Cognition). By building on state-of-the-art neuropsychological test development, the toolkit permits evaluation of a full range of cognitive functions using brief (1-5 minutes), validated procedures. The tests included, but went beyond, what is currently measured by WinSCAT and the Reaction Self Test on the International Space Station (ISS). Importantly, the toolkit permitted rapid assessment of performance in cognitive, social-emotional, and sensorimotor domains. This study had the following specific aims: Development of short-duration adaptive versions of neuropsychological tests for space flight. Establish learning curves for neuropsychological tests and validate sensitivity to sleep deprivation. Cognition software development and optimization for space flight. NASA’s Johnson Space Center (JSC) field testing, astronaut learning curves, and astronaut norms for performance feedback algorithm development. Complete ISS feasibility study.
approach: The investigators completed data acquisition in the Human Exploration Research Analog (HERA) 14-day missions (16 crew in 1-week missions, and 16 crew in 2-week missions total). They also completed data acquisition in six Hawaii Space Exploration Analog and Simulation (HI-SEAS) crewmembers in an 8-month mission. In addition, they collected Cognition data at three Antarctic research stations along with 13 control subjects at the German Space Agency to compare changes over mission-duration. Lastly, the investigators completed inflight data collection on seven astronauts. Two of them participated in the 12-month mission.
results: The findings support the feasibility of Cognition administration in astronauts and astronaut surrogate populations, on both the Windows and iPad platform, and in space analog environments. Participant feedback provided during debriefs (N>60) provided helpful insights for current and future improvements of the battery. Cognition is currently deployed in several key studies funded by NSBRI, NASA, and European Space Agency (ESA), and it was selected as a core component in the project to develop a standardized behavioral measures toolkit (BCM) for space flight operations, demonstrating the need for and the success of the Cognition battery.

title: Dynamic Team Role Allocation in Long Duration, Exploration Missions: Identification of Roles, Triggers, and Measurement Tools
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Long-duration, exploration missions present a unique environment characterized by many stressors (e.g., social isolation, danger, confinement, interpersonal dynamics, periods of over/under stimulation), with little ability to escape. Research has found that within such environments interpersonal dynamics occupy a key role in effective functioning. While the last few years has witnessed an increase in research examining the composition requirements of high performance teams, little work has examined these issues in light of teams embedded in long-duration, exploration missions. The investigators sought to determine the following with regard to long-duration, exploration missions: Key social and team technical (task) roles which influence team function. Behavioral and communicative markers which can be used to assess the degree to which key identified social and team technical roles are being fulfilled. Contextual aspects that trigger a need for the dynamic shift of social roles. Optimal combinations (i.e., profiles, algorithms) of social roles for the maintenance and regulation of team functions. Markers that can be used to select for those most likely to fit social profiles and how these profiles change across the duration of the mission (i.e., the team’s life cycle) In determining these factors, the investigators sought to provide a series of scientifically-grounded and experimentally validated taxonomies, guidelines, and measurement tools for team selection/composition. In exploring these questions, the investigators took a multi-pronged
approach: consisting of analysis of retrospective data (e.g., astronaut diaries, historical accounts of teams operating in isolated and confined environments, astronaut interviews), scientific literatures on group dynamics, personality, team roles, stress, and diversity, interviews, and experimentation in NASA analogs. APPROACH: With respect to analog environments, data was collected within the Human Exploration Research Analog (Campaigns 2-4) and at two NSF research stations in the Antarctic during the Winter-Over 2018 season. Additional data was gained through interviews with subject matter experts and through the application of historiometry to archived information.  Participants were asked to complete several types of questionnaires: Prior to the start of the mission, participants were administered individual difference measures, such as a demographic survey, personality measures, and measures of collective orientation. During the mission, participants completed the following: Role questionnaire which assessed the task and social roles present during the prior mission segment. Measures which assessed teamwork quality, team satisfaction, and team effectiveness. Journal protocol which prompted them to recount key tasks, as well as describe interactions and situation so that key roles and triggers could be extracted. A single semi-structured interview conducted over the phone which was no longer than an hour. In addition, investigators collected audio and video recordings in order to access communication logs from points where key triggers and role shifts occur (approximately 30 minutes prior to 30 minutes afterward). This allowed them to establish a situational baseline as well as information about what occurs after the role shift. At the end of the mission, participants completed a survey that examined the task and social roles that occurred throughout the mission. At the end of the mission, participants completed a survey that examined the task and social roles that occurred throughout the missions.
results: Regarding the nature of team roles, evidence was found for the dynamic nature of team roles and the fact that within the context of spaceflight team roles are most often shared or distributed throughout the team. Results indicated not only a specific team role often shared amongst members of the crew, but correspondingly that crew members often engaged in multiple roles throughout the course of the mission. With respect to the dynamic nature, results also indicated the way contextual factors may impact the appearance and functionality of task and social roles (as a set) as well as specific roles. Contextual factors that were found to differentially relate to the enactment of roles included temporal factors, workload variations, sleep deprivation, boredom and isolation. Emerging evidence for the increased importance of social roles as mission duration increases and the potential that failures in social roles may remain hidden and take longer to notice than task roles. Results also began to speak to the notion of person-role fit within this context as is seen in the broader organizational literature on roles but has rarely been examined with relation to informal team roles nor within the context of long duration spaceflight. The results also suggest that personality may predispose a crew member to occupy roles and that there is systematic variance between personality and team role dimensions and frequency of role enactment. However, results from the operational interviews and data collected within the analog that illustrates differential relationships between personality and role enactment over time also speak to moderators on the person-role fit relationship. Two potential new measures were created, team role measure and TRIAD (Tracking Roles in and Across Domains). More specifically, based on all the evidence gathered throughout the project, a refined team role taxonomy was created which had behavioral markers expected to be indicative of each role. The TRIAD measure produces a different view on team roles as it does not examine roles in terms of the types of team-directed behaviors that occur but in terms of a set of underlying dimensions that have been argued to cut across all roles in varying degrees. As the measures were created towards the end of the project they still require further validation and research.

title: Wearable Biosensor Monitor to Support Autonomous Crew Health and Readiness to Perform
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: The purpose of this technology demonstration was to evaluate the Astroskin system with crews during flight analog studies and obtain data that will support decisions for transitioning the system to operational use during flight. Additionally, evaluation during a Human Exploration Research Analog (HERA) campaign provided a unique opportunity to demonstrate operational feasibility including long-term crew health monitoring capabilities, during exercise protocols as a measure of crew fitness, system usability and crew comfort, and Bluetooth communication in this environment. Nine men and seven women, ages ranging from 30 and 52, participated in this study. This study had the following specific aims: Evaluate comfort, usability and performance of the Astroskin system on ambulatory crews during 30-day HERA missions. Obtain baseline data used for further development of algorithms and tools that facilitate decision making for medical support. Demonstrate performance of the Bluetooth protocol for real-time transmission and data verification in an analog environment.
approach: The Astroskin system is a prototype wearable garment used for continuous physiological monitoring. The reusable, washable garment connects to a plug-in device which provides signal conditioning, data storage, wireless data transmission via Bluetooth radio, and battery power. Conductive fabric sensors are embedded in the garment which requires no adhesive connection to the skin as with traditional wet electrodes. Prior to the mission, chest and waist measurements were obtained from each participant to assure correct sizing of the garment. Garments were made available in small, medium, and large sizes and each participant was given two garments (a prime and back-up) for the mission. Data were stored on the Astroskin device. Data were streamed real-time via Bluetooth to a mobile device for viewing and verification by crew. After each recording session data were downloaded from the Astroskin device to crew laptops using software then made available to the investigators. The battery in the Astroskin device was recharged after each 24-hour monitoring session by connecting the device to a USB port on crew laptops. Participants completed a survey on their iPads after each day they wore the Astroskin. Personnel at the HERA facility provided crews with an open network port allowing them to connect to the survey website from within the habitat. Survey data were stored on a Qualtrics secure server and downloaded by the investigator after each mission day. The survey included three categories of questions: 10 questions on garment and headband comfort; 5 questions on interference or impact on performance of activities; and 12 questions pertaining to operations of the garment and plug-in device. The questions consisted of four fixed choice responses on an ordinal scale measuring levels of agreement/disagreement (e.g., very comfortable to very uncomfortable).
results: Investigators discovered that real-time data streaming via Bluetooth to an onboard mobile device significantly reduces battery life resulting in less than 24-hour recordings and that current software for real-time data streaming does not store data on the mobile device. In addition, the inability to view streaming data is a risk to studies in the analog environment and may result in signal loss or poor signal quality. The current prototype garment design is less than optimal for female crew which resulted in movement of ECG sensors and poorer signal quality. The ability to wash the garment is a potential issue for extended duration missions requiring cleaning options or stowage of multiple garments. Participants experienced significant discomfort after wearing the headband sensor when worn for 24 hour periods. Real-time data streaming requires higher capacity battery and/or lower power Bluetooth transmitter. The analog setting helped investigators to better understand some constraints and requirements related to the design and use of a biomonitoring system (e.g., interference from other equipment). Crew input from the surveys provided useful insights on how to improve the garment design.

title: Spaceflight Habitability Acceptability Questionnaire (SHAQ) Development and Validation
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: The primary objective of this study was to develop and validate a Space Flight Habitability and Acceptability Questionnaire (SHAQ), to assess the behavioral health and performance impacts of volume, layout, and other design features of vehicles and habitats for long-duration exploration missions and other operational environments. A secondary objective was to characterize the behavioral health and performance risks associated with reduced volume and the lack of individual crew quarters in missions of shorter duration (up to 45 days). SHAQ responses served as the primary outcome metric to study the behavioral health and performance effects of habitat area layouts. This study had the following specific aims: Empirically assess the initial sensitivity, construct validity, divergent validity, and concurrent validity of SHAQ over eight 45-day Human Exploration Research Analog (HERA) missions. Refine SHAQ based on the
approach: Investigators evaluated the quantitative responses to SHAQ as the primary measure. For concurrent validity, habitability-related items from the System Usability Scale (SUS) were administered during SHAQ sessions. Construct and divergent validity was assessed through measures of individual and team behavioral health and performance from complementary HERA investigations such as BHP Standard Measures in HERA. Operational acceptability was assessed during post-mission debrief interviews. Using a within-subjects repeated-measures design, the researchers collected SHAQ data from HERA 16 crewmembers in reference to the Sleep/Bedroom, Hygiene/Bathroom, Work/Office/Workshop, and Food Preparation/Kitchen/Galley habitat areas in the HERA operational environment, private hotel rooms, and individual home habitats.
results: of the HERA validation study. Draft a NASA Technical Report and/or manuscript for publication that (a) provides the results of SHAQ research and development efforts and (b) offers habitability recommendations for future deep space exploration missions. Author a SHAQ User Guide for public dissemination providing details on administration, scoring, and data management and interpretation. APPROACH: Investigators evaluated the quantitative responses to SHAQ as the primary measure. For concurrent validity, habitability-related items from the System Usability Scale (SUS) were administered during SHAQ sessions. Construct and divergent validity was assessed through measures of individual and team behavioral health and performance from complementary HERA investigations such as BHP Standard Measures in HERA. Operational acceptability was assessed during post-mission debrief interviews. Using a within-subjects repeated-measures design, the researchers collected SHAQ data from HERA 16 crewmembers in reference to the Sleep/Bedroom, Hygiene/Bathroom, Work/Office/Workshop, and Food Preparation/Kitchen/Galley habitat areas in the HERA operational environment, private hotel rooms, and individual home habitats. RESULTS: SHAQ has high construct validity, internal consistency and reliability, concurrent validity, and discriminant validity (e.g., significantly higher facilitation of group activities in HERA Work/Office/Workshop and Food Preparation/Kitchen/Galley areas versus. Hygiene/Bathroom and Sleep/Bedroom areas; significantly lower ratings of privacy, comfort, and convenience in HERA versus. hotel). The resulting data and validated SHAQ instrument can be used to inform recommendations and thresholds on habitat size, layout, and design options to support individual and team behavioral health and performance in operational environments.

title: Asynchronous Techniques for the Delivery of Empirically Supported Psychotherapies
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Astronauts are exposed to extreme environments and behavioral health risks during space missions. These stressors may place astronauts at elevated risk for behavioral health consequences including delirium, adjustment disorders, asthenia, and mood and anxiety problems, especially during long-duration missions. An expected barrier to delivering treatment to astronauts during long-duration missions is the lag in real-time communication between astronauts and mental health specialists on Earth. Therefore, the objective of this study was to identify technologies that will best facilitate the use of psychotherapeutic techniques when real-time communication is not possible.
approach: Phase I involved systematic reviews of the existing literature on (a) psychotherapy techniques currently and historically used on space missions and; (b) existing technologies (e.g., video diaries, virtual reality immersion) with the potential for use in the asynchronous delivery of psychotherapuetic techniques to astronauts. Phase II used the knowledge gained from Phase I to inform the design of a three-arm randomized clinical trial aimed at evaluating the feasibility, acceptability, and efficacy of the most promising technologies, alone and in combination, for asynchronous delivery of empirically supported psychotherapeutic skills. Products of this study included best practice guidelines for asynchronous delivery of empirically supported psychotherapuetic techniques during long-duration space missions. A total of 56 “astronaut-like” participants experiencing elevated psychological distress were randomly assigned to one of the three treatment conditions. Protocols were updated to allow for remote recruitment. An additional 89 participants were enrolled remotely from varying Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) universities and science laboratories. In total, 145 participants were enrolled to the randomized clinical trial (RCT) out of 300 individuals screened. Upon finishing the 7-week treatment, participants completed a post-treatment assessment and an exit interview over the phone. A 1-month follow-up assessment was also administered to participants
results: All survey data was collected via Qualtrics and exported to SPSS for analysis. An excel codebook was created to describe the contents, structure, and layout of the final data base. Main study analyses indicated that there were significant reductions in depression, anxiety, and stress, and improvements in work, life and social functioning from baseline to 1-week post treatment. These findings were apparent in all treatment conditions. There were no time by group treatment effects. There were also no differences across conditions regarding level of support provided, confidence in the program, level of comfort (e.g., sharing personal information, thoughts and feelings), and level of skill. There was a significant group difference in the number of logins into the MyCompass program with participants in the delayed video support condition logging in more than those in the MyCompass only and the delayed-text support conditions.

title: Automation in Procedures: Guidelines for Allocating Tasks for Performance
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: As crewed missions move deeper into space and communication latency increases, strategies for carrying out tasks must shift. Astronauts will be unable to depend on real-time support from flight controllers; controllers will not be able to perform procedures in the same way they do for the International Space Station (ISS), nor to advise on changed applicability of procedures in real-time. This change threatens to increase astronaut workload, decrease efficiency, and increase the risk of suboptimal task execution. Automation is an important resource for adapting to this altered environment. To help rather than harm, however, automation must be effectively integrated with the humans it supports. This research aimed to: 1) identify and refine candidate strategies for allocating tasks to automation and the factors when guidelines apply, 2) define effectiveness measures for these task allocation strategies, 3) conduct empirical assessment of the effectiveness of human-automation integration(HAI) based on the proposed allocation strategies, and 4) integrate findings as proposed task allocation strategies with automation. The
approach: to automation investigates the use of procedures as the basis of automation. By using a human-oriented procedure to organize automation, automation is designed to be more comprehensible to operators. For procedure automation, the actions in a procedure are enabled for automatic execution when instrumentation is available to perform the action. The degree of automation can be varied by changing which actions are designated for automatic execution. Strategies for determining which steps should be automated range from pre-defined allocations to flexible adjustment while the procedure is being executed. APPROACH: Ground TRACLabs and its partners from NASA and San Jose State University evaluated human performance for different task allocation strategies for procedure automation and used the
results: to articulate a set of allocation strategies. In addition, they defined operational scenarios for the evaluation, including a set of multi-step procedures and simulation that works with these procedures, provided procedure automation software for executing these procedures on the simulation, and performed ground-based human subject testing where subjects used the procedure automation to perform the tasks. The investigators selected the task allocation strategies for evaluation that included both predefined and flexible allocation of tasks and measured and analyzed human and automation performance for each of these strategies under both nominal and off-nominal circumstances. NASA’s Human Exploration Research Analog (HERA) A study was completed in the HERA facility during Campaign 2 evaluating PRIDE electronic procedure software. Sixteen subjects participated, four per mission. Each subject was trained for two hours prior to the two-week mission, then performed seven 1-hour sessions during the mission. Investigators embedded two study-designs within the larger seven-session activities. The Step-List Study tested the hypothesis that performance using procedures with actions grouped into functional units of work called steps (Step Format) would be better than using procedures without this grouping (List Format). The Problem-Solving Study investigated 1) the effects of repetition on problem solving, 2) the effects of a secondary manual task done in conjunction with the primary habitat task where problem occurs, and 3) the effects of encouragement to plan in advance on subsequent execution. Several exploratory tasks were distributed over the mission as well, including the Automation-Manual Investigation comparing human performance with an electronic procedure to the same procedure done using as much automation as possible. RESULTS: Ground Investigators analyzed data comparing manual execution of the new procedure system (PRIDE Interface) to a system analogous to procedures for ISS (Legacy Interface). They assessed whether manual performance with PRIDE would be as good as or better than with the legacy system. This lays the foundation for integrating automated execution into the flow of procedures designed for humans. They found speed and accuracy of manual procedure execution was better using the PRIDE interface over Legacy interface. When using the PRIDE interface, less than three percent of procedures had errors. For Legacy Interface, 33 percent of procedures had errors. Using PRIDE interface took less time than Legacy interface for all trials. Using the original PRIDE interface it was hard to predict what can be automated, what should be automated, and the consequences of attempting to automate elements that cannot or should not be automated. Methods to identify what cannot or should not be automated were an important direction for development. Support for constructing and checking an advance automation plan also was identified as valuable. Automation plans may be more complex than was easily supported by the original approach of automating between the focus bar and a breakpoint. Users may find it useful to specify spans of procedure lines to automate. Since steps are a central unit of work in procedures, supporting step-level automation control may be valuable. HERA HERA Step-List Study: Investigators found significant effects of format on both markup errors and mode-execution errors given a correct markup. This suggests the Step Format made it somewhat easier to assign execution mode (Manual or Automated) and execute from those assignments; there was no influence of Format on time measures. These results suggest that the Step format reduces errors in setting function allocation relative to List format and they merit further investigation. HERA Problem Solving Study: Behavior across users and days for the HERA experiment is both less successful in accomplishing the task-specified goals and more variable in the strategies adopted, than in the earlier study of problem-solving behavior. The most striking result is the degree of variation in strategy and outcome across this user group. Some users were successful in using electronic procedure software to recover from an unexpected situation where the procedure could not be executed directly and normally. Other users were not, and their difficulties included an assumption that automation would prevent any harmful action, reluctance to do anything not directly specified in their daily tasks, and uncertainty about what might be causing the specific value or its importance. There are many possible contributors to the reduced likelihood of accomplishing the task goal in HERA over that in the ground study. The task was structurally more complexly in HERA, because the user needed to identify and execute the recovery procedures for two habitat systems instead of one. Additionally, the absence of experimenter available for the ground study, and differences in training may have increased the difficulty of the problem-solving tasks in HERA. HERA Automation-Manual Investigation: Error analyses suggest that the mode differences (manual versus automated), between two low error rates, would be expected again in similar conditions. Thus executing with maximal automation may reduce errors relative to manual execution. Executing procedures with maximal automation may also reduce execution timing relative to executing the same procedures by manual alone. Small reductions in execution timing with automation were observed. Faster execution time with automation versus manual only modes should be investigated further.

title: Impact of Age, Genetics Variants and High LET Track Structure on Mammary Cancer Risk Estimates
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: A key NASA objective is to obtain quantitative data defining the risk of carcinogenesis following galactic cosmic ray (GCR) exposure. Current radiation quality factors used to determine cancer risk for space radiation do not provide the accuracy needed, and debate exists as to the relevance of the experimental studies they’re based upon. To formulate better risk estimates, key data is needed including how age, genetic susceptibility, and radiation quality affect carcinogenic potential in irradiation sensitive tissues. Towards this aim, investigators used a novel resource of a large collection of normal mammary epithelial cell strains, from women aged 16 to 80, including many in the age of astronauts, to address these important questions. They obtained quantitative data regarding radiation quality effects; ROS and DNA damage signaling, radiation-induced centrosome defects, and enrichment of stem cell populations using this cohort of strains from various aged individuals. In addition, they also investigated genetic susceptibility, including how loss of p16 expression, a sporadic event in individual cells of normal women in vivo and often observed in breast tumors, affects radiation quality effects and centrosome aberration frequency. Additionally they analyzed strains containing a BRCA1 or an ATM heterozygote genetic background, representing ~0.32 and ~1% of the normal population respectively, to determine how these genetic variants may make them more sensitive to high LET exposures. These studies provide critical data, which can be used to model how genetic susceptibility, age, and radiation quality interplay in defining the cancer risk of mammary cells to high LET radiation. The intent of this study was to determine how age, genetic susceptibility, and radiation quality modify the risk of high LET radiation-induced cancer. A cohort of mammary epithelial cell strains isolated from women of various age groups was used for these studies. Centrosome studies were performed using both a novel flow cytometry based assay, which provided a less subjective and more rapid way to define centrosome defects, as well as a standard microscopy-based method. Previous studies have revealed that changes in stem cell numbers are associated with an increased risk of cancer. Thus these studies assessed how radiation exposure and radiation quality affect stem cell populations, and whether age plays a role in the differences observed.
approach: Frozen vials of primary cells from eighteen individuals were obtained from an HMEC Bank at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (LBNL), generated by Dr. Martha Stampfer. Early passage (p=2) cells were expanded and used for subsequent experiments. Approximately seventy p4 vials were frozen down from each individual’s strain to have sufficient cell stocks to perform all experiments in the study. At Brookhaven National Laboratory (BNL) cells were exposed to three different doses (0, 0.05, and 0.5 Gy) of cesium, Si 93, and Ti 300 MeV/u in triplicate. Each strain was cultured in a T25 or a T75 flask at BNL, exposed to radiation, and then one day post exposure, cells were either sent back live to LBNL or trypsinized and frozen down for analysis after long term culture post radiation exposure. At LBNL, cells were plated at seeding densities to enable analysis at 85% confluency at different time points post radiation exposure (3, 9, and 14 days). These studies required extremely labor-intensive tissue culture, scoring for centrosome defects using microscopy, and flow cytometry determination of stem cell population changes. As a majority of studies to date typically defined genomic instability at early times post exposure (3 days) post exposure, investigators assessed centrosome aberrations at two later time points as well, weeks post exposure; these are time points likely more relevant and useful in modeling cancer risk. Their aim was to compare early effects at day three to the persistent effects of radiation exposure at longer times. They examined how centrosome levels are affected by the age of the individual the strain was derived from and the radiation quality of the exposure. They also defined the percentage of stem/progenitor cells in these various exposed populations at long times post exposure to define if radiation influences the growth of this population and how age may impact this endpoint. Furthermore, to gain additional information from this cohort of samples, the investigators also performed assays using a smaller subset to assess the phosphorylation profile of select proteins involved in DNA damage response and miRNA expression from various age groups following high or low LET radiation exposure.
results: Genetic instability was quantified based on levels of centrosome aberrations. This work sought to address whether age was an important defining characteristic in describing the effectiveness of the various radiation quality exposures to induce centrosome aberrations. These studies revealed a significant dose dependent increase in centrosome aberrations. In assessing age effects, the investigators noted that the percentage of cells with supernumerary centrosomes increases linearly with age particularly when exposed to Ti as compared to low LET. For Ti, the slopes for low dose (LD) and high dose (HD) appear parallel, with high dose exhibiting an approximately 2 fold increase in centrosome aberrations relative to low dose, for the same age. The baseline for centrosome aberrations in unexposed cells shows a slight increase with age that is not significant. In evaluating the distribution of the number of centrosomes in aberrant cells, results indicate a linear increase in the proportion of cells with >3 centrosomes with both low and high doses of Ti exposure. Time course studies with assessments at day 3, 9, and 12 post exposure revealed that, in comparison to day 3 and day 9, there is a significant age dependent linear increase in the frequency of centrosome aberration at day 12. Interestingly, the fraction of cells exhibiting aberrant pATF2 foci post Ti exposure at Day12 decreased with increasing age, suggesting that the pattern of repair signaling is opposite of what is seen with centrosome aberrations. In summary, this work suggests both age and radiation quality affects the levels of radiation induced-genomic instability. No datasets exist for the study. A final report was archived.

title: The Contribution of Delta Rays to the Chromosome Aberration Dose Response in Human Cells Irradiated with HZE Particles of Different Energy but the Same LET
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Highly energetic heavy ions (HZE), of the type found in galactic cosmic rays, deposit energy in the form of ionizations along the tracks they take as they travel through a cell. These ionizations are tightly spaced along these tracks and this spacing makes them highly damaging to cellular structures. Some of the particles energy is also imparted to electrons (delta rays) which can travel great distances and produce damage, albeit less severe, in cells far removed from the original particle track. The ranges of these electrons are proportional to the energy of the original HZE particle. While these delta rays by themselves are not likely to produce much in the way of measurable damage, investigators have evidence that these electrons can add damage to that forming along independent HZE particle tracks that will eventually be expressed in the form of chromosome exchanges of greater complexity. Chromosome exchanges
approach: Investigators irradiated human skin cells with low and high energy beams matching linear energy transfer (LET), energy deposited per unit track length and fluences so that the only variable will be particle energy.
