A dose response curve for chromosome exchanges irradiated with low particle fluences was constructed. At the same time they looked for breaks that fail to rejoin. One experiment was conducted at a low dose rate which prevented damage from delta rays from being added to chromosome exchanges forming along primary particle tracks by spreading damage formation out in time and allowing some breaks to be repaired or exchanges to be completely formed before other breaks occurring later can be added to them. Investigators also grew populations from single surviving cells allowing them to measure the transmissibility of chromosome exchanges a number of cell generations removed from the irradiation. Chromosome aberrations are tightly linked to cancer development. With this study they hoped to gain a better understanding of the processes underlying chromosome exchange formation following irradiation with HZE particles similar to those astronauts might encounter in space. Investigators aimed to determine the shape of the exchange dose response curve for these particles at low doses and at low dose rate, processes involving the mis-repair of radiation induced damage that could lead to carcinogenesis. At the same time they looked at terminal deletions and incomplete exchanges
results: when radiation breaks a chromosome by severing the DNA of which it is composed. The cell has means to repair the chromosome and can splice the DNA together. On some occasions, if one chromosome break is close to another break, the cell might make a mistake and join the broken ends to inappropriate partners. Two or more breaks can be involved in the process; the greater the number of breaks, the more complicated the resulting chromosome exchange will be. Investigators plan to test the hypothesis that these exchange complexity increases will be related to the primary particle energy and resultant maximum delta ray range. Higher particle energies will result in longer delta ray maximum ranges allowing more primary particle tracks to be close enough to irradiate a cell with delta electrons for any specific fluence (particle tracks per unit area; equivalent to dose). APPROACH: Investigators irradiated human skin cells with low and high energy beams matching linear energy transfer (LET), energy deposited per unit track length and fluences so that the only variable will be particle energy. A dose response curve for chromosome exchanges irradiated with low particle fluences was constructed. At the same time they looked for breaks that fail to rejoin. One experiment was conducted at a low dose rate which prevented damage from delta rays from being added to chromosome exchanges forming along primary particle tracks by spreading damage formation out in time and allowing some breaks to be repaired or exchanges to be completely formed before other breaks occurring later can be added to them. Investigators also grew populations from single surviving cells allowing them to measure the transmissibility of chromosome exchanges a number of cell generations removed from the irradiation. Chromosome aberrations are tightly linked to cancer development. With this study they hoped to gain a better understanding of the processes underlying chromosome exchange formation following irradiation with HZE particles similar to those astronauts might encounter in space. Investigators aimed to determine the shape of the exchange dose response curve for these particles at low doses and at low dose rate, processes involving the mis-repair of radiation induced damage that could lead to carcinogenesis. At the same time they looked at terminal deletions and incomplete exchanges resulting from the cell’s failure to repair damage. These lesions are likely to kill the cell and eliminate it from a population that might develop into cancer. Finally, they looked for exchanges found only in a fraction of the cells making up a clonal population indicating genomic instability, the process which drives carcinogenesis. RESULTS: For curvature to be observed in the dose response, the delta rays from one primary particle would have to produce chromosome breaks that were close enough to be involved in an exchange with other breaks produced by a separate and independent primary particle, a process termed track interaction. The investigators believed that the range of the delta rays would be of utmost importance in this process. As each of the different particle beams deposits the same amount of energy as it travels through the cell, those with shorter tracks deposit more energy along those tracks. Therefore, the lower energy particles produce a more concentrated distribution of energy induced damage closer to the primary particle track (path it takes through the cell), while the higher energy ions spread this same amount of damage over a longer distance. While the delta rays travel longer distances and can potentially encounter more independent tracks the concentration of that damage is less making it a more remote chance that a track interaction event could occur. The calcium ion beam is taken to represent an optimal energy where the delta rays have sufficiently long range to pass near independent tracks and produce damage with adequate density to allow track interaction events to occur with measurable frequency. No datasets exist for this study. A final report was archived.

title: Epigenetic Effects of Radiation on Epithelial Cell Self-renewal
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Aberrant self-renewal is a fundamental property of cancer cells that can be conferred by non-mutational (epigenetic) means. Early events in radiation-induced carcinogenesis must either cause the expansion of pre-existing cells with extensive self-renewal potential or the acquisition of extensive self-renewal potential by cells that have repressed it. A current weakness in cancer risk assessment models is the lack of consideration of epigenetic factors that influence malignant transformation. Recent data indicate that radiation can promote changes in the epigenetic properties of cultured human cell populations and intact rodent organs. Using a three-dimensional cell culture system that supports tissue-like behavior of human breast cells, investigators aimed to: 1) determine the effects of ionization density and dose on the frequency of self-renewal versus differentiation, 2) identify biochemical pathways that show persistent changes as functions of ionization density and dose, and 3) use genetic manipulations to test the mechanistic involvement of discrete pathway components in persistent radiation quality effects. These experimental studies employed new assays to improve the mechanistic understanding of radiation quality effects on the gain of aberrant self-renewal capacity and loss of responsiveness to differentiation signals - two related cancer development processes. The intent of this study was to develop a breast tissue-specific risk model of major processes in radiation carcinogenesis. Enhanced self-renewal and loss of differentiation are important surrogate endpoints that can be used directly in estimates of cancer risk and in reducing the uncertainties in predicting radiation quality effects.
approach: To avoid selection bias associated with expansion in adherent cultures the investigators performed irradiation experiments using thawed primary epithelial cell-enriched human breast tissue fragments (organoids) in suspension. Their general scheme involved the following steps: 1) overnight incubation of thawed organoids in serum-free medium, 2) acute irradiation, 3) overnight recovery, 4) dissociation to single cells, and 5) growth and differentiation assays.
results: In initial experiments, investigators detected dose-dependent increases in the percentages of side-population (SP) cells present after irradiation with up to 5 Gy of X-rays. SP cells identified using this technique are those cells that do not retain the DNA-binding dye, Hoechst 33342, usually because they express high levels of the ATP-binding Cassette Transporter ABCG2 that actively pumps out the Hoechst dye. This assay is one of the oldest and most trusted techniques for identifying and sorting stem and early progenitor cells in a variety of tissues and species. During the spring 2011 run (NSRL11A), organoid aliquots from two specimens were exposed to 50 and 100 cGy doses of gamma rays, as well as 25 and 50 cGy doses of Si and Fe. After overnight recovery, the control and irradiated samples were dissociated to single cells, and aliquots shipped back to Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (LBNL) for SP assays. Changes in proportions of SP cells were noted, but no consistent pattern emerged. Because of uncertainties inherent in the shipment of live cells cross-country for analysis, this assay was abandoned in favor of assays that could be performed onsite at Brookhaven National Laboratory (BNL), or after fixation. The first such assay involved staining and sorting for c-kit, a cell surface marker that others have shown to be highly expressed by luminal estrogen receptor negative progenitors in both mouse and human mammary glands. Investigators found that approximately one percent of the cells within unirradiated organoids expressed c-kit, and that the level was fairly constant in irradiated samples, with the exception of one set of samples irradiated with the highest dose (0.5 Gy) of Fe ions, where the percentage of c-kit(+) cells was significantly decreased. Beginning with the fall 2011 run (NSRL11C), investigators examined the effects of radiation on a second set of cell surface markers, CD44 and CD24. The fraction of CD44hi/CD24Lo cells has proven useful for distinguishing stem-like cells in both malignant and non-malignant human breast tissues. To evaluate the possibility that the trypsinization procedure itself would alter the relative abundance of CD44hi /CD24Lo cells, investigators subjected aliquots of the same organoid preparation to trypsin for differing amounts of time. The results demonstrated that trypsinization for periods between 5 and 20 minutes did not lead to differences in the fractions of CD44hi/CD24Lo cells, confirming that the dissociation procedure itself was not a selective influence. Results obtained with organoids from several individuals indicated that the baseline fraction of cells with this phenotype was relatively stable for each specimen, but ranged between 0.5 and 5% among specimens. During the fall 2011 run (NSRL11C), organoid aliquots from two specimens were exposed to 50 and 100 cGy of gamma rays, 25 and 50 cGy doses of Si as well as 10 and 25 cGy doses of Fe. The results indicated that, at the low to moderate doses of radiation employed, no significant changes in the fractions of CD44hi/CD24Lo cells were detectable 24 hours after irradiation, regardless of ion or charge density. To assess the differentiation potential of primary human mammary epithelial cells (HMECs) derived from control or irradiated organoids, 24 hours after irradiation the organoids were dissociated with trypsin to single cells. The isolated cells were then incubated at clonal densities in adherent cultures for seven days before fixation and staining with specific antibodies for keratins 14 (basal marker) and/or 19 (luminal marker). In preliminary experiments, when irradiated with 1 Gy of X-rays, the percentages of mixed colonies containing both luminal and basal cells were significantly higher for one specimen and marginally higher for another specimen, than for corresponding unirradiated controls. However, during the fall 2011 run (NSRL11C), when organoid aliquots from different specimens were exposed to the ions and doses indicated above, the specimens did not show statistically significant differences in the percentages of mixed colonies generated from unirradiated versus irradiated organoids. Subsequent exposure of organoids from one of these latter specimens to 1 Gy of X-rays at LBNL also did not yield statistically significant differences in the percentages of mixed colonies. The variability observed was therefore likely to be attributable to heterogeneity among the specimens themselves, rather than to beam characteristics or uncontrolled technical issues. During the fall 2011 run, investigators also assessed the overall colony-forming efficiency of individual cells from a single specimen (N158) that were irradiated as organoids, maintained as organoids for 24 hours post-irradiation, and dissociated to permit single cells to form colonies. Organoids from the same individual were exposed to gamma rays or 1 GeV/amu Fe ions. The results demonstrated that graded low doses of gamma rays do not elicit measurable toxicity in this standard assay, suggesting that when left intact, the local physical environment exerts a protective effect on potential clonogens for the sparsely ionizing reference radiation. In contrast, exposure to graded low doses of 1 GeV/amu Fe ions does result in increasing cytotoxicity, despite the integrity of the local physical environment. Beginning with the spring 2012 run (NSRL12A), investigators examined the effects of radiation on another set of cell surface markers, MUC1 and Thy1 that has proven useful for distinguishing different types of colony-forming cells (CFCs) in non-malignant human breast tissues. These CFCs share expression of EPCAM and CD49f, but luminal-restricted CFCs express MUC1, while less differentiated bipotent CFCs express Thy1. Investigators determined, using specimens from several individuals, that the proportion of luminal-restricted CFCs increased, while that of bipotent CFCs decreased in organoids exposed to moderate levels of sparsely ionizing X-rays and gamma rays. However, this correlation was not observed for organoids exposed to approximately equitoxic doses of Fe. The results suggested possible qualitative differences in the epigenetic responses of progenitor cells in intact glandular structures to the effects of sparsely and densely ionizing radiation. However, this distinction did not hold up in experiments performed with additional specimens during the fall 2012 run (NSRL12C). Over the course of three years, investigators conducted a variety of differentiation and self-renewal assays with primary human organoid preparations exposed to sparsely and densely ionizing radiation. While radiation-associated changes were observed in some cases, no definitive trends were documented. Investigators speculate that radiation-induced changes may have been affected by pre-existing inter- and intra-individual cellular heterogeneity in the organoid preparations. This heterogeneity may have had technical causes such as differences in preparation or handling of specimens, and/or it may represent true biological variation (e.g., differences in position within the originating tissue or genetic variability among specimen donors).

title: Creating a Taxonomy of Variables Affecting Cognitive Aid Design via an Investigation of Hybrid Aids
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Crewmembers on the International Space Station (ISS), similar to operators from other industries, complain about using current checklist-like procedures to complete tasks. Issues include procedures having too much or too little detail and poor usability. Due to obstacles, mistakes still occur and time to accomplish procedures is misestimated. NASA crew presently use static paper or electronic “cue cards” and procedures that provide guidance on both nominal and off-nominal tasks. Existing tools may not account for the lack of recent training, be optimized for the task, or the number of users, and/or be resilient to resumption after interruption. A more interactive cognitive aid can overcome the limitations of these cue cards and procedures by matching task, individual, team structure, and environment. Investigators designed a prototype of a hybrid aid for medical equipment maintenance tasks, while at the same time building a library of tools to create similar aids for other procedures. Second, they developed a taxonomy of cognitive aid design that considers the most important variables affecting performance with aids: user knowledge and experience, time pressure on performance, task criticality, and the number of operators expected to interact with the aid.
approach: Through a literature review, two controlled experiments, and a validation study, investigators examined the potential attributes of cognitive aids as they interact with task demands, time pressure, and number of team members. All studies were performed using a dual-task/interruption paradigm to better approximate the environments where cognitive aids are likely to be used. The investigators hypothesized that a taxonomy of cognitive aids for non-experts will need to contain a variety of information on aid design for number of operators, highly spatial versus highly verbal sub-tasks, highly visual versus highly auditory sub-tasks, and combinations thereof. A second product to come from these studies was a software program that supports the development of hybrid cognitive aids, the Hybrid Aid Toolkit (HAT). The HAT was developed in iterative design cycles, with portions of it being used to create testable aids in the experiments as features were implemented. Wizard-of-Oz techniques were used to fill in features not yet implemented. HAT development was complete before the validation study and usability data from that study allowed a last iteration before a software release at the end of the project.
results: Experiment 1 examined the effects of sensory resource conflict by manipulating which resources were demanded by the task (visual, auditory) and which were demanded by the aid (visual, auditory). The amount of resource conflict did not have as much of an effect as the sensory modality of the aid: the visual cognitive aid outperformed the auditory aid no matter what the modality of the task. A follow-up experiment allowed operators to interact with the aid by speaking, to make interaction with the auditory aid more natural. The results replicated the first experiment with the visual aid supporting the highest performance from operators. In the second experiment, operators were randomly assigned to use the aid alone or in a team of two. For part of the task, participants performed under time pressure and for part they experienced no time pressure (task sections were counterbalanced). Time pressure adversely affected the accuracy of single operators but not teams. Time to complete the task varied greatly. Dependence on the cognitive aid was high, but did not significantly vary according to the conditions. Participants who scored highly on conscientiousness ratings also scored their team more highly on teamwork ratings. Workload is increased by time pressured environments, even when operators can rely on others and even when a cognitive aid is in place. When designing an emergency aid, minimalistic design should be applied to not overload an already high cognitive load. Aid design should incorporate elements that promote elements of conscientiousness, which will require further research to ascertain. In the third experiment, an extreme age groups design was utilized to understand the best way to design an aid when spatial resources are low or reduced. Analysis showed age differences in performance, with younger adults making fewer initial errors, fewer changes, and completing the task faster than older adults. Spatial ability was analyzed separately and found to be related to performance measures: those who score better on spatial ability measures were more likely to make fewer errors and complete the task faster. In each of these experiments, the design of the HAT was iterated resulting in a final prototype used for the validation study with participants from Johnson Space Center. In the validation study, the type of task and aid was manipulated, where the HAT-created cognitive aid was compared to a traditional static aid. Operators performed better when given the HAT-created cognitive aid compared to the static aid on all tasks, however they rated it as less usable. Usability data showed that this was likely because participants perceived the static procedure to be more simple to interact with but that when using it, they were unaware the were committing errors. The results of this validation study established the effectiveness of the interactive cognitive aid and suggested design changes that were later iterated into the software. The literature review focused on cognitive aid research published in the last twenty years. General findings were that the literature on cognitive aids is vast and split across many domains, with mixed findings regarding aid effectiveness, proper design, and even nomenclature. In this review, we bring together these disparate findings and organize them at their most basic level: which cognitive processes do the aid need to support? Which processes do they support? Such processes included cognitive, perceptual, communication, and higher-order processes. Support of these processes could serve two goals: directly affecting the outcome of the task or indirectly affecting the outcome by making the cognitive aid more effective. This divided research studies on cognitive aids into those which introduced a direct support and those which introduced a usability change to the aid itself, which then affected the outcome of the task. Emergent themes for these articles are discussed, the empirical articles listed for future potential meta-analysis, and gaps in the literature summarized. Last, the review presented the design-related variables for cognitive aids in a design taxonomy, based on the empirical literature and provide a process for using the taxonomy in planning/designing new cognitive aids. These variables included task criticality, operator experience level, number of operators, and presence or absence of time pressure.

title: Gemini Medical Operations
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: With each passing year, radioisotope techniques become more important in biological research and clinical medicine. With the flight of Gemini IV, medical radioisotope investigations were extended, for the first time, into the realm of near space. The radioisotope studies that started with Gemini IV have subsequently proven to be an efficacious means of studying various aspects of man's response to this new environment. To date, the human radioisotope studies performed for the Gemini program have included plasma volumes, red cell masses, and red cell survivals. The objective of this experiment was to study various clinical aspects of astronauts in space, such as plasma volume, heart rate, workload, blood pressure, hematology, and orthostatic intolerance.
approach: All determinations of plasma volume and red cell mass were preceded by a 15-minute recumbent interval. Background blood samples were obtained prior to each radioisotope series to correct for any previously injected radioactivity. All plasma volume measurements were accomplished with iodinated human serum albumin. The erythrocyte survival half-times were measured from the disappearance of chromium-tagged red cells and were corrected for changes in red cell mass. A sample obtained 24 hours after the injection of the radioactive cells was used as the zero time for each survival determination. This prolonged mixing time was used to allow removal of cells inadvertently injured during the tagging procedure.
results: Plasma volume, red blood cell mass, and erythrocyte survival determinations were performed for the Gemini astronauts before and after Gemini orbital flights IV, V, and VII. Plasma volume decreases similar to those seen after bed rest and water immersion were found in Gemini IV and V. While each of these flights was affected by different stresses and the data accumulated are not as complete or extensive as desired, the results suggest that the plasma volume changes associated with the shorter flights may have been compensated for in the longer Gemini VII flight.

title: Mechanisms for Induction of Bystander Effects by High Energy Particles in Cells and Tissues
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: In space, astronauts are exposed to a complex and unique radiation environment composed of trapped proton and electron radiation, galactic cosmic rays (GCR; energetic protons and heavy charged ions, HZE), and solar particle events (SPE), primarily protons. Although these radiations can
approach: The methodology is embedded in the
results: in appreciable cumulative doses to astronauts during long-duration missions, the exposures occur at low fluences and fluence rates, such that particle traversals through individual cells in an astronaut’s body may be well separated in tissue location and time. Under such conditions, so-called non-targeted effects such as bystander responses may have increased significance. The radiation-induced bystander effect is the occurrence of biological responses in unirradiated cells near to or sharing medium with cells actually traversed by radiation. It is hypothesized that at the low fluences of protons and HZE particles to which astronauts are exposed in space, a significant fraction of the cellular changes may be due to bystander responses, in addition to the damages caused in cells directly traversed by ionizing particles or their associated delta rays. The specific aims for this study are: Test the hypothesis that bystander effects occur at particle fluences so low that only 1-2 % of cells in a culture dish are traversed by an energetic proton or HZE particle. Test the hypothesis that cells that have survived an initial traversal and sent a bystander signal, can again send a signal when traversed once again by a particle or can subsequently respond as bystanders to a hit in a neighboring cell by extending low fluence work to studies using repeated exposures of cells to low fluences and mixed (actually sequential) beams of more than one particle type. Test the hypothesis that non-nuclear damage-initiated, metabolically produced reactive oxygen species (ROS) in hit cells are involved in the early steps of bystander signaling. Chemical countermeasures to reduce the bystander responses based on removal of ROS or prevention of their formation will also be studied. Previous studies have indicated that ROS are at least partially involved in transmittal of the Fe ion-induced bystander signal from hit to unirradiated cells. Test the hypothesis that radiation-induced bystander signals can be sent between differing cell types, but the characteristics of the responses depend on the cell types and the types of radiation. APPROACH: The methodology is embedded in the results below. RESULTS: At very low iron ion (1 GeV/n) fluences, i.e., 2-50% of cells traversed by an ion, or very low proton (1 GeV) fluences, i.e., 2-200 protons/cell, there was increased damage in cells in both irradiated and bystander populations. That finding--that about 100-fold lower particle fluence is needed to produce DNA damage in irradiated or bystander populations with Fe ions than with protons of the same energy--suggests that linear energy transfer (LET) or particle track structure, including delta-rays, is a determinant of the minimum dose needed for the effect. Studies with 300 MeV/n Fe ions (higher LET) show a shift to even lower minimum particle fluence for induction of the effect, consistent with LET being important. Ongoing analysis of samples irradiated with silicon and carbon, of intermediate LET, appear to yield consistent data. The studies with mixed cell types (fibroblasts and keratinocytes) in 2D and with the same cells in a 3D model of epithelial tissue (aim 4) have been completed. The data in monolayers show that with either X-rays or protons (low LET radiations), there is a 1.5-2-fold increase in micronuclei (MN) formation in bystander fibroblasts or keratinocytes after either cell type is irradiated, but there is no significant increase in MN in bystander fibroblasts in co-culture with irradiated keratinocytes. In the 3D studies, the data in irradiated cells show that the fraction of fibroblasts with DNA damage when irradiated in the 3D constructs is significantly less (4-fold at the shortest time of 1 h) than in cells irradiated in 2D monolayers. With time after irradiation, the fraction of damaged cells decreases such that at 24 h it is back to background in cells in 3D, but remains elevated out to 72 h in cells in 2D. In contrast to the irradiated cells in 3D, the level of damage in the bystander portion of the 3D model is low at 1 h, but increases to a peak at 12 h after protons and a maximum at 24-48 h after Fe ion exposure. The data further show that bystander signals can travel considerable distances (mm) and that, although scavengers have no effect on DNA damage in irradiated cells in 3D, the level of DNA damage in bystander cells in 3D is reduced nearly to control, unirradiated, levels by scavenging hydrogen peroxide, superoxide and nitric oxide in the medium shared by the construct halves, findings similar to those in 2D. In studies to assess intercellular signaling between normal fibroblasts and tumor cells, this study has shown that there is no bystander signaling with a human chrondrosarcoma cell line (HTB94) irradiated with X-rays, protons or iron ions. However, irradiated HTB94 cells can send signals to bystander fibroblasts, to elicit DNA damage, although the tumor cells do not respond to signals from the fibroblasts.

title: Interactive Space Vehicle Design Tool with Virtual Reality
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Optimal space vehicle design is critical to maximize crew operational efficiency, comfort, and equipment storage. Traditionally, designers and engineers have utilized physical mock-ups early in their design process for task performance and layout evaluation, but high-fidelity mock ups can be costly and time consuming to produce and reconfigure. Therefore, many design decisions have been set in place by the time a high-fidelity mock-up is created, thus diminishing its usefulness. Engineering drawings allow early assessment of vehicle design, but do not allow experimental evaluation with a physical presence of people interacting with the system. Recent advancements in technology have enabled the use of digital designs to ‘virtually’ evaluate habitats in ways not possible with physical mock-ups, for example to explore the vehicle from a simulated microgravity perspective while in 1G. Due to the rapid advancement of technology, practical application of how these capabilities can best be used in the vehicle design process to minimize the potential for costly design errors is still evolving. The goal of this experiment was to evaluate the spectrum of visualization tools in their ability to facilitate rapid mock-up and flexible design of microgravity vehicles and habitats. To enable efficient and rapid mock-up of vehicle concepts, the spectrum of visualization tools can be used earlier in the design process to achieve improved system design. Investigators will define, characterize, and establish metrics by which these tools can be used, with focus applications in early-stage spacecraft habitat design. From the
approach: In this project, investigators characterized, evaluated and contrasted a spectrum of reality design tools: 1. Physical Reality (PR); 2. Augmented Reality (AR); 3) Hybrid Reality (HR); and 4. Virtual Reality (VR). This evaluation was directed toward the specific application of spacecraft vehicle and habitat design from the perspective of engineering, human factors, operations and habitability. The second phase of the study performed an experimental evaluation of these capabilities in the context of early-stage habitat design to validate the framework. Alternative realities are achieved by influencing human sensing Modalities. Three Modalities were investigated: Visual, Auditory, and Tactile. In this context, investigators include an individual’s perception of motion, orientation, and proprioception within the Tactile modality. Within each sensing Modality, sub-dimensions were identified comprising the technical elements by which the Modality is altered within XR environments. Some sub-dimensions lie along a continuum, while others are discrete technology choices the user may make. The technical requirements of a sub-dimension can be linked to the Spectrums outlined above. In this way, the framework provides a mapping between different sensing Modalities and the environmental aspects influenced by a given technology choice. The
results: of this initial definition phase, an experimental evaluation of the proposed methodologies will be performed. This study had the following specific aims: Create a virtual reality design tool for space vehicles and habitats. Evaluate tool effectiveness in a vehicle mock-up experiment. APPROACH: In this project, investigators characterized, evaluated and contrasted a spectrum of reality design tools: 1. Physical Reality (PR); 2. Augmented Reality (AR); 3) Hybrid Reality (HR); and 4. Virtual Reality (VR). This evaluation was directed toward the specific application of spacecraft vehicle and habitat design from the perspective of engineering, human factors, operations and habitability. The second phase of the study performed an experimental evaluation of these capabilities in the context of early-stage habitat design to validate the framework. Alternative realities are achieved by influencing human sensing Modalities. Three Modalities were investigated: Visual, Auditory, and Tactile. In this context, investigators include an individual’s perception of motion, orientation, and proprioception within the Tactile modality. Within each sensing Modality, sub-dimensions were identified comprising the technical elements by which the Modality is altered within XR environments. Some sub-dimensions lie along a continuum, while others are discrete technology choices the user may make. The technical requirements of a sub-dimension can be linked to the Spectrums outlined above. In this way, the framework provides a mapping between different sensing Modalities and the environmental aspects influenced by a given technology choice. The objective of this framework is to allow users to transition between Spectrums and Modalities more easily and to identify areas in which to focus development based on their specific needs. From the detailed framework, high-level guidelines were provided to assist stakeholders within spacecraft habitat design (SHD) in choosing an XR category to suit their evaluation objectives. The stakeholders identified were evaluators in Program Management, Human Systems Integration, Operations and Training, Engineering, and Manufacturing and Assembly. Information for the stakeholder groups on their evaluation needs was acquired by reviewing the evaluation criteria against which stakeholders perform SHD evaluations, from documentation provided by NASA personnel, and interviews with subject matter experts. These data were then aggregated into a series of tables incorporating the anticipated advantages, disadvantages, and applicable phases in the design process. A list of tools that can be used by evaluators within an XR classification was also compiled. These guidelines and tool lists should continue to be expanded and adapted as hardware and technology development continues, in order to ensure it remains contemporary. This research provides a functional set of practices that can be used to help SHD evaluators achieve their mission to reduce the risk of incompatible spacecraft habitat design. The investigators defined a framework that links theoretical Spectrums to technical requirements within a sensing Modality and define four XR Classification groups. They converted the detailed framework developed into a functional set of guidelines and potential practice cases for stakeholders in spacecraft habitat and design, with a focus on design evaluation. From these findings, they experimentally investigated the ability of subjects to perceive volume in spacecraft habitats across the XR spectrum. One of the most important aspects of SHD evaluation is to understand the spacecraft’s volume, layout, and its impact on the crew. It was noted across the literature, interviews, and NASA documents that virtual representations of interiors, while instructive, are not realistic enough to provide a true evaluation of volume considerations. This mismatch may be due to the 2D projection of a 3D space, the capacity of the human eye and brain to integrate information, or the lack of personal sense within a virtual volume when not visualized. To investigate this, investigators experimentally evaluated what scaling difference across volume representations were present in VR, HR, and AR as compared to PR. Further, they performed a side-by-side comparison of the four XR environments for volumetric evaluation purposes. Across the literature, comparisons of PR and VR are widely documented, particularly at early stages of design. The comparison of PR and VR with AR and HR, though, are less well documented. This was also reflected in the reduced familiarity our subject matter experts had with these technologies and how they could best be implemented in their SHD evaluations. Investigators performed direct performance comparisons across all four XR Classifications, in a manner similar to that has been done previously. The investigators characterized and defined the four categories of design tools and established a set of high-level guidelines from the literature for how each approach was typically used, to be documented as a table of advantages, disadvantages and comments. This characterization will include specific definitions of these categories, metrics by which to evaluate them, and system requirements. To the extent possible, investigators will also project into future technology development on the horizon from interaction with experts in academia, government and industry, such that this benchmark assessment is not limited to current state-of-the-art. RESULTS: Equal-fidelity mockups were made in each XR environment, depicting a single, common interior vehicle layout. Investigators detailed the steps taken to construct all four environments and highlighted the various advantages and limitations of each alternative reality approach. Moreover, a novel hybrid reality setup that includes intuitive interactions, realistic haptics, and a fully virtual audiovisual scene was implemented. Their experimental results indicate that VR is the most likely to produce results consistent with a real physical mock-up. Each of the metrics was internally consistent and many results were consistent even across experiments. There remain challenges merging physical and virtualized content, perhaps contributing to the poorer overall performance of HR and AR. These environments show promise, though, particularly as the state-of-the-art in XR technology advances. This research contributes to the understanding of alternative reality technologies and their application in all stages of spacecraft habitat design and evaluation. This research will assist in evaluating requirements and can be used to improve habitability, ergonomics and space allocation, and to meet engineering constraints. This research identifies how emerging and existing alternative reality technologies can be incorporated by SHD stakeholders across various phases of design evaluation to reduce the risk of incompatible spacecraft habitat environments.

title: Eye-Head Coordination During Target Acquisition
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: A number of investigators have assessed the role of vestibular-based subsystems both during and immediately following exposure to microgravity. While providing information specific to one or more sensorimotor subsystems there is little documentation of changes in the strategies used for coordination among subsystems or for those strategies supporting performance of natural, goal-directed behaviors. In particular, there may be several strategies selected for use during the process of adaptation to microgravity. These strategies may become more reliable for missions of increasing duration. Prime among these strategies are: (1) the reduced use of head movements during the early phases of the mission, (2) the reliance on either an internal coordinate system (intrinsic)or environmental coordinates (extrinsic) during different phases of space flight for spatial orientation, and (3) compensation for the changing role of proprioceptive information during flight. These strategies, we believe, can be evaluated using goal-directed head and eye coordination tasks. Therefore, the primary objective of this study was to investigate the emergence or alteration of goal-oriented strategies required to maintain effective gaze when the interactive sensorimotor systems required for this function have been modified following extended exposure to the stimulus rearrangement of space flight.
approach: For baseline data collection, all subjects sat in a chair facing a visual display which consisted of miniature LED targets in the shape of a cross. The LEDs were illuminated to create either a static or moving visual pattern. The following physiological measures were taken preflight and postflight: (1) Eye movements: monitored by electrodes placed vertically above and below the right eye, horizontally over the left and right temples, with a ground behind the left ear, and (2) Head movements: measured by a tri-axial rate sensor fixed to the head. All responses were collected on a Data Acquisition System which consisted of Macintosh computer, Data Acquisition box with Anti-aliasing filters, and custom acquisition and control software. The following measurements constituted the experiment: Predictable Target Acquisition (PTA): Used both head and eyes to acquire +/-20°, +/-30°, and +/-60° horizontal and +/-15°, +/-20° and +/-50° vertical targets in a predetermined sequence. Unpredictable Target Acquisition (UTA): Used both head and eyes to acquire +/-20°, +/-30°, and +/-60° horizontal and +/-15°, +/-20° and +/-50° vertical targets in a random sequence. Smooth Pursuit Tracking (SP): Moving eyes only or eyes /head together to follow a moving target. Target motion is sinusoidal using four frequencies (SP1=0.2 Hz, SP2=0.33 Hz, SP3=0.8 Hz, SP4=1.4 Hz) in both the horizontal or vertical planes, or ramp to an unpredictable displacement. NOTE: The ramp portion of smooth pursuit was never completed on any of the Mir 18/STS-71 crewmembers. Head Shakes (HS): Keeping eyes on center target, oscillate head in the horizontal or vertical plane in cadence with an auditory tone at 0.2, 0.33, and 2.0 Hz. Repeat with vision occluded. Memorized Head Rotations (MHR): View a sequence of target illuminations while head is stationary, then attempt to recreate the pattern by rotating the head to remembered target positions with vision occluded. A cruciform target arrangement was used to provide the visual stimulation for target acquisition, pursuit tracking,memorized head rotations, and sinusoidal head oscillations (as a spacecraft fixed target). The target arrangement, placed approximately 75 cm from the subject's retinal plane, was used to provide a variety of static, time optimal, and dynamic visual stimuli to the subject in both the horizontal and vertical planes. Each axis of the cross was approximately 1.25 m long and contained a line of 495 miniature LEDs with a spacing between LEDs of 2.54 mm. Illumination of the LEDs were under microprocessor control, and multiple LEDs could be illuminated at any given time. Software drivers were developed to enable concurrent or sequential illumination of “special” standard target positions in the horizontal (0°, ±20°, ±30°) and vertical (0°, ±15°, ±20°, ±30°) planes, as well as to present both sinusoidal and non-predictable,constant-velocity ramp-type target motion along either axis. The device was also equipped with the capability of controlling remote or eccentric LEDs beyond the effective ocular-motor range (EOM range). For these experiments at least one set of these targets was located at ±60° horizontal and ±50° vertical. Targets within the EOM range are defined as those that can be acquired with the eyes alone and do not require a head movement to foveate the target. This target device was planned to be positioned 75 cm in front of the subject, but provisions could be made to enable entering the subject-to-target distance so that the illuminated LED targets would actually represent true angular positions with respect to the subject, and the LED representing a given angular displacement would change if the subject-to-target distance changed. Head position measurements were calibrated by activating a low-power laser mounted at the browpiece of the head cap. Following adjustment of the laser to align with the 0° target (with head in the zero-position), visual feedback from the laser allowed the subject to accurately align the head with a given calibration target. Movements were made successively between the central target and each calibration target in both the horizontal and vertical planes. At least two trials to all targets were performed at the beginning of the experiment, and repeated if for any reason the head cap is disturbed or removed. Target Acquisition: Following eye and head calibration, the subject acquired targets with both head and eye movements using a time-optimal strategy (move the head and eyes together as quickly and as accurately as possible to acquire the target). Target acquisition was performed successively between the 0° target and each of the horizontal and vertical targets used for eye calibration as well as the eccentric targets intentionally located outside the EOM range (±60° horizontal; ±50° vertical), thereby forcing an appreciable head movement. Tests were performed using both predictable and unpredictable target sequences. In the predictable sequence all targets for a given displacement and plane were illuminated simultaneously, and the subject made gaze shifts using the time optimal strategy, maintaining fixation upon each target for a minimum of 2 seconds before returning to the center target. For these trials, the investigator quantified the dynamics of target acquisition to predictable, visible targets in terms of the relative contributions of eye and head to gaze as well as how these dynamic relationships change with respect to target amplitude and mission duration. Data from these trials were then compared with data previously collected on other astronaut subjects. For the unpredictable target acquisition trials, the targets were successively illuminated in a random sequence and the subject was paced through each target acquisition by the visual stimulus device. This task allowed characterization of latency changes in acquiring newly-visible targets. The timing between successive illuminations was randomized to prevent the subject from anticipating the onset of changes in target position. Each target was acquired at least two times for each type of acquisition stimulus per session. Pursuit Tracking Studies: The pursuit tracking studies were designed to measure the effectiveness of both smooth pursuit eye movements and combined eye-head tracking in acquiring and maintaining gaze on a moving target. All trials required crewmembers to track a small, smoothly moving target, first with just their eyes (smooth pursuit), and subsequently using eye movements in concert with active, self-generated head movements (combined eye-head tracking). By comparing
results: from preflight, inflight, and postflight testing, differences between the smooth pursuit and combined eye-head tracking responses to similar types of target motion helped further discriminate the loci of neural pathways that are affected by exposure to microgravity. Subjects were positioned 75 cm from and facing a display surface upon which the target was presented. In the initial set of trials, the target moved horizontally with respect to the subject; the trials were then repeated using vertical target motion. The stimulus involved predictable target motion. The target oscillated at 0.3 Hz with a peak deflection of ±30° horizontally or ±20° vertically. For each trial, tracking was performed for at least 6 cycles. The responses to the non-predictable stimuli helped identify operational impacts on the ability to visually acquire moving targets due the effects of exposure to microgravity. They also helped elucidate and quantify changes in the central processing mechanisms brought about by this exposure. The responses to the predictable stimuli helped extend understanding of the operational impacts of microgravity exposure by assessing the ability to maintain fixation on a moving target once acquired. Sinusoidal Head Oscillations (Head Shakes): To assess adaptive (and readaptive) changes in the active VOR during (and after) space flight, its gain and phase characteristics were measured in each subject using three frequencies: 0.2, 0.8, and 2.0 Hz. The VOR was characterized in this manner in both the vertical (pitch) and horizontal (yaw) planes, with the subject either fixating or imagining a far (75 cm) target. To perform this test, the subject was first positioned so that the wall-fixed target (cruciform target's center LED) was located at the center of his/her visual field. The subject then attempted to maintain visual fixation on the target while smoothly oscillating his/her head in the plane of interest in cadence with an audio tone that was sinusoidally modulated at the frequency of interest. The angular displacement of head oscillation was selected by the subject to maximize comfort. Following a collection of responses to a minimum of 10 cycles at each frequency, the subject's visual field was occluded by electronically activating a polymer dispersed liquid crystal (PDLC) goggle assembly (also known as an Electronic Light Occluding goggle [ELOG]) worn by the subject. Immediately upon occlusion of the visual field, the subject repeated the individual frequencies while attempting to maintain visual fixation on the remembered location of the target. The subject repeated this entire procedure in the each plane for each visual condition. Throughout the experimental period, the subject's head and eye movements were continuously measured using a specially designed angular rate sensor system and an EOG system, respectively. Gain and phase of the VOR were determined for each frequency of stimulation by comparing the eye movement velocity to the head movement velocity, and changes in these parameters were assessed as a function of inflight adaptation to microgravity and readaptation to 1-G. Special attention was paid to cross-axes head movements, and changes in head movement control. Memorized Head Rotations: Using a scheme similar to the memory-guided ocular saccade paradigm employed by two cosmonauts on the ARAGATZ mission, the crewmembers’ ability to recreate horizontal and vertical head rotations following the occlusion of vision was studied. For this task, the visual stimulus device successively illuminated a pseudorandom combination of 4-6 of the LED targets in either the horizontal or vertical plane for approximately 2 seconds each. With the aid of the headmounted laser (otherwise used for aligning the head with the targets during the head calibration trials), the subject rotated the head in a time-optimal way to successively align the laser spot with each illuminated target. After acquisition of the last illuminated target (at 0°), the headmounted laser was extinguished, vision was occluded using the ELOGs, and after a variable, prespecified time (5-30 sec) the subject was required to recreate the head rotation pattern as closely as possible without the aid of visual feedback. [Note: there was some concern with respect to calibrating head rotations when the targets were acquired with vision and laser feedback. In the event that preflight trials suggested that this task influenced the without-vision trials, the visually guided trials with laser were eliminated from the protocol]. Sixteen trials were performed per session in both the horizontal and vertical planes. Analysis involved determining the head position errors between the vision-available and vision-occluded parts of a trial, and efforts were made to correlate head rotation position errors with target displacement, time period following vision occlusion before the remembered response is performed, and mission duration. Spontaneous, Gaze, and Positional Nystagmus: Inflight spontaneous nystagmus was tested with the subject visually fixating on a spacecraft fixed target, imagining the same spacecraft fixed target with vision occluded, and then with eyes closed (for 20 seconds each). Gaze nystagmus, with vision occluded was evaluated following a change in eye position by requiring the subject to deviate the eyes within the orbit as far as possible to the right, left, up, and down for 20 seconds each followed by a return of the eye to the center gaze position for each deviated position. No attempt was made to evaluate positional nystagmus in flight. Pre/Postflight: Both spontaneous and gaze nystagmus were evaluated with the inflight procedures (substituting the spacecraft fixed target for a wall fixed target). Positional nystagmus tests consisted of eye movement recording for approximately 30 seconds. Verbal Responses: Following each experiment condition, crewmembers provided verbal quantitative descriptions of perceived self and/or visual surround motion or changes in orientation/position. Primarily, they were asked to specify distinct difference between the preflight, inflight, and postflight sensations, and specifically, to describe the perceived amplitude and rate of the rotational and/or translational components of self/surround motion. RESULTS: Six crewmembers from Mir 18, STS-71 and Mir 19 participated in this experiment. Three of four preflight data collection sessions were performed at L-120 (120 days before launch), L-45 and L-15. The fourth session at L-80 was cancelled. Data collected for one subject on L-15 was partial due to illness. Inflight measurements were not taken because of hardware failure. Postflight data was lost because the protocol collection sessions were reduced from 9 to 6 sessions. Because of these time constraints and protocol reductions, data can only be compared for Predictable Target Acquisition (PTA) and Smooth Pursuit 2 (SP2) tracking at 0.33 Hz. Findings strongly suggest that the effects seen on short duration missions (delayed target acquisition, reduced head velocity following flight, high gain in the visual vestibulo-ocular system, failure to suppress the VOR during eye/head target pursuit, etc.) are present following long duration missions. That is, long duration flights tend to produce long lasting effects. Recovery, particularly in the pursuit system was not observed in all crewmembers 64 days after flight.

title: Preflight and Postflight Parallel Swing Tests
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: An otolith is a structure in the inner ear, specifically in the vestibular labyrinth. They are sensitive to gravity and linear acceleration. The vestibular otolith receptors respond to linear motion and gravity. If motion cues from visual and skin receptors were reduced or eliminated, responses to roll and linear translation attributable primarily to the otolith receptors could be examined. The Miami University Parallel Swing and its associated restraint system made this examination possible. This investigation examined two types of responses associated with roll and linear translation stimulation: perceived self-motion path and eye movements. These responses were examined before and after orbital flight. Because the otoliths are gravity receptors, it was hypothesized that adaptation to the loss of stimulation due to gravity during flight would alter responses to which the otoliths contribute. This investigation assessed changes in responses associated with otolith receptor activity following prolonged space flight. The
approach: On STS-8, a subject performed head tilts (roll and pitch) and followed a self-motion reporting procedure. On STS-41B (a.k.a. STS-11), two subjects repeated the STS-8 protocol, and examined the hypothesis that the brain's reinterpretation of otolith information would affect eye movement reflexes. The STS-41B subjects were exposed to the same motion stimuli as on STS-8 and reported their self-motion in the same manner. In addition, their eye movements were recorded in the dark using an infrared-sensitive video camera. A second purpose of DSO 433 was to examine possible changes in linear self-motion detection thresholds following weightlessness. Ocular counterrolling during static head tilt was recorded preflight and immediately postflight.
results: led to the development of an otolith tilt translation reinterpretation hypothesis which, in conjunction with the sensory conflict hypothesis, provides a conceptual framework for comprehending space motion sickness. APPROACH: On STS-8, a subject performed head tilts (roll and pitch) and followed a self-motion reporting procedure. On STS-41B (a.k.a. STS-11), two subjects repeated the STS-8 protocol, and examined the hypothesis that the brain's reinterpretation of otolith information would affect eye movement reflexes. The STS-41B subjects were exposed to the same motion stimuli as on STS-8 and reported their self-motion in the same manner. In addition, their eye movements were recorded in the dark using an infrared-sensitive video camera. A second purpose of DSO 433 was to examine possible changes in linear self-motion detection thresholds following weightlessness. Ocular counterrolling during static head tilt was recorded preflight and immediately postflight. RESULTS: STS-8: This investigation obtained data from one subject. The results indicated that prolonged exposure to weightlessness resulted in reinterpretation by the brain of signals from the otolith organs. The subject was exposed to roll around the head (X axis) and linear translation along the head (Y axis). The subject reported self-motion perception following exposure to the two types of motion. Preflight, the subject's self-motion reports corresponded with the actual motion; roll was perceived as roll and translation as translation. Immediately postflight, the self-motion sensation associated with roll differed dramatically from that reported preflight. At R+2.5 hours, roll motion was perceived primarily as linear translation along the Y axis. At R+36 hours, self-motion sensations were approximately the same as those observed preflight. The STS-8 observations led to the following hypothesis: During prolonged weightlessness, the adaptive brain learns to interpret all signals from the otolith linear accelerometer as linear translation. In weightlessness, the otoliths do not produce a signal indicating head tilt (roll or pitch) because linear acceleration due to gravity is absent. Following return to earth, and before the brain re-adapts, the interpretation that all otolith signals indicate is that linear motion persists. However, the otoliths produce a signal during head tilt (roll) because gravity is present. Consequently, the observer reports that roll motion is perceived as linear translation plus a roll component due to the semicircular canals. Following re-adaptation to normal gravity, true perception of roll motion returns. STS-41B (a.k.a. STS-11): Preflight and postflight self-motion reports following roll and linear translation were nearly the same as those reported on STS-8. Eye movements recorded preflight indicated that the linear translation stimulus produced nearly pure horizontal translation of the eyeball, and that roll stimuli produced nearly pure ocular counterrolling (eye torsion). Immediately postflight, the eye movements differed dramatically from those seen preflight. For one subject, who was seen at R+70 minutes, both roll and linear motion stimulation produced horizontal translation of the eyeball. For the second subject, seen at R+2 hours, roll stimulation produced horizontal eye movements in combination with a small amount of torsion. Self-motion reports indicated that roll was perceived as a combination of linear translation and roll. The roll component of the perceptual report was probably due to semicircular canal stimulation. At R+2 days, both subjects' self-motion reports had returned to the preflight state. However, some horizontal eye movement was still present. By R+3 days, both perceptual reports and eye movement were approximately the same as preflight. In conclusion, the otolith reinterpretation hypothesis derived from STS-8 was supported by the results from STS-41B. The eye movement results were consistent with a hypothesis that the reinterpretation of the otolith signals occurs in the brain stem in the nuclei associated with vestibular-ocular reflexes (VOR). The results suggested ways in which an astronaut's performance might be disturbed during the immediate postflight period. The results imply that performance of tasks that require accurate perception of complex self-motion should be avoided. It was also suggested that SAS symptoms and orientation disturbances are related to the period in which the brain is learning to reinterpret the otolith signals in weightlessness. This suggestion is consistent with the reports indicating that head tilts, particularly in the pitch plane, are provocative. This suggestion can be evaluated by performing appropriate inflight observations and employing appropriate preflight countermeasures during future missions. A second purpose of DSO 433 was to examine possible changes in linear self-motion detection thresholds following weightlessness. The large threshold elevation reported for STS-8 was not seen with the STS-41B subjects. Results for ocular counterrolling during static head tilt are not available. DSO 433 was renamed to DSO 449 prior to the STS-51D flight, and additional subjects' data were obtained on DSO 449. Information archived for this experiment was provided by the William E.Thornton collection.

title: Frames of Reference and Internal Models
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: On Earth, information from the vestibular system is combined with information from gravity sensors in the joints, touch sensors in the skin, and visual information to coordinate body movements and maintain body stability. However, when space flight crews first experience weightlessness, there is an initial awkwardness in moving within the spacecraft. There is also disorientation because the signals coming from the vestibular system no longer correspond with visual and other sensory information sent to the brain. The Frames of Reference and Internal Models investigation was designed to enhance the understanding of how the central nervous system (CNS) interprets and integrates sensory data for the production of a coordinated motor response. During the act of catching a ball on Earth, the CNS estimates the trajectory of the ball, accurately taking into account its downward acceleration due to gravity. This could involve a real-time estimation of ball acceleration based on visual information, but more likely involves the use of a priori information about the effects of gravity on free-falling objects. This in turn may involve the integration of sensory cues about the actual gravitational environment. The purpose of this investigation was to test the following hypotheses: 1. If subjects could measure the ball's acceleration, they would correctly estimate time-to-contact (TTC) in both 0-G and 1-G. 2. A first-order estimate, which assumes no acceleration, predicts TTC correctly in 0-G but overestimates the drop duration at 1-G. 3. If the brain instead uses a second-order internal model to account for gravity's accelerating effects on the ball, motor activity will be correctly timed to impact at 1-G, but the same second-order internal model applied in 0-G will underestimate the true TTC. The scientific objective of this experiment involved a ball catching activity in which the CNS was tested to see how it adjusts for the lack of gravitational acceleration acting on the ball in weightlessness.
approach: Subjects were seated in a chair and restrained by the body restraint system (BRS). To complete the scientific
results: When these experiments were performed on the ground prior to flight, the astronaut subjects generated the peak of anticipatory biceps activity, that occurs about 40 ms prior to impact and independent of initial ball speed, as has been seen previously in other Earth-based studies. Subjects also rotated their forearm just prior to contact so as to move the hand upward to meet the ball. This upward movement was not generated by the peak of muscle activity described above, because the movement was initiated somewhat earlier than the measured EMG activity. Rather, this measurement represented two separate responses – upward movement to meet the ball and limb stiffening to stiffen the hand – both of which can tell us when the brain expects the ball to arrive. To see whether the brain uses an internal model of gravity when estimating the ball's arrival time, researchers compared the time course of these two responses between 1-G (pre- and postflight) and 0-G (inflight) conditions. Anticipatory muscle activity occurred earlier relative to impact in 0-G compared to 1-G. This difference could not be explained by the repeated practice on this task that the astronauts had leading up to the flight because the timing returned to preflight values upon return to Earth. Nor can the shift simply be explained by the fact that subjects had more time to react in 0-G than in 1-G; dropping the ball from higher heights to increase the drop duration on Earth led to no differences in timing. One might also guess that muscle activity must start sooner during flight to overcome the fact that the muscles tend to be more relaxed in 0-G; but researchers found that supporting the forearm with an externally applied force to counteract gravity on Earth reduced the tonic activation of the biceps (as would be expected in 0-G) while causing no significant changes in timing of the anticipatory EMG peak. Thus, the timing shifts observed during flight were best explained by a failure to fully compensate for the lack of ball acceleration in 0-G. The timing of forearm movements also changed during flight. On the ground, such movements were monotonically upward and accurately synchronized to impact, but these movements started much too early in 0-G. Unlike the simple shift observed for muscle activity onset, however, limb movements stopped or even reversed direction after the initial false start. The change from monotonic movement on Earth to the non-monotonic movements observed during flight showed that movements were not simply slower in microgravity, as was observed, or simply due to reduced muscle tone in 0-G. Instead, the evidence suggested that, once triggered, the CNS could correct the ongoing movement by updating estimates of TTC based on visual feedback. While one might predict that catching responses would occur too early when subjects are first faced with microgravity conditions, it would be surprising if the brain was unable to adapt to this novel environment. Some evidence for adaptation exists. Although forearm movements started prematurely for all inflight tests, on flight days 9 and 15 the amplitude of the early, erroneous movement diminished and a later upward rotation developed just prior to impact. On the other hand, re-adaptation to Earth conditions occurred almost immediately. Average data from early postflight sessions (R+0, 1, 2) did not differ significantly from preflight or later postflight sessions. This indicated that subjects could rapidly retune internal models to the 1-G environment. The key test in this experiment involved determining the magnitude of time shifts for different initial ball velocities (v 0 ). The second-order internal model hypothesis predicted the nonlinear increases in time shifts (d) for decreasing values of v 0 using reasonable, fixed values of the TTC threshold (?). These ? values were biologically plausible. Allowing for the time it takes a neural signal to travel from the brain to the periphery, threshold values of TTC used to initiate a given behavior should be somewhat greater than the lead time of the behavior itself. That is, if the brain wants to activate a muscle x ms prior to ball impact, it has to use a TTC threshold of x+y ms, where y represents the time it takes for the message to get from the brain to the muscles. A response initiated at ?=75 ms within the brain was consistent with the arrival of the EMG peak in the muscle 40 ms prior to impact, due to neural transmission delays. Similarly, ? values of 300-400 ms were compatible with movement onset that normally occurred 200 ms prior to impact, given the time necessary to overcome limb inertia. In contrast, a first-order TTC estimate would require unreasonably long ? values (? > 1.2 seconds; i.e., longer than the total drop time of the ball in 1-G) to reproduce the time shifts observed in 0-G. Furthermore, a first-order TTC estimate cannot, with a fixed ?, predict the substantial changes of initiation time as a function of v 0 . Finally, had the subjects been able to directly measure the acceleration of the ball in real time, one would expect to see no time shift at all (with respect to impact) between 0-G and 1-G, irrespective of ?. The data from these experiments were compatible with the third hypothesis; i.e., that to catch a falling ball the CNS: (1) employs a second-order estimate of TTC, (2) uses an internal model to predict gravity's effect on the ball, and (3) applies this internal model initially even in microgravity. Furthermore, it appeared that the brain gradually adapts the internal model with prolonged exposure to 0-G.
