title: Eye-Hand Coordination
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: The objective of this experiment was to evaluate changes in the perception of motion levels in crewmembers during space flight and immediately postflight.
approach: A hand tracking task of a moving point on recording papers was made preflight, in flight, and postflight to note any changes in sensitivity. A modified servo recorder, self-contained, weighing approximately five pounds was used by a mission specialist during approximately 3 - 15 minute sessions in flight and 2 - 15 minute sessions pre- and postflight. Data was recorded on board and returned for analysis. The tracings were scored and consisted of sweep, peak, and reaction times (before and after the trial) for the sine and ramp data. The vertical distance between the signal and the response at the peak was measured in decimeters. Peak differences were converted to centimeters and are referred to as "peak". Overshoots were recorded as negative values while undershoots were positive for the peak measurements. The horizontal distance between the signal and the response, which is referred to as "sweep" was measured on the axis and at half the amplitude of the signal. In the sweep measurements, leads were recorded as negative values and lags were positive. The sweep measurements on the axis were selected and defined as the lag response. These lag responses were converted to time measured in milliseconds and are referred to as "time-lag." The horizontal distance between the signal and the response was measured at the beginning of the wave pattern and at the end of the wave. These lag responses were converted to reaction times in milliseconds and are referred to as "RT-Before and RT-After.” Unequal sub-samples among the frequencies within the replications exist for the peak and time-lag measurements. Sub-samples for frequencies 2, 5, and 10 were approximately 4, 10, and 20 respectively. Only one sample for each frequency within the replications is present for the RT-Before and RT-After measurements for the sine and ramp waves. There were approximately 18 to 20 measurements of reaction time in the square wave pattern. Several problems were encountered while recording the data. Sometimes the pen used to record the subject's tracing stopped writing and at other times the pen tore the paper. These individual points were recorded as missing. For some measurements, whole sessions were questionable and these data were not used in these analyses.
results: The peak differences generally deceased over flights (time) for both sine and ramp waves, while the same pattern was seen only for the half amplitude factor on the time-lag data. The full amplitude factor showed very mixed results for the three flights. Generally, the performance was better (smaller peak difference and less lag) for the half amplitude than for the full amplitude and generally the performance improved as the frequency decreased. No significant flight or replication effects were detected from the before and after reaction time data of the sine and ramp waves as well as the reaction time from the square signal. The data suggest that the subjects improved in performance over time, although the limited replication data did not necessarily support this, and that the tracking in space (in flight) essentially did not alter the crewmembers' performance.

title: Microgravity Induced Changes in the Control of Muscles
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: The overall goal of this project was to investigate the effects of microgravity on the neural control of motor units within a given muscle and the coordination of a group of muscles controlling a given joint. The main objectives were: 1. To document the effects of microgravity on the control of motor units in the Vastus Medialis (VM), an antigravity muscle of the leg used to a much lesser extent in space than on Earth. 2. To study the effects of microgravity on the First Dorsal Interosseous (FDI), a hand muscle used less in space than on Earth but is nevertheless utilized more than the antigravity muscle of the leg being considered. 3. To study the effects of microgravity on the activation of a group of muscles controlling one joint. 4. To determine the course of recovery from microgravity after being re-exposed to gravity. The information gained in this project will assist in understanding why muscles weaken in space and should enable the development of improved countermeasures for maintaining muscle force viability. This is an important issue that is relevant for enhancing the safety of astronauts in space and improving their health during and following extended exposures to microgravity. In regard to Earth-based research, the understanding of the neurological modifications that occur in microgravity should provide an accelerated time-scale model for the neurological effect on motor control due to aging. Additionally, the equipment that will be developed for studying the behavior of motor unit motor control can be used by neurologists to assess the degree of severity of upper motor neuron disease such as stroke and Parkinson's disease.
approach: Subjects participated in three pre-flight test sessions at L-45, L-43 and L-41 and six postflight test sessions between R+0, 1 or 2, 3, 5, 7, and 14). The procedures focused on two areas of neural control of muscle: 1) the regulation of the discharge activities of motor units that make up a given muscle, and 2) the coordination among different muscles that contribute to a given task. Both properties were studied using intramuscular and surface electromyographic (EMG) techniques. The procedures investigated two different muscles, the First Dorasl Interosseous (FD), a small hand muscle that controls the index finger, and the Vastus Medialis (VM), a muscle of the thigh that controls knee extension. These particular muscles were selected becasue they experience different patterns of usage in microgravity. The pre- and postflight protocols are similar. The subject is seated in a custom-made test chair. The hand and leg muscles were tested sequentially in the same test session. Surface EMG sensors were placed on four thigh muscles and one hand muscle. Maximal voluntary strength measures were taken during knee extension/flexion and index finger abduction. These measurements were made with custom dynamometers attached to the test chair. Afterward the indwelling EMG electrode was placed in the thight muscle. EMG signals from the wires were recorded while the subject execute the two force trajectories: one at a relatively low force level and the other at a relatively hight force level. Each test contraction lasted no more than one minute, with ample rest periods provided between the contractiosn. The same force trajectories and recordings were made from the hand muscle, except the recordings were made from either a surface EMG electrode "array" placed over the FDI muscle or a 25-gauge needle was inserted in the FDI muscle adjacent to a surface EMG array.
results: The investigators composed a final report but there are limited results available because the investigation was discontinued.

title: Light Flash Observations
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: During the Apollo missions 12-17 and Skylab missions 2-4, the crews observed and recorded the frequency and character of light flashes through their eyes. After approximately 17 minutes of dark adaptation, tiny dots and thin streaks of white light were seen at frequencies of approximately three events per minute by crewmembers when on translunar coast (TLC) or transearth coast (TEC) or over the polar part of Skylab orbits. When near the South Atlantic Anomaly (SAA), where the proton flux was over 1000 times greater than in other parts of the orbit, the frequency increased to approximately nine events per minute for Skylab altitudes of 443 km. Nearly 20 years ago, it was hypothesized that astronauts were likely to see flashes of light from cosmic ray particles when they were outside the shielding provided by the Earth’s magnetic field. The site of action of these particles, and whether cosmic particles actually caused the light flash phenomenon, were topics of conjecture in 1970, when this phenomenon was first reported. The causes for luminous phosphenes included ionizing radiation, mechanical pressure, electrical currents, magnetic fields, stimulation of the cerebral cortex, or pathological conditions of the Central Nervous System (CNS). In 1970, these phenomena were believed to be caused by ionizing heavy nuclei such as carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen, which transversed the spacecraft and the body when outside the Earth’s magnetic shielding. The conjecture that the major mechanism for these visual phenomena was Cerenkov radiation was controversial. Simulation studies were used to determine whether carbon, nitrogen, oxygen or other ions with equivalent ionizing characteristics could cause the same phenomena seen by astronauts. The exact mechanism in which the retina was stimulated by ionizing particles traveling at velocities below those necessary for emission of Cerenkov light was unclear. Experiments in which nitrogen ions were stopped in the cerebral cortex showed that the brain and optic nerve were not stimulated. Several mechanisms existed by which cosmic particles could produce visual sensations. They were: 1) electrical excitation
approach: Special features of the experiment included measurement of the characteristics of the cosmic-particle environment in the vicinity of the eye, measurement of dark adaptation, and continuous onboard accumulation of the light flash observations from astronauts and particle detectors throughout one complete 90-minute orbit. Two revolutions of the Earth were devoted to this experiment. During revolution 110, the silicon telescope-spectrometer was deployed to measure the trajectory, atomic charge Z, and velocity of cosmic particles with a stopping power of 10 kilo-electron volts per micrometer or greater. During revolution 111, two crewmembers donned special masks in order to become completely dark-adapted. After approximately 10 minutes, the two observers reached dark adaptation and made continuous observations of visual sensations. At each event, a push-button signal from the observing astronaut was recorded on the digital tape and the verbal description was recorded on the onboard tape recorder. The third crewmember operated the experiment control unit, which received data from silicon detectors and silver chloride AgCl(Cd) crystals. The crystals were used to register particle tracks in four sectors of orbit, those corresponding to the northern latitudes, equatorial latitudes, the SAA, and the southern latitudes. After the flight, the digital tapes, voice tapes, detector boxes, and masks were returned to the investigators. The digital tapes were transcribed, and each event was related to the orbital position of the spacecraft. Events from the silicon detectors, pushbuttons and control unit were read from the digital tape by a specially constructed microprocessor. The push-button events and time marks were related to the verbal reports. The energy and trajectory information were inadequate because of a paucity of recorded events. The AgCl(Cd) crystals were transported to the University of Frankfurt, Germany, where they had been produced and calibrated. The crystals were analyzed for the abundance of tracks produced by protons, alpha particles, or heavier ions. The characteristics of the cosmic particle environment inside the spacecraft were determined by converting the spectrum and abundance of particles outside the spacecraft to the number of particles with various stopping powers and residual ranges, using aluminum shielding data for 512 sectors of solid angle around the spacecraft.
results: ing in near-ultraviolet (UV) radiation in the vicinity of the retina, 2) ionization by cosmic ray particles through the retina, 3) local ionization by the products from a nonelastic collision of the high-velocity proton and carbon, nitrogen, or oxygen, or 4) a shock wave phenomenon from charged particles passing through the tissue matrix. The purpose of the experiment was to ascertain quantitatively the frequency, character, latitudinal dependence, and identity of cosmic particles that caused the light flash phenomenon during the Apollo-Soyuz Test Project. The ultimate objective was the assessment of radiation hazards of long-term Earth-orbiting and interplanetary missions. APPROACH: Special features of the experiment included measurement of the characteristics of the cosmic-particle environment in the vicinity of the eye, measurement of dark adaptation, and continuous onboard accumulation of the light flash observations from astronauts and particle detectors throughout one complete 90-minute orbit. Two revolutions of the Earth were devoted to this experiment. During revolution 110, the silicon telescope-spectrometer was deployed to measure the trajectory, atomic charge Z, and velocity of cosmic particles with a stopping power of 10 kilo-electron volts per micrometer or greater. During revolution 111, two crewmembers donned special masks in order to become completely dark-adapted. After approximately 10 minutes, the two observers reached dark adaptation and made continuous observations of visual sensations. At each event, a push-button signal from the observing astronaut was recorded on the digital tape and the verbal description was recorded on the onboard tape recorder. The third crewmember operated the experiment control unit, which received data from silicon detectors and silver chloride AgCl(Cd) crystals. The crystals were used to register particle tracks in four sectors of orbit, those corresponding to the northern latitudes, equatorial latitudes, the SAA, and the southern latitudes. After the flight, the digital tapes, voice tapes, detector boxes, and masks were returned to the investigators. The digital tapes were transcribed, and each event was related to the orbital position of the spacecraft. Events from the silicon detectors, pushbuttons and control unit were read from the digital tape by a specially constructed microprocessor. The push-button events and time marks were related to the verbal reports. The energy and trajectory information were inadequate because of a paucity of recorded events. The AgCl(Cd) crystals were transported to the University of Frankfurt, Germany, where they had been produced and calibrated. The crystals were analyzed for the abundance of tracks produced by protons, alpha particles, or heavier ions. The characteristics of the cosmic particle environment inside the spacecraft were determined by converting the spectrum and abundance of particles outside the spacecraft to the number of particles with various stopping powers and residual ranges, using aluminum shielding data for 512 sectors of solid angle around the spacecraft. RESULTS: There were 82 visual events reported by two crewmembers during a 90-minute orbit at an altitude of 225 kilometers (km). The results of the light flash experiment indicated that the abundance of ions that caused the light flash phenomena was minimal between latitudes 30° N and 30° S. The frequency of light flashes between latitudes 30° N/50° N and 30° S/50° S was 25 times higher than noted in the equatorial latitudes. Increased flash phenomena were not reported through the SAA, as was expected after reviewing a Skylab 4 report of increased activity through the SAA. However, at the 225-km altitude of Apollo-Soyuz, the proton flux was much less than that of the Skylab 4 altitude of 443 kilometers. Also, the shielding of the Apollo spacecraft was greater than that of Skylab. This distribution of flashes was correlated with the distribution of cosmic particles with stopping power greater that 15 kilo-electron volts per micrometer in the eye. The frequency of reported light flash events was strongly dependent on latitude. At the points of closest approach to the geomagnetic poles, the observed events occurred at one to two per minute; however no events occurred near the equator. These observations were consistent with the change in abundance of cosmic particles with latitude that was also noted during the Skylab 4 mission. The increased rate of visual events near the south geomagnetic pole can be explained by increased dark adaptation of the crewmembers. The observed event rate correlated with a cosmic particle abundance for heavy particles with energy losses > 5 kilo-electron volts per micrometer. The AgCl(Cd) detector results suggested that 60 events of 15 kilo-electron volts per micrometer or greater would be observed during three-minute intervals in the northernmost portions of the orbit. The highest observed event rate at high latitudes was only 14 events per three minutes near the south magnetic pole. This rate implied a 23-percent efficiency for the detector. However, near the equator, where only a few events were observed, the detectors recorded the equivalent average of 73 events per four cm 2 /minute. An explanation of this inconsistency was that the fading time from the heavy ions was long relative to the orbit sectors. Thus, identification of the heavy particle environment in each sector could not be expected. Also, particles interacting in the crystals hours before the experiment might have been included in the event. Assuming the complete retina target area of four cm 2 , the efficiency of visualizing the events was 36 percent for the northernmost sector. In the SAA sector, the detector efficiency diminished to eight percent. Thus, the AgCl(Cd) detector data did not correlate well with either the observed event rate or the calculated abundances. There were no reports of high frequency throughout the SAA, as was expected from a previous Skylab 4 report of markedly increased flash activity. At the 225-km altitude of Apollo-Soyuz, the proton flux of particles was 14 times less than at the 443-km altitude of Skylab 4. Also, the aluminum shielding of the Apollo command module was much greater than that of Skylab. The more favored hypothesis for the events seen in the SAA, particularly at higher altitudes, was the mechanism of proton nonelastic nuclear collision with carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen in tissues of the retina. This mechanism was similar to that proposed for neutron interactions, which also cause discrete flashes. If the average cross-section for interactions such as (p, p’, 3a) on carbon, nitrogen, or oxygen was assumed to be approximately 450 millibars in the proton energy range of 175 million electron volts (MeV) or less, only one event per three minutes would occur during Apollo-Soyuz altitude of 225 km. Under the reduced shielding conditions of Skylab 4, 51 times more protons would interact with the eye tissues of one observer, or 26 events might be observed during a three-minute interval. The average rate was 28 events per three minutes on Skylab 4. Thus, the nuclear collision hypothesis for the origin of light flashes in the SAA had some validity.

title: Functional Task Test (FTT) Muscle Performance Reliability Study
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Space flight induces a host of physiological changes that have detrimental effects on normal human function in normal gravity (1-G). Upon entry into a gravitational environment, astronauts must cope with impairments in strength, balance, and the ability to ambulate. The primary objective of the Functional Task Test (FTT) project is to develop and evaluate an integrated set of functional and physiological tests, and then use those tests to determine how postflight changes in sensorimotor, cardiovascular, and muscle physiology impact functional performance (e.g. standing, ladder climbing, and hatch opening). Because the FTT project necessitates the development of novel tests, the reliability of each component test must be determined prior to data collection. Therefore, the purpose of this pilot study is to determine the reliability of novel tests designed by the Exercise Physiology Laboratory at Johnson Space Center (JSC) to quickly and safely assess muscle performance. Prior to initiating the flight-related portion of the FTT project, the reliability of these novel muscle performance tests must be determined. Specific Aims: (1) To determine the reliability of each test designed to quickly and safely assess muscle performance. (2) To determine the time requirement of each of the muscle performance tests.
approach: Ten (5 males, 4 females) healthy, recreationally active volunteers were recruited by the Johnson Space Center Human Test Subject Facility to participate in this investigation. All subjects completed an Air Force Class III equivalent physical examination prior to participation. Subjects received verbal and written explanations of test protocols before providing written informed consent. Test protocols and procedures were reviewed and approved by the NASA Johnson Space Center Committee for the Protection of Human Subjects. Subjects completed a battery of lower- and upper-body muscle performance tests on three separate occasions, each separated by at least 48 hours. The battery included the following tests (in order): 1) Primus® muscle force control test; 2) knee extension interpolated twitch test; 3) knee extension muscle force control test; 4) leg press maximal isometric force test; 5) leg press maximal power test; 6) leg press power endurance test; 7) bench press maximal isometric force test; 8) bench press muscle force control test; 9) bench press maximal power test; and 10) bench press power endurance test. Intra-class correlation coefficients and coefficients of variation were calculated to determine the reliability of each muscle performance parameter.
results: The force control variables demonstrated low-to-moderate reliability, probably due to the low target force. The Primus® and the bench press both assessed upper-body force control. The bench press provided better reliability than the Primus®. Central activation capacity, maximal isometric force, RFD values, and maximal power values demonstrated excellent reliability. Reliability of the fatigue index metric during the leg press power endurance test was relatively low; however, reliability of the total work metric was excellent. Conclusions After discussing the findings with the FTT principal investigator (Jacob Bloomberg), the FTT investigative team, and ECP, the invetigators have decided to remove the Primus® force control test as well as the leg press and bench press maximal power tests from the battery because these tests provided poor reliability and redundant information, respectively.

title: Solid Tumor Risk Estimation: Incorporating Intercellular Interaction Effects
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Under this NSCOR grant, investigators made a number of findings that help provide a mechanistic framework for biologically-based risk models. Investigators requested and received a cost extension to finish off experimental characterization of proton and iron irradiation studies to address angiogenesis processes that are important in radiation carcinogenesis and can be viewed as bottlenecks to carcinogenesis advancement. The significance of this in the carcinogenesis risk context lies in the challenge it presents to the standard radiogenic cancer paradigm. This paradigm holds that cancer may be understood as an autonomous expansion of an initiated cell clone, followed by the chance genetic creation of a cancer cell in that clone that then inevitably expands to become a diagnosed cancer. At the basis of these events is thought to be the DNA lesion. Investigators argue that essential population-level and tumor-environmental dynamics can alter this picture dramatically, either promoting cancer development or slowing the course of existing cancers. Their basis extends beyond DNA damage to include the familiar “hallmarks” of cancer that constitute “bottlenecks” to tumor advancement – population-level logistic growth effects, acquisition of angiogenic potential, and competency for invasion, to name three. Investigators have shown that radiation can progress or limit cancers by modifying these bottlenecks. Because these bottlenecks may be significant enough to increase the likelihood of transforming an initiated cell, or to change the likelihood an existing cancer advances to clinical detection over a lifetime, they must be included in the overall assessment of radiogenic cancer risk. It follows that existing models that fail to include such bottleneck effects are inherently flawed in that they do not include all radiation actions bearing on the development of manifest cancer disease.
approach: Proton-induced gene regulation was investigated in a number of human cell types that actively contribute to carcinogenesis progression, including not only cancer cells but also primary non- transformed stromal and microvascular endothelial cells. A baseline was obtained by analysis of the proton-induced global gene expression signature in the primary human non-transformed cells. Both human lung microvascular endothelial cells (HLMVEC) and normal human dermal fibroblasts (NHDF) were irradiated (0Gy and 2Gy) and genome-wide array analysis was performed on RNA isolated six hours after proton exposure.
results: Investigations to this end show that cancer-progression-modifying tumor-host interactions indeed occur at a number of levels, including: 1) reduction of angiogenesis by protons, with enhancement by 56Fe (similar to gamma); 2) reduction in the ability of both targeted and non-targeted cells to invade following proton exposures; in contrast with 3) augmentation in ability of tumor and host stromal cells to follow chemotactic stimuli following exposure to 56Fe ions; 4) Reduction in support for tumor proliferation and survival following proton radiation; effects opposite to 5) the stimulation of support for tumor proliferation and survival observed with 56Fe (and gamma). In addition, 6) mouse age generally, as differentially modified by radiation, was found to have a significant effect on cancer progression. Lastly, investigating the potential influence of intercellular interactions within the tumor on radiation modulation of cancer progression, investigators found that 7) cell-cell interactions among the cancer stem cell (CSC) and non-stem tumor compartments, known to be differentially affected by radiation, can critically affect carcinogenesis course. 1) Reduction of angiogenesis by protons, with enhancement by 56Fe (similar to gamma): Using pan-genomic arrays, expression of key pro-angiogenic and inflammation-associated genes including VEGF-1A, C-MYC, IL-8, and IL-6, were found generally to be downregulated by protons (1GeV). RT-PCR reconfirmed this down-regulatory trend for a number of specific angiogenesis-regulating genes, including VEGF, IL-8, HIF-1A, and IL-6, c-MYC, FGFR1 and ANGPT1, in human lung microvascular endothelial cells (HLMVEC), normal human dermal fibroblasts (NHCF), and A549 lung carcinoma 6 hours after receiving doses of sizes 0.5, 1 and 2Gy. In contrast, when the fibroblast, endothelial and tumor cells were gamma-irradiated at the same doses, the expressions of VEGF, IL-8, HIF-1A and IL-6, were upregulated in a dose-dependent manner relative to control (0Gy) 6hr post-irradiation. Having established the proton-induced downregulation of these angiogenic genes (6 hours post-irradiation), regulation of the corresponding proteins was examined. ELISA assays specific for VEGF and IL-8 were performed after irradiation of endothelial (HLMVEC), fibroblast (NHDF) and tumor (A549) cultures. At 24h hours post-irradiation, levels of secreted IL-8 in the culture supernatants were reduced by 31% and 50% in endothelium and tumor cells respectively. Secreted VEGF was also significantly reduced in proton-irradiated fibroblast (17%) and tumor cells (34%) versus sham-irradiated controls (although results with endothelial cells were indeterminate). These findings indicate a dose-dependent downregulation of important angiogenic genes and, for the most part, a significant reduction in protein levels following proton irradiation. For comparison, 56Fe-induced gene regulation was investigated in the same cell types as for protons. Again, a baseline was obtained by analysis of the iron ion-induced global gene expression signature in the primary human non-transformed cells. Both human lung microvascular endothelial cells (HLMVEC) and normal human dermal fibroblasts (NHDF) were irradiated (0, 0.2, 0.4, and 1Gy) and genome-wide array analysis was performed on RNA isolated 6 hours after radiation (or sham) exposure. Expression of key pro-angiogenic and inflammation-associated genes including, VEGF-1A, C-MYC, IL-8, and IL-6, were found to be upregulated. The expression patterns of a number of the angiogenesis-regulating genes, including: VEGF, IL-8, HIF-1A, IL-6, c-MYC, FGFR1 and ANGPT1 were again investigated using quantitative RT-PCR. Results from the quantitative assessment of a number of these genes are shown. Significant upregulation of expression was observed for these genes in both the irradiated HLMVEC and NHDF cells, compared to sham-irradiated controls (p 2) Reduction in the ability of both targeted and non-targeted cells to invade following proton exposures: Beyond the suppression of genes critical in angiogenesis, investigators determined that proton irradiation could also suppress the ability of cells to invade under chemoattractant conditions in vitro. The invasion of the proton-irradiated endothelial, fibroblast, and tumor cells was investigated using a matrigel invasion assay. Compared with untreated controls, proton-irradiated cells (2Gy) showed significantly reduced invasion through the matrigel extracellular matrix. Quantification of the results demonstrated that following proton irradiation, the invasive capacity of A549, NHDF and HLMVEC cells was reduced, by 46, 15 and 14% respectively. Next, the invasion/migration of endothelial (HLMVEC) in response to soluble factors produced by either proton-irradiated fibroblast (NHDF) or proton-irradiated tumor cells (A549) was analyzed. In an effort to mimic the crosstalk that occurs under in vivo conditions between fibroblast, cancer cells and microvascular endothelial cells, a co-culture transwell chamber system was used. Irradiated or sham-irradiated tumor or fibroblast cells were seeded in the lower chamber. The upper chamber used was an invasion chamber in which untreated endothelial cells were seeded. Since it is known that both fibroblast and cancer cells produce angiogenic factors (e.g. VEGF) that chemoattract endothelial cells, investigators studied how proton irradiation would alter this paracrine interaction. Compared to the matched sham-irradiated cell populations, both the 2-Gy proton-irradiated fibroblasts and tumor cells were less effective (19% and 16% respectively) at inducing endothelial cells to invade and traverse to the underside of the membrane. They propose that the reduced invasion of endothelial cells was, in part, a direct consequence of the demonstrated reduced secretion of angiogenic factors from the proton-irradiated cells. Indeed, addition of either recombinant VEGF or IL-8 to the irradiated compartment counteracted the anti-migratory effect of proton irradiation. 3) Augmentation in ability of tumor and host stromal cells to follow chemotactic stimuli following exposure to 56Fe ions: Extending the finding of increased expression of genes critical in angiogenesis, investigators determined that iron ion irradiation could also augment the ability of cells to invade under chemoattractant conditions in vitro. Thus far, the invasion of the iron ion-irradiated fibroblast (NHDF) and tumor (A549) cells has been investigated using a matrigel invasion assay. Compared with untreated controls, iron ion-irradiated cells (0.2Gy) showed significantly increased invasion through the matrigel extracellular matrix; even more so than 1Gy. Quantification of the results demonstrated that, following 0.2Gy iron ion irradiation, the invasive capacity of A549 and NHDF cells was increased by 47% and 18% respectively. Investigators next analyzed the invasion/migration of HLMVEC in response to soluble factors produced by either iron ion-irradiated A549 or iron ion-irradiated NHDF cells. In an effort to mimic the crosstalk which occurs under in vivo conditions between fibroblast, cancer cells and micro-vascular endothelial cells, a co-culture transwell chamber system was used. Irradiated or sham-irradiated A549 or NHDF cells were seeded in the lower chamber. The upper chamber used was an invasion chamber in which untreated HLMVEC cells were seeded. Since it is known that both fibroblast and cancer cells produce angiogenic factors (e.g. VEGF) that are chemoattractant to endothelial cells, investigators studied how iron-ion irradiation would alter this paracrine interaction. They found that, compared to the matched sham-irradiated cell populations, both the 0.2-Gy iron-irradiated fibroblast and tumor cells were more effective at inducing endothelial cells to traverse to the underside of the membrane. Investigators hypothesized in this case that increased secretion of angiogenic factors from the iron ion-irradiated cells was responsible for the increased invasion of endothelial cells. Addition of small molecule inhibitor of VEGF, SU11248 to the irradiated compartment counteracted the pro-migratory effect of iron ion irradiation. Invasion of tumor (A549), fibroblast (NHDF) and human lung microvascular endothelial cells (HLVMEC) towards conditioned media from 56Fe-exposed cells was also analyzed. A dose-dependent upregulation in invasion was observed. Interestingly, breaking this trend was a dramatic upregulation of invasion of fibroblast cells towards CM from tumor cells irradiated at 0.2Gy, and a downregulation of tumor cells towards CM from LMEC cells irradiated at 0.2Gy. As a matter deserving further investigation, an upward deviation in the vicinity of 0.2Gy from linearity has been consistently noted for the pro-progression effect of 56Fe radiation. 4) Reduction in support for tumor proliferation and survival following proton radiation: To investigate the modulation of additional aspects of tumor progression by proton radiation, the ability of endothelial (HLMVEC) cells to proliferate was examined in a transwell co-culture assay with proton-irradiated or sham-irradiated tumor (A549) or fibroblast (NHDF) cells. Cancer cells are already known to secrete pro-angiogenic factors e.g. VEGF and IL-8 that can recruit endothelial cells and stimulate their proliferation. Decreased cell proliferation was observed for endothelial cells sharing media with proton-irradiated fibroblasts or proton-irradiated cancer cells, but not for endothelial cells sharing media with the sham-irradiated matched controls. In contrast, when this same assay was conducted using photon-irradiated fibroblast or tumor cells, an increased, rather than a decreased, proliferation of endothelial cells was observed. Next examined was the degree to which proton-irradiated cells (cancer, fibroblast, or endothelial), plated in the upper chambers of transwell plates modulates the proliferation of fibroblast or endothelial cells in the lower chambers. A measurable reduction in proliferation of both fibroblasts and endothelial cells associated with proton-irradiated cancer cells was detected compared to that of controls. Investigators further investigated whether addition of the angiogenic factors VEGF or IL-8 could restore the original proliferation capacity. The proton radiation-induced reduction in responding cell proliferation was partially ameliorated by the addition of VEGF (20ng/ml) or IL-8 (20ng/ml) to the irradiated cell compartment (normalized to sham-irradiated controls). The data suggests that proton-induced suppression of these specific angiogenic factors may well play a direct role in inhibiting adjacent cell proliferation. Such proton-induced suppression of cell proliferation could well have ramifications for treatment optimization. The reduction in proliferation/survival was most pronounced for the NHDF stromal fibroblasts that shared media with 2Gy-irradiated tumor cells. Proliferation levels of the fibroblast cells that shared media through transwells with proton-irradiated tumor cells were less than 50% of their matched fibroblast controls that shared media with sham-irradiated tumor cells. In line with other growth factor rescue experiments, addition of recombinant VEGF or IL-8 partially restored the proliferation levels to 71% and 90% respectively. Similar results were observed for the other cell combinations. To ascertain the dose dependence of survival of endothelial (HLMVEC), fibroblast (NHDF), or tumor (A549) cells, and whether proton-irradiation induced inhibition of IL-8 might actually contribute to the radiation sensitivity of these cells, clonogenic assays were performed with or without the addition of recombinant human IL-8 (20ng/ml). Cells were irradiated at 1, 2 and 4Gy of protons. It was found that treatment of cells with recombinant IL-8 significantly spared the 2-Gy proton irradiated cells from clonogenic inhibition. The SF2 (survival fraction after 2Gy) of proton and photon/gamma (results not shown) was found to be 0.68 and 0.78 respectively, with the cell killing effect of proton being slightly higher than that of photon radiation. 5) Stimulation of support for tumor proliferation and survival observed with 56Fe (and gamma): The ability of the HLMVEC cells to proliferate was examined in a transwell co-culture assay with iron ion irradiated or sham-irradiated A549 tumor (or NHDF fibroblast) cells. Contrary to protons, increased cell proliferation was observed for endothelial cells sharing media with iron ion-irradiated fibroblasts or iron ion-irradiated cancer cells, but not for endothelial cells sharing media with the sham-irradiated matched controls. 6) Mouse age generally, as differentially modified by radiation, and was found to have a significant effect on cancer progression: Tumor progression dynamics for young (Y) and middle-aged (MA) mice, with or without iron irradiation at 1GeV/u, were studied for LLC implanted in syngeneic C57BL/6 mice with and without 5x0.2Gy of iron irradiation. Progression was gauged in terms of two quantities: tumor growth rates after approximately exponential growth starts, and “effective” initial tumor volumes, which is proposed to account for differential tumor/stromal “reorganization” times following injection and before growth of the tumor mass. To do this, the two quantitative aspects of tumor development just mentioned were taken to be the growth rate c and the “effective initial tumor volume” b, obtained by extrapolating the fitted exponential curve backwards to time zero and interpreted as mainly a measure of either stromal incorporation into the tumor, or how supportive the microenvironment was prior to the near exponential growth phase. Growth data were fitted to V = b*exp(ct), with b the geometric mean of the b’s for individual mouse fits, and c the arithmetic mean of the c’s for individual mouse fits. The data show generally that tumor growth rates are dependent on host age, and that there was a statistically significant decrease in average growth rates c for the unirradiated middle age (MA) as compared to the unirradiated young (Y) hosts, with only a modest increase in the effective initial volume. As regards perturbation by irradiation, the following results were found: i) the effective initial volume b was very significantly decreased by irradiation in both young (Y) and middle-aged (MA) mice; ii) the overall progression decrease by irradiation in the young (Y) mice was due exclusively to a dramatic decrease in effective initial volume; while iii) the more modest decrease in progression by irradiation in middle-aged (MA) mice was due to a slight increase in growth rate compensating for a substantial decrease in effective initial volume; and iv) modest decreases in both average growth rates and effective initial volumes were noted for irradiated middle-aged (MA) mice compared to irradiated young (Y) mice. To gain some molecular-level understanding, protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks were constructed from the gene array data. Demonstrated were highly regulated protein interactions for tumors of the young (Y) iron-irradiated mice compared with those of the unirradiated groups and of the middle-aged (MA) iron-irradiated compared with those of the unirradiated groups. Overall, the network based on data from tumors growing in irradiated versus unirradiated young (Y) mice demonstrated more regulation of activity than did the network based on data from tumors growing in the irradiated versus unirradiated middle-aged (MA) mice. The general directions of the significantly regulated proteins due to irradiation also coincided with the direction of regulations of genes; mostly down in young (Y) hosts, and a slight bias upward in the middle-aged (MA) hosts. As was also true for the gene regulations, iron irradiation induced a greater genetic response overall in young (Y) compared to middle-aged (MA) hosts. Interestingly, two central network hubs, FASN (fatty acid synthase) and AKT1 genes, were found to be downregulated within the tumors of young (Y) mice in response to iron-irradiation. FASN is a key metabolic enzyme responsible for lipogenesis and it plays a central role in energy homeostasis. It has been shown that FASN can be highly expressed in aggressive and metastatic tumors. AKT1 is one of three homologous isoforms of the AKT (PKB) protein kinase family that control a wide variety of cellular functions including proliferation, survival, and metabolism. Given the wide range of pro-growth cellular functions AKT1 modulates, it is not surprising it is also implicated in tumor progression and metastases. Using Ingenuity Pathway Analysis (IPA) software, specific pathways were constructed around FASN and AKT1 that included those genes directly or indirectly up or down regulated for tumor samples from young (Y) or middle-age (MA) mice with and without iron irradiation. Comparisons between groups were done by calculating the log2-fold change, with increasing levels of up- (red) or down- (green) regulation indicated by the darker shades of the respective color and with grey indicating genes present in the network without a 2-fold change under the perturbation studied. In the case of young (Y) unirradiated versus irradiated mice, FASN is seen to be downregulated. By contrast, no FASN regulation was detected between the tumors from the middle-aged (MA) irradiated and unirradiated groups, consistent with the reduced degree of suppression of progression by irradiation noted for these hosts. 7) Cell-cell interactions among the cancer stem cell (CSC) and non-stem tumor compartments, known to be differentially affected by radiation, can critically affect carcinogenesis course: In recent years cancer stem cells (CSCs) have been hypothesized to comprise only a minor subpopulation in solid tumors that drives tumor initiation, progression, and metastasis; the so-called "cancer stem cell hypothesis." While a seemingly trivial statement about numbers, much is put at stake. If true, the conclusions of many studies of cancer cell populations could be challenged, as the bulk assay methods upon which they depend have, by, and large, taken for granted the notion that a "typical" cell of the population possesses the attributes of a cell capable of perpetuating the cancer, i.e., a CSC. In support of the CSC hypothesis, populations enriched for so-called "tumor-initiating" cells have demonstrated a corresponding increase in tumorigenicity as measured by dilution assay, although estimates have varied widely as to what the fractional contribution of tumor-initiating cells is in any given population. Some have taken this variability to suggest the CSC fraction may be nearly 100% after all, countering the CSC hypothesis, and that there are simply assay-dependent error rates in the ability to "reconfirm" CSC status at the cell level. To explore this controversy more quantitatively, investigators developed a simple cellular automaton model of CSC-driven tumor growth dynamics. Assuming CSC and non-stem cancer cells (CC) subpopulations coexist to some degree, we evaluated the impact of an environmentally dependent CSC symmetric division probability and a CC proliferation capacity on tumor progression and morphology. Their model predicts, as expected, that the frequency of CSC divisions that are symmetric highly influences the frequency of CSCs in the population, but goes on to predict the two frequencies can be widely divergent, and that spatial constraints will tend to increase the CSC fraction over time. Further, tumor progression times show a marked dependence on both the frequency of CSC divisions that are symmetric and on the proliferation capacities of CC. Together, these findings can explain, within the CSC hypothesis, the widely varying measures of stem cell fractions observed. In particular, although the CSC fraction is influenced by the (environmentally modifiable) CSC symmetric division probability, with the former converging to unity as the latter nears 100%, the CSC fraction becomes quite small even for symmetric division probabilities modestly lower than 100%. In the latter case, the tumor exhibits a clustered morphology and the CSC fraction steadily increases with time; more so on both counts when the death rate of CCs is higher. Such variations in CSC fraction and morphology are not only consistent with the CSC hypothesis, but lend support to it as one expected byproduct of the dynamical interactions that are predicted to take place among a relatively small CSC population, its CC counterpart, and the host compartment over time. Overall conclusions: Cell-cell interactions between the tumor and host, and between tumor cell subcompartments, affect radiation-induced cancer progression, and thus cancer risk, in a highly radiation-quality-dependent fashion. Investigators focused on two radiation types, 56Fe and protons, and found them to generally encourage and discourage, respectively, a number of molecular and functional indicators of progression. This fact must be considered alongside the risks of cancer cell creation when making conclusions as to astronaut safety during long-term space flight. Closer to home, the favorable tumor-host dynamical effects noted for proton radiation in space may work to supplement its well-established physical attributes as a therapeutic modality.

title: Test and Evaluation of Liquid Cooling Garments
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: This research evaluated the physiological functioning and subjective comfort of subjects while donned in five liquid cooling garments. The goal was to identify the optimal features of each of the garments to maintain core temperature and comfort under intensive physical exertion.
approach: Four males and two females between the ages of 22 and 46 participated in this study. The garments evaluated were the Minnesota Advanced Cooling Suit (MACS-Delphi), Russian Orlan, NASA Liquid Cooling and Ventilation Garment (LCVG), MACS-Delphi without hood, and Russian Orlan without hood. Subjects were tested on different days in two different environmental chamber temperature/humidity conditions. Each session consisted of stages of treadmill walking/running (250W to 700W at different stages) and rest. Skin and core temperatures, energy expenditure, heart rate, evaporative/nonevaporative sweat rate, and ratings of thermal comfort and heat sensation, overall and on specific body areas were measured throughout each session.

title: The Effectiveness of Manual Control During Simulation of Flight Tasks (PILOT)
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Russian flight investigations have found evidence of functional disorders affecting psycho-physiological capacity and navigational skills during initial periods of weightlessness. Deterioration of these skills has potential impact on mission safety, as crewmembers are required to perform complex and dynamic activities throughout a mission. Previous studies of performance have been limited to the first week in weightlessness. The PILOT experiment was designed to evaluate how crewmembers perform work tasks during a long-duration mission. Specific goals of the experiments were to: 1) evaluate how operator performance is affected by prolonged exposure to microgravity; 2) determine the stresses involved in performing work tasks during various phases of long-duration flight; 3) assess how well crewmembers retained their skills at performing work tasks during and after a long-duration flight; and 4) compare ground training performance and crewmembers' physical and mental sate with actual in flight performance and state. approach: Two crewmembers, subject 1 and subject 2, were scheduled to participate in the experiment. This experiment used a ground-based Russian spacecraft control simulator and a Mir-based workstation system to simulate the re-docking of a Soyuz module to the Mir station and collect performance data. Both the simulator and workstation contained a television receiver, simulation control devices and physiological sensors. The two systems were telemetrically connected in a closed loop system, with the ground-based unit transmitting simulated vehicle states to the operator at the Mir workstation. The workstation, in turn, transmitted operator actions and physiological information to the ground-based simulator. Audio and video systems uploaded and displayed the ground-based simulator version of the orbital station Mir to the test subjects. Crewmembers were instructed not to take psychotropic medication, consume alcohol or perform strenuous physical exercise within 24 hours of data collection. Preflight data collection was scheduled four times preflight for both subjects during training exercises on the simulator at the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Russia. During each data collection session, the subjects completed three cycles of experimental tasks in approximately 45-50 minutes. Medical monitoring sensors called "Gamma-1" were applied to the body to detect heart rate, cranial blood flow and blood pressure. The data collection sessions established a baseline for individual levels on manual control performance (work performance) and functional state (skill retention). The same work tasks were to be performed during flight while the subject was positioned at the Mir workstation. The experiment was scheduled to be performed on flight days 5 (FD5), FD20, FD40, and FD82 by subject 1 and FD24, FD57 and FD86 by subject 2. Heart rate, cranial blood flow and blood pressure were to be measured using the same medical equipment as preflight. At the completion of each data collection session, the subject was to complete a self-report describing his functional state and manual control performance. All data was to be transferred from the Mir to the Shuttle (STS-71) for return to earth. Postflight, both subjects were scheduled to be debriefed the third day after landing (R+3) during a 30-minute verbal question-and-answer session using a structured questionnaire developed by Russian investigators. A self-evaluation of the difficulty and quality of task performance was to be collected during this debriefing. Simulator sessions were to be performed on R+7 and R+30 using the same equipment as the preflight data collection sessions.

title: Design and Evaluation of Automated Electronic Checklists for Robotics Operations
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: The investigators aimed to develop a prototype electronic procedure system and use it to study how the automated features of this system should be implemented to enhance situation awareness (SA), operator workload, and task execution in the context of robotic arm operation. Future long-duration, long-distance mission crews will have to operate more independently from the ground and rely more on automated spacecraft systems to support them while executing mission tasks. NASA has relatively little experience designing systems to support this concept of operations so the overall goal was to provide to NASA design guidelines for implementing these automation features in electronic procedures and empirical evidence that demonstrates how the operator and task performance are affected. Investigators used well defined International Space Station (ISS) robotic arm operations as their proxy for future arm or rover operations. They included capabilities in the electronic procedures that are not currently available, such as automatic multi-step execution or verification and control of current robot system states (e.g., arm configuration, camera control). The primary objective of this project was to provide empirical evidence supporting design guidelines for automated electronic checklists for robotics operations. While planning to use the ISS robotic arm operations as their proxy for general arm or rover operations but they will develop scenarios that test a crew’s ability to operate more autonomously than in ISS operations. This study had the following two specific aims: Develop a prototype display for robotics operations that integrated the electronic procedures with the displays for performing robotic tasks. The design process began with a hierarchical task analysis
approach: to drive out functional and information requirements for the display. Additionally, critical system states were identified using “Object-Process Methodology,” a task modeling approach that extends the task analysis to a computable level. We augmented our prototype design with the capability for automated execution of procedural steps. This prototype was integrated into the MIT (Massachusetts Institute of Technology) ISS robotic workstation simulation that has previously been used in several National Space Biomedical Research Institute (NSBRI) projects. Perform a human-in-the-loop study that provided empirical evidence about the effects of the prototype system architecture, including varying levels of automation, on task performance, operator situation awareness, and mental workload. The study investigated how the allocation of procedural step execution between human operator and automation affects situation awareness (SA), mental workload, and task performance. Shifting more procedure steps to the automation may ease workload and speed task completion, but may also degrade the operator’s SA and ability to detect and resolve errant conditions. The experiment scenario included interrupting events that required switching between different procedures. APPROACH: Initial efforts focused on developing a prototype electronic procedure system with new automated capabilities and integrating this capability into the robotic workstation simulator. First, informed by actual robotic arm procedures conducted on the ISS, investigators defined and developed a set of robotic task scenarios that includes system setup, support of a series of simulated spacewalk activities, and system shutdown. Within these scenarios, the possibility for a variety of failures and associated failure recovery steps were designed and built into the simulation so that they can test responses to non-normal situations. Investigators used tools including Hierarchical Task Analysis (HTA) and Object-Process Methodology (OPM) to break down each task goal into its components and necessary actions and to define system states throughout the flow of the simulated robotic arm operation. Secondly, investigators used the HTA and OPM analyses to design the computer code that creates the simulated integrated control panel and procedure checklist system. In doing so, they created a new type of human-machine electronic procedure interface that integrates automation and system information into an electronic display. By integrating a functional electronic control panel, procedure, and checklist into their simulator, they created a system that presents information equivalent to two separate systems and laptops that are currently used on the ISS during robotic operations. This, in turn, reduces the required number of displays and equipment, an important feature for future space missions that will have strict mass and power constraints. Following the development of the prototype automated electronic procedure system, investigators completed a human-in-the-loop experiment to investigate how the allocation of procedural step execution between the human operator and automation, or level of automation, would affect task performance, situation awareness, and mental workload. The key independent variable in the experiment was the level of automation used during task completion. The simulator was capable of allocating the automation to perform all or a subset of the procedural steps including state selection, identification verification, and confirmation. Three levels of automation were tested--Full Auto, Full Manual, and Auto Set/ Manual Verify. If the automation was tasked with doing all of the procedure steps, then the system is in Full Auto mode in which we expected low subject mental workload and high performance but also low situation awareness. In Full Manual mode, all steps were allocated to the human operator, and we expected high situation awareness but also high workload and possibly lower task performance. In the intermediate automation allocation, Auto Set/ Manual Verify, the automation was tasked with setting the states while the human operator verified the state change. In this intermediate automation level, investigators expected high task performance and situation awareness, and intermediate workload.
results: Results are largely consistent with the investigators' initial hypotheses, that Full Automation mode results in faster task completion times with practically no errors and low subject mental workload, measured objectively with a visual secondary task and subjectively using the NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX). The reduction in completion time comes primarily from the automatic selection of cameras and entry of arm parameters for Space Station Remote Manipulator System (SSRMS) movement performed by the automation, rather than manually. The elimination of manual control tasks reduces the visual demands of the task and frees attentional resources for monitoring system state and task progress. This behavior was observed in the improvement of the operator’s ability to detect system events and states in the Full Manual condition. However, the use of automation also degraded the operator’s ability to comprehend of current system state and predict future states compared to Full Manual mode. The intermediate automation mode, Auto Set/Manual Verify, was generally preferred by the subjects as the best compromise to speed up task completion while maintain their situation awareness of the task and also resulted in the best overall performance across time, workload, and awareness.

title: Etiology of Back Pain in Microgravity
variables: Size, length; Bone, spine, Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI)
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: The purpose of this experiment was to develop a balanced traction to elongate the spine to the degree experienced by astronauts. The effects of traction on the spine exposed to the 6 degree head down tilt (HDT) model is compared to effects on the spine with traction and horizontal bed rest (HBR). The second part of this study (ARCbedrest129) was designed to determine the electrical activity and intramuscular pressures of the muscles along the lumbar spine while upright and while in 6 o HDT or HBR position.
approach: Healthy volunteers were tested in the MRI before and after 3 days exposure to a balanced traction device that placed a load on the spine by suspending a load corresponding to 5% of the body weight from each leg with a cable-pulley system. The volunteer was at bed rest in the 6 o HDT or in HBR position. Activity was not restricted. HDT with traction was compared with HBR with traction. The second part of the study conducted a few days after this one estimated the electrical activity of lumbar spine muscle through surface electrodes for specified hours of normal activity. Through a catheter inserted into the muscle on either side of the lumbar spine, the pressures were recorded during upright and then at three time intervals during of HDT or HBR. Electrical activity was recorded concurrent with intramuscular pressure. Subjects were randomized into 2 groups of three. Group 1 underwent HBR followed by HDT in balanced traction. Group II underwent HDT in balanced traction followed by HBR. There was a two-week recovery period between the two forms of 3d-bed rest.
results: Repeated measures ANOVA indicated that total body length increased more (mean±SE) during HDT with balanced traction (22±8 mm) than during HBR (16±4 mm). Spine length between L5 and C7 also increased more during HDT with traction (25±8 and 14±9 mm). Ultrasonography showed increases in lumbar disc height during HDT and HBR (2.9±0.8 mm vs. 3.3±0.6 mm), but there were no differences among groups. Seventy percent of the increase in disc height occurred during the first 5 hours of bed rest. Within the first hour of standing, there was a 10 mm decrease in body height, about 80% of the normal diurnal variation in our subjects. The intensity of pain in the back, abdomen and head was greater during HDT with traction than during HBR with traction. Reflexes were normal in both groups. Intramuscular pressure in erector spinae muscles that averaged 8.4±0.7 mm Hg did not change during the study and was similar in HBR and HDT. Ankle joint torque during plantar- and dorsi-flexion did not change during the study and was similar in HBR and HDT with balanced traction. Conclusions: Results suggest that HDT with balanced traction may combine the advantages of both models to simulate total body and spinal lengthening, as well as back pain associated with microgravity. Note: Both studies were carried out on the same group of subjects. The measurements of intra muscular pressure in HR 129 were reported separately, but the protocols for each study were the same. Therefore, it is more complete to have both HR 117 and HR 129 reported together as the first part and the second part of the study as described.

title: Hardware Evaluation: International Space Station Portable Pulmonary Function System (PPFS)
variables: Fractions of expired oxygen and carbon dioxide
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: The National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Human Research Program’s Integrated Research Plan specifies that acquisition of data regarding the changes in maximum exercise oxygen consumption (VO2max) during and following space flight is a high priority to support future space exploration endeavors. In order to support such measurements, a metabolic gas analysis system capable of being used in a spacecraft is required. One such device, known as the Pulmonary Function System, was developed for International Space Station (ISS) use and was validated in the Exercise Physiology Laboratory at NASA-Johnson Space Center (JSC). The PFS is currently being used to support studies of resting metabolism and cardiac function on board the ISS, but is not portable and is confined to a relatively immobile rack location. The exercise equipment on board the ISS changed locations since earlier expeditions, and the cycle ergometer used for exercise testing was moved to a different module than the PFS. Thus, the need for a portable metabolic gas analysis device for ISS use arose. The Portable Pulmonary Function System (PPFS) was developed by a contractor to the European Space Agency (ESA) to fill this need. The PPFS is a sized-optimized variant of the PFS which is capable of being used in any location on board the ISS that has available power and data connections. Aerobic capacity (VO2pk) is determined by two factors: the body’s ability to deliver oxygen to the working muscles, and the muscles’ ability to extract that oxygen. In normal subjects, cardiac output, or the amount of blood the body is able to pump per minute, increases with increasing workload providing a relationship between cardiac output and VO2pk. During long-duration space flight and bed rest, changes in the cardiovascular system lead to a decrease in aerobic capacity. The Exercise Physiology Laboratory prepared for an investigation designed to study the changes in VO2pk and cardiac output during space flight. The flight study is titled “Evaluation of Maximal Oxygen Uptake (VO2max) and Submaximal Estimates of VO2max Before, During and After Long Duration International Space Station Mission.” In order to measure these changes, a new portable metabolic gas analysis system, the Portable Pulmonary Function System (PPFS) was used to measure both VO2pk and cardiac output. The purpose of this study was to determine the accuracy of PPFS measurements.
approach: Subjects performed an initial peak cycle test protocol used to determine pre-flight VO2max for astronauts. The cycle ergometer used for all testing was a LODE Excalibur Sport (Groningen, NL). During the initial test, subjects with a body mass of > 65 kg, cycled for three minutes at 50, 100, and 150 Watts (W) followed by an increase of 25 W every minute until peak exertion was reached. If the subject’s body mass was © (ParvoMedics, Salt Lake City, UT) system was used to perform metabolic gas analysis. The VO2and work rate data from the test was used to prescribe the protocol for the second and third tests. The second and third tests were trials designed for comparison of the metabolic gas analysis systems and cardiac output measurements. The testing protocol used was an extension to maximum of the ISS periodic fitness evaluation (PFE) test. The comparison tests consisted of three five minute stages designed to elicit 25%, 50%, and 75% of the individual’s previously determined VO2max. These three stages are identical to those of the ISS PFE test. These stages were followed by 25W/min work rate increases until subjects reached their maximum. Comparison tests were performed in a counterbalanced order, with one test performed using the ParvoMedics TrueOne © system paired with echocardiography (Phillips iE-33™) to measure Qc, and one test performed using the PPFS to obtain metabolic gas analysis data and Qc measurements using a re-breathing technique. These tests were conducted within one month after the initial test, and were separated by at least one week in order to minimize the potential effects of residual soreness or fatigue. For all tests, prior to the start of exercise, subjects rested quietly for five minutes in the supine and the seated position while resting measurements of heart rate (HR) and rhythm and blood pressure (BP) were taken. HR and rhythm were measured electrocardiographically (Q-Stress, Quinton Instruments, Seattle, WA) and BP was measured using a mercurial sphygmomanometer and stethoscope. HR and rhythm and metabolic expired gas were measured continuously throughout the exercise test protocol. BP was measured one time each stage and ratings of perceived exertion were reported during the last 30 seconds of each stage. In the recovery period, BP was recorded and the subject was monitored for any adverse effects caused by maximal exertion.
results: All of the metabolic gas analysis data, irrespective of the device used for measurement, fell within normal physiological ranges. Thus, there are no gross errors present in either the PPFS or the Parvomedics device. In general, the PPFS-measured absolute values of VO2 were lower than those measured by the Parvomedics system. Please refer to website http://ntrs.nasa.gov/ for the NASA Technical Paper, which includes graphs, charts, and more detailed information regarding this experiment.

title: Magnifying Lens Study
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: The purpose of this study was to observe changes in the relationship between head and eye movements due to wearing 2.2x magnifying telescopic lenses. This study was conducted in the late 1980’s. Pre-studies were conducted with in-house subjects prior to the Magnifying Lenses Study which was composed of 10 subjects.
approach: Study 1, Magnifying Lenses Study: 5 in-house subjects participated in this study. Each subject had electrodes placed above and below the right eye. Dark adaptation was accomplished by the subject wearing red goggles for 20 minutes prior to data collection. The subject was placed approximately 26 inches from a center target with 1 LED 3.25 inches above and below it. After a pre-test eye calibration (tracking LEDs with eyes), rectangular head calibration (moving head up and down and pausing at limits) and a sinusoidal head calibration (moving head back and forth between limits as directed by a tone @0.5 hz and +/- 7.5 deg displacement), an initial baseline was collected for fixation of an actual target condition and fixation of an imaginary target condition. At this point, the subjects donned the magnifying goggles. Red plastic was placed behind the lenses to maintain dark adaptation. Data was collected immediately for both actual and imaginary fixation conditions. Hereafter, data was collected every 8 minutes for both target conditions. After 40 minutes the magnifying goggles were removed and the red goggles were immediately donned. Data was immediately collected at 0, 8 and 16 minutes for both target conditions. Each test concluded with post-test and eye calibrations. This protocol is unique in that it requires the subject to focus on a center target while making voluntary pitching head movements as directed by a tone. A “beep” at each limit helped the subject match the head movement with the tone. The head movements and the fixation on the center target were continuous throughout the entire test. During the data collection, which lasted 55 seconds, the subjects were asked to fixate an actual or imagined target without blinking. Blinking was acceptable during times data was not collected. Study 2, Shorter Duration Magnifying Lenses Study: This protocol was modified from the earlier one. The duration of the test protocol was approximately 35 mins. Five in-house subjects participated in this study. Each subject had electrodes placed above and below the right eye. Dark adaptation was accomplished by the subject wearing red goggles for 20 minutes prior to data collection. The subject was placed approximately 26 inches from a center target with 1 LED 3.25 inches above and below it. After a pre-test eye calibration (tracking LEDs with eyes) and a sinusoidal head calibration (moving head back and forth between limits as directed by a tone@ 0.5 hz and +/- 7.5 deg displacement), an initial baseline was collected for fixation of an actual target condition and fixation of an imaginary target condition. At this point the subjects donned the magnifying goggles. (Red plastic was placed behind the lenses to maintain dark adaptation.) Data was collected immediately for both actual and imaginary fixation conditions. After 2 mins, data was again collected for both actual and imaginary fixation conditions. At this point, the magnifying lenses were donned and data was collected for both fixation conditions at 0, 5, and 10 mins (after donning the magnifying lenses). After 10 mins, the magnifying lenses were removed, and the subjects donned the original dark adaptation goggles. Data was collected for both fixation conditions 0 and 3 mins after removing the magnifying lenses. Each test concluded with post-test head and eye calibrations. This protocol is unique in that it required the subject to focus on a center target while making voluntary pitching head movements as directed by a tone. A “beep” at each limit helped the subject match the head movement with the tone. The head movements and the fixation o the center target were continuous throughout the entire test. During the data collections, which lasted 55 seconds, the subjects were asked to fixate an actual or imagined target without blinking. Blinking was acceptable during times data was not collected. Study 3, Magnifying Lenses Study After Wearing Lenses During 1 Hour of Normal Routine Activities: Two in-house subjects participated in this study. Each subject had electrodes placed above and below the right eye. Dark adaptation was accomplished by the subject wearing red goggles for 20 minutes prior to data collection. The subject was placed approximately 26 inches from a center target with 1 LED 3.25 inches above and below it. Data was collected in two separate sessions on the same day. Eye and head calibrations were performed in each session. During Session 1 data was collected at 0, 5, and 10 mins after initiating pitching head movements for both actual and imaginary fixation conditions. After completing data collection in Session 1, the subject was disconnected from the head and eye movement monitoring system and donned the magnifying lenses. The subject wore the magnifying lenses for 1 hour, performing normal routine activities at work (walking, reaching for objects, etc.). After the 1 hour of wearing the lenses, the subject was reconnected to the head and eye movement monitoring system. Data was collected at 0, 4, and 10 mins after initiating pitching head movements for both actual and imaginary fixation conditions. The magnifying goggles were then removed and replaced by the original dark adaptation goggles. Data collection for both fixation conditions was collected at 0, 5, and 10 mins after removal of the magnifying goggles. This protocol required the subject to focus on a center (actual or imagined) target while making voluntary pitching head movements as directed by a tone. A “beep” at each limit helped the subject match the head movement with the tone. The head movements and the fixation on the center target were continuous only during the two separate test sessions. During the data collections, which lasted 55 seconds, the subjects were asked to fixate an actual or imaged target without blinking. Blinking was acceptable during times data was not collected. Passive Pitch Magnifying Lens Study Method: Test subjects were recruited for two 1-hour (approximate) test sessions. During one test session the subjects wore the magnifying lenses. During the other test session, the subject wore dark adaptation goggles. The subjects wore electrodes by placing infant EKG electrodes (silver/silver-chloride) above and below each left eye after scrubbing the surface of the skin around the eye with an alcohol swab. After electroding, the subjects dark adapted for 20 minutes, using the standard red goggles. Each subject was then restrained in a comfortable position in the prototype Mode C PAT chair. At this time the LEDS were attached. The subject either continued to wear the red goggles or exchanged them for the magnifying lens goggles. (The starting condition of wearing the magnifying lenses or the dark adaptation goggles was alternated between subjects. The subjects never wore the magnifying lenses until they were seated in the Mode C. The dark adaptation is maintained throughout the test as red plastic is placed in front of the magnifying lenses.) A Velcro foam-padded strap secured the subject’s head to the chair rest. An eye calibration system consisting of two leads and a center target were placed in the center of the subject’s field of view. The subjects directed which way the system should be moved (up, down, left, right,) so that both LEDs could be seen and the center target was in their straight-ahead gaze. The magnifying lenses established the viewing constraints due to the limited field of view (approximately 15 degs). The LEDS were placed vertically approximately 2.5 inches apart and approximately 32 inches from the subject. Data was not ready to be collected. The subjects were instructed to gaze at the center target while the amplifier was reset. When the LEDs lit, the subjects were instructed to track the lights, trying to make clean, smooth, and sharp eye movements. The subjects were instructed to fixate on the particular LED that was lit at the time until the next one came on, trying not to anticipate the lighting of the other LED. The subjects were instructed that they should not move their head in any way during the 30 minute test. During each test, data (eye calibrations) was collected 6 times over 30 minutes. The duration of each data collection was 30 seconds. Between data collections, the subjects were passively pitched for 5 minutes in the Mode C at a frequency of 0.5 hz and an amplitude of +/- 7.5 degs. During the passive tilt, the subjects fixated on the center target.
results: Although not clear in all cases, it appears that there is a much greater decrease in amplitude across time when the subjects wear the magnifying lenses than when they wear the standard dark adaptation goggles.

title: Use of Fludrocortisone or Salt Load to Expand Plasma Volume in Ambulatory Subjects
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: It is known that a fall in blood pressure occurs after space flight on return to Earth's gravity. This is associated with a reduced volume of plasma, an adaptation made for the weightless environment, and currently restored by the ingestion of large volumes of water and salt tablets on landing. Earlier work revealed that the synthetic corticosteroid, flurocortisone, clinically useful in patients with low blood pressure, could expand plasma volume in subjects exposed to the bed rest model for space flight. The purpose of this study was to compare the effectiveness of salt ingestion with the administration of a synthetic corticosteroid to prevent orthostatic hypotension.
approach: A previous study (HR77) had tested 4 subjects with fludrocortisone (Florinef) and 4 subjects with a saline load after 7 days of – 6o bed rest. Florineff restored plasma volume to pre-bedrest levels, but a saline load did not. The response in ambulatory subjects was opposite to this post bed rest response. This study plans to repeat the earlier study in the same subjects, reversing the protocol (giving Florinef to subjects who were treated with a saline load before and giving a saline load to subjects treated with Florinef earlier).
