Postflight assessments were conducted immediately before and immediately after rehabilitation if crewmembers had not returned to preflight levels by R+29.
results: from these exercise tests showed decreases from baseline in aerobic condition (heart rate responses to individualized standard work rates) of the Skylab 2 crew during and after flight. The Skylab 3 crew increased the amount of inflight exercise and showed no change in aerobic condition during the flight, but showed a decrease postflight. On Skylab 4, 2 of the 3 crewmembers completed a greater volume of exercise than the crew of Skylab 3. The inflight exercises produced a physiologically significant increase (22%) in inflight peak oxygen consumption (VO 2peak ) and peak work rate (20%) for one crewmember, while the other two showed a slight upward trend (3-6% and 0-2%, respectively) during the flight. This data, in conjunction with an insignificant change in postflight submaximal heart rate (3 to 9 BPM higher than preflight), may suggest an uncoupling between aerobic capacity and cardiovascular adjustments to exercise postflight. However, there were no studies that compared the inflight and postflight submaximal and peak responses of these linked systems. Thus, two hypotheses were drawn based on the Skylab results: 1) The inflight cardiorespiratory responses to supine cycling will not be different than pre- and postflight values where posture is not a part of the testing. 2) The inflight cardiorespiratory responses to treadmill exercise will be different than pre- and postflight values where posture is a part of ground-based testing. A 1977 Russian study evaluated a Russian "micro-cycle" countermeasure program. This program provided the equivalent volume of exercise as running 12.9 km (8 miles) per day for three consecutive days for a 70 kg person (no exercise was done on the fourth day). Exercising subjects maintained their baseline work capacity levels after 45 days at -4° head down tilt bed rest (the effects of head down tilt bed rest is a close approximation to effects of weightlessness). A 1980 Russian study used a slightly reduced countermeasure protocol. The average volume of exercise for this study was equivalent to running 10 km (6.2 miles) per day, for approximately 6 days per week for a 70 kg person. Exercising U.S. subjects reported this amount of exercise to be greater than the average amount of preflight exercise, which is equivalent to approximately 3-4 miles per day for 3-4 days per week. The subjects showed a decrease in heart rates (91% of the maximal heart rate to 47%) when evaluated at a constant work rate. This data suggested that the subject showed an increase in aerobic capacity. The micro-cycle countermeasure program was used during a yearlong Mir flight. The heart rate response to standard exercise increased during flight, suggesting a decrease in exercise conditioning. Adherence to the micro-cycle program, as well as postflight aerobic responses, was not reported. A 1992 report by Siconolfi and Charles reported that astronauts were able to maintain the VO 2peak levels after 7 to 11 days of space flight, even when the volume of inflight exercise was equivalent to only 25-75% of their preflight exercise volumes. The ability to maintain aerobic responses on short-duration flights might not require the higher than normal volumes or intensities used on the longer duration Skylab 4 and Russian flights. Given the long duration of the Mir flight, and the high volume of exercise in the Russian countermeasure program, a third hypothesis was proposed: 3) The Russian countermeasure program will increase aerobic capacity during the flight and this increase will be evident after the flight. The main objective of this investigation was, therefore, to evaluate whether exercise countermeasures would mitigate the normally observed decreases in cardiorespiratory responses to exercise associated with long-duration exposure to microgravity. Aerobic capacity was assessed from a graded exercise test performed on a cycle ergometer (CYCLE protocol), as well as a modification of the Russian treadmill test (SPORT protocol). Heart rate (ECG) and metabolic gas analysis were recorded. The gas analysis included measurement of oxygen consumption (VO 2 ), carbon dioxide output (VCO 2 ), expired volume (V E ), and respiratory rate (RR). All measurements were repeated during the first minute of recovery. Resting (supine) heart rate (HR) and blood pressure were assessed before exercise. Preflight baseline data collection (BDC) occurred at 120, 32 and 31 before flight for the Mir 18 crew. Postflight BDC occurred at 5, 6, 12, and 15 days after landing (table 1). One inflight data collection session occurred on FD5 of STS-71; all other inflight data collection sessions were canceled due to time constraints. Postflight assessments were conducted immediately before and immediately after rehabilitation if crewmembers had not returned to preflight levels by R+29. RESULTS: Before Flight versus After Flight (table 2) Subject A (90% Exercise Countermeasures): External work (speed and watt) and associated internal work (VO 2peak ) decreased. At a standard work rate (CYCLE protocol) efficiency was maintained with slight increases in arteriovenous oxygen difference (a-vO 2 ) and HR. At self-selected exercise rates (SPORT protocol), VO 2 was maintained while external work (speed) had a slight increase. However, capillary flow (Q C ) decreased (mainly due to HR) but was totally moderated with an increase in a-vO 2 . The slower HR decreased Q C , but allowed greater extraction of O 2 by the tissues (a-vO 2 ). This may support training-induced maintenance of blood volume. Subject B (70% Exercise Countermeasures): External work (speed and watts) and associated internal work (VO 2peak ) decreased. At a standard work rate (CYCLE protocol), efficiency decreases were linked to decreases in Q C , mainly due to stroke volume (SV), but this was somewhat moderated with an increase in a-vO 2 . At self-selected exercise rates (SPORT protocol) VO 2 was maintained while external work (speed) had a slight increase. However, Q C decreased (mainly due to SV) but was totally moderated with an increase in a-vO 2 . This is similar to classical detraining. Subject A versus B Comparisons: External work (speed and watt) and associated internal work (VO 2peak ) decreased. Seventy percent (70%) compliance (by self report) to the exercise countermeasures did not prevent cardiorespiratory deconditioning, indicated at both peak and submaximal exercise responses, while 90% compliance was more, but not completely, effective. Exercise countermeasures may have been effective by maintaining stroke volume. Self-selected peak running speeds showed a decrement in external work 5 days after flight without a concomitant decrease in metabolic work. This may suggest a change in biomechanics or neuromuscular function (figure 5). CYCLE provides standard work rates for comparisons (e.g. efficiency), while the SPORT protocol provided neuromuscular evaluation or perceived work that has a greater operational impact. Before Flight versus During Flight (table 3) Results from the SPORT protocol demonstrated a clear differentiation between a subject's compliance to exercise countermeasures while the CYCLE test had a more mixed result. Not all in-flight parameters could predict the after flight responses. This suggested that ground-based testing and in-flight testing are not equivalent. The effects of long-duration space flight should be evaluated before versus after flight and early versus late (flight days). This may impact how exercise countermeasures are monitored during long-duration flight. Note that supine cycling, which is thought to represent microgravity testing, did not produce similar responses during the flight. Conclusions The sample size of this investigation was too small to make general inferences for long-duration space flight; however, the following results apply to the three subjects: (1) subjects completing a greater percentage of the prescribed exercise were closer to preflight levels of performance, (2) maintenance of submaximal performance, regardless of modality, appears to be linked to stroke volume, and (3) both CYCLE and SPORT protocols should be continued because they independently assess different--cardiorespiratory and neuromuscular--aspects of performance.

title: Visuo-Motor Coordination during Space Flight
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Astronauts have reported that visuo-motor performance degrades early in a space mission. During later stages of the flight, gross motor skills fully recover, while fine motor skills remain disturbed. Little quantitative data is available on visuo-motor performance in weightlessness. During the brief microgravity episodes of parabolic flight, individuals performing simple pointing movements, while prevented from viewing their hands, produced movements that were consistently deviated upwards. Pointing responses produced after several hours of Space Shuttle flight exhibited no such bias. In contrast, performance in a demanding compensatory-tracking exercise remained degraded throughout a 13-day mission. The Visuo-Motor Coordination During Space Flight experiment was one of three Sensory Motor and Performance investigations performed during the 1998 Neurolab mission. By identifying and analyzing motor-skill compensation and motor-skill deficiencies, investigators will learn more about the dependence of human motor functions on normal gravity and the adaptation to weightlessness. Furthermore, this will extend the knowledge of how prolonged exposure to microgravity impacts sensory motor performance. Information to be gained from this experiment is important to investigators who seek to better understand the role of gravity as a fundamental reference frame for spatial orientation and the adaptive capabilities of the human visuo-motor system. The information is also of potential value to scientists seeking insight into the limitations of visuo-motor performance in humans on Earth. In addition, testing devices, such as those developed for this experiment, will be valuable for assessing motor disorders in Earth-based patients.
approach: Using the Visuo-Motor Coordination Facility (VCF), investigators assessed changes in the eye-hand coordination of astronauts during their adaptation to microgravity. As the VCF projected visual targets onto a screen, astronauts pointed at the targets as they moved from place to place, grasped at them as they changed in size, and tracked them as they moved in a circle. During the test, the subject wore a specially designed glove that allowed precise tracking of hand movements and response times. The glove, equipped with light emitting diodes (LEDs) at the thumb and index fingertips, provided a trail that was recorded by the VCF. Other hardware included two cameras, a video-analysis system based on the Sharp-CORE board, and a PC compatible computer. The computer reconstructed 3-D locations from 2-D data and stored the
results: on a disk; it also generated the stationary and moving targets of various sizes and shapes that the subject tracked on the screen. The Visuo-Motor Coordination (VMC) of Neurolab crewmembers was evaluated at 30, 29, 15 and 14 days before launch, on Flight Days 1, 7, and 14 and on the day of landing, as well as 2 and 9 days after landing to detect changes in performance and chronicle the adaptation of the nervous system as the subject adjusted to microgravity. During the test sessions, subjects performed exercises including double-step pointing, double-step grasping, circular tracking, and a group of reaction time tasks. During double-step pointing, the subject pointed an index finger at sequentially presented visual targets that suddenly changed location. For double-step grasping, the subject used the thumb and index fingertips to grasp at a target that, in a percentage of trials, changed size. For circular tracking, the subject tracked targets that moved in circular paths with the index finger. For the reaction time tasks, the subject quickly pressed the hand reaction switch when the targets changed. Reaction time tasks included predictive hand tracking in a reaction-time task, predictive eye tracking in a reaction time task, and a general reaction-time task. For the Predictive Hand Tracking in a Reaction-Time task, the subject tracked, by hand, a target moving along a predictable trajectory. For the Predictive Eye Tracking in a Reaction-Time task, the subject visually tracked a target moving along a predictable trajectory. For the general Reaction-Time task, the subject observed a stationary target in the center of the computer screen. RESULTS: Twelve of 12 nominally scheduled sessions were performed by the payload crewmembers. Five additional sessions were performed by the Orbiter crewmembers. Data appear to be of good quality based on initial evaluation while the hardware performed flawlessly. Pointing responses were slowed distinctly in microgravity, but the speed of tracking movements was not affected. The secondary task had comparable effects on tracking performance in space and on Earth.

experiment_type: Shuttle Extended Duration Orbiter Medical Project (EDOMP)

objectives: The primary objective of this investigation was to measure selected hormone and electrolyte components of the blood early in space flight. The blood components selected reflect the status of fluid and electrolyte metabolism. Measurement of these variables may help investigators determine whether responses predicted by the fluid redistribution hypothesis occur. According to this hypothesis, losses of body fluid and electrolytes
approach: The Inflight Blood Collection System was used to collect samples by venipuncture from 6 subjects on 2 missions 1 or 3 times before flight; on mission days 2, 4, and 6 during flight; and within 2 hours (R+0) and 3 days (R+3) after landing. The concentrations of electrolytes and other blood components were determined using established clinical laboratory procedures such as spectrophotometry and radioimmunoassay.
results: from the headward shift of fluid brought about by exposure of the human body to weightlessness. Estimation of early changes previously was not possible because of inflight scheduling priorities and constraints. The most dramatic changes in the adaptive response to weightlessness are believed to occur in the first hours of a mission. APPROACH: The Inflight Blood Collection System was used to collect samples by venipuncture from 6 subjects on 2 missions 1 or 3 times before flight; on mission days 2, 4, and 6 during flight; and within 2 hours (R+0) and 3 days (R+3) after landing. The concentrations of electrolytes and other blood components were determined using established clinical laboratory procedures such as spectrophotometry and radioimmunoassay. RESULTS: The earliest inflight blood collection time of 31 hours may not have been early enough. High levels of antidiuretic hormone (ADH) may have been related to space motion sickness. Angiotensin I levels increased while aldosterone was suppressed at the inflight times measured. Cortisol secretion appeared to have been stimulated by high levels of adrenocorticotropic hormone. Most hormones increased at landing. Serum sodium decreased slightly during flight, and potassium decreased in the first 4 days but increased on flight days 6 and 7. The results, especially those for hormone levels, indicated that the fluid redistribution hypothesis does not explain changes in the regulation of body fluid and electrolytes during weightlessness. Renal function and other factors involved in fluid and electrolyte regulation, such as atrial natriuretic factor and prostaglandin E, need to be measured during flight.

title: Study of In-flight Fluid Changes
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: The objective of the experiment was to assess the redistribution of fluid volumes, including losses and changes in composition and pressure as influenced by the loss of hydrostatic forces during space flight. The investigators wanted to obtain information about body fluid regulation under operational Shuttle conditions. Skylab and ASTP data had shown that a major fluid volume shift occurred before flight day 3(FD3), but the time course of the shift was still not understood. Measurements of changes in leg volume were made pre- and postflight on Apollo 16 and 17 and subsequently on Skylab 2, 3, and 4. The volume measurement was accomplished by using a modification of a measurement system for fitting support stockings. Single-point calf girth measurements were also done in flight on Skylab 2, 3, and 4. The postflight leg volume measurements made on these missions were late in the recovery period after the return of fluid was largely over. On Skylab 4, in-flight changes in leg volume were documented using a tape measure. A repeat of the leg volume study was performed on the Apollo-Soyuz Test Project (ASTP) system. Previous space flights had also suggested that the weightless environment presented significant challenges to man's ability to maintain homeostasis, and included weight loss, increased aldosterone secretion, and loss of sodium and potassium. Furthermore, it was hypothesized that some of the factors involved in fluid metabolism changes were also involved in the space adaptation syndrome (SAS).
approach: The tape measure methodology used in the Skylab and ASTP studies was tedious and time consuming. Because of this, it was not practical to make measurements early on-orbit or at recovery when crew time was limited; however, these were the times when the fluid shift was most critical. There wasn't an opportunity to repeat the studies until the Space Shuttle became operational. Other methods of volume determination, such as water displacement, were impractical in the weightless environment of space or were logistically difficult and time and equipment intensive. A simpler, much more rapid scheme for obtaining volumes was therefore devised and
results: ed in the stocking plethysmograph used during the Shuttle program. The method was first tested on STS-5, and then used on STS-7 and 8, then later routinely used on Shuttle flights. On STS-5, a plastic marking window was used. It was found that it did not produce uniform friction on the measuring tapes, thus introducing significant errors in measurements. A uniform and consistent metal marking window was designed and used on STS-7 and 8. Prior to STS-7, a series of repeatability and validity tests were run to compare the stockings to a tape measure. In addition, the stocking method was compared to the water displacement method. Details about the design of the stocking plethysmograph can be found in Moore TP, Thornton WE. Space shuttle inflight and postflight fluid shifts measured by leg volume changes. Aviation, Space, and Environmental Medicine. 1987. On STS-8, urine collections were done for 3 days preflight, in 12 hour pools throughout the mission, and for 3 days after the flight to determine the time course of the metabolic changes. Urine was collected in bags containing lithium chloride and boric acid. Postflight assays of lithium concentration gave the total void volume, and boric acid served as the preservative. Specimens collected in flight could not be frozen, so aliquots of the pre- and post-flight specimens were kept at room temperature for the duration of the mission and were compared to specimens frozen immediately, to determine the effect of storage conditions. Samples were analyzed for volume, electrolytes, cortisol, aldosterone and antidiuretic hormone (ADH). Records of food and fluid intake were also kept. Approximately 2 hours before landing, a blood sample was drawn into a heparinized tube and was analyzed immediately postflight. RESULTS: The earliest inflight stocking plethysmograph data from STS-7 and 8 was obtained at 11 and 13 hours Mission Elapsed Time (MET). The conclusion was that by the this time inflight, the fluid shift from the legs was essentially complete, since later inflight measurements showed no significant further leg volume loss. As much as 4 liters of fluid shifted from the legs within the first few hours of flight. On STS-8, excretion of ADH and then cortisol increased greatly during the first 24 hours of flight but returned to levels only slightly above normal on the second day. Later the excretion rate of urine volume and then aldosterone increased. The results indicate that homeostatic mechanisms are indeed affected by flight conditions. This experiment was extended to subsequent missions (as DSOs 446 and 461) to further understand the time course of the fluid shift. Results from all 3 experiments can be found under LSDA records for DSOs 446 and 461.

title: Gastrointestinal Function During Extended Duration Space Flight
experiment_type: Shuttle Extended Duration Orbiter Medical Project (EDOMP)
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: The absence of gravity might reduce gastrointestinal motility (the smooth muscle action that mixes the food and propels it through the gastrointestinal tract), which could decrease appetite and absorption of fluids, nutrients, and medications. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effect of space flight on the gastric emptying rate and intestinal transit time.
approach: Two astronauts were studied at 60, 45, and 30 days before launch, on the fifth day of flight and nine days after landing. Their gastric emptying rates were determined by following the concentrations of acetaminophen in their saliva, and of acetaminophen and its metabolites in their urine, after an oral dose of acetaminophen. The absorption rate of this drug after an oral dose is directly proportional to the gastric emptying rate. The concentrations of the drug and its metabolites were measured by high-performance liquid chromatography and analyzed with a pharmacokinetic simulation computer program. Intestinal transit time was measured indirectly with a lactulose-hydrogen breath test. Lactulose is a sugar that passes undigested through the small intestine, but is fermented by bacteria in the colon, producing hydrogen that is then exhaled. The period from the ingestion of lactulose to the peak in breath hydrogen represented the transit time from the mouth to the cecum (the first part of the large intestine). Performing the acetaminophen absorption test and the lactulose-hydrogen breath test at the same time in each subject allowed the intestinal transit time to be determined by subtracting the gastric emptying time from the mouth-to-cecum transit time. These methods had been validated in six subjects in an earlier 10-day head-down bed-rest study.
results: Results from the subjects varied. Gastric emptying seemed to be prompt, as salivary acetaminophen levels peaked within 15 minutes of a dose. Intestinal transit time, however, seemed to increase during the flight. Too few astronauts were studied for conclusions to be drawn. It was recommended for future studies that hydrogen concentrations be measured simultaneously in the breath and in the air inside the spacecraft, that the astronauts provide several baseline breath samples before ingesting lactulose, and that breath samples be collected for longer than four hours after lactulose ingestion.

title: Astronaut Vision Issues and One Carbon Metabolism: Expanded Polymorphism Evaluation and Evaluation in a Potential Analog Population
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Several crewmembers who have flown on long-duration missions to the International Space Station (ISS) have developed ophthalmic issues now identified as Spaceflight Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS). The one-carbon metabolic pathway, a broad set of metabolic reactions responsible for the activation and transfer of one-carbon units for many biosynthetic processes in the body, has been identified as a possible contributor to the development of SANS. This investigation seeks to identify genetic variation in the one-carbon metabolism pathway, the effect of these polymorphisms on enzyme function, and potential relationships to SANS. Additionally, this research will investigate the utility of a clinical population that shares many similar symptoms with SANS: patients with Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS). This investigation will expand upon a previous study, “Risk of visual impairment and intracranial hypertension after space flight: Evaluation of the role of polymorphism of enzymes involved in one-carbon metabolism” (One_Carbon), which examined five single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) and the association with a genetic predisposition for ophthalmic issues among crewmembers. This investigation has four Specific Aims: 1) Test for SNPs of the 85 major genes associated with one-carbon metabolism (a total of 523 SNPs) in ISS crewmembers and relate these data to existing one-carbon biochemistry and metabolomic data, along with existing vision and related medical data. 2) Gather ancestry data from the crewmembers and characterize the extent to which ancestry is predictive of ophthalmic issues after long-duration space flight. 3) Evaluate the data collected in this (and the initial) one-carbon metabolism genetics studies and cardiovascular data. To this end, we will request VO2 max (pre-, in-, and post-flight), Framingham Risk Score, resting heart rate along with diastolic and systolic blood pressure (pre-, in-, and post-flight), exercise heart rate and blood pressure (both diastolic and systolic, pre-, in-, and post-flight), data obtained as part of the Vascular Compliance Study (heart rate, blood pressure, cardiac output and stroke volume), medications, diagnoses, Body Mass Index (BMI), and % body fat data from the Lifetime Surveillance of Astronaut Health (LSAH) project for evaluation relative to the one-carbon genetic and biochemical data. 4) Compare one-carbon metabolism genetics, biochemistry, and ophthalmologic data from ISS crewmembers to the same measures from patients in one of four treatment groups: (1) women diagnosed with PCOS without Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (IIH), (2) women diagnosed with PCOS and IIH, (3) women diagnosed with IIH without PCOS, and (4) control participants diagnosed with neither PCOS nor IIH.
approach: This investigation will examine genetic data from a total of 79 crewmembers who have participated in missions on the ISS. Genetic data for two crewmembers who did not participate in the previous One_Carbon study will be obtained from a fasting blood sample. A medication and supplement log will also be obtained from the participants at this time. Genetic data from the 77 crew who participated in the previous study will be obtained from archived blood samples after those crew have provided consent. Ancestry data will be collected from all subjects via a questionnaire/survey to determine if ancestry is predictive of genetic/ophthalmic issues after long-duration space flight. Consent will also be requested for data sharing of cardiovascular, vision and eye imagery data for evaluation relative to the one-carbon genetic and biochemical data. In the PCOS arm of this study, a total of 150 participants will provide blood samples for biochemical and SNP analysis. Ophthalmologic testing in the PCOS population will include optic nerve ocular coherence tomography, fundus photography, and ultrasound examination, cycloplegic refraction (with visual acuity), and intraocular pressure. The
results: of these analyses will be compared to data from an age-matched control group that is not affected by PCOS or IIH and to the ISS crew data. Per the original PI informed consent briefing, the genetic test data will not be archived with the LSDA. If data is requested for this experiment, must obtain original PI approval and subject must be re-consented. RESULTS: The investigators anticipate the results of this research will help characterize the genetic mechanism that influences the development of SANS in crew during spaceflight and provide guidance for preventing and treating these eye changes in astronauts. Further, this research will expand understanding of genetic influences on the one-carbon metabolic pathway and aid in the treatment and preventing of vision and other related diseases in the broader population.

title: Targeting Protein Cross Talk Signaling as a Biological Predictor for Space Radiation Cancer Risk

objectives: One of the important concerns of 'late effects' after space radiation exposure is the onset of cancers. Investigators proposed that two key proteins, nuclear factor kappa Beta (NF-kB) and tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-a), sequentially co-ordinate and control this cascade of events. A novel role of these proteins in radiation-induced tumor development is identified through recent in vitro and in vivo studies after low linear energy transfer (LET) radiation exposure. In this project investigators addressed: (i) how low doses of high LET radiation trigger initial damage signals that remain persistent and are maintained in the memory of the cell/tissue, (ii) how these signals are amplified, (iii) how these amplified signals are transmitted to
approach: es, in which irradiated normal vascular endothelial cells in an intact tissue setup or organ culture will be allowed to communicate with the co-existing non-targeted normal or pro-tumorigenic cells from lung, skin, and breast tissue. This study had the following specific aims: Study the significance of low doses (0, 0.2, 0.4, or 0.8 Gy) of high-LET radiation exposure on an altered autocrine signaling mechanism that initiates, amplifies, and sustains a positive feedback cycle, i.e., triggering NF-kB -->TNF-a --> NF-kB signaling in the targeted cells.
