title: The Role of the Bone Marrow Microenvironment in Space Radiation-Induced Leukemogenesis
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Hematopoietic stem cells (HSC) comprise less than 0.1% of the bone marrow (BM) of adults, yet they produce all blood cells that are responsible for constant maintenance and immune protection of the body. In addition to the requirement for high cell output, the concentration of the different blood cell lineages produced are precisely controlled to allow not only preservation of normal homeostasis, but also the prompt response to specific stimuli and demands. Previous studies have suggested that exposure to galactic cosmic radiation (GCR) and solar particle event (SPE) radiation that occur or may potentially occur during space flight may increase the likelihood of carcinogenesis, with leukemia being one of the most frequent radiogenic cancers, and the ones with the smallest latency period. The investigators hypothesize that GCR and SPE radiation can have a deleterious impact not only at the level of the mature immune cells and their committed progenitors, as is currently thought, but at the earlier developmental stage of the HSC. Genetic lesions induced by this exposure can lead directly to leukemic transformation, and may also cause these cells to generate a functionally compromised immune system lacking the ability to effectively fight challenges such as pre-leukemic transformations and viral/bacterial infections. As such, investigators hypothesize that astronauts would be doubly at risk, due to both the potential for induction of leukemia by SPE/GCR radiation, and the reduced ability of the astronauts’ immune systems to identify and eliminate malignant cells or pathogens in the body.
approach: In ground-based studies performed at NASA Space Radiation Laboratory (NSRL) and Wake Forest, investigators spent four years assessing the risk of leukemogenesis from space radiation by examining the effects of simulated SPE/GCR exposures on human hematopoiesis, testing the hypothesis that the quality and quantity of cells being produced can be altered not only from direct exposure of HSC themselves, but also via indirect, biological bystander effects arising from exposure of MSC within the critical hematopoietic niche. Human HSC and MSC were immunomagnetically-sorted with antibodies to CD34 and Stro-1 respectively and exposed to: A) sham irradiation; B) 1 Gy of 137Cs gamma-irradiation (LET = 0.91 keV/µm); C) 1 Gy of 50 MeV protons (primary SPE energy; LET = 1.26 keV/µm); D) 20 cGy of 1 GeV/n 56Fe ions (model GCR radiation; LET = 151 keV/µm); or E) 1 Gy of 50 MeV protons followed 15 minutes later by 20 cGy of 1 GeV/n 56Fe ions at NSRL. Immediately following irradiation, aliquots of HSC and MSC were cultured for chromosomal aberration (CA) analyses and DNA/RNA isolations, one aliquot of HSC was immediately assessed for functionality/ differentiative potential using the highly sensitive and quantitative, luminescence-based Hemogenix HALO® assay, and the remainder of the cells were placed in an MSC-based HSC maintenance/expansion culture system, testing four different combinations: 1) unirradiated HSC plated over unirradiated MSC; 2) unirradiated HSC plated over irradiated MSC; 3) irradiated HSC plated over unirradiated MSC; and 4) irradiated HSC plated over irradiated MSC. Hematopoietic cells were then collected after seven days, and methylcellulose or HALO® assays were used to assess the impact of irradiation of the HSC, the MSC, or both cell types on hematopoietic colony-forming potential.
results: Direct Effects on Human HSC: Methylcellulose and HALO® assay data showed that gamma-rays and 50 MeV protons exerted fairly similar effects on HSC function, both reducing by 50–80% the ability of HSC to form both more primitive (HPP-CFC and CFU-GEMM) colonies, as well as more differentiated myeloid (CFU-GM), erythroid (BFU-E), megakaryo-cyte/platelet (CFC-Mk), and lymphoid (CFC-T and CFC-B) colony types. The marked deleterious effect of protons on the ability of human HSC to give rise to cells of the T and B lymphoid lineages is of particular note, given the body of published work showing that astronauts, even on fairly short missions, exhibit pronounced immune alterations. In contrast to the result seen with gamma-rays and 50 MeV protons, 1 GeV/n 56Fe ions had much less pronounced effect on HSC colony-forming potential, exerting no significant effect on their ability to give rise to the most primitive HPP-CFC colonies, but reducing the colony-forming potential in the remaining lineages by 20–40%, depending upon the specific colony type. Exposing sequentially to protons then iron ions, however, proved to be highly deleterious to HSC function, reducing the ability of HSC to produce all colony types by 80–90%. This decrease was, in all cases statistically different than the effects seen with either iron ions alone or protons alone. Indirect/Biological Bystander Effects on Hematopoiesis following Exposure of the Niche to SPE/GCR: Irradiation of MSC with gamma-rays or protons produced similar effects on the most primitive HSC, reducing HPP-CFC output 30–40%. Importantly, irradiation of both HSC and MSC produced a negative additive effect on the most primitive HSC, reducing HPP-CFC output ~75%. The results with 56Fe ions were far more unexpected, as irradiation of MSC alone reduced HPP-CFC output 30%, yet co-culture of both irradiated HSC and MSC somehow restored the HPP-CFC potential. Additive Negative Effects on Hematopoiesis Following Sequential Exposure to SPE then GCR Radiation: Perhaps the most remarkable results came from the sequential treatment with protons and iron ions. While sequential treatment reduced HPP-CFC output 70%, treating the MSC with this sequential dosing regimen actually increased HPP-CFC output of the co-culture roughly 20%. Unexpectedly, however, co-culturing HSC and MSC that had both been sequentially exposed to both ions resulted in an 80% reduction in HPP-CFC output. Very similar results were obtained when the investigators examined the next most primitive colony type, CFU-GEMM, and more differentiated myeloid CFU-GM. Striking results were also obtained when they examined the effect proton and iron ion irradiation of the MSC had upon co-cultured HSC’s ability to generate megakaryocyte and lymphoid (CFC-T and CFC-B) colonies. Alterations to Human Hematopoiesis Assessed in vivo: The investigators conditioned NOD/SCID/IL-2rgamma null (NSG) mice by administering 2 sequential doses of busulfan spaced 24 hours apart. Conditioned NSG mice were then transplanted with 2x10(5) human HSC that had been exposed to one of the following irradiation schemes (n=9 per group) at the NSRL: 1) sham irradiation; 2) 1 Gy of 137Cs gamma-irradiation; 3) 1 Gy of 50 MeV protons; 4) 20 cGy of 1 GeV/n 56Fe ions; or 5) 1Gy of 50 MeV protons followed immediately by 20 cGy of 1 GeV/n 56Fe ions. Mice were then sacrificed at 4–6 months post-transplant, their spleen and bone marrow harvested, and analyzed by multicolor flow cytometry to ascertain the levels of human hematopoietic engraftment and assess whether exposure to SPE/GCR altered the engraftment potential and/or differentiative capacity of the HSC. In addition to affecting overall levels of engraftment, treatment with protons, 56Fe ions, or sequential exposures also led to pronounced skewing of the differentiative potential of the human HSC, as shown by the relative lineage distribution of the engrafted human cells in the bone marrow and spleens of the transplanted mice. Commitment to the erythroid lineage was significantly impaired following exposure of human HSC to all radiation types tested, and there was a significant expansion of both the T and B lineages. In addition to this lineage skewing, 5 of the 14 recipients of 56Fe ion-irradiated human HSC (obtained from 2 different healthy donors) exhibited dramatic splenomegaly, with one mouse’s spleen reaching ~30X the normal size. To ascertain the cause of splenomegaly, spleens were analyzed by histopathology and immunophenotyping. The spleen exhibited an abnormal morphology, populated largely by cells with a rounded, highly monotonous appearance consistent with lymphoid cells. Immuno-histochemistry with human-specific anti-bodies confirmed that the vast majority of the cells populating the spleen were human, and they expressed CD3 and CD7. Many of these cells also expressed terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT), a marker frequently associated clinically with human lymphocytic leukemias. The absence of any staining in an untransplanted NSG mouse spleen stained with the same panel of antibodies verified their specificity. The observed histopathology and immunophenotyping led a team of clinical hematopathologists to concur that human T-ALL developed in these mice. No datasets exist for this experiment. A final report was archived.

title: Advanced EKG
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Cardiac autonomic function and electrical stability will be better preserved in artificial gravity (AG-treated) subjects than in head down bed rest (HDBR) controls.
approach: Supine high-fidelity 12-lead ECG recordings were done for 5 minute durations at 3 time points in this study: Pre-bedrest (BR-07), and post-bedrest (BR+0, BR+4). Breathing was controlled (15 breaths/min = 0.25 Hz). The Mason-Likar electrode configuration was used, as was a sampling rate of 1000 samples/s/channel. An expanded amplifier bandwidth (300 Hz low pass) was used. Electrocardiographic Methods: A conventional ECG was used, plus multiple advanced ECG parameters were measured via specialized software (Cardiosoft). Beat-to-beat heart rate variability (HRV, multiple stochastic & deterministic types) was measured. Other measurements included: beat-to-beat QT interval variability (QTV, with application of SVD to QTV), T-wave morphology by singular value decomposition (SVD) using signal averaging, “SAECG” (including “late potentials” via 12-lead-to-Frank (XYZ) transform), spatial mean QRS/ventricular gradients, spatial QRS-T angles, and other left ventricular mass parameters. High frequency QRS ECG (150-250 Hz) using signal average was done. Estimates of baroreflex sensitivity (BRS) using peak-to-trough excursions in RR intervals during slow breathing (6 breaths/min=0.1 Hz) without a beat-to-beat BP device.
results: Many parameters showed a prominent “day effect”, i.e., effect of head down bed rest (HDBR) itself, but with no “day x group” effect (i.e., no difference in the response between groups). For example, in both groups on BR+0 compared to pre-HDBR, the following parameters showed this effect: (1)Heart rate (2) “Sympathetic” HRV indices [LF/(LF+HF); LF/HF of HRV], ± _QTc interval (mild) and (3) “Parasympathetic” HRV indices and parameters, _“LV mass” parameters by ECG. A relevant “day x group” effect (i.e., effect of countermeasure) was found only for (1) “Mixed” HRV parameters (but only when BR+04 result also included in the ANOVA), (2) QT Variability Index (_QTVI), and (3) possibly for “estimated BRS”. Brief daily AG treatment by short-radius centrifuge during each of 21 days of HDBR does not appear to protect against HDBR-related losses of supine cardiac autonomic function nor of “LV mass” as estimated by ECG, perhaps due to a hydration effect. One exception to this may be that the AG treatment may have helped to better preserve “baroreflex sensitivity” as estimated by the 0.1 Hz breathing technique, based strictly on the group-related difference on BR+0 (albeit no day x group effect). One potential concern is the greater increase in QTVI in the AG group compared to the HDBR-control group—i.e., on BR+0, with further worsening on BR+04. This finding may hint at the possibility of creating an autonomic nervous system milieu that might eventually be more arrhythmogenic in AG-treated groups. Therefore, the AG countermeasure appears to be potentially helpful for orthostatic tolerance (i.e., estimated BRS + tilt data). It is not helpful, or may even be potentially harmful, for cardiac electrical stability (i.e., QTVI data). Several autonomic parameters, including BRS, can be influenced by hydration status. Thus, it will be important in future experiments to correlate the HDBR-induced changes in cardiac autonomic parameters with those in plasma volume. Similarly, ECG-based measures of LV mass might actually reflect LV volumes (and/or the volume of LV muscle, which includes water). Thus, the significant “day” effect observed on ECG-based “LV mass” parameters in this study may relate to decrements in plasma volume, and/ to changes in volume within the LV cavity or LV myocardium itself. Results should thus ultimately be corroborated by the echo results obtained in this study (although echo has some similar limitations) or ideally by cardiac MRI in future studies. Note that consistent with the findings of Buchheit et al (AJP Heart Circ Physiol 291, 451-58, 2006), in the present study, there was also a strong correlation between VO2max and resting baseline “parasympathetic” HRV parameters. For example, on BR-07 in this study, the correlation between VO2max and HF/(HF+LF) was R = 0.62, p = 0.035.

title: Dependence of Radiation Quality on Charged Particle-induced Early and Late Damages in Chromosomes
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Tumor formation in humans or animals is a multi-step process. An early stage of cancer development is believed to be genomic instability (GI) which accelerates the mutation rate in the descendants of the cells surviving radiation exposure. A relationship between GI and tumor metastasis, as well as between GI and adaptation to drug treatment, has also been suggested. Evidence for GI induced from radiation exposure has been established in the last two decades. GI is defined as elevated or persistent genetic damages occurring many generations after the cells are exposed, and can be manifested in several biological consequences including mutation, apoptosis and damages in chromosomes. Genomic instability can be induced by both low- and high-LET radiation. Space radiation consists of a mixture of different types of ions covering a wide range of masses and energies. Its associated health risks to astronauts in flight are of special concern for prolonged space missions beyond the protective terrestrial magnetosphere. Before such missions can be undertaken, a much more detailed understanding of these biological effects is required to allow planning and implementation of protective countermeasures. This experiment investigated GI induced from exposures to energetic ions of the types and energies encountered during space flight. The overall goals of this study were (1) to determine the relationship between the quality and fluence of energetic charged particles and the induction of delayed damages in chromosomes, which is commonly referred to as chromosomal instability and (2) to understand the relationship between chromosomal instability and other events at the cellular and molecular level that play a role in the maintenance of genome integrity.
approach: The investigators selected well-developed and widely used methodologies for quantification of GI. The three models included human T-lymphocytes collected from healthy subjects, and haemopoietic cells extracted from CBA/CaH and from C57BL/6J mice, which differ in radiosensitivity. The cells were exposed in vitro to protons, Si, and Fe ions which represent three of the most important particle types in space. Chromosomal instability was analyzed in both the total population of the cells surviving after multiple generations post irradiation (non-clonal assay), as well as in clonal populations derived from single cells surviving particle irradiation (clonal assay). The non-clonal assay is less labor intensive and allows analysis of samples exposed to particles of different types, energies, and doses, whereas the clonal assay was designed to tackle the question of genetic background influence on the induction of GI. Several techniques for chromosome analysis was used which include multi-color fluorescence in situ hybridization (mFISH) and the multi-color banding in situ hybridization (mBAND). Measurements of telomere length and expressions of genes involved in genomic stability were performed in cells from unstable, as well as stable, clones. The clonal expansion assay is arguably more suitable than the non-clonal assay for determining the correlation between chromosomal instability and other biological consequences.
results: In this project, GI was investigated for both low- and high-LET radiation across different species and different cell types using both cell models and animal models. The degree of GI is apparently dependent on the quality of radiation, as well as on the biological systems. Consequently, the relative biological effectiveness (RBE) value can be different for different cell types and different endpoints. In this study, the RBE value for Fe ions can be high for initial chromosome aberrations in human lymphocytes. However, the value was found to be close to 1 when late damage was assessed. Early damage in the biological system does not necessarily predict residual damage, which is more closely related to late radiation risks such as cancer.

title: Cyber Partners: Harnessing Group Dynamics to Boost Motivation for More Efficient Exercise
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Astronauts may have difficulty adhering to exercise regimens at vigorous intensity levels during long space missions. Keeping up with exercise prescriptions is important for aerobic and musculoskeletal health during space missions and afterwards. A key impediment to maintaining intense levels of exercise is motivation. However, finding ways to motivate astronauts to be physically active at the levels necessary to lessen the effects of bone and muscle loss and aerobic capacity has not been explored. Typically individuals become bored with training regimens over time or find them less enjoyable if they do not have strategies to maintain their motivation. Although traditional group exercise leads to higher exercise adherence than individual exercise programs, structured group exercise programs are not possible for astronauts during space missions. Exercise video games have been marketed as a way to increase people’s motivation and enjoyment to exercise by being entertaining, engaging and providing a means by which to interact with other players. Although many exercise games involve competition among players, few take advantage of group dynamics to motivate play and there has been little attempt to analyze what game features and interpersonal interactions would best motivate users to continue exercising with these games. Using individuals closely matched in age and fitness to current astronauts, this research was designed to determine whether recently documented motivation gains in task groups can be harnessed to improve motivation in interactive exercise games using virtual, software-generated (SG) partners. Exercising with an SG partner offers a number of advantages such as availability, flexibility, and autonomy over a live human partner. This study had the following specific aims: Develop software to create SG exercise partners and interface with exercise equipment (cycle ergometer) similar to equipment available on the International Space Station (ISS). Test various design features of an SG partner within designed exercise video games to determine the most effective features for enhancing motivation to exercise, enjoyment, confidence, and connectedness. Test whether exercising with an SG partner over a 24 weeks, compared to exercising alone, leads to better aerobic capacity and muscle strength, adherence to exercise regimen, enhanced exercise enjoyment, self-efficacy, and sense of social connectedness.
approach: To address the second aim, investigators tested an SG partner in one of three modes against an individual control condition: (a) co-acting mode, where the subject cycled with the SG partner but whose performance was independent of the partner (i.e., they were not teammates), (b) conjunctive-teammate mode, where scores were based on the slower performer, and (c) choice mode where subject could choose co-acting mode or conjunctive teammate mode for all trials. The experiment routines consisted of (a) 30 minutes of continuous aerobic exercise on a cycle ergometer at or above 75% of maximum heart rate and (b) high-intensity interval training involving four repetitions of four minutes at or above 90% heart rate (HR) max. Investigators tested an additional 38 chronic exercisers. Subjects were allowed to adjust the power output (watts) during workouts. The main outcome variable was average watts cycled above target prescribed watts. To address the third aim, investigators tested an SG exercise partner in one of two modes: (a) conjunctive-teammate mode and (b) conjunctive teammate who is not always superior (NAS) and is sometimes surpassed by the subject, plus (c) individual control condition. Subjects exercised six days a week for 24 weeks, using the following aerobic routines: (a) 30 minutes of continuous aerobic exercise on a stationary cycle at or above 75% HR max, (b) 4x4 minute intervals at or above 90% HR max with three minutes of active rest, (c) 6x2 minute intervals at varying intensities with two minutes of active rest, and (d) 30 second sprint intervals at maximal effort with 20 seconds of active rest. In addition, investigators first tested whether the Conjunctive or NAS groups adhered more to the protocol than Controls. Conjunctive and NAS conditions averaged 15 more days completing the protocol than the Controls. However, group differences were not statistically different. In terms of the primary dependent measure, effort analyses are based on the continuous and four minute interval sessions. Subjects were not allowed to increase their intensity on the two minute intervals. Similarly, the dependent measure for the 30 second sprints was number of intervals completed, which all subjects completed. During Week 20, NAS subjects increased their effort more (M = 8.9 watts) compared to Controls (M = 1.5 watts) and Conjunctive subjects (M = 3.9 watts) on the four minute interval workout.
results: In regards to target prescribed watts, results showed no condition main effects from baseline; however, during the four minute interval sessions conjunctive trended toward greater exercise effort than control and coactive conditions. The four minute intervals likely represent the most motivationally demanding workout at 90% HR max. Increases in effort above target watts positively correlated with enjoyment, self-efficacy, and team perceptions during the four minute intervals. No relationships were found with less intense continuous exercise. Although this study did not find significances between group increases in performance effort, participants significantly increased their effort with the exercise video game (i.e., simulated bike paths). Throughout the duration of the study, NAS subjects always outperformed Controls on the four minute intervals. All groups had large significant increases in VO2max from baseline to midpoint, then values leveled off from midpoint to final. Social connectedness rose significantly from midpoint to final, and those with an SG partner increased their teams' perceptions from midpoint to final. Subjects in NAS and Conjunctive conditions had higher self-efficacy beliefs than Controls after one week with the SG partner. Enjoyment remained stable, above response scale midpoint, across 24 weeks.

title: Serial Changes in Site Specific Bone Density and Structure with Paralysis
variables: Activity, exercise; Weight load, whole body
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Study 1: The purpose of the first study is to investigate the effect of paralysis on bone density and structural parameters of the tibia. Study 2: The purpose of the second study was to investigate bone mass and structure in the tibia after resection of the fibula.
approach: Study 1: were two male and two female adults aged 17-32 years who had sustained a spinal cord injury at least 4 years prior to the study. Cross-sectional structural parameters including area (A), principal area moments of inertia (Imax, Imin), polar area moments of inertia (J), and major principal axis orientation of the tibia and fibula were computed every millimeter along the scan length for the three scans of the leg using the lower energy for its larger dynamic range. Study 2: Subjects who had undergone a fibular resection at least 2 years earlier were recruited (n=3). Fibular resection was carried out in all 3 men to remedy avascular necrosis in the hip. In addition to anthropomorphic data (BW, Ht, tibial length) a set of 3 scans of the tibia on right and left sides as above was done as well as a DXA scan of the right and left calcaneus to measure areal bone density, an indication of loading symmetry. Structural parameters of the tibia and fibula as enumerated above were performed on one leg and on the tibia of the other leg.
results: Study 1: Body weights in paraplegics were greater than in controls. Two male subjects had lower values for cross-sectional areas and density as well as lower structural parameters in the midshaft, distal tibia and femoral midshaft. Data supporting bone loss in the two female paraplegics was not convincing except at the tibial midshaft where the data was not scaled to body size. In one male subject, cross sectional areas and principal moments of inertia of the tibia were not symmetrical. Conclusions of study 1: The large variation in results of just a few subjects point to the need for longitudinal studies and more subjects to definitively measure changes in structural parameters due to paralysis and unloading. Study 2: Subject 1. The cross-sectional area of the tibia on the side of the fibular resection (rt) was increased 2% at the midshaft and 33% at the distal third compared to the unaffected tibia. The principal and polar moments of inertia on the right tibia were increased 51% and 89% at the midshaft and distal third, respectively. The midshaft was also more symmetric, but not the distal section. Subject 2: The tibia on the resected side (left) showed an increase in cross-sectional area (8% at midshaft and 10% at distal third) and an increased minimum moment of inertia of 22 % in the mid and 47% in the distal third. Imax increased by 9% in both sites. Subject 3: The increases in the cross-sectional area were 32% at the mid and 27% at the distal third, compared to the unaffected left side. Imin increased by 74% and 95% at the distal third and Imax increased 15 and 24 % in the same respective regions, an indication the tibia is more symmetric. Calcaneal density was not consistent in the 3 subjects and showed R and L differences outside the 0.6% observed in normal men. Calcaneal density was less (by 5.7 and 8 %) in the affected than the unaffected limb in two subjects who also had functional problems in gait. The lower heel density may be an indication of less load on the affected limb and was not present in the subject who reported normal gait and skiing activity post surgery. Conclusions: All three subjects with fibular resection showed an increase in cross-sectional area as well as structural parameters related to stiffness and strength, an indication of increased loading of the tibia from the ipsilateral side of the fibular resection resulting in increased bone deposition. This points to a role of the fibula in driving the shape of the tibia cross-section and in load bearing.

title: Electronic Procedures for Crewed Missions beyond Low Earth Orbit (LEO)
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: In future missions, NASA plans to venture beyond Low Earth Orbit (LEO). Communication between the spacecraft and Earth will be subject to longer delays, and in some cases, will be unavailable. These spacecraft will require systems that will allow the crew to perform procedures without assistance from Mission Control. Crewmembers will rely much more heavily on the automated, computer-based tools available within their vehicle or habitat. Given the increased autonomy from the ground, missions will likely be even more dependent on procedures for day-to-day operations and survival. Crewmembers will need to be able to independently operate procedures without missing important steps, keep track of who is working each procedure (i.e., their crewmate, or the system automation), and maintain a view into the vehicle or habitat system’s health and status, along with the effects of their actions on those systems. Two key questions addressed in this research were: 1) When incorporating automation into electronic procedures, how much automation should be provided? 2) What is the importance of a relevant graphical system display in the execution of electronic procedures, and how important is the visual integration of that display with electronic procedures? Of primary interest was the effect of these different procedure configurations on human performance, namely situational awareness (SA) and workload. This study had the following specific aims: Determine the effect of level of automation of procedure step execution on SA, and other human-system performance metrics. In a complex, multiple-procedure scenario, determine the effect of procedure management aids (e.g., availability of task allocation information) on SA and other human-system performance metrics. Determine the effect of the level of integration of system and procedural information on SA and other human-system performance metrics.
approach: Two studies were completed as part of this research project. Study 1 addressed level of automation of electronic procedures (Aims 1 and 2), and Study 2 addressed procedure/display integration (Aim 3). One of the key measures of interest in both studies was Situation Awareness, which was measured using the Situation Presence Assessment Method (SPAM). SPAM uses time to answer a query about the system as a measure of SA. Accuracy, workload, trust, usability and subjective preferences were also measured in both studies. Study 1 involved 27 crew-like subjects learning and performing tasks with PRocedure Integrated Development Environment (PRIDE) procedures and a habitat simulation system developed by TRACLabs. Subjects completed the scenario-based procedures while seated at a workstation intended to simulate a Habitat Control Station. The station consisted of two computers: the Procedures computer used to complete electronic procedures using PRIDE, and the Mission Control Center (MCC) computer where subjects answered computer-based questions from a mock MCC throughout the test session. MCC questions were SA queries or simple progress questions. For the within-subjects study, subjects completed the procedures under conditions of: 1) no automation, 2) mixed automation, and 3) high automation. Another experimental factor was the location of a procedure management aid (always visible or on request). Study 2 involved 20 crew-like subjects learning and performing tasks with an electronic procedures system and a flight control simulation. Subjects completed the scenario-based procedures, which included responding to alarms, performing malfunction procedures, and monitoring spacecraft launches, while seated at a workstation intended to simulate a future space vehicle control station. The station consisted of two computers: the Procedures computer used to complete electronic procedures using Orion-like procedures developed by the Crew Interface Rapid Prototyping Laboratory, and a Mission Control Center (MCC) computer where the subjects answered computer-based questions from a mock MCC throughout the test session. MCC questions were SA queries or Bedford workload rating scales. For the within-subjects study, subjects completed the procedures under one of the following configurations: 1) procedures-only (no system display, telemetry only), 2) serial procedures (procedure was shown with an associated system display in toggle fashion, only for commands or on request), and 3) simultaneous procedures (procedure and related system display were shown on the same monitor). In addition to accuracy, workload, trust, usability and subjective preferences, performance data were collected from an eyetracker and a prototype functional Near Infrared Spectroscopy (fNIRS) sensor.
results: The Electronic Procedures for Crewed Missions beyond Low Earth Orbit study was completed to determine: 1) the effect of level of procedure automation on performance, and 2) the effect of level procedure/display integration on performance. Two studies were performed using high-fidelity electronic procedures systems. Results from the first study indicate that a mixed level of automation is preferred because it keeps operators engaged in the task, while providing efficiencies. Results from the second study indicate that relevant graphical displays that are visible at the same time as electronic procedures provide important context. The simultaneous display of procedures and system information was highly preferred over designs that showed electronic procedural steps alone, or designs with only limited access to graphical displays.

title: Human Endothelial Cells in 2-D and 3-D Systems; Non-Cancer Effects and Space-Related Radiations
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Though not prone to carcinogenic change the endothelial cell is of critical importance to the normal functioning of all tissues and organs of the body. Endothelial cells constitute the linings of the blood circulatory system, and disruption of this function can lead to multiple changes, from minor to catastrophic. Cardio-vascular diseases are the leading cause of death in developed societies. Endothelial cells have been studied in monolayers [2-dimensional ] for many years, however it is clear that cell behavior in the third dimension [tissue-like structures] is not necessarily well represented by such studies. In recognition of the crucial role of the endothelial cell, the radiation sensitivity of the chromosomes of normal human umbilical vein endothelial cells [HUVEC] to low LET radiation was studied. It was determined that chromatid-type aberrations in late G2 cells were exquisitely linearly sensitive to radiation doses in the range 0.0125 to 0.8 Gy. This response was approximately 3 times more sensitive than that of early-mid G2 cells, and approximately 15 times more sensitive than for chromosome-type aberrations in non-cycling G1 cells [dose range, 0.5-8.0 Gy]. More recently 3-dimensional capillary like tubular structures from the culture of HUVECs in collagen gel matrices have become available. This investigation proposes to irradiate 2D [cell monolayers] and 3D [capillary-like cell structures] with Fe ions at 1GeV with doses where a bystander effect may apply [ 2D versus 3D culture
approach: Normal human endothelial cells were encouraged to develop into the capillary-like structures of the human circulatory system. At various stages of development these structures were exposed to proscribed doses of energetic iron particles or protons as found in space, and responses assessed..
results: in no difference in the responsiveness of human endothelial cells. Space related radiations are not more effective than low LET radiations for these cells with their crucial role in the maintenance of normal bodily functions. APPROACH: Normal human endothelial cells were encouraged to develop into the capillary-like structures of the human circulatory system. At various stages of development these structures were exposed to proscribed doses of energetic iron particles or protons as found in space, and responses assessed.. RESULTS: The most significant achievement of this investigation was the development of a human model tissue system. 3-D human micro-vasculature models have been successfully developed from normal human umbilical vein endothelial cells. These structures have been characterized by multi- photon microscopy and have been irradiated with high energy iron ions and protons. Irradiation of mature vessels led to a breakdown of the vessels after low doses of iron ions. DNA damage foci [53BP-1] formation was examined in endothelial cell nuclei in 2-D monolayers and in the cell nuclei of the 3-D micro-vasculature structures. Both protons at 0.22 keV/micrometer and Fe ions at 150 keV/micrometer showed similar kinetics of foci formation with peak yields at 1 hr and a 10 fold decline at 48hrs. However, there were dramatic differences in the efficiency of focus formation. At the peak, there was approximately one 53 BP-1 focus for each Fe ion traversal and approximately 1 focus for every 1,000 proton traversals. Human endothelial cells can form 3-D micro-vasculature like structures and show quantitative morphological and DNA damage responses after space-like radiations at moderate to high doses. At the fluences likely to be experienced in cells by man in space the question might reasonably be asked about the micro-vasculature; does this matter? Probably not.

title: Occupant Protection Data Mining and Modeling Project
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Current NASA Occupant Protection standards and requirements are based on extrapolations of biodynamic models, which were based on human tests performed during pre-Shuttle human flight programs. In these tests, occupants were in different suit and seat configurations than are expected for the Multi-Purpose Crew Vehicle (MPCV) and Commercial Crew programs. As a
approach: In order to develop updated standards, adequate injury assessment tools must be chosen and developed. In the case of dynamic loads, the THOR ATD was chosen as the appropriate human surrogate. For the data mining portion of the task, recreation of the conditions of each impact case was needed to determine injury risk. Since physical recreation of each case is not feasible, a numerical model of the THOR ATD was desired. An existing THOR FE model was refined and validated. To supplement available THOR ATD validation data, additional THOR ATD testing was conducted at two facilities and ATD response data was collected. The FE model responses were then be assessed against the physical ATD responses. Once the ATD model was validated, it was used for the data mining portion of the study. Because analogous space flight injury biomechanics data are very limited, data mining of other analogous environments were used. These datasets were chosen as they have similarities with the landing environment expected in future vehicles. The existing human injury and response data from other sources include historical military volunteer testing, automotive Crash Injury Research Engineering Network (CIREN), IndyCar impacts, and NASCAR impacts. These data sources can allow better extrapolation of the ATD responses to off-nominal conditions above the nominal range that can safely be tested in humans. These elements were used to develop injury risk functions for each of the injury metrics measured from the ATD.
results: , there is limited statistical validity to the Occupant Protection standards. Furthermore, the current standards and requirements have not been validated in relevant space flight suit and seat configurations or expected loading conditions. To address the limitations of the current NASA standards, this study addressed the following two objectives: 1) Develop a finite element (FE) model of a Test Device for Human Occupant Restraint (THOR) Anthropomorphic Test Device (ATD), and 2) Conduct data mining of existing human injury and response data using the THOR FE model. APPROACH: In order to develop updated standards, adequate injury assessment tools must be chosen and developed. In the case of dynamic loads, the THOR ATD was chosen as the appropriate human surrogate. For the data mining portion of the task, recreation of the conditions of each impact case was needed to determine injury risk. Since physical recreation of each case is not feasible, a numerical model of the THOR ATD was desired. An existing THOR FE model was refined and validated. To supplement available THOR ATD validation data, additional THOR ATD testing was conducted at two facilities and ATD response data was collected. The FE model responses were then be assessed against the physical ATD responses. Once the ATD model was validated, it was used for the data mining portion of the study. Because analogous space flight injury biomechanics data are very limited, data mining of other analogous environments were used. These datasets were chosen as they have similarities with the landing environment expected in future vehicles. The existing human injury and response data from other sources include historical military volunteer testing, automotive Crash Injury Research Engineering Network (CIREN), IndyCar impacts, and NASCAR impacts. These data sources can allow better extrapolation of the ATD responses to off-nominal conditions above the nominal range that can safely be tested in humans. These elements were used to develop injury risk functions for each of the injury metrics measured from the ATD. RESULTS: The first objective of this study was to assess the THOR for use by NASA in developing and validating occupant protection standards. THOR was impact tested in various orientations and multiple peak acceleration levels, and responses to these impacts differed from human responses under identical impact conditions and do not replicate human bracing for impact. As part of this study, a FE model of the THOR was developed, calibrated, and optimized. The FE model proved a good match to the ATD. The FE model simulations (at a wide range of impacts that military subjects participated in) historically revealed that the FE model correlated to lower-peak acceleration impacts better than to higher-peak accelerations. The second objective of this study was to mine existing human injury and exposure data. The U.S. Air Force maintains thousands of human-impact-test results. Data collected from 1976 to 2004 have been downloaded and converted into a user-friendly MATLAB data structure format. The team created injury assessment reference values (IARVs) for several metrics mined from existing injury literature. The IARVs for the spine and chest deflection subsequently were refined based upon statistical models of combined non-injurious and injurious literature data. This work culminated in the development of an acceptable risk of injury from space flight, which included a newly developed operationally relevant injury scale.

title: A Multi-faceted Approach to Examine Team Adaptation and Resilience within Isolated, Confined, and Extreme Environments
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Long-duration exploration mission (LDEM) crews worked and lived together in an isolated, confined, extreme (ICE) environment for a period of up to 30 months. Physical and psychological stressors are inherent in such a mission, triggered by living in a small habitat, in continual close proximity to others, separated from family and friends, while carrying out a dangerous mission with a high workload, and doing so without real- time support from mission control. In addition to on-going, low-grade chronic stressors, a crew on a LDEM was likely to experience several unanticipated acute stressors, including perhaps one or more emergencies. Therefore, a successful LDEM crew would need to self-adapt as a mission progresses, working through and recovering from various challenges, and sustaining their resilience. Each LDEM crewmember needed to adapt and maintain personal resilience. But, equally important, the crew also needed to adapt and sustain their resilience as a team. Researchers have traditionally examined adaptation and resilience from an individual perspective, but to ensure that LDEM crews were ready for the challenges they would face, there was a need to better understand how adaption and resilience would operate at the team level. Doing so would allow for the development of validated countermeasures that can be deployed prior to and at appropriate times during a mission, increasing a LDEM crew’s ability to handle the stressors associated with ICE environments and enabling them to adjust when unexpected challenges emerge. This study addresses both the fundamental need to learn ore about team adaptation and resilience, as well as the need to develop and test potential countermeasures.
approach: Investigators looked at data that was previously collected during NASA’s Human Exploration Research Analog (HERA) missions. They indexed the nature of different episodic events, the teams confronted, and associated them with members’ adaptation and resilience by using computer aided text analysis (CATA) of members’ communications. The investigator team had developed a CATA scoring mechanism for multiple dimensions of team processes and resilience which would yield multi-dimensional networks per event. They also explored the construct validity of the data yielded by the sociometric badges as a potential alternative or complementary source of network data. After reviewing the archived HERA data, investigators gathered data from 36 to 45 Saturation Dive Teams (SAT) over two to three years from three organizations, each with their own organizational culture. Each crew’s 28-day mission runs in parallel with two other crews who are also diving in rotating 8-hour shifts. The three crews worked on the same mission but did not dive or live together simultaneously - each crew lived in their own separate and isolated hyperbaric chamber. Approximately half of the SAT teams received one or more countermeasure(s) and half served as controls for testing the efficacy of the intervention(s).
results: Behavioral Health and Performance has conducted literature reviews and operational assessments exploring threats to crew cohesion and performance. They highlight how future-long duration exploration mission (LDEM) crews will, by necessity, have greater autonomy and control than prior crews. This research helped to address the risk to future space exploration crews by enhancing NASA’s understanding of the ‘’key threats, indicators and life cycle of the team for autonomous, long duration and/or distance exploration missions.’’ The investigator team’s work with crews within three LDSM analog environments demonstrated how a diary protocol approach can be used to measure and yield rich, qualitative data about taskwork and teamwork challenges over time. Some evidence of ‘’survey fatigue’’ over time was noted, but participants did not report any resistance or reluctance to complete them. The acceptance may be because the focus of the diary was perceived as very relevant to them. Overall, the diary approach yielded rich qualitative and quantitative data and enabled the collection of longitudinal data in all 3 analog settings. The findings from the experiment also confirmed that the ICE teams experienced both task-related and non-task related challenges. Crews in some settings may experience more task related challenges than non-task related challenges while crews in other settings may experience the reverse. However, per the findings from the experiment, all crews would benefit from learning how to deal with both types of challenges. The challenges appeared to fall into 4 primary categories: 1.        Personal Needs 2.        Living Environment 3.        Interpersonal 4.        Taskwork A close examination of the HERA campaigns 5 and 6 crew data suggested that challenges occurred throughout the mission, but different types of challenges were more predominant at different mission phases. Crews adapted less effectively to more disruptive challenges, particularly task-related ones. They reported handling recurring tasks and interpersonal challenges less effectively. This highlighted the importance of dealing with challenges, and in particular interpersonal challenges, when they arose, rather than allowing them to fester or drain a team’s adaptability. Across the three analogs, a total of 19 types of responses or adaptations to challenges were identified. These fell into seven response categories. Adapting Strategies and Adapting Actions were the two most deployed response categories, but the pattern of responses differed across analogs. The differences that were exhibited made sense, because the types of challenges experienced, and the nature of the mission varied across the three analogs. In general, crews reported that they handled challenges more effectively when the adaptation processes, they deployed aligned with the nature of the challenge, but other adaptation processes worked at time times as well. The team also discovered that making any type of adjustment helped with Personal challenges, which suggests that it is unhealthy to ignore Personal challenges, and that doing “something” is better than doing nothing in those instances. The team also found that when teams handle challenges more effectively, they report higher levels of resilience, maintain a better mood, and believe they are completing their mission goals and tasks more effectively. In short, it pays to prepare crews to handle and adapt to challenges constructively. A key focus of this research was to test whether it is possible to inoculate crews against future challenges so they can navigate them more effectively. It was seen that crews that participated in a structured adaptation inoculation exercise were less adversely impacted by challenges that emerged over the course of a mission. In sum, this short, simple, team-led countermeasure showed meaningful results across a 6-week mission. Participants believed that future space crews would benefit from this type of exercise.

title: 6 Degree Headdown Tilt with Balance Traction to Emulate Spinal Lengthening Experienced by Astronauts during Microgravity
variables: Size, length; Bone, spine, Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI)
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: The purpose of ARCbedrest117 was to develop a balanced traction to elongate the spine to the degree experienced by astronauts. The effects of traction on the spine exposed to the 6 o head down tilt (HDT) model is compared to effects on the spine with traction and horizontal bed rest (HBR). The second part of this study (ARCbedrest129) was designed to determine the electrical activity and intramuscular pressures of the muscles along the lumbar spine while upright and while in 6 o HDT or HBR position.
approach: Healthy volunteers were tested in the MRI before and after 3 days exposure to a balanced traction device that placed a load on the spine by suspending a load corresponding to 5% of the body weight from each leg with a cable-pulley system. The volunteer was at bed rest in the 6 degree HDT or in HBR position. Activity was not restricted. HDT with traction was compared with HBR with traction. The second part of the study conducted a few days after #117 estimated the electrical activity of lumbar spine muscle through surface electrodes for specified hours of normal activity. Through a catheter inserted into the muscle on either side of the lumbar spine, the pressures were recorded during upright and then at three time intervals during of HDT or HBR. Electrical activity was recorded concurrent with intramuscular pressure. Subjects were randomized into 2 groups of three. Group 1 underwent HBR followed by HDT in balanced traction. Group II underwent HDT in balanced traction followed by HBR. There was a two-week recovery period between the two forms of 3d-bed rest.
results: Repeated measures ANOVA indicated that total body length increased more (mean±SE) during HDT with balanced traction (22±8 mm) than during HBR (16±4 mm). Spine length between L5 and C7 also increased more during HDT with traction (25±8 and 14±9 mm). Ultrasonography showed increases in lumbar disc height during HDT and HBR (2.9±0.8 mm vs. 3.3±0.6 mm), but there were no differences among groups. Seventy percent of the increase in disc height occurred during the first 5 hours of bed rest. Within the first hour of standing, there was a 10 mm decrease in body height, about 80% of the normal diurnal variation in our subjects. The intensity of pain in the back, abdomen and head was greater during HDT with traction than during HBR with traction. Reflexes were normal in both groups. Intramuscular pressure in erector spinae muscles that averaged 8.4±0.7 mm Hg did not change during the study and was similar in HBR and HDT. Ankle joint torque during plantar- and dorsi-flexion did not change during the study and was similar in HBR and HDT with balanced traction. Conclusions: Results suggest that HDT with balanced traction may combine the advantages of both models to simulate total body and spinal lengthening, as well as back pain associated with microgravity. Note: Both studies were carried out on the same group of subjects. The measurements of intra muscular pressure in ARCbedrest129 were reported separately, but the protocols for each study were the same. Therefore, it is more complete to have both ARCbedrest117 and ARCbedrest129 reported together as the first part and the second part of the study as described.

title: Rapid Measurements of Bone Loss Using Tracer-Less Calcium Isotope Analysis of Blood and Urine
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: The purpose of this research was to develop a method for rapid detection of changes to bone mineral balance by measuring the endogenous isotope composition of calcium in the blood and urine of bed rest subjects. An isotopic ratio analysis would provide a method to evaluate the occurrence of incipient bone loss in advance of changes to bone density as detectable by conventional x-ray methods.
approach: Blood, urine, and diet samples were obtained for analyses. Subjects were separated into two groups. The blood collection groups collected blood prior and during the study with and overnight fast and vitals check before breakfast. Likewise, after the study, blood collections sessions were collected from the subject four times daily. The first collection followed with an overnight fast and vitals check and before breakfast. The last collection was late in the evening as possible without impacting the subject’s schedule. The second and third collections were evenly spaced intervals between the first and last collections. The urine collection sessions were divided into two groups, each collecting void by void aliquot samples in pre-acidified tubes. In addition, a 24 hour session pool was collected, which sampled 5ml aliquots and collected before, during, and after bed rest. Medication and Dietary sessions were collected in two groups by measuring the over the counter medications including pain killers and antacids, and study medications given to the subject as required. Calcium fortified food intake was collected and analyzed, as well as, homogenate samples of each meal in the menu cycle.
results: How soon after the start of bed rest does a bone loss signal appear in urine and blood? All-subject average urinary Ca isotopes begin to show bone loss on the third day of bed rest. This signal persists throughout the bed rest and recovery periods and becomes statistically significant by day nine of bed rest. Ca isotopes in urine reflect the onset of negative bone mineral balance (BMB) at least ten times faster than radiological techniques like DEXA, which can detect changes in bone mass that require several months of bed rest to produce. What factors other than BMB can affect soft tissue Ca isotope composition? Several factors other than BMB possibly could affect soft tissue Ca isotope composition. Extraneous factors like changes in dietary Ca isotope composition and differences in geographic and dietary history between subjects can be adequately controlled for under the strict conditions of bed rest studies by normalizing each subjects Ca isotope composition to his or her individual average pre-bed rest value. The former factor—changes in dietary d44/42Ca—is harder to control for, but based on the data does not seem to obscure the bone loss signal under the carefully controlled experimental conditions of bed rest, in which all subjects are fed the same menu on the same ten day rotation. The mass of Ca in soft tissues is large enough to dampen meal-to-meal variations in d44/42Ca of absorbed Ca. This damping effect is enhanced in 24-hour pooled urine samples, which for that reason are ideal for Ca isotope analysis.

title: Response of Thyroid to Space-like Radiation Fields
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Glandular tissues are sensitive to carcinogens and ionizing radiation; thus, they are common sites for tumor development. Thyroid tissue is a glandular tissue that can grow into unhindered three-dimensional shapes and can be used as a realistic model to investigate how other tissue types respond to ionizing radiation on different levels. It is important to understand the effects of ionizing radiation on the body's tissues to ensure the protection of crewmembers during long-duration space flight. A mission to Mars is of particular concern, because astronauts would be subjected to more types of chronic low-dose and acute high-dose radiation as they travel away from the protection of Earth's atmosphere. The objective of this study was to characterize the pattern of radiation regulated gene expression in thyroid tissue using low-dose ionizing radiation. Tissue models were subjected to various doses of low, medium and high linear energy transfer (LET). This radiation exposure protocol enabled the investigator to determine which gene profiles reflect the critical changes in structure and function of tissue that lead to changes in cells. The
approach: In a simulated low Earth orbit model, thyroid tissue models, or analogs, were chronically exposed to gamma rays delivered at a low-dose rate. The thyroid tissue analog will thus become "primed" by the low-dose exposure, after which it was subjected to galactic cosmic ray models of low, medium and high linear energy transfer (LET). The "priming" effect was induced to test the investigator's hypothesis that low-dose chronic exposure invokes cell and tissue level homeostatic mechanisms that cause structural and functional changes reflected in their gene expression profiles. It is believed that after thyroid tissue cells transition to the "primed" state, they will exhibit an altered response to an acute radiation exposure and will show an increased resistance to changes that lead to cellular disease relative to "unprimed" cells.
results: ing information will improve radiation exposure risk assessment for long-duration space flight. The thyroid tissue analog will thus become "primed" by the low-dose exposure, after which it was subjected to galactic cosmic ray models of low, medium and high linear energy transfer (LET). The "priming" effect was induced to test the investigator's hypothesis that low-dose chronic exposure invokes cell and tissue level homeostatic mechanisms that cause structural and functional changes reflected in their gene expression profiles. It is believed that after thyroid tissue cells transition to the "primed" state, they will exhibit an altered response to an acute radiation exposure and will show an increased resistance to changes that lead to cellular disease relative to "unprimed" cells. RESULTS: These studies indicate that protons and HZE particles (carbon and iron) have unique signatures and result in more dramatic responses to low dose radiation than gamma rays. In fact the data results showed that protons have the greater response, in terms of the number of modulated genes, than carbon or iron ions. In the studies of acute responses and those of the challenge exposures indicated that protons behave more like HZE particles than they do gamma-rays or low LET radiation. The findings of several of experiments reveal protons and carbon were more affecting of gene expression than gamma-rays or iron ions. Suggesting that they have the potential to cause greater effects than would be predicted based on their intermediate LET’s influence. The investigators three-dimensional tissue analog model represents an intermediate state between the isolated follicles found in flask-grown cultures and the highly organized multifollicular assembly of the intact thyroid gland. The identification of differences in gene expression found when comparing FRTL-5 cells grown in flasks with those grown in bioreactors supports the biological differences measured previously using these culture conditions. The results indicate that the tissue analogs and flask-grown follicles have substantially dissimilar responses to radiation stress. Thus, the method of culturing (flasks vs. bioreactors) dramatically impacts how these cells respond to ionizing radiation. It is likely that cells in the bioreactor cultures and the flask cultures represent different microenvironments that are controlled by different regulatory factors, and in turn respond differently to ionizing radiation. From this perspective, it will still be necessary to determine which of these gene expression patterns represent the best approximation of the radiation response in vivo. However, the previous reports of normal tissue-like properties of engineered organoids suggest that our bioreactor-generated thyroid tissue will exhibit radiation-induced changes in gene expression that more closely approximates the in vivo condition. Thereby providing a reasonable approximation to in vivo and thus reducing the need for animals in ascertaining risk. In conclusion, the results support that at low doses of radiation the gene expression response of tissues is significantly less than would be predicted from cells grown in vitro.
