title: ATD (Anthropomorphic Test Dummy) Injury Metric Development
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Anthropomorphic test devices (ATDs) – the Hybrid III and THOR – used to test the Occupant Protection requirements are not well correlated to low injury risk, as these devices were designed for automotive use. Automotive research is directed at preventing severe injuries in very low probability events. NASA vehicles, such as the Orion, require a lower risk of injury during dynamic phases of flight because the occupants will experience dynamic loading during every flight. The objective of this study is to develop injury risk functions for the Hybrid III and THOR ATDs. This study is focused on five areas of the body, each evaluating a unique injury response mechanism lower neck injury in rearward loading, vertical neck loading, upper and lower neck under lateral loading, thorax in lateral loading and pelvis in lateral loading. The biomechanics and potential injuries of each location were investigated using the following specific aims: Identify appropriate datasets for THOR comparison Test THOR in same conditions as historical testing Use historical human data to establish tolerance and injury risk focusing on lateral responses and sex differences Use Bayesian analysis combined with survival analysis along with human tolerance to estimate injury risk. Use
approach: Historical human data will be selected from the Wright-Patterson Collaborative Biodynamics Network (CBDN) and National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) databases. The data will be selected based on loading dynamics and subject demographics. Once these data are selected, the THOR ATD will be tested in identical conditions. A Bayesian analysis along with survival analysis will be used to relate the
results: of prior data mining and existing literature as prior distribution Develop new Injury Assessment Reference Values based on the new statistical analysis APPROACH: Historical human data will be selected from the Wright-Patterson Collaborative Biodynamics Network (CBDN) and National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) databases. The data will be selected based on loading dynamics and subject demographics. Once these data are selected, the THOR ATD will be tested in identical conditions. A Bayesian analysis along with survival analysis will be used to relate the resulting THOR responses to improve injury risk predictions. The results of the Occupant Protection Data Mining and Modeling Task will be used as prior distributions. Matched- pair tests between postmortem human surrogates (PMHS) and each ATD are used to determine ATD- specific injury criteria. The merit of the matched-pair design is the one-to-one correlation of the results from external loads to both surrogates. To achieve specific aim 1, historical PMHS test cases for the five areas of the body focused on in this experiment were selected from the Medical College of Wisconsin (MCW) database for matched-pair testing. Selection of these cases were made based on their similarity to spaceflight loading dynamics and astronaut demographics. The first area of the body that was tested to evaluate a unique injury response mechanism was lower neck . Lower neck injury in rearward loading was tested when two different PMHS historical data sets were used for this study. A group of five intact PMHS were seated and belted in a custom metal seat on an accelerator sled and were subjected to low or high velocities. A group of 13 PMHS were isolated at the T2 level. The PMHS in the second group were exposed to 4 different severities. A matched-pair test for each PMHS was conducted for both the THOR and Hybrid-III 50th percentile male ATDs. For the intact PMHS test conditions, the full ATD was placed in the same custom chair and subjected to the same input conditions. For the head-neck complex PMHS tests, the head and neck were removed from the rest of the ATD and tested on the same sled-pendulum test rig. Internal accelerometers and neck load cells were used to capture dynamic data. Vertical neck loading was tested by using PMHS from multiple studies. They were organized into 2 groups: upright and inverted; denoted by groups A and B respectively. In total, there were 42 subjects (26 males and 16 females). The upright subjects were isolated at T2-T3 and the applied loading rates ranged from 0.05 to 8.9 m/s. The specimens for the inverted subjects were raised approximately 0.53 m and dropped to the platform of a drop apparatus with velocities of 2.3 to 3.3 m/s. Matched pair tests could not be completed because the necks of both the Hybrid III and THOR are much less compliant than the human neck, and therefore could not match the posture and alignment of PMHS. Upper and Lower neck were tested under lateral loading. Biomechanical data were gathered for 11 subjects and organized into 3 groups: : (1) fully restrained torso with belts securing both the torso and extremities, (2) torso secured with a three-point center-mounted buckle, and (3) a different design of the three-point belt in which the specimens were positioned on a custom-designed seat rigidly fixed to the platform of a sled. The subjects were seated facing forward and upright. Tension force and extension bending moment data at the upper and lower neck were analyzed in this report to develop neck IRCs. Matched-pair tests were conducted for Groups A and B. Both the THOR and Hybrid-III were placed in the same seat and belt setup as each PMHS group and given the same sled dynamics. Thorax was tested in lateral loading conditions. Seventeen PMHS were used in this part of the study, each instrumented with 3 chest band strain gauge suites wrapped around the circumference of the thorax at the level of rib 4, xiphoid process, and rib 10. The PMHS was seated on a custom seat which was fixed to an accelerator sled, and each test was conducted at 6.7 m/s. The Hybrid-III lacks instrumentation on the ribs to calculate chest deflection and therefore could not be used for matched-pair testing. The THOR was also not used for matched- pair testing for this injury metric because its internal rib sensors demonstrated very little deflection in side impacts. Pelvis was tested in lateral loading when biomechanical data was gathered from 2 different data sets. A total of 63 tests were performed, split between two groups. The first data set included 10 PMHS, with thirty -seven tests performed, seated in a driving posture and unbelted without lateral support. The second group had 12 subjects tested in a similar manner. The Hybrid III-ATD does not have acetabulum/ hip internal load cells and hence is incapable for matched-pair tests in this study. RESULTS: Injury risk correlations derived from PMHS and ATD comparisons were used to improve upon the injury metrics previously developed under the Occupant Protection (OP) Data Mining and Modeling Task. For upper and lower neck assessments, forces and interaction criteria had differences of risk levels between the magnitudes of metrics. Forces curves were noted to be similar to the upper and lower necks, while the moment curves were amplifies at the lower neck due to the kinematics of the cervical column during lateral acceleration. The inverted drop test series indicated that age of the specimen is a significant covariate. It was noted to be negatively associated with the risk of injury. A comparison between the forces at all risk levels indicated a greater magnitude of force with the upright than the inverted model, reflecting the differences between the bony in the former versus soft tissue and distractive nature of injuries sustained in the latter set up. All injury risk methods had an additional calculation at 35-45 years of age, since age was found to be a significant covariate. The results from the upright experimental model indicated that age is a significant variable and increasing age was associated with higher risk of injury. These results suggest that for compression- related injuries, specimen age should be used as a covariate or individual specimen data may be scaled to derive risk curves. Results for distraction or extension-related injuries showed that specimen age does not need to be used as a covariate in the statistical analysis. The findings from these tests and survival analysis indicate that age factor modulates human cervical spine tolerance to impact injury.

title: Effects of High Versus Low Autonomy on Space Crewmember Performance (Autonomy)
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: In future space missions to an asteroid or Mars, crewmembers will be given more autonomy to plan and carry out their activities due to the long distances involved and the tasks that will be needed to explore a planetary surface. The impact of increased autonomy on crew performance has not been evaluated formally. In addition, while the evidence is largely anecdotal, strict adherence to timelines sent from mission control has been reported to be fatiguing and stressful for astronauts. Furthermore, such stressors can affect interpersonal interactions,
approach: The investigators conducted a series of pilot studies in this project: NEEMO 12 and 13, and the Haughton-Mars Project in 2008 (HMP 2008). In the series of pilot studies reported below, crewmember and mission control subjects filled out a weekly Study Questionnaire, which included mood and interpersonal interactions questions from the Profile of Mood States, the Group Environment Scale, and the Work Environment Scale, as well as a critical incident log. Additionally, new measures were developed and tested in the Mars 500 105-day Simulation but not on any of the simulations described in this report. The investigators had planned to test these in the NEEMO 14 mission, but this mission was postponed due to operational reasons unrelated to the research done on this experiment. The independent variable was low versus high autonomy, and the dependent variables were scores on the measures of crewmember mood, team behavior, cohesion, task performance, and the crew-mission control interaction. It was not expected that autonomy would adversely affect mood, group interactions, and performance. In fact, it was expected that mood, group interactions, and performance would be the same or better during high autonomy periods.
results: ing in increased team conflict and reduced morale and productivity. The long-term goal of this experiment was to conduct a scientific hypotheses-testing study involving a series of on-orbit missions to the International Space Station (ISS) in which the investigators measured the effects on crewmember mood, team behavior, cohesion, task performance, and the crew-mission control interaction of “high” autonomy conditions (where crewmembers plan much of their work schedule and perhaps experience a “Mars-like” communication delay with family members and mission control personnel back on Earth). This was contrasted with “low” autonomy conditions (where mission control personnel communicate in real-time with the crew and develop the work schedule, much as happens now). The impact of high versus low crew autonomy on mission control personnel was also be studied. Before engaging in the flight experiment, the investigators were asked by NASA/JSC management to test the feasibility and safety of their methods during pilot studies involving a series of ground-based space analog missions (e.g., NEEMO, Houghton-Mars Project, Mars-500 105-day Simulation), where key elements of the flight experiment can be evaluated. Thus, the short-term goal was to conduct such feasibility pilot studies involving such missions. This is the purpose of the current “Autonomy” pilot project, which deals with NEEMO and HMP simulations. Under separate funding from NASA and the NSBRI, the investigators also studied the Mars-500 105-day Simulation, but this will not be reported here. APPROACH: The investigators conducted a series of pilot studies in this project: NEEMO 12 and 13, and the Haughton-Mars Project in 2008 (HMP 2008). In the series of pilot studies reported below, crewmember and mission control subjects filled out a weekly Study Questionnaire, which included mood and interpersonal interactions questions from the Profile of Mood States, the Group Environment Scale, and the Work Environment Scale, as well as a critical incident log. Additionally, new measures were developed and tested in the Mars 500 105-day Simulation but not on any of the simulations described in this report. The investigators had planned to test these in the NEEMO 14 mission, but this mission was postponed due to operational reasons unrelated to the research done on this experiment. The independent variable was low versus high autonomy, and the dependent variables were scores on the measures of crewmember mood, team behavior, cohesion, task performance, and the crew-mission control interaction. It was not expected that autonomy would adversely affect mood, group interactions, and performance. In fact, it was expected that mood, group interactions, and performance would be the same or better during high autonomy periods. RESULTS: NEEMO One study involved the NASA Extreme Environment Mission Operations (NEEMO) program. The purpose of this program is to study human survival in the Aquarium underwater laboratory in preparation for future space missions. The Aquarius is located near Key Largo, Florida. Missions typically last 10 to 14 days and involve research and other activities conducted by 4 or more “aquanauts”, who are usually astronauts or other NASA personnel. These activities are conducted within the habitat or during simulated EVAs in the ocean. “Mission control” personnel located topside monitor crewmember progress and timeline the schedule. The investigators studied two NEEMO missions: 12 and 13. NEEMO 12 consisted of two weeks of low autonomy, where the crewmember work schedules were timelined by the topside mission control. Subjects included three NASA crewmembers and 6 topside personnel. NEEMO 13 consisted of one week of low autonomy and one week of high autonomy (where the crew had more flexibility to plan their own work schedule). Subjects included four NASA crewmembers and eight topside personnel. At the end of each week, subjects completed a measure of mood [Profile of Mood States (PMS)], items from two measures of social climate [Group Environment Scale (GES), Work Environment Scale (WES)], and a critical incident log. Due to the small number of data points, investigators could only analyze the data descriptively by examining change scores of the subscales of their measures from the first to the second week, separately for the two missions. Preliminary analyses suggested that the autonomy condition was successfully employed in NEEMO 13 with no adverse results. There seemed to be clear differences between the low and high autonomy weeks by the results, the crewmembers reported more direction from the mission commander (reflected by an increase in “Leader Control”) as well as a decrease in fatigue from the low to the high autonomy weeks during NEEMO 13 as compared to NEEMO 12, which only had low autonomy conditions. For the topside personnel, work pressure was stable in NEEMO 13, whereas it rose in the second week during NEEMO 12. However, confusion increased during the high autonomy second week of NEEMO 13 as compared to the second week of NEEMO 12 (where it declined), suggesting that the topside personnel were not as clear in their roles when the crew took over more of the schedule. HMP 2008 A second pilot study involved some of the summer 2008 crewmembers working on the Haughton-Mars Project (HMP) on Devon Island in Canada. The location was an old, large impact crater which had similarities to the Martian surface in appearance and geological characteristics. People participating in this program dress up in space suits, travel in a Mars rover, and conduct tasks similar to those anticipated during an actual expedition to Mars. There is no formal “mission control” and the participants have great freedom to plan their activities each day. Hence, there is great autonomy in the work schedule. Investigators studied the last three weeks of the 2008 mission. Eight non-NASA scientists and graduate students served as subjects. As in their previous work, they completed weekly POMS, GES, WES and critical incident log measures. Since they had no contrasting low autonomy period with which to compare their results, investigators decided to compare the subscale scores of the HMP subjects with those from published adult norms in the POMS, GES, and WES manuals, and with subscale scores from mission control subjects who participated in their previous on-orbit studies. The HMP group reported greater levels of in-group leader direction and innovation and less need for outside direction as compared with other work groups on Earth, which presumably had more managerial control. These findings suggest that they were working under fairly high autonomous conditions. In addition, they reported being more cohesive than as compared with other work groups as well. They also reported being more tired than mission control groups, but this might have been an artifact of their working in the Canadian north in the summertime, when there is constant daylight and the work if more physically taxing than sitting in front of a mission control console. Taken together, these results suggest that people working under relatively high autonomous conditions are not adversely affected and may even bond together more cohesively than other work groups. The results of these pilot studies suggest that in isolated and confined conditions that are meant to simulate those encountered during space missions, high autonomy is safe, well-received by crewmembers, and offers some potential advantages over low autonomy conditions. The crews have reported that they enjoy the high autonomy condition, and there have been no untoward effects to date. There have been some suggestions that high autonomy improves mood and cohesion, with more innovation and reliance on the crew leader. Outside mission monitors reported less work pressure but some confusion concerning their role. Clearly, these results are suggestive based on limited pilot data, but they point to the safety and possible advantages of high autonomy on crew functioning during actual space missions.

title: Comparison of Bone Bending Stiffness in Elite Female Synchronized Swimmers and Judo Athletes
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: There is a great deal of information on the bone densities of athletes with different loading histories, but limited information on the effect of sports activities on the structure and mechanical properties of bone. It is known that gymnasts have high density bone because of their exposure to high-impact loads. It is also known that swimmers have lower density bone because of their exposure to a buoyant environment. We asked the question: Are the bones of synchronized swimmers, stimulated primarily by non-impact loads and muscular contractions, weaker than those of gymnasts?
approach: Thirty seven young (20-22 years) women were recruited from Olympic level synchronized swimming (n=13) and gymnastic (n=8) clubs as well as from an untrained population (n=16) of college students. All gave informed consent for the study. Historical information was acquired before the tests for muscle in the athletes and the non-invasive test of length and bone strength in the ulnas and tibias of all subjects. The MRTA delivers a "buzz" and then detects the response of the bone on which the probe is centered on the skin surface. The response curve to the vibratory stimulus is analyzed by software that generates a measurement for E (the modulus of elasticity) and for I (the moment of inertia) for the ulna and the tibia. The instrument had been previously validated in the bones of monkeys (correlation of non-invasive measurement with a three-point bending test in the same bone extracted at necropsy was found to be 0.95, highly significant).
results: The synchronized swimmers (SYN) were taller than the gymnasts (GYM) and the untrained women (UNT), partly due to a longer tibia in SYN. The SYN also had higher body weights and lower BMI measurements then GYM or UNT groups. Years of training in GYM exceeded those in SYN by 3.5 years. The BMD in the wrist was highest in GYM, lowest in SYN and intermediate in UNT. In contrast, the ulnar EI was similar in GYM and SYN and 50% higher than in UNT. Ulnar EI was related to Ulnar width, but not to wrist density. EI in the tibia was similar in both athletic groups, and twice the value of the UNT. The knee flexor strength correlated with tibial EI. We concluded that in spite of different loading histories that could be related to bone mineral density in the wrist, the bending stiffness of synchronized swimmers and gymnasts was similar and in the athletes, much higher than in the untrained women. EI (bending stiffness) in the ulna could be related to the width of the bone and in the tibia, to muscle strength. It seems clear that vigorous physical training of the type used in synchronized swimming can increase bone strength without necessarily increasing bone density.

title: Dose-Rate Effects and Components of Systems Governing Variations in Susceptibility for Carcinogenic and Acute Radiation Risks following Gamma-Ray, Proton, or HZE Irradiation
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: The central hypothesis is that dose-rate effects in the 1 to 0.005 Gy/min range will be the same for protons vs. gamma-rays for chromosomal aberration induction. Second, levels of chromosomal radiosensitivity, and their dose-rate dependence will be similar for cells from individuals with genetic differences in radiosensitivity. Such a biomarker may help identify differences among individuals in a component contributing to their susceptibility to these effects.
approach: The approach for this investigation is unavailable.
results: For low passage normal human fibroblasts and for MCF10A human mammary epithelial cells, the dose rate effect for induction of chromosomal aberrations seen for gamma-rays in the range of 70cGy/min (HDR) to 0.005cGy/min (LDR) was virtually identical for protons with energies of 1000MeV or 50MeV and corresponded to a dose rate reduction factor(DREF) of about 2.0 for all these radiations. There was a smaller, but still a significant dose rate effect for 1GeV/n Fe ions corresponding to a DREF of about 1.3 despite the fact that the LET for the Fe ions was approximately 150 keV/micrometer. For the MCF10A cells, the responses (aberration induction, cell killing and gamma H2AX formation at low dose rates) in 2D or 3D culture were identical. Indistinguishable dose rate effects were also seen for ATM +/- cells compared to ATM +/+ cells with the two cell strains that were derived from individuals who were siblings from the same family.

title: The Effects of Space Radiation on Stem Cells and Vascular and Cardiac Disease
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: The integrity of organs and tissues is maintained through continued cell production to replace damaged or senescent cells. In particular, stem cells are pivotal to this process providing the primary source for production of functional cells. In the heart, cardiac stem cells (CSCs) reside in close proximity to stromal cells or mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) that produce proteins that control the growth and development. Stem cells are quiescent cells that cycle through self replication very slowly. This decreases the ability of these cells to repair damage to DNA and may lead to increased risks of vascular and heart disease. In this study, investigators aimed to evaluate the effects of exposure of stem cells to space flight-relevant radiation.
approach: To determine the effect of space flight relevant radiation on stem cells, stem cell populations were exposed to radiation in vitro. Two types of stem cell populations were used for these experiments including: a) Human Fetal Heart (HFH) derived plastic adherent CSCs: The heart tissue was digested with collagenase and cells cultured in standard plastic culture flasks in media supplemented with recombinant human stem cell factor (rhSCF). Over 1 to 2 weeks, adherent cells were grown from the tissue as CSCs. These CSCs were passaged using trypsin treatment. b) Bone Marrow (BM) Derived Mesenchymal Stem Cells (MSCs): The human MSCs were isolated from BM from normal donors and expanded using standard culture conditions and stored frozen in liquid nitrogen. The MSCs have a standard phenotype expressing CD105, CD90 and CD73 but negative for CD45. Early passage (P3 to P5) cells were thawed and cultured in T162 cm2 culture flasks and were finally grown in T75 flasks, T25 flasks, chamber slides, e-plates, and six well plates for irradiation at Brookhaven National Laboratory (BNL) for irradiation.
results: To study the effects of radiation on activation of repair genes and induction of DNA damage, cells were analyzed for gamma-H2AX staining by flow cytometry and immunofluorescence. Gamma-H2AX marks sites of double-strand breaks. CSCs or MSCs grown either in 6 well plates or in 2 well chamber slides were exposed to radiation at BNL. For immunofluorescence, 15 minutes, 1, 2, 6, 12, 18, and 24 hours after, cells were fixed in cold acetone: methanol (1:1). Media was collected at each time for cytokine analysis later. The fixed cells were analyzed for DAPI (red-nucleus) and immunofluorescence staining with gamma-H2AX antibody (green). For flow cytometry, cells were trypsinized and stained with FITC conjugated gamma-H2AX antibody and propidium iodide (PI) at 15 minutes, 1, 2, 6, 12, and 18 hours after radiation and analyzed. HFH74 cells showed a 2-4 fold increase in the staining up to 2 hours following 100 cGy of proton irradiation. At later time points, this increase was lost. Following HZE ion irradiation however, an increase in gamma-H2AX was observed at 6 hours or 18 hours. Significant induction of gamma-H2AX was not observed in NHMSC cells following proton irradiation; however, an increase in gamma-H2AX was observed at 6 hours or 18 hours following Iron irradiation. In the case of Iron irradiation, a significant increase in cell death was observed up to two hours following 20 cGy exposure in both the cell lines. However, it appears that cells were able to recover from this initial damage. Since flow cytometry provides an average number of positive events in a cell population, investigators are currently analyzing gamma-H2AX staining using immunofluorescence. One potential effect of space flight-relevant radiation may be to induce aging of stem cells and therefore investigators compared the CFU-F formation potential of cells after radiation exposure. In NHMSC cells following Iron irradiation (10cGy), a surviving fraction (SF) of 0.43 ± 0.0 was observed. Following continuous gamma irradiation for 12 hours, a SF of 0.91 ± 0.1 at 50mR/h and 0.8 ± 0.1at 100mR/h was observed. HFH74 cells showed a plating efficiency of only 7% even in matrigel coated plates, therefore the growth of the cells with and without radiation was followed in real time using cell electronic sensing system (ACEA Biosciences). As expected, with all types of irradiation in HFH74 cells increased growth delay was observed with increasing radiation dose. However, in NHMSC cells, except following proton irradiation, significant differences in growth were not observed with the increasing doses of radiation. No datasets exist for this study. A final report was archived.

title: Feasibility Pilot Study on Acute Biological and Behavioral Responses to the Solid State Lighting Modules for the International Space Station
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Currently, the International Space Station (ISS) uses General Luminaire Assemblies (GLAs) that house fluorescent lamps for illuminating the astronauts’ working and living environments. Solid-state light in the form of Light Emitting Diodes (LEDs) is an attractive candidate for replacing the GLAs on the ISS as well as all future manned space vehicles and habitats. With respect to space flight, the advantages of LEDs over conventional incandescent and fluorescent lighting systems include lower upmass, power consumption, and heat generation, as well as fewer toxic materials. In addition, LEDs have greater resistance to damage and longer lamp life expectancy. Engineers at Kennedy Space Center (KSC) have developed a prototype Solid-State Lighting Assembly (SSLA) that has been installed on board the ISS. In a consensus document between the KSC engineers, lighting experts from Johnson Space Center (JSC), research management from JSC and NASA’s biomedical research partner, the National Space Biomedical Research Institute (NSBRI), it was recommended that the SSLAs could provide reasonably equivalent light compared to the GLAs currently onboard ISS. Two crewmembers onboard the ISS have assessed the recently installed SSLA prototype to be acceptable for supporting vision. With regard to the efficacy of the SSLAs for astronaut circadian regulation, there was less certainty. It was suggested that further research was needed to determine the biological and behavioral efficacy of the SSLAs. This project was a feasibility, pilot study. The goal was to develop and run a multiday study with a small cohort of healthy, male, astronaut-aged volunteers. The primary study objective was to determine the best way to test the acute effects of the prototype LED light designed for use on the ISS. Specific measures were taken on visual performance, color discrimination, alertness and cognitive performance through neurobehavioral testing, measures of plasma melatonin levels, as well as total sleep time, sleep latency and sleep efficiency using electroencephalography (EEG), electrooculography (EOG), and electrocardiography (EKG).
approach: The methodology is embedded in the
results: below. RESULTS: This project successfully completed each of the proposed specific aims. Collaborators from four institutions developed and refined controlled, ground-based protocols that assessed the visual, neuroendocrine, alerting, and sleep effects relative to different Correlated Color Temperature (CCT) outputs of the Solid State Lighting Assembly (SSLA). Both the Thomas Jefferson University Institutional Review Board and the NASA Committee for the Protection of Human Subjects approved the study protocols. During the time those activities were completed, two high fidelity simulations of the ISS Crew Sleeping Quarters (CQs) with internal illumination provided by an SSLA were constructed with engineering support from JSC, KSC, and the Lighting Sciences Group. Over 200 astronaut-aged, male volunteers were screened to assure they were physically healthy, psychologically sound, drug-free, and had stable sleep-wake rhythms. Ten subjects were selected from that pool of volunteers to enter the multiday study. Nine of the subjects completed the full multiday study providing data on melatonin secretion, subjective alertness, objective alertness, neurobehavioral responses, and sleep parameters. Eight of those subjects also participated in independent experiments on visual performance and color discrimination inside the CQs. Collateral support from the National Space Biomedical Research Institute made it possible to extend the number of subjects studied, enhance the testing of visual performance and color discrimination as well as augment analysis of polysomnography for both sleep and alertness measures. As hypothesized, the results of the visual performance and color discrimination testing showed that CCT of 2,300 K and 6,500 K SSLA light supported visual performance as well as indirect midday daylight and common 3,500 K CCT fluorescent light. Also as hypothesized, color vision was significantly compromised under dim 2,300 K SSLA light versus brighter indirect daylight, 3,500 K fluorescent light, and 6,500 K SSLA light. Currently a dim 2,700 K SSLA pre-sleep lighting countermeasure is being considered for use on the ISS. If this setting is operationally used, the astronauts should be made aware of the potential color discrimination difficulties and be advised to save any tasks requiring color discrimination for the other lighting conditions. Going forward additional visual testing should be done in high fidelity mock ups of other spaces onboard ISS as they have very different lighting configurations and reflectant surfaces. From the outset, the multiday study was intended as a pilot study to determine the feasibility of using a variety of physiological and behavioral measures within the very confined spaces of the replica ISS CQs. Despite the overall study being insufficiently powered, some statistically significant effects were observed. These included: 1) evening plasma melatonin sample; 2) one evening neurobehavioral test; and 3) one morning neurobehavioral test. The evening melatonin and neurobehavioral results support the hypothesis that evening exposure to dim, long wavelength-shifted SSLA light better prepares an astronaut-aged male subjects for sleep. Further, the morning neurobehavioral results support the hypothesis that bright, short wavelength-shifted SSLA light is more alerting than dimmer, long wavelength-shifted SSLA light. These observations are tempered, however, by the fact that the results may have been due to an order effect not the lighting. A fully powered, crossover study is needed to confirm these observations from the multiday pilot study. As intended, the multiday study provided the ability to determine which dependent variables studied could yield statistically significant results through power analyses. The results of the power analyses varied depending of the study measure being assessed. The number of subjects needed for statistically significant results in future studies will be determined by the dependent variables selected for study. To prepare for manned space missions, NASA utilizes Earth-based research in specific environments with elements that are similar or analogous to some of the conditions of space flight. Analog research environments can be in extreme locations such as Antarctica, rugged deserts, the ocean floor, or inside of a volcano. The work reported here represents a middle ground between research done in highly controlled laboratory conditions and NASA’s experimental field environments. Finally, the issue of gender needs to be addressed in planning a multiday protocol of seven days or longer. In discussions between the collaborative scientific team and NASA management, it was determined that this feasibility study should include only male subjects to reduce variability across the small sample size. Future studies should include both genders to more accurately reflect the sex distribution in the astronaut corps and future space flight crews. The sleep deficits experienced by astronauts during space flight can be considered a threat to the success of space missions. The resulting physiological and behavioral changes caused by sleep and circadian disruption can lead to diminished alertness, cognitive ability, and psychomotor performance. A significant portion of the global population suffers from chronic sleep loss and/or circadian-related disorders. Development of an in-flight lighting countermeasure that helps resolves circadian and sleep disruption in astronauts is likely to help optimize use of light therapy for patient populations with affective, circadian, and sleep disorders.

title: Individual Variations in Measures of Muscle and Bone in Ambulatory Subjects
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Muscle strength has been shown to predict bone mineral density (BMD) in women, but there is limited data in healthy non-athletic men. The purpose of this study was to determine the relationship of muscle strength and bone mineral density in men, and to define the effect of exercise patterns in non-athletes on BMD and muscle strength. A secondary objective was to test a newly developed instrument, the Mechanical Response Tissue Analyzer, to determine a mechanical property of bone related to its strength (EI or bending stiffness) non-invasively.
approach: Fifty healthy men, aged 28 to 51 years were recruited for an ambulatory study and gave informed consent. Volunteers were instructed in the daily recording of physical activities and outfitted with a step meter to be worn at all times except during bathing, sleeping and recreational exercise (softball games, etc.). The exercise log was reviewed each week for accuracy with an exercise physiologist. A five-day diet record was also provided with instructions to enter all foods eaten for four week-days and at least one weekend day. Each subject had a series of bone density measurements (Hologic QDR 1000) and a series of strength tests using isotonic weight equipment (Universal and Nautilus). Bending stiffness of the right ulna and right tibia was estimated with a new instrument (MRTA) on 3 separate occasions and on the left ulna and tibia, on one occasion. A single measurement of bone density of the wrist was carried out with a Norland densitometer and the calcaneal bone density by a single energy densitometer, (Osteon, Inc). The right calcaneus was measured three times and the left, twice.
results: We obtained the first data on bending stiffness in the ulna and tibia of adult males with our non-invasive instrument and found the left tibia to be stronger than the right. The ulnas of right-handed men showed lower values for EI in the left ulna than in left-handed men whose left and right ulnas were equal. EI was related to the mineral density of the right ulna, and both right and left tibias. EI was also related to the width of the ulna and the strength of the biceps. We concluded that the measurement of EI was reproducible, and was influenced by arm strength. We found that BMD at all sites was related to the muscle strength in the back and the biceps (recorded in pounds). Body weight correlated with tibia and whole body BMD. Comparison of exercisers and non-exercisers walking mileage showed no difference in miles per day (3.9 miles a day), age, body weight, dietary protein or fat intakes in these two groups. Kcal/d were greater in exercisers than non-exercises due to intakes of carbohydrate. BMD and muscle strength were significantly greater in the exercisers than in the non-exercisers, indicating that hours spent doing recreational exercise is a better predictor of BMD than daily walking. Calcaneal BMD was not related to walking steps, but could be correlated with the amount of time engaged in high load exercise (i.e. loads of more than two body weights).

title: Tissue-Specific Acute and Late Molecular Surveillance of Particle Radiation Effects
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: The space atmosphere is comprised of wide spectrum of highly energetic and charged particle radiation. Exposure to this type of radiation in the galactocosmic environment or unplanned solar particle events (SPE) may pose a potential health hazard to humans in long-term manned space explorations. A large database of information is available on the mutagenic potential of particle radiation on cultured cells; however, limited information is available for multicellular tissue responses. This is primarily due to constraints in the selection of adequate markers in the appropriate tissue systems. Transgenic rodent mutation model systems are widely accepted by regulatory agencies as an appropriate in vivo systems to access the potential carcinogenicity of a variety of test articles. In these systems, multiple copies of the inert reporter gene are integrated into every cell of the genome, making it possible to use it as a tool to measure, both quantitatively and qualitatively, mutations in every tissue of the animal. This experiment uses a transgenic mouse mutation model system to evaluate the immediate and long-term mutagenic potential of simulated space radiation beams in different tissue. Knowledge gained in this ground-based work is directed at understanding how tissue and organ respond to exposures both on the lunar surface as well as in deep space. Information gathered from this research will aid in reducing the uncertainties associated with predicting risks both in the estimation of risk to astronaut health and the design of appropriate countermeasures to ameliorate any potential negative effects in space flights.
approach: Animals were exposed to a range of low dose-rate simulated solar particle event (sSPE) radiation at the NASA-sponsored Research Laboratory (NSRL) at Brookhaven National Laboratory (BNL). Peripheral blood was harvested from animals from 1 to 12 days after total body irradiation (TBI) to quantify the level of circulating reticulocytes (RET) and micronucleated reticulocytes (MN-RET) as an early indicator of radiation-induced genotoxicity. Bone marrow lymphocytes and hippocampal tissues from each animal were collected at 12 days and up to two months, to evaluate dose-dependent late effects after sSPE exposure.
results: This project demonstrated that the lacZ model system is indeed an efficient and effective model system that can be used to evaluate tissue-specific genomic damage as a function of particle radiation quality. In addition to measuring reporter transgene modifications, aspects of the in vivo system were studied by using a multi-pronged approach to evaluate particle radiation induced perturbations in different organ systems, including cytogenetic damage and recovery in reticulocytes (RETs) populations and lymphocytes and alterations in gene expression profiles in the CNS and the liver tissue. Through this effort, temporally-regulated dose, dose-rate and radiation quality- and dosing regimen-dependent of changes in (i) mutation in the reporter transgene, (ii) gene expression profiles in micro-dissected hippocampus sections from the brain and liver tissues, (iii) persistence of total chromosome/chromatid aberrations as well as chromosome-specific lesions, and (iv) dynamic early changes in levels of RETs and MN-RETs in peripheral blood have bben identified. Mutation analysis of two different tissues in the same animals highlights the importance of tissue specificity considerations in risk analysis. Sequential exposure to particle radiations with different LETs resulted in alterations in gene expressions profiles that are distinctly different from single ion exposures. The results, from this experiment, to date suggest that low dose rate sSPE radiation impacts the hematopoietic system. However, such events are transient. On the other hand, gene expression profiling in the hippocampus demonstrated that sSPE induced down regulation of neurotrophic genes important to functional integrity of CNS. The results indicate that the concept of dose response must be expanded to not only include quantitative changes in the level of response, but also qualitative changes in the profile of genetic expression. Obviously, higher doses of sSPE displays a gene expression spectrum that is qualitatively different from those obtained from animals that were exposed to lower doses.

title: Effects of Altered Gravity on Spinal Cord Excitability
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Skeletal muscle is made up of many "motor units." Each unit consists of a group of muscle fibers and a motor neuron that innervates them. For each nerve impulse, the muscle fibers perform a single twitch contraction (contract and immediately relax). This single twitch of a single motor unit could be considered the quantal unit of exercise. Prolonged weightlessness
approach: During experiment operations, the test subject was fitted with five electrodes. Electromyography (EMG) activity was recorded differentially from two recording electrodes applied to the soleus muscle. The locations of these electrodes on the posterior surface of the leg were critical. A single reference electrode was applied to the anterior surface of the same leg. The electrical stimulus to the posterior tibial nerve was applied through an adjustable, spring-loaded electrode located behind the knee. A knee brace provided a rigid and stable structure on which to mount the stimulating electrode. The stimulus circuit was completed through a stimulus return path electrode positioned just above the knee cap. Following application of the electrodes, the subject was restrained in a sitting position. The feet were strapped to a foot brace that established fixed and consistent knee (120 degrees) and ankle (90 degrees) angles that varied somewhat between subjects. During the “Locate Phase” of the experiment, the subject received electrical shocks (600 microseconds in duration, 40-90 volts amplitude) at the rate of one shock every three seconds. The purpose of this phase was to allow the operator to locate the posterior tibial nerve (the stimulating electrode could be adjusted for optimum data collection), and determine the shock strength (the electrical shock was varied to find the minimum and maximum values required for the experiment). No data was stored during the Locate Phase. During the “Data Collection Phase” of the experiment, sixty test shocks were delivered at the rate of one every five seconds. The stimulus was incrementally increased and then slowly decreased within the determined maximum range. The
results: in a loss of muscle strength and volume and decreased bone density, particularly in the legs. At this time, the only effective treatment for these problems appears to be in-flight exercise. No form of physical activity can be maximally efficient or effective, however, if motor neuron recruitment is compromised. This may be the case, as previous observations have suggested that Achilles' tendon tap responses and Hoffmann Reflexes in the soleus muscle are abnormal after several days in space. However, most of these data were obtained days after landing or were incidental observations during experiments designed for other purposes. The effect of weightlessness on spinal cord excitability has not been fully studied. The objective of this experiment was to determine if spinal cord excitability gradually decreases during prolonged spaceflight, and if so, to measure the extent of the change, and how long it continues after return to the ground. APPROACH: During experiment operations, the test subject was fitted with five electrodes. Electromyography (EMG) activity was recorded differentially from two recording electrodes applied to the soleus muscle. The locations of these electrodes on the posterior surface of the leg were critical. A single reference electrode was applied to the anterior surface of the same leg. The electrical stimulus to the posterior tibial nerve was applied through an adjustable, spring-loaded electrode located behind the knee. A knee brace provided a rigid and stable structure on which to mount the stimulating electrode. The stimulus circuit was completed through a stimulus return path electrode positioned just above the knee cap. Following application of the electrodes, the subject was restrained in a sitting position. The feet were strapped to a foot brace that established fixed and consistent knee (120 degrees) and ankle (90 degrees) angles that varied somewhat between subjects. During the “Locate Phase” of the experiment, the subject received electrical shocks (600 microseconds in duration, 40-90 volts amplitude) at the rate of one shock every three seconds. The purpose of this phase was to allow the operator to locate the posterior tibial nerve (the stimulating electrode could be adjusted for optimum data collection), and determine the shock strength (the electrical shock was varied to find the minimum and maximum values required for the experiment). No data was stored during the Locate Phase. During the “Data Collection Phase” of the experiment, sixty test shocks were delivered at the rate of one every five seconds. The stimulus was incrementally increased and then slowly decreased within the determined maximum range. The resulting EMG response from each shock was recorded from the soleus muscle. After the last shock was applied, a computer analyzed and displayed the recorded data, allowing the crew member to determine if the test was successfully completed. At the end of the session, the computer analyzed the data and determined the minimum and maximum of spinal cord excitability for each session. Subsequently, the ratio of H-max to M-max (the measure of spinal cord excitability) was determined. Data was saved on the hard drive and down-linked to ground operations as soon as possible. During flight, H-Reflex recruitment curves were recorded four times during each subjects stay onboard the Station: three times early in flight (pre-docked and docked) and once late in the mission. The principal investigator added an additional early session during Expedition 3, after results received during Expedition 2 indicated that an additional session would better define the rate of change in this reflex. For comparison, the experiment was also run three times preflight and four times post-flight. RESULTS: This study of spinal cord excitability using the Hoffman reflex was completed by a total of eight subjects over ISS Expeditions 2-4. H-Reflex measured how excitable the nerve cells were by applying small electrical shocks behind the knee. Each shock produced a reflex response in the calf muscles (the H-Reflex response); the data collected indicated that this response decreased significantly while in microgravity. The study found that spinal cord excitability decreased by about 35% in weightlessness, and stayed at this new level for the duration of the mission. Although there was notable improvement in the H-Reflex response the day after landing, it took about ten days back on Earth for astronauts to fully recover their muscle strength and spinal cord excitability. This difference in excitability means that only a portion of muscle fiber units are contracting in response to signals from the nervous system and explains functionally why muscle mass declines in weightlessness, even with exercise. Reduced excitability means that there might be limits on the degree to which heart muscle strength, leg muscle tone, and bone density (for which muscle contraction is an important regulating factor) can be maintained through exercise on long-duration missions. Because this decrease in excitability is only observed on orbit and not during bed rest, an analogue for weightless space travel, the results highlight the possibility that reduced excitability with corresponding loss of muscle and bone might be partly a nervous system response and not simply due to disuse of the legs. Based on the results of this study, decreased spinal cord excitability could be an issue for long-duration stays in partial-gravity environments such as are found on the moon and Mars. Future designs of exercise equipment that provide feedback on work actually performed would help crewmembers compensate for decreases in exercise efficiency.

title: Evaluation of Functional Skeletal Muscle Performance Following Space Flight
experiment_type: Shuttle Extended Duration Orbiter Medical Project (EDOMP)
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Muscular deconditioning after long exposure to microgravity could interfere with the safe completion of critical tasks during space flight or during emergency or routine landing or egress. The objective of this study was to evaluate changes in the strength of the arm muscles after space flight and to determine whether extravehicular activity during flight affects those changes.
approach: Before and after space flights of 9 to 14 days, the strength of the arm muscles of three astronauts who performed extravehicular activities during flight and one who did not was assessed. The muscles that act on the elbow and the muscles that turn the forearm and wrist were tested with LIDO isokinetic dynamometers. These dynamometers provide variable resistance so that movements continue at the same speed (i.e., they are isokinetic) regardless of the force applied. Both concentric and eccentric strength were measured. Concentric strength is the strength of a muscle as it contracts to move a body part, while eccentric strength is the strength of the muscle as it is gradually lengthened while resisting the motion of a body part.
results: The astronauts who took part in extravehicular activity, as well as in the astronaut who did not, appeared to experience operationally relevant losses (>10%) of arm strength. However, the changes were not statistically significant. The effects of EVA on muscle performance require further study. Loss of muscle mass during space flight could increase the risk of injury during routine activities. According to rehabilitation standards, 40% of the astronauts were at increased risk of a back injury, and 20% were at increased risk of a leg injury. Because these standards are based on losses in a single muscle group, while space flight affects many major muscle groups, the risks may be even higher.

title: Evaluation of Cardiac Rhythm Disturbances During Extravehicular Activity
experiment_type: Shuttle Extended Duration Orbiter Medical Project (EDOMP)
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: This study represents the first systematic evaluation of dysrhythmias during extravehicular activity (EVA). Twenty-four-hour electrocardiograph (ECG) tracings of Shuttle crew members (n=7) were recorded before, during and after spaceflight including EVA. A comparison of the incidence and severity of dysrhythmias across subjects and time was performed.
approach: Participating crewmembers were required to wear either a Holter ECG recorder or the standard operational bio-instrumentation system (OBS) ECG monitors. The protocol involved 3 specific phases: Phase 1, before flight - acquisition of 3 separate 24-hour Holter recordings; Phase 2, during flight - 24 hours of data collection during and after each EVA (including one 24-hour period within 2 days of landing). Phase 3, after flight - 24 hours of Holter monitoring on postflight days R+0, R+7, and R+30.
results: Although limited by sample size, the data suggested that the incidence of dysrhythmias is no greater during EVA than in any other phase of a mission. The cardiac response during EVA was statistically no different from the response during the preflight and postflight phases. With the advent of Space Station and the necessity for increased EVA, knowledge of both electrophysiologic and cardiovascular changes will be needed. The data from this study suggested that EVA does not precipitate deleterious cardiac events during space flight.

title: Preflight Adaptation Training (PAT)
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: This study assisted in developing a standardized Motion Perception Vocabulary and Reporting System that provided for quantitative descriptions of perceptual responses that occur during each phase of space flight. Such descriptions provided insight into neurosensory adaptation and readaptation processes associated with varying mission durations, and importantly, toward the evaluation of neurosensory countermeasures. These data are being directly applied to the development of preflight adaptation trainers and training procedures. Astronaut participation is essential for the development of accurate sensory stimulus conditions effective for pre-adapting crewmembers to microgravity and return to Earth's gravity.
approach: Preflight, crewmembers practiced using a Quantitative Motion Perception Reporting Vocabulary to describe their self/surround motion during brief exposures to several sensory stimulus rearrangement conditions produced by the PAT Tilt-Translation Device (TTD) in both pitch and roll orientations. Inflight (early and late), during entry, and at wheels stop, crewmembers reported perceived self/surround motion elicited by slow, low amplitude head movements in the pitch, roll, and yaw planes with eyes open and with eyes closed. Postflight, crewmembers were re-exposed to the PAT-TTD conditions and made comparisons between self/surround motion perceptions associated with head movements on-orbit, during entry, and immediately postlanding with those elicited by the various PAT-TTD conditions.
results: Significant findings include: 1) PAT-TTD stimulus conditions can elicit perceptual responses consistent with the hypothesis that during exposure to microgravity all otolith signals are interpreted as linear translation (Otolith Tilt-Translation Reinterpretation - OTTR). 2) Exposure to PAT-TTD stimulus conditions has elicited sensations and symptoms very similar to those experienced immediately postflight for up to 7-10 days. 3) Exposure to PAT-TTD motion profiles postflight has elicited sensations of near weightlessness. 4) Linear vection can be elicited postflight where none was perceived preflight and 5) Data indicated that a 180 degree or 270 degree phase angle between tilt motion and surround translation elicit motion perception sensations more similar to those associated with pitch head movements made immediately following landing than the other phase relations presented. Conclusions: Data from eight crewmembers 1) support the OTTR model of neurosensory adaptation to microgravity; 2) indicate that the PAT-TTD can reproduce some of the sensory stimulus characteristics present on-orbit; and 3) support the idea that the PAT-TTD may be effective in helping to pre-adapt crewmembers. Preflight Adaptation Training is expected to speed neurosensory adaptation on-orbit, thus reducing spatial orientation disturbances and space motion sickness. Preflight preparations for on-orbit experiences will lead to a dual-adapted state which will also help speed readaptation upon return to Earth.

title: Role of Visual Cues in Spatial Orientation
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: The Role of Visual Cues in Spatial Orientation experiment was one of three sensory motor and performance experiments performed during the 1998 Neurolab mission. This experiment focused on how the balance between visual and vestibular cues shifts toward the visual system in microgravity. Using virtual reality, this investigation was designed to study how visual scene content and symmetry influenced the astronauts perception of up and down, to determine how quickly a moving visual scene would produce the illusion of self-motion, and to explore how the direction of perceived "down" altered the ability to recognize shapes and interpret curvature from shading. Information gained from this experiment will help investigators understand why, in the absence of gravity, astronauts become dependent on visual stimuli. This information is also of potential value to medical researchers seeking insight into inner ear impairments and other balance disorders in Earth-bound patients, as well as related rehabilitative testing and training methods for those individuals. As an added value, portable head-mounted displays similar to the one developed for use in this experiment may prove useful for patients, perhaps someday even providing visual prostheses for the vestibularly impaired.
approach: The Role of Visual Cues in Spatial Orientation experiment was performed using NASA's Virtual Environment Generator (VEG), a head-mounted display, which allowed the subjects to view a succession of visual scenes rendered by the VEG graphic computer. The VEG also tracked the motion of the head, so scenes that were displayed appeared stable when the head moved. The astronauts participated in three types of spatial orientation experiments: 1) the Virtual Tilting Room Test (ROOM) 2) the Linear Vection Test (VECTION) 3) the Object Recognition Test (OBJECT). Tests were performed with the astronaut free-floating and, alternately, wearing a constant force spring harness that provided artificial "down" cues to the shoulders and hips. Preflight ROOM, OBJECT and VECTION tests were performed 1 year before launch in NASA's training airplane, the KC-135, and in the laboratory at 90, 89, 60 and 59 days before launch. The OBJECT test was performed on flight day 3, and the ROOM and VECTION tests were performed on flight day 4, with an additional session performed by one subject on flight day 16. Postflight, all three tests were performed on the day of landing and 1, 2, 4 and 6 days after landing. The ROOM test allowed investigators to study the influence of visual scene symmetry, scene rotation, orientation expectation, and tactile/proprioceptive cues on perceived self-tilt. Subjects wearing the VEG head mounted display viewed the interior of a virtual room. Two presentation types were used, static and continuously rotating at constant angular velocity. The VEG joystick, also called the Subject Interface Device (SID), recorded subject responses. The subject made comments using a microphone and entered notes after testing using the IBM Thinkpad laptop computer. During both the ROOM and VECTION tests, subjects wore the Subject Restraint System for testing under free-floating and simulated "standing upright" conditions. When free-floating, the subject's body was not in contact with the Spacelab; loose cloth tethers clipped between the restraint harness, D-rings on the center aisle, and rack handrails prevented the subject from drifting. When the subject was "standing," constraint force springs connecting the harness to the floor allowed the subject to stand erect with his feet on the floor, with proprioceptive and tactile compressive loading on the trunk and lower extremities. Several hypotheses were tested during the ROOM sessions, including: 1) Visual reorientation illusions could be created in the frontal (roll) plane using a VEG-controlled, visual stimulus. Inversion illusions could be elicited in subjects susceptible to them, because the visual cues for static self-tilt perception are usually derived from the ambiguous underlying horizontal and vertical visual symmetries in conventional room interiors 2) A subject's indication of the subjective vertical can be predicted in rooms with differing degrees of visual symmetry (dotted, walled, or furnished rooms). A subject's self-tilt report in static and rotating virtual rooms depends (in a predictable way) not only on scene symmetry, but on expectation, which is determined by internal sensory cues associated with 0-g fluid shift and saccular unloading. The latter will be manipulated using preconditioning visual and haptic stimuli 3) As subjects adapt to weightlessness, their self-orientation becomes less biased by internal sensory cues and increasingly veridical. The VECTION test was used with and without haptic cues to determine how quickly a moving visual scene would produce the illusion of self-motion. Haptic cues are clues that allow orientation by providing input from the restraint system that, for example, forces the feet against the floor, thereby giving the feeling of standing. The VEG was programmed to present a binocular "looming vection" display to the subject in successive 30-second tests. The stimulus velocity and subject orientation were manipulated across tests. Objects in the scene moved radially on the display, simulating subject movement along a path parallel to the visual axis. Previous research on the role of visual cues in 0-g spatial orientation has addressed the phenomenon of rotational vection about the roll axis of the head (roll circular vection). The
results: suggested an increasing dependence on visual and haptic cues and indicated that less weight was given to otolithic cues (probably because their response to head tilt seems initially unfamiliar in 0-g). Otolith organs physically responded equally well to linear acceleration and head tilt. Therefore, it is important to know whether otolith responses to linear acceleration were also given less weight. If so, the linear, as well as angular, component of visually induced self-motion should show changes in 0-g. If all otolith cues are discounted in 0-g, the following was hypothesized for the VECTION test: 1) the latency of linear vection onset to constant velocity visual stimulation would be shorter; and 2) vection magnitude would increase faster and with fewer dropouts than on Earth. The OBJECT test used two types of stimuli to study the influence of perceived "down" on the visual recognition of complex figures and interpretation of shading gradients. Whether an item was determined to be concave or convex depended on how the visual system interpreted the shading. Hypotheses for the OBJECT test included: 1) For complex figure recognition and shading gradient interpretation, the critical factor would be subjective orientation of the "perceptual down," the exocentric frame of reference cognitively adopted by the subject, not gravity 2) Because subjects can voluntarily change their exocentric reference frame, the experiment should show that this change results in object recognition and concavity/convexity interpretation. RESULTS: Eight of 8 nominally scheduled sessions were performed early in flight. One additional session was performed on flight day 16 before a hardware failure that prevented further additional sessions. Data appear to be of good quality based on the initial evaluation. Results from this experiment are expected to add insight into how the nervous system establishes a new balance between information gathered from the eyes, inner ear, and joints. This could help in the design of the next generation spacecraft, in the testing of patients with neurological diseases, and in understanding the relative role of vision in human spatial orientation not only in space, but also in our lives on Earth.

title: The Effect of Daily Activity and Age on Bone	 Density in Men
variables: Activity, exercise; Weight load, whole body
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: The purpose of these studies was to determine the relationship between declining activity level with age and calcaneal density as well as in vivo calcaneal stresses from external and internal forces during walking and running
approach: The first study: A mathematical model previously derived using experimental data of exercise effects on bone mass was used to calculate the sensitivity of calcaneal bone density to age-related changes in body weight, walking speed, and daily walking duration over the age range of 30-70 years. Changes in body weight and walking speed with age were obtained from the literature. The assumption was made that walking provides the primary mechanical load stimulus to the calcaneus. The second study towards a simple Ground Reaction Force (GRF) measurement from external forces was guided by the hypothesis that the reciprocal of foot-ground contact time or the reciprocal of the stride-period-normalized contact time would predict the peak horizontal and vertical GRF during gait. GRF data was collected from 24 subjects while they walked or ran at a variety of speeds. The third study was directed toward a more detailed study of the internal forces from joints, muscles, and tissues during walking and running. It utilized force plate measurements and hi-speed cine-radiography data collected at the Herrick-Davis Motion Analysis Laboratory, Henry Ford Hospital, Detroit, MI. A finite element model coupled with contact of the foot was constructed to determine the forces acting on the calcaneus during walking and running. The GRF data (units in BW) was transformed to a reference system fixed on the foot with the forefoot and the Achilles tendon as the 2 points of contact.
results: A decline in daily walking duration with age may be a major factor in the decrease in bone density up to the age of 50 years. A 39% reduction in daily walking from 30 to 50 years of age can account for a bone loss of 0.2% per year and a reduction of 79% over the same period can account for a bone loss of 0.8% per year. Past age 55, individuals tend to walk more slowly and lose BW, two factors that combined with reduced duration in walking, may accelerate bone loss. Collectively, the second and third studies showed that all parameters were significantly correlated to the reciprocal of foot-ground contact time and the reciprocal of stride-period-normalized contact time. The calculated force-time profiles of the joint contact, ligament, and Achilles tendon forces varied with the time history curve of the moment about the ankle joint. The forces acting on the calcaneus at peak loading during walking occur at 70-80% of stance and during running, earlier or at 60% of stance. The model predicted peak talocalcaneal and calcaneocuboid joint loads of 5.4 and 4.2 BW during walking and 11.1 and 7.9 BW during running. The maximum predicted Achilles tendon forces were 3.9 BW for walking and 7.7 BW for running. Conclusions: Temporal measures can predict force parameters of gait and may be an alternative to direct GRF measurements for determining daily histories of habitual lower limb loading quantities needed for a bone-remodeling stimulus. The bone-remodeling algorithm predicts that running can substantially increase calcaneal bone density. Large magnitude forces and calcaneal stresses are generated late in the stance phase, with maximum loads occurring at 70% of the stance phase during walking and at 60% of the stance phase during running, for the gait velocities analyzed. The trajectories of the principal stresses, during both walking and running, corresponded to each other and qualitatively to the trabecular architecture of the calcaneus.

title: Development and Use of Human 3-Dimensional Tissue Culture Models for the Study of Space Radiation Effects on the Central Nervous System
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Human space exploration involves exposure to types of radiation not normally encountered on earth. The effect of these particles on the human central nervous system (CNS) is of particular concern since impairment of cognitive function could not only compromise missions but cause later effects on the quality of life. Studies in animals have shown that space radiation particles can have adverse effects on cognition and behavior. The effect on neurogenesis has also been documented and proposed to be a cause of cognitive loss. Information regarding the effects of space radiation on the CNS is, however, still in its infancy due to the difficulty of extrapolating data from animals and cell lines to the intact human being. The primary objective of this investigation was to increase the understanding of the effects of space radiation on the human central nervous system with an emphasis on neurodegeneration. There were two primary goals: Develop 3-dimensional tissue models for neural tissue, achieving a more accurate representation of human neural tissue by incorporating human neuron, astrocytes, and endothelial cells into the model. Apply the 3-dimensional models to develop assays to support projected studies of the effects of space radiation on neurodegeneration.
approach: The study began with the development of the human brain tissue model. At least 3 human cell types were acquired for each of the components of the model: neurons, astrocytes and endothelial cells. This ensured the best possible model and provided back-up cells. Then, a multistep protocol was developed for the generation and differentiation of normal human neurons from stem cells. Expression of neuronal markers and degeneration markers in 3D monocultures was successfully detected. The strategy for constructing tissue models was to embed neurons and astrocytes into protein gel matrices after they had been differentiated into the respective cell type and then induce morphological or “end stage” differentiation while they were in the matrix. Endothelial cells were added, given the right factors, and allowed to grow into the matrix and form blood vessels as in vivo during angiogenesis. Different media types and different pairings of cell types were tested. As a
results: , it was found that the requirement of endothelial cells was not entirely compatible with that of neurons and astrocytes. Endothelial cells, which line the vessels and are in contact with blood in vivo require serum for vessel formation. Neurons and astrocytes, normally behind the blood brain barrier (BBB), require serum-free conditions to differentiate in matrices. However, a prototype neurovascular unit using the above protocol was created by reducing the serum concentration and relying on trophic support from astrocytes for the maintenance of vessels. At this stage, it was determined that tissue models were developed enough to be incorporated into assays that assess tight junctions and provide an additional relevant endpoint. Assay development was directed towards determination of the effects of space radiation on the Blood-Brain Barrier (BBB). Assays to determine the function of the endothelial barrier were developed. For the first assay, trans-endothelial resistance measurement was achieved by using equipment that measures electric cell-substrate impedance sensing (ECIS). Resistance monitoring of monolayers was easy and continuous. This assay is useful for determining parameters such as the time course of the effects of radiation. A second assay was developed using tissue inserts to determine the rate of labeled molecules permeation through the cell layer on the insert. This provides a direct measurement of the passage of molecules of varying sizes through the endothelial cell layer. This assay does not utilize the neurovascular unit but can still include a cell mixture of endothelial cells and astrocytes or pericytes. Endothelial cells are plated on one side of the membrane and the other cell types are plated on the other side of the membrane. Thus it represents the human blood-brain-barrier more closely than endothelial cells alone. 2 additional assays were developed for localization of the junction proteins that seal the BBB using immunolabeling of these molecules: the first examining the junction proteins in normal monolayers and the second, examining the junction proteins in the 3-D human tissue models. Further assays include endpoints more directly applied to human neuro-degenerative diseases. One such endpoint is the metabolization and localization of the protein involved in Alzheimer’s disease – the amyloid precursor protein (APP). RESULTS: The primary goal of this investigation has been achieved. Human 3-D tissue models have been developed sufficiently for use in novel assays to determine degenerative markers. Other assays were developed for use in future studies that address a pivotal part of the brain involved heavily in many neuro-degenerative disorders – the brain blood capillaries. Work going forward includes improving the longevity of these models and substituting neurons from stem cells for the neuroblastoma used in the prototype model.

title: Evaluation of the Validity, Acceptability and Usability of Biomathematical Models to Predict Fatigue in an Operational Environment
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Biomathematical models hold promise as tools that can be used to manage fatigue risks in an operational setting. There are numerous models available to predict fatigue-related performance impairment arising from sleep loss, circadian misalignment, and sleep inertia. It is imperative that any model considered for use during space flight missions be validated in an operational setting in order to ensure that predictions are reliable and consistent. Given the complexity of the underlying causes of fatigue, there are wide individual differences in response to mission stressors. However, the majority of candidate models provide predictions based on average human responses, making it difficult to use the models to make operational decisions for individuals. In addition, there are no published reports on the acceptability, usability, and feasibility of any of the current models. Effective incorporation in a space flight environment requires model-based software systems that are easy to use by a wide-range of operators and are integrated with other scheduling constraints that are relevant in space flight operations. This study had the following specific aims: Validate model predictions in a space flight analog. Evaluate acceptability, usability, and feasibility of the selected sleep-wake model software user interface. Incorporate model predictions into Playbook and assess usability and acceptability of model in the context of scheduling and planning.
approach: Investigators aimed to identify which models are the best candidates for inclusion in four Human Exploration Research Analog (HERA) missions. Crewmembers were trained on how to use the modeling software for the selected models and evaluated the usability of the current model software. Investigators asked crewmembers to collect measures of cognitive impairment and simulated operational data throughout the mission using actigraphy, sleep logs, the Psychomotor Vigilance Task (PVT), User Experience Questionnaire (UEQ), Samn-Perelli fatigue Scale (SPS), and the Robotic On-Board Trainer (ROBoT). Investigators used this
results: Investigators studied crews of four individuals during 4.5 missions in the HERA (n = 20). Crewmembers were allowed five hours of sleep during the week and eight hours of sleep on weekends. Crewmembers completed a reaction time test and fatigue ratings five times a day approximately every three days over 45 days. The investigators compared objective performance on the reaction time test to the predictions of biomathematical models designed to predict fatigue. They found that performance deteriorated over the course of the mission on average, however, there were wide individual differences in performance trajectories between crewmembers. Self-reported fatigue did not change over the mission. Biomathematical models were able to predict average performance, but not performance at the individual level.
