RESULTS: As hypercapnia is a potent cerebrovasodilator, investigators hypothesized that HDT+CO2 would result in an increase in cerebral blood flow. Instead they found the opposite. By bed rest day 7 there was a 25.1% global decrease in cerebral blood flow compared with baseline. Additionally, there was a significant time-by-SANS interaction indicating that the change in perfusion over time varied as a function SANS status. The non-SANS group significantly decreased perfusion between BDC-13 and between measurements at baseline and HDT29. The SANS group significantly decreased perfusion between baseline and HDT7. However, they then experienced a significant increase in perfusion at HDT29 compared with HDT7. At HDT7, there was a strong trend for the SANS group to have decreased perfusion values compared with the non-SANS group. At HDT29, the SANS group had significantly greater perfusion than the non-SANS group. These results represent the first MRI assessment of cerebral perfusion in a space flight analog. In this study, investigators showed that the combination of strict HDT along with chronic 0.5% CO2 results in altered cerebral perfusion that is SANS dependent. These results underscore the need for further studies to determine if the changes in perfusion documented here are clinically relevant, whether or not similar changes occur during space flight, and whether or not altered perfusion contributes to the development of SANS or headaches among astronauts.

title: Induction of Bystander Effects by High LET Radiation In Cells and in Tissue Models
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: The mission of NASA’s space radiation biology program is to provide knowledge on the effects of high energy charged particles on biological systems at the molecular, cellular, tissue, and organism levels in order to enable better prediction of risks of carcinogenesis and damage to normal tissues from exposures of astronauts to the ionizing radiation in space. With charged particles such as alpha-particles and low energy protons, significant differences from direct DNA damage-mediated responses have been demonstrated in a number of biological systems. Occurrence of these effects, including bystander effects and genomic instability, calls into question the use of a simple linear extrapolation of cancer risks from high dose data to low doses. This is of particular relevance to NASA because the occurrence of bystander effects in cells exposed to heavy ions or energetic protons, as found in space, has not been evaluated to date. The overall goals of this study are to test the hypothesis that heavy ions and energetic protons efficiently cause bystander effects in neighboring cells not directly traversed by the radiation and to study the mechanisms involved. There were four specific aims: 1. Determine induction of bystander effects by heavy ions compared to X-rays and protons in cultured human diploid fibroblasts and keratinocytes using endpoints specific for each cell type and including production of micronuclei, apoptosis, clonogenicity and increased gene expression. 2. Test the hypothesis that heavy ion-induced bystander effects can be modified by exposure of cells to reactive oxygen species (ROS), an overlying oxidative stress. 3. Test the hypothesis that exposure to low LET radiation alters the heavy ion-induced bystander effects. 4. Begin development of 3-D tissue models for assessment of bystander effects from heavy ions and energetic protons.
approach: The methodology for this study isn’t available.
results: The investigators have developed a novel transwell insert co-culture system in which irradiated and unirradiated cells share medium, but are physically separated, and used this approach to demonstrate medium-mediated bystander responses in AG01522 normal human fibroblasts after X-ray exposure. At the NASA Space Radiation Laboratory (NSRL) at Brookhaven National Laboratory they have used this co-culture system, as well as irradiating cells at low particle fluences, to study bystander responses induced by heavy ions (1 GeV/n Fe, 1 GeV/n Ti and 290 MeV/n C) and protons (1 GeV/n). They have used iron, titanium, carbon and protons because they represent particles found in space that span a range of LET values from 0.24 to about 150 keV/micrometer, thus allowing us to test the LET dependence of various bystander responses. Investigators found substantial effects in directly irradiated AG01522 fibroblasts and h-TERT immortalized human keratinocytes using endpoints including clonogenic survival, micronuclei (MN) formation and p21 expression. For example, with the clonogenic survival assay in the AG01522 cells, we have found relative biological effect (RBE) values at 10% survival are 2.5, 2.3, 1.0 and 1.2 for 1 GeV/amu Fe, 1 GeV/amu Ti, 290 MeV/amu C and 1 GeV/amu protons, respectively, compared to 250 kVp X-rays, indicating the greater effectiveness of Fe and Ti for inducing cell killing. Fe and Ti are also very effective inducers of MN in these cells, although C ions are less effective, similar to protons. Using their insert system,investigators have demonstrated that irradiation with 1 GeV/amu Fe ions induces a 2-3 fold increase in MN formation in unirradiated bystander AG0 cells, which is similar in magnitude to that seen with X-rays. The increase in damage in bystander cells is independent of the dose to the hit cells between 0.1 and 2 Gy Fe ions, although it is somewhat lower at 0.05 Gy. The insert system allows investigators to study the timing of bystander signaling by altering the time at which the co-culture of irradiated and unirradiated cells is started or how long the two cell populations are together. Using this approach, they have shown that when irradiated and unirradiated bystander cells are combined in shared medium immediately, one hour or three hours after irradiation, a full bystander MN formation effect is observed. However, when combining the irradiated and unirradiated cells is delayed six hours after irradiation, the bystander effect is lost. Furthermore, bystander micronuclei formation is observed even when the bystander cells are co-cultured with irradiated cells for only one hour if they are combined immediately after irradiation. This suggests that the signal transduction to bystander cells from irradiated cells occurs at a short time after irradiation, and these early stage signals sent by irradiated cells are crucial to the induction of bystander effects. The results with iron ions are similar to those with X-rays, suggesting that the bystander MN formation in this system is independent of LET. Protons also induce a medium-mediated bystander effect in terms of MN production, although the magnitude is less than seen with Fe ions or X-rays. In addition to X-irradiation, the investigators have now shown gamma-H2AX foci formation in unirradiated bystander cells that shared medium with Fe ion-irradiated cells at different time points after co-culture. The data indicate that a 2-3-fold increase in percentage of bystander cells with gamma-H2AX foci occurs as early as one hour after irradiation, and lasts at least 24 hours. Compared to the directly irradiated cells, which have a high yield of gamma-H2AX foci at early times after irradiation and return to control levels by 24 hours, bystander cells have slower kinetics of disappearance of gamma-H2AX foci. Fe ions and X-rays induce a similar pattern of gamma-H2AX foci in unirradiated bystander cells, suggesting gamma-H2AX foci induction in bystander cells is independent of LET of the radiation. The investigators were interested in studying the effects of very low fluences of particles where only one to two percent or less of the cells would be traversed by particles. Dr. Rusek and his team of NSRL physicists have developed procedures for obtaining these very low fluences, and, most importantly, being able to accurately quantify the particle fluences, determine the beam uniformity and determine the purity of the beam. They have now demonstrated that very low fluences of energetic protons and iron ions induce bystander MN formation and 53BP1 foci (another surrogate for DNA DSBs) in non-irradiated bystander fibroblasts that share medium with irradiated cells. Results show that while there is no significant increase in MN formation in cells directly irradiated with low fluences (2e3 to 5e6 particles/cm2 for protons and 2e3 to 2.25e5 particles/cm2 for iron ions) of protons and iron ions, there is 1.5-2-fold increase in MN formation in bystander cells in the insert system. On the other hand, 53BP1 forms foci in both directly irradiated and bystander cells with low fluences of protons and iron ion, with the percentage of irradiated cells with 53BP1 foci being a little higher than that of bystander cells. It is noteworthy that within the range of low fluences used, 53BP1 foci formation is independent of dose. This suggests that the linear no-threshold hypothesis for relationship of radiation-induced damage to dose may not hold at very low doses. Furthermore, although the the typical dose response plateau pattern of irradiation-induced bystander effects, the fluence at which the threshold occurs is still unclear. At 2e3 particles/cm2, which equals 0.4 mGy of iron ions or 0.57 microGy of protons, there is bystander MN formation with iron ion irradiation but not with protons. The lowest proton fluence that induces the bystander effect is 2e5 particles/cm2, which equals 57 microGy. These data suggest that there might be a threshold for irradiation-induced bystander effects at about 60 microGy for protons and somewhere below 400 microGy for Fe ions. With regard to aim 2 the investigators have reported previously that ROS play a significant role in transmission of signals from irradiated to bystander cells after exposure to X-rays or Fe ions. They have now begun studies to determine the effect of low levels of oxidative stress on responses of irradiated and bystander cells to subsequent irradiation. Their preliminary data show that if bystander AG0 cells are exposed to a low, non-toxic level of hydrogen peroxide before co-culturing with irradiated cells, there does not appear to be any radiation-induced bystander MN formation, but if bystander cells are oxidatively stressed after the start of co-culturing with irradiated cells, the radiation-induced bystander MN formation is not changed compared to the sham control. Further studies are needed to confirm those results. Relevant to aim 3, the investigators have been among the pioneering groups at NSRL to investigate the effects of “mixed,”, actually sequential, irradiations with iron ions and protons. Their preliminary data suggest that in irradiated cells the induction of micronuclei is greater when the two particle exposures are separated by three or 24 hours compared to when given within five minutes. However, depending on the time between irradiations, bystander cells appear to “adapt” to the second signal, i.e., a smaller bystander response was seen when irradiated cells were “hit” twice with 3-24 hours between the hits, than when the same dose was given in a single irradiation. Clearly, these data need repeated, but the results are intriguing. Previously, the investigators reported progress on aim 4 showing significant signaling from X-irradiated fibroblasts to unirradiated keratinocytes and vice versa (endpoints of MN formation and p21 expression). However, interestingly, after Fe exposure their data suggest that with some endpoints there is no signaling from irradiated keratinocytes to unirradiated fibroblasts or keratinocytes, and the effect is delayed from irradiated fibroblasts to unirradiated keratinocytes. Additional investigation is still underway, and they have made progress developing a 3D tissue model using these two cell types that will allow them to test the importance of microenvironment to cell-cell signaling.

title: Team Cohesion Monitoring Badge: Development of Galvanic Skin Resistance Modality
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: The research team developed a monitoring and regulation system designed to unobtrusively measure and support team collaboration and cohesion under grant NNX13AM77G (Measuring, Monitoring, and Regulating Teamwork for Long Duration Mission). One key component of the system was a monitoring badge, a wearable body sensor array designed to assess the frequency, duration, and quality of collaborative interactions between team members as it worked together to accomplish team tasks, as well as physiological metrics such as heart rate (HR) and heart rate variability (HRV). The investigators were able to evaluate the high frequency interaction data streamed by the badges. They also had promising experimental evidence indicating that positive and negative affective reactions to specific team member interactions can be predicted from badge data. Specifically, interactions between team members that involved a cognitive stressor were associated with negative affect and performance failures for the stressed team member. HR predicted both affective states. However, negative affect was predicted by a significant interaction between HR and HRV. This was a very promising finding, because it indicated that the psychosocial status of team members can be inferred analytically from interaction metrics combined with HR and HRV data streams that are monitored by the badges.  This study had the following specific aims: Extend technology development of the sensor platform to integrate a GSR sensor, develop relevant software, and redesign the badge casework. Validate the utility of the GSR sensor to improve discrimination of positive and negative affective states.
approach: The technology development team devised the hardware, embedded software, and stored software components for adding GSR as an additional sensing modality to the existing badge platform. The design was a system-wide backward compatible in that the usability and existing functions of the badge platform did not undergo any changes. The GSR sensor was optionally pluggable to the badge using a wired interface, upon detection of which the badge and base station software self-configured to sense, collect, and store GSR data following existing protocols used for other sensing modalities. Validation research evaluated the utility of the GSR data to significantly improve the prediction of positive and negative affective states beyond the prediction attained using just the existing HR and HRV data streams. This ground-based human research adapted the previous validation experimental protocol used to validate the HR/HRV relationship with positive and negative affect. Two experimental conditions were contrasted: (a) interaction monitoring with HR/HRV versus (b) interaction monitoring with HR/HRV plus GSR. A cognitive stressor was selectively applied to specific interactions as a within person manipulation. The utility of the GSR data will be established if enabled significantly improved predictions of positive and negative affective states beyond HR/HRV.
results: In the phase 4 validation experiment, prior phase 3 validation design was adapted and extended to evaluate the efficacy of the GSR sensing modality as part of the TIS sensor array. The effectiveness of the GSR sensor as a predictor of affective responses to stressed interactions was examined. In particular, the research was primarily focused on its ability to add to the prediction of affect beyond the HR and HRV metrics that were previously validated. The validation experiment was designed to create differential degrees of stress across conditions by using a strong CT (i.e., similar to phase 3 validation which yielded a 78% failure rate) versus a moderate CT (i.e., an easier CT with a target failure rate of approximately 50%). This allowed an evaluation of the sensitivity of the GSR sensor to different degrees of stress. In addition, interactions within conditions were differentially stressed (i.e., resource exchanges with CT versus without CT) which allowed an examination within individuals. The final results showed that heart rate had more consistent relationships with the key study variables (PA, NA, cognitive testing) than GSR. GSR only related to NA, and its relationship was redundant with information conveyed by HR alone. As previously discussed, HR is indicative of both sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous system activity, whereas GSR is solely an indicator of the sympathetic nervous system. It is interesting and perhaps consistent with this conceptualization that GSR only related to NA; however, given the literature, It was anticipated that GSR would aid in the prediction of NA for this reason. Although HR may simply be a more effective physiological measure, there are alternative reasons why this result may have occurred. The GSR sensors used may simply be less precise than the more established HR sensors that were utilized. It is also possible that GSR and HR may not be sufficiently “in phase.” That is, if galvanic skin responses occur more slowly than HR responses, the interaction-level analyses would not effectively capture the relevant information from the GSR metrics; recall the failure of GSR SD to relate to any of the key study variables. However, previous research has shown that GSR and HR responses tend to occur on the same timescale. It was also plausible that skewness within physiological data affected the analyses. To address that possibility, all the analyses were replicated using log-transformed data. The relationships between GSR / GSR SD and key study variables were unchanged. On balance, It is concluded that GSR using the sensors employed in this research does not offer incremental validity for the TIS badge. Although there is sufficient ambiguity to note that these findings are not definitive, the research described in this report does not support a GSR sensor as a strong prospect for improving the TIS technology.

title: Hyperpolarized Noble Gas Magnetic Resonance Imaging
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Conventional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) systems that provide three-dimensional internal imaging of the body have been off-limits for use in spacecraft due to their large size and power requirements. A new technology utilizes hyperpolarized (HP) noble gases, such as xenon and helium to perform similar, but superior, non-invasive imaging of the body. The HP noble gas MRI does not require a large magnetic field, unlike the conventional medical MRI machine, so it offers a potential for a more practical device that is both small in size, low on power demands and easy to use. HP noble gas MRI may be the ideal imaging tool for use in space. This three-year ground-based study evaluated HP noble gas MRI as a means to: 1) help acquire new information about the physiological structure and function of organs and systems of the body while they are affected by microgravity; 2) diagnose disease in microgravity environments; and 3) develop real-time treatments for space-related illnesses.
approach: From previous research, a very low-field MRI system using a signal generated from HP helium-3 and xenon-129 was built. This investigation began the phase of feasibility testing on this prototype unit as a diagnostic tool capable of imaging the function and structure of the lungs, heart and brain. The detailed protocol for testing was developed using a conventional commercial MRI scanner operating at 1.5 and 0.2 Tesla, a reliable and proven platform. The procedures were transferred for use on the prototype HP gas MRI and compared to those developed initially on a conventional MRI. The HP noble gas imaging studies were conducted on the ground using both animal and human subjects. Imaging was aimed at determining lung structure, gas diffusion in the lung, cardiac perfusion, lipid membrane structure, blood flow, and general organ structure. Other specific goals were to: 1) develop small, distal lung airway imaging at resolutions below 1 mm; 2) measure regional ventilation and perfusion irregularities of the lung; 3) detect right to left shunt in subjects with foramen ovale, a condition that needs to be detected prior to EVA (space walks); and 4) test the imaging of lung ventilation and perfusion at very low magnetic fields (0.015 Tesla).
results: In addition to the investigators’ lung studies, advances have been made in their effort to develop hyperpolarized 129Xe MRI for the assessment of brain structure and function. The three most significant advances in this area include: 1. The method of chemical shift imaging was validated in the laboratory, 2. Hyperpolarized 129Xe MRI CSI was carried out in rat brain. 3. In vivo Functional Brain Imaging Using Hyperpolarized 129 Xe was demonstrated. Previously, the investigators reported that the rigorous airway diameter quantification algorithm they developed has been tested on an anthropomorphic lung phantom, and presented the results. Five subjects who have had their airways scanned using HP 3He MRI have also been imaged with CT. The algorithm computing the local ventilation coefficient of variation from HP 3He MRI images previously developed was applied to all ventilation data sets available. The resulting heterogeneity maps, viewed in the context of the ventilation maps, clearly demonstrate the capture of the ventilation heterogeneity characteristics. The algorithms for mapping ventilation have been applied to four non-asthmatics and 13 asthmatic subjects. Statistical significant differences were observed in the heterogeneity scores as well as ventilation distribution standard deviation for various cases of comparison. The results of this study support the idea that HP 3He MRI can serve as a diagnostic tool that can be regularly used to evaluate astronaut physiology, how that differs from their earth status, how it progresses with continued space flight, and how it alters in the presence of disease or impairment.

title: Phoenix Scout Lander: Countermeasures Testbed for Spaceflight Ground Controllers
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: A multi-institutional team of investigators provided fatigue management education to the scientists and engineers working on the Mars Phoenix Lander project. This project was funded by NASA/JSC Behavioral Health and Performance (BHP) research program element and provided an operational opportunity, in a Mars Time Analog, to evaluate countermeasures in a real-time, field setting. Investigators sought to evaluate the acceptability, feasibility, and efficacy of a photic countermeasure used to treat fatigue, circadian misalignment, and sleep loss associated with the Phoenix Mars Lander mission. The proposed research could have significant implications for both sleep disorders medicine and space life sciences. The
approach: The Phoenix spacecraft landed on Mars on May 25, 2008 and the scientists and engineers supporting the Phoenix Mars Lander worked on a Mars sol schedule until August 11, 2008 when the official schedule reverted to an Earth schedule. A multi-institutional team of investigators provided fatigue management education to the scientists and engineers working on the Mars Phoenix Lander project. The investigators also recruited 19 subjects to participate in a research study to investigate the work hours, sleep, circadian rhythmicity, and performance of individuals living on a Mars sol schedule in an operational environment. Investigators sought to evaluate the acceptability, feasibility, and efficacy of countermeasures used to treat fatigue, circadian misalignment, and sleep loss associated with the Phoenix Mars Lander mission. Investigators provided three educational sessions to the scientists, engineers, and support personnel working on the Phoenix Mars Lander project in the week prior to the mission. During those 1-hour sessions, the scientific team provided information on sleep, circadian rhythms, and appropriate countermeasures to facilitate entrainment to a Mars sol schedule and to maximize alertness and performance during work hours. Investigators provided a blue light box to research subjects as well as instructions for when to seek and avoid light to facilitate entrainment to the Mars sol schedule. Ocular light exposure of a specific narrowband wavelength (±30 nm half-peak bandwidths) was encouraged using a light delivery system developed by Apollo Light Systems Inc., (American Fork, UT). Research subjects continuously wore actigraphs on their wrists to monitor sleep and light exposure. They completed daily logs indicating work times and the fatigue countermeasures they used, and provided subjective evaluations of sleep and alertness. Subjects also accomplished daily performance testing and completed 48-hour urine collections about every two weeks to permit analysis of a melatonin conjugate to estimate circadian timing. Subjects wore a Motionlogger on their wrists throughout the study period to provide sleep/wake activity and light exposure information. Each subject was given a personal digital assistant that contained two programs: a sleep-work log that was completed each day and a 5-minute version of the Psychomotor Vigilance Test (PVT) and Karolinska Sleepiness Scale (KSS) that was completed twice per day. Subjects were requested to complete the Automated Neuropsychological Assessment Metrics (ANAM4) at the beginning and end of each work shift. The ANAM battery also included a mood scale.
results: of the proposed research could lead to the development of a new treatment regimen for sleep disturbances of various etiologies during space flight missions, where crewmembers, mission controllers, and support personnel are scheduled to live on non-24 hour days, which could enable these individuals to avoid the decrements in alertness and performance associated with sleep deprivation. title: Self-Generated LBNP for Deep-Space Missions
archive_status: Data preservation is complete.  All datasets are privacy-protected.  Data is available via data request.
objectives: Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-Ocular Syndrome (SANS) is considered an unexplained major risk for future long-duration spaceflight. Evidence thus reviewed supports that chronic, mildly elevated intracranial pressure (ICP) in space (as opposed to more variable ICP with posture and activity on Earth) is largely accounted for by loss of hydrostatic pressures and altered hemodynamics in the intracranial circulation and the cerebrospinal fluid system. In space, an elevated pressure gradient across the lamina cribrosa, caused by a chronic but mildly-elevated ICP, likely elicits adaptations of multiple structures and fluid systems, which manifest themselves as SANS in the neurologic and ocular systems. A chronic mismatch between ICP and intraocular pressure (IOP) in space may alter the optic nerve head, lamina cribrosa and optic nerve subarachnoid space in a manner that is maladaptive to Earth and contributes to the pathogenesis of SANS. The goal of this research is to investigate key measures of cephalad fluid shifts associated with transition from upright seated to supine using a self-generated LBNP device (SELF) without and with expansion exercise. This device is unique in that it is integrated with exercise, requires no power to run and allows LBNP generation in an active or passive manner. This research will include acute studies to document short-term effects of SELF on internal jugular vein dimensions, pressure (static SELF condition), systemic blood pressure, and heart rate. This aim of this study us to characterize the short-term (30 minutes) responses to SELF and evaluate SELF as a method to counteract headward fluid shifts In acute ground-based simulations of microgravity (supine bed rest without head elevation) investigators will use non- invasive technologies and ultrasound imaging to determine if fluid shift alterations reduce jugular vein congestion, a contributor to the development of SANS. To meet this aim, the researchers will quantify internal jugular vein dimensions and pressure (when feasible) in volunteers using a balanced cross-over design before, during, and after simulated microgravity with and without use of the self-generated LBNP.
approach: The investigator included 11 healthy subjects (female and male) in a cross-over design study, assessing cross-sectional area and pressure (when possible) of right and left internal jugular veins during a microgravity simulation using supine bedrest without head elevation. Two different countermeasure of half hour of SELF LBNP were used: 1) Static LBNP: Extend legs to create LBNP and then lock with support rod. 2) Exercise LBNP: Extend legs to create LBNP and continue to bear the load of keeping legs extended by NOT using support rod. The researchers measured blood pressure and heart rate by a continuous, non-invasive finger arterial pressure monitoring device, left and right internal jugular vein cross-sectional areas, and, when possible, pressures using the VeinPress device in each condition. Subjects started with the baseline control conditions of 5 minutes rest, 30 minutes seated and 30 minutes supine SELF LBNP. Strict horizontal supine posture (without head elevation) was chosen instead of HDT as the microgravity model because previous studies document that the venous congestion in microgravity is comparable to that seen during horizontal supine posture at 1g. Supine subjects were not given a pillow, as it is documented that some head-up tilt on a pillow is enough to allow adequate drainage of the optic veins. After baseline and control periods, subjects were exposed to the following acute SELF LBNP protocol: LBNP One (static SELF LBNP or exercise SELF LBNP), Break (water, bathroom, etc.) , five minute baseline, and LBNP Two (whichever countermeasure they did not do in LBNP One) where the order of LBNP One and LBNP Two are randomly assigned in a counterbalanced fashion across subjects.
results: This integrated countermeasure of self-generated LBNP may make return to gravity easier and reduce postflight recovery. The self-generated LBNP device is very timely with NASA’s need to provide an integrated countermeasure for SANS and musculoskeletal atrophy, while at the same time providing a physiologically-integrated exercise device that is safe, low mass, low volume, human powered, and simple for deployment in a confined deep space vehicle. It is also anticipated that the self-generated LBNP device for 30 minutes to 1 hour of exercise and up to 4 hours passively during three days of simulated microgravity will prevent venous congestion, elevated intraocular pressure (IOP), increased intracranial pressure, and cerebral edema formation. This will all help maintain higher intracranial compliance.

title: Etiology and Countermeasure for Back Pain Associated with Microgravity
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: The purpose of this investigation was to compare the effect of spine compression with a harness to the physiologic condition of an upright position on the lumbar spine.
approach: Twelve men and three women (aged 24.4 ±4.8 yrs, mean±SD) with no prior history of back pain volunteered for the 2-day study. On day 1, the baseline scan of the lumbar spine in a supine subject was obtained followed by a scan after 30 minutes exposure to a compression load of 50% of body weight applied by a harness. On the second day, supine subjects were scanned followed by a scan after 30 minutes in an upright position (kneeling in lieu of standing).
results: Both spinal compression with a harness and upright posture increased the anterior disk height and decreased the posterior disk heights. This resulted in a curvature of the spine that was similar after 30 minutes in both loading conditions (14.1±5.3 o after harness and 11.5±6.0o after upright posture). Spinal compression with a specially designed harness has the same effect as the physiologic loading of the spine in the kneeling upright position within the first hour after loading when 80% of the changes occur. Further studies will be required to evaluate the effect of the harness in space flight.

title: Elucidating the Relationship Between the Effects of Various Radiation Qualities and Cancer Development Processes using Novel Flow-based Assays
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Current radiation quality factors used for determining cancer risk for space radiation do not provide the accuracy needed, and there is debate as to the relevance of the experimental studies they're based upon. Therefore, one of NASA's primary goals is to improve the understanding of the carcinogenic process related to high LET exposures to better define the risk. Recently the current understanding of carcinogenesis has improved, and a number of cancer hallmarks have been identified. Some hallmarks, or surrogate cancer endpoints include genetic instability, telomere length changes, and aberrant cellular signaling. Identifying relationships between early and late cell signaling profiles, later surrogate cancer endpoints, and radiation qualities will aid in determining a better risk assessment for cancer formation. In addition, using relevant cell types, such as human epithelial cells in which the majority of cancers develop is also key. In this proposal investigators will studied critical phosphorylation signaling at early and late time points as well as surrogate cancer endpoints of telomere length changes and genomic stability as measured by centrosome amplification, at these same late times post exposure. Epithelial and fibroblast cells from the same individuals were used to better understand the etiology of cancer, and why certain cell types more easily become carcinogenic. Investigators also performed studies to understand the heterogeneous nature of high LET radiation. Energy deposition from high LET ions is dense in the track cores,
approach: Cells were set up in flasks or chamber slides prior to irradiation, irradiated at the various doses and then fixed at multiple time points thereafter. A methanol and a combination of paraformaldehyde and methanol fixation were used depending on what was optimal for the antibody. Fixed slides were sent back to our home institution from Brookhaven in PBS to stain with the appropriate primary and secondary antibodies. Cells exposed in flasks were trypsinized and fixed at various times after exposure, and then sent back on ice in methanol. Aliquots of fixed cells were then stained for various phospho-proteins and analyzed via flow cytometry. For analysis at longer timepoints after exposure (weeks) cells were grown to confluence while at Brookhaven, then frozen down before leaving (~ 1 week post exposure). Cells were then thawed back at the home institution, and expanded to then analyze for telomere length changes and centrosome defects. Cells were stained with pericentrin antibody, then fixed with a methanol fix for flow cytometry based analysis of centrosome dysfunction, and were hybridized to a telomere probe to allow detection of telomere length changes.
results: ing in closely spaced and complex damages, and delta rays originating from cores provide additional exposures similar to X-rays. Using carefully chosen charge, energy, and LETs of particles to obtain differing populations of cells hit by tracks and delta rays alone they investigated how phosphorylation profiles change. APPROACH: Cells were set up in flasks or chamber slides prior to irradiation, irradiated at the various doses and then fixed at multiple time points thereafter. A methanol and a combination of paraformaldehyde and methanol fixation were used depending on what was optimal for the antibody. Fixed slides were sent back to our home institution from Brookhaven in PBS to stain with the appropriate primary and secondary antibodies. Cells exposed in flasks were trypsinized and fixed at various times after exposure, and then sent back on ice in methanol. Aliquots of fixed cells were then stained for various phospho-proteins and analyzed via flow cytometry. For analysis at longer timepoints after exposure (weeks) cells were grown to confluence while at Brookhaven, then frozen down before leaving (~ 1 week post exposure). Cells were then thawed back at the home institution, and expanded to then analyze for telomere length changes and centrosome defects. Cells were stained with pericentrin antibody, then fixed with a methanol fix for flow cytometry based analysis of centrosome dysfunction, and were hybridized to a telomere probe to allow detection of telomere length changes. RESULTS: SUMMARY OF RESEARCH ACCOMPLISHMENTS: Track structure studies based on phospho-kinetics in normal hTERT immortalized fibroblast cells. Normal hTERT immortalized fibroblasts were exposed to a very comprehensive range of carefully chosen high LET ions and energies, to help identify the importance of track structure in defining biological effects. Various phospho-proteins known to be activated following radiation were analyzed for phospho-kinetics including gamma H2AX, pSMC1, and pATF2. Fibroblasts were exposed in triplicate independent experiments to: Fe 300, 600, and 1000 MeV/u; Ti 300, 326, and 386 MeV/u; Si 93, 173, 300, and 1000 MeV/u at timepoints between 0.5 and 24 h. Various comparisons for early and late timepoints were made between equal LET, energy, or Z2/beta2 (roughly equivalent to the number and intensity of delta rays). These studies revealed Z2/beta2 to be a primary determinant in the phosphorylation response. In addition, residual levels of foci (24 h post exposure) correlated well with the predicted energy deposition per nucleosome. This body of work was completed and submitted to Radiation Research recently and is currently in revision (no major revisions required). Conclusions from this work include that: 1) most high LET particles induce a greater induction of gamma H2AX and higher level of residual signaling as compared to equal doses of low LET; 2) at early timepoints ATM-mediated phospho-inductions are much lower following all high LET ion exposures as compared to low LET, indicating that the ATM protein is hampered in fully activating downstream proteins following high LET irradiation as compared to low LET exposures; 3) ions with high delta-ray component (Z2/b2) appear to show a greater persistent phosphorylation signal. Phospho-protein kinetics of primary isogenic mammary epithelial and fibroblast cells. To determine how phospho-kinetics may differ based on cell type and status (immortalized vs primary) we compared phosphorylation profiles of gamma H2AX, and pATF2 from primary isogenic (from same tissue biopsy) mammary fibroblasts and mammary epithelial cells. These genetically matched mammary cells where exposed to a variety of different radiation qualities: Fe 300 MeV/u, Ti 300 MeV/ u, Si93 MeV/u, cesium, and X-ray. Initial induction was assessed at 2h post exposure and the amount of residual signaling was assessed at 24 hour post exposure. We chose the 2 h timepoint as for most radiation qualities this timepoint either showed higher levels or the same levels as observed at 0.5 h. Our results indicate that gamma H2AX induction following high LET exposure is greater than following low LET exposure. For example, cells exposed to Si93 MeV/u exhibit a greater induction than following X-ray exposure. Comparing mammary epithelial and fibroblast cells, initial gamma H2AX inductions were similar for all high LET ions, although the Ti ion was uniquely higher for epithelial cells. At late times post exposure, epithelial cells revealed a much greater degree of residual gamma H2AX signal, indicative of a higher amount of unresolved damage in epithelial cells as compared to fibroblasts. This suggests that epithelial cells are more sensitive to high LET damage than fibroblast cells, since the genetic background of the lines cannot be the culprit of this difference as they are from the same individual and tissue section. A second phospho-protein that kinetics were studied in these lines post various radiation quality exposures was pATF2. ATF2 is known to have various functions within the cell however phosphorylation at this particular site (Ser490/498) has been documented to be specifically required for its role in DNA repair. As has been noted in past studies, pATF2 induction was lower than what was observed for gamma H2AX at early times, with levels saturating at about 0.5 Gy. Unexpectedly initial pATF2 induction in fibroblasts was greater than what was observed for epithelial cells for both high and low LET radiation, which is in contrast to the kinetics we observed for gamma H2AX. However, residual signaling for pATF2 was similar for both the fibroblasts and the epithelial cells. Also of interest was the fact that in general for fibroblast line pATF2 levels decreased with time; however, for epithelial cells in many cases the highest levels were observed at the latest timepoint (24h). This is very different from the findings with gamma H2AX, and suggests again that epithelial cells may have more difficulty responding to effects of high LET exposure. The difference observed between the phospho-protein results may also suggest that levels of pATF2 do not directly correlate with the level of double strand breaks (based on gamma H2AX levels), but instead might reflect others things such as perhaps the levels of oxidative stress present in cells. Similarly to the skin fibroblast study currently in revision, we had wanted to analyze data on a per cell basis on exported flow data. We are currently working with a statistician to finalize this work for publishing in next few months. High LET effects on telomere length of primary mammary epithelial and fibroblast cells. To better understand the relationship between radiation exposure and carcinogenesis we analyzed how the phospho-kinetic response following various radiation quality exposures corresponded to the surrogate cancer endpoint of telomere length shortening. The Flow cytometry-based telomere length assay, or flow FISH was used to determine how various qualities of radiation affected telomere lengths of cells differentially. A dose-dependent shortening of telomeres for both mammary epithelial and fibroblast cells following high LET exposures was observed. For low LET exposures, mammary fibroblasts were fairly resistant to shortening effects even at the highest doses, whereas mammary epithelial cells exhibited a dose-dependent shortening even with low LET exposure. The Fe ion irradiations appeared to show the least difference between cell types, in particular Fe 300 MeV/u, which revealed nearly the same change in telomere length over the majority of the doses. Fe 300 MeV/u has the highest delta ray component of all the radiation qualities tested and this may be one of the major drivers in terms of effects, given both cell types failed to show a resistance to the effects. Overall mammary epithelial cells were more sensitive to the effects of radiation and showed a greater decrease in telomere shortening per dose than did fibroblast cells, consistent with the fact that they reveal a greater sensitivity to radiation induced carcinogenesis. We have also exported individual cell flow cytometry data to define how telomere lengths change on an individual cell basis. Preliminary data has revealed that fibroblasts do not show an increase in cells with short telomeres with increasing X-ray dose, yet epithelial cells did reveal an increase in cells showing short telomeres with increasing dose. This additional analysis will allow us to understand in more detail the underlying reasons for the mean changes in telomere shortening for each cell type. Given that mean lengths can change, for example to show an overall longer length, yet the underlying reason for this mean change could be more cells containing shorter telomeres were lost. A finding of an increase in telomere length upon exposure to protons has been noted in the literature, thus detailing the underlying reason for the mean change in shortening should help us to better understand cell type differences and the mechanism involved in radiation-induced telomere shortening. This work is planned to be combined with phospho-kinetic data and as noted above should be submitted in next few months. High LET effects on centrosome amplification in primary mammary epithelial and fibroblast cells. The second surrogate cancer endpoint, which investigators have studied in relationship to radiation quality, dose, and cell type, was centrosome amplifications. Again a flow-based assay was developed and used to identify increases in size or number of centrosomes as a function of dose and radiation quality, using the pericentrin antibody, which envelops the centrosome of the cell. Our preliminary study with mammary epithelial cells following levels days post X-ray exposure was performed to determine the temporal kinetics of centrosome formation and decline following radiation exposure. These studies revealed that at ~day 9 after exposure significant increases in centrosome aberrations were observed as denoted by the percent of cells showing higher pericentrin levels than the 80-90th percentile of controls. Further studies looking at dose and radiation quality effects were then initiated. We have also performed some studies to better understand how flow cytometry results may compare to the more common way of analysis, immunofluorescence and microscopic scoring of aberrant cells. These studies revealed based on Fe 1000MeV/u results, that similar results in terms of pattern of peak levels observed for both the microscopy and FACS assay were at 0.1 Gy. Why an intermediate dose may show higher levels of centrosome aberrations is uncertain; however, it may be that higher doses kill off cells with aberrant levels thus this is the dose where radiation induces damage, yet it is not enough to kill the exposed cells. Binned results for other ions and energies in assays looking at centrosome aberration frequencies were also performed. These studies revealed the greatest percentages of centrosome aberrations were obtained following Fe300 MeV/u exposures for mammary epithelial cells (far right bin for each radiation quality, showing percent of cells having pericentrin levels >80th percentile as compared to controls). Further statistical analysis was performed on individual centrosome cell data to more carefully define differences at lower doses. The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test (K-S test) was used for these studies; it provides a nonparametric test for the equality of a continuous, one-dimensional probability distribution. It was used to investigate how different doses and radiation qualities compared in terms of the level of pericentrin fluorescence (equal to aberrant centrosomes at high levels over controls) following exposure. The K-S test quantifies a distance between the empirical distribution function of the sample and the cumulative distribution function of the control distribution. Based on KS test investigators were able to note a significant difference from control levels with all radiation qualities and at all doses for mammary epithelial cells. Results with fibroblast cells from the same tissue (mammary) have shown that fibroblasts are much more resistant to forming centrosome aberrations and that levels in general were below detection using the flow-based assay. They went on to confirm this via the microscopy method following Fe1000 MeV/u exposure, and again found no increase in centrosome aberrations over control levels using this method as well. Thus it appears similarly to the telomere shortening, mammary epithelial cells are more sensitive to the formation of centrosome aberrations following radiation exposure as compared to mammary fibroblasts from the same individual. This again points to a heightened sensitivity for epithelial cells to radiation and potentially also carcinogenesis given these endpoints have been linked to cancer and a pre-malignant state. Conclusions: The findings of this body of work point to the importance of radiation quality and cell type in determining the effectiveness of high LET exposure. Epithelial cells for the most part appear to show a greater sensitivity to high LET exposure and of particular importance also a greater induction in the two surrogate cancer endpoints investigated, telomere length shortening and centrosome aberration frequencies. Mammary cells, both fibroblast and epithelial cells, appear to show a less robust response to radiation in terms of phosphorylation of various DNA repair proteins after exposures as compared to a skin fibroblast line (82-6). However all lines revealed a greater response to high LET as compared to low LET radiation. These studies allowed investigators to study how well early phospho-protein profiles predict a cell’s response to other endpoints more closely aligned to cancer. They determined that there was not a direct correspondence between the ion/energy that showed the highest residual level of double-strand breaks (based on persistent gamma H2AX at 24 h) and the ion/energy that showed the highest level of centrosome defects and/or telomere shortening. For example, for phospho-protein signaling at 24 h Ti300 MeV/u reveals the greatest residual levels for mammary epithelial cells, whereas for centrosome aberrations, Fe 300 MeV/u generates the greatest number of aberrant cells weeks post exposure, and Si 93 MeV/u shows the greatest effect on telomere shortening, again weeks post exposure. However, studies in skin fibroblast cells, with a more comprehensive set of energies for each ion, suggest that the ions/energies that are the most effective when compared to other energies are Ti300, Si93, and Fe300 MeV/u. Thus in each case the ion/energy showing a more dramatic response for our mammary epithelial cells when compared to other energies of the same ion are the ones in which in the skin fibroblast study revealed more effectiveness. Thus, perhaps if additional energies had been used for surrogate cancer endpoints and phospho-kinetics for the mammary cell studies we would have seen a pattern similar to what was observed with the skin fibroblast cells, whereby the ions with the lowest energy, having the greatest delta ray component, were the most effective in each case. Why different types of ions show a preference for inducing greater levels for particular endpoints is uncertain and would require further investigation.

title: Comparison of Bending Stiffness in the Dominant and Non-dominant Tibias of Women
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: There is limited information on the mechanical properties of the long bones of healthy women compared to the amount of data on the density of bone. We were interested in determining the mechanical strength of a long bone and evaluating it in reference to the strength of the muscles of the same bone. We were also interested in determining gender differences in the laterality of tibial strength since previous data in normal men revealed the left tibia was stronger than the right.
approach: Twenty women (age 44±11 yrs) were recruited from the working staff of Ames Research Center. All gave informed consent for the study and provided brief historical information on general health and physical activity. The tests for muscle strength were carried out by quantifying the forces required to extend and flex the leg with a LIDO instrument. A non-invasive test of bone strength was performed in the tibia of a relaxed recumbent subject with the probe of instrument positioned on the center of the ‘shin’ bone. The MRTA delivers a “buzz”, detects the response of the bone to a brief vibration at the same site on which the probe is centered and then analyzes the response curve by software that generates a measurement for bending stiffness or EI (E is the modulus of elasticity and I the moment of inertia) for the tibia. The instrument had been previously validated in the bones of monkeys by correlating the non-invasive measurement with three-point bending in a mechanical instrument in the same bone (0.95 was the significance of the
results: of the in vivo test vs. the extracted bone tested with a mechanical instrument). Gender comparisons were done on a population of 22 normal men, aged 39±7 yrs studied earlier (ref #4). RESULTS: In contrast to the findings in men, there was no difference in the bending stiffness of the right and left tibias (150±71 vs. 151±47Nm2). Values in women averaged 28% lower than in men, appropriate for the 24% difference in body weight (men weighed 80±10 vs. women 61±10 kg). Women were shorter than the men but had the same body mass index (BMI = wt/ht2 = 23) and tibial length. Flexion and extension of the right and left legs were also similar (83±22 vs. 84±31 in Nm for flexion and 177±38 vs. 168±51 Nm for extension) and unrelated to EI. We concluded that tibial strength is appropriate for its load carrying function in both sexes, symmetrical in women, but not in men.

objectives: Blood volumes are not routinely measured before and after Shuttle missions, yet were suspected to influence postflight crew performance. To support the hypothesis that blood volume is reduced post space flight, this experiment measured changes in blood volume after space flight.
approach: The subjects had to lie supine while having a venous catheter inserted in their arm. After 20 minutes, a blood sample was taken, and the subject breathed 100 percent oxygen for one minute. Sixty cubic centimeters of carbon monoxide was added to the breathing system and was breathed for 10 minutes. A final blood draw was made.
