objectives: On Earth, upright posture establishes a linear gradient of blood pressure along the length of the body. The change from upright to supine body position is followed by an increase in local pressure from 100 to 200 mmHg in the feet and a decrease at the head level from 100 to 70 mmHg. Considering the combined effect of central and local controls for arteriolar tone, these mechanisms may work cooperatively in the lower body and antagonistically in the upper body, i.e. above the heart level, baroreceptor-induced changes in arteriolar tone may be negated by local myogenic factors, as suggested by cutaneous micro-vascular responses in a study by Aratow et al. that compared responses in the forehead and foot to two tilt angles. This study proposed to further document the different responses in cutaneous microvascular flow to graded postural changes in humans.
approach: Ten healthy subjects (7 male and 3 female) ranging in age from 26 to 47 years (median 27.5), with average weight of 67 kg and height of 171 cm agreed to participate in the study. Flow meters were attached with adhesive tape to the neck and to the leg of each subject. Instrumented subjects were placed upright on a motorized tilt table against a footplate and mildly restrained with a canvas strap across the chest. After stabilization of cutaneous flows, subjects underwent the following stepwise protocol: (Each angle was maintained for 30 seconds with 10 minute transitions between angles) 90 o , 54 o , 30 o , 12 o , 0 o , -6 o , -12 o , -6 o , 0 o , 12 o , 30 o , 54 o , 90 o . In 8 subjects, Ga/ln-in-silastic strain gauge plethysmography measured percent changes in leg and neck volumes.
results: Cutaneous flows (avg±SE) at the calf and neck increased significantly from standing to 12o head-up-tilt (247±55% and 161±15%). From 12 o to –12 o tilt, flows continued to increase at the calf to 479±91% of control, but decreased at the neck to near baseline (119±13% of control, NS). Tilting from head-up to head-down produced significant increments in mean neck volume of 3.8±0.5% above standing control and significant decrements in mean leg volume of 1.8±0.2% below control. Responses of body segment volumes to tilt were practically instantaneous, indicating that blood volume translocation accounted for most of the change. The researchers concluded that flow increases from standing to supine posture can be attributed to baroreceptor-mediated vasodilation at both sites with the added effect of increased pressure at the neck. The subsequent decrease in flow at the neck with head-down-tilt may be due to a myogenic response to increased local arteriolar pressure. The great dissimilarity of flow responses at the two sites suggests that the cutaneous microcirculation of the calf is more sensitive to gravitational stresses than that of the neck.

title: Study of Lunar Dust and Lunar Simulant Activation, Monitoring, Solution and Cellular Toxicity Properties
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: With the plan to potentially return humans to the Moon, it is imperative to understand the hazards that may be faced and to determine ways to minimize them. Understanding the effects of lunar dust on both human physiology and mechanical equipment is one of the most pressing concerns, as problems related to lunar dust during the Apollo missions have been well documented. While efforts were made to remove the dust before reentering the lunar module, via brushing of the suits or vacuuming, a significant amount of dust was returned to the spacecraft, causing various problems. For instance, astronaut Harrison Schmitt complained of “hay fever” effects caused by the dust, and the abrasive nature of the material was found to cause problems with various joints and seals of the spacecraft and suits. It is clear that, in order to avoid potential health and performance problems while on the lunar surface, the negative properties of lunar dust must be quenched. This studied focused on several related areas of research regarding lunar soil: 1) understanding the activation and deactivation processes of lunar soil, as well as how to monitor these processes, 2) understanding the properties of lunar soil in solution (dissolution), and 3) understanding the effects of lunar soil on cellular systems. Initial studies were carried out using several different materials. Due to the scarcity of pristine lunar soil, tests were conducted with lunar simulant, JSC-1A-vf, and quartz and titania, which have been used as positive and negative controls, respectively, in toxicological studies. Knowledge of the activation and deactivation processes is important due to the likely passivation of the active surfaces of lunar soils prior to their transfer to long-term storage. In order to determine methods for dust mitigation on the lunar surface, investigators must first activate the materials and determine the best methods for deactivation. Additionally, the particles themselves may not require activation in order to be toxic. Therefore, dissolution and cellular toxicity studies were performed to determine if any toxic properties of lunar soil are due simply to their chemical makeup.
approach: There is no standard protocol for experiments aimed at understanding the solubility and dissolution characteristics of mineral dusts. The investigators have previously developed a protocol using lunar dust simulant (JSC-1A-vf). In this protocol, 0.5 mg/mL mixtures of dust and the solution of interest were placed in sealed containers and rotated for 72 hours in order to ensure consistent mixing. At the completion of this time period, the mixtures were filtered, and the
results: ing solution was tested using Inductively Coupled Plasma Mass Spectroscopy (ICP-MS) for the presence of metals. These results were compared to tests run concurrently on solutions containing no dust. The current work used jet-milled lunar dust, Apollo sample 14003, and 3 different solutions: distilled water, pH 4.0 buffer (citrate-phosphate), and pH 7.14 buffer (phosphate-buffered saline). RESULTS: After only 2 hours in distilled water, the pH of the lunar dust mixture was significantly higher than that of the control. Over the 30-day testing period, both the control solution and dust mixtures showed increases in pH with respect to the starting pH. While a number of species were measured using ICP-MS after 3, 14, and 30 days, only silicon, calcium, and magnesium were present in quantities above the detection limit of the instrument. While the effects of water on lunar dust are of interest for its possible use as a plant growth medium, studies of dust in the body become more complicated. Fluids in the body are buffered and much more complex in their composition. In an attempt to understand the effects of pH on lunar dust, the investigators performed 3-day dissolution experiments at pH 4.0 and pH 7.14. In contrast to the distilled water testing, many more ions are released into solution in the buffered solutions, especially at lower pH.

title: Advanced Technology Development of Laser-polarized Noble Gas Magnetic Resonance
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: This study is a continuation of previous research into the development of laser-polarized noble gas nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR). NMR is an emerging biomedical technology that has applications for ground-based and possibly, space-based, non-invasive imaging of the body. Using laser-polarized noble gases (helium and xenon), this technology is a novel multi-functional tool that allows traditional high resolution magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of tissues, as well as non-invasive measurements of tissue perfusion. NMR does not require a large magnetic field like traditional MRIs; thus, it is comparatively lightweight and low-power, making it feasible for use in space flight. Possible space-based applications for NMR in non-invasive research and diagnostics include exploring the effect of microgravity on the cardiopulmonary system and lung perfusion and measuring cardiopulmonary function (e.g. ventilation, perfusion, gas exchange and concentration). Additionally, ground-based applications include clinical diagnosis and treatment of lung disease and non-invasive measurement of localized blood flow in a variety of organs.
approach: The investigators developed and tested a second-generation low-field MRI system for optimized open-access human lung imaging. The B0 coils are based on an eighth-order, bi-planar, constant-current four-coil design, providing up to 0.01 tesla with a homogeneity of 50 ppm in a 40 cm diameter spherical volume with an inter-coil distance of ~ 90 cm. The B0 coils are mounted on circular aluminum flanges that are slotted to minimize eddy currents. A water-cooled Alpha current supply provides up to 100 amperes, which run in series through all four coils with stability better than 10 ppm. The magnet is housed in an RF-shielded enclosure that provides noise attenuation better than 80 db at the 50-500 kHz range. Three planar gradient coils have been designed and constructed to provide up to 0.2 G/cm with a linearity suitable for 256 x 256 images with a 40 cm field of view. The gradient coils have greatly improved heat sinking compared to the first-generation system, and can thus generate fast (~ 1 ms) pulsed magnetic field gradients without the need for long delays between echo acquisitions. The second-generation system also features a commercial RF control and acquisition console designed to operate at kHz frequencies without modification, while a single RF transmit/receive (B1) coil reduces cross-coupling noise in a fully 50 O impedance-matched system. The investigators studied several options for B1 coils, and determined the most useful and practical to be a single solenoidal coil worn by the subject around the chest. As a demonstration of the second-generation low-field imager’s capability, two subjects were imaged a total of six times, in both horizontal (supine) and vertical (sitting) body orientations. IRB approval was obtained for 3He inhalation/imaging from the Partners Human Research Committee (Massachusetts General/Brigham & Women’s Hospitals) under an inter-institutional IRB agreement with the Harvard University Committee for the Use of Human Subjects. Each subject inhaled ~ 500 cm3 of laser-polarized 3He gas from a Tedlar bag. We employed 2D and 3D gradient-recalled echo sequences. 2D projection images were acquired in both orientations without slice selection over a 50 cm FOV, in ~ 5 seconds. 3D images were acquired over a 50 x 50 x 12 cm FOV, in ~ 30 seconds.
results: The 3D imaging technique provides a clear representation of the lungs. After rendering, the pleural boundaries are clear and the cardiac cavity is clearly visible. In the 2D slices, the effect of the diaphragm is seen on the lower portion of the lungs. When the subject is sitting vertically, the characteristic curvature from the diaphragm at the bottom of the lungs seen when the subject is supine is no long visible, and the lungs are distended slightly.

title: Time Course of Metabolic Adaptations during Loading and Unloading
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: The alterations in skeletal muscle structure and function induced by space travel or endurance training are the
approach: A novel top-down approach was applied to model whole-body metabolism and to bridge organism to cellular level. Thus, a minimal, but comprehensive, systems model of metabolism was developed which included: (a) brain, heart, liver, adipose tissue, and skeletal muscle, (b) a cardiorespiratory controller, (c) pancreas and liver, and (d) the cardiovascular system. Modeling transport processes across membranes constituted an essential feature of the integration process linking the various scales. For model validation, molecular and cellular measurements were used to assessed tissue and whole body metabolism. To maintain intact regulatory mechanisms, a novel methodological approach with emphasis on the use of in vivo measurements was applied, specifically, proteomics and metabolomics using state-of-the-art stable isotope techniques. This multi-scale model of metabolism enabled testing of physiologically-feasible time profiles of the adaptations to loading/unloading in every organ/tissue, which would otherwise require collection of hundreds of samples in thousands of animals. Specifically, this model can be used to predict tissue metabolism (e.g., fuel efficiency, buffering capacity, and muscle endurance) as well as whole body metabolism (e.g., insulin resistance, lactate acidosis, work capacity).
results: of a chronic mechanical stimulus (or lack of it) a series of metabolic interactions spanning from the cellular to the organism level. Reduced activation of the weight bearing muscles alters gene expression of myosin heavy chain isoforms to meet the functional demands of weightlessness and results in muscle atrophy, reduced capacity to process fatty acids, and reduced muscle endurance. On the other hand, endurance training induces an up-regulation of oxidative enzymes and results in increased fatty acid oxidation capacity and muscle endurance. The few human and animal studies comparing skeletal muscle structure and function before and after unloading suggest that the adaptations are time and biological-level dependent. While some parameters may be altered within a week (muscle mass, insulin resistance), others may take longer to show changes (work efficiency, VO2max). Similar conclusions may be drawn from endurance training studies. Thus, to establish countermeasures aimed at restoring astronauts’ work capacity, it is critical to determine: (1) the time course of muscle atrophy, (2) the bioenergetic, metabolic, and fuel-processing factors that contribute to the reductions in endurance associated with muscle atrophy, and (3) the effects of skeletal muscle atrophy on whole-body metabolism. To answer these questions a multi-scale model of energy metabolism -linking cellular to whole organism processes is needed in combination with appropriate cellular to whole-body measurements collected during the period of adaptation. The objective of this study was to identify the time course of the adaptations to loading and unloading and to integrate them using a multi-scale model of skeletal muscle and whole body metabolism, in order to predict the system integrated response after periods of space travel or endurance training. Accordingly, a team of two computational modelers with expertise on scales ranging from cellular to whole body and three experimentalists with expertise in complementary methodologies in rodents were formed to reach the study’s objectives. The specific aims of this study were: To identify and model the time course of the structural, metabolic and functional adaptations to loading and unloading, To develop and validate a multi-level (cell-muscle-whole body) computational model skeletal muscle metabolism in the context of the whole body. To predict the integrated response of muscle fibers, whole skeletal muscle, and whole body during periods of loading and unloading, in particular astronaut’s muscle energetics and function, as well as his/her whole body metabolism and performance. APPROACH: A novel top-down approach was applied to model whole-body metabolism and to bridge organism to cellular level. Thus, a minimal, but comprehensive, systems model of metabolism was developed which included: (a) brain, heart, liver, adipose tissue, and skeletal muscle, (b) a cardiorespiratory controller, (c) pancreas and liver, and (d) the cardiovascular system. Modeling transport processes across membranes constituted an essential feature of the integration process linking the various scales. For model validation, molecular and cellular measurements were used to assessed tissue and whole body metabolism. To maintain intact regulatory mechanisms, a novel methodological approach with emphasis on the use of in vivo measurements was applied, specifically, proteomics and metabolomics using state-of-the-art stable isotope techniques. This multi-scale model of metabolism enabled testing of physiologically-feasible time profiles of the adaptations to loading/unloading in every organ/tissue, which would otherwise require collection of hundreds of samples in thousands of animals. Specifically, this model can be used to predict tissue metabolism (e.g., fuel efficiency, buffering capacity, and muscle endurance) as well as whole body metabolism (e.g., insulin resistance, lactate acidosis, work capacity). RESULTS: In this research, investigators documented and validated models to provide the desired simulations for integration into the Digital Astronaut program. In the model validation process, investigators compared simulations with experimental data from finished/published animal/human studies. The quantified validation of these models provides the Digital Astronaut project with defensible and credible evidence supporting the use of model simulations to predict muscle performance and atrophy. Model M.1: Simulations were compared with experimental data to validate model predictions of a) cellular metabolic responses from muscle atrophy (by unloading) and training (by exercise loading) of rodents and b) gender differences and fiber types on oxygen uptake kinetics during exercise. Model M.2: Simulations were compared with oxygenation data from skeletal muscle measurements of venous blood and muscle tissue data with various levels of arterial oxygen content and exercise. This validation procedure ensured model robustness under hypoxic stress so that whole-body metabolic function can be evaluated. Model M.3: Simulations were compared with experimental data from skeletal muscle under ramp and constant load tests at different exercise intensities. This validation procedure identified model limitations in predicting metabolic responses to higher exercise intensities. Model M.4: Simulations were compared with experimental data from cardio-respiratory and skeletal muscle responses to exercise in adults: (a) before and after training and (b) before and after bed rest. Investigators provided the Digital Astronaut program with uniform and well-documented computer codes that were or can readily be converted to another format, e.g., MATLAB. The documentation includes: 1. Background theory, variable, derivations, conceptual model structure, fundamental assumptions and implementation documentation including developer’s notes. 2. Well-documented and commented code (FORTRAN and/or MATLAB) with references to all supporting documentation, including definition of all variables and units. 3. Users guides that explain the implementation of the stand-alone code. 4. Outcome of all verification and validation testing, including determination of model limitations. 5. Copies of all publications resulting from this work.

title: Pathophysiology and Treatment of Spinal Pain Associated with Microgravity
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: The purpose of this first back pain study was to determine whether the head-down tilt (HDT) bed rest model would elicit back pain and spinal lengthening similar to that in astronauts during space flight.
approach: Eight male subjects, aged 38±6 years with an average weight of 80.8±10.4 kg and height of 182.6±5.5 cm volunteered for a 21 day study. There was a 4-day control period, 16 days of HDT to simulate microgravity and 1 day of recovery standing upright. Subject heights were measured on 2 control days, the first 8 and last two days of bed rest. All subjects completed a pain questionnaire daily. The questionnaire asked the subjects to rate the back pain on a scale of 1-5, note any activity that eased or worsened the back pain and to describe sleep patterns.
results: There was an increase of 2.1±0.5 cm by the 3rd day of HDT and no further increase. An increase in height during the night after a day of normal ambulation was less than the increase on the 3rd day of HDT. The intensity of back pain in the lower back increased to 2.5 (dull pain) and then decreased to basal levels by the 9th day. Although spinal lengthening in space is twice that experienced during HDT, the type, level, distribution and time course of back pain during HDT was similar to that experienced during space flight. The pain subsided when the spinal lengthening stopped. Astronauts report dull back pain between days 1 and 6 of space flight and it is noted that a knees to chest position reduces the pain in astronauts as well as in volunteers in this study.

title: Investigation of Neural Strategies of Visual Search
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Human performance is easily impaired in a variety of aerospace tasks - such as remotely docking a spacecraft, or flying an aircraft in poor visibility, or finding and tracking a particular target airplane on a crowded air-traffic control display. These impairments occur because aerospace environments can degrade or remove the sensory cues used to drive and coordinate voluntary actions, and display systems may not be optimally matched to the human user. Fortunately, much progress has been made recently in the field of neuroscience toward understanding the physiological mechanisms responsible for voluntary motor behaviors. Visual search is the process that allows us to quickly respond to important items in our surroundings, even in the presence of other irrelevant stimuli. Understanding how individual neurons participate in this process is critical for identifying the factors that limit the speed and accuracy of visual search. Knowledge of these neural factors could be used to design visual displays that conform to the temporal and spatial constraints imposed by human neurobiology, thereby directly improving human performance in man-machine interfaces and virtual environments. Arguably the most important class of movements made by primates during visual search are eye movements, because control of the position of the eyes determines which visual information is sampled and for how long. Decades of anatomical and physiological research have provided a detailed outline of the brain pathways that are responsible for the control of eye movements in primates. These pathways involve a network of areas including visual areas of the cerebral cortex (which provide information about the content of the visual scene), motor regions of the cerebellum and brainstem (which form the final motor commands), and several regions that lie in-between (and which possess a mixture of sensory and motor properties). It is these latter, intermediate, brain regions that are most likely responsible for forming the decision about where the eyes should move next during visual search, because they lie at the interface between the visual areas that provide evidence about the location of stimuli and the motor regions that execute the movements. One of these structures, the superior colliculus (SC), has long been known to play a pivotal role in the control of saccadic eye movements. However, most studies of the SC have focused on its contribution to the motor execution of saccades. Because of the importance of the SC in the decision processes that precede saccade generation, examination of this structure during visual search is likely to reveal fundamental aspects of the visual neural computations involved in identifying, localizing, and selecting visual targets. The main goal of this project would be to measure how neurons in the superior colliculus (SC) change their activity during a visual search task. Specifically, we propose to measure how the activity of these neurons is altered by the discriminability of visual targets and test whether these changes can predict the changes in the subjects' performance. Understanding how the information encoded by these neurons constrains overall search performance will foster the development of more predictive models of human performance and ultimately lead to the design of better aerospace displays and interfaces.
approach: By recording from single neurons in the brains of non-human primates as they perform visual search, the investigators have a window into the internal processing steps that support visual search and how these change over time on a millisecond time scale – data that cannot be obtained from behavioral experiments with humans. In addition, they conducted parallel behavioral experiments with humans to confirm the applicability of this approach.
results: 1) Analysis of brain mechanisms during visual search The initial goal of this project was to investigate the neural mechanisms underlying visual search. Toward this goal, the investigators analyzed neuronal activity in the SC of two subjects while performing a visual search and discrimination task. They recorded from saccade-related neurons (n=85) in the SC of two subjects during a luminance discrimination task. Subjects initially fixated a central fixation cross on a random noise background, and two boxes at six degrees on either side of fixation demarcated possible target locations. On cued trials one box briefly reversed contrast, indicating the likely location of the upcoming target (75% valid). After a random interval, two Gaussian-blurred discs were added, with a luminance increment (SNR = 0 to 4) added to one disk. The subject was rewarded for making a saccade to the brighter disc. The analysis of the neural data was aimed at addressing a basic question about how prior information affects performance during visual search: does it change the sensitivity to the visual input itself or does it weight the visual inputs without changing the underlying evidence? The former explanation is the traditional interpretation, whereas the latter explanation is a more recent interpretation based on signal detection theory and applications of Bayesian inference. The results of the analysis favor the weighted evidence interpretation. The subjects’ performance in the task showed a clear cue validity effect: higher percent correct when the cue correctly indicated the target location. Neurons in the superior colliculus showed a neural correlate of this cueing effect: higher activity on validly cued trials compared to invalidly cued trials. However, ROC analysis indicated that this effect was almost entirely due to a bias in activity caused by the presence or absence of the cue in the neuron’s response field. The ability of the neuron to visually discriminate between target and distracter was largely unaltered by the presence or absence of a cue. These findings are consistent with the idea that saccadic choice behavior is guided by a weighted integration of sensory evidence, and that the activity recorded in the superior colliculus lies after the point at which those weights are applied. In addition, the investigators have modeled these results using approaches from signal detection theory and Bayesian statistics. Based on the feedback and comments received during the Bioastronautics Investigator’s Workshop in Galveston Texas in January 2005 – in particular, that human studies should be emphasized over animal studies, the investigators adjusted their research goals and initiated an additional set of studies aimed at making their neurophysiological studies more directly relevant to issues of human performance. The remaining projects were aimed at understanding human performance during visual search and the underlying biological mechanisms. 2) Shared decision signals for different components of visual search Eye movements generated during visual search have two components: saccades that rapidly redirects the line of sight to new objects, and smooth pursuit that smoothly changes the line of sight to follow moving objects. Most models of visual search account for saccades, but do not include smooth pursuit. The investigators extended their model of eye movement decisions to incorporate pursuit as well as saccades. The data used in this study included approximately 8,000 combined pursuit and saccade movements during a visual search task. This data set allowed investigators to answer the question: how can pursuit and saccades by guided by a common decision signal and yet still display differences in timing and choices? On the one hand, their results provide additional evidence that pursuit and saccade choices are determined by a common decision signal – in particular, the speed-accuracy curves for pursuit and saccade have the same shape. On the other hand, they also identified two specific differences between pursuit and saccades in how the putative decision signal is read-out to determine the eye movement choices. First, the pursuit system employs a lower response threshold than saccades; this difference accounts for approximately seventy percent of the time-shift as well as the occurrence of trials in which the two motor choices disagree. Second, the saccadic system is subject to an additional motor delay that is not present in the pathways for pursuit; this difference accounts for the remainder of the time-shift observed between the two responses. 3) Eye movement selection when reward probability is dynamically manipulated The investigators have also developed a novel task to examine how knowledge of target probability affects visual search. In these new studies, they have compared the ability of humans to learn a Markov process. Markov chains (stochastic processes where probabilities are assigned based on the previous outcome) are commonly used to examine the transitions between behavioral states, such as those that occur during foraging or social interactions. However, relatively little is known about how well primates can incorporate knowledge about Markov chains into their behavior. Saccadic eye movements are an example of a simple behavior influenced by information about probability, and thus are good candidates for testing whether subjects can learn Markov chains. In addition, when investigating the influence of probability on saccade target selection, the use of Markov chains could provide an alternative method that avoids confounds present in other task designs. To investigate these possibilities, investigators evaluated human behavior on a task in which stimulus reward probabilities were assigned using a Markov chain. On each trial, the subject selected one of four identical stimuli by saccade; after selection, feedback indicated the rewarded stimulus. Each session consisted of 200-600 trials, and on some sessions, the reward magnitude varied. On sessions with a uniform reward, subjects (n = 6) learned to select stimuli at a frequency close to reward probability, which is similar to human behavior on matching or probability classification tasks. When informed that a Markov chain assigned reward probabilities, subjects (n = 3) learned to select the greatest reward probability more often, bringing them close to behavior that maximizes reward. On sessions where reward magnitude varied across stimuli, subjects (n = 6) demonstrated preferences for both greater reward probability and greater reward magnitude, resulting in a preference for greater expected value (the product of reward probability and magnitude). These results demonstrate that Markov chains can be used to dynamically assign probabilities that are rapidly exploited by human subjects during saccade target selection 4) Eye movement selection when sensory information is minimal or absent Deciding where to look next demands the integration of bottom-up intrinsic image salience with top-down information of goals, motivation, and past experience of reward. Most research has focused on the characteristics of the image regions we choose to fixate; less attention has been given to the role of top-down influences despite research showing that top-down influences are important in determining the next saccade in natural scanning tasks. In these experiments, the investigators explicitly manipulated prior experience by “hiding” reward locations and asking human and monkey subjects to conduct an eye movement search for the rewarded locations. Over the course of single experimental sessions, subjects redirected their gaze to the estimated center of the rewarded target distribution. Later in the session, the distribution of subjects’ eye movements reflected the shape and spread of the distribution. Thus, using this novel eye movement search task, investigators can control the association of a spatial region with reward and assess how implicit learning contributes to where we look next.

title: Total System Approach
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: NASA has established the goal of returning human expeditions to the moon and extending exploration to Mars. Extended manned missions of these types require massive quantities of food to be flown into space. This presents two challenges when dealing with a food system. These challenges are maintaining the quality of the food throughout its shelf life which may be in excess of five years, and to assure the mass and volume of the food system are minimized. A Total System
approach: is an operating system that considers each parameter of an overall process and seeks to optimize each of these parameters to maximize the output. In the case of the NASA food system, the output would be a food system with low mass packaging using high barrier packaging materials. The purpose of this project was to evaluate the processes related to the packaging of the current NASA food system being used for the International Space Station (ISS) and the Shuttle (STS). The evaluation will define the current processing parameters and identify ways to improve the processes. These parameters include those related to sealing, internal atmosphere of the package, and materials. Parallel to this evaluation, a literature review will be conducted in an effort to identify available materials with high potential for long-duration missions, possible packaging defects, and ways to prevent them in the future, ways to improve oxygen elimination, and the impact of these on product shelf life. Even though the current packaging system processing parameters have been documented, these parameters have not been evaluated from the perspective of improving packaging integrity and mass reduction. This is due largely to the success of the current packaging system using the current high payload vehicles such as the STS and Russian Progress vehicle. Payload for long-duration missions of years rather than months, like ISS missions, will require a greater quantity of food in proportion to other supplies than do the missions of today. Thus, the need for reduced packaging mass becomes critical in order to execute future missions. APPROACH: The outline below describes specific processing points that were evaluated. These processing points are parts of the Total Packaging System. Any improvements that can be made in each of these areas may benefit the overall packaging system. 1. Literature review - Identify high potential materials, minimize pinholes and critical defects, optimize Modified Atmosphere Packaging (MAP) flushing , and improve shelf life. 2. Define existing packaging system - food processing 3. Effects of Temperature on Materials - heat seal 4. Effects of temperature variation 5. Seal Width (possible area of mass reduction) 6. Quality - defects , seal Integrity, vacuum 7. Oxygen quantities - MAP flushing quality 8. Using current system 9. Modified system 10. Gases other than nitrogen - Material quality, film, septum, gases (i.e. ppm 02), Packaging design/configuration
results: Optimal sealing parameters for each type of material currently being used by the space food system have already been incorporated into the packaging procedures. As new materials are added to the system, it is recommended that the procedure used in the heat seal evaluation be used to determine the optimal seal setting for each material. Although the seal reduction evaluation showed considerable mass saving, it is not recommend that the seals be reduced below the 3/8” standard. The safety and health of the crew is more important than minimal mass savings when it comes to a mission’s success. Reducing the seals would increase the potential for package failure from contaminants in the seal leading to food spoilage and food borne illness. The data that was gathered during the Modified Atmosphere Packaging (MAP) evaluation shows that the current methods used in the space food packaging system is inefficient and seals in a significant amount of air in some cases. It is highly recommended that the optimal equipment setting determined during the evaluation be incorporated as soon as possible to improve the quality of food in the space food system. The gusseted pouch design yielded very good results in making the rehydratable packages easier to produce while minimizing mass, volume, and waste. It reduced the production process from using three pieces of packaging equipment to one. It reduced the packaging from two pouches to one and decreased the total amount of packaging mass by approximately 63%. The literature review and MAP gas research stated that argon is a viable gas with great potential. Argon gas is more efficient, does not require a vacuum cycle, and can be used with liquid products, like the thermostabilized foods which currently have residual air in the headspace. More research and development is required for the use of argon gas for MAP applications because it is not widely used and requires equipment modifications. Also, it would need to be determined whether the levels of argon released from opened packages in an in enclosed environment would be hazardous to crew health.

title: Ocular Counter Rolling and Subjective Visual Vertical
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: To assess whether head down bed rest diminishes inner ear (otolith) sensitivity, the ocular counter-rolling response to postural tilting was measured before and after bed rest. Furthermore, to assess whether head down bed rest alters the perception of spatial orientation, the subjective visual vertical (SVV) was assessed before and after bed rest each using settings of a visual line to upright.
approach: Ocular Counter-Rolling (OCR) refers to the rotation of the eye about the line of sight. Measures of an otolith-mediated reflex was made using a Personnal Computer (PC)laptop-based head and eye tracker, developed by the investigators (MacDougall and Moore). Torsional eye movement (rotation about the line of sight) was calculated using images acquired from a miniature digital camera at a rate of 30 Hertz. Subjects were seated while wearing lightweight goggles with one digital video camera attached. Subjects looked straight ahead for 10 seconds and were then instructed to lie on their right side. After a period of 60 seconds, to allow semicircular canal input to diminish, the subjects looked straight ahead for 10 seconds. This process was repeated with the subject lying on their left side. The gain of OCR was calculated from the actual head roll position (i.e., upright, 90 degrees to the right or left) and the amount of roll eye movement. Following removal of the video goggles, perception of the spatial upright was assessed using settings of a visual line to the Subjective Visual Vertical (SVV) using hardware and software developed for the Neurolab STS-90 vestibular experiment. Subjects were asked to adjust (using a handheld controller) the orientation of a luminous bar on a laptop display which is visible through a circular cut-out and shroud. The shroud was used to control for orientation cues from the computer itself. Subjects made 10 settings from start positions randomly offset of ±15° either side of the vertical meridian while seated with their head in the upright position. This sequence was repeated with the subject lying on their right side and left side. Subjects completed two pre-bed rest test sessions at approximately 2 sessions before bed rest and up to five post-bed rest test sessions. It was expected that if bed rest induces deconditioning of otolith-ocular reflexes that this would not be reversed by Artificial Gravity (AG) exposure since the positioning of the subject on the centrifuge only allows for partial gravity stimulation of the otoliths during AG exposure. It is also expected that only a small decrease in OCR gain will be observed post bed rest, due to the partial unloading of the saccule.
results: Results indicated that OCR was unaffected by bed rest and bed rest plus artificial gravity. Performance on the subjective visual vertical task was unaffected in the control group, but revealed a significant increase in error for 48 h after bed rest in the treatment (artificial gravity) group. Intermittent application of linear acceleration along the long body axis may have increased the weighting of the idiotropic vector, resulting in an increased of the SVV toward the long body axis during 90 degrees roll tilt. This experiment has concluded in ground-based studies sponsored by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration's Human Adaptation and Countermeasures Division. This experiment was conducted during the Artificial Gravity Bed Rest Study. LSDA does not expect to receive results from this study however, more information can be found through the publication listed.

title: Analysis of a Clinical Database as a Means to Validate Non-invasive Assessment of Intracranial Pressure Using the Cerebral and Cochlear Fluid Pressure (CCFP) Analyzer
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Visual impairment intracranial pressure (VIIP) is a top risk for human space flight, yet there are no reliable means to monitor intracranial pressure (ICP) non-invasively, particularly in flight. A lumbar puncture (LP) is invasive and isn’t a viable option for in flight monitoring, and are only used on crewmembers exhibiting significant VIIP symptoms. Development and validation of a noninvasive means of monitoring ICP would
approach: This study was a retrospective chart review of Ear and Balance Institute patients. Personnel at the Ear and Balance Institute reviewed physical and electronic charts and compiled data into coded, de-identified spreadsheets and file structures. This data was transmitted to the investigative team in Houston, who performed the analysis. The analysis had several components that addressed the specific aims of this study: 1) evaluate both evoked and passive TMD waveforms as measured by CCFP and compare with LP data; and 2) determine the age-dependent distribution of cochlear aqueduct patency.
results: in collection of data that could define the involvement of elevated ICP in the VIIP syndrome. The Cochlear and Cerebral Fluid Pressure (CCFP) analyzer measures tympanic membrane displacement (TMD) in both evoked and passive modes. These TMD waveforms change in response to ICP alterations, allowing a noninvasive means to monitor ICP changes. Additional clinical validation of the CCFP analyzer is necessary to better understand the device’s utility. The Ear and Balance Institute has over 1,000 patient records of CCFP tests, many with accompanying LP measures. Analysis of the results of these tests has helped validate the use of the CCFP technology as a surrogate measure of ICP. The purpose of this retrospective clinical study was to examine this unique CCFP and LP data set, in order to identify characteristics that could contribute to follow-on studies employing the CCFP analyzer. APPROACH: This study was a retrospective chart review of Ear and Balance Institute patients. Personnel at the Ear and Balance Institute reviewed physical and electronic charts and compiled data into coded, de-identified spreadsheets and file structures. This data was transmitted to the investigative team in Houston, who performed the analysis. The analysis had several components that addressed the specific aims of this study: 1) evaluate both evoked and passive TMD waveforms as measured by CCFP and compare with LP data; and 2) determine the age-dependent distribution of cochlear aqueduct patency. RESULTS: Because the CCFP had been used as a clinical screening tool, many patients had begun medical intervention between administration of the CCFP test (Vm) and the LP, or had been undergoing treatment prior to any test being administered. Another caveat associated with this analysis is that CCFP measures had not been collected at the same time as LP. To address these issues, analysis focused on patients whose LP was performed in close temporal proximity to CCFP (within an average of approximately five days), and those who had no interventions between measures. These factors have reduced the number of charts available for analysis (approximately 70 out of 1000 available with CCFP and LP measures). Nearly all patients in this database had ear-related pathology, with the largest contributors being superior semicircular canal dehiscence (SSCD), and perilymph fistula that likely affect CCFP response. Despite these factors, a negative correlation between tympanic membrane displacement in an evoked CCFP test and LP opening pressure was found in the non-SSCD patient population in the seated position, and expectation-maximization estimates suggested that Vm in the supine position trends negatively with LP. These results are encouraging as to the potential utility of the CCFP as an ICP screening tool in a non-clinical population, and deserve further investigation in an experimental setting.

title: Assessing and Mitigating the Impact of Transmission Delays on Teleoperations
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: The objective of this study was to examine coupled human-system performance in the presence of temporally varying communication delays between the human controller(s) and remotely operated robot(s), and to propose countermeasures for delay-induced performance decrements. This DRP will be conducted in support of the NASA Enabling Technology Development and Demonstration (ETDD) Program’s Human Exploration Telerobotics (HET) Project, in which ground-station operators will control robotic assets on board the International Space Station (ISS). Specifically, the DRP will concentrate on the element led by NASA ARC that is focused on ground-to-orbit control of the “Synchronized Position, Hold, Engage, and Reorient Experimental Satellites” (SPHERES) free-flying robots on the International Space Station (ISS). The DRP will focus on the range of time delays encountered in the ground-based control of the robotic assets on the ISS, ranging from 20-50 ms (effectively for line-of-sight communication) up to 2-10 s for multiple satellite ground-station relayed (Tracking and Data Relay Satellite System, or TDRSS, and associated ground network) communication, and, in particular, as delay instantaneously varies because of real-time changes in communication paths and data buffering. The aims of the proposed work were: 1) to employ human-in-the-loop (HITL) testing to empirically investigate the impact of variable communication delays, with latencies spanning from tens of milliseconds up to approximately five seconds, on coupled human-system performance for telerobotic systems; 2) to evaluate empirically the efficacy of existing time delay compensation schemes for this range of latencies for telerobotic tasks and control modes that have different required movement precision levels; and 3) to use the data
approach: Investigators conducted human-in-the-loop (HITL) performance experiments using visual display of a dynamic simulation representative of a variety of SPHERES operations requiring different movement precision under this range of time-delay conditions. Next, they examined HITL performance under these conditions employing mitigation techniques for short time delays such as prediction algorithms that generated compensatory in command signal lead and, for longer delays, predictive “feed-forward” graphical overlays that “look ahead” and provided a virtual view showing the future pose and location of the robot. The goal of the second of the studies was to understand the performance trades between these techniques in a wider variety of environmental and latency conditions than is usually achievable during in situ experimentation. Based on these empirical HITL
results: ing from these studies to identify the trade points between latency compensation schemes as a function of time delay and required task precision and then design and test strategies for gracefully switching between mitigation techniques as telerobot system time delays vary. The guidelines, tools, mitigation techniques and performance metrics developed from this research will help provide a rational basis for the design of teleoperation tasks to be carried out in the presence of communication delays. These products will in turn assist subsequent task, technology design, and validation experiment decisions regarding acceptable or desirable delay compensation techniques and define at what point to engage more autonomous operational modes. APPROACH: Investigators conducted human-in-the-loop (HITL) performance experiments using visual display of a dynamic simulation representative of a variety of SPHERES operations requiring different movement precision under this range of time-delay conditions. Next, they examined HITL performance under these conditions employing mitigation techniques for short time delays such as prediction algorithms that generated compensatory in command signal lead and, for longer delays, predictive “feed-forward” graphical overlays that “look ahead” and provided a virtual view showing the future pose and location of the robot. The goal of the second of the studies was to understand the performance trades between these techniques in a wider variety of environmental and latency conditions than is usually achievable during in situ experimentation. Based on these empirical HITL results, investigators designed and tested a strategy for combining and gracefully switching between mitigation techniques as telerobot system time delays vary across the millisecond to second range. To conduct the DRP studies, investigators built their experiment testbed derived from elements of the HET ground-to-orbit SPHERES task, encompassing ground operator user interfaces as well as computer-based simulations of the SPHERES robots and ground-ISS communication links. This strategy allowed them to run HITL tests that will reduce the operating environment to offer sufficient flexibility and control for human performance experiments, yet still maintain salient features of the HET tasks key for face-validity and applicability of the results. The results from the experimental studies will help define more focused and scientifically revealing experiments that could subsequently be conducted on the ISS. RESULTS: Movement time and trajectory data from all twenty participants, pooled across all experiment conditions, were significantly positively correlated, indicative of a speed-accuracy tradeoff in their performance. Analyses of Variance (ANOVAs) conducted separately on path length and movement time (transformed to correct for data skew) produced identical results. These ANOVAs showed a significant effect of rotation angle and an interaction between rotation angle and axis, but did not reveal a significant effect of the sequence of rotation axis. General features of the data indicate that the MDF, whether expressed in terms of movement time or path length, reaches a peak at or near 120 degrees for all axes and that the peak’s magnitude was significantly greater for rotation about the roll axis. The results from this study indicate that the MDF, i.e., the effect of the control-display rotation, is not isotropic with respect to axis of rotation: roll produces a distinctly larger nonlinearity and peak magnitude. Investigators conjecture this is due to the displacement arising from the roll misalignment being projecting into the participant’s two key body reference axes, i.e., the lateral (left-right) axis and the vertical axis (usually aligned with gravity), which contrasts with pitch and yaw disturbances being projected into only one of these axes in the frontal plane.

title: Effects of Long-Duration Microgravity on Fine Motor Skills: 1-year ISS Investigation
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Fine motor skills will be critical during long-duration space missions, particularly those skills needed to interact with technologies required in next-generation space vehicles, spacesuits, and habitats. They will be necessary for performing tasks in transit or on a planetary surface, such as information access, just-in-time training, subsystem maintenance, and medical treatment. Few, arguably no, studies have been completed in long-duration microgravity to investigate the type of functional fine motor performance required to interact with advanced technologies (e.g., touch technologies, gesture interfaces). There has also not been a complete, systematic study of fine motor performance to include different phases of microgravity adaptation, long-term microgravity, and the sensorimotor recovery period after transition to Earth gravity. In addition, the fine motor control studies conducted to date have not been conclusive regarding the effects of microgravity. The aim of this study was to determine the effects of long-duration microgravity and of different gravitational transitions on fine motor performance. This study had the following specific aims: Determine the effects of long-duration microgravity on fine motor performance. 1) How does fine motor performance in microgravity trend/vary over the duration of a year-long space mission? 2) How does fine motor performance on orbit compare with that of a closely matched subject on Earth? Determine the effects of different gravitational transitions on fine motor performance. 1) How does performance trend/vary before and after gravitational transitions, including the periods of early flight adaptation, and very early/near immediate postflight periods?
approach: ISS Subjects completed a set of fine motor tasks on an iPad computer, with a stylus and finger. The tasks included: Pointing, Dragging, Shape Tracing, and Pinch-Rotate. Response times and errors for each task were captured and sent to the International Space Station (ISS) server for downlink once a week. Subjects performed the task approximately once a week for the first 3 months of the flight, and every 14 days for the remainder of the flight. Due to postflight crew time constraints, a short version of the Fine Motor Skills test battery (5 minutes) was used for the early postflight data sessions. The short sessions were completed on landing day (Return +0), R+1, and R+3, and regular-length sessions (15 minutes) were completed on R+5, R+15, and R+30. The study included two one-year subjects and seven standard duration (six-month) astronauts. Eight ground-matched subjects completed the study with the same schedule as the flight crew, lagged by a few weeks. HERA To complete the tasks, participants used an iPad with the test battery software and a stylus. The stylus was tethered to the tablet. Some tasks were completed with only the finger or stylus; some were completed with both input methods. Investigators used a number of test battery tasks that examined various aspects of fine motor performance: (a) multidirectional pointing task, in which the participants selected targets of different sizes at various distances; (b) dragging task, in which a target was dragged from one position to another; (c) shape-tracing task; and (d) pinch-rotate task, in which a geometric object was pinched and rotated using the touchscreen to match an object presented on the screen. Each session consisted of multiple trials of all four tasks. In the debrief session, participants were asked to complete short surveys about the tasks and the hardware. This was a small pilot test for the ISS portion of the study evaluating the software and hardware during HERA Campaign 1, mission 3.
results: Results indicate no significant decrements inflight during the six-month and one-year missions; however, small, but significant decrements were found in the days and weeks following landing, indicating the impact of the gravitational transition back to Earth. The Fine Motor Skills test battery software was released for public use through the NASA Technical Reporting process, and the app will soon be available on the Apple app store. The test battery can be used to measure fine motor decrements in elderly or diseased populations. The software may also prove beneficial in rehabilitation of fine motor skills in elderly patients, people with motor disorders, and patients with brain injuries.

title: Spatial Organization within Prostate Cancer Spheroids
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Multicellular spheroids have a remarkable capacity to mimic solid tumors to a greater extent than cell monolayers. Spatial organization within spheroids is seminal to their in vivo-like behavior and is instrumental in the acquisition of drug resistance and expression of antigens that can serve as biomarkers for carcinogenesis. This research provides a comprehensive analysis of the spatial profile and assembly of multicellular spheroids, using prostate cancer cells as a model system. Spheroid differentiation and viability will be determined as a function of radial position. This analysis was performed on spheroids produced using conventional methods and in a rotating-wall vessel (RWV). The knowledge gained from this research will ultimately improve the fidelity of multicellular spheroids in the extent to which they resemble micrometastases and avascular regions of larger tumors. The objective of the proposed research was to improve the understanding of how culture conditions affect the spatial profile and assembly of multicellular cancer spheroids, using prostate cancer cells as a model system. During the study, the investigators fulfilled the following specific aims: 1) Developed mathematical models of spheroid formation with population balances and Monte Carlo technique. 2) Elucidated the biological and physical mechanisms underlying spheroid formation of prostate cancer cells with the mathematical models. 3) Assessed the ability of the mathematical models to predict spheroid self-assembly of prostate cancer cells. 4) Characterized the spatial composition of prostate cancer spheroids with respected to viability, differentiation and multidrug resistance.
approach: The methodology for the study is embedded in the
results: section below. RESULTS: Aggregation of attachment-dependent animal cells represents a series of motility, collision, and adhesion events applicable to such diverse fields as tissue engineering, bioseparations, and drug testing. Aggregation of human prostate cancer cells in liquid-overlay culture was modeled using Smoluchowski's collision theory. Using well (LNCaP) and poorly differentiated (DU 145 and PC 3) cell lines, the biological relevance of the model was assessed by comparing aggregation rates with diffusive and adhesive properties. Diffusion coefficients ranged from 5 to 90 microm(2)/min for single LNCaP and PC 3 cells, respectively. Similar diffusivities were predicted by the persistent random walk model and Einstein relation, indicating random motion. LNCaP cells were the most adhesive in the study with reduced cell shedding, 100% adhesion probability, and enhanced expression of E-cadherin. There was an increase in DU 145 cells staining positive for E-cadherin from nearly 20% of single cells to uniform staining across the surface of all aggregates; fewer than 30% of PC 3 aggregates stained positive. Aggregation rates were more consistent with adhesive properties than with motilities, suggesting that aggregation in the study was reaction-controlled. Relative to other assays employed here, aggregation rates were more sensitive to phenotypic differences in cell lines and described size-dependent changes in aggregation at a finer resolution. In particular, model results suggest similar aggregation rates for two-dimensional DU 145 and PC 3 aggregates and upwards of 4-fold higher rates for larger three-dimensional DU 145 spheroids, consistent with expression of E-cadherin. The kinetic model has application to spheroid production, to cell flocculation and as an adhesion assay. Neoplastic multicellular spheroids are in vitro models of solid tumors employed in drug testing and basic research. This study compares differentiation in static and mixed prostate cancer spheroids. Staining intensity of prostate specific antigen (PSA) was down-regulated upon mixing, from 0.21 +/- 0.03 to 0.13 +/- 0.03 in LNCaP multicellular spheroids, and from 0.13 +/- 0.04 to 0.03 +/- 0.02 in DU 145 multicellular spheroids. This was accompanied by 65% increase in the expression of cytokeratins 8 and 18 in DU 145 spheroids. PSA expression extended 60 micro m within static spheroids and was disrupted in mixed culture. Diminished PSA expression and spatial organization suggests a more aggressive cancer. Higher cytokeratin expression could result from either differentiation towards a luminal phenotype or activation of the Ras pathway during dedifferentiation. Thus, the existing paradigm of differentiation established for normal tissue does not apply for our neoplastic spheroids. Cell dedifferentiation is attributed to improved interstitial transport and synthesis of extracellular matrix.

title: New Automated System for Real-Time Bio-Imaging of a Vascular Cell Function in Microgravity
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: It is critical to NASA's mission for human exploration and development of space to understand the influence of the space environment, specifically microgravity, on human physiology. Previous work has shown that microgravity can modify host cell-cell and cell-matrix interactions, and thereby exert potentially deleterious effects on human vascular and immune functions and regeneration processes. For simulated microgravity, such as in a rotating wall vessel (RWV), adhesion assays as currently conducted have important limitations. First, to remove a cell sample from the RWV, rotation must be stopped, interrupting the simulated microgravity, not just for the sample, but for all cells in the chamber. Second, adhesion assays can take over an hour to perform when one considers cell preparation, transfer of cells from the microgravity chamber to the assay, and incubation periods. While these delays may be acceptable for general adhesion research, it is important to minimize elapsed time when studying gravitational effects, so that the cells won’t have time to recover from microgravity. In this project, investigators developed a novel human tissue bio-imaging technology applicable to microgravity research to overcome these shortcomings. Lessons learned from development of this Earth-based system can form the basis for a future space-flight culture and assay system to allow NASA to monitor microgravity-inducible physiological events during space flights. The purpose of this project was to develop a novel human tissue bioimaging technology applicable to microgravity research. This system was to integrate automated bioreactor sampling and real-time bioimaging. This will enable researchers to monitor, for the first time, effects of simulated microgravity on an important vascular function--adhesion between white blood cells and the blood vessel wall, without interruption of the culture conditions and with essentially no delay between sample extraction and cell-function assay. Technology developed in this project ultimately has potential applications for monitoring astronaut immune system function on long-term space flights. Task Objective: To develop a new, automated system for real-time bio-imaging of effects of microgravity on cell-cell adhesion through completion of the following objectives: 1. Design and develop a system to automatically extract and deliver cell samples from a rotating wall vessel to an assay system at predetermined intervals. 2.Design and develop a small, integrated, real-time digital bio-imaging system to produce digital images of cell samples. 3.Integrate into the bio-imaging system an assay of vascular cell function that utilizes the unique Amgel matrix system and sensitive real-time computer tracking of adhesive cell interactions. The system developed for this purpose can be adapted to assay other effects of simulated microgravity on cultured cells. It can also be useful as a compact, portable flow-cell based adhesion assay to measure adhesion of leukocytes or other cells under shear-stress conditions similar to those found in the blood stream.
approach: The methodology for the study isn’t available.
results: Objective 1: Development of the cell extraction and delivery system Even though extraction of fluid from a rotating RWV was a relatively straightforward engineering project, extraction of the cells from a rotating system is not trivial. Beyond the technical issue of a leak-free rotating interface between the chamber and external tubing, there is the issue that cells are often not uniformly distributed within the chamber. Although various models have been proposed to describe the location of cells in such a system, models do not always agree. Investigators determined the best sample points empirically. Their current system reliably delivers cells at a uniform concentration from two separate locations (after an initial mixing period of approx. 10 minutes.) without interrupting rotation. In the first year, feasibility was confirmed with a largely manual system of valves and a syringe pump system that used a command line interface for each action of the pump. However, entering of individual commands made experimentation cumbersome and time consuming. The control process was improved by transitioning to a graphical control program where embedded script files are created and programmed into the syringe pump. These pre-programmed script files are executed directly from the laptop graphical control program. This software configuration for control of the syringe pump streamlines the control process and also increases the reliability of the commands. In addition, a system of several manual valves in various locations has been replaced by one central multivalve that controls the entire system. These advances represent major improvements in efficient extraction of cells, optimization of valves and control points, miniaturization, and automation of the system. Objective 2: Development of the real-time bio-imaging system One of the problems with previous adhesion assay systems for cells undergoing shear stress is that a research microscope is required for imaging of the process. This necessarily requires relatively long tubing between the RWV and the assay chamber, which increases the time between rotation and assay. The research microscope also costs more than all of the other components of the system the system combined. Therefore, a completely new, low cost, custom-designed optical system was developed to reliably image cell adhesion under flow conditions in our adhesion assay system. The mini-microscope was tested extensively in real experiments, and has provided video image data of sufficient quality for the high-speed motion analysis necessary for flow-chamber cell adhesion data. In addition, the investigators have converted from a tape-storage system to direct digitization, streamlining data analysis and improving fidelity of motion tracking. Objective 3: Integration of the bio-imaging system and the cell adhesion assay In preparation for biological experiments, a new flow chamber was developed, with an improved sealing mechanism, to provide a more portable and robust flow chamber. Although beyond the scope of the current project, these modifications are an important step in development of a space flight system. In order to accommodate budget cuts and shortened time frame, however, it was necessary to focus on developing a basic flow-chamber-based adhesion assay, setting aside the work on the Amgel matrix system and the real-time computer tracking. This has resulted in a complete system for assay of the microgravity effect on leukocyte adhesion that, although lacking the real-time computer analysis system originally planned, will permit state-of-the-art analysis as good as current systems in use for conventional adhesion studies.

title: Hypobaric Hypoxia in Space Data Mining
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Extravehicular activity (EVA) is a vital component of human space exploration. The pressure differential between the internal cabin of a spacecraft and a space suit pressurized to 4.3 psia introduces the risk of decompression sickness (DCS). The risk of DCS is currently reduced with lengthy denitrogenation protocols. To reduce both the denitrogenation time and the risk of DCS during EVA, the option of an intermediate habitat pressure of 8.2 psia with 34% oxygen (herein referred to as 8.2/34) has been proposed for NASA’s exploration missions. However, the proposed atmosphere creates partial pressure of inspired oxygen inspired oxygen (PIO2) of 128 mm Hg, which is equivalent to breathing air at approximately 4,000 feet altitude. Coincidentally, one of the denitrogenation protocols used during the Shuttle Program was a staged protocol that exposed astronauts to 10.2 psia and 26.5% oxygen (10.2/26.5). The Shuttle-staged protocol
approach: Retrospective environmental data were examined to determine shuttle mission time at 70.3 kPa (10.2 psia) and partial pressure of oxygen (ppO2) and partial pressure of carbon dioxide (ppCO2) values for missions that performed a Staged pre-breathe protocol. Private medical conferences and post-flight debriefs were examined and data related to 14 possible hypoxia symptoms were compared with equivalent data collected during normoxic Space Shuttle operations at 101.3 kPa (14.7 psia) using logistic regression.
results: ed in a mildly hypoxic PIO2 of 127 mm Hg, almost identical to that of the proposed 8.2/34 environment. Terrestrial data suggests that this hypoxic dose is acceptable for unimpeded mission operations; however, the interaction between adaptation to microgravity, the space flight environment, and mild hypobaric hypoxia is uncertain. This study had the following specific aims: Determine accurate environmental exposure doses and durations for crewmembers during the shuttle program including hypoxia and elevated carbon dioxide (CO2). Identify and evaluate any available flight data from the Shuttle program that may aid in clarifying the physiologic and health effects of exposure to mild hypobaric hypoxia in microgravity. Review terrestrial hypoxia literature with respect to very mild hypoxia at altitudes of 6000 feet or less. APPROACH: Retrospective environmental data were examined to determine shuttle mission time at 70.3 kPa (10.2 psia) and partial pressure of oxygen (ppO2) and partial pressure of carbon dioxide (ppCO2) values for missions that performed a Staged pre-breathe protocol. Private medical conferences and post-flight debriefs were examined and data related to 14 possible hypoxia symptoms were compared with equivalent data collected during normoxic Space Shuttle operations at 101.3 kPa (14.7 psia) using logistic regression. RESULTS: Over the Space Shuttle program, there were 134.1 days (788.8 person-days adjusted for crew size) under the 70.3 kPa (10.2 psia) Staged condition (average 3.17 ± 2.2 days per mission, maximum 8.1 days) and 258.81 days at 101.3kPa (14.7 psia) and 2192.95 total person-days of normoxic operations. An average of 4.31 potentially hypoxia-related symptoms per mission day was documented under Staged conditions compared with 4.08 per mission day during normoxic operations. Logistic regression analysis found none of the hypoxia signs and symptoms to be significantly associated with the 70.3 kPa (10.2 psia) condition versus the 14.7 psia condition. Terrestrial experience indicates that chronic exposure to a PIO2 of 876 kPa (137 mmHg) is well-tolerated by healthy humans. Shuttle experience indicates that similar levels of hypoxia in space at a pressure of 70.3 kPa (10.2 psia) resulted in no increased reporting of possible hypoxia related symptoms, and no obvious crewmember performance issues related to completion of mission objectives. However, these results may not be representative of how chronic mild hypoxia interacts with physiologic changes due to microgravity over long duration missions.

title: ATD (Anthropomorphic Test Dummy) Injury Metric Sensitivity and Extensibility Study
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Currently, injury assessment reference values (IARV) are based on volunteer and post-mortem human subjects tested in non-space flight setups specific to the environment of interest. In automotive research, the occupant is put in the "super-slouched" position and is subjected to either frontal or side impacts at specific velocities with a three-point restraint and airbags. In military research, test configurations are commonly based on ejection seats. These tests employ seating geometries, restraint, and loading directions that are not consistent with space flight configurations. Acute seat pan angles, non-extended legs (fetal position), combined axis loading, as well as other seat, restraint, and loading conditions may induce unforeseen changes in injury risk. Because the current data available do not account for these variations, a sensitivity and extensibility study was needed. This study had the following specific aims: 1. Validate the response of each finite element model against matched physical Anthropomorphic Test Dummy (ATD) tests in the baseline seat from existing datasets. 2. Quantify ATD and human numerical model response variance and sensitivity to a limited set of small perturbations in seat, and restraint initial conditions. 3. Quantify the effects of spacecraft-specific seating and restraint configurations on ATD and human numerical model responses.
approach: In Phase I, 35 Hybrid III, 26 THOR, and 212 human volunteer tests were chosen to validate the Humanetics 50th percentile Hybrid III, NASA version of the 50th percentile THOR-K, and the Global Human Body Models Consortium (GHBMC) simplified 50th percentile male (GHBMC M50-OS) finite element (FE) models, respectively. Seat and restraint configuration models matching chosen test configurations were developed. Each unique test condition was simulated and model response was evaluated. The sled pulse from each configuration was applied to the appropriate model and instrumented acceleration and force signals were extracted. Each simulated metric was compared to the matched physical responses of the ATD or human volunteer to quantitatively compare physical and simulated signals. The CORA (CORrelation and Analysis) comprehensive score metric was used to evaluate the model response against the matched physical test across several signals and ranged from 0 to 1, with unity being a perfect match, and 0 representing no correlation. In Phase II, the Humanetics 50th percentile Hybrid III, NASA version of the 50th percentile THOR-K, and the Global Human Body Models Consortium simplified 50th percentile male (GHBMC M50-OS) FE models were used to examine the effects of loading condition and environmental parameters on injury metric response. Boundary conditions were parameterized and categorized as loading condition variables or environmental variables, the latter of which are expected to be less controllable than the former. Loading condition parameters included acceleration pulse shape, relative magnitude, and peak
results: ant acceleration. Environmental variables included belt forces, seat orientation with respect to gravity at impact time, and initial positioning on the model with respect to the seat vertex. Parameters were varied using a Latin Hypercube Design of Experiments to generate 455 simulations per model. A total of 1365 simulations were developed for this study, 97.9% of which reached termination without error. Ten injury metrics were compared using statistical methods detailed above. In Phase III, the Humanetics 50th percentile Hybrid III, NASA version of the 50th percentile THOR-K, and the Global Human Body Models Consortium simplified 50th percentile male (GHBMC M50-OS) FE models were positioned and belted in FE representations of three spacecraft-like seat and restraint systems as well as the simplified seat model from Phase I and II. The Latin hypercube design (LHD) designed in Phase II of this study was developed based on a factorial matrix of loading direction, and acceleration pulse rise time, consisting of 20 unique acceleration profiles. However, these profiles were never directly simulated. RESULTS: Phase 1 In respect to the overall average comprehensive CORA score, both the Hybrid III and THOR models had a CORA score of at least 0.8, as hypothesized for this phase. The THOR had the highest score of the 3 models with all directional average scores scoring at least 0.8; however, the THOR lacked data for the +X-direction. The Hybrid III had the second highest overall average comprehensive CORA score, with only the +X-direction loading group scoring under 0.8. On the other hand, the GHBMC model had only a single direction group, +Z, that scored above 0.8. Active bracing of the human volunteers may have contributed to the low CORA scoring. Phase 2 It was determined for each region that the loading condition variables generally were more predictive of injury metric outcome compared the environmental variables. In some regions, including the neck, lumbar spine, and lower extremities, the GHBMC response more closely resembled the THOR. In the head, thorax, and pelvis, the GHBMC had results closer to that of the Hybrid III. It was determined that discrepancies exist in injury prediction fidelity of both ATDs when comparing to human volunteer response that vary by body region and specific metrics. Further work should examine these potential differences using more vehicle-specific seats, harnesses, and helmets. Phase 3 A total of 915 simulations were run for this study, 97% of which reached termination without error. The Hybrid III and GHBMC exhibited higher rotational head injury metric distributions when equipped with a helmet compared to the simplified seat model.
