However, for the THOR, median BrIC decreased compared to the simplified seat. For each occupant model, pelvis acceleration tended to be pretty similar across the loading seat models. With the Hybrid III model, there was no statistically significant difference in matched pelvis accelerations between any of the spaceflight-like configurations and the simplified seat. However, with GHBMC the pelvis acceleration in each seat model was decreased compared to the simplified seat.

title: Quantitative Computerized Tomography
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Hip and spine morphology data was collected by quantitative computed tomography (QCT) technology in bed rest subjects. The QCT scan was used to measure true bone density volume, not just bone mineral density (BMD) per unit area. The QCT measured both cortical and trabecular bone. A more sensitive QCT technique was used to obtain these measurements which revealed how bone mass is geometrically distributed over a 3-dimensional space.
approach: QCT was used to evaluate bone mass and geometry. Scans were performed pre- and post-bed rest for long-duration (70-day) bed rest subjects. Consistent with space flight measures, bed rest subjects received follow-up QCT scans six months and one year after completion of bed rest. The QCT measurement was performed using a standard clinical CT scanner and a set of calibration phantoms. The first step was to scan the calibration phantoms. The rectangular phantom was placed flat on the scan table and the torso phantom was placed upon it. The scan table was adjusted so that the center of the torso phantom was at the isocenter of the scanner (all images in the test were taken with the scan table a specific height). Three axial images were taken of the phantoms at the center of the torso phantom. The torso phantom was then removed and the subject was asked to lie supine with his/her lumbar spine over the rectangular calibration phantom with their feet elevated and oriented toward the scanner. A scout scan was taken for positioning (a sagittal image through the center of the spine). A series of axial images was then taken covering the vertebra L1 and L2 (from the endplate of T12 to the endplate of L3). The subject was then repositioned so the phantom was beneath his/her hips and a coronal scout scan was then taken. A series of axial scans were then taken covering the region from 1 cm superior to the femoral head to 5mm inferior to the lesser trochanter.
results: This experiment has concluded. Tabular results are available for the public .

title: Habitability Ground and Analog Testing
experiment_type: NASA Extreme Environment Mission Operations (NEEMO) Project
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: This study served as a precursor for a related study that is taking place on the International Space Station (ISS). The purpose of this investigation was to allow for ground-based analog testing of tools and methods intended for use in subsequent inflight studies using NASA’s Human Exploration Research Analog (HERA) facility and NASA Extreme Environment Mission Operations (NEEMO). Crewmembers collected videos and questionnaires that helped characterize the habitability in ground-based analog environments using the iPad-based Space Habitability Observation Reporting Tool (iSHORT). These naturalistic techniques provided crewmembers with the opportunity to self-report habitability and human factors observations near real-time, which is not systematically done during current ISS missions. Automated tracking of person location enabled researchers to study traffic patterns within the environment.
approach: The investigation primarily consisted of the iSHORT tool development, the testing of both the iSHORT and targeted video data collection techniques, and the development of tools and methods to aid in the design and assessment of habitable volume for long-duration space flight. Data collected using iSHORT walk-through videos, task-based videos, and habitability questionnaires assisted in documenting/quantifying details about crew performance of tasks. These tools will provide ISS crewmembers with the opportunity to self-report habitability and human factors observations near real-time. Data was collected from the iSHORT on the first mission during HERA Campaign 1. During HERA Campaigns 2 and 3 and NEEMO 18 the iShort was used an operational tool only. No statistical analyses was performed.
results: All of the participants successfully captured and provided commentary on the desired habitat areas using walk-through and task-based videos. Throughout all seven mission days, the participants’ observations provided excellent comments and suggestions regarding the habitability of the HERA and effectively utilized all of the iSHORT methods of making the observations (i.e., text, video, audio, and photo).

title: Inflight Exerciser and Work Tolerance
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: The response of the cardiovascular system to a quantified workload is a frequently used index of the general physical condition of an individual. The objective of the Inflight Exerciser and Work Tolerance (M003) experiment was to evaluate the day-to-day general physical condition of the Gemini 4 , Gemini 5, and Gemini 7 astronauts during space flight by evaluating the cardiovascular system. In this examination, variation in heart rate, blood pressure, and respiration rate to a calibrated workload was studied preflight and inflight, as the basis for measuring the response of the cardiovascular system.
approach: The exercise device used for the experiment consisted of a pair of rubber cords. The cords were attached to a nylon handle at one end and to a nylon foot strap at the other. A stainless steel cable limited the stretch length of the rubber bungee cords and limited the isotonic workload of each pull. The device exercised the arms by holding the feet stationary while the astronaut pulled the handle. In flight, a bioinstrumentation system was used to collect the cardiovascular data. These data were simultaneously recorded by the onboard biomedical magnetic tape recorder (for real-time evaluation) and telemetered to the ground-based monitoring stations. Exercise periods lasted for 30 seconds, during which time the astronaut stretched the bungee cords through a full extension one time per second. Ten exercise periods were performed by subject A of the Gemini 4 mission, while seven exercise periods were performed by subject B. Exercise periods were performed three times daily by the Gemini 5 astronauts. During the Gemini 7 mission, the exercise was scheduled twice daily. Additional isometric and isotonic exercises were performed by the Gemini 7 astronauts approximately three times daily. Heart rate was determined by counting beats during 15-second intervals for 2 minutes before and after exercise, as well as during the first and last 15-second intervals during each exercise. Blood pressure measurements were obtained before and after each exercise period.
results: Comparison of data from preflight exercise periods with data obtained during flight revealed little difference in heart rate response for all astronauts. In addition, comparison of data collected from the inflight exercise periods from the first to the last day of Gemini 5 revealed little difference in heart rate response. Gemini 4 astronauts exhibited a moderate rise in heart rate during exercise, with a rapid return to near pre-exercise levels within 1 minute following exercise. The astronauts' heart rates returned more rapidly to pre-exercise values than did the Mercury 9 astronaut tested (a 34-hour mission). The heart rate of the Gemini 4 astronauts returned to pre-exercise values 45 to 60 seconds after cessation of exercise. The one astronaut of the Mercury 9 mission had a mean post-exercise heart rate during flight that was slightly increased for approximately 2 minutes after exercising. However, the environmental control system of the Gemini spacecraft was superior to that of the Mercury spacecraft; therefore, the data were not strictly comparable. Evaluation of the heart rate data revealed no significant difference between the heart rate responses (of both Gemini 4 astronauts) to exercise during the mission and the responses obtained before the mission. Thus, using the rate of return of the heart rate to pre-exercise values as an index of physical condition, there was no evidence of cardiovascular deconditioning at any time during the Gemini 4 mission. Results were similar for Gemini 5 and 7 astronauts. During Gemini 4, blood pressure changes were minimal. Generally, blood pressure measurements, before and after exercise periods on Gemini 5 were not remarkable. Post-exercise systolic pressures of both astronauts tended to be higher than pre-exercise values. Generally, post-exercise diastolic pressures were slightly higher than, or were identical to, pre-exercise values. After the fourth day of flight, both astronauts used the exerciser frequently between scheduled medical data passes. Both Gemini 5 astronauts remarked that exercise was essential and beneficial on long-duration space flights. The results were similar for Gemini 7 astronauts. On the basis of the data obtained during the missions, investigators concluded the following: 1) The response of the cardiovascular system to a calibrated workload was relatively constant for a given individual during space flights lasting up to 14 days. 2) Crewmembers were able to perform mild-to-moderate amounts of work under the conditions of space flight and within the confines of the Gemini spacecraft. This ability continued essentially unchanged for up to 14 days in flight. 3) Using a variant of the Harvard Step Test as a cardiovascular deconditioning index, no decrement in the physical condition of the crewmembers was apparent during space flights of up to 14 days. No decrement was observed under the stress of the relatively mild workloads imposed in this experiment.

title: Effect of Radiation on Human Peripheral Blood Dendritic Cells
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: The objective of this study was to investigate the effect of proton, heavy ion, and gamma radiation on human dendritic cells (DCs) and their ability to process antigens and, thus, impact the immune system. Increased exposure of the body to ionizing radiation suppresses the formation of bone marrow tissue, which, in turn, suppresses development of blood cells within bone marrow. This affects the differentiation, maturation, and function of dendritic cells, which are believed to be the link between innate and cell-mediated immunity. Thus, it is suspected that the increased exposure to ionizing radiation during long-term space flight may severely impair the immune system unless appropriate countermeasures are taken.
approach: Cultured human monocyte-derived dendritic cells were exposed to proton-, heavy ion- and gamma-radiation. The life cycle and formation of DCs were studied by determining the effects of the radiation on the differentiation of non-lymphocyte white blood cell precursor cells into immature dendritic cells. Then, the ability of these immature DCs stimulate cellular immunity were determined. In addition, this study determined the ability of activated mature DCs to present antigen to T-lymphocytes (T-cells). Countermeasures to prevent the harmful effects of proton-, heavy ion- and gamma-radiation on myelosuppression and the subsequent immune suppression were also identified.
results: The investigators have accomplished the following based on the data obtained from 12 healthy normal subjects: 1. Compared with un-irradiated PDC or MDC, there were no significant differences in the percentage of cytokine-producing PDC or MDC subject to low-dose g-radiation. 2. There is an irradiation dose dependent reduction of the mean channel fluorescence intensity (MFI) of intracellular IFN-a (P = 0.004) and TNF-a (P = 0.000) of the plasmacytoid DC upon stimulation with 5 uM of CL097. 3. The amount of IL-12 (p = 0.007) and TNF-a (p = 0.028) produced by individual MDC was significantly reduced upon the activation through TLR-8 with CL097 in an irradiation dose-dependent manner. In summary, the suppression of PDC to synthesize IFN-a and TNF-a by low-dose g-irradiation is unprecedented and suggests the possible attenuation of innate immune surveillance, whereas the reduced production of IL-12 and TNF-a by low-dose g-irradiated MDC might negatively impact the ability of MDC to mediate adaptive immunity and effector T-cell function. As DC are essential for the development of an immune response and clearance of microbial infection, low-dose g-radiation might pose a serious threat to long-term health in space.

title: Efficacy of Antimicrobials on Bacteria Cultured in a Spaceflight Analog
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: As humans travel into outer space, microorganisms will travel with them. While the current NASA standards limit the presence of infectious agents, they are not completely eliminated, and space flight missions maintain antibiotics as the primary countermeasure after infection. The consequence of infectious disease during the human exploration of space is greatly dependent on the efficacy of the countermeasures used to minimize the impact of the infection. As antimicrobials are the primary post-infection countermeasure against infectious disease aboard spacecraft, understanding the pharmacodynamics of antibiotics during a mission is of critical importance to mitigate the health, safety, and performance risk for the crew. Previous space flight experiments have indicated alterations in bacterial antibiotic resistance, though the specific mechanisms behind these changes have not been elucidated. Previous experiments have confirmed that the space flight environment alters a variety of microbial characteristics. Most notably, alterations in microbial virulence in Salmonella typhimurium and virulence characteristics in S. typhimurium and Pseudomonas aeruginosa have been demonstrated in response to space flight, thus influencing the perception of infectious disease risk during missions. Several space flight experiments have shown alterations in antibiotic resistance. Ground-based space flight analog systems provide a practical
approach: to understanding this change. The rotating-wall vessel (RWV) culture apparatus was developed to produce a low-shear, low-turbulence environment for suspension culture that models aspects of space flight. This analog does not completely reproduce all of the effects of microgravity, but has been shown to be predictive of trends that will be seen during space flight. This study investigated the response of three medically significant microorganisms grown in the RWV to antibiotics that could be used on space flight missions. APPROACH: The minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) of antibiotics currently manifested during space flight missions was evaluated on three medically significant model organisms (Salmonella typhimurium, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Staphylococcus aureus) that have either been isolated from space flight vehicles or have a clear route of infection.
results: Generally, the organisms did not display significant differences when compared to appropriate controls; however, a few interesting exceptions were noted. S. Typhimurium exhibited alterations in antibiotic sensitivity to azithromycin, which interferes with protein synthesis, but only at one concentration when longer exposure times were adopted. Interestingly, P. aeruginosa displayed reproducible changes in resistance to azithromycin depending on the level of fluid shear, which was modulated through the incorporation of beads added to the RWV; suggesting a more complex shear associated mechanism with this antibiotic. Methicillin resistant S. aureus (MRSA) strain N315 also demonstrated an enhanced resistance under microgravity-analogue culture conditions to levofloxacin, a DNA gyrase inhibitor.

title: A Study of Radiation Doses Experienced by Astronauts During EVA
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: The space radiation environment is dominated by high-energy electrons and protons, and their fluxes are a function of orbital position and time. In general, particle fluxes are higher in the South Atlantic Anomaly and Polar Horns, and with solar flares or other high solar activity, the particle fluxes can temporarily increase considerably. Shielding from the spacecraft structure and/or space suits changes the space radiation reaching the surface of a crewmember's body by removing low energy particles and generating secondary radiation. The radiation environment inside the spacecraft consists primarily of high energy protons and secondary particles, which include neutrons generated by the interactions of the high energy protons and the shielding material of the spacecraft structure. Activity external to the spacecraft exposes humans to much higher radiation levels as a
approach: Twelve sensor badges were used in this experiment. They were grouped into four sets (EV1 to EV4) of three badges, each containing a specific head, torso and leg badge. All badges were read at regular intervals while on the space station, and specifically before and after any EVAs. During an EVA, the astronauts were required to wear all three badges. Crewmembers wore three active dosimeter badges (placed on the leg, torso, and near the eye) during Extravehicular Activity (EVA). The badges were placed in temporary pockets sewn into the Extravehicular Mobility Unit (EMU) undergarments. The leg and torso badges were located either on the Thermal Comfort Undergarment (TCU) or the Liquid Cooled Ventilation Garment (LCVG) worn inside the EMU, and the eye badge was placed on the Communications Carrier Assembly (CCA). The badges were read individually before and after EVA using an electronic reader. Following EVA activities, the radiation data was downloaded to the onboard computer and batch-downlinked to the ground once per week. The dose readings were recorded onboard the spacecraft and analyzed against time and position in EVA, the orbit, altitude and attitude of the ISS, and any shielding effects provided by the ISS.
results: of decreased shielding. The type and flux of radiation inside the space suit depends on the shielding afforded by the particular part of the suit. Consequently, different parts of the body (e.g., arms, body, eyes) receive different levels of radiation. The aim of this investigation is to determine the levels of radiation dose received to the skin, eyes, and blood forming organs (BFOs) of crewmembers during EVA. APPROACH: Twelve sensor badges were used in this experiment. They were grouped into four sets (EV1 to EV4) of three badges, each containing a specific head, torso and leg badge. All badges were read at regular intervals while on the space station, and specifically before and after any EVAs. During an EVA, the astronauts were required to wear all three badges. Crewmembers wore three active dosimeter badges (placed on the leg, torso, and near the eye) during Extravehicular Activity (EVA). The badges were placed in temporary pockets sewn into the Extravehicular Mobility Unit (EMU) undergarments. The leg and torso badges were located either on the Thermal Comfort Undergarment (TCU) or the Liquid Cooled Ventilation Garment (LCVG) worn inside the EMU, and the eye badge was placed on the Communications Carrier Assembly (CCA). The badges were read individually before and after EVA using an electronic reader. Following EVA activities, the radiation data was downloaded to the onboard computer and batch-downlinked to the ground once per week. The dose readings were recorded onboard the spacecraft and analyzed against time and position in EVA, the orbit, altitude and attitude of the ISS, and any shielding effects provided by the ISS. RESULTS: Data derived from the study has helped determine the overall dose levels experienced in EVA, the variation of dose received by the skin, eyes, and BFOs, and the orbital factors and degree of shielding afforded by the EVA suit and the spacecraft structure. From this information, recommendations and guidelines for possible implications in radiation protection will be made. EVARM results show that geomagnetic storms do increase the radiation doses to which spacewalking astronauts are exposed, although these storms are not very common. Shielding from the ISS significantly affected the dose each badge received. To determine radiation doses received by specific organs, results showed that one torso badge was not enough, and that badges must be placed more accurately near the organ to be monitored. Expedition 4: data were received for eight extravehicular activities (EVAs). Two astronauts participated in each EVA, during which both were expected to wear all three head, torso and leg badges. However, some of the badges were not worn at certain times. Head badges were not worn on five of the EVAs (#1, 2, 6, 7 and 8) and leg badges were not worn on EVA #3. These unworn badges were left inside the space station and read normally. This was taken into consideration in the analysis of the data. Expedition 5: Six EVAs occurred during Expedition 5. Two astronauts participated in each EVA, during which both were expected to wear all three head, torso and leg badges. However, some of the badges were not worn at certain times. These unworn badges were left inside the space station and read normally. This was taken into consideration in the analysis of the data. Expedition 6: Three EVAs occurred during Expedition 6. Two astronauts participated in each EVA, during which both were expected to wear all three head, torso and leg badges. All badges were worn as expected, therefore six individual EVAs were obtained. In addition to EVA measurements, an inflight internal dose measurement intercomparison was made between EVARM badges and the NASA Intra-vehicular Charged Particle Directional Spectrometer (IVCPDS) instrument. In conclusion, although radiation doses have been measured in Shuttle and Mir missions for many years, the emphasis has been on the dose received to blood forming organs (BFOs) in crew quarters. Extremity dosimetry has not been well addressed, primarily because the crew radiation environment is dominated by high-energy protons that mainly affect doses to the BFOs. Missions on the International Space Station (ISS) will require significantly more Extravehicular Activity (EVA), and it will be important to measure skin and eye doses as well as dose to BFOs. Radiation doses have previously been measured by chemical thermoluminescent dosimeters that require considerable processing before and after use. This investigation used electronic badge radiation dosimeters, based on silicon transistor technology, which can measure small radiation doses. Data derived from these dosimeters helped determine which parts of the human body are exposed to the highest doses of radiation and under which EVA situations this arises.Data derived from the study will help determine the overall dose levels experienced in EVA, the variation of dose received by the skin, eyes, and BFOs, and the orbital factors and degree of shielding afforded by the EVA suit and the spacecraft structure. This information is required to determine radiation protection criteria for the ISS crew. In addition, the new badge option will eventually allow EVA crew to measure and monitor their radiation doses on an as-required basis, allowing for safety decisions based on total body dose received to all critical organs during the flight career of crewmembers.

title: Intraocular Pressure
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Intraocular pressure (IOP) has been shown to be an objective and quantitative measure of fluid shifts toward the head in the 10-degree head-down tilt bed rest model of microgravity. However, insufficient numbers of measurements have been made in microgravity to correlate bed rest changes with changes that occur in weightlessness. A study by Mader and Meehan (Mader et al., 1990) has quantified IOP changes that occurred with a 10-degree whole body head-down tilt over 48 hours. An immediate rise in IOP was documented upon assuming the head-down position. For the next 48 hours, variations in IOP were observed. Upon resuming the sitting position, there was a significant drop in IOP below the initial sitting values. The
approach: A series of measurements were taken (on one eye only) preflight at Launch-6 (L-6) weeks, L-4 weeks, and L-10 days (dates are approximate) using the Tono-Pen (a clinical instrument commonly used by non-physicians in an ophthalmologist's office for measuring IOP). All preflight measurements were taken with the subject in the seated position. During flight, measurements were taken as soon as possible on orbit, post-sleep on flight day (FD) 2 and on the final flight day post sleep. Additional measurements were desired on orbit (pre- and post sleep), but were optional. Postflight measurements were taken at return (R)+0 and during the postflight physical on R+3. One drop of the short-activity topical anesthetic (proparacaine 0.5 percent) was instilled into the left eye and the subject instructed to look straight ahead. During flight, the drop of proparacaine was brought into contact with the lower conjunctival fornice to be absorbed onto the cornea by capillary action. The operator performed the following steps: 1. Replaced the tonometer tip cover. 2. Instilled one drop of proparacaine into left eye. 3. Gently tapped the cornea 3-6 times until a beep is heard. 4. Recorded the data displayed on the Tono-Pen LCD screen. 5. Repeated the procedure 5 times. Measurements were taken in the subject's left eye at each data collection point (in prior studies, there have been no significant differences between the measurements taken in 2 healthy eyes of an individual). The data collection sessions were approximately 5 minutes per subject; however, 15 minutes was scheduled to allow for the effects of the proparacaine to abate (the anesthetic deadens the eye for approximately 15 minutes). Neither the anesthetic nor the pressure measurement with the Tono-Pen caused discomfort to the eye when used properly.
results: of this study support the theory that distension of the retinal veins is a mechanism for the sudden changes in IOP that occur with changes in position. Assuming that head-down tilt is a valid model for fluid shifts in microgravity, the results from this study predict a similar sustained IOP increase in microgravity and a corresponding temporary drop in IOP (to below preflight values) upon return to Earth. Significant increases in IOP could result in visual impairment affecting crew performance and operations. This study was designed to test the following hypothesis: Intraocular pressures will rise immediately upon entering microgravity due to fluid shifts toward the head, and will drop to below preflight levels upon return to 1-G. The objectives of this study were: 1. To establish a database of changes in intraocular pressures that can be used to evaluate crew health, 2. To validate 10-degree head-down tilt bed rest as a model for fluid shifts toward the head in microgravity, 3. To facilitate the interpretation of data by providing a quantitative measure of microgravity induced fluid shifts toward the head, 4. To validate the hand-held tonometer as an effective tool for diagnostic and scientific data collection that can be used in on orbit investigations. APPROACH: A series of measurements were taken (on one eye only) preflight at Launch-6 (L-6) weeks, L-4 weeks, and L-10 days (dates are approximate) using the Tono-Pen (a clinical instrument commonly used by non-physicians in an ophthalmologist's office for measuring IOP). All preflight measurements were taken with the subject in the seated position. During flight, measurements were taken as soon as possible on orbit, post-sleep on flight day (FD) 2 and on the final flight day post sleep. Additional measurements were desired on orbit (pre- and post sleep), but were optional. Postflight measurements were taken at return (R)+0 and during the postflight physical on R+3. One drop of the short-activity topical anesthetic (proparacaine 0.5 percent) was instilled into the left eye and the subject instructed to look straight ahead. During flight, the drop of proparacaine was brought into contact with the lower conjunctival fornice to be absorbed onto the cornea by capillary action. The operator performed the following steps: 1. Replaced the tonometer tip cover. 2. Instilled one drop of proparacaine into left eye. 3. Gently tapped the cornea 3-6 times until a beep is heard. 4. Recorded the data displayed on the Tono-Pen LCD screen. 5. Repeated the procedure 5 times. Measurements were taken in the subject's left eye at each data collection point (in prior studies, there have been no significant differences between the measurements taken in 2 healthy eyes of an individual). The data collection sessions were approximately 5 minutes per subject; however, 15 minutes was scheduled to allow for the effects of the proparacaine to abate (the anesthetic deadens the eye for approximately 15 minutes). Neither the anesthetic nor the pressure measurement with the Tono-Pen caused discomfort to the eye when used properly. RESULTS: Acceptable data was acquired from 9 subjects on missions STS-31, 32, 34, 41, 52 and 53. Sufficient data was not collected on STS-33, 44, and 50. There was a mean increase in intraocular pressure during the first two days of space flight. This increase of approximately 20 percent above baseline values decreased during the remainder of the flight but was elevated above baselines on landing day.

title: In-Suit Doppler Ultrasound for Determining Risk of Decompression
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: The overall objective of this RME was to evaluate the possibility of reduced pre-breathe requirements for extravehicular activity (EVA), without compromising operational safety or increasing the risk of decompression sickness (DCS) to astronauts. The process was defined in three steps: (1) develop an in-suit Doppler system to quantify the free gas phase in microgravity during EVA; (2) measure the incidence of microbubbles during operational EVA by using the in-suit Doppler ultrasound system; (3) conduct additional ground-based studies to evaluate risk of DCS with reduced pre-breathe.
approach: The In-Suit Doppler System is designed to monitor and record blood flow sounds from the pulmonary artery. The In-Suit Doppler System hardware was activated during EVA preparation activities and data was collected throughout the course of the EVA. The crewmember first donned the Liquid Cooling Ventilation Garment (LCVG), and then placed the Doppler subsystems in the appropriate pockets of the LCVG. The crewmember then placed the transducer over the chest region in the area of the pulmonary artery and listened to the blood flow sounds on audio headphones to ensure proper placement. The crewmember then secured the transducer to the chest with an adhesive overdressing, removed the headphones, and capped the headphone jack. The crewmember then completed EMU donning. The Doppler unit remained powered on throughout the pre-breathe and EVA period (maximum 12 hours). Following the EVA, the crewmember doffed the EMU and Doppler System. Prior to the next EVA, he connected the Doppler unit by the Interface Cable to the Payload General Services Computer (PGSC), and downloaded the data to a data storage device. The Doppler was then turned off and was be ready for the next EVA.
results: This was a hardware evaluation study. Results aren’t available.

title: Soft Contact Lens Application Test
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Ocular counterrolling is a principal measurement of otolith function in humans, and is consequently of great interest in the study of space motion sickness and adaptation to weightlessness. There has been success with ocular torsion analysis of video and photographs of eyes to which soft contact lenses with visible markings have been attached. Contact lenses have been frequently used to measure, by optical or mechanical means, the motions of the eye relative to an external frame of reference. Prior to this investigation, only rigid (hard) contact lenses had been used for this purpose. Hard lenses are usually poorly tolerated by the subjects unless a topical anesthetic is used, and the investigator must also maintain a large trial kit of lenses to fit all subjects. The objective of this experiment was to determine the effectiveness of a method of application and fixation of specially marked hydrogel (soft) contact lenses to the eyes during orbital flight. If distilled water is introduced into the eye, the lens becomes adherent to the corneal surface for a five to ten minute time interval. Investigators aimed to quantitatively document the dependency of lens adhesion on factors such as lens diameter, thickness, construction type, extent of subject blinking, tearing, etc. so that the lenses might be used in torsion measurement. This was done in 1g by "dehydrating" the lens-eye interface with sterile water. In zero-g KC-135 flights, there had been difficulties in achieving fixation, therefore a simple inflight demonstration was requested.
approach: The placement method called for mounting the lens in the eye, application of distilled water droplets and wicking away the excess. Two methods of irrigating the lenses, verified in KC-135 flights, were used. Method 1 called for holding the squeeze bottle in front of the eye and squirting water on the lens; the water forms a blob that covers the lens and sometimes the upper lids. Method 2 involved producing a blob of water on the end of the squeeze bottle and then bringing the blob up to the eye; the water rapidly transfers to the eye once it contacts the eye. Once the distilled water was in the eye it needed to be wicked away so that the contact lens could adhere to the cornea. A lint free paper towel (e.g. Kim Wipe) was held to the corner of the eye and put in contact with the water bolus. The surface of the contact lens may also have been dabbed to assure all the water had left the eye. Investigators wanted to test the best methods of irrigation and removal, as there was not sufficient sustained time on the KC-135 to do so. Both irrigation then removal of water, as well as simultaneous irrigation and removal were tested. Once the lens was in the eye, investigators needed to know how long and how well the lens stuck to the eyeball. After waiting about 15 seconds, the crewmember attempted to move the lens once again, first by vigorous eye movements, then by pressing on the lens with his finger, to determine if it shifts position. When the lens was properly adhered, pressing on it rotated the entire eye and contact lens together, and the effect could be felt and seen in the mirror. The crewmember was asked to do this every 45 seconds to determine whether the lens slips freely, sticks slightly, or adheres rigidly to the eye. The lens was not expected to adhere any longer than 10 minutes under the best of conditions. To repeat the test, the lens was bathed in physiological saline solution and the process could be repeated without requiring reinsertion of the lens on the eye. The crewmember was asked to repeat the test using different amounts of water and different times of wicking away the excess water to achieve the best lens adhesion to the eye. After all tests were complete, the eye was irrigated with saline to loosen the lens, which was then removed.
results: Inflight, the installation was extremely simple, but in spite of a wide range of maneuvers lasting several hours, the lens would not adhere using the prescribed procedures. After extraordinary difficulty, the subject managed to get a lens in place, confirming the results from KC-135 flights. The same was experienced postflight. Because of this, the concept was redesigned for use on subsequent flights; it was only after procedures were modified that reliable adherence would occur. It was hoped that the use of multiple small applications of water would improve performance in future flights. Information archived for this experiment was provided by the William E.Thornton collection.

title: Leg Plethysmography

objectives: Space flight, due to the loss at hydrostatic pressure gradient,
approach: Preflight: Each participating crewmember was requested to make six leg volume change recordings. Each recording consisted of a standing and supine measurement. Training was integrated into the first preflight measurement and plethysmograph stocking fitting session. In flight: Each plethysmograph measurement required two persons: one as a subject and one to mark the leg volumes. If both crewmembers did the plethysmographs concurrently, then a total of 15 minutes was used to obtain data on both crewmembers. Otherwise, it was a two person operation with each measurement taking 15 minutes. On Mission Day 1, measurements on each subject at 3, 6, 12 and 24 hours Mission Elapsed Time (MET) were acquired. The crewmember was given the stocking to take home to make six additional measurements during the first week postflight, to be done at their convenience.
results: in significant fluid shifts. These shifts are characterized by the movement of fluid from the lower extremities toward the thorax and upper portions of the body. The body recognizes this as a fluid overload and consequently loses some of it in the form of increased urine output and/or decreased intake. Then on re-entry, the reverse occurs.
