title: Photographic Documentation of Body Fluid Shift
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: The known large shifts of fluid from lower to upper body assumed a fresh importance through the possibility that the central nervous system (CNS) or inner ear pressures might be altered and contribute to or even cause space motion sickness (SMS). There is currently no satisfactory way to measure shifts to the head and there is always a need for simpler procedures for other areas. The objective of this experiment was to gather data on the course and amount of fluid lost from the legs and gained by the head region to assess the role of fluid shift in SMS.
approach: A background grid with a standard STS 35mm Nikon camera, interior film, and flash were set up at known distances and angles and the subject placed his heel in a fixture at a known position. He sequentially rotated his leg 180° through five positions while pictures were made at each position. The head was photographed in three positions and without fixation. Data may be manually reduced by reconstruction of cross sections from the multiplane views and volumes calculated from these. Three photo views of the leg and head against a background grid were collected as early and as late as possible during flight. Photographs were collected on as many crewmembers as possible.
results: Satisfactory in-flight and postflight pictures were made of all crewmembers. Results from the investigator’s analysis are currently unavailable.

title: Food Processing vs. Packaged Food System Trade Study
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: The Food Processing vs. Packaged Food System Trade Study addresses the efficiencies and adequacies of growing produce and processing baseline crops into edible ingredients as compared to the efficiencies and adequacies of the utilizing the existing prepackaged food system. Specifically, the research was parceled into four specific aims: 1. To determine the requirements on vegetable, fruit, and baseline crops growth and bulk ingredient supply in terms of the estimated pounds required. 2. To determine requirements for food preparation and/or processing equipment at the extraterrestrial habitat. 3. To provide a quantitative assessment of mass penalties and human factors impacts of each proposed menu option. 4. To provide an assessment of feasibility of implementing the proposed systems and identify associated technology gaps. Recent AFT work to prepare for deep space surface missions identified the shortcomings of using the current prepackaged food system in long exploratory mission application. The degradation of the quality of thermostabilized products and degradation of nutritional content indicates the inadequacy of the current food system for a five-year mission. This trade study is central to the decision process on whether to continue work on bioregenerative crop development for future space flight missions. Additionally, the trade study supports the decision process on whether to develop food preparation and food processing technologies and, if so, to what extent the development should occur. Because the food system has huge implications to the upmass considerations of the mission as well as measurable impact to the psyche of the crew members, the appropriate decision on the food system will directly relate to the adequacy of the food system for the mission.
approach: Two 10-day menus were developed in preparation for a Mars habitat mission. The first was built on the assumption, as in previous menu development efforts for closed ecological systems, that the food system would be vegetarian, whereas the second menu introduced shelf-stable, prepackaged meat and entrée items from the current International Space Station (ISS) food system.
results: The trade study answered the key question to which it was targeted – is it better to take the food to Mars or grow the food on the surface? – with the ambiguous “yes.” While the advantages of growing the food at the surface involve a tremendous upmass savings, higher acceptability, and higher potential menu variety, it cannot be discounted that even a small addition of prepackaged food prompted a significant decrease in crew time utilization and decreased the likelihood of food scarcity. The results indicate the food system design should focus on a solution that is mixed with food sources, leveraging the advantages of both farming crops and stowing the food supply. Five food systems were postulated based on three menu designs of equal caloric contribution. The first food system was based on meals derived from crops grown at the Martian habitat with minor dry ingredient additions. The second food system used the same meals as the first but was based on meals derived from a smaller number of crops grown at the Martian habitat, stable bulk commodities (rice, beans, wheat) shipped from Earth, and minor dry ingredient additions. The third and fourth food systems mirror the first and second system food sources, respectively, except both the third and fourth systems are supplemented with prepackaged meat products. The final food system was based solely on existing space food. Many recipes were reproduced to ascertain the amount of raw material, the necessary cookware, and time that was required to complete a meal. The equivalent system mass (ESM) and the food metric value (FMV) for each of the five food systems were then compared to determine which food system is preferable based upon resource utilization and other food system metrics. For a crew of 6 on a 600-day habitat mission, Food System 3 had the lowest equivalent system mass at 8566 kilograms and the lowest food metric value at 176 kilograms. This food system had both the second lowest mass shipped and second lowest volume shipped but was third in active crew time hours. The ESM for food system 3 was driven primarily by the low mass of stowed ingredients and a crew time utilization that was less than food system 1 or 2. The modified food quality index was not very different between food systems 1-4, and therefore, the value impacted the final results very little. The combination of the food processing data with the ESM calculations of other linked subsystems (e.g. biomass production, water) will present the most accurate view of the food processing cost to mission planners.

title: Utilization of the SVS as an AR system for Mission Operations
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Abstract Augmented reality is a technique whereby computer generated images are superimposed on live images for visual enhancement. Augmented reality can also be characterized as dynamic overlays when computer generated images are registered with moving objects in a live image. This technique has been successfully implemented, with low to medium levels of registration precision, in an NRA funded project entitled, Improving Human Task Performance with Luminance Images and Dynamic Overlays. Future research is already being planned to also utilize a laboratory-based system where more extensive subject testing can be performed. However successful this might be, the problem will still be whether such a technology can be used with flight hardware. To answer this question, the Canadian Space Vision System (SVS) will be tested as an augmented reality system capable of improving human performance where the operation requires indirect viewing. This system has already been certified for flight and is currently flown on each shuttle mission for station assembly. Successful development and utilization of this system in a ground-based experiment will expand its utilization for on-orbit mission operations. Current research and development regarding the use of augmented reality technology is being simulated using ground-based equipment. This is an appropriate
approach: for development of symbology (graphics and annotation) optimal for human performance and for development of optimal image registration techniques. It is anticipated that this technology will become more pervasive as it matures. Because it’s known what and where almost everything is on the International Space Station (ISS), this reduces the registration problem and improves the computer model of that reality, making augmented reality an attractive tool, provided it’s known how to use it. This is the basis for current research in this area. However, there is a missing element to this process. It is the link from this research to the current ISS video system and to flight hardware capable of utilizing this technology. This is the basis for this proposed Space Human Factors Engineering project, the determination of the display symbology within the performance limits of the Space Vision System that will
results: This study demonstrated differences in alignment performance with respect to accuracy and speed for different augmented reality overlays and improved accuracy compared to alignment without overlays. The different overlays appeared to affect hand controller errors in different ways, suggesting that geometric differences among them may induce perceptual or cognitive difficulties in the operator. Additional research into these relationships may provide valuable insights into optimizing human interfaces for robotic controls.

title: Microorganisms in the Spacecraft Environment
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: The mass spectrometric
approach: to bacterial identification that was developed is extremely fast and utilizes instrumentation that can be used for a variety of other tasks. Thus, for some applications in areas such as environmental microbiology, medical diagnosis, and biodefense it may offer advantages over sequencing approaches. The low shear modeled microgravity
results: point out that different organisms can respond quite differently to these conditions. Similar low shear conditions are found in the human body and hence the results of studies done using the rotating bioreactor (HARV) may be more representative of how a pathogenic organism will respond to factors such as antibiotics than traditional culture studies. The original project had two long-term objectives: (1) To develop general and specific microbial monitoring systems that utilize technologies that can be readily implemented in spacecraft. (2) To better understand the long-term effects of the space environment on representative bacteria. Three project tasks were to address these objectives. The primary task was to develop microbial monitoring technology that can be used on long term space missions. 16S ribosomal RNA, (16S rRNA), is the single most useful molecule for bacterial identification and therefore it was the target of choice in the monitoring work. In order to develop a general sentinel system for pathogens and other problematic organisms without prior knowledge of what organism might be encountered, we sought to take advantage of our earlier discovery that there are a large number of informative subsequences in 16S rRNA (“signature sequences”) whose presence in a unknown sample provide information that can be used to provide information on phylogenetic position (genetic affinity) or specific identity. For routine monitoring we proposed to look for the presence of specific genera and species as expected indicators of anticipated problems such as contaminated water or air. In a more sophisticated mode, we would seek to determine the genetic affinity of any problematic organism without prior knowledge of what it would be. APPROACH: Three approaches were investigated for this purposes; (A) microarrays of 16S rRNA targeted probes; (B) mass spectrometry and (C) solution hybridization with detection by fluorescence using molecular beacons. The essence of the second task was to conduct experiments with the objective of understanding how a low gravity/high background radiation environment affects bacteria over extended time periods. The third project task which was abandoned due to the early project termination was extension of the core monitoring technology to detection of microbial escape from an advanced life support system. RESULTS: The key advantage of mass spectrometry is that the core instrumentation is compatible with space flight and potentially has many uses. The investigators initially made a detailed investigation of the feasibility of using the information obtained by digesting 16S rRNA from an unknown organism with a base specific nuclease such as ribonuclease T1 and identifying the mass of all the resulting fragments. Their analysis of this scenario identified two key issues. The first was loss of information due to the inability of mass spectrometry to distinguish fragments with the same composition but different sequence (e.g. CACAAAG vs. AAAACCG). It was found that fragments of length six and larger contained useful information and that enough of such fragments would be available to allow identifications to be made. The second difficulty is that the mass of cytosine and uracil are so close together that the relatively low resolution instruments that likely would be available during a space flight would not be able to distinguish them. The investigators therefore implemented an alternative experimental protocol in which the rRNA is first converted to DNA and then regenerated as RNA with a mass labeled analog of uracil. Using this protocol they successfully identified five out of five bacteria in test runs. A subtraction algorithm was devised to deconvolute the spectra. This approach was applied to the analysis of the spectra obtained from a complex human cheek sample. They were able to identify the same dominant organisms that were found by a more traditional cloning and sequencing approach. In the array area, the investigators developed an evolutionary programming approach to the design of a universal array of less than 1000 15mer signature sequence probes. No organism is uniquely identified by a single probe. Instead, the design is such that any organism will test positive with at least 40 probes. The pattern obtained then serves to determine the genetic affinity of the unknown organism. With less than a thousand probes, this "signature chip" can in principle determine the genetic affinity of any bacterium. The investigators have completed extensive computational validation of the concept, and developed an optimized set of signature sequences. These have been tested in small scale for methods development and optimization of spacer offset sequences, rRNA fragmentation methods, and labeling and analysis methods. Based on these results, a custom microarray was obtained from Combimatrix. Tests of this chip with E. coli resulted in a positive identification. However, many probes either failed to hybridize or gave false positive signals. This was expected because the behavior of individual hybridization probes is notoriously unpredictable from sequence information alone. These bad probes will need to be eliminated from the chip and replaced with alternatives that work. It therefore was necessary to revise the software so that it could start a new optimization using a partially specified set of probes, e.g. those that work. This is now complete and further testing of the arrays is continuing. The third approach to microbial monitoring that the investigators expected would be useful for routine monitoring was molecular beacons. Beacons carry a fluor that is initially quenched. When reaching their target in the 16S rRNA, the beacon probe hybridizes to the 16S rRNA resulting in exposure of the fluor and generation of a strong fluorescent signal. This solution hybridization approach would be advantageous because it would require minimal sample preparation and could be conducted with easily prepackaged reagents. The key problem is that the signal produced is insufficient for identification of small numbers of bacteria. The proposed solution to this problem was to use a “beacon swarm” in which multiple probes would target the 16S rRNA molecule in multiple signature sites but emit fluorescence at a single wavelength. With ten targets a single molecule of target would produce an order of magnitude more fluorescence than is normally produced. To date, the investigators have not been able to successfully demonstrate feasibility of the approach; possibly because of unintended interactions between the individual beacon probes. Since molecular beacons are unlikely to resolve the routine monitoring need, the investigators have revised efforts began during a prior NSBRI award to develop small arrays that target a modest number of informative organisms. Thus, an array is envision that would test for E. coli, enterics in general, gram positives and gram negatives in general, Staphylococcus and Streptococcus, etc. Probes were previously designed for many of these targets and tested but not in an array format. The investigators have constructed small arrays with these probes and begun testing them. Most of them work. The primary problem is false positives. The offending probes were removed and replaced with alternatives. A second major project goal was to better understand the response of bacteria to the space environment. In order to do this, the investigators examined the growth of representative bacteria under simulated microgravity conditions using the NASA developed rotating wall bioreactor (HARV). An initial comparison of aerobic and anaerobic results revealed that there was no gene uniquely responding to these two growth conditions as would occur if the response was actually to gravity and that its response is quite different from that of its close relative Salmonella.

title: Food Fortification Stability Study
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: NASA has established the goal of traveling beyond low-Earth orbit and extending manned exploration to Mars. The length of proposed Mars missions and the lack of resupply missions increases the importance of nutritional content in the food system, which will need a five year shelf life. The purpose of this research was to assess the stability of vitamin supplementation in traditionally processed space flight foods. It is expected that commercially available fortification nutrients will remain stable through a long-duration exploration mission at sufficient levels if compatible formulation, processing, and storage temperatures are achieved.
approach: Five vitamins (vitamin E, vitamin K, pantothenic acid, folic acid, and thiamin) were blended into a vitamin premix such that the vitamin concentration per serving equaled 25% of the recommended daily intake after two years of ambient storage. Four freeze-dried foods (Scrambled Eggs, Italian Vegetables, Potatoes Au Gratin, Noodles and Chicken) and four thermostabilized foods (Curry Sauce with Vegetables, Chicken Noodle Soup, Grilled Pork Chop, Rice with Butter) were produced, with and without the vitamin premix, to assess the impact of the added fortification on color and taste and to determine the stability of supplemental vitamins in spaceflight foods.
results: The addition of fortification to space flight foods appears to be a plausible mitigation step to inadequate nutrition concerns when considering the ease of adding vitamin premix to the formulations for provisions and the sustainability of the vitamins through the initial processing steps. Vitamin fortification with this premix did not have immediate impact to sensory and color of the food. At this stage, the caveat to introduction is the preciseness to which vitamins can be added. The total amount of vitamin premix required for the largest space production run equates to 10 - 20 grams, a tiny percentage of the formulation. As demonstrated by Italian Vegetables and Grilled Pork Chop, the homogeneity may be difficult to achieve with such small amounts so pouch-to-pouch variability, over-fortification, and under-fortification may ensue. Future analysis should reveal the extent to which this issue should be a concern. No data sets exist for this experiment. A final report was archived.

title: Protocols for Asynchronous Communication in Space Operations: Communication Analysis
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Effective and efficient communication between Mission Control and space crews is essential for successful task performance and mission safety. The importance of team communication is heightened when unforeseen problems arise, such as system failures that are time-critical and require extensive coordination and collaboration between space and ground crews. During long-duration missions and missions beyond Low Earth Orbit, space-ground communications will involve delays up to 20 minutes one-way, a reality that poses a formidable challenge to team communication and task performance. The overall aim of this study was to develop and validate medium-specific communication protocols that enable flight controllers and space crews to establish and maintain common ground (i.e., mutual task and situation awareness) and coordinate problem solutions in response to different operational tasks during periods of communication delays. This study had the following specific aims: Determine the impact of communication delays on communication, teamwork, and task performance in relation to varying task demands, i.e., procedural tasks versus tasks requiring analysis and decision making, and different communication media (voice vs. text). Develop and validate communication protocols to support joint problem solving and decision making by mission controllers and space crews during periods of asynchronous communication. To achieve these objectives several ground-based studies were conducted using a space analog and laboratory setting. The first set of studies aimed to determine how transmission delays of various lengths impact team communication and performance under different media conditions. Findings then informed the design of medium-specific communication protocols. Their feasibility for space missions was assessed in two analog environments, NASA’s Human Exploration Research Analog (HERA) and NASA’s Extreme Environment Mission Operations (NEEMO). A complimentary laboratory study was conducted to examine whether the availability of protocols enhanced remote team members’ communication and task performance during periods of communication delay.
approach: The first study consisted of an analysis of the communications between astronauts and Mission Control personnel recorded as part of the Advanced Exploration Systems Autonomous Mission Operations Project: Crew Autonomy Experiment - 1 (AMO) study conducted in NASA’s Deep Space Habitat (DSH). Investigators analyzed the crew-mission control communications that occurred during the baseline condition of that study. In a second laboratory study, investigators examined the impact of communication delay in relation to different communication media. Findings from these studies informed the design of medium-specific communication protocols as they highlighted which aspects of the communication process need support to ensure successful communication between remote partners under asynchronous conditions. The effectiveness and feasibility of communication protocols for space operations was subsequently assessed in two studies,
results: ing in refinements of the protocols and the design of a communication training module. In a companion laboratory study investigators explored the impact of transmission delay on team communication and task performance in relation to varying task demands and different communication media. Spatially distributed teams of three collaborated in a computer-based task environment and communicated either by voice-over-internet or via a texting tool. The micro-world for the study was AutoCAMS 2.0 which simulates the life support system of a spacecraft and requires team members to monitor and control different subsystems, and to diagnose and repair failures. Each team was required to perform procedural and problem solving tasks during one synchronous and one asynchronous flight segment with a 5-minute one-way delay in communications transmission. Each flight segment lasted for 90 minutes. In order to guarantee the requirement of communication and collaboration on the experimental tasks, task-related expertise concerning diagnostic and repair procedures was differentially distributed among team members. The Flight System Engineer (FSE) received extensive training on AutoCAMS systems, diagnoses, and repairs, and had access to a comprehensive reference manual. The two Pioneer crewmembers were given basic training on AutoCAMS and were instructed to contact the FSE for guidance on diagnosis and repair whenever a failure occurred on their system. In all NEEMO and HERA missions, communication delay occurred on consecutive mission days. Communication between crew and Mission Control was delayed by 5 minutes or 10 minutes one-way. In some simulations communication medium was limited to voice or text on a given day with transmission delay, or the crewmembers could choose their communication medium. Copies of the communication protocols were given to trained participants at the start of a mission to serve as a reference aid on days with a communication delay. Surveys were administered throughout a mission asking participants to rate the effectiveness of the protocols and their interactions with mission control, and in a final survey to provide feedback on individual elements of the communication protocols. RESULTS: AMO Analysis of the AMO data provided first insights into the effects of transmission delays on team communication. Specifically, investigators observed that transmission delays disrupted the timing and structure of turns such as communications by different team members. Communications by different speakers co-occurred (i.e., step-ons in which team members talked over each other) or were out of sequence (i.e., related turns by partners did not follow each other as one partner inserted a turn before the addressee could respond to the initial contribution). Both types of disruptions likely increased team members’ cognitive workload and jeopardized common ground. Step-ons compromised mutual understanding insofar as parts of a message were inaudible and required additional turns to repair which, given the transmission delay, were likely associated with considerable costs both in terms of time and workload as partners had to wait for critical information and keep track of concurrent tasks. Laboratory Analyses of team performance revealed that transmission delay impacted time required to initiate a successful repair and more importantly, that its effect varied by communication medium. When communication was delayed, teams used a comparable amount of time to repair system failures, irrespective of the communication medium used. However, when communication was synchronous, voice teams outperformed text groups. Likewise, teams’ accuracy in performing system repairs was influenced by communication medium. Overall, teams communicating by text undertook more incorrect repairs than teams communicating by voice. Analysis of FSE/Pioneer communications revealed that communication delay influenced both the rate of turns by team members and the length of their contributions. Team members made fewer but longer contributions when they communicated under time delay than when no time delay was present. Moreover, these effects were more pronounced for teams communicating by voice than those communicating via text. This finding suggests that team members using text may have been more concise than team members in the voice condition. However, subsequent content analyses of Pioneer Crew/FSE interactions during transmission delay revealed that text communication was also associated with an increased potential for misunderstanding. Text teams were more likely than voice teams to split up related information and present it in separate turns. Related communications by distributed team members were also further apart in text- than in voice-based communications. Text communication also included more threats to common ground, in particular missing responses and anaphora (i.e., terms whose meaning could not be established within a turn but depended on information provided in preceding turns). NEEMO and HERA Trained crewmembers generally rated protocol elements and conventions as fairly critical to ensuring effective communication during asynchronous conditions. Very high ratings across crews for several items—providing a topic, using a log to track related messages, and announcing complex or critical messages—reflect the value of protocols for keeping track of message threads. Compliance with the protocols was also high as crewmembers generally followed the protocols in their communications on mission days with a transmission delay. Overall these findings suggest that asynchronous communication may be facilitated by protocols that aid conversational partners in keeping track of conversational threads and the temporal sequence of messages. Results from this study led to the development of a communication training module that can be used to prepare crewmembers and members of Mission Control for the challenges of communication delay. Moreover, the communication protocols not only target how to speak or write during asynchronous conditions but also point to specific technological solutions.

title: Probabilistic Analysis of Renal Stones in US Astronauts
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: During all space flight missions to date, renal stone incidence is actually lower than what would be expected in the general population or in the analog population utilized by the Longitudinal Study of Astronaut Health. (LSAH). After astronauts return to earth, however, the incidence rate increases and surpasses both the rate of the general population and the LSAH analog population, with the astronaut incidence rate of calcium oxalate stones approximately doubling that of the general US population. If these trends persist with the reintroduction of even fractional gravity, renal stones during a Mars mission could become a serious problem, not only in terms of astronaut health, but also in terms of the resources required to adequately treat the condition.
approach: Given the nature of these data, the Glenn Research Center (GRC) Integrated Medical Model (IMM) team developed a proof of concept probabilistic simulation of renal stone formation during a long-duration exploration mission. While somewhat limited in scope, this simulation included both probabilistic and deterministic components. The deterministic components were developed to support the probabilistic analysis.
results: Key findings from this work include: 1. As the stone grows larger, the governing equation says the rate of growth will increase, which is why the probabilistic analysis picks up the seed size as being influential. 2. The probabilistic model demonstrates identical sensitivity for Calcium and Oxalate, suggesting that a more detailed surface chemistry simulation needs to be conducted. 3. The sensitivities for the dwell time of a stone show pronounced differences between the 2.0L/day and 2.5L/day cases resulting in a 68.6% change in the probability of one stone reaching the effective diameter of a nephron from heterogeneous growth only. This result has a standard deviation of 0.237. As part of the validation process for this module, the task underwent a subject matter expert review of the work done to date. The review was favorable with indication that an increase model fidelity was required, as outlined in Steps 1-3 below. 1. Determine expected incidence rate of renal stones during exploration missions and how this rate is affected by new countermeasure activities. 2. Provide a probabilistic simulation that allows the Exploration Medical Capabilities Element of the Human Research Program to develop medical kits appropriate to the level of risk of renal stone formation. 3. Provide a probabilistic simulation that allows the Exploration Medical Capabilities Element of the Human Research Program the ability to quantitatively evaluate the effect of different operations scenarios on the ability of a given medical kit to adequately treat an ill or injured crew member. No data sets exist for this study. A final report was archived.

title: Hyperpolarized 129Xe MRI of the Brain, Lungs and Plants Augmented with MRI Pulse Sequence Development--NNX07AP80G
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Investigators are developing a new diagnostic technology: magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and spectroscopy of hyperpolarized noble gases. Large non-equilibrium nuclear spin polarizations can be created in the spin-1/2 noble gases, 3He and 129Xe, using the technique of spin-exchange optical pumping. Such large polarizations greatly enhance the magnetic resonance detection of 3He and 129Xe, enabling high-resolution MRI studies of the lung and airways, as well as dissolved tissue-phase investigations of organs and tissues, such as the brain, using lipophilic 129Xe. An important feature of hyperpolarized noble gas MR is that it does not require a large magnetic field, unlike the conventional water proton MR method used in medical MRI. Low magnetic field MRI with hyperpolarized noble gases can allow investigators to use a small, light-weight, low-power devices. This capability provides potential for advances in both portable ground-based and practical space-based MR systems. This ground-based investigation with hyperpolarized noble gas MR will affect biomedical research in two important ways: (1) by providing the potential to acquire novel information about physiological structure and function of the lung and the brain in space-flight and in terrestrial gravity, and (2) by developing a new diagnostic technology that has clinical applications for diagnosis of pathology. An important feature of hyperpolarized noble gas MR is that it does not require a large magnetic field, unlike the conventional thermally polarized water proton MR method used in a medical MRI. As a
approach: Investigators developed large volume hyperpolarized 3He and 129Xe systems that take advantage of inexpensive, compact, and mechanically robust high-power diodelasers (in excess of 100 W of radiant energy), which have recently become available. By bringing together an optimized continuous flow optical pumping chamber with a storage and delivery system, a dedicated gas generation system was constructed to produce the large volumes of hyperpolarized gas necessary for this project.
results: , at low magnetic fields (0.01 Tesla) the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of hyperpolarized noble gas MR is much larger than the SNR of conventional thermally polarized MR. Low field MR utilizing hyperpolarized noble gases should be practical in a small, light-weight, low-power device, providing the potential for both portable ground-based and practical space-based MR systems. Specific magnetic and biological properties of hyperpolarized 3He and 129Xe MRI include: (i) airway and lung gas space imaging (for diagnosis of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), e.g. emphysema, asthma, and for studies of respiratory function); (ii) the imaging of lipid structures in the brain (for the diagnosis and staging of demyelinating diseases such as multiple sclerosis, and in research on brain function); and (iii) angiography and measurement of blood flow (for diagnosis of stroke and ischemia, and for research into the function of the brain and cardiopulmonary system). The recent progress made lays the foundation for the continued development of hyperpolarized xenon MRI for brain imaging. Specifically, imaging of lipid structures in the brain (for the diagnosis and staging of demyelinating diseases such as multiple sclerosis) and angiography and measurement of blood flow (for diagnosis of stroke and ischemia, and for research into the function of the brain and cardiopulmonary system), are now viable research goals. Because HP 129Xe is an MR signal source with properties very different from those generated from water-protons, it may yield structural and functional information not detectable by proton-based MRI methods. Thus brain imaging with hyperpolarized xenon should be of great benefit to the diagnosis and treatment monitoring of a number of neurological diseases. APPROACH: Investigators developed large volume hyperpolarized 3He and 129Xe systems that take advantage of inexpensive, compact, and mechanically robust high-power diodelasers (in excess of 100 W of radiant energy), which have recently become available. By bringing together an optimized continuous flow optical pumping chamber with a storage and delivery system, a dedicated gas generation system was constructed to produce the large volumes of hyperpolarized gas necessary for this project. RESULTS: The overall goal of this proposal was to develop hyperpolarized noble gas magnetic resonance imaging (HP MRI) for the assessment of pulmonary and nervous system damage that may be incurred during human space flight. Hyperpolarized noble gas MRI is showing dramatic results for diagnostic imaging of the lungs, brain, and other parts of the body, some of which have been resistant to conventional proton MRI. Most notably, investigators have achieved high resolution dynamic images of the lungs and airways using hyperpolarized 3He, and have measured cerebral perfusion and functional activity in the brain using hyperpolarized 129Xe (HP 129Xe). The number of space flight-related pathologies which may benefit from this technique are vast and range from pulmonary dysfunction caused by microgravity to cognitive and neurobehavioral problems resulting from the stress and isolation of extended term space travel. This novel technology should also offer a rapid, sensitive method to detect treatment effects and thus may expedite the development of therapeutic strategies for treating space flight related injury, such as aerosol administration of drugs via the lungs, which may obviate the need for medicinal injections during space flight.

title: Mechanistic Study of the Risk of Low Doses of HZE Particles on Human Cell Pre-Malignant Transformation
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Establishing the scientific basis of radiation cancer risk is a primary goal for the NASA Space Radiation Program. There are large uncertainties in
approach: es to extrapolate experimental or human epidemiology data from high to low doses, and from high LET to low LET radiation. In this study, investigators used the cell transformation (pre-malignance) assay, which occurs much earlier than carcinogenesis after radiation exposure, to elucidate mechanisms and to provide important quantitative data on radiation quality effects related to cancer risks from low doses of HZE particles. This study had two specific aims: Investigate how p63 promotes HZE particle-induced human epithelial cell transformation through the JAG1/Wnt4-Myc pathway. Investigate how p63 promotes HZE particle-induced human epithelial cell transformation through the CD95-JNK-Jun pathway. APPROACH: Investigators studied the effects of two pathways on HZE particle-induced transformation by knocking down the components involved in this pathway in HZE particle-transformed human epithelial cells. In addition, they looked at the effects of the two pathways on HZE particle-induced transformation by examining the kinetic changes of the pathway in non-transformed human epithelial cells and fibroblasts at different times after low dose of HZE particles irradiation. They also studied the effects of the p63->JAG1/Wnt4->Myc pathway on HZE particle-induced transformation by up-regulating the pathway in non-transformed human fibroblast cells and examined the effects of HZE particle on the cell transformation.
results: Investigators successfully irradiated human epithelial cells from the lung, breast, colon, and esophagus and examined the messenger RNA (mRNA) level and MYC of cell cycle regulators. The cell transformation was detected by growing colonies in soft-agar. Non-irradiated cells served as the controls. It was determined that down-regulating p63 diminishes the transforming characteristics of human epithelial cells. Epithelial cells showed an increased MYC level compared to non-transformed cells.

title: Reusable Handheld Electrolytes and Lab Technology for Humans (rHEALTH Sensor)
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: The goal of the rHEALTH sensor is to provide rapid, low-cost, handheld complete blood count (CBC), cell differential counts, electrolyte measurements, and other lab tests based on a reusable, flow-based microfluidic platform. For Phase II, we developed an rHEALTH prototype to be delivered to NASA for reusable CBC, cell differential counts, and electrolyte measurements. Each subassembly and individual assay will be tested individually prior to full integration into the system level prototype. The rHEALTH sensor is a compact, portable device that employs cutting-edge fluorescence detection optics, innovative microfluidics, and unique capabilities. Based on its streamlined design, the rHEALTH sensor is able to perform a suite of different assays using a single drop of blood. Furthermore, the entire system allows cost-effective operation because of its nanoliter operating volumes. This is in contrast to existing point-of-care diagnostics devices such as the iSTAT and Piccolo systems which only perform one panel of assays per disposable reagent cartridge. The
results: is a highly practical, cost-effective, and powerful sensor. The successful completion of the Phase II program is a significant milestone for our rHEALTH sensor. It means that we would have been successful in shrinking hospital-sized clinical laboratory into a portable device.

title: Hyperpolarized Noble Gas Magnetic Resonance Imaging
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: A novel biomedical imaging technique, hyperpolarized (HP) noble gas magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is capable of generating high-resolution images of the lung, heart, and brain by using the spin-1/2 noble gases, 3He and 129Xe. The HP gases, created via spin-exchange optical pumping, have greatly enhanced MR detectability. Unlike conventional proton MRI, HP gas MRI does not require a large magnetic field and, therefore, can be performed in very low magnetic fields (~ 0.01 Tesla). Thus, a small, portable, low-power MRI system, practical for space flight, may be designed to implement very low field HP gas MRI. The imaging capacity of HP gas MRI itself is also relevant to space flight research. Under prior NASA funding, the investigators have obtained (i) cerebral blood flow measurements and (ii) lung gas transfer measurements using HP 129Xe MRI in rats. Additionally, in humans they have (i) obtained high-resolution images of the distal airways in lungs up to the 7th generation, (ii) created models of the three-dimensional lung airway tree, and (iii) obtained very low field (0.015 Tesla) images of the lungs, using HP 3He MRI. They now propose to apply this novel technique to investigations of the physiological and functional states of the lungs, heart, and brain. Studies will focus on regional ventilation and perfusion inhomogeneities of the lungs, patent foramen ovale and pulmonary embolism of the heart, and cerebral function and blood flow of the brain. Their proposed ground-based investigations with HP gas MRI will impact space flight research in three important ways: (i) by facilitating the acquisition of novel information about the physiological structure and function of organs and systems most affected by changes in microgravity; (ii) by developing a new technology that may have clinical applications for the diagnosis of pathologies endemic to microgravity environments; and (iii) by developing treatment strategies that address the continuum of a space-induced illness.
approach: Investigators developed large volume hyperpolarized 3He and 129Xe systems that take advantage of inexpensive, compact, and mechanically robust high-power diodelasers (in excess of 100 W of radiant energy), which have recently become available. By bringing together an optimized continuous flow optical pumping chamber with a storage and delivery system, a dedicated gas generation system was constructed to produce the large volumes of hyperpolarized gas necessary for this project.
results: Hyperpolarized (HP) noble gas MRI using 3He or 129Xe provides highly detailed images of the lungs and brain, and offers the immense advantage of providing information on physiological function, including lung ventilation (3He or 129Xe), lung perfusion (129Xe), and cerebral blood flow (129Xe). For example, HP gas MRI allows investigators to pinpoint precise sections of the lungs where gas is reaching, and where gas is not reaching (ventilation defects), something other measurements of lung function cannot do. Because of its greater sensitivity, HP gas MRI can detect pulmonary or cerebral dysfunction at earlier stages, allowing treatment or counteracting measures to be provided earlier and with greater effectiveness. In addition, HP gas MRI provides imaging of physiological function without exposing subjects to ionizing radiation or chemical contrast agents. This increases safety, and also allows investigators and/or care providers to non-invasively image subjects repeatedly over time. HP gas MRI has countless applications to evaluating vascular and pulmonary problems that could arise in human space flight. Such applications include investigating the effects of microgravity and pressure changes on the physiological functioning of the lungs, and studying the effects of microgravity and pressure changes associated with space flight on vascular functioning. In addition, HP gas MRI is ideal for evaluating aerosol drug administration, a delivery method of particular interest for space flight because it avoids the need for injections of medicines in space. In this study, investigators further developed hyperpolarized noble gas MRI for use in examining pulmonary and brain function in animal models and in humans, building upon previous work by the PI funded by NASA. HP gas MRI has immense potential for applications to the study of the physiology of the lungs and brain, and for helping diagnose and inform treatment for adverse reactions to microgravity and low pressure environments. Low-magnetic-field MRI, which is made possible by HP gas MRI, is particularly advantageous in this regard because it provides extraordinarily detailed images of lung and brain function with lightweight, low-cost, easy-to-operate equipment that could be used in space environments. With the assistance of generous funding from NASA, the investigating team was able to make significant advances in many areas of HP gas MRI, including pulmonary ventilation analysis and low-magnetic-field MRI.

title: Biomedical Investigations with Laser-Polarized Noble Gas Magnetic Resonance
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: The investigators developed a laser-polarized noble gas nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) as a novel biomedical imaging tool for ground-based and eventually space-based applications. This emerging multidisciplinary technology enables high-resolution gas-space magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-e.g., of lung ventilation-as well as studies of tissue perfusion. In addition, laser-polarized noble gases (3He and 129Xe) do not require a large magnetic field for sensitive detection, opening the door to practical MRI at very low magnetic fields with a lightweight, low-power device. The investigators pursued two specific aims in this research. The first aim was to develop a low-field ( The investigators developed a large Helmholtz coil assembly for use in low field noble gas MRI of human lungs. The coil assembly has been used to create a magnetic field of 20 gauss with better than 100 ppm field uniformity over a 30 cm diameter volume centered between the coils. The Helmholtz coil assembly is housed inside a wire-mesh cage to provide shielding from any background electromagnetic noise. The investigators also constructed low-rf pulse/drive coils and associated electronics employing low-cost audio amplifiers with custom trigger/gate circuitry. Using this 20 gauss low-field system, they obtained high SNR signals from a laser-polarized 3He phantom, and acquired a proton NMR signal in a single acquisition. They recently began the design of signal detection coils for low field MRI of human lungs, since they are not available commercially at the audio frequencies used with low field MRI. The investigators have also begun the construction of low-noise receiver electronics for these coils.
approach: The investigators began development and testing of xenon interphase exchange NMR, a new technique designed to measure the exchange of xenon atoms between the gas and dissolved phases in porous media such as the lung. They used xenon interphase exchange NMR to determine the surface-area-to-volume ratio (S/V) of four samples of porous high-density polyethylene polymer (materials commonly used in filtering, wicking, etc.) They machined each of the four samples to fit tightly in a 0.5" glass cell that excluded free gas around the polymer core. The team performed NMR experiments on a GE Omega/CSI 4.7 T spectrometer operating at 55.3 MHz for 129Xe. They filled the samples and a similar empty cell with thermally- polarized xenon, and made NMR measurements of the sample porosity f, 129Xe partition coefficient b, and dissolved-phase 129Xe T1. For interphase exchange measurements, they evacuated the sample and admitted approximately 1 bar of laser- polarized 129Xe gas into the cell. The team performed a saturation/recovery experiment in which they selectively saturated the dissolved-phase 129Xe polarization and observed its recovery after a variable waiting time due to diffusive exchange from the gas-phase. They determined S/V by fitting this recovery of the dissolved-phase 129Xe NMR signal to an expression they derived for non-equilibrium interphase diffusion. In addition, the team performed independent measurements of S/V for each POREX sample using optical confocal microscopy, a well-established technique which requires sectioning of the sample. They found the NMR and optical measurements of S/V to be in qualitative agreement.
results: The results with phantoms indicate the potential for MRI experiments at low field strengths in a large, open-access system, despite low-field limitations of narrow bandwidth RF coils, and gradient pulses that are not necessarily small compared to the applied field. Further system optimization and human inhalation studies are planned for the follow-on NASA grant for this project.

title: Sleep Monitoring
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Prior to Skylab, very little objective information had been obtained concerning the ability of man to sleep in space. Only by continuous EEG (electroencephalographic) monitoring can such information be obtained, and the technical problems associated with acquisition and analysis in space are significant. Before the advent of manned spaceflight, there was some concern about the possible adverse effects of this weightless environment upon sleep characteristics. During the Gemini program, however, it became apparent that fairly long duration space flight was not associated with drastic alterations of sleeping behavior. Astronauts could sleep in space and, on at least some occasions, did so fairly well. In the Gemini and Apollo programs, though, it became clear that in many instances insomnia was a problem. Sleep loss, while not absolute, was sufficient in some instances to
approach: A complete system for analyzing sleep during space flight was designed for this 'experiment and included data-acquisition hardware, onboard-analysis components, and a capability for real-time telemetry. Automatic analysis of the electroencephalogram (EEG), electro-oculogram (EOG), and head-motion signals was accomplished by onboard equipment. The system's output, consisting of sleep-stage information, was telemetered in near 'real time to Mission Control, where a profile of sleep stage versus time was accumulated. The analog signals (EEG, EOG, and head motion) were also preserved by onboard magnetic-tape recorders, thus allowing a more detailed postflight analysis. The recording cap was worn during the 59-day mission (Skylab 3). The electrodes, attached inside the elastic cap, were joined by wires to a miniature connector at the vertex, which permitted rapid linkage with the preamplifier assembly. The cap contained seven electrodes; four electrodes (left and right central positions, C l and C 2 , and left and right occipital positions, 0 1 and 0 2) provided a composite EEG channel (Cl and C2 paired and referenced to 0 1 and 0 2 paired); two (one lateral to and one above the left eye) provided one EOG channel; and one served as a ground. Following the sleep period, the preamplifier was disconnected, and the used cap was discarded; i. e., a new cap was used for each recording session.
