title: Dark Focus In-house Study
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: The definition of dark focus is the resting state of visual accommodation is that refractive state to which the eye tends to return in the absence of any visual stimulus, as in complete darkness. Seven healthy in-house subjects (4 males; 3 females), ranging in age from 27 - 55 years old, participated in this study. Neurobiological research indicates that changes in visual accommodation are associated with stresses that may occur during space mission. Measures of accommodation may be used to index onset and extent of space motion sickness and other stress of spacelfith. An accurate measure of accommodation may be used to signal that visual performances may be degraded.
approach: To participate in the study, the subjects were not asked to alter their normal daily routine. Prior to each test session, the subjects completed a short questionnaire that documented their recent pre-test activities. All subjects reported that they were in their usual state of fitness, and that they had a sufficient amount of sleep within the last 24 hours. Although caffeine consumption was not specifically controlled, subjects reported having three of fewer cups of coffee throughout an entire 24 hour period on test days. Six of the seven subjects were nonsmokers, and the 1 subject who was a smoker routinely smoked 2-3 cigars each morning. On average, each subject had sat in front of a video display terminal 1-2 hours prior to each test session. Only 1 subject required glasses for corrected vision, and did wear corrective lenses when performing the test. Measurements of dark focus were made twice daily, in the morning and afternoon, on four consecutive days. The test sessions were scheduled for approximately the same time of day for each subject across the four days. During each test session, three measurements of dark focus were made in a dark room. The subject was instructed to look in to he Dark-focus Measuring Device (DFMC) using his/her dominant eye while keeping the other eye closed. Sliding the focus adjustment rod back and forth, the subject adjusted the focus of the fiberoptic light until a sharply focused light image appeared. The subjects was instructed to close his/her eyes while the operator recorded the measurement of the dark focus then offset the focus of the fiberoptic light by sliding the focus adjustment rod prior to repeating the test procedure two times for a total of 3 measurements.
results: Results are not available for this study.

title: Mechanism of Clustered DNA Double-strand Break Repair in Response to HZE Particles in Human Cells
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: DNA damage and consequent mutations initiate the multi-step carcinogenic process. Substantial evidence indicates that high charge and energy (HZE) particles, component of galactic cosmic rays, induced clustered DNA damages are difficult to repair, and in some instances are irreparable. This has been associated with the increased relative biological effectiveness of chromosomal aberrations, mutagenesis, and carcinogenesis. However, it is unclear why clustered lesions are difficult to repair, and the mechanisms by which unrepaired clustered DNA lesions trigger carcinogenic events are not known. The goals of this research were to utilize the unique capability to quantitatively estimate the ability of cells to repair clustered DNA lesions in response to a spectrum of HZE particles, and to dissect the genetic factors that may potentially be involved in the processing of complex DNA lesions. The specific aims of this study were to test the following hypothesis: The cellular ability to repair HZE particles induced clustered DNA damage is modulated by radiation quality and cell cycle stages, utilizing newly established in situ and imaging technology. Homologous recombination plays a key function in facilitating the repair of double-strand breaks (DCBs) associated with clustered DNA lesions, using key homologous recombination factors deficient cells. Fanconi Anemia (FA) complex may orchestrate the repair of complex DSBs induced by HZE particles, using a panel of FA pathway deficient human cells.
approach: Investigators studied the effects of radiation on human cells using their newly developed in situ and image technology. In addition they assessed the effects of Fe particles irradiation on DNA and chromosomal instability in human cells.
results: Investigators identified a novel mechanism by which space radiation triggers immune signaling in human cells. They conclude that the immune signaling initiated by the space radiation will contribute to the carcinogenesis risks. In regards to RAD51, investigators found it’s critical for complex DSB repair in S/G2 cells in response to Fe-particle irradiation, it blocks MRE11-mediated degradation of nascent DNA strands in response to Fe-particle exposure, its depletion upregulates expression of innate immune signaling genes by accumulating self-DNA in the cytoplasm of S/G2 phase cells, and it suppresses chromosome breakages following Fe-particle exposure. No datasets exist for this study. A final report was archived.

title: Functional Foods Baseline and Requirements Analysis
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: NASA, in planning for long-duration missions, wants to provide the necessary nutrition to ensure sustainment of crew health and performance. To this end, the Human Health Countermeasures (HHC) Program has identified several desired nutrients, optimally delivered from food sources, with the potential to benefit health beyond nutritional maintenance. It is expected that these nutrients, and any nutrients identified in the future, will be required to be delivered in the food system to mitigate or prevent health issues, and that determination of compatible formulation, processing, and storage conditions will enable these functional foods to meet shelf life requirements. The purpose of this study was to determine the current concentrations of these previously unmeasured nutrients in the food system and their stability to different processing conditions, formulation matrices, and storage temperatures reflective of potential vehicle architecture to inform functional food capabilities and requirements development for long-duration space flight.
approach: Twelve foods that were thought to have a significant concentration, or a concentration significantly greater than most space flight foods, of bioactive compounds (lycopene, lutein, omega-3 fatty acids, phenolics, sterols, and flavonoids) were selected for the study from the International Space Station (ISS) food provisions. Recently produced food samples were sent by overnight shipment to the Food Composition Laboratory of the Linus Pauling Institute at Oregon State University for bioactive compound analysis. Three packages of each product were blended together for the analysis to reduce package-to-package variability. Duplicate samples of the food were placed in 4°C, 21°C, and 35°C environmental chambers within the Space Food Systems Laboratory for storage and re-analysis at periodic time points.
results: Efficacious concentrations of lycopene, lutein, and omega-3 fatty acids were measured in limited space flight foods, but a meal plan addressing health issues requiring these compounds could not be created without a secondary risk of menu fatigue. Likewise, two grams of sterols a day may be difficult to achieve with the current space diet. Total polyphenol delivery appears stable and adequate, but individual phenolic compounds vary in stability and were not specifically evaluated in this study. The data suggests that some bioactive compounds, like lycopene and lutein, degrade and then plateau at some equilibrium concentration. The anthocyanin stability appears to be related to storage temperature and processing method, and lutein stability in leafy vegetables may be impacted by storage temperature. This work indicates that cold storage, increased variety, and processing optimization will be required to provide and sustain several bioactive compounds in current space flight foods. Implementation of countermeasures will require validation to five years to enable provisioning of an acceptable food system for a mission to Mars. No datasets exist for this study. A final report was archived.

title: Vestibular-Cerebrovascular Interactions and Their Contribution to Post-Spaceflight Orthostatic Intolerance
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Postflight orthostatic intolerance, a long-standing NASA problem following space flight, is still poorly understood. Recent studies have indicated that vestibular responses to space flight affect the cerebrovascular response to orthostasis. The goal of this research is to examine the role of vestibular inputs in cerebral blood flow regulation and the effect of these inputs on orthostatic tolerance. This work may lead to new methods to diagnose and treat orthostatic intolerance in space travelers and the general population. Our general hypothesis is that otolith mediated vestibular inputs act as a feed forward mechanism causing cerebral vasodilation to compensate for the decrease in cerebral perfusion pressure during the upright posture. This project's four specific aims are to: Determine the effect of tilts in the pitch plane with and without visual feedback on cerebral blood flow and cerebral autoregulation in healthy elderly with and without vestibular hypofunction and healthy young subjects. Determine the effect of otolith versus otolith and canal stimulation on cerebral blood flow in healthy elderly with and without vestibular hypofunction and healthy young subjects. This aim will be accomplished by varying the radius of rotation of subjects on a short arm centrifuge Determine the effect of canal versus canal and otolith stimulation on cerebral blood flow in elderly subjects with normal and reduced vestibular function. This aim will be accomplished by using earth vertical axis rotations vs. head tilt while supine or prone Determine the effect of training subjects to associate otolith input as tilt on cerebral blood flow during orthostatic stress in elderly subjects with intact and impaired vestibular function. This aim will be accomplished by training subjects with tilt or centrifugation to interpret otolith signals as either translation or tilt by providing visual scenes to reinforce this perception.
approach: The methodology for the study isn’t available.
results: Specific Aim 1: Determine the effect of orthostatic stress (tilts) on cerebral blood flow and cerebral autoregulation in elderly subjects with intact and impaired vestibular function. The purpose of this aim was to determine whether the vestibular system plays an important role in the changes in cerebral blood flow when you go from a supine to upright. Major Finding: Loss of vestibular function in both younger and older subjects is associated with greater decreases in cerebral blood flow when upright. Specific Aim 2: Determine the effect of static otolith stimulation on cerebral blood flow. The purpose of this aim was to determine whether continual stimulation of the otoliths without associated canal or other sensorimotor cues affects cerebral blood flow. This aim was accomplished by performing centrifugation to selectively stimulate the otoliths. Major Finding: Changes in cerebral blood flow were consistent during otolith stimulation, even in the absence of other cues of tilt. Specific Aim 3: Determine the effect of dynamic canal plus otolith versus otolith stimulation on cerebral blood flow. This aim was accomplished by examining cerebral blood during both centrifugation (otolith stimulation) versus dynamic pitch tilt (otolith and canal stimulation) in a group of young subjects with intact vestibular function. Major Finding: Changes in cerebral blood flow were mediated primarily by otolith activation. Specific Aim 4: Determine the effect of training subjects to associate otolith input as tilt on cerebral blood flow during orthostatic stress in elderly subjects with intact and impaired vestibular function. The goal of this aim is to determine if enhancing vestibular function could be used as a countermeasure to improve cerebral blood flow when upright. Major Finding: Stimulation of the vestibular nerve with subsensory stochastic noise causes improvement in both vestibular function and cerebral blood flow responses to tilt.

title: NSCOR: Space Radiation and Gastrointestinal Cancer: A Comprehensive Strategy for Risk Assessment and Model Development
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Gastrointestinal (GI) tumors are common in the U.S, and colorectal cancer (CRC) is the third most common cancer, accounting for 10% of all cancer deaths. Precancerous lesions are present in about 10% of adults at age 40 (younger than the average age of astronauts) and increases to about 25% in older adults. Due to the high frequency of CRC among the US population, even a small exposure to space radiation will have a major impact on the risk estimates and planning for future long-term missions into space. The overarching goal of this NASA Specialized Center of Research (NSCOR) study is to model the relative risk of colonic and stomach tumorigenesis

title: Feedforward Active Noise Reduction Headphones for Otoacoustic Hearing Assessment of Space Station Crews
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Acoustic data from the International Space Station (ISS) indicate that there is a significant risk to crew members' hearing. However, no method currently exists to monitor the hearing acuity of ISS crews. The objective of this project is to provide a means for reliable hearing assessment of ISS crews over extended space missions.
approach: This experiment proposed an innovative design for digital active noise reduction in functional audiometer headsets (Creare headset system). The noise reduction system was designed to attenuate background noise and thus permit hearing assessment tests in space and relatively high noise environments on Earth. The research efforts included laboratory-scale technology development and assessment, clinical trials of the device, and design of a space qualified instrument.
results: The following activities were performed: obtained and analyzed noise measured within the International Space Station (ISS) service module; characterized the performance of passive designs and materials used in noise reduction headsets; quantified the performance of both passive and active commercial-off-the-shelf (COTS) noise reducing headsets in the presence of ISS noise; measured the performance of a preliminary bench top version of a feedforward active noise reduction algorithm in ISS noise; performed an initial clinical evaluation of hearing assessment methods with passive hearing protection in noisy environments; supported evaluation of the passive hardware by NASA personnel; fabricated and tested the performance of a custom passive noise-reducing headset in combination with otoacoustic hearing evaluations; and began development of bench top hardware for testing feedforward active noise reducing headsets for this application. Distortion product otoacoustic emision (DPOAE) testing can be a reliable way to assess hearing during long duration stays on the ISS. Threshold hearing testing using Békésy audiometry may also be feasible. Furthermore, the Creare headset system should enable hearing assessment tests to be administered in less controlled Earth environments than is currently possible. This technology can be employed by all DoD and civilian facilities where hearing tests are performed, such as field hospitals, physicians offices, occupational health clinics, and grade schools.

title: The Effect of Skeletal Unloading on Bone Formation
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Skeletal unloading
approach: The methodologies are embedded in the
results: in an inhibition of bone formation associated with a decrease in osteoblast number, impaired mineralization of bone, and altered proliferation and differentiation of osteoprogenitor cells. Although such changes are likely to be mediated by multiple factors, resistance to the skeletal growth promoting action of insulin like growth factor-I (IGF-I) appears to play an important role. IGF-I mRNA and protein levels rise during skeletal unloading, but the ability of IGF-I to stimulate proliferation of bone cells in vivo and in vitro when taken from unloaded bone is markedly impaired. This resistance to IGF-I is associated with a failure of IGF-I to activate its receptor and the subsequent IGF-I signaling pathways. BMSC from unloaded bone show a reduction in integrin expression, and inhibition of integrin signaling reproduces the findings of IGF-I resistance. Specific Aims: 1. Determine the point(s) at which skeletal unloading blocks IGF-I stimulated bone formation. a. Determine whether skeletal unloading alters the mesenchymal pool committed to osteoblast differentiation. b. Determine whether skeletal unloading alters the ability of IGF-I to bind to and activate the IGF-I receptor (IGF-IR) in those cells committed to osteoblast differentiation c. Determine the relative contributions of the ras/MAPK and PI3K/Akt pathways to the proliferative response to IGF-I. d. Determine whether skeletal unloading alters the protein levels and/or activation of the components of the pathway(s) mediating the proliferative response to IGF-I. e. Determine whether skeletal unloading alters the nuclear translocation of ERK, PI3K, and Akt and cellular levels of cyclin D1, p21cip, and p27kip 2. Determine the ability of skeletal unloading to block the response of BMSC to other growth factors such as EGF, PDGF and FGF with respect to: a. Proliferation b. Growth factor receptor number, binding, and activation c. Activation of the ras/MAPK and/or PI3K/Akt pathways 3. Determine the interaction between IGF-I and integrin signaling as affected by skeletal unloading in the regulation of osteoprogenitor cell proliferation. a. Determine the mRNA and protein levels of the various integrins in osteoprogenitor cells from normally loaded and unloaded bone b. Determine which integrins potentiate IGF-I responsiveness with respect to proliferation and activation of the IGF-IR and the ras/MAPK and PI3K/Akt pathways c. Determine whether the effect of integrins on IGF-IR activation requires direct interaction with the IGF-IR d. Determine whether correction of integrin levels, if altered by skeletal unloading, will restore IGF-I responsiveness with respect to proliferation and activation of IGF-I signaling pathways. APPROACH: The methodologies are embedded in the Objectives above and the Results below. RESULTS: 1) Determine the points at which skeletal unloading blocks IGF-I stimulation bone formation. Skeletal unloading does not alter the binding of IGF-I to its receptor. Investigators used an analog of IGF-I, namely des IGF-I, which does not bind to IGF-binding proteins and demonstrated that like IGF-I itself binding to the bone marrow stromal cells (BMSC) from loaded and unloaded bones is equivalent. The down stream events such as activation of the MAPK pathway and the subsequent proliferative response to IGF-I are impaired in BMSC from unloaded bones, but this follows the failure to activate the IGF-I receptor. We have shown that skeletal unloading reduces the expression of a number of integrins, and the use of the integrin inhibitor echistatin reproduces the effects of skeletal unloading on IGF-I responsiveness. Thus, the investigators believe that the loss of bone during skeletal unloading is due to IGF-I resistance caused by the failure of integrins to enable IGF-I to activate its receptor. In contrast when the animals are reloaded, they are able to restore IGF-I responsiveness, integrin expression, and accelerated bone formation. 2) Determine the ability of skeletal unloading to block the response of BMSC to other growth factors. Investigators examined in depth the effect of skeletal unloading on the resistance to PDGF. To their surprise, BMSC from unloaded bones respond quite well to PDGF with respect to activation of the PDGF receptor (via phosphorylation) and proliferation. Furthermore, the integrin antagonist echistatin, which blocks the response of BMSC to IGF-I, fails to block the response of BMSC to PDGF. Thus, the resistance to IGF-I caused by skeletal unloading appears to be specific to IGF-I and is not generalized to all other growth factors. 3) Determine the interaction between IGF-I and integrin signaling as affected by skeletal unloading. As noted above the investigators found that the expression of a number of integrins is reduced in the BMSC from unloaded bones. They are having some difficulty showing that the protein levels are reduced because of the lack of good antibodies to rat integrins. However they have developed methods to selectively knockout specific integrins to determine which if any are critical for BMSC response to IGF-I. These experiments are being performed in both rat BMSC and a human osteoblast cell line for which better integrin antibodies are available. Using this latter cell line, the investigators have had success in showing that at least one of the integrins of interest binds directly to the IGF-I receptor, as shown by co-immunoprecipitation. Furthermore, they have developed an in vitro model using pulsatile fluid flow to test whether integrins per se can activate the IGF-IR when load is applied in the absence of IGF-I. The results show that load can activate the IGF-IR, which appears to be dependent on selected integrins and the matrix containing selected integrin ligands on which the cells are plated.

title: Metric Development to Quantify Change in Mission Risk Due to a Physician-Trained Crew Medical Officer
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: NASA currently requires a physician-trained Crew Medical Officer (CMO) for missions exceeding 210 days in length. This is based on the nominal 180-day length of an International Space Station (ISS) mission, which affords relatively quick and easy return to Earth for treating complicated cases. As NASA considers various Design Reference Missions (DRMs) for exploration, there are DRMs of only a few weeks duration that could not quickly return to Earth. Accordingly, they may well carry a medical risk level high enough to warrant the judgment of a physician-trained CMO. In contrast, the current assumption that missions to Mars would be less medically risky with a physician-trained CMO may be invalid. Due to rigorous preflight screening, which lessens the likelihood of a disease state, and the limited nature of the envisioned medical kits, perhaps NASA's treatment options are limited enough that the judgment of a physician-trained CMO would not appreciably reduce medical mission risk. This study had the following specific aims: To develop a Medical Judgment Pathway Metric (MJPM) for assessing clinical judgment based on evidenced-based practice for treating two common conditions from the Exploration Medical Condition List (EMCL). To validate the MJPM by a multi-disciplinary expert medical team to confirm principal components of the MJPM. To test the MJPM in an analog population using populations that mirror those of the astronaut corps in terms of both age and training.
approach: This investigation was completed by Summa Health Systems with advice from the Integrated Medical Model (IMM) team about the suitability of the metric for modeling. This study achieved two aims: 1. Develop a MJPM assessing clinical judgment; and 2. Demonstrate evidence of validity and reliability of MJPM scores. The individual MJPM items, domains, and sections of the MJPM were built based on existing standardized frameworks. Content validity was determined by a convenient sample of eight experts. The MJPM instrument was pilot tested in four medical simulations with a team of three medical raters assessing 40 participants with four levels of medical experience and skill.
results: Raters were highly consistent in their MJPM scores in each scenario as well as their evaluation of the expected patient outcome. For each simulation scenario, average rater score cut-scores significantly predicted expected loss of life or stabilization.

title: Middleware for Exploration Medical System
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: The middleware is an intelligent data management and communications software that facilitates the acquisition, integration, management, and distribution of data from on-orbit vehicle medical and environmental devices, sensors, and systems. The software reduces crew time and ensure the accuracy of data collection and timeliness of data delivery. The objectives of the Middleware were to: Reduce or eliminate the time required of an on-orbit crew and ground personnel [which include Surgeon, Biomedical Engineer (BME), and Medical Operations Data Specialist] to access, transfer, and manipulate medical data. Support the integrated demonstration that the on-orbit crew has the ability to access medical data/information via an intuitive and crew-friendly solution to assist/aid in the treatment of a medical condition. Develop a common data management framework and architecture that can be ubiquitously used to automate repetitive data collection, management, and communications tasks for all crew health and life sciences activities. Ensure crew access to medical data during periods of reduced or unavailable ground communication. Develop a common data management framework and architecture that allows for scalability, extensibility, and interoperability of data sources and data users. Lower total cost of ownership for development and sustainment of peripheral hardware and software that utilize the Middleware for data management. Provide better crew health via reduction in crew errors, crew time, and ground time.
approach: The Exploration Medical System was designed to demonstrate the integration of complimentary and disparate pieces of medical informatics software. The Middleware software, as part of the larger Exploration Medical System, has potential training and simulation opportunities for future astronauts and ground personnel. In addition, the Exploration Medical System can serve as software infrastructure for future development and integration of medical devices and software.
results: The development, integration, and testing of all EMSD components - electronic medical record, assisted medical procedures software, Middleware infrastructure, and associated Middleware "adapters" were completed.

title: Electronic Medical Records for Exploration Medical System
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: The Electronic Medical Record (EMR) is an electronic system that provides a repository for medical data, images, videos, and reports and makes the information accessible to the crew in flight via a graphical user interface to assist in the diagnosis and treatment of acute and chronic medical conditions. The system is used to access medical data for all medical encounters, especially during periods of exploration missions when contact with ground resources (e.g., flight surgeon) will either be minimal or absent. During these periods of autonomous medical care, the crew will need such a system for urgent and non-urgent medical events. The objectives of the EMR were to: Reduce or eliminate the time required of an on-orbit crew (i.e., clinician and non-clinician) to store, access, and process medical data, images, and reports. Reduce the time required of the ground crew to access medical data, images, or reports. Ensure Crew Medical Office (CMO) access to all relevant crewmember medical data, images, or reports for improved quality of care. Ensure crew access to personal medical data, images, or reports during periods of restricted ground communication. Ensure crew ability to capture onboard medical data regardless of the state of the communication link to the ground. Ensure privacy protection of onboard crewmember medical data.
approach: Development of the OpenEMR application programming interfaces (APIs), required for integration into the Exploration Medical System, can be made available to the OpenEMR open source community for potential inclusion into future releases of the EMR software. These APIs enhance the ability to import and export data into/out of the EMR database.
results: All required development of the EMR for integration into the greater Exploration Medical System Demonstration (EMSD) project has been completed. This includes the development of APIs, data forms, and associated intermediate software "adapters" and databases.

title: Epidemiologic Analyses of Risk Factors for Bone Loss and Recovery Related to Long Duration Space Flight
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Bone loss is estimated to occur at a rate of one percent per month in space, particularly in weight-bearing bones in the legs and spine. This rate of loss is equivalent to what a human might lose in a year with advancing age on Earth. It remains unknown what this loss signifies for future fracture risk in crewmembers. While unloading of the skeleton in the weightless environment of space is considered the key factor contributing to bone loss, there are likely other factors that also play a role. Current prevention strategies have not been effective at preventing this bone loss. Improved understanding on the risk for fracture following long-duration space flight, as well as the factors contributing to bone loss in microgravity, and its recovery, are needed in order to develop better prevention strategies for the benefit of crew health, both during and after long-duration space exploration, and mission success. This study had the following specific aims: Investigate the risk of microgravity exposure on long-term changes in bone health and fracture risk. Provide a summary of the current evidence available on potential risk factors for bone loss, recovery and fracture following long-duration space exploration.
approach: Data assembly at NASA-Johnson Space Center (JSC) on risk factors known to be related to bone loss and fracture risk was completed in early 2012. The investigators performed analyses on these available data to help better understand the variability in hip bone mineral density (BMD) loss and recovery, postflight. Risk factor data included, medication use, bone turnover markers, and surrogates of exercise status inflight, such as changes in strength measures, and lean muscle mass. Data assembly and data cleaning were completed. The investigators noted that there were limited data on risk factors available beyond the initial return post long-duration flights, so analyses were restricted to the immediate post-flight period.
results: Following review of all the different measures available for analyses, the investigators identified several different risk factors which may help identify those at greatest risk for bone loss during long-duration missions. These included pre-flight measures of elevated bone resorption, as well as surrogate markers of better muscle strength and greater aerobic capacity preflight. Results suggest that individuals with high bone resorption markers preflight may benefit most from anti-resorptive therapy before a long-duration mission. Findings also suggest that those who are the most physically fit preflight may have bones that have adapted to greater than average loading stimuli and therefore may be more susceptible to enhanced bone resorption once unloaded in microgravity, reinforcing the importance of maintaining adequate physical conditioning during long-duration space flight. Of note, the results are from data largely prior to US crewmembers having access to the Advanced Resistive Exercise Device (ARED), which may have helped overcome this important risk factor. The data from this study is medical and thus is housed with the Lifetime Surveillance of Astronaut Health (LSAH). A final report was archived in the LSDA.

title: Wound Healing
experiment_type: NASA Extreme Environment Mission Operations (NEEMO) Project
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: The purpose of this experiment was to evaluate digital still camera procedures written for the Photodocumentation of Skin Injuries and Allergic Reactions medical requirement for International Space Station (ISS) crews. Photodocumentation of injuries and illnesses provides visual images to support diagnosis and documentation of cutaneous injuries and illnesses.
approach: Test subjects reported all minor and major injuries, infections, allergies, and hypersensitivities incurred during the mission to the crew surgeon, including the time when the injury occurred or illness began. Using the onboard digital still camera, the area(s) of concern were photographed to document the injury/illness. A small ruler was positioned within the field of view to provide scale. Photos were taken both at a distance of 3-5 feet to include some anatomic landmarks for orientation and as a close-up view with an oblique light source positioned at a 45 degree angle to the area. Images were downloaded to the laptop computer and downlinked to the crew surgeon, so the image quality could be evaluated and procedures revised if necessary. Photographs were taken at 24-hour intervals until the injury/illness healed.
results: Results for this investigation are not available.

title: A Tool for the Automated Collection of Space Utilization Data
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: The objective of this study was to develop and validate an automated data collection system that delivers useful data in the analysis of space utilization and vehicle habitability pertaining to crew activities on the International Space Station (ISS) as well as potential long duration space missions. The investigation utilized two independent technologies, 3D Radio Frequency Identification (RFID)-Real Time Location System (RTLS) and Microsoft Kinect 3D volumetric and anatomical scanning tools, integrating them into a single solution in the Human Exploration Research Analog (HERA) platform. This comprehensive data collection provided data regarding: (a) the number of crew present in each area of the vehicle at any given time, (b) the quantity of time crew spend at each workstation in the performance of tasks, (c) the physical orientation of crew while utilizing the provided volume, (d) frequent or common translation paths and traffic flow patterns within the volume, (e) operational flow/volume required for mission tasks by single or multiple crew in the vehicle, and (f) 3D biomechanical and postural data related to individual and team based tasks.
approach: The first portion of this project focused on the integration of the 3D RFID-RTLS and Kinect hardware technologies involved and the initial development of software interfaces. The second portion included the development and refinement of the system and its software interfaces; and the third portion includes full validation of the completed system in the HERA analog environment.
results: The Space Utilization Data System (SUDS) has been completed and with the full scope of functionality originally planned when it was first proposed. It provides a facile system for collection of 3D volumetric data, rough order of magnitude postural data, and time and motion tracking over time. It fully records and recreates the full 3D environment being assessed, and the volumes occupied by the occupants of the scene. It has been designed with future updates in mind through programming methods used, and the ability to support alternative devices for inclusion in the system. Laboratory testing has demonstrated its accuracy and functionality in various regards, and future work is recommended to further document its capabilities. The system is ready for use and implementation in analog testing environments and use in human-in-the-loop testing.

title: AR/VR and Hybrid Reality for Verification Assessments: Phase 1
archive_status: Data preservation is complete.  All datasets are privacy-protected.  Data is available via data request.
objectives: NASA has a growing interest in using extended reality (XR) technologies (virtual reality, augmented reality, and hybrid reality) verification and validation activities for the Spaceflight Program. To meet NASA minimum specifications, hardware systems are required to be verified human rated. Analysis, inspection, demonstration, and testing are several methods by which verification activities can be completed. Method determination depends on the requirement type, form factors of products, and test facility availability where verification activities can take place. Verification activities can be costly, as developers must often build high-fidelity physical mockups for certain verification tests. Leveraging XR technologies in human-in-the-loop testing requires little to no hardware, construction costs, or storage facilities, which is significant in cost savings. XR allows NASA systems to be replicated by a high-fidelity virtual reality simulation which approximates the appearance, size, and functionality of a real-world experience. The validity of verification outcomes from XR methodologies are currently unclear. The researchers for this investigation will communicate directly with NASA subject matter experts (SMEs) on using XR for activities that can help this study. The biggest concern is that verification data collected with XR technology would not be comparable to data collected in a physical mockup using traditional methods. This could
approach: The literature review was carried out by the project team, an overview was created of how XR technology was used for verification and related activities, such as operational testing, examining evaluations, and training. Gathered information on XR training was the start towards understanding the strengths and weaknesses of XR for different tasks. The researchers interviewed experts and stakeholders, that allowed the researchers an understanding on XR technologies success. It also helped pinpoint the strengths, weaknesses, and barriers to implementation, while giving lessons on verification. This study included a pilot study to replicate verification activities using “equivalent” virtual and physical mockups.
results: in additional risk when used for flight readiness decisions. Taking this into consideration, NASA currently limits use of XR technologies for developmental test activities only. NASA needs data and theoretical knowledge to develop guidelines for how XR technology can be applied without increasing human health and performance risk for the future. This research will help NASA understand XR technologies strengths, limitations, and gaps. This project has the following aim: 1.           To gather and synthesize available knowledge and generate new data that will help stakeholders make informed decisions regarding the use of XR technologies for verification-related activities. Approach: The literature review was carried out by the project team, an overview was created of how XR technology was used for verification and related activities, such as operational testing, examining evaluations, and training. Gathered information on XR training was the start towards understanding the strengths and weaknesses of XR for different tasks. The researchers interviewed experts and stakeholders, that allowed the researchers an understanding on XR technologies success. It also helped pinpoint the strengths, weaknesses, and barriers to implementation, while giving lessons on verification. This study included a pilot study to replicate verification activities using “equivalent” virtual and physical mockups. Results of the virtual and physical mockups are compared and provide validation for XR Verification Framework. The deliverables of Phase I are used for a separate Phase II investigation. Phase II will consist of a more comprehensive study to replicate and build upon the pilot study results. The research was conducted according to the timeline and major milestones presented below: The projected duration of the project was 12 months. ·        Literature Review – ATP + 3 months ·        Interviews – ATP + 3 months ·        Requirements Framework – ATP + 5 months ·        Pilot study protocol peer review – ATP + 5 months ·        Pilot study – ATP + 7 months ·        Research report summarizing results of the pilot test, lessons learned, – ATP + 12months. Results: The results from the literature review, interviews, and the pilot study generated a report that helped future developers and researchers better understand when and how XR technologies are applied and when they should be avoided in hardware system verification and validation. Results from the literature review and SME interviews produced XR Verification Decision Framework. It is the first draft for NASA to make decisions on program requirements regarding XR technologies. The framework is the foundation for identifying gaps in research. The PI team created a VR duplicate of a high-fidelity physical mockup, the Habitable Airlock. Outcomes were observed to be about the same for both mockups with two exceptions. The appropriateness of VR mockups relative to a PR mockup was evaluated, but it is both resource intensive and impractical for NASA partners. PR and VR mockup for two verification-like tasks were compared, Hand Signal Identification and Field of View. These results support the cautious conclusion from phase 1, that VR might be best suited for demonstrations.

title: CREWS: Crew Recommender for Effective Work in Space
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Team composition, the configuration of member attributes and their relationships, is a critical enabling feature of fostering effective teamwork and likely plays an important role in the effectiveness of future long-duration space exploration (LDSE). Limited research on team composition in environments analogous to LDSE exists, and how team composition can be used to optimize crew functioning and performance is unclear. The research aims are to: Identify the effects of team composition on team functioning in LDSE and the critical factors of team composition driving this effect. Identify particular patterns of this effect with different team compositions. Identify methods for composing teams for LDSE. Develop a predictive team composition model for use in composing teams and identify potential issues with already composed teams. Provide recommendations for composing teams for LDSE.
approach: To address these aims, investigators propose a 3-year, multi-method research effort, in which they: (1) develop an agent-based model (ABM) team composition for LDSE based on empirical data linking key model inputs (e.g., individual difference variables, network relational factors, task characteristics) to team functioning (e.g., social integration, team processes, team cohesion, team conflict) in LDSE-relevant contexts; (2) conduct virtual experiments using characteristics and relationships identified in Phase I to identify the team functioning patterns that arise under different member compositions, and create a predictive model of team composition; and (3) conduct an initial validation of the model developed in Phase 2 in the Human Exploration Research Analog (HERA) and NASA Extreme Environment Mission Operations (NEEMO) analogue environments using specific manipulations of key factors (e.g., compositions; situational characteristics). Research products will be developed including a predictive model of team composition in LDSE, evidence in support of the model, and a mockup of a proposed interface to assist in the staffing and management of LDSE crew and mission teams. In Phase I, investigators will develop an ABM of effective crewmember composition in the LDSE context based on: systematic review of the literature relevant to the LDSE context; primary data collected previously in the lab and analog environments; and new data collection efforts in analog environments (i.e., HERA, 24-hour hackathon). In Phase II, model attributes will serve as the inputs for virtual experiments via computational modeling. These virtual experiments will inform a predictive model of effective composition for LDSE crews. During Phase III, investigators will collect initial validation evidence for the predictive model from analog- definition research conducted in HERA. They will use their research to develop a mockup of a crew staffing and management tool, and to inform recommendations for staffing, training, countermeasures, and future research.

title: Artificial Intelligence for Tracking Micro-Behaviors in Longitudinal Data and Predicting Their Effect on Well-Being and Team Performance
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: NASA advocates psychosocial dimensions of team functioning to be critical to the success of long-distance  missions. A number of factors affect team functioning, including team composition, emergent states and other  moderating factors. Studies in analog environments reveal that stress and physical exhaustion account for the  majority of team conflicts, with team creativity and performance on 10 intellective tasks decreasing over time.  These findings suggest that team functioning during long duration missions can change in a dynamic manner and  can be affected by brief, often unconscious, micro-behaviors between the team members, which are best  measured via observation. Future long-distance space exploration will have a number of challenges that increase  the risk of inadequate cooperation, coordination, collaboration, and psychosocial adaptation, and can lead to  behavioral health and performance decrements. In this proposed research, it is hypothesized that micro-behaviors  captured via audiovisual recordings, quantified via linguistic and acoustic measures, and automatically detected  via artificial intelligence (AI) can provide unique insights into operationally- relevant team performance, beyond  self-report team functioning measures.  Micro-behaviors are small, often unconscious gestures, words and tone of voice which can influence how  included (or not) the people around us feel. The most common type of micro-behaviors are micro-aggressions.  Micro aggressions can have detrimental impact to well-being and team performance. Micro-affirmations reflect  inclusion and caring and can counter-act the harmful effects of micro-aggressions. This research will have three primary aims: 1. Leverage advance multimodal data analytics to detecting micro-behaviors in longitudinal team  interactions. 2. Identify emotional reactivity to micro-behaviors. 3. Incorporate knowledge on micro-behaviors to predict operationally relevant team performance.
approach: Previously collected peer and mission control ratings, physiological, audio and team task performance data from  HERA 4 and 5 campaigns will also be analyzed. Machine learning algorithms will be leveraged to learn complex  multimodal patterns of micro-behaviors.  This study will deploy a mixed-methods approach to detect micro-behaviors by coding 25% of the data with  human coders, this will be followed by automatic detection of micro-behaviors in the remaining a 75% data  through AI algorithms. Crew interactions will be identified automatically via detection of turn-taking and speech  overlap. Reliability checks will be conducted manually to address any discrepancies.
results: Results from this research contribute to a greater understanding of factors that affect team operation and performance in isolated and confined environments (ICE), and the effective management of future space crews. Particularly relevant to this project is the focus on micro-behaviors, that is small, often unconscious gestures, words and tone of voice which can influence how included (or not included) the people in the team feel. The proposed AI methods allow us to track micro-behaviors on a moment-to moment basis, thus potentially yielding a more complete picture of team dynamics. Exploratory analysis suggests that negative micro-behaviors included increased sentences with passive voice for both the sender and the target, potentially due to the subtlety of their expression. Negative micro-behaviors also depicted fewer second-person personal pronouns (e.g., “you”) compared to turns without those behaviors. While this finding for negative micro-behaviors might initially be nonintuitive, since blaming language tends to include a large number of second-person pronouns, this result might also reflect fact that negative micro-behaviors are many times indistinct and not sharply expressed. Positive micro-behaviors had significantly higher positive affect, lower percentage of angry language, and higher percentage of language related to achievements compared to negative micro-behaviors. Acoustic turn similarity between sender and target was the highest for instances of positive micro-behaviors (i.e., indicating convergence between speakers) and the lowest for instances of negative micro-behaviors (i.e., indicating divergence between speakers). The PI team leveraged machine learning classifiers and dialog state tracking models, combined with natural language processing techniques relying on lexicon-based methods and data-driven methods, to learn complex multimodal patterns of micro-behaviors and automatically detect positive and negative microbehaviors between team members. The experimental findings indicate that the psycholinguistic markers extracted using the linguistic inquiry and word count (LIWC), STRESSnet dictionaries, and acoustic features can achieve an f1-score up to 55% in a three-class classification problem, which is well-above the 33% chance accuracy. The findings also suggest that modeling turns between the sender and target of micro-behaviors is significantly more effective in detecting micro-behavior than only modeling the sender’s information. Finally, the PI team demonstrate the effect of introducing context for detection purposes. Dialog state tracking approaches that model the linguistic interaction between team members and incorporate contextual information about the task and sentiment of the conversation can further yield improved performance, depicting an f1-score of 57.73%. These results suggesting the preliminary feasibility of such system using unobtrusive speech measures. Training these large-scale ML models with more data (e.g., additional mission tasks) can potentially yield improved results and increase the robustness of these automated systems. Physiological reactivity to micro-behaviors was measured in order to better understand how a target of micro-behavior experiences the focal event. Physiological reactivity was measured in terms of heart rate (HR), for which continuous data from the TIB task of the C4 campaign was captured. For this purpose, the team defined two intervals. The first interval was defined as starting 1 min before the micro-behavior and ending at the micro-behavior occurrence, referred to as ‘Before’. The second interval, referred to as ‘During/After’ was defined as starting from the micro-behavior occurrence and ending 1 min into or after the micro-behavior, depending on whether the micro-behavior ended before the 1 min. Results indicate a large inter-individual variability in terms of the physiological reactivity responses. A subset of team members, such as P1, P2, and P3, depict increased physiological reactivity to negative micro-behaviors and decreased physiological reactivity to positive micro-behaviors, which is anticipated. However, other team members, such as P4, P5, and P6, depict opposite trends. These results suggest that different team members might depict different sensitivity to micro-behaviors. Future analysis should also acknowledge and take into account additional confounding factors that might affect physiological reactivity (e.g., physical activity, daily stressors) and other buffering mechanisms. The team examined to what extent the linguistic content of a micro-behavior was associated with team performance outcomes. The team studied the dependence of team performance on linguistic features extracted using the Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC) dictionary, which captures affective, cognitive, and physical processes, as well as drives and motives, extracted from conversation turns corresponding to positive and negative micro-behaviors through a linear mixed-effect (LME) model. LIWC features included: (1) two measures of affective processes, including positive and negative emotion; (2) three measures of cognitive processes, that included discrepancy (e.g., would, can, want, could), certainty (e.g., really, actually, of course), differentiation (e.g., but, not, if, or); (3) three measures that capture physical processes related to food, body, and sex; and (4) five measures that capture drives and motives, including affiliation (e.g., we, our, us, help), achievement (e.g., work, better, best, working), power (e.g., own, order, allow, power), reward (e.g., opportunity, win, gain, benefit), and risk (secure, protect, pain, risk). Results indicated that increased use of language associated with positive emotion during positive microbehaviors is associated with an increase in team performance. On the contrary, increased use of negative emotion language during negative micro-behaviors is associated with a decrease in performance. When running the same LME model using data from all turns, the language associated with positive emotion appears to be positively associated with team performance reaching almost significance level, but the language with negative emotion does not depict a significant association with team performance. This potentially suggests that the affective content of micro-behaviors can be an indicator of team performance, but the affective content present over the entire conversation does not necessarily predict team performance, thus highlighting the importance of studying team interaction in the context of microbehaviors.

objectives: Investigators aim to develop a cutting-edge integrative model which details how team member attributes, combinations thereof, and interpersonal perceptions affects the emergence of relational states in isolated and confined environments (ICE). approach: The research is a US-Russian collaborative effort in which they the researchers leverage existing data previously collected in the Mars 105 and Mars 500 simulations; collect new data using analog-definition research in NASA’s Human Exploration Research Analog (HERA); and use a novel data analysis approach to create an interpersonal model that can be used in ICE. title: Self-Guided Multimedia Stress Management and Resilience Training
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Stress and anxiety-related problems are some of the most common and costly behavioral health problems in society. For those working in operational environments (i.e., astronauts, flight controllers, military), stress and anxiety-related problems before, during, or after missions can seriously compromise efficiency, safety, and performance. To address behavioral health issues like stress, it is important to maximize the privacy, validity, and acceptability of the training and countermeasures used. Technology-based behavioral health programs (e.g., computer or web-based programs) are effective for treating behavioral health problems. These programs increase availability of evidence-based interventions to individuals who are not able or willing to receive such in-person treatments. Prior research validated the autonomous multimedia resilience training program the investigators created (i.e., Stress Management and Resilience Training for Optimal Performance; SMART-OP). SMART-OP interactively trains users to manage stress and build resilience over six weekly training sessions lastly approximately 45 minutes each.
approach: The investigators propose to evaluate the effectiveness, usefulness, and usability of SMART-OP with a sample of flight controllers and instructors (including those in training flow) at Johnson Space Center (JSC) by comparing it to an attention control group. Additionally, they will examine the effects of self-guided stress management and resilience training on biomarkers for stress (i.e., cortisol, a-amylase), heart rate, and cognitive and behavioral performance. Based on several meetings with the Space Flight Resource Management (SFRM) Working Group, investigators learned that trainees are not progressing through the training flow satisfactorily and that they identified stress as a potential contributor to poor trainee performance. Additionally, stress was identified as an area of concern to address with flight controller and instructors. Since SMART-OP significantly reduced perceived stress, increased perceived control over stressors, and was rated as highly useful, SMART-OP could provide helpful stress management training for flight controllers. Also, since SMART-OP is evidence-based, confidential, and self-directed, it may be more acceptable to flight controller trainees than other programs.
results: from a randomized controlled trial with a stressed but otherwise healthy sample (N=66) indicated that SMART-OP decreased perceived stress, improved perceived control over stress, and was rated as significantly more useful than an attention control group that received marketed videos and published material on stress management. SMART-OP was also rated as “excellent” in terms of user-friendliness, acceptability, and had low dropout, and high homework adherence. APPROACH: The investigators propose to evaluate the effectiveness, usefulness, and usability of SMART-OP with a sample of flight controllers and instructors (including those in training flow) at Johnson Space Center (JSC) by comparing it to an attention control group. Additionally, they will examine the effects of self-guided stress management and resilience training on biomarkers for stress (i.e., cortisol, a-amylase), heart rate, and cognitive and behavioral performance. Additionally, stress was identified as an area of concern to address with flight controller and instructors. Since SMART-OP significantly reduced perceived stress, increased perceived control over stressors, and was rated as highly useful, SMART-OP could provide helpful stress management training for flight controllers. Also, since SMART-OP is evidence-based, confidential, and self-directed, it may be more acceptable to flight controller trainees than other programs. RESULTS: This experiment is in progress. However, preliminary results are available. Study Implementation: The majority of work during 2013-2014 was spent on various aspects of implementing the study at JSC. The study is designed to be conducted in a self-guided fashion where possible which means the study participant needs to conduct much of the assessment and all of the stress management training independently (i.e., without research coordinators). IRB protocols and approvals were obtained at JSC and UCLA to conduct the study. Biweekly teleconferences with NASA BHP personnel addressed various areas of study implementation and maintained regular communication. Progress during this period covered several areas including reserving and setting up a study room on site to conduct the study including assessments. Study computers and iPads were programmed and authenticated for use in the study. Additional study materials were purchased including heart rate monitors. There were several logistical/technical issues/hurdles that were addressed to give the UCLA research team required access to conduct the study from afar. Accomplishing this involved regular communication with JSC BHP and IT staff and personnel. The UCLA research team made two trips to JSC to address various aspects of study implementation including giving several informational session presentations for study recruitment; adding software and other information to JSC computers for assessments and stress management training sessions; testing computers for functionality and reliability; and testing the downloading of training session and assessment data for functionality. Assessment Procedures: The UCLA research team created several assessment tasks required for the study. The tasks involved computer programming so that study participants could conduct much of the assessments in a self-guided fashion. These involved creating online questionnaires, programming for computerized tasks designed to frustrate/stress users, modification of the neuropsychological battery for use in current study, creation of study protocols instructing the user how to conduct assessments and stress management training sessions on their own. The JSC Nutritional Biochemistry Lab (NBL) is leading a portion of the assessment procedures which involve collection of saliva and urine to measure stress biomarkers (cortisol and alpha amylase). This part of the assessment procedures was developed jointly between the UCLA and NBL teams, protocols formulated, and then the procedures were tested during the visits of the UCLA team to JSC.

title: NSCOR: Mechanisms Underlying the Risk of HZE Particle-induced Solid Tumor Development
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Space radiation from high charge and energy (HZE)-particles with high-LET is different from radiation with low-LET on Earth. Understanding the mechanism by which mammalian cells respond to space radiation induced the DNA damage is a key issue to evaluate the risk of space radiation on astronauts’ health at any endpoint. Lung cancer is the most common fatal cancer among men and women worldwide. Lung cancer is believed to be one of the major risks of HZE-particle exposure-induced carcinogenesis, although a quantitative and mechanistic understanding of this risk is lacking. The Emory NSCOR will address this important knowledge gap. In addition, the NSCOR team will answer the question concerning whether and how different qualities (LET) of radiation affects lung tumorigenesis. These
approach: es to address the role of miR-21 dependent and independent stress responses in HZE particle-induced lung cancer. There are four projects: 1. Determine whether the lung cancer suppressor, Gprc5a, protects against HZE particle-induced lung carcinogenesis, and whether miR-21 overexpression blunts this protective effect. 2. Determine whether HZE-particle radiation exposure
results: will not only provide important information that will aid in the facilitation of the NASA Mars project, but will also provide the public with useful information concerning lung carcinogenesis and the benefits of cancer prevention. The Emory University-Georgia Health Sciences University NSCOR will investigate the mechanisms by which HZE particles, a component of space radiation, induce lung cancer. HZE exposure elicits complex DNA damage, together with a broader cell/tissue stress response that likely includes changes in expression of tumor suppressor proteins, persistent elevation of reactive oxygen species, and alterations in the pattern of DNA methylation. The central hypothesis of this NSCOR is that this broader stress response amplifies the carcinogenic risk from a primary DNA damage event. Preliminary studies suggest that a small noncoding RNA, microRNA-21 (miR-21) plays a key role in coordinating the HZE particle-associated stress response. Center investigators will use genetic, epigenetic, and biochemical approaches to address the role of miR-21 dependent and independent stress responses in HZE particle-induced lung cancer. There are four projects: 1. Determine whether the lung cancer suppressor, Gprc5a, protects against HZE particle-induced lung carcinogenesis, and whether miR-21 overexpression blunts this protective effect. 2. Determine whether HZE-particle radiation exposure results in hyper-reliance on error-prone DNA repair pathways, whether miR21 mediates this effect, and whether dysregulation of DNA repair contributes to lung carcinogenesis. 3. Determine the nature of the HZE-particle induced ROS stress response, whether it contributes to HZE particle-induced lung carcinogenesis, and the role of miR-21 in this process. 4. Determine the scope of HZE-particle radiation-induced alterations in DNA methylation patterns, whether these alterations contribute to lung carcinogenesis, and the role of miR-21-dependent targeting of DNA methyltransferase 1 (DNMT1) in this process. These four projects have a synergy through their collaboration on studying the mechanism underlying how mammalian respond to HZE particle-induced DNA damage, which contributes to tumor development. APPROACH: The methodology is embedded in the Results below. RESULTS: This experiment is in progress. Preliminary findings are noted below. Project 1: The main purpose of this project is to identify the targets of miR-21 and their regulation and effects on IR-induced carcinogenesis. Investigators found that miR-21 could directly target SOD3 and indirectly target SOD2 to enhance HZE particle-induced ROS and transformation in the human lung epithelial cells. They have also found that the miR-21-EGFR loop is over-activated in the DNA double strand break (DSB) repair deficient cells and mice, which is stimulated by endogenous DNA DSB formation that occurs during DNA replication. They found that the increased level of miR-21 and EGFR is correlated with an increased frequency of radiation-induced tumorigenesis. These results demonstrate for the first time that DNA DSBs have a functional link with the up-regulation EGFR-miR-21 loop. These findings provide an important explanation for why DNA DSB repair deficient mice have a high frequency of spontaneous tumorigenesis, and also provides additional explanation concerning why radiation-induced DNA DSBs enhances tumorigenesis. Project 2: The hypothesis underlying project 2 is, “exposure to HZE-particle radiation, or altered miR-21 expression status, results in hyper-reliance on error-prone repair pathways, which accounts for the excess relative risk of HZE-particle radiation in lung carcinogenesis.” The experimental approach is to test whether a history of HZE radiation exposure influences the fidelity (and not just the efficiency) of the response to future DNA damage. These experiments used a reporter cell line that has been engineered to report mutagenic repair of enzymatically-induced DNA double-strand breaks. Investigators exposed replicate cultures to HZE particle radiation and challenged at intervals by expression of a rare-cutting nuclease that cuts within integrated reporter transgenes. In this system, deletion of a sequence within one of the reporter transgenes leads to green fluorescence, and translocation between two transgenes integrated into different chromosomes leads to red fluorescence. Project 3: DNA damage inflicted by radiation or chemotherapeutic drugs induces a cellular stress response by as yet undefined mechanisms and consequences for cell survival and genomic stability. The goals for Project 3 are to determine the nature of HZE-particle induced stress response and the resulting DNA damage and genomic instability that contributes to HZE-particle induced lung carcinogenesis. Investigators found that elevated ROS co-exist with biomarkers of cellular senescence, genomic instability and nitric oxide (NO). They found that Fe particle irradiation, but not an equivalent X-rays dose, induced a senescence-like response, which increases genomic instability and can be abrogated by p38MAPK inhibition. They have initiated measuring nitric oxide production, which, following radiation exposure follows a temporal pattern overlapping with ROS, but does not appear to affect genomic instability or the senescence-like response. Investigators will pursue their studies about the persisting effects of PARP-1 inhibition at early times following exposure to HZE. They will follow-up on the response leading to NO production as this is a potential, convenient biomarker that is easy to measure in exhaled air, reporting such persistent responses and signaling lung distress. Project 4: The primary goal of this project is to define the epigenetic determinants of HZE radiation exposure induced lung carcinogenesis and the extent to which this is mediated by miR-21. The hypothesis is that there may be an epigenetic “memory” of high LET radiation exposure wherein alterations in DNA methylation resulting from acute radiation exposure and local DNA damage have the potential to become ‘fixed’ if they are subsequently replicated, leading to permanent changes in DNA methylation and new gene expression programs. To test this hypothesis, triplicate cultures of immortalized human bronchial epithelial cells (3KT) were exposed to low LET (X-ray) (onsite at Emory) or high LET of various doses (0, 0.3, 1.0 Gy) and sources (Si, Fe) at the Brookhaven National Laboratory facility. Samples were collected from a fraction of the exposed population after 48 hours and the remaining cells were maintained in continuous culture for an additional 20 population doublings (~3 months) with weekly collection for genomic DNA, RNA, and cellular protein. Unexposed cultures underwent the same handling procedures and were maintained in parallel. The methylation status of > 485,000 CpG residues across the human genome was analyzed using the Illumina Infinium Human Methylation 450K platform. Two independent experiments have been performed for the high LET Fe series, with a 0.1 Gy dose added to the second series.

title: Wearable Health Monitoring Systems
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: The objective of this proposal is to demonstrate the feasibility of producing a wearable health monitoring system for the human body that is functional, comfortable, bendable in 3 dimensions, durable, water-proof, washable, and light-weight. This new technology area of wearable health systems, sometimes referred to as smart-clothing, promises to allow for a secondary human nervous system that connects various different electronic devices positioned on or around the human body. As the shrinking in size and weight of electronic circuits has progressed, it is now possible for the modern human astronaut to carry increasing numbers of different electronic devices and sensors such as thermometers, gas monitors, microphones, altimeters, digital processors, digital memory, and push-button controls. These devices allow the astronaut to access data about their current environment and health status, and communicate with other astronauts and/or databases to send and receive information of value. As the variation in the number of devices and sensors that can be deployed increases greatly, a new technology is required to allow the seamless integration of these devices with the human astronaut so that the devices can be electrically powered, operated, re-charged, and communicate with each other over a digital pathway.

title: Microgravity-Driven Optic Nerve/Sheath Remodeling Simulator - MONSTR Sim
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Visual Impairment/Intracranial Pressure (VIIP) syndrome occurs in a significant fraction of astronauts undergoing long-duration space flight. VIIP is characterized by a spectrum of ophthalmic changes, including optic nerve sheath distention and kinking, optic disc edema, choroidal folds, and flattening of the posterior eye globe. Most significantly, astronauts with VIIP can suffer permanent loss of visual acuity. The cause(s) of VIIP are not well understood, but the syndrome has ophthalmic features similar to those seen in patients with idiopathic intracranial hypertension, strongly suggesting that elevations in intracranial pressure and/or reductions in intraocular pressure play an important role in VIIP. Notably, observations in VIIP are consistent with a major alteration in the pressure difference across the lamina cribrosa. Given the probable role of these altered pressures in VIIP, any VIIP computational model should include biomechanical models of the relevant ocular tissues. Importantly, VIIP develops slowly (over weeks); further, the anatomic changes observed in ocular connective tissues (e.g. the optic nerve sheath) appear to be permanent in some cases. This strongly suggests that tissue remodeling is an important aspect of VIIP, and thus any attempt to understand VIIP must consider remodeling effects. In view of the above, investigators hypothesize that cephalad fluid shifts in microgravity affect intracranial pressure (ICP) and intraocular pressure (IOP), leading to altered biomechanical loads on the tissues of the posterior globe and optic sheath. This altered biomechanical environment in turn causes connective tissue remodeling, an important contributing factor to vision changes in the VIIP syndrome. Investigators will develop modeling tools to allow the above hypothesis to be tested, and which will provide a test bed for identification of which clinically observable attributes play key roles in the development of the VIIP syndrome. These tools will be developed through 4 specific aims: Develop validated tools for computing IOP and ICP in microgravity. These tools will be based on modeling of fluid shifts between the eye and various compartments in the cardiovascular, cerebrospinal and lymphatic systems. Develop validated finite element-based tools for computing the biomechanical environment and subsequent connective tissue remodeling in the optic nerve head, optic nerve sheath, and posterior globe. These tools will be complemented by a model of the eye's optical performance Integrate the models from aims 1 and 2 to produce a unified, open and extensible software package that can predict ocular biomechanics and ocular connective tissue remodeling under microgravity conditions. Use the integrated model of aim 3 to study clinically observable attributes and determine the role they may play in the development of VIIP.
approach: This project is primarily constructed around the use of free software, most of which is open source. In addition, MATLAB will be used for a number of purposes. The free software to be used includes: FEBio, a nonlinear finite element code specifically created for modeling tissue biomechanics, will be used to model the biomechanical response of the eye to changing pressures, as well as to describe chronic ocular tissue remodeling in VIIP. Gmsh, a script-driven a 3D finite element mesh generator, will be used to help prepare FEBio input files in an automated fashion for parametric models. OSLO-EDU, a free “light” version of OSLO (Optics Software for Layout and Optimization), will be used for modeling the optical performance of the eye. Models will be validated through lab studies of porcine and post mortem human eyes, as well as clinical studies involving a small group of patients experiencing idiopathic intracranial hypertension.

title: Nanoscale Test Strips for Multiplexed Blood Analysis

objectives: The goal of the nanoscale test strips, or nanostrips, is to provide rapid, low-cost, powerful multiplexed analyses in a diminutive form so that whole body health checks can be performed on a single drop of blood. The
approach: is conceptually similar to pH or urinalysis test strips which allow multiplexed measurements in a linear format. The main difference is that we are proposing test strips at the nanoscale, shrunk in size over a billion-fold in volume, allowing multiple sensing elements to be included in a tiny area. In Phase I, we fabricated, tested, and demonstrated functional parathyroid hormone and vitamin D nanostrips for bone metabolism. Furthermore, we developed thrombin aptamer and immune IgG antibody nanostrips. For Phase II, we will develop a breadth of nanostrips designed to address key space-flight medical needs. These will be for assessment of bone metabolism, immune response, cardiac status, liver metabolism, and lipid profiles. We plan to enhance our technology capabilities by developing a Rapid Nanostrip Assay Capability, mix-and-run assay capability, in-house aptamer production, advanced lyophilization technology, and nanostrip accelerated stability tests. The nanostrips will be read out in a time-of-flight flow-based manner utilizing our rHEALTH sensor.

title: Portable Cathode-Air-Vapor-Feed Electrochemical Medical Oxygen Concentrator
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Future space exploration missions present significant new challenges to crew health care capabilities, particularly in the efficient utilization of on-board oxygen resources. The International Space Station and future exploration vehicles require a light weight, compact, portable oxygen concentrator technology (OCT) that can provide medical grade oxygen from the ambient cabin air. Current OCTs are heavy, bulky, have a narrow operating temperature range (ambient to 40 degree Celsius), and require 15 to 30 minutes start-up time to reach their full operating capacity. Lynntech's proposed electrochemical OCT solves these issues by operating the OCT with a cathode-air vapor feed, unlike conventional electrochemical OCTs which require a liquid water feed. This is possible due to the use of in-house developed proprietary nanocomposite proton exchange membrane and catalyst technologies. Cathode-air vapor feed operation eliminates the need for a bulky on-board water supply, significantly reduces the complexity of the balance-of-plant, and greatly increases the system efficiency. OCT will be a quarter the size and weight of conventional OCTs, be capable of instant start-up, and have a wide operating temperature range. Lynntech will develop a Phase II prototype that is capable of delivering 4 SLPM of 60% oxygen and deliver it to NASA for further testing.
